units.la: Caput Cyri amputatum Diodorus eum cruci adfixum esse memorat. Xenophon in Cyropædia, placidâ ait mortem obiisse domi suæ. Quæ causa est, cur aliqui non hunc, sed Cyrum Medum Darii fratris successorem à Massagetarum regina interfectum, ipsiusque nominis similitudinem, erroris causam fuisse existimant.
units.tr: Caput Cyri amputatum] Diodorus records that he was fastened to a cross. Xenophon in the Cyropaedia says that he died peacefully in his own home. This is why some think it was not this Cyrus, but Cyrus the Mede, successor of Darius's brother, who was killed by the queen of the Massagetae, and that the similarity of their names was the cause of the error.

units.la: Darius Hic edictum confirmauit de reædificando templo Hierosolym. Quare multa eius mentio est apud Aggæum, Zachariam, Esdram.
units.tr: Darius] This king confirmed the edict concerning the rebuilding of the temple at Jerusalem. Hence his name is often mentioned in Haggai, Zechariah and Ezra.

units.la: Domi fe Gerberibus lacerari Vide Suid. in Patræmia Ζωσύρου τάλαντα.
units.tr: Domi fe Gerberibus lacerari] See Suidas under Patraemia, [Ζωσύρου τάλαντα].
Epitome of the Histories of Pompeius Trogus
BOOK II. SUMMARY.

units.la: 1 Scytharum otigo, antiquitas, de qua cum Ægyptiis bellica. Ægyptios fugant, contendunt. 3 Scytharum fortitudo Asiamque reddunt tributa.
units.tr: 1 The antiquity of the Scythians, about which they contend in war with the Egyptians. They rout the Egyptians. 3 The valour of the Scythians, who make Asia pay tribute.

units.la: 2 Descriptio Scythiæ, & riam. morum gentis, quæ in plau- 4 Amazonum à Scythis stris degens iustitiam colit origo, reginæ, res gestæ. & continentiam. 5 Bellum Scytharum ad- uersus B
units.tr: 2 A description of Scythia and the customs and character of its people, who live in wagons, cultivate justice and self-restraint. 4 The origin of the Amazons from the Scythians, their queens, and their deeds. 5 The Scythians' war against the

units.la: uersus seruos, quos lepido Persæ ad Thermopylas mi‐ strategemate reprimūt. Da‐nus Seythis deinde Ionibus & Atheniensibus arma in‐fert.
units.tr: slaves, whom they hold in check by a clever stratagem; the Persians at Thermopylae. Darius then makes war on the Scythians, then on the Ionians and Athenians.

units.la: 6 Atheniensium origo, victa, post multam stragem gloriatio, iudustria, artes, re‐ges.
units.tr: 6 The origin of the Athenians; their defeat; after much slaughter, their boasting; their industry, arts and kings.

units.la: 7 Respublica Athenien‐sis, Solonis legibus & poli‐tico strategemate firmata.
units.tr: 7 The Athenian commonwealth, established by Solon's laws and a political stratagem.

units.la: 8 Pififtratus, post fortiter gesta in Megarenses, tyran‐ nidem per 33. annos occu‐pat.
units.tr: 8 Pisistratus, after his brave campaigns against the Megarians, seizes tyranny for 33 years.

units.la: 9 Eiusdem filius Hippias fugit. Eodem fere momen‐ tria pulsus, Persarum ex‐citum in Græciam addu‐cit. Inde Marathonia pugna in qua victi Persæ, Atheniẽ‐ses victores.
units.tr: 9 His son Hippias flees. At about the same time, having been driven out, he leads a Persian army into Greece. Then the battle of Marathon, in which the Persians were defeated and the Athenians were victorious.

units.la: 10 Dissidium de regno inter Darii filios, Xerxes & bellum instaurat cum vali‐ dissimo exercitu.
units.tr: 10 A dispute over the kingdom between the sons of Darius; Xerxes renews the war with a very strong army.

units.la: 11 Fortitudine Spartano‐rum, quorum rex Leonidas, præ‐lio superatus.
units.tr: 11 The courage of the Spartans, whose king Leonidas was overcome in battle.

units.la: N relatione rerum ab Scythis gesta‐rum, quæ satis ample magnifice fuerunt, principium ab origine repe‐tendum est. Non enim minus illa‐stria initia, quam imperium habue‐re: nec virorum imperio magis, quam feminarum virtutibus clarucre. Quippe cum ipsi Parthos, Bactria‐nosq;, feminæ autem eorum Amazonum regna condi‐ derint : pros sus vt res gestas virorum mulierumq; con‐side‐. fideruntibus incertum sit, vter apud eos sexus illustrior fuerit. Scytharum gens antiquissima semper habita, quanquam inter Scythas & AEgyptios diu contentio de generis vetustate fuerit: AEgyptiis praedicantibus, institorum, cum alia terra nimio feruore solis arderent, alia rigerent frigoris immanitate, ita vt non modo primae generare homines, sed neductas quidem recipere ac tueri possent, priusquam aduersus calorem vel frigus velamenta corporis inuenirentur, vel locorum vitia quaesitis arte remediis mollirentur; AEgyptii ita temperatam semper fuisse, vt neque hiberna frigora, nec aestiui solis ardores incolas eius permerent: Solum ita fecundum, vt alimentorum in vsum hominum nulla terra feracior fuerit. Iure igitur ibi primum homines natos videri debere, vbi educari facilime posset. Contra, Scythæ cæli temperamentum nullum esse vetustatis argumentum putabant: quippe naturam cum primum incrementa caloris ac frigoris regionibus diffinxit, statim ad locorum patientiam, animalia quoq; generasse: sed arborum atq; frugum pro regionum conditione, apte genera variata. Et quanto Scythis sit caelum asperius quam Ægyptiis, tanto & corpora & ingenia esse duriora. Ceterum si mundi, quà nunc partes sunt, aliquando vnitas fuit, siue illuuies aquarum principio rerum terras obrutas tenuit; siue ignis, qui & mundum genuit, cuncta possedit: vtrisq; primordij Scythas origine præstare. Nam si ignis prima possessio rerum fuit, qui paulatim extinctus, sedem terris dedit, nullâ prius quà Septentrionalem partem, hiemis rigore ab igne secretâ, adeo vt nunc quoq; nulla magis rigeat frigoribus. Ægyptū vero, & totum Orientē, tardissime temperatum: quippe qui etiā nunc torreti calore solis exæstuet. Quod si omnes quondam terra submersæ profundo fuerunt, pro-
units.tr: Since the account of the deeds done by the Scythians is fairly full and splendid, I must begin with their origin. For their beginnings were no less illustrious than their empire; nor did they become famous more through the rule of men than through the virtues of women. For while the men founded the Parthians and Bactrians, their women founded the kingdoms of the Amazons. So, since the deeds of men and women are recorded alike, it is uncertain which sex was more distinguished among them. The Scythian people has always been regarded as the most ancient, although the Scythians and the Egyptians have long disputed the antiquity of their race. The Egyptians claimed that, since some lands burned with the excessive heat of the sun and others were stiff with the immense cold, men could not have been first generated, nor could they even be received and sustained once born, until coverings for the body had been devised against heat or cold, or the defects of places had been softened by artificial remedies. Egypt, they said, had always been so tempered that neither the winter frosts nor the summer heat of the sun wore out its inhabitants; its soil was so fertile that no land was richer for the sustenance of men. It is right, therefore, that men should be thought to have been born first there, where they could most easily be reared. On the contrary, the Scythians held that the temperature of a climate is no proof of antiquity. Nature, as soon as she first divided the regions by degrees of heat and cold, at once produced animals adapted to the endurance of each place, and the kinds of trees and crops varied appropriately with the condition of the regions. And as the sky is harsher for the Scythians than for the Egyptians, so their bodies and minds are hardier. Moreover, if the world, in the parts it now has, was once a single whole, whether the flood of waters covered the lands at the beginning of things, or fire, which also begat the world, possessed everything, in either case the Scythians excel in origin. For if fire was the first possessor of things, and gradually, once extinguished, gave place to the lands, the northern part was the first to be cut off from the fire by the rigour of winter, so that even now no region is more stiff with frost. But Egypt and the whole East were tempered most slowly, since even now they glow, scorched by the heat of the sun. And if all lands were once submerged in deep water,

units.la: {B} 2 profecto editissimam quang̃ partem decurrentibus aquis primum detectam ; humilimo autem solo eandem aquam diutissime immoratam:Et quanto prior quaq; pars terrarum siccata sit, tanto prius animalia genera-re coepisse. Porro Scythiam adeo editiorem omnibus 5 terris esse, vt cuncta flumina ibi nata in Maeotim, tum deinde in Ponticum, & AEgyptium mare decurrant.
units.tr: {B} 2 certainly the highest part of the land was first uncovered by the flowing waters, while the lowest ground was longest held by the same water; and the earlier any part of the lands dried out, the earlier animal kinds began to be generated. Moreover, Scythia lies so much higher than all other lands that all the rivers born there flow down into the Maeotis, and then into the Pontic and the Egyptian sea.

units.la: AEgyptum autem quae tot regum, seculorum cura impensaq; munita sit, & aduersum vim incurrentium aquarum tantis structa molibus, tot fossis confissa, vt 10 cum his arceantur, illis recipiantur aquae, nihilominus, nisi excluso Nilo, non potuerit, nec possit videri hominum vetustate vltima, quae aggerationibus regum, sive Nili trahetis limum, terrarum recentissima videatur, His igitur argumentis superatis AEgyptiis, antiquiores semper Scythae vissi.
units.tr: But Egypt, which was fortified by the care and expense of so many kings over so many ages, and built with such great masses against the force of the rushing waters, and cut through with so many ditches that by these the waters are shut out and by those received, nevertheless could not, unless the Nile were shut out, and cannot be seen to be the most ancient of men, since it seems the most recent of lands, by the embankments of kings and the mud the Nile drags down. Therefore, these arguments having overcome the Egyptians, the Scythians always appeared the more ancient.

units.la: 2. Scythia autem in Orientem porrecta, includitur ab uno latere Ponto, & ab altero montibus Riphaeis: à tergo Asia & Phasi flumine. Multum in longitudinem & latitudinem patet. Hominibus inter se nulli fines: neq; enim agrum exercent; nec domus illis villa, aut tectum, aut sedes est, armenta & pecora semper pascentibus, & per incultas solitudines errare solitis. Vxores liberosq; secum in plaustris vehunt: quibus, coriis imbriū hyemisq; causa tectis, pro domibus vtuntur. Iustitia gentis ingeniis culta, non legibus. Nullum scelus apud eos furto gravius: quippe sine tecti munimento pecora & armenta habentibus, quid inter fyluas superesset, si furari liceret? Aurum & argentum non perinde ac reliqui mortales appetunt. Lacte & melle vescuntur. 3 Lanea vsus ac vestium ignotus: & quanquam continuis frigoribus vrātur, pellibus tamen ferinis ac murinis vtuntur. Hac continentia, illis morum quoq; iustitiam edidit, nihil alienum concupiscentibus: Quippe ibidem diuitiarum cupido est, vbi & vsus. Atq; vtinam reliquis mortalibus similis moderatio, & abstinentia alieni foret: profecto non tantum bellorum per omnia
units.tr: 2. Scythia, stretching eastward, is bounded on one side by the Pontus and on the other by the Riphaean mountains; behind it lie Asia and the river Phasis. It extends far in length and breadth. Its people have no boundaries among themselves: they do not work the land, and have no house, villa, roof or fixed seat, since they always pasture herds and flocks and are accustomed to wander through uncultivated wastes. They carry their wives and children with them in wagons, which, covered with hides against rain and winter, serve them in place of houses. The justice of the people is cultivated by natural disposition, not by laws. No crime is graver among them than theft: since they keep herds and flocks without the shelter of a roof, what would remain in the woods if theft were allowed? They do not desire gold and silver as other mortals do; they live on milk and honey. 3 They have no use of wool and know no clothing; and although they are burned by continual frosts, they wear the skins of wild beasts and mice. By this self-restraint, nature also gave them justice of conduct, since they covet nothing belonging to others: for the desire for riches exists exactly where the use of them does. And would that other mortals had the same moderation and abstinence from what is another's! Certainly wars would not be carried on through all ages over all lands, nor would iron and arms take more men than the natural condition of fate.

units.la: 5 secula terris omnibus continuaretur, neq; plus hominū ferrum & arma, quam naturalis fatorum conditio raperet. Prorsus vt admirabile videatur, hoc illis naturā dare, quod Graci longa sapientium doctrina, praeceptiq; philosophorū consequi nequeunt, cultosq; mores inculta
units.tr: 5 It seems quite remarkable that nature gives them what the Greeks cannot attain by the long teaching of the wise and the precepts of the philosophers, and that cultivated manners are surpassed by uncultivated

units.la: barbaria collatione superari. Tanto plus in illis proficit vitiorum ignoratio, quam in his cognitio virtutis.
units.tr: barbarism in comparison. So much more does ignorance of vice profit them than knowledge of virtue profits the others.

units.la: 3 Imperium Asia ter quasiuere, ipsi perpetuo ab alieno imperio aut intacti, aut inuicti mansere. Darium regem Persarum, turpi ab Scythia fugmouerunt fuga: Cyrum cum omni exercitu trucidauerunt: Alexandri Magni ducem Sopyriona pari ratione cum copiis vniuersis deleuerunt: Romanorum audiuere, non sensere
units.tr: 3 Three times they sought to win Asia; they themselves, always untouched by foreign rule, remained unconquered. They put Darius, king of the Persians, to shameful flight out of Scythia; they slaughtered Cyrus with his whole army; in the same way they destroyed Sopyrion, the general of Alexander the Great, with all his forces. They heard of the arms of the Romans, but did not feel them.

units.la: arma. Parthicum & Bactrianum imperium ipsi condiderunt. Gens laboribus & bellis aspera: vires corporū immensa: nihil parare quod amittere timeant: nihil victores, praeter gloriam concupiscunt. Primus Scythis bellum indixit Vexoris rex AEgyptius, missis primo lenonibus, qui hostibus parendi legem dicerent. Sed Scythae iam ante de aduentu regis a finitimis certiores factii, legatis respondent: tam opulenti populi ducem stoide aduersus inopes occupasse bellum, quod magis domi fuerit illi timendum: quod belli certamen anceps, praenia victoria nulla, damna manifesta sint. Igitur non xspectaturos Scythas dum ad se veniatur, cum tanto
units.tr: They themselves founded the Parthian and Bactrian empires. The people is rough from labours and wars, immense in bodily strength, possesses nothing that they fear to lose, and as conquerors desire nothing but glory. The first to declare war on the Scythians was Vexoris, king of Egypt, who first sent heralds to tell them to obey the law of their enemies. But the Scythians, already warned of the king's approach by their neighbours, answered his envoys: it was foolish for a king of so wealthy a people to attack a needy people, and he had more to fear at home; the outcome of war was doubtful, there was no prize of victory, and the losses were certain. Therefore the Scythians would not wait until he came to them, since there were far more things to covet there among the enemy, but would go out to meet them of their own accord for plunder.

units.la: ibi plura in hostis concupiscendafint, vltro prede iuros obuiam. Nec dicta, res morata: quos cum tanta eleritate venire rex addidicisset, in fugam vertitur, xercitu, cum omni apparatu belli relicto, in regnum
units.tr: Nor was the matter delayed by words. When the king learned that they were coming with such speed, he turned to flight, leaving his army and all the equipment of war behind, and withdrew into his kingdom.

units.la: B se recepit. Scythas ab Aegypto paludes prohibuere: Inde reuersi, Asiam perdomitam vectigalem fecere, modico tributo magis in titulum imperij, quàm in victoriae pramium imposito. Quindecim annis pacandae Asiae immorati, vxoriũ flagitatione reuocantur; per legatos denunciantibus, ui redeant, subolem fe ex finitimis quaerituras, nec passuras vt in posteritatem Scytharum genus per feminas intercidat. His igitur Asia per mille quingentos annos vectigalis fuit. Pendendi tributi finem Ninus rex Assyriorum imposuit.
units.tr: B He withdrew. The marshes kept the Scythians out of Egypt. Returning from there, they made Asia, once subdued, pay tribute, imposing a modest tax more as a mark of dominion than as the reward of victory. Remaining fifteen years to pacify Asia, they were recalled by the demands of their wives, who sent word that unless they came home by force, the women would seek offspring from the neighbouring peoples and would not allow the Scythian race to die out in posterity through its women. For these reasons Asia paid tribute for fifteen hundred years. King Ninus of the Assyrians put an end to the payment of the tribute.

units.la: Sed apud Scythas media tempore duo regij iuuenes, Ylinos & Scolopitus, per factionem optimatum, domo pulsi, ingentem iuuentutem secum traxere; & in Cappadociae ora, iuxta amnem Thermodonta conse- derunt, fubiectofq; Themiscyreos campos occupauere. Ibi per multos annos spoliare finitimos assueti, confiratione populorum per insidias trucidantur. Horum vxores, cum viderent exsilio additam orbitatem, arma sumunt finesq; suos, fuinimoucntes primo, mox etiam inferentes bella, defendunt. Nubendi quoq; finitimis animum omisere; seruitutem, non matrimonium appellantes: singulare omnium seculorum exemplum. Auxere rempublicam fiue viris; iam etiam cum contemptu virorum fe tuentur. Et ne feliciores alie aliis viderentur, viros qui domi remanserant, interficiunt. Vltionem quoq; caesorum coniugum, excidio finitimorum consequuntur. Tum pace armis quaesita, ne genus interiret, concubitum finitimorum inéunt. Siqui mares nascerentur, interfuebant; Virgines in eundem ipsis morem, nō otio, neq; lanificio, sed armis, equis, venationibus exercebant, nuflis infantis dexterioribus mammis, ne sagittarum ictus impedirent, unde Amazones dictae sunt. Dua bis regina fuere, Marthefia & Lapeto, qua
units.tr: Meanwhile among the Scythians, two royal youths, Ylinos and Scolopitus, were driven from home by a faction of the nobles and drew a great body of young men with them. They settled on the coast of Cappadocia, near the river Thermodon, and occupied the neighbouring Themiscyrean plains. There, long accustomed to plundering their neighbours, they were trapped and slaughtered by a conspiracy of the peoples. Their wives, seeing that exile had added bereavement to their loss, took up arms and defended their territory, first repelling invaders and soon waging war themselves. They also gave up any thought of marrying their neighbours, calling it slavery rather than marriage: a unique example in all ages. They increased the commonwealth by their own strength, and now they even defend themselves with contempt for men. Lest some seem more fortunate than others, they kill the men who had remained at home. They also avenge their slain husbands by destroying neighbouring peoples. Then, having sought peace through arms, so that their race would not perish, they had intercourse with their neighbours. If any males were born, they killed them. The girls they trained in the same way as themselves, not in idleness or wool-working, but in arms, horses and hunting; they cut off the right breasts of the infants so that these would not hinder the aim of their arrows, whence they were called Amazons. They had two queens, Marthesia and Lapeto, through whom

units.la: 1 Quod Ninus rex Assyriorum imposuit. qua in duas partes agmine diuiso, inclyta iam opibus, vicibus gerebat bella, solaeque terminos alternis defendentes: & ne fuccesibus deesset auctoritas, genitas se Marte praedicabant. Itaq; maiore parte Europae subacta, Asiae quoq; nonnullas ciuitates occupauere. Ibi Ephesō, multisq; aliis vrbibus conditis, partem exercitus cum ingenti praeda domum dimiserunt. Reliquae, quae ad tuendum Asiae imperium remanserant, cōcursu barbarorum cum Marthesia regina intorficiuntur. In huius locum filia eius Orithya regno succedit: Cui praeter singularem belli scientiam, eximia seruate in omne euum virginitatis admiratio fuit. Huius virtute tantum additum gloriae & famae Amazonum, vt Herculi rex, cui 12 stipendia debebat, quasi impossibile imperauerit, vt arma regire Amazonum sibi affertet: Eo igitur profectus longis nouem nauibus, comitante principum Graecia iuuentute, inopinantes aggreditur. Duae tum sorores, Amazonum regna tractabant, Antiope & Orithya, sed Orithya foris bellum gerebat. Igitur cum Hercules ad littus Amazonum applicuit, infrequens multitudo cum Antiopa regina, nihil hostile metuente, erat. Quare efsectum est vt pauca repentino tumultu excitae, arma sumerent facilemq; victoriā hostibus darent: Multae in- tag, casa, captaq. In his duae Antiope sorores captae sunt, Menalippe ab Hercule, Hippolyte a Thefeo. Sed Thefeus obtenta in praemium captiua, eandem in matrimonium assumpsit, & ex ea genuit Hippolytum. Hercules postea victoriam, Menalippen captiuam sororī reddidit, & pretium, arma regina accepit. Atq, ita su- ꝯ tus imperio, ad regem reuertitur. Sed Orithya, vbi cōperit bellum sororibus illatum, & raptore esse Athenis ensium principem, bortatur comites, frustra, & Pontifinum & Asiam edomitam esse dicit, si Graecorū nan fam. tam bellis, quam rapinis pateant. Auxilium deinde à Sagillo rege Scythiæ petit: Genus seScytharum esse; cladedem virorum, necessitatem armorum, belli causas ostendit; assectusque, virtute ne segniores viris feminas habere Scythæ viderentur. Motus ille domestica gloria, mittit cum ingenti equitatu filium Panasagorum in auxilium. Sed ante prælium dissensione orta, ab auxiliis deserta, bello ab Atheniensibus vincuntur: receptaculum tamen habuere castra sociorum, quorum auxilio intactæ ab aliis gentibus, in regnum reuertuntur. Post Orithyam, Penthesilea regno potita est, cuius Troiano bello inter fortissimos viros, cum auxilium aduersus Græcos ferret, magna virtutis documenta extitere. Interfecta demum Penthesilea, exercitusque eius absumpto; pauca, quae in regno remanserant, agre se aduersus sinitimos defendentes, vsq; tempora Alexandri Magni durauerunt. Harum Minithyia, siue Thalestris regina, concubitu Alexandri per dies 13. ad subolem ex eo generandam obtento, reuersa in regnum, breui tempore cum omni Amazonum nomine intercidit. 20
units.tr: 1 That Ninus, king of the Assyrians, imposed (this). Through whom, the army being divided into two parts, they waged wars in turn, defending the borders alternately, and, so that their successes might lack no authority, they declared that they were born of Mars. Thus, with the greater part of Europe subdued, they also seized several cities of Asia. There, having founded Ephesus and many other cities, they sent part of the army home with great booty. The rest, who had remained to defend the empire of Asia, were killed by a rush of barbarians together with Queen Marthesia. In her place her daughter Orithya succeeded to the kingdom. Besides her remarkable skill in war, she was admired for her extraordinary preservation of virginity throughout her life. Through her valour so much glory and fame was added to the Amazons that the king to whom Hercules owed twelve years of service ordered him, as if it were impossible, to bring him the arms of the Amazons. Hercules therefore set out with nine long ships, accompanied by the young nobility of Greece, and attacked them unawares. Two sisters then ruled the kingdom of the Amazons, Antiope and Orithya, but Orithya was waging war abroad. So when Hercules landed on the shore of the Amazons, a scattered crowd was there with Queen Antiope, who feared nothing hostile. Hence it came about that the few who were roused by the sudden tumult took up arms and gave the enemy an easy victory. Many were cut down, and many taken captive. Among them two sisters of Antiope were captured: Menalippe by Hercules, Hippolyte by Theseus. But Theseus, having obtained the captive as his prize, took her in marriage, and by her he begot Hippolytus. Afterwards Hercules returned Menalippe to her sister in exchange for the queen's arms as his reward. And so, having been freed from his service, he returned to the king. But Orithya, when she learned that war had been waged on her sisters and that the abductor was the leader of the Athenians, urged her companions, saying that in vain was Pontus and Asia subdued if the Greeks lay open not only to wars but to plunderings. Then she sought help from Sagillus, king of Scythia: she pointed out that they were of Scythian stock, the slaughter of their men, the necessity of arms, and the causes of the war; and she appealed to their valour, so that the Scythians should not seem to have women less brave than men. Moved by that domestic glory, he sent his son Panasagorus with a great cavalry force to help. But before the battle a quarrel arose, the Amazons were deserted by their auxiliaries, and they were defeated by the Athenians in war. Nevertheless they had the camp of their allies as a refuge, and by their help, unharmed by other peoples, they returned to their kingdom. After Orithya, Penthesilea held the kingdom, and when she brought aid against the Greeks in the Trojan War, she gave great proofs of her valour among the bravest men. At last Penthesilea was killed and her army destroyed; the few who had remained in the kingdom, defending themselves with difficulty against their neighbours, endured until the time of Alexander the Great. Of these, Minithyia, or Queen Thalestris, having obtained intercourse with Alexander for thirteen days to beget offspring from him, returned to her kingdom, and in a short time perished together with the whole name of the Amazons.

units.la: § Scytha autem tertia expeditione Asiana, cum annis octo à coniugibus & liberis abfuissent, seruili bello domi excipiuntur. Quippe coniuges eorum longa exspectatione virorum fessa, nec iam teneri bello, sed deletos rati, seruis ad custodiam pecorum relictis nubunt: 25 qui reuersos cum victoria dominos, velut aduenas, armati finibus prohibent. Quibus cum varia victoria fuisset, admonentur Scytha mutare genus pugnae, memores non cum hostibus, sed cum seruis prœliandum; nec armorum, sed dominorum iure vincendos: verbera 30 in aciem, non arma adferenda; omissoq; ferro, virgas acflagella, steraq; seruilis metus paranda instrumenta. Probato omnes cōsilio, instructi sicut praeceptū erat, postquam ad hostem accessere, inopinantibus verbera intentant: adeoq; illos perculerunt, vt quos ferro non poterant, metu verberum vincerent; fugamq; non vt hostes vicii, sed vt fugitiui ferui capesserent. Quicunq; capi potuerunt, supplicia crucibus luerunt. Mulieres quoq; male sibi conscia, partim ferro, partim suspendio vitam finierunt. Post hac pax apud Scythas fuit, vsq; tempora Iancyri regis. Huic Darius rex Persarum, sicut supra dictum est, cum filiæ eius nuptias non obtinuisset, bellum intulit: & armatis septingentis millibus hominum Scythiam ingressus, non facientibus hostibus pugnæ potestatem, metuens ne interrupto ponte Istri, reditus sibi intercluderetur, amisis octoginta millibus hominum trepidus refugit: quæ iactura, abundante multitudine, inter damna numerata non est. Inde Asiam & Macedoniam domuit: Ionas quoq; nauali prælio superat. Dein cognito quod Athenienses Ioniis auxilium contra se tulissent, omnem impetum belli in eos conuertit.
units.tr: § The Scythians, however, in their third expedition to Asia, having been away from their wives and children for eight years, were met at home by a slave war. For their wives, weary of long waiting for their husbands, and thinking them no longer alive but destroyed, married the slaves who had been left to guard the herds; these, when their masters returned victorious, as if they were strangers, armed, barred them from their lands. When the struggle went with varying success, the Scythians were warned to change their kind of fighting, mindful that they had to contend not with enemies but with slaves, and that they must be conquered by the right of masters, not by arms: they were to bring whips into the line, not weapons; and, laying aside the sword, to prepare rods and scourges and the instruments of servile fear. When all approved this counsel, they took up their arms as instructed; and when they came near the enemy, they threatened them with whips while they were unaware. And so they struck them down, so that those whom they could not conquer with the sword they conquered by fear of the lash; and the slaves took to flight not as conquered enemies but as runaway slaves. All who could be caught were punished on crosses. The women too, conscious of their guilt, ended their lives, some by the sword, some by hanging. After this there was peace among the Scythians until the time of King Idanthyrsus. Against him Darius, king of the Persians, as was said above, made war when he had not obtained his daughter in marriage. He invaded Scythia with seven hundred thousand armed men, but when the enemy did not give him the chance of battle, fearing lest the bridge over the Ister be broken and his return cut off, he fled in alarm, having lost eighty thousand men; this loss, in such an abundant multitude, was not counted among the disasters. Thence he subdued Asia and Macedonia, and he also overcame the Ionians in a naval battle. Then, learning that the Athenians had brought aid to the Ionians against him, he turned the whole force of his war against them.

units.la: ·6· Nuncquoniam ad bella Atheniensium ventum est, quæ non modo vltra spem gerendi, verumetiam vltra gesti fidem peracta sunt; operaq; Atheniensium effeƈtu maiora quam voto fuere, paucis verbis origo repetenda est; & quia, non vt quærere, à sordidis initiis ad summa creuere. Soli enim præterquam incremento, etiam origine gloriantur: quippe non aduenæ, neq; passim collecta populi colluuies originem verbi dedit: sed eodem innati solo, quod incolüt; & quæ illis sedes, eadem origo est. Primi lanificij & olei & vini vsum docuere: Arare quoq; & serere frumenta, glandem vescentibus monstrarunt. Littera certe ac facundia, & hic ciuilis ordo disciplinæ, veluti templum Athenas habent. Ante Deucalionis tempora regem habuere Cecropem; quem,
units.tr: 6 Now that we have come to the wars of the Athenians, which were carried out not only beyond the hope of waging them but beyond the credibility of their achievement, and since the Athenians' efforts were greater than their wishes, we must briefly trace their origin; and because they rose from humble beginnings to the highest eminence, not by seeking it... Indeed the Athenians glory not only in their growth but also in their origin: for they were not newcomers, nor did a chance gathering of people give them their name, but they were born from the very soil they inhabit, and their origin is the same as their dwelling place. They first taught the use of wool-working, of oil and of wine; they also showed how to plough and sow grain, and how to feed on acorns. Certainly letters and eloquence, and this civil order of discipline, are their temple, as it were, at Athens. Before the time of Deucalion they had Cecrops as king, whom,

units.la: vt omnis antiquitas fabulosa est, biformem tradidere, quia primus marem femina matrimonio iunxit. Huic successit Cranaus, cuius filia Athis regioni nomen dedit. Post hunc Amphiction regnauit, qui primus Minerua urbem sacrauit, & nomen ciuitati Athenas dedit. Huius temporibus, aquarū illuuies maiorem partē populorum Graciæ absumpsit: Superfuerunt quos refugia montium receperunt, aut ad regem Thessalię Deucalione ratibus euecti sunt; à quo propterea genus hominum conditum dicitur. Per ordinem deinde successionis regnum ad Erichtheum descendit, sub quo frumenti satio apud Eleusin à Triptolemo reperta est, in cuius muneris honorem noctes initiorum sacrata. Tenuit & Aegeus Thesei pater Athenis regnum, à quo per diuortium decedens Medea, propter adultam priuigni ætatem, Colchos cum Medo filio ex Aegeo suscepto, concessit. Post Aegeum Theseus, ac deinceps Thesei filius Demophoon, qui auxilium Græcis aduersus Troianos tulit, regnum possedit. Erant inter Athenienses & Dorienses simultatium veteres offensæ, quas vindicaturi bello Dorienses, de euentu prælij oracula consuluerunt:
units.tr: as all antiquity is fabulous, they handed down as two-formed, because he was the first to join a male to a female in marriage. Cranaus succeeded him, and his daughter Athis gave her name to the region. After him Amphictyon reigned, who first consecrated the city to Minerva and gave the city the name Athens. In his time a flood of waters destroyed most of the peoples of Greece; some survived, whom the refuges of the mountains received, or who were carried in boats to Deucalion, king of Thessaly; for this reason the human race is said to have been restored through him. Then, in the order of succession, the kingdom passed to Erichthonius, under whom the sowing of grain was discovered at Eleusis by Triptolemus, and in honour of this gift the nights of the initiations were consecrated. Aegeus, the father of Theseus, also held the kingdom at Athens, and when Medea departed from him by divorce, on account of the grown age of her stepson, she withdrew to Colchis with her son by Aegeus, Medus. After Aegeus, Theseus reigned, and afterwards Theseus' son Demophoon, who gave aid to the Greeks against the Trojans, possessed the kingdom. There were old grudges and enmities between the Athenians and the Dorians, which the Dorians, about to avenge them by war, consulted oracles about the outcome of the battle:

units.la: Cranaus, Athis. Amphiction ad cuius tempora Deucalionis diluuium referetur. Erichtheus, sub quo frumenti satio nem Græcos docet Triptolemus. Ægeus. Theseus. Demophoon. Codrus, qui flagranti ergà patriam charitate se Responsum superiores fore, ni regem Athenien-sium occidissent. Cum ventum esset in bellum, militibus ante omnia, custodia regis praecipitur. Athenien-sibus eo tempore rex Codrus erat; qui & responso Dei, & praeceptis hostium cognitis, permutato regis habitu, pannosus, sarmenta collo gerens, castra hostium ingreditur: ibi in turba obsistentium, à milite, quem falce astu convulnerauerat, interficitur. Cognito regis corpore, Dorienses sine proelio discedunt. Atque ita Athenienses virtute ducis; pro salute patriae morti se offerentis, bello liberantur.
units.tr: Cranaus, then Amphictyon, in whose time the flood of Deucalion is dated. Erichtheus, under whom Triptolemus taught the Greeks the sowing of grain. Aegeus. Theseus. Demophoon. Codrus, who, burning with love for his country, when the oracle had answered that the Dorians would prevail unless they killed the king of the Athenians, ... When the war came, the soldiers were ordered above all to guard the king. The Athenians at that time had Codrus as their king. Having learned both the god's answer and the enemy's orders, he changed his royal dress for that of a ragged man, carried brushwood on his neck, and entered the enemy camp. There, in the crowd of those who opposed him, he was killed by a soldier whom he had cunningly wounded with a sickle. When the king's body was recognised, the Dorians withdrew without a battle. And so the Athenians were freed from war by the courage of their leader, who offered himself to death for the safety of his country.

units.la: 7 Post Codrum nemo Athenis regnauit: quod memoria mominis eius tributum est. Administratio reipublica annuis magistratibus permissa. Sed ciuitati nulla tunc leges erant: quia libido regum pro legibus habebatur. Legitur itaq; Solon, vir iustitiæ insignis, qui {1}velut nouam ciuitatem legibus conderet: qui tanto tempore inter plebem fenatumq; egit (cum fi quid pro altero ordine tulisset, alteri displiciturum videretur) vt ab vtrisq; parem gratiam traheret. Huius viri inter multa egregia, illud memorabile fuit. Inter Athenien{10}fes & Megarenfes de proprietate Salamina infula, prope vfq; interitum armis dimicatum fuerat. Post clades multas capitale esse apud Athenienses cœpit, fi quis legem de vindicanda infula tulisset. Solicitus igitur Solon, ne aut tacendo parum reipublica consuleret; aut {15}censendo,sibi:subitam dementiam simulat,cuius venia non dicturus modo prohibita,sed & facturus erat. Deformis habitu, more vecordium in publicum euolat; factoq; concursu hominum, quo magis consilium diffimulaíet, insolitè sibi versibus suadere populo cœpit, {20}quod vetabatur: omniumq; animos ita cœpit, vt exitio bellum aduersus Megarenfes decerneretur, infulaq; deuiĉtis hostibus Atheniensium fieret.
units.tr: 7 After Codrus no one reigned at Athens, and this was granted in memory of his name. The administration of the commonwealth was entrusted to annual magistrates. But the state then had no laws, because the will of the kings was held in place of laws. Solon, a man distinguished for justice, was then chosen, as if to found a new state by laws. He spent a long time among the common people and the senate, so that, whenever he proposed something that seemed likely to displease one order, he might win equal favour from both. Among the many outstanding things this man did, one was especially memorable. Between the Athenians and the Megarians there had been a fight, almost to the point of destruction, over ownership of the island of Salamis. After many defeats it began to be a capital offence among the Athenians for anyone to propose a law about claiming the island. Solon, anxious lest he either serve the commonwealth poorly by keeping silent, or serve himself by speaking, feigned a sudden madness, though he was going to speak not only in defiance of the prohibition but also to act upon it. Disfigured in appearance, he rushed into the public square like a madman; when a crowd had gathered, and so that he might better conceal his purpose, he began to recite verses to the people, in an unusual way, on the very subject that was forbidden. He so moved the minds of all that war against the Megarians was decreed to destroy them, and the island was made Athenian once the enemy was conquered.

units.la: 8 Interea Megarenfes memores illati Atheniensibus belli, & deserti,ne frustra arma mouisse viderētur, {25}matronas Atheniensium in Eleufinis sacris noctu oppressuri, nauēs conscendunt: Quare cognita, dux Athenienfium Pififtratus iuuentutem in insidiis locat, iussis matronis soluto clamore, ac strepitu, etiam in accessu hostium, ne intellectos fe sentiat, sacra celebrare; egreffos nauibus Megarenfes inopinantes aggressus, deleuit; ac protinus classe captiua intermixtis mulieribus, vt {30}speciem captarum matronarum præberent, Megaram contendit. Illi cum & nauium formam, & petitā prē-dam dam cognoscerent, obuij ad portum procedunt, quibus cesis, Pisistratus paulum a capienda vrbe abfuit. Ita Pisistratus autem astute tyrannidem occupat & regnat per 33. annos. Megarenses suis dolis hosti victoriam dedere. Sed Pisistratus quasi sibi, non patrie vicisset, tyrannidem per dolum occupat: quippe voluntarijs verberibus domi afsectus, laceratoq; corpore in publicum progreditur: aduocata concione, vulnera populo ostendit; de crudelitate principum, a quibus hac fe passum simulabat, queritur: adduntur vocibus lacryme, & inuidiosa oratione multitudo credula accenditur: amore plebis inquisitum fe senatui affirmat; obtinet ad custodiam corporis sui satellitum auxilium, per quos occupata tyrannide per annos 23. regnauit.
units.tr: 8 Meanwhile the Megarians, mindful of the war waged against the Athenians, and fearing that their arms would seem to have been raised in vain, boarded ships to surprise the Athenian matrons at night during the Eleusinian rites. Their plan was discovered. The Athenian leader Pisistratus placed the young men in ambush, and ordered the matrons to perform the sacred rites with loud shouting and noise, even as the enemy approached, so that the Megarians would not sense that they had been detected. Pisistratus attacked the Megarians as they came out of their ships, unsuspecting, and destroyed them. Then, with the captured fleet, the women mixed in among the men so as to look like captured matrons, he made for Megara. When the Megarians recognised the shape of the ships and the prey they had sought, they came out to the harbour to meet them, and when they had been cut down, Pisistratus was only a short distance from taking the city. Thus Pisistratus, shrewdly, seized the tyranny and reigned for 33 years. The Megarians, by their own tricks, gave the enemy victory. But Pisistratus, as if he had conquered for himself and not for his country, seized the tyranny by a trick. Having inflicted voluntary blows on himself at home and with his body torn, he went out into public. Calling an assembly, he showed the people his wounds and complained of the cruelty of the leading men, by whom he pretended to have been treated in this way. Tears were added to his words, and by a hateful speech the credulous crowd was inflamed. He declared that he had been sought out by the people's love and was in danger from the senate. He obtained for the guarding of his person a bodyguard of armed men, with whose help, having seized the tyranny, he reigned for 23 years.

units.la: 9 Post eius mortem Diocles, alter ex filiis, per vim fuprata virgine, a fratre puella intersecitur. Alter Hippias nomine, cum imperium paternum teneret, interfectorem fratris comprehendi iubet: qui cum per tormenta conscios cedis nominare cogeretur, omnes amicos tyranni nominauit: quibus interfectis, quaerenti tyranno, an adhuc aliqui conscij essent, neminem ait fuisse, quem amplius moriqeftiat, quam ipsum tyrannum: qua voce eiusdem fe tyranni victorem, post vindictam pudicitie sororis ostendit. Huius virtute cum
units.tr: 9 After his death, Diocles, another of the sons, having violently ravished a maiden, was killed by her brother. Another, named Hippias, while he held his father's power, ordered the murderer of his brother to be seized. When under torture he was forced to name his accomplices, he named all the tyrant's friends. When they had been killed, and the tyrant asked whether any accomplices were still left, he replied that there was no one whom he hated more than the tyrant himself. By these words he showed himself the victor over the same tyrant, after avenging his sister's chastity.

units.la: admonita ciuitas libertatis effet, tandem Hippias regno pulsus in exilium agitur: qui profectus in Persas, duce Dario inferenti Atheniensibus bellum, sicuti supra significatum est, aduersus patriam suam offert. Igitur Athenienses audito Dario aduentu, auxilium a Lacedemonis socia tum ciuitate petiuerunt. Quos vbi viderunt quatridui tencri religione, non exspectato auxilio, in tructis decem millibus ciuium, & Plataeensibus auxiliaribus mille, aduersus fexcenta millia boftium, in campos Marathonios in praelium egrediuntur. Miltiades & dux belli erat, & auctor non expectandi auxilij,quem tanta fiducia ceperat, vt plus præsidij in celeritate,quam in socijs duceret. Magna igitur in pugna euntibus alacritas animorum fuit, adeo vt cum mille 5 passus inter duas acies essent, citato cursu ante iaclum sagittarum ad hostem venerint: nec audacia eius,euentus defuit. Pugnatum est enim tanta virtute, vt hinc viros,inde pecudes putares. Victi Persæ in naues consugerunt;ex quibus multæ suppressæ,multæ captæ sunt. In 10 eo prælio tanta virtus singulorum fuit, vt cuius laus prima esset, difficile iudicium videretur. Inter cæteros tamen Themistoclis adolescentis gloria emicuit, in quo iam tunc indoles futura imperatoria dignitatis apparuit: Cynagiri quoq; militis Atheniensis gloria, magnis {1}15 {/}scriptorum laudibus celebrata est; qui post prælij innumeras cædes, cum fugientes hostes ad naues egisset, onu-stam nauem dextra manu tenuit, nec prius dimisit, quam [manum] amitteret: tum quoq; amputata dextra, nauem sinistra comprehendit; quam & ipsam cum amisisset, ad postremum morsu nauem detinuit: Tantam in eo virtutem fuisse, vt non tot cædibus fatigatus; non duabus manibus amissis victus; truncus ad postremum, & veluti rabida fera dentibus dimicauerit. Ducenta millia Persæ eo prælio: sine naufragio amisere.
units.tr: Once the city had been roused by his courage to seek liberty, Hippias was at last driven from the kingdom into exile. He set out to the Persians, and, with Darius leading war against the Athenians, as has been said above, he turned against his own country. The Athenians, having heard of Darius's approach, sought help from the Lacedaemonians, their allies. But when they saw that the Lacedaemonians were held back by religious scruple for four days, they did not wait for the help. Drawing up ten thousand citizens and a thousand Plataeans as auxiliaries, they went out to battle on the Marathonian plains against six hundred thousand enemies. Miltiades was both the leader in war and the author of the decision not to wait for aid; he had been so filled with confidence that he counted more protection in speed than in allies. Great eagerness of spirit was therefore shown by those advancing into battle, so that, when there were a thousand paces between the two armies, they ran at full speed and reached the enemy before the arrows were thrown; nor did their boldness lack success. For the fighting was carried on with such courage that you would think the men were on one side and beasts on the other. The defeated Persians fled to their ships, of which many were sunk and many captured. In that battle the courage of individuals was so great that it would be hard to judge whose praise was first. Among the others, however, the glory of the young Themistocles shone out, in whom even then appeared the future quality worthy of a commander. The glory of Cynaegirus, an Athenian soldier, also, celebrated by the great praises of writers, is famous. After countless slaughters in the battle, when he had driven the fleeing enemy to their ships, he seized a loaded ship with his right hand and did not let go until he lost the hand. Then, with the right hand cut off, he grasped the ship with his left; and when he had lost that too, at last he held the ship with his teeth. So great was his courage that, though worn out by so many slaughters and with both hands lost, he fought on, a maimed trunk, and, like a raging wild beast, with his teeth. In that battle the Persians lost two hundred thousand, not counting the wrecks.

units.la: {20} fere. Cecidit & Hippias tyrannus Atheniensis, auctor & concitor eius belli, diis patriæ vltoribus pœnas repetentibus.
units.tr: Almost. The Athenian tyrant Hippias also fell, the author and instigator of that war, as the gods, avengers of the fatherland, exacted punishment.

units.la: Interea & Darius cum bellum refstauraret, in ipso apparatu decidit, relictis multis filiis, & in regno, & ante regnum suscep tis. Ex his Artemenes maximus natu, ætatis priuilegio, regnum sibi vindicabat; quod ius, & ordo nascendi, & natura ipsa gentibus dedit.
units.tr: Meanwhile Darius also, while he was renewing the war, died in the very preparation of it, leaving many sons, both born during his reign and before it. Of these, Artemenes, the eldest, claimed the kingdom for himself by the privilege of age; this right, and the order of birth, and nature itself, have given to nations.

units.la: Porro Xerxes controuersiam non de ordine, sed de nascendi {a}scendi felicitate referebat. Namq; Artemenem primũ quidem Dario, sed priuato prouenisse; se regi primum natum. Fratres itaq; suos qui ante geniti essent, priuatum patrimonium, quod eo tempore Darius habuisset, non regnũ sibi vindicare posse: se esse quem primum in regno iam rex pater sustulerit. Huc accedere, quod Artemenes nõ patre tantum, sed & matre priuata adhuc fortuna, auo quoq; materno priuato, procreatus sit: se vero & matre regina natum, & patrem nõ nisi regem vidisse; autem quoq; materuum Cyrum se regem habuisse, non heredem, sed conditorem tanti regni: & sic in æquo iure virtuq; fratrem pater reliquisset, materno tamen se iure & auito vincere. Hoc certamen concordi animo ad patruum suum Artaphernem, veluti ad domesticum iudicem, deferunt; qui domi cognita causa, Xerxem præposuit. adeoq; fraterna contentio fuit, ut nec victor insultauerit, nec victus doluerit; ipsoq; litis tempore innuicem munera miserint; iucunda quoq; in-ter se non solum, sed credula conuiuia habuerint; iudicium quoq; ipsum fine arbitris, fine conuitio fuerit. Tanti moderatius, tum fratres inter se regna maxima diuidebant, quam nunc exigua patrimonia partiuntur. Igitur Xerxes bellum a patre captum aduersus Græciam, quinquennium infinituit. Quod vbi primum didicit Demaratus rex Lacedæmoniorum, qui apud Xerxem exulabat, amicior patriæ post fugam, quam regi post beneficia, ne inopinato bello opprimerentur, om-nia in tabellis ligneis magistratui perscribit, easdem cera superinductâ delet: ne aut scriptura fine tegmine indicium daret, aut recens cera dolum proderet. Fido deinde feruo perferendas tradit, iussoq; magistratui Spartanorum tradere. Quibus perlatis, Lacedemone quæstioni res diu fuit, quod neq; scriptum aliquid
units.tr: Xerxes, however, argued the dispute not about order but about the good fortune of birth. For Artemenes was indeed born first to Darius, but while Darius was still a private man; Xerxes was the first son born to a king. Therefore his brothers who had been born before him could not claim the kingdom, since their inheritance was only the private estate Darius had possessed at that time; he was the one whom the father, already king, had raised up first in the kingdom. Added to this was that Artemenes was born not only to a father, but also to a mother still in private fortune, and to a grandfather who was likewise a private man; whereas he himself was born to a queen mother, had seen his father only as king, and had as his maternal grandfather Cyrus, a king, not an heir but the founder of so great a kingdom. Thus, though the father had left the brother in equal right and merit, he himself would prevail by his maternal and ancestral right. They brought this contest, in a spirit of harmony, to their uncle Artaphernes, as to a domestic judge; he, having heard the case at home, preferred Xerxes. And the rivalry between the brothers was so free of bitterness that neither the winner insulted nor the loser grieved; during the very course of the dispute they sent each other gifts, and they held pleasant and even trusting banquets together; the judgment itself was given without witnesses and without reproach. Brothers then divided the greatest kingdoms among themselves more moderately than now they share small inheritances. Therefore Xerxes continued for five years the war his father had begun against Greece. When Demaratus, king of the Lacedaemonians, who was living in exile with Xerxes, and who after his flight was more friendly to his country than to the king for his favours, learned of this, so that they should not be overwhelmed by an unexpected war, he wrote everything on wooden tablets for the magistrate, and then erased the same writing by spreading wax over it, so that neither the writing without a covering would reveal the secret, nor fresh wax would betray the trick. He then handed them to a faithful slave to be carried, and ordered him to deliver them to the Spartan magistrate. When they had been brought, the matter at Lacedaemon was long a question, because nothing had been written...
Artaphernes settles the quarrel between the brothers.

units.la: Inter quos lite durante nulla appa-ret animo-rum conten-tio: imo gra-tia multa, & quidem ra-riffima.
units.tr: While the dispute lasted, no sign of rivalry appeared in their minds; on the contrary, there was much goodwill between them, and of a very rare kind.

units.la: Xerxes am-bitione du-ctus bellum aduersus Græcos in-taurat.
units.tr: Xerxes, driven by ambition, renews the war against the Greeks.

units.la: Demaratî ftratagema politicum,vt Græcorum saluti consu-leret.
units.tr: Demaratus' political stratagem, to provide for the safety of the Greeks.

units.la: quid viderent, nec frustra missas suspicarentur, tantoq; rem maiorem, quanto fit occultior, putabant. Harentibus in coniectura viris, soror regis Leonida consilium scribentis inuenit. Erasa igitur cera, belli consilia deteguntur. Iam Xerxes septingenta millia de regno armauerat, & trecenta millia de auxiliis: ut non immerito proditum fit, flumina ab exercitu eius siccata, Graciaq; omnem vix capere exercitum eius potuisse: Naues quoq; decies centum millia numero habuisse dicitur. Huic tanto agmini dux defuit. Ceterum si regem spectes, diuitias, non ducem laudes: quarum tanta copia in regno eius fuit, vt cum flumina multitudine consumerentur, opes tamen regiae superesserent. Ipse autem primus in fuga, postremus in praelio semper visus est; in periculo timidus; sicubi metus abesset, inflatus; deniq; ante experimentum belli fiducia virium, veluti natura ipsius dominus, & montes in planum deducebat; & connexa vallium aequabat; & quaedam maria pontibus sternebat, quædam ad nauigationis commodum per compendium ducebat.
units.tr: They did not know what the tablets showed, and they suspected they had not been sent for nothing; the more hidden the matter, the more important they thought it was. While the men were still puzzling over it, the king's sister found the message of Leonidas, who was writing it. The wax was therefore scraped away, and Xerxes' plans for war were revealed. Xerxes had already raised seven hundred thousand men from his kingdom and three hundred thousand from his allies. It is not without reason that it is recorded that rivers were drained dry by his army, and that Greece could scarcely hold his army. He is also said to have had a fleet of one thousand two hundred ships. This great host lacked a commander. But if you look at the king, you will praise his wealth, not his generalship; there was such an abundance of riches in his realm that, although the rivers were consumed by the multitude, the royal resources nevertheless remained. He himself was always seen to be first in flight and last in battle; timid in danger, and puffed up wherever fear was absent. Finally, before he had tested the war, relying on his strength, as if he were master of nature itself, he levelled mountains into plains, filled in linked valleys, and bridged some seas, while others he led by a shortcut for the convenience of sailing.

units.la: 11 Cuius introitus in Graciam quam terribilis, tam turpis ac fœdus discessus fuit. Namq; cum {k}Leonida rex Spartanorum cum quatuor millibus militū angustias Thermopilarum occupasset, Xerxes cōtemptu pau-citatis, eos pugnam capessere iubet, quorum cognati {l}Marathonia pugna interfecti fuerant; qui dum vlcisci suos quærunt, principium cladis fuere: succedente deinde inutili turba, maior cædes editur. Triduo ibi cum dolore & indignatione Persarum dimicatum: quarta die, quum nunciatum esset Leonida, à 20. millibus hostium summum cacumen teneri, tunc hortatur socios recedere, & se ad meliora patriæ tempora referuet: sibi cum Spartanis fortunam experiendam; plura se patriæ quam vitae debere: ceteros ad prasidia Gracia seruandos. Audito regis imperio discedere ceteri, soli Lacedæmonij remanserunt. Initio huius belli scitantibus Delphis oraculum, responsum fuerat, aut regi Spartanorum, aut urbi cadendum. Et idcirco rex Leonida cum in bellum proficiscereetur, ita suos firmauerat, ut irent ad moriendum animo circumstantes. Augustias proterea occupauerat, ut cum paucis aut maiore gloria vinceret, aut minore damno reipublicæ caderet. Diuisus igitur socius, hortatur Spartanos, meminerint qualitercunque, præliantibus, cadendum esse; caueren-t, ne fortius manifesto quam dimicasse videantur; nec exspectandum ut ab hoste circumuenirentur, sed dum nox occasionem daret, securis et latis superueniendum: nunquam victores honestius quam in castris hostium periturei. Nihil erat difficile persuadere persuasis mori: flatim arma capiunt; et fexcenti viri, castra quingentorum millium irrumpunt; flatimq; regis prætorium petunt, aut cum illo, aut si ipsi oppressi essent, in ipsius potissimum sede moriturio: Tumultus totis castris oriretur. Spartani posteaquam regem non inueniunt, per omnia castra victores vagantur; cadunt, sternunt, omnia: vt qui sciant se puguare non spe victoriae, sed in mortis ultionem. Prælium a principio noctis in maiorem partem diei tractum: Ad postremum non victi, sed vincendo fatigati, inter ingentes stratorum hostium caterinas occiderunt. Xerxes duobus vulneribus terrestri prælio acceptis, experiri maris fortunam statuit.
units.tr: 11 His entry into Greece was as terrible as his departure from it was shameful and disgraceful. When Leonidas, king of the Spartans, had occupied the narrow pass of Thermopylae with four thousand soldiers, Xerxes, despising their small number, ordered them to join battle. Their kinsmen had been killed at the battle of Marathon, and while they sought to avenge them they became the beginning of the disaster. Then, when an useless crowd came up behind them, a greater slaughter followed. For three days the fighting went on there, to the grief and indignation of the Persians. On the fourth day, when it was reported to Leonidas that twenty thousand of the enemy held the highest peak, he urged his allies to withdraw and keep themselves for better times for their country. He said that he and the Spartans would try their own fortune; he owed more to his country than to his life; the others should be kept for the defence of Greece. When the others heard the king's command and left, only the Lacedaemonians remained. At the start of this war, the Delphic oracle had been consulted and had answered that either the king of the Spartans or the city would have to fall. So when King Leonidas set out for war, he had strengthened his men so that they went to die with resolute spirit. He had therefore occupied the narrow pass so that with a few men he would either win with greater glory or fall with less loss to the commonwealth. Having divided his forces, he urged the Spartans to remember that, however things turned out, they must fight to the death. They were to take care not to appear to have fought more bravely than they had fought in fact, and not to wait until the enemy surrounded them, but to attack with swords and spears while the night gave them the chance. They were never to die more honourably than as victors in the camp of the enemy. It was not hard to persuade men who were already persuaded to die. At once they seized their arms, and six hundred men burst into a camp of five hundred thousand and made straight for the royal headquarters, intending either to die with the king or, if they themselves were overwhelmed, to die in his very seat. Tumult arose throughout the whole camp. When the Spartans could not find the king, they wandered through all the camp as victors, cutting down and overthrowing everything, as men who knew they were fighting not in hope of victory but in revenge for death. The battle, begun at the start of the night, was carried on for most of the following day. At last they fell, not conquered, but worn out with conquering, among the huge heaps of enemy dead. Xerxes, having received two wounds in the land battle, decided to try his fortune at sea.

units.la: 12 Sed Athenienses dux Themistocles, cum animaduertisset Ionas, propter quos bellum Persarum fusceperaret, in auxilium regis classe venisse, solicitare eos in partes suas statuit. Et cum colloquendi copiam non haberet, quo applicaturi erant, symbolos proposui, et faxit faxis proscribi curat: Quae vos Iones dementia tenet? quod facimus agitatis bellum inferre olim conditoribus vestris, nuper etiam vindicibus cogitatis? An ideo mana vestra condidimus, ut essent qui nostra delerent? 5 quid si non haec & Dario prius, & nunc Xerxe belli causa nobisfum foret, quod vos rebellantes non destituimus? Quin vos in haec nostra castra exista obsidione transitu? Aut si hoc parum tutum extat, vos commissio praelio ite cesim; inhibete remos, & a bello discedite. Ante na10 ualis praelij congressionem miserat Xerxes quatuor millia armatorum Delphos, ad templum Apollinis diripiendum: prorsus quasi non cum Graecis tantum, sed cum diis immortalibus bellum gereret: quae manus tota imbribus, & fulminibus delera est, ut intelligeret, Quam
units.tr: 12 But the Athenian commander Themistocles, seeing that the Ionians, for whose sake the Persians had undertaken the war, had come with their fleet to help the king, resolved to win them over to his side. Since he had no opportunity to speak with them, he had messages drawn up and written on arrows, and shot into the place where they were about to land. They read: "What madness holds you, Ionians? Why do you intend to make war on those who founded you, and lately even on those who have avenged you? Did we found our homes only so that there would be men to destroy ours? What if this were not the cause of war for us, both with Darius before and now with Xerxes, because we did not abandon you when you rebelled? Why not come over to our camp here, leaving the enemy's side? Or if this seems too unsafe, then at least hold back from joining battle, stop your oars, and withdraw from the war." Before the naval engagement, Xerxes had sent four thousand armed men to Delphi to plunder the temple of Apollo, as if he were waging war not only with the Greeks but with the immortal gods. That whole band was destroyed by rain and thunderbolts, so that he might understand how no human strength could stand against the gods.

units.la: 15 nulla esset hominum aduersus deos vires. Post haec Thespias, & Plateas, & Athenas vacuas hominibus incendit: & quoniam ferro in homines non poterat, in aedificia igne grassatur. Namque Athenienses post pugnam Marathonium pramonente Themistocle, victoriam il- lam de Persis, non finem, sed causam maioris belli fore, 20 200. naues fabricauerunt. Aduentante igitur Xerxe, consulentibus Delphis oraculum, responsum fuerat: salutem muris ligneis tuerentur. Themistocles nauium praesidium demonstratum ratus, persuadet omnibus, 25 patriam municipes esse, non moenia; ciuitatem, non in aedificiis, sed in ciuibus positam: Melius itaq; salutem nauibus, quam vrbi commissuros: huius sententia et iam Deum auctorem esse. Probato consilio, coniunges liberosq; cum pretiosissimis rebus abditus insulis, relicta 30 vrbe, demandant: ipsi naues armati conscendunt. Exemplum Athenienses & alia vrbes imitatae. Itaq; ut adunata omnis sociorum classis, & intenta in bellum manuale esset; angustiasq; Salaminij freti, ne circumueniri C niri à multitudine posset, occupasset; differsio inter ciuitatum principes oriuntur: qui cum deserto bello ad sua tuenda dilabi vellent, timens Themistocles, ne discessu sociorum vires minuerentur, per servum fidum Xerxi nuntiat, uno in loco eum contractam Graeciam capere facillime posse: Quod si civitates quae iam abire vellet, dispersentur, maiore labore ei singulas consectandas. Hoc dolo impellit regem signiu pugnae dare. Graeci quoq; adventu hostium occupati, proelium collatis viribus ceperunt. Interea rex, velut spectator pugnae, cum parte navium in litore remanet. Arthemisia autem regina Halicarnassi, quae in auxilium Xerxi venerat, inter primos duces belli acerrime ciebat: quippe ut in viro mulierem timorem, ita in muliere virilem audaciam cerneres. Cum anceps proelium esset, Ionei iuxta praeceptum Themistoclis, pugnae se paulatim subtrahere coeperunt, quorum defectio animos ceterorum fregit. Itaq; circumspicientes fugam petuntur Persae, & mox proelio victi, in fugam vertuntur. In qua trepidatione multa capta naues, multa merses, plures tamen non minus senitiam regis, quae hostem timentes, domum dilabatur.
units.tr: 15 After this he set fire to Thespiae, Plataea and Athens, which were empty of people. Since he could not get at the men with the sword, he attacked the buildings with fire. For after the battle of Marathon, when Themistocle had warned that that victory over the Persians would not be the end but the cause of a greater war, the Athenians built two hundred ships. So when Xerxes drew near, and they consulted the Delphic oracle, the answer had been that they should protect their safety with wooden walls. Themistocles, judging that the protection of the ships was what had been pointed out, persuaded everyone that the homeland consists of its citizens, not its walls, and that a city lies not in its buildings but in its people. It was better, therefore, to entrust their safety to ships than to the city. This plan, he said, was already approved by God as its author. When the plan was approved, they left the city, and entrusted their children and their most precious possessions to hidden islands. The Athenians themselves boarded the ships armed. Other cities imitated the Athenian example. And so, that the whole allied fleet might be gathered together and kept ready for the war at sea, and that they might not be surrounded by the mass of the enemy, they occupied the narrow strait of Salamis. Then disagreement arose among the leaders of the cities, who wanted to abandon the war and slip away to defend their own lands. Fearing that the strength of the allies would be weakened by their departure, Themistocles sent a message through a faithful slave to Xerxes, saying that he could very easily capture Greece if he gathered it into one place. If the cities that were already wanting to leave were scattered, it would be much harder for him to pursue them one by one. By this trick he drove the king to give the signal for battle. The Greeks too, when the enemy arrived, joined battle with their forces combined. Meanwhile the king remained on the shore with part of his fleet, like a spectator of the fight. Artemisia, queen of Halicarnassus, who had come to help Xerxes, drove on most fiercely among the leading commanders of the war. Indeed, in her you could see a woman's fear in a man, and in a woman a man's boldness. While the battle was still uncertain, the Ionians, following Themistocles' advice, began gradually to withdraw from the fight, and their desertion broke the spirits of the rest. So the Persians, looking about for flight, were pursued, and soon, beaten in battle, they turned to flight. In that panic many ships were captured, many sunk, but more, not less, of the king's own forces, fearing the enemy, scattered and made their way home.

units.la: 13 Hac clade perculsum, & dubium consilij Xerxem P.Mardonius aggreditur. Hortatur vt in regnum abeat, nequid seditionis moueat fama aduersi belli, & in maius, sicuti mos est, omnia extollens: sibi 300. millia 25 armatorum lecta ex omnibus copiis relinquat; qua manu aut cum gloria eius perdomiturum se Græciam, aut si aliter euenerit ferat, sine eiusdem infamia hostibus cessurum. Probato consilio, Mardonio exercitus traditur; reliquas copias rex ipse deducere in regnum parat. 30 Sed Græci auditA regis fuga, consilium ineunt pontis interrumpendi, quem ille Abydo veluti victor maris secerat, vt intercluso reditu, aut cum exercitu deleretur, aut
units.tr: 13 Struck by this disaster and uncertain what to do, Xerxes was approached by Mardonius. Mardonius urged him to return to his kingdom, so that the rumour of the unfortunate war should not stir up any sedition, and, as is the custom, magnifying everything: he himself should keep for him three hundred thousand armed men chosen from all the forces. With this army, he said, he would either subdue Greece to the king's glory, or if things turned out otherwise, he would bear it, and would yield to the enemy without any disgrace to Xerxes. The plan was approved, and the army was handed over to Mardonius; the king himself prepared to lead the remaining forces back into his kingdom. But the Greeks, hearing of the king's flight, planned to break the bridge which he had built at Abydos, as if he were the victor of the sea, so that, with the way back cut off, his army would either be destroyed or, reduced to desperation by the hopelessness of their situation, would be forced to seek peace on the conquered terms. But Themistocles feared that the enemy, cut off, might turn their despair into courage, and by force open a way that otherwise would not be open to them. He kept saying that there were enough enemies still left in Greece, and that their number should not be increased by holding them back, since they ought to be conquered by strategy...

units.la: desperate desperatione rerum, pacem victus petere cogeretur. Sed Themistocles timens, ne interclusi hostes desperationem in virtutem verterent, & iter quod aliter non pateret, ferro patefacerent, fatis multos hostes in Graecia remanere dictitans, nec augeri numerum retinendo oportere, cum vincere consilio ceteros non posset, eundem ferunt ad Xerxem mittit, certioremq; consilij facit; & occupare transfitum maturata fuga iubet. Ille perculsus nuntio, tradidit ducibus milites producendos, ipse cum paucis Abydon contendit. Vbi cum solutum pontem bibernis tempestatibus offendisset, piscatoria scapha tredidit traiecit. Erat res spectaculo digna, & aestimatione fortis humanae, rerum varietate miranda, in exiguo latentem videre navigio, quem paulo ante vix aequor omne capiebat, carentem etiam omni seruorum ministerio, cuius exercitus propter multitudinem, terris graves erant. Nec pedestribus copiis, quas ducibus assignaverat, felicius iter fuit: siquidem quotidiano labori (Nec enim vlla est metuentibus quies) etiam famis accesserat. Multorum deinde dicerum inopia contraxerat & pestem; tantaque foeditas morientium fuit, ut via cadaveribus impleretur, aliisque & bestiis, illecebris solicitata exercitum sequerentur.
units.tr: Driven by the desperation of their situation, the defeated would be forced to seek peace. But Themistocles, fearing that the trapped enemy would turn despair into courage and, by force, open a passage that would otherwise not be open to them, kept saying that many enemies were still left in Greece and that their number should not be increased by holding them back, since he could not defeat the rest by strategy. They say he therefore sent a messenger to Xerxes to inform him of the plan and to urge him to seize the crossing by a hasty retreat. Xerxes, struck by the news, handed the troops over to his generals to lead out, and himself hurried to Abydos with a few men. There, finding the bridge broken up by the winter storms, he crossed in a fishing boat. It was a sight worth seeing, and wonderful for the variety of its circumstances and for a human being's estimate of what is brave: to see in a tiny boat the man whom, a little before, the whole sea could barely hold, now stripped even of all the service of his slaves, whose armies had been burdensome to the lands because of their numbers. Nor was the march by the land forces, which he had assigned to his generals, any more fortunate. For to their daily toil (for there is no rest for those who are afraid) hunger had also been added. Then, through the lack of food for many days, they had also caught a plague, and the dying was so foul that the road was filled with corpses, and beasts, lured by these, followed the army.

units.la: 14 Interim Mardonius in Graecia Olynthum expugnat. Athenienses quoq;, in spem pacis, amicitiamq; regis solicitat, spondens unde eorum vrbi etiam in maius restitutionem. Possea quam nulle pretio libertatem videt his venalem, uncenfis quae adificare caperant, copias in Boeotiam transfert. Eo & Graecorum exercitus, qui centum millium fuit, equitus est. Ibi, proelium commissum, sed fortuna regis cum duce mutata non est. Nam victus Mardonius, veluti ex naufragio cum paucis profugit: castra reficta regalis opulentia capta. Vnde
units.tr: 14 Meanwhile Mardonius captured Olynthus in Greece. He also tried to win over the Athenians, with hope of peace and the friendship of the king, promising that their city would be restored, and even on a larger scale. But when he saw that no price could buy liberty for them, he burned what they had begun to build and moved his forces into Boeotia. There the Greek army, which numbered a hundred thousand, also came. There a battle was joined, and the fortune of the king changed along with its commander. For Mardonius, defeated, fled with a few men, as if from a shipwreck; the camp, which had been rebuilt, was captured with the royal wealth. From this

units.la: { } primum Græcos, diuisò inter se auro Persico, diuitiarum luxuria uepit. Eodem forte die quo Confecto bello cum de præmiis ciuitatum agerctur, omnium iudicio Atheniensium virtus cæteris prælata. Inter duces quoque Themistocles, princeps ciuitatum testimonio iudicatus, gloriam patriæ suæ auxit.
units.tr: first the Greeks, having divided the Persian gold among themselves, were seized by the luxury of riches. On the same day, when the war was finished and the rewards of the cities were being discussed, by the judgment of all the Athenians' valour was preferred to the others. Among the commanders too, Themistocles, judged by the testimony of the cities to be first, increased the glory of his country.

units.la: 15 Igitur Atheniensis aucti, & præmiis belli & gloria, urbem ex integro condere moliuntur. Cum mœnia maiora complexi fuissent, suspecti esse Lacedæmoniis cœpere, recte reputantibus, quibus ruina urbis tantum incrementi detulisset, quantum fit datura munita ciuitas. Mittunt ergo legatos, qui monerent ne nummimen-ta hostibus & receptacula futuri belli exstruent. Themistocles, vt vidit spei vrbis inuideri, non existimans abrupte agendum, respondit legatis, ituros Lacedaemonem, qui de ea re pariter cum illis consulant. Sic dimissis Spartanis, hortatur suos vt opus maturent. Dein ipse interiecto tempore in legationem proficiscitur, & nunc in itinere infirmitate simulata, nunc tarditatem collegarum accusans, sine quibus agi iure nihil posset, dicm de die proferendo, spatium consummando operi quaerebat: cum interim nunciatur Spartanis, opus Athenis maturari, propter quod denuo legatos mittunt ad inspiciendam rem. Tum Themistocles per seruum magistratibus scribit Atheniensium, legatos vinciani, pignusq; teneant, ne in se gratius consulatur. Adiit deinde concionem Lacedæmoniorum, indicat permunitas Athenas esse, & posse iam illatum bellum non armis tantum, sed etiam muris sustinere: Siquid ob eam rem de se crudelius statuerent, legatos eorum in hoc pignus Athenis retentos. Graviter deinde cassigat eos quod non virtute, sed imbecillitate sociorum potentiam quaerent. Sic dimissus, veluti triumphatis Spartanis, a civibus excipitur. Post haec Spartani ne vires otio corrumperent, & ut bellum illatum a Persis Græciæ bellum vlciscerentur, vltro fines eorum depopulantur. Ducem suo, sociorumq; exercitui deligunt Pausaniam, qui pro ducatu regnum, Græciæ affectans, proditionis præmium cum Xerxe, nuptias filiæ eius pacisci tur, reddito captivis, ut fides regis aliquo beneficio obstringeretur. Scribit praeterea Xerxi, quoscunque ad se nuntios misisset, interficeret, ne res loquacitate hominum proderetur. Sed dux Atheniensium Aristides belli focus, collegæ conatibus obviam eundo, simul & in rem sapienter consulendo, proditionis consilia dissecuit. Necmulto post accusatus Pausanias, damnatur. Igitur Xerxes cum proditionis dolum publicatum videret, ex integro bellum instituit. Græci quoq; ducem constituunt u Cimonem Atheniensem filium Miltiadis, quo duce apud Marathonem pugnatum est, iuuenem, cuius magnitudinem futuram pietatis documenta prodiderunt. Quippe patrem ob crimen peculatus in carcerem coniectum, ibiq; defunctum, translatis in se vinculis ad sepulturam redemit. Nec in bello iudicium diligentium fefellit: siquidem non inferior virtutibus patris Xerxem terrestri, navalique bello superatum, trepidum recipere se in regnum coegit.
units.tr: 15 Therefore the Athenians, enlarged both by the rewards of war and by glory, set about building their city anew. When they had enclosed it with larger walls, they began to be suspected by the Lacedaemonians, who reasoned correctly that the ruin of the city had brought such growth as a fortified city was going to produce. So they sent envoys to warn them not to build fortifications and strongholds for the enemy and a base for a future war. Themistocles, seeing that the hope of the city was being begrudged, and not thinking the matter should be handled abruptly, replied to the envoys that they would go to Sparta and consult with them on that matter together. So, when the Spartans had been dismissed, he urged his people to hasten the work. Then, after an interval, he himself set out on the embassy, and now, pretending illness on the journey, now accusing the slowness of his colleagues, without whom nothing could lawfully be done, he sought to put off the day from day to day, and to use up time to finish the work. Meanwhile it was reported to the Spartans that the work was being hurried at Athens, on account of which they sent envoys again to inspect the matter. Then Themistocles, through a slave, wrote to the magistrates of the Athenians that they should arrest the envoys and hold them as a pledge, so that he would not be treated more harshly. He then went before the assembly of the Lacedaemonians, showed that Athens was now well fortified, and that it could now withstand a war brought against it not only with arms but also with walls. If they decided anything more cruel about him on account of this, their envoys were being held at Athens as a pledge. He then sharply rebuked them because they sought power not by virtue but by the weakness of their allies. Thus dismissed, as if he had triumphed over the Spartans, he was received by his fellow citizens. After this, lest the Spartans corrupt their strength by idleness, and so that they might avenge on Persia the war brought against Greece, they laid waste their territory of their own accord. They chose Pausanias as leader of their own and their allies' army. Aiming at the kingship of Greece in place of the leadership, he bargained with Xerxes for the reward of treachery, namely the marriage of his daughter, in return for handing back the prisoners, so that the king's good faith might be bound by some kindness. He further wrote to Xerxes that he should kill whatever messengers he sent to him, so that the affair would not be betrayed by men's talkativeness. But Aristides, the Athenian commander, a stronghold of the war, by opposing his colleague's efforts and at the same time by advising wisely on the matter, cut through the treacherous plans. Not long afterwards Pausanias was accused and condemned. Therefore Xerxes, seeing that the trickery of the betrayal had been made public, renewed the war. The Greeks also appointed as their leader Cimon the Athenian, son of Miltiades, under whose command the battle was fought at Marathon, a young man whose future greatness the proofs of his piety revealed. For when his father had been thrown into prison on a charge of embezzlement and died there, he took the chains upon himself and redeemed the body for burial. Nor did his conduct in war disappoint the judgment of those who valued him: for, no less than his father in virtue, he defeated Xerxes in both land and naval war and forced him, in fear, to retreat into his kingdom.
