Cicero, in the Partitiones oratoriae: the most learned inventress of all things; and in the letters to his friends, book 4: the most noble gymnasium of the world. {*} Demaratus: when he dissuaded the king from the war, he said among other things, "Greece will defeat you also for this reason, that it cannot contain you. Such a huge army has not strength but weight. Nothing is so great that it cannot be attacked." Seneca, On Benefits, book 6.

units.la: {b} Vt non immerito proditum] Aristides Sophista de apparatu Xerxis inter alia sic: ὁ ἥλιος συνεκρύψατο τὸν ... ἦν δὲ πλήθος ἡ μὲν θάλασσα πλοῖα, ἡ δὲ γῆ πεζῶν, ὁ δὲ ἀὴρ βελῶν: telis ob curabatur ipse sol, mare navibus, terra copiis pedestribus, aer sagittis redundabat.
units.tr: {b} That it was not unjustly reported: Aristides the Sophist, on Xerxes' preparations, says among other things: "The sun was hidden [ὁ ἥλιος συνεκρύπτετο] ... the sea was crowded with ships, the land with foot soldiers, and the air with arrows [ἦν δὲ πλήθος ἡ μὲν θάλασσα πλοῖα, ἡ δὲ γῆ πεζῶν, ὁ δὲ ἀὴρ βελῶν]." The sun was obscured by missiles, the sea by ships, the land by infantry, and the air by arrows.

Quod de Aristomene quoque Messenio duce præstantissimo scriptum reliquit Pausanias: Qui & Leonidæ virtutem excellentem, inter alia his verbis prædicat in Laconicis : Λεονίδᾳ κալὸν ὀμμα ὑπερσοφία (ἰμοὶ δοκεῖν) τὸν τε ἀνω χρόνον σύμπαντα, καὶ τὸν ἐπ᾽ ἀσπίσι. Leonidæ præclara & egregia facta superiorum omnium temporum rebus gestis meo iudicio antecellebant.
units.tr: {k} Leonidas: Cicero also mentions him, in book 1 of the Tusculan Disputations, where his heart was found hairy when his belly was opened. Pausanias likewise records this of Aristomenes the Messenian, a most outstanding leader. He also praises the excellence of Leonidas in his Laconica, in these words: "Leonidas' fine eye [Λεονίδᾳ καλὸν ὄμμα] ... in my opinion surpassed all the time before him and the time of the shields [ὑπερσοφία ... τὸν ἐπ᾽ ἀσπίσι]." That is, in my judgment the famous and outstanding deeds of Leonidas surpassed the achievements of all earlier times.

units.tr: Killed in the battle of Marathon: ten years before, in book 1. Themistocles, leader of the Athenians: whom Aristides praises in his Platonic oration 2, along with Herodotus, Thucydides and Plutarch.

units.la: Haius sententia etiam Deum auctorem esse] ἀποζῶν θεμιστοκλῆς (ait Plutarchus) τοῖς ἀνθρωπίνοις λογισμοῖς προσαγέσθαι τὸ πλῆθος, ὥσπερ ἐν τρα̈γῳδίᾳ μηχανὴν ἀρεὰς, σημεῖα δαιμόνια καὶ χρησμοὺς ἐπῆγεν ἀνδρὶς. Cum humanis rationibus Themistocles promouere se populum posse dissideret, diuinis propositis signis & oraculis eidem suam persuadere sententiam conatus est. Signum de quo dicitur erat Draconis è templo fuga. Quam Themistocles ita interpretabatur, quasi Dea urbe relicta, viam Atheniensibus ad mare ostenderet, navalem secum Persis insensam eandem esse pugnam significans. Plut. Themist.
units.tr: He also said that God was the author: Themistocles, relying on human reasoning, could not win over the people, so (says Plutarch) he brought in, as in a tragedy a stage machine, divine signs and oracles, trying to persuade them of his own opinion. The sign in question was the flight of the dragon from the temple. Themistocles interpreted it as though the goddess, having left the city, was showing the Athenians the way to the sea, signifying that the naval battle would be the same against the Persians. Plutarch, Life of Themistocles. [ἀποζῶν θεμιστοκλῆς]

units.la: In muliere virtutem audaciam] Obid Xerxes dixisse fertur: ὡς οἱ ἀνδρες γυναῖκες γεγόνασιν, καὶ δὲ γυναῖκες ἀνδρες ἐγενοντο: è viris fœminas, ex fœminis viros factos esse. Suid. in voc. Ἀγρίμια.
units.tr: Courage in a woman: Xerxes is said to have remarked: "As men have become women, so women have become men [ὡς οἱ ἄνδρες γυναῖκες γεγόνασιν, καὶ ... γυναῖκες ἀνδρες ἐγενοντο]," that men were made from women and women from men. Suidas, s.v. Agrimia.

units.tr: Mardonius: the king's cousin, who had earlier urged the war, against the opinion of Artabanus.

units.tr: {r} The royal wealth of the sumptuous bedding: for when Xerxes fled from Greece, he left the golden and silver couches, the tables and all the royal equipment with Mardonius. Herodotus, books 9 and 10.

units.tr: {f} The army of Mardonius destroyed: among the dead, according to Herodotus, when the bones were stripped of flesh, the skull of a certain man was found without a suture.

units.la: {t} Accusatus Paufanias damnatur] Damnatus in fano Minerua in quod tanquam asylum fe receperat, occlusus fame atque inedia interficitur, cum Agefilaus & Alcithoe parentes eius primi lapides ad obftrudas templi fores comportaffent,vt est apud Plutarchum in parallelis minoribus. Ita vir Magnus, magnam belli gloriam turpi motu commaculauit,ait Æn. Probus in Paufania, 2
units.tr: {t} Pausanias accused and condemned: condemned in the temple of Minerva, into which he had withdrawn as to a sanctuary, he was shut in and killed by hunger and starvation, when his parents Agesilaus and Alcithoe brought stones to block up the doors of the temple, as is related in Plutarch's Parallel Lives (minor). Thus a great man, by a shameful act, stained the great glory of his war, says Aemilius Probus in his Life of Pausanias, 2.

units.la: {u} Cimenem] De cuius virtutibus rebusq; gestis praeter Plutarchum, Probum, Herodotum, Valerium, vide quoque Aristidem oratorem in ea,quam supra dixi orat. plac. 2. Atque itacum hoc fecundo Iuftini libro desiuit Herodoti nouem librorum historia,qui à Cic. 1. dell. 2f patet historiæ dicitur, & profanis omnibus historiarum scriptoribus antiquitate.prastat: quem iniuste Plutarchus (quod mirum est in tam sapiente viro) peculiari libro vituperat,Caimerarius contra & H. Stephanus iure defendunt aclaudant.
units.tr: {u} Cimon: concerning his virtues and deeds, besides Plutarch, Probus, Herodotus and Valerius, see also the orator Aristides in the Platonic oration I mentioned above, number 2. And so with this the second book of Justin ends; the history of Herodotus in nine books, which Cicero (in ... ) calls the history of history, surpasses in antiquity all the profane writers of histories. Plutarch unjustly criticises it in a separate book (which is remarkable in so wise a man), while Camerarius and H. Stephanus rightly defend and praise it.

units.tr: 10 1 Xerxes and Artabanus, the treacherous killer: they pay the penalties; the war of the Persians is renewed, and at last they are overthrown by the Macedonians and Athenians. 6 The third war of the Messenians. Sparta's commonwealth and its lawgiver, Lycurgus. 7 The peace treaty is broken; the Spartans are hard pressed by the Pelopidas' valour, whose outstanding services to the commonwealth are described. Peace is again sanctioned and violated, whence the Sicilian war. 5 The Messenians' crimes.

units.la: 25 ERXES rex Persarum terror an- tea gentium, bello in Græcia infelicter gessit, etiam suis contemptui esse cœpit: Quippe a Artabanus præsectus eius, deficiente quotidie regis maiestate, in spem regni adductus, cum septem robustissimis filiis regiam veperi ingrediturb, nam amicitiæ iure semper illi patebat, trucidatoq; rege, voto suo obsistentes c filios eius,dolo aggreditur. Secutior de Ar- 35 taxerxe puero admodum, fingit regem a Dario, qui erat adolescens,quo maturius regno potiretur, occisum; impellit Artaxerxem parricidium parricidio vindica- re: Cum ventum ad domum Darij esset, dormiens in- ueniens
units.tr: King Xerxes, once the terror of the nations, waged an unfortunate war in Greece, and then began to be despised even by his own people. For Artabanus, his prefect, as the king's majesty daily declined, was drawn into hope of the kingdom. He went into the palace at evening with his seven most robust sons, for by the right of friendship he always had access to it. He murdered the king and, with a plot, attacked the sons who stood in the way of his wish. Then, to Artaxerxes, a boy still very young, he falsely claimed that Darius, who was an adolescent, had been killed by the king, so that the younger man might take the kingdom the sooner. He urged Artaxerxes to avenge a parricide with a parricide. When he came to Darius's house, he found him sleeping, and, as if Darius were pretending to sleep, he was killed.

units.la: a Artabanus. b Amicitiæ. c Filios. uentus, quasi somnum fingeret, interficitur. Dein cum vnum ex regis filiis sceleri suo superesse Artabanus videret, metuereta, de regno certamina principum; assumit in societatem consilij Bacabasum, qui prasenti statu contentus, rem prodit Artaxerxi, vt pater eius occi- sus fit; vt frater falsa parricidij suspicione oppressus; vt denig, ipsi parerentur insidiae. Ills cognitis Artaxerxes, verens Artabani numerum filiorum, in posterum diem paratum esse armatum exercitum iubet, recognituros & numerum militum, & in armis induffriam fingulorum. Itaq; cum inter cateros ipse Artabanus armatus afflicteret, rex simulat se breuiorem loricam habere; iubet Artabanum secum commutare: exuentem se, ac nudatum, gladio traiecit: Tum & filios eius corripi iubet. Atq; ita egregius adolescens, & eadem patris, & se ab insidiis Artabani vindicauit.
units.tr: a Artabanus. b Friendship. c The sons. Then, seeing that one of the king's sons was left to survive his crime, Artabanus feared the contests of princes over the kingdom. He took Bagabates into partnership in his plan. Bagabates, content with his present state, betrayed the matter to Artaxerxes: that his father had been killed, that his brother was oppressed by a false suspicion of parricide, and that finally, plots were being laid against Artaxerxes himself. When Artaxerxes learned this, fearing the number of Artabanus's sons, he ordered an army to be made ready under arms the next day, and the number of soldiers and the diligence of each man in his arms to be reviewed. So, while Artabanus himself was standing armed among the others, the king pretended that he had a shorter breastplate and ordered Artabanus to exchange with him. As Artabanus took it off and was stripped, the king ran him through with a sword. Then he ordered his sons to be seized as well. And so the outstanding young man avenged both his father and himself against the plots of Artabanus.

units.la: 2 Dum hac in Persis geruntur, interea Graecia omnis ducibus Lacedemoniis & Athenieniss in duas diuisa partes, ab externis bellis, velut in viscera sua, armis conuertit. Fiunt igitur de vno populo duo corpora; & eorundem castrorum homines in duos hostesles exercitus diuiduntur. Hinc Lacedemonij communia quondam ciuitatum auxilia, ad vires suas trahebant: inde Athenienses & vetustate gentis, & gestis rebus illustres, proprijs viribus considebant. Atq; ita duo potentissimi Graeciae populi, instituti Solonis & Lycurgi legibus pares, ex aemulatione virium in bellum ruebant: Namq; Lycurgus cum fratri suo Polybita Spartanorum regi succesisset, regnumq; sibi vindicare potuisset, Charillo filio eius, qui natus postumus fuerat, cum ad aetatem adultam peruenisset, regnum summa fide reflituit: vt intelligerent omnes, Quanto plus apud bonos pietatis iura, quam omnes opes vale- rent.
units.tr: The wicked Artabanus fell into the pit he had dug. And the young prince Ratesmas was dragged to punishment. The peoples, accustomed to arms, when external war ceases, turn the steel against themselves. Rivalry of strength is the fuel of war. On the commonwealth of Sparta. The piety of Lycurgus towards his country and his nephew Charilaus. In the meantime, while the infant grows up and he administers his guardianship, he gave laws to the Spartans, who had none; he was more famous for the example he set than for the invention of the laws. For he decreed nothing by any law of which he did not himself first give proof in his own person. He bound the people to obedience to their rulers, and the rulers to justice in their commands. He urged thrift on all, believing that the toil of soldiering would be easier with a constant habit of frugality. He ordered that each thing be bought not with money but by exchange of goods; he abolished the use of gold and silver, as the material of all crimes.

units.tr: The wicked Artabanus fell into the pit that he had dug. The young prince Ratesemates was dragged to deserved punishment. The people, accustomed to arms, cease from external war and turn the sword against themselves. Rivalry of strengths, the tinder of war. On the commonwealth of the Spartans. Lycurgus's devotion to his country and to his nephew Charillus. Meanwhile, while the infant grew stronger and he administered his guardianship, he gave laws to the Spartans, who had none. He was more famous for his example than for the invention of the laws, since he enacted nothing by any law which he did not first give as an example in himself. He bound the people to the obedience of their princes, and the princes to justice in their commands. He persuaded all to thrift, thinking that the labour of soldiering would be easier with a constant habit of frugality. He ordered that each thing be bought not with money but by exchange of goods, and he abolished the use of gold and silver, as the material of all crimes.

units.la: 3 Administrationem reipublicæ per ordines diuifit : Regibus potestatem bellorum; magistratibus iu- 15 dicia, & annuos successores; Senatui custodiam legum ; populo sublegendi Senatum, vel creandi quos vellet magistratus, potestatem, permisit. Fundos o- mnium æqualiter inter omnes diuisit, vt æquata patrimonia neminem potentiorem altero redderent.
units.tr: 3 He divided the administration of the commonwealth among orders: to the kings he gave the power of war; to the magistrates, judgments and yearly successors; to the Senate, the guardianship of the laws; to the people, the power of choosing the Senate or of creating whatever magistrates they wished. He divided the lands equally among all, so that equal patrimonies would make no one more powerful than another.

units.la: 20 Conuiuari omnes publice iussit, ne cuius diuitiæ , vel luxuria in occulto essent. Iuuenibus non amplius vna veste vti toto anno permissum, hęc quemquam cultius quam alterum progredi , nec epulari opulentius, ne imitatio in luxuriam verteretur.. Pue25 ros puberes non in forum ,sed in agrum deduci præcepit, vt primos annos non in luxuria, sed in opere, & in laboribus agerent. Nihil eos somni causa substernere ,& vitam sine pulmento degere, neq; prius in vrbem redire , quam viri facti essent , statuit.
units.tr: He ordered that all should dine in public, so that no one's wealth or luxury might be hidden. Young men were not permitted to wear the same garment for a whole year more than once, lest one should go about more finely dressed than another, or feast more lavishly, lest imitation turn into luxury. He ordered that boys who reached puberty should not be taken into the forum but into the country, so that they might spend their early years not in luxury but in work and labour. He decreed that they should sleep on nothing but rushes for the sake of sleep, live without a relish, and not return to the city before they had become men.

units.la: 30 Virgines sine dote nubere iussit , vt vxores eligen- tur, non pecunia ; seueriusque matrimonia siat viri coercerent , cum nullis dotis frœnis teneren- tur. Maximum honorem non diuitum & poten- tium
units.tr: He ordered that girls marry without a dowry, so that wives would be chosen, not for money; and that husbands, since they were bound by no dowry restraints, would more strictly restrain marriages. He wanted the greatest honour to belong not to the rich and powerful,

units.la: Conuiuia publica esse iubet. Iuuenes ad frugalitatem reuocat. tium,sed pro gradu aetatis senum esse voluit. Nec sane vsquam terrarum locum honoratiorem senectus habet. Hæc quoniam primo solutis antea moribus, dura videbat esse, auctorem eorum Apollinem Delphicum fingit, & inde se ea ex præcepto numinis detulisse, vt consuefciendi tadium metus religionis vincat. Dein vt aeternitatem legibus suis daret, iureiurando obligat ciuitatem, nihil eos de eius legib. mutaturos, priusquam reuerteretur: & simulat se ad oraculum Delphicum proficisci, consulturum quid addendum, mutandumq; legibus videretur. Proficiscitur autem Cretam, & ibiq; perpetuum exilium egit, abiicique in mare ossa sua moriens iussit, ne relatis Lacedæmonem, solutos se Spartani religione iurisiurandi in dissoluendis legibus arbitrarentur.
units.tr: Public banquets he ordered to be held. He called the young back to frugality, but he wanted the elders to hold rank according to their age. Nor indeed does old age have a more honoured place anywhere on earth. Since these customs seemed harsh to a people whose morals had previously been loose, he invented Apollo of Delphi as their author and claimed that he had brought them from the god's command, so that the fear of religion might overcome the weariness of habit. Then, to give his laws eternity, he bound the citizens by oath that they would change nothing of his laws until he returned. He pretended that he was setting out for the oracle at Delphi, to consult what ought to be added to or changed in the laws. He went to Crete and there lived out a perpetual exile, and, dying, he ordered that his bones be thrown into the sea, so that the Spartans, if he were brought back to Sparta, would not think themselves released from the religion of their oath and free to dissolve the laws.

units.la: 4 His igitur moribus ita breui ciuitas conualuit,vt cum Messeniis propter stupratas virgines suas, in solemni Messeniorum sacrificio, h bellum intulissent, grauissima se exsecratione obstrinxerint, non prius quam Messeniam expugnassent, reuersuros tantum sibi vel 20 de viribus suis, vel de fortuna spondentes. Quae res initium dissensionis Græciæ, & intestini belli causa & origo fuit. Itaq; cum contra præsumptionem suam annis decem in obsidione vrbis tenerentur,& quaerelis vxorū post tam longam viduitatem reuocarentur: veriti, ne 25 hac perseueratia belli, grauius sibi quam Messeniis nocerent: quippe illis quantum iuuentutis bello intercidaret,mulierum fecunditate suppleri, sibi & belli damna assidua, & fecunditatem vxorum, absentibus viris, nullam esse.Itaq; legûnt iuuenes ex eo genere militum, 30 qui post iusiurandum in supplementum venerant,quibus Spartam remissis promiscuos omnium feminarum concubitus permiserc:maturiorem futuram conceptionem rati, si eam singula per plures viros experirentur. Ex his nati, ob notam materni pudoris, Parthenia vocati, qui cum ad annos 30. peruenissent, metu inopiae, nulli enim pater existebat, cuius in patrimonium successio pervareretur, ducem Palantum assumunt, filium Araci, qui auctor Spartanis fuerat, iuuentutis ad generandam subolem domum remittendae: vt sicuti dudū patrem eius nascēdi auctorem habuissent, sic ipsum spei ac dignitatis suae haberent. Itaq; nec salutatis matribus, e quarum adulterio infamiam collegisse videbantur, ad sedes inquirendas proficiscuntur; diuq; & per varios casus iactati, tandemque in Italiam deferuntur; & occupata arce Tarentinorum, expugnatis veteribus incolis, sedes sibi constituunt. Sed post annos plurimos dux occupant. 15 eorum Palantus, per seditionem in exilium proturba-
units.tr: 4 By these customs the state grew strong so quickly that when the Messenians had seduced their virgins during a solemn sacrifice of the Messenians, they went to war, binding themselves by the gravest curse not to return until they had conquered Messenia, pledging to lose either their strength or their fortune. This was the beginning of the dissension among the Greeks and the cause and origin of an internal war. So, when, contrary to their presumption, they were held for ten years in the siege of the city, and their wives complained, calling them back after so long a widowhood, they feared that by this persistence in war they would harm themselves more than the Messenians: for the Messenians could make up for the youth lost in war by the fecundity of their women, whereas for them the losses in war were constant, and the wives, with their husbands absent, had no fecundity at all. So they selected young men from that class of soldiers who had come as reinforcements after the oath, and, sending them back to Sparta, allowed them promiscuous intercourse with all the women, reckoning that conception would be more mature if each woman tried several men. Those born of these unions, called Parthenians because of the known shame of their mothers, when they reached thirty years of age, out of fear of poverty (for no father existed in whose patrimony a succession could be claimed), took as their leader Phalanthus, son of Aristocrates, who had been the author for the Spartans of sending home the young men to beget offspring, so that, just as they had once had their father as the author of their birth, so they might have him as the source of their hope and dignity. Thus, without greeting their mothers, from whose adultery they seemed to have gathered their infamy, they set out to seek lodgings, and, tossed about for a long time through various chances, they were at last carried to Italy; and, having seized the citadel of the Tarentines and overcome the old inhabitants, they established their seats there. But after many years their leader Phalanthus was driven into exile by sedition.

units.la: tus, Brundusium se contulit, quo expulsi sedibus suis veteres Tarentini concesserant: Is moriens persuadet, ut offa sua, postremasq; reliquias conterant, & tacite spargi in foro Tarentinorum curent: hoc enim modo 20 recuperare illos patriam suam posse. Apollinem Delphis cecinisse. Illi arbitrantes eum in ultionem sui, ciuium fata prodidisse, praeceptis parere: sed oraculi diuersa sententia fuerat: perpetuitatem enim urbis, non amissionem hoc facto promiserat. Ita ducis exulis consilio, 25 & hostium ministerio, possessio Tarentina Parthenis in aeternum fundata: ob cuius beneficij memoriam Palantio diuinos honores decreuere.
units.tr: Palantus, driven into exile by a sedition, withdrew to Brundisium, where the old Tarentines had retreated after being expelled from their homes. On his deathbed he persuaded them to crush his bones and last remains and to have them quietly scattered in the forum of the Tarentines, for in this way they could recover their homeland. Apollo had given this answer at Delphi. Thinking that the god, in revenge against himself, had betrayed the fate of the citizens, they obeyed his instructions. But the meaning of the oracle had been different, for by this deed it had promised the city's perpetuity, not its loss. Thus, by the counsel of the exiled leader and the service of the enemy, the Parthenian possession of Tarentum was founded for all time. In memory of this benefit they decreed divine honours to Palantus.

units.la: 5 Interea Messenij cum virtute non possent, per infidias expugnantur. Dein cum per annos 80. grauia 30 seruitutis verbera, plerunq; & vincula, ceteraq; capta ciuitatis mala perpesi essent, post longam poenarum patientiam, bellum restaurant. Lacedaemonij quoq; eo conspiratius ad arma concurrunt, quo aduersus seruos dimicaturi videbantur. Itaq; cum hinc iniuria, inde indignitas animos acueret, Lacedæmonij de belli etiem tu oraculo Delphis consulto, iubentur ducem belli ab Atheniensibus petere. Porro Athenienses cum responsum cognouissent, in contemptum Spartanorum {k}Tyrtæum poetam claudum pede misere: qui tribus præliis fusus, eo vsq; desperationis Spartanos adduxit, vt ad supplementum exercitus, seruos suos manumitterent, hisq; interfectorum matrimonia pollicerentur, vt non numero tantum amissorum ciuium, sed & dignitati succederent. Sed reges Lacedæmoniorum, ne contra fortunam pugnando maiora detrimenta ciuitati infunderent, reducere exercitum voluerunt, ni interuenissez Tyrtæus, qui composita carmina exercitui pro concione recitauit; in quibus hortamenta virtutis, da-
units.tr: 5 Meanwhile the Messenians, unable to prevail by valour, were overcome by treachery. Then, after suffering for eighty years the heavy lashes of slavery, often chains, and the other evils of a captured city, they took up the war again after a long endurance of punishment. The Lacedaemonians also rushed to arms all the more united, since they seemed about to fight against slaves. So, while injury on one side and indignity on the other sharpened their spirits, the Lacedaemonians consulted the oracle at Delphi about the war and were ordered to ask the Athenians for a leader. The Athenians, when they learned the answer, sent them, in contempt of the Spartans, the lame poet Tyrtaeus. He was defeated in three battles, but he brought the Spartans to such despair that, to make up their army, they freed their slaves and promised them marriage with the widows of the slain, so that the freedmen might succeed not only to the number of the lost citizens but also to their rank. But the Spartan kings, lest by fighting against fortune they should bring greater losses on the state, wanted to lead the army home. They would have done so, had Tyrtaeus not intervened. He recited to the army, before an assembly, songs he had composed, in which were exhortations to courage and ...

units.la: {k} Bellum instauratur inter Spartanos & Messenios. Suos cladibus fasi, a- tos, eloquentia poetica. multorum fælatia, belli consilia conscripserat. Itaq; tantum ardorem militibus iniecit, vt non de salute, sed de sepultura solliciti, tesseras, insculptis suis & patrum nominibus, dextro brachio deligarent: vt sio- mnes aduersum prælium consumpsissent, & temporis 20 spatio confusa corporum linteamenta effent, ex indicio titulorum tradi sepultura possent. Cum sic animatum reges exercitum viderent, curant rem hostibus nunciare. Meffeniis autem non timorem res, sed æmulationem mutuam dedit. Itaque tantis animis 25 concursum est, vt raro vnquam cruentius prælium fuerit: Ad postremum tamen victoria Lacedæmoniorum fuit.
units.tr: {k} The war is renewed between the Spartans and the Messenians. Their men, broken by defeats, [were roused] by poetic eloquence. Tyrtaeus had written the counsels of war for the benefit of many. And so he kindled such ardour in the soldiers that, anxious not for their safety but for their burial, they tied to their right arms tokens inscribed with their own names and their fathers' names, so that if they fell in the coming battle and the bodies were confused with their linen wrappings, they could be handed over for burial by means of the inscribed titles. When the kings saw the army so inspired, they took care to announce the matter to the enemy. But for the Messenians the news caused not fear but mutual rivalry. So they joined battle with such spirit that there was scarcely ever a bloodier fight. In the end, however, victory fell to the Lacedaemonians.

units.la: 6 Interiecto tempore tertium quoq; bellum Messeniī reparauere: in cuius auxilium Lacedæmonij, inter 30 reliquos socios etiam Athenienses adhibuere; quorum fidem cum suspectam haberent, superuacaneos simulantes, à bello eosdem dimiserunt. Hanc rem Athenien- jes fes grauiter ferentes, pecuniam quæ erat in stipendium Perfici belli ab vniuersa Græcia collata, à Deo Athenas transferunt, ne deficientibus à fide socijs Lacedæmoniis, præda ac rapina esset. Sed nec Lacedæmonij quieuere: qui cum Messeniorum bello occupati essent, Peleponnenses immisere, qui bellum Athenientibus facerent. Paruæ tunc temporis, classe in AEgyptum missa, vires Athenientibus erant: Itaque nauali prælio dimicantes, facile superantur. Interiecto deinde tempore, postquam reditum suorum aucti, & classis, & militum robore, prælium reparauere. Iam & Lacedæmonij, omissis Messeniis, aduersus Athenienses arma verterant. Diu varia victoria fuit: ad postremum æquo Marte vtrinq; discessum. Inde revocati Lacedæmonij ad Messeniorum bellum, ne medium tempus otium Athenien̂sibus relinquerent, cum Thebanis pacisĉ untur, vt Bœotiorum imperium his restituerent, quod temporibus Perfici belli amiserant, vt illi Atheniensium bella suscipe-rent. Tantus furor Spartanorum erat, vt duobus bellis implicit́i, suscipere tertium non recusarent, dummodo inimicis suis hostes acquirerent. Igitur Athenienses, aduersus tantam tempestatem belli, duos duces deligunt, Periclem spectata virtutis virum, & Sophoclem scriptorem tragœdiarum: qui dimisso exercitu, & Spartanorum agros vastauerunt, & multas Achaiæ ciuitates Atheniensium imperio adiecerunt.
units.tr: 6 After an interval the Messenians renewed a third war. For help in it the Lacedaemonians called in, among their other allies, the Athenians as well. But when they suspected their loyalty, they dismissed them from the war, pretending that they were superfluous. The Athenians took this badly. They transferred to Athens from Delos the money that had been collected from all Greece for the Persian war, so that, if the Lacedaemonian allies should fall away from their faith, it would not be left open to plunder and rapine. Nor did the Lacedaemonians stay quiet. While they were occupied with the Messenian war, they sent the Peloponnesians to make war on the Athenians. At that time the Athenians had few forces, since they had sent a fleet to Egypt, so, fighting at sea, they were easily defeated. After an interval, when their fleet and soldiers had been restored to strength by the return of their men, they renewed the battle. Now the Lacedaemonians, having set the Messenians aside, had turned their arms against the Athenians. For a long time the victory was variable, and in the end they parted on equal terms. Then the Lacedaemonians were recalled to the Messenian war, lest they leave the Athenians time to rest in the meantime. They made a treaty with the Thebans to restore to them the leadership of Boeotia, which they had lost during the Persian war, on condition that the Thebans should take up the wars of the Athenians. Such was the madness of the Spartans that, though entangled in two wars, they did not refuse to undertake a third, provided they could gain enemies for their enemies. Therefore the Athenians, against so great a storm of war, chose two leaders, Pericles, a man of proven virtue, and Sophocles, a writer of tragedies. Dismissing the army, they laid waste the fields of the Spartans and added many cities of Achaea to the empire of the Athenians.

units.la: 7 Hus malus fracti Lacedæmonij, in annos 30. pepigerunt pacem: sed tam longum otium inimicitiæ non tulerunt, Itaque quintodecimo anno rupto fœdere, cum contemptu deorum hominumq;, fines Atticos populantur: Et ne prædam potius, quam pugnam expetisse viderentur, hostes ad prælium provocant. Sed Athe-
units.tr: 7 Broken by these evils, the Lacedaemonians made peace for thirty years. But such a long period of idleness their enmity could not bear. So in the fifteenth year, the treaty broken, they ravaged the Attic fields with contempt for gods and men. And so that they might seem to seek battle rather than plunder, they challenged the enemy to fight. But the Athenians

units.la: Athenienses, consilio Pericli ducis, populationis initi riam differunt in tempus vltionis,fuperstaciuam pugnā existimantes, cum vlcisci hostem fine periculo possent. Deinde interiectis diebus naues conscendunt, & nihil sentientibus Lacedæmoniis, totam Spartam deprædatur,multog, plura auferunt,quam amiserant. Prorsus vt in comparatione damnorum, longe pluris fuerit vltio,quam iniuria. Clara quidem hæc Periclis expeditio habita; sed multo clarior priuatı pacr monij contemptus fuit. Huius agros,in populatione ceterorum um,intactos hostes reliquerant, sperantes acquirere ı illi pose, aut periculum ex inuidia, aut ex suspicione prouisionis infamiam: Quod ante prospiciens Pericles & futurum populo prædixerat; & ad inuidiæ impetum ueclinandum,agros ipsos dono reipublica dederat: Atq, ita unde periculum quæsitum fuerat,ibi maximam gloriam inuenit. Post hac interiectis diebus,nauali prælio dimicatum est:victi Lacedæmonij fugerunt. Nec cessatum deinceps est, quin aut terra, aut mari varia præliorum fortuna inuicem se trucidarent. Denig, sepe tot malis,pacem in annos quinquaginta fecere,quam non nisi sex annis seruauerunt. Nam indutias quas proprio nomine condixerant,ex sociorum persona rumpebant: quippe quasi minus periurij contraherent: si ferentes sociis auxilia, potius quam si aperto prælio dimicafsent. Hinc bellum in Siciliam translatum:quod priusquam exponam, de Sicilia situ pauca dicenda sunt.
units.tr: postponed their vengeance to a later time, under the counsel of their leader Pericles, thinking that a battle was unnecessary, since they could punish the enemy without danger. Then, after a few days, they boarded their ships, and while the Lacedaemonians suspected nothing, they plundered the whole of Sparta and carried off far more than they had lost. Thus, when the damages were compared, the vengeance was far greater than the injury. This expedition of Pericles was indeed considered famous, but the contempt for his private property was much more famous. The enemy had left his fields untouched while they ravaged the others, hoping either to gain them, or to bring danger on him through envy, or infamy through suspicion of collusion. Pericles, foreseeing this, had both predicted it to the people and, to turn aside the force of envy, had given the fields themselves as a gift to the state. And so where danger had been sought, there he found the greatest glory. After this, a naval battle was fought after a few days; the Lacedaemonians were defeated and fled. Nor did they cease from then on, but by land or by sea they slaughtered each other with varying fortune in their battles. At last, after so many evils, they made peace for fifty years, which they kept for only six. For they broke the truces that they had agreed in their own name, through their allies, since they thought they would incur less perjury by bringing aid to their allies than if they fought in open battle. Hence the war was transferred to Sicily, and before I explain it, a few things must be said about the position of Sicily.
ON BOOK III OF JUSTIN
SCHOLIA OF THEOPHILUS CANGIFERUS

units.la: Artabanus praefectus eius] Diodorus eum vocat tregiorum stipatorum principem.
units.tr: Artabanus, his prefect] Diodorus calls him the commander of the three hundred bodyguards.

units.la: Nam amicitia iure semper illi patebat] Idem Diod. narrat lib. 11. Artabanum opera Mithridatis Eunuchi & cubiculari regii noctu clam intra cubiculum regis ad- missum esse.
units.tr: For by right of friendship he always had access to him] Diodorus also relates in book 11 that Artabanus was secretly admitted by night into the king's bedchamber through the work of Mithridates, the royal eunuch and chamberlain.

units.la: Filios eius] Qui eo tempore tres adhuc erant superstites: Darius natu maior & Artaxerxes, in aula regia, & Hystaspes, qui tum erat apud Bactrianos. Diod. lib. 11. qui paulum variat ab iis, quae apud nostrum auctorem sequuntur.
units.tr: His sons] At that time three of them were still alive: Darius, the elder, and Artaxerxes, at the royal court, and Hystaspes, who was then among the Bactrians. Diodorus, book 11, who differs slightly from what our author follows.

units.la: Spartanis] qui antea κακοσυμπαθ... ex omnibus Graecis pessime morati erant. Herod. lib. 1.
units.tr: To the Spartans] who earlier were of bad disposition [κακοσυμπαθ...], and among all the Greeks had the worst manners. Herodotus, book 1.

units.la: Leges instituit] Quod factum esse annis centum ante primam Olympiadem scribit Eusebius lib. 10. de praeparat. Euangel. cap. 3. Hisce legibus se opponens Alcander Lycurgo auctori alterum oculum excultit, eumq; fecit μονόφθαλμον, Paulsan Lacon. Lycurgum vocat Herodotus δικαιον ἀνδρα τῶν Σπαρτιατῶν virum inter Spartanos probatum.
units.tr: He instituted laws] Eusebius, in book 10 of the Preparation for the Gospel, chapter 3, writes that this was done a hundred years before the first Olympiad. Opposing these laws, Alcander struck out one eye of Lycurgus, the author, and made him one-eyed [μονόφθαλμον], as Pausanias the Laconian reports. Herodotus calls Lycurgus "a just man [δικαιον ἀνδρα] among the Spartans," that is, a man approved among the Spartans.

units.la: Auctorem eorum Apollinem Delphicum fingit] Val. Max. lib. 1. cap. 34. (sed iuxta Plutarchum in Lyc. & Strabonem lib. 10. haec non ficta, sed acta sunt. Et Herod. lib. 1. recitat versus Pythiae ad Lycurgum sciscitandi oraculi ergo advenientem. Ἥκεις ἀ λυκόεργα ἱκὸν τοῦ τίοντα ἠὸν Ζηνὶ φιλῷ κοὶ θεῶν ἀλύμπια δώματ' ἔχοντ', &c.
units.tr: He feigns that their author was Apollo of Delphi] Valerius Maximus, book 1, chapter 34. (But according to Plutarch in the Life of Lycurgus and Strabo, book 10, these things were not invented but actually done.) Herodotus, book 1, also recites the verses of the Pythia, addressed to Lycurgus when he came to consult the oracle: "You come, Lycurgus, to my rich temple, dear to Zeus and to the gods who hold Olympian homes," etc. [Ἥκεις ἀ λυκόεργα ἱκὸν τοῦ τίοντα ἠὸν Ζηνὶ φιλῷ κοὶ θεῶν ἀλύμπια δώματ' ἔχοντ', &c.]

units.la: Etsi idem adferat cum Paulsaniam Laconicis, quod nonnulli harum legum non Lycurgum, sed Minoem auctorem agnoscant ... translatas esse ... ex Cretensibus ... ad Spartanos per Lycurgum translatas existimant.
units.tr: Although the same author adds, with Pausanias on Laconian matters, that some of these laws are acknowledged to be the work not of Lycurgus but of Minos... that they were transferred... from the Cretans... to the Spartans through Lycurgus, they think.

units.la: Ibiq; perpetuum exilium egit, abiicig] Dissentiunt de loco mortis ac sepulturae apud Plutarchum Apollothemis, Timagus, Aristoxenus.
units.tr: There he spent perpetual exile, and was cast out] Apollothemis, Timagus and Aristoxenus disagree, in Plutarch, about the place of his death and burial.
{g} Bel.

units.la: h B. Illum intulisse] Nonæ Olympiadis anno altero, secundum Pausan. Mœssen. De hoc bello vide prætet citatos à Bong. Lactantium. lib. 1. cap. 20. qui nonnihil variat.
units.tr: h B. That he brought it on] In the second year of the ninth Olympiad, according to Pausanias of Messene. Concerning this war, see besides the authorities cited by Bongarsius, Lactantius, book 1, chapter 20, who differs somewhat.

units.la: i Ducem Palantum] Strabo lib. 6. auctor est, eos coniurasse cum servis Helotibus in Spartanorum civium necem hoc modo, ut simulatq; in foro pilei laconici collocarentur, impressio fierent in cives congregatos, & urbs occuparetur. Quo dete&to consilio Parthenie (ita enim legendum esse recte Bong. rfius monuit, & apud Strabonem dicuntur σωσὶῶν) viram figa redemerunt.
units.tr: i Leading Palantus] Strabo, book 6, reports that they conspired with the Helot slaves to kill the Spartan citizens in this way: as soon as the Laconian caps were placed in the forum, they were to fall upon the citizens gathered there and seize the city. When this plot was detected, they bought off Parthenie (for so Bongarsius rightly reminds us that the reading should be, and in Strabo they are called σωσὶῶν) with a fine.

units.la: k Tyrtæum] Qui elegiaco carmine id bellum descripsit, ut liquet è Paulania, qui aliquot cius versus narrationi suæ inter-serit.
units.tr: k Tyrtaeus] Who described that war in an elegiac poem, as is clear from Pausanias, who inserted some of its verses into his narrative.

units.la: l Peloponnenses] Hæc igitur ἀφορμὴ prima exstitit belli Peloponnesiaci, quod Thucydides 8. libris persequitur, vetustate proximus ab Herodoto, lectuque multis nominibus utilissimus.
units.tr: l The Peloponnesians] This, then, was the first cause [ἀφορμὴ] of the Peloponnesian War, which Thucydides pursues in eight books, closest in age to Herodotus, and in many respects most useful to read.

units.la: m Periclem] Anaxagoræ philosophi discipulum, qui dicendo fulgurate, tonare, permisisse Græciam aitin oratore Cic ex Aristophane Alia ipsius encomia vide apud Thucyd. lib. 2. & Plutarchum Pericle.
units.tr: m Pericles] A disciple of the philosopher Anaxagoras, who, by his speaking, is said to have thundered and lightened and so thrown Greece into confusion, as Cicero says, from Aristophanes. For other praises of him, see Thucydides, book 2, and Plutarch's Life of Pericles.

units.la: n Et ad invidia impetum declinandum] Simile exemplum Livius de Hannibale & Fabio Max. dictatore commemorat lib. 2 decad. 5.
units.tr: n And to avert the force of envy] Livy records a similar example about Hannibal and Fabius Maximus the dictator, book 2 of the fifth decade.
Pompeius Trogus, Epitome of the Histories
Book IV. Summary.

units.la: 1 Siciliæ insulæ situs, fo-ra natura. Ætnæ mōtis, Scyl-læ irem & Charybdis mira-culum. 2 Nominæ, incolæ vete-res, tyranni Siciliæ, cui Carthaginenses inhiant. 3 Rheginenses ab Himera-nis oppressi. Athenienses imperium Siciliæ ambiunt, & prospere agunt initio. 5 Athenienses à Gylippo 4 In incepto pergentes, po Lacedæmoniorum duSyracusam Lacedæmonios ce terra marique fraugunaccersunt. fit Græcorū cóu-tur, ducibus Demosthene 5 cursu, & bellum in Siciliam & Nicia indecoro fato subtransferrũt. lars.
units.tr: 1 The situation of the island of Sicily, its natural fertility, the wonder of Mount Etna and of Scylla and Charybdis. 2 Its name, its ancient inhabitants, and the tyrants of Sicily, for whom the Carthaginians lust. 3 The Rhegians oppressed by the Himerans. The Athenians seek dominion over Sicily and at first act successfully. 4 Proceeding with the undertaking, they are driven back by sea and land. The Syracusans summon the Lacedaemonians. 5 The Athenians are defeated by Gylippus, the Spartan leader, and the Greek war is transferred to Sicily, where it is fought with ill-starred fortune.

units.la: ICILIAM ferunt angustis quondam faucibus Italiæ adhæsisse; direptam, velut à corpore, maiore impetu superi maris, quod toto vndarũ onere illuc vehitur. Est autē ipsa terra tenuis ac fragilis; & cauernis quibusdam fistulisq, ita penetrabilis, vt ventorum tota ferme flatibus patcat; necnon & ignibus generandis nutriendisq, foli ipsius na35 turalis materia: quippe intrinsecus stratum sulphure & bitumine traditur: quæ res facit, vt spiritu cum igne inter interiora lacte, frequenter & complurib9 locis nunc flammas, nunc vaporem, nunc fumum eructet.
units.tr: Sicily is said to have once clung to the narrow jaws of Italy, and to have been torn away, as if from a body, by the greater force of the upper sea, which is carried there with the whole weight of its waves. The land itself is thin and fragile, and so pierced by caverns and channels that it lies open almost entirely to the blasts of the winds. Moreover, the soil itself has natural material for generating and feeding fires: it is said to be layered within with sulphur and bitumen. This causes the spirit, together with fire, to belch out in many places, now flames, now vapour, now smoke, from among its inner recesses.

units.la: Inde denique, Ætna montis per tot secula durat incen-20 dium. Et vbi acrior per spiramenta cauernarum ventus incubuit, harenarum moles egerũtur. Proximum Italiæ promontorium, b Rhegium dicitur, ideo quia Græce abrupta hoc nomine pronuntiantur. Nec mirum si fabulosa est loci huius antiquitas, in quem res tot coiere 25 mira. Primum quod nusquam alias tam torrens fretũ, nec solum citato impetu, verumetiam sæuo; neq, experientibus modo terribile, verumetiam procul videntibus: Vndarum porro in se concurrentium tanta pugna est, vt alias veluti tergà dantes in imum desidere, alias 30 quasi victrices in sublime ferri videas: nunc hic frenitum ferventis æstus, nunc illuc gemitum in voraginem desidentis exaudias. Accedunt vicini, & perpetui Ætnæ montis ignes, & insularũ Æolidum, veluti ipsis vndique alatur incendium. Neq, enim in tã angustis terminis aliter
units.tr: Hence it is that the fire of Mount Etna has burned for so many centuries. And where a fiercer wind presses down through the vents of the caverns, masses of sand are cast out. The nearest promontory of Italy is called Rhegium, because in Greek such broken places are called by this name. Nor is it surprising that the antiquity of this place is full of fable, since so many marvels have gathered there. First, nowhere else is the strait so turbulent, and not only with swift onrush but with savage force, terrible not only to those who experience it but even to those who watch from afar. Moreover, the waves clash together in such a battle that you may see some sink to the bottom as if turning their backs, while others are borne aloft as if victorious; here you hear the roar of seething surge, there the groan of water sinking into the abyss. Add the neighbouring and perpetual fires of Mount Etna and of the Aeolian islands, as if the fire were fed on every side. For so great a fire could not have burned for so many centuries within such narrow bounds unless it were nourished by the sustenance of moisture.

units.la: D .2 aliter durare tot seculis tantus ignis potuisset, nisi humoris nutrimentis aleretur. Hinc igitur fabulæ Scyllam & Charybdim peperere; hinc latratus auditus; hinc monstri credita simulacra, dum navigantes magnis vorticibus pelagi desidentis exterriti, latrare putant vndas, quas sorbentis æstus vorago conlidit. Eadem causa etiam Ætna montis perpetuos ignes facit. Nam aquarum ille concursus, raptum secum spiritum in imum fundum trahit, atque, ibi suffocatum tamdiu tenet, donec per spiramenta [terra diffusus, nutrimenta] ignis incendat. Iam ipsa Italiæ, Siciliæ, vicinitas, promontoriorum altitudo ipsa ita similis est, ut quantum nunc admirationis, tantum antiquis terroris dederit; credentibus, cœuntibus in se promontoriis, ac rursum discedentibus, solida intertipi abfumiq; nugia. Neq; hoc ab antiquis in dulcediuem fabulæ compositum, sed metu & admiratione transeuntium. Ea est enim procul inspicientibus natura loci, ut sinuosa maris, non transitum putes; quo cum accesseris, discedere, ac seiungi promontoria, quæ antea iuncta fuerant, arbitrere.
units.tr: Hence fables gave birth to Scylla and Charybdis; hence the barking that was heard, and hence the supposed likenesses of a monster, since sailors, terrified by the great whirlpools of the sinking sea, think the waves are barking, which the vortex of the swallowing surge dashes together. The same cause also makes the perpetual fires of Mount Etna. For that concourse of waters drags the air it has seized down to the bottom of the deep, and holds it there suffocated for so long, until it kindles fire, spread through the vents of the earth as its nourishment. Now the very nearness of Italy and Sicily, and the very height of the promontories, is so much alike that it has given the ancients as much terror as it now gives wonder: they believed the promontories came together and then parted again, and that solid things were swallowed up and vanished. Nor was this invented by the ancients for the sweetness of a tale, but arose from the fear and amazement of those who passed by. For the nature of the place is such that to those looking from afar the winding sea does not appear to be a passage; but when you have come near, you judge that the promontories which had formerly been joined are separating and parting.

units.la: 2 Siciliæ primo Trinacriæ nomen fuit; postea Siciliæ cognominata est. Hæc a principio patria Cyclopum fuit: quibus extinctis, Cocalus regnum insulæ occupauit: post quem singulæ ciuitates in tyrannorum imperium concesserunt, quorum nulla terra feracior fuit. Horum ex numero Anaxilaus iustitia cum ceterorum crudelitate certabat, cuius moderationis haud mediocrem fructum tulit: Quippe decedens cum filios paruulos reliquisset, tutelamq; eorum Micalo, spectata fidei seruo, commisisset; tantus amor memoriæ eius apud omnes fuit; ut parere seruo, quam deferre regis filios mallet, principesq; ciuitatis obliti dignitatis suæ,
units.tr: 2 Sicily was first called Trinacria; afterwards it was named Sicily. At the beginning it was the homeland of the Cyclopes. When they were destroyed, Cocalus seized the kingdom of the island. After him the individual cities submitted to the rule of tyrants, and no land was more fertile than theirs. Among these, Anaxilaus contended for justice against the cruelty of the others, and he reaped no small fruit of his moderation. For when he died, leaving young sons, and entrusted their guardianship to Micalus, a slave of proven loyalty, there was such a love for his memory among everyone that they preferred to obey a slave rather than hand over the king's sons, and the leading men of the city, forgetting their own dignity,

units.la: / sua, regni maiestatem administrari per seruum patere-
units.tr: own, and suffered the majesty of the kingdom to be administered through a slave.

units.la: rentur.Imperium Siciliæ etiam Carthaginenses tentauere, diuq; varia victoria cum tyrannis dimicatum. Ad posteremum amisso Hamilcare imperatore cum exercitu, aliquantisper quieuere, victi.
units.tr: The Carthaginians also attempted the rule of Sicily, and for a long time the struggle with the tyrants went on with varying success. At last, with their general Hamilcar and his army lost, they were defeated and for a while kept quiet.

units.la: 3 Medio tempore cum Rhegini discordia laborarêt, ciuitasq; per dissensionem diuisa in duas partes esset, veterani ex altera parte ab Himera in auxilium vocati, pulsis ciuitate, contra quos implorati fuerant; & mox cæsis, quibus tulerant auxilium, vrbem cum coniugibus & liberis sociorum occupauere; authorn facinus nulli tyranno comparandum: quippe vt Rheginis melius fuerit vinci, quam vicisse. Nam sine victoribus captiuitatis iure seruiissent, siue amissa patria exulare necesse habuissent, non tamen, inter aras & patrios lares trucidati, crudelissimis tyrannis patriam cum coniugibus ac liberis prædam reliquissent. Catinienses quoq; cum Syracusanos graues & atrocitatem
units.tr: 3 Meanwhile, while the Rhegians were troubled by discord, and the city, divided by dissension, was split into two parts, veterans from the other faction were summoned from Himera to help. They drove out of the city those against whom they had been called in, and soon, after slaughtering those whom they had come to aid, they seized the city together with the wives and children of their allies. It was a deed comparable to no tyrant's; indeed, it would have been better for the Rhegians to be conquered than to have conquered. For without their conquerors they would have served by the right of captivity, or, having lost their homeland, would have been forced to go into exile; yet they would not, slaughtered between their altars and their ancestral hearths, have left their country with their wives and children as plunder for the cruellest tyrants. The Catinians too, when the Syracusans were grievous and of atrocious

units.la: Rheginenses ciuili seditione laborantes, ab Himeranis oppetiti stultitiæ suæ poenas dant grauissimas. auxilium ab Atheniensibus petiuere: qui seu studio maioris imperij, quod Asiam Graeciamq; penitus occupauerant; seu metu facta pridem à Syracusanis classis, ne Lacedaemoniis illæ vires accederet, Lamponium ducem cum classe in Siciliam misere, vt sub specie ferendi Catinienfibus auxilij, tentaret Siciliæ imperium. Et quoniam prima initia, frequenter cæsis hostibus, prospera fuerant; maiore denuo classe, & robustiore exercitu, Lachete & Cariade ducibus, Siciliam petiuere; sed Catinienses siue metu Atheniensium, siue tædio belli, pacem cum Syracusanis, remissis Atheniensium auxiliis, fecerant.
units.tr: The Rhegians, labouring under civil sedition, pay the gravest penalties for their folly at the hands of the Himerans. They sought aid from the Athenians, who, either from zeal for greater empire, since they had thoroughly occupied Asia and Greece, or from fear that the fleet recently built by the Syracusans might join the forces of the Lacedaemonians, sent Lamponius with a fleet to Sicily, so that under the pretext of bringing aid to the Catinians he might attempt the rule of Sicily. And since their first beginnings, with the enemy often slain, had been successful, they sought Sicily again with a larger fleet and a stronger army, under the leaders Laches and Charias. But the Catinians, either from fear of the Athenians or from weariness of war, had made peace with the Syracusans, sending back the Athenian aid.

units.la: 4 Interiecto deinde tempore, cum fides pacis à Syracusanis non seruaretur, denuo legatos Athenas miserunt, qui sordida veste, capillo barbaq;, promissis, & omni squaloris habitu ad misericordiam commouendam acquisito, concionem deformes adeunt; adduntur precibus lacrymæ: & ita, misericordem populum supplices mouent, vt damnarentur duces, qui ab his auxilia deduxerant. Igitur classis ingens d'icvitur; creantur duces Nicias, & Alcibiades, & Lamachos; tantiq; viribus Siciliā repetitur, vt ipsis terrori essent, in quorum auxilia mitterentur. Breui post tempore, reuocato ad reatum Alcibiade, duo prælia pedestria secunda Nicias & Lamachos faciunt: munitionibus deinde circundatis, hostes etiam maritimis commeatibus in urbe clausos intercludunt. Quibus rebus fracti Syracusani, auxilium à Lacedæmoniis petierunt. Ab his mittitur Gylippus, solus, sed [in] quo instar omnium auxiliorum erat. Is audito geuere belli, iam inclinato statu, auxiliis partim in Gracia, partim in Sicilia contractis, opportuna bello loca occupat. Duobus deinde prœlis victus, congressus tertio, occiso Lamacho & hostes in fugam compulit,& socios obsidione liberauit. Sed cum Atheniensēs à bello terrestri in nauale se transtulissent, Gy20 lippus classem Lacedæmone cum auxiliis arcessit: quo cognito, & ipsi Athenienses in locum amissi ducis Demosthenem & Eurymedonta cum supplemento copiarum mittunt: Peloponnesii quoq; communi ciuitatium decreto, ingentia Syracusanis auxilia misere; & quasi 25 Græcia bellum in Siciliam translatum esset, ita ex vtraq; parte summis viribus dimicabatur.
units.tr: 4 Some time later, since the faith of the peace was not kept by the Syracusans, they again sent envoys to Athens. In squalid dress, with hair and beard neglected, and with every appearance of squalor assumed to move pity, they came before the assembly in wretched state; tears were added to their prayers. In this way the suppliants moved the merciful people so that the leaders who had led the aid away from them were condemned. Therefore a huge fleet is voted; Nicias, Alcibiades and Lamachus are made commanders; and Sicily is attacked with such forces that they became a terror to those in whose aid they had been sent. Shortly afterwards, Alcibiades was recalled to answer the charge, and Nicias and Lamachus fought two successful land battles. Then, after surrounding the city with fortifications, they cut off the enemy, shut up in the city, from supplies by sea. Broken by these events, the Syracusans sought aid from the Lacedaemonians. From them Gylippus was sent, alone, but he was worth the aid of all the others. Hearing of the nature of the war, and that the state of affairs was already tilting, he occupied places suitable for the war, with forces partly gathered in Greece and partly in Sicily. Then, defeated in two battles, he joined battle a third time, killed Lamachus, drove the enemy into flight, and freed his allies from the siege. But when the Athenians had transferred the war from land to sea, Gylippus summoned a fleet with reinforcements from Lacedaemon. On learning of this, the Athenians themselves sent Demosthenes and Eurymedon in place of the lost leader, with a supplement of troops. The Peloponnesians too, by common decree of their cities, sent great aid to the Syracusans; and it was as if the war of Greece had been transferred into Sicily, so fiercely was the fighting carried on by both sides.

units.la: 5 Prima igitur congressione nauali certaminis, Athenienses vincuntur. Castra quoq; cum omni publica ac priuata pecunia amittunt. Super hæc mala, cum 30 etiam terrestri prœlio victi essent nunc Demosthenes censere cœpit, vt abirent Sicilia, dum res, quamuis afflicta, nondum tamen perdita forent; neq; in bello male auspiauspicato amplius perseuerandum esse; domi grauiora, & forsitan infelicitora bella, in qua feruare hos urbis apparatus oporteat. Nicias seu pudore male acta rei, seu metu deflituta spei ciuium, seu impellente fato ma- 5 nere contendit. Reparatur igitur nauale bellum, & animata prioris fortuna procella, ad spem certaminis renocantur: sed insciria ducum, qui inter angustias maris tuentes se, Syracusanos aggressi fuerant facile vincuntur. Eurymedon dux in prima acie fortissime, 10 dimicans, primus cadit: triginta naues quibus praesuerat, incenduntur. Demosthenes & Nicias, & ipsi victi, exercitum in terram deponunt: tutiorem fugam rati itinere terrestri. Ab his relictas centum triginta naues Gylippus inuasit; ipsos deinde insequitur, fugientes par-. 15 tim capit, cadit partim. Demosthenes amisso exercitu, a captiuitate, gladio, & voluntaria morte se vindicat: Nicias autem ne Demosthenis quidem exemplo, vt sibi consuleret admonitus, cladem suorum auxit & dedecore captiuitatis.
units.tr: 5 In the first naval battle, therefore, the Athenians were defeated. They also lost their camp with all their public and private money. Besides these disasters, when they had been beaten in a land battle too, Demosthenes now began to advise that they should leave Sicily, while their affairs, though shaken, were not yet lost; that they should not persist any longer in a war begun under bad omens; and that they must keep these preparations of the city for wars at home, which would be heavier and perhaps more unlucky. Nicias, whether from shame at the bad conduct of the affair, or from fear because the hope of the citizens was failing, or impelled by fate, insisted on staying. So the naval war was renewed, and with their former fortune revived, they were recalled to hope of battle. But through the inexperience of their leaders, who fought among the narrows of the sea and attacked the Syracusans, they were easily defeated. Eurymedon, the leader, fighting most bravely in the front line, fell first; the thirty ships under his command were burned. Demosthenes and Nicias, themselves defeated, landed the army, thinking a land march the safer flight. Gylippus attacked the hundred and thirty ships left behind by them; then he pursued the men themselves, capturing some as they fled and killing others. Demosthenes, having lost his army, saved himself from captivity by the sword and by voluntary death; but Nicias, not even warned by Demosthenes' example to look to his own safety, increased the disaster of his men and the disgrace of captivity.
ON BOOK IV OF JUSTIN.
THE NOTES OF THEOPHILUS CANGISER.

units.tr: 25 ᵃ They say Sicily] A fuller description, better suited to these times, is to be sought in the Geography of Marius Aretius, in that volume which contains several learned writers on Sicilian affairs and was printed at Frankfurt a few years ago by the Wechel press.

units.la: 30 ᵇ Rhegium] Ῥήγιον τῆς ἡγιοῦς τῆς Διαρεῖος καὶ Διαχολῆς Suid. Vnde Sicilia Straboni est ἀποτομὴ καὶ ἀποσπασμὸς τῆς ἤπειρου abrupta & auulsa pars continentis.
units.tr: 30 ᵇ Rhegium] Suidas: Rhegion [Ῥήγιον τῆς ἡγιοῦς τῆς Διαρεῖος καὶ Διαχολῆς]. Hence Strabo calls Sicily a cutting-off and tearing-away [apotomē kai apospasmos tēs ēpeirou] of the mainland, an abrupt and torn-off part of the continent.

units.la: ᶜ Sicania cognominata est] Thucydidi, vt habet Plinius lib. 3. cap. 8.
units.tr: ᶜ Sicania was so named] According to Thucydides, as Pliny has it, book 3, chapter 8.
See Max., book 3, chapter 2.

units.la: Nā Xerxes è Græcia fugiēs aureos & argenteos lectos atq; mensas omnemq; regium apparatum reliquerat apud Mardonium. Herodot. lib. 9.
units.tr: For Xerxes, fleeing from Greece, had left behind with Mardonius his golden and silver couches and tables and all his royal equipage. Herodotus, book 9.

units.la: Inter eas Herodoto teste, cū offa carnibus nudarētur, cuiuldam hominis caput absq; satura t pertuin est.
units.tr: Among these things, as Herodotus attests, when the bones were stripped of their flesh, the head of a certain man, without a suture, pertains here.

units.la: Damnatus in sano Mineruæ in quod tanquam asylum se recepetat, occlusus fame atque inedia interficiitur, cum Agefilaus & Alcithoe parentes eius primi lapides ad obstruēdas templi fores comportassent, vt est apud Plutarchum in parallelis minoribus. Ita vir Magnus, magnam belli gloriam turpi morte commaculauit, ait Æn. Probus in Paufania.
units.tr: Condemned, he was shut up in the temple of Minerva, into which he had withdrawn as into a sanctuary, and was killed by hunger and starvation, after his parents Agesilaus and Alcithoe had first carried stones to block up the doors of the temple, as is found in Plutarch's Parallel Lives (the minor ones). Thus a great man stained his great military glory with a shameful death, says Æn. Probus in his Life of Pausanias.
The Epitome of the Histories of Pompeius Trogus
BOOK III.
SUMMARY.

units.tr: 3 The laws given to the Spartans by Lycurgus, and how they are ratified and kept. ... the various aspects of ...
