units.tr: 4 War waged on the Messenians on account of the raped virgins, and the migration of the Spartan bastards into Italy. 7 The peace treaty is broken. The Spartans are pressed by the valour of Pericles, whose outstanding services to the commonwealth are described. Peace is again sanctioned and violated, whence the Sicilian war.
5 The Messenians ... of their crimes.

units.la: ERXES rex Persarum terror antea gentium, bello in Gracia infeliciter gesto, etiam suis contemptui esse coepit: Quippe Artabanus praefectus eius, desidente quotidie regis maiestate, in spem regni adductus, cum septem tobusitus filiis regiam vesperi ingreditur, nam amicitiae iure semper illi patebat, trucidatoq; rege, voto suo obsistentes filios eius, dolo aggreditur. Securior de Artaxerxe puero admodum, fingit regem à Dario, qui ex rat adolescens, quo maturius regno potiretur, occisum; impellit Artaxerxem parricidium parricidio vindicare: Cum venturum ad domum Darii esset, dormiens in- cum...
units.tr: Xerxes, king of the Persians, once the terror of the nations, after his war in Greece had gone badly, began to be despised even by his own people. For Artabanus, his prefect, as the king's majesty declined daily, was led into hope of the kingdom. In the evening, with his seven sons, he entered the royal palace, since by right of friendship he always had access to it. Having slain the king, he treacherously attacked his sons, who stood in the way of his wish. Feeling safer about Artaxerxes, a very young boy, he pretended that the king had been killed by Darius, who was an adolescent, so that he might the sooner obtain the kingdom. He urged Artaxerxes to avenge parricide with parricide. When he was about to go to Darius's house, while Darius was sleeping, ...

units.la: Xerxes potentissimus princeps sed Persis inusitus, à praefecto suo interficitur.
units.tr: Xerxes, a most powerful prince but unusual for the Persians, is killed by his prefect.
He who had made insolent assaults on Europe perished at home.

units.la: Darius per calumniam horrendam opprefus. uentus, quasi somnum fingeret, interficitur. Dein cum vnum ex regis filiis sceleri suo superesse Artabanus videret, metueretq; de regno certamina principum; assumit in societatem consilij Bacabasum, qui præsenti statu contentus, rem prodit Artaxerxi, vt pater eius occisus sit; vt frater falsa parricidij suspicione oppressus; vt deniq; ipsi parारentur insidiæ. His cognitis Artaxerxes, verens Artabani numerum filiorum, in posterum diem paratum esse armatum exercitum iubet, recognituros & numerum militum, & in armis industriam fingulorum. Itaq; cum inter ceteros ipse Artabanus armatus assisteret, rex simulat se breuiorem loricam habere; iubet Artabanum secum commutare: exuentem se, ac nudatum, gladio traiecit: Tum & filios eius corripi iubet. Atq; ita egregius adolescens, & eadem patris, & se ab insidiis Artabani vindicauit.
units.tr: Darius, overwhelmed by a horrible calumny, was killed while he lay asleep, as if feigning sleep. Then, when Artabanus saw that one of the king's sons survived to be a witness to his crime, and feared contests among the princes over the kingdom, he took into partnership of his counsels Bagabasus, who, content with the present state of affairs, betrayed the matter to Artaxerxes: that his father had been killed, that his brother was oppressed by a false suspicion of parricide, and that plots were finally being prepared against himself. Having learned this, Artaxerxes, fearing Artabanus's number of sons, ordered an armed army to be ready the next day, so that they might review also the number of soldiers and the diligence of each man in arms. So when Artabanus himself stood armed among the others, the king pretended that he had a shorter breastplate, and ordered Artabanus to exchange armour with him. As Artabanus was undressing and became naked, the king ran him through with his sword. Then he ordered his sons to be seized as well. And so the excellent young man avenged both his father and himself against the plots of Artabanus.

units.la: 2 Dum hæc in Persis geruntur, interea Græcia omnis ducibus Lacedæmoniis & Atheniensibus in duas diuisa partes, ab externis bellis, velut in viscera sua, arma conuertit. Fiunt igitur de vno populo duo corpora; & eorundem castrorum homines in duos hostiles exercitus diuiduntur. Hinc Lacedæmonij communia quondam ciuitatum auxilia, ad vires suas trahebant: inde Athenienses & vetustate gentis, & gestis rebus illustres, propriis viribus considebant. Atq; ita duo potentissimi Graciæ populi, instityti Solonis & Lycurgi legibus pares, ex æmulatione virium in bellum ruebant: Namq; Lycurgus cum fratri suo Polybitæ Spartanorum regi succesisset, regnumq; sibi vindicare potuisset, Charillo filio eius, qui natus postumus fuerat, cum ad aetatem adultam peruenisset, regnum summa fide reflituit: vt intelligerent omnes, Quanto plus apud bonos pietatis iura, quam omnes opes valerent rent. Medio igitur tempore dum infans conualescit, tutelamq; eius administrat, non habentibus d Spartanis c leges instituit; non inuentione earum magis, quam exemplo clarior: Siquidem nihil lege vlla in alios sanxit, cuius non ipse primus in se documenta dare-t. Populum in obsequia principum, principes ad iustitiam imperiorum firmauit. Parcimoniam omnibus suasit, exiguum laborem militiæ, assiduaq; frugalitatis consuetudine faciliorem fore. Emi singula non pecunia, sed compensatione mercium iussit: auri argentiq; vsum, velut omnium scelerum materiam, sustulit.
units.tr: 2 While these things were happening in Persia, all Greece, under the leadership of the Lacedaemonians and the Athenians, was divided into two parts, and turned its arms from foreign wars, as if against its own vitals. Thus one people became two bodies, and men of the same camps were divided into two hostile armies. Hence the Lacedaemonians drew to their own strength the auxiliaries of the states, which had once been common; the Athenians, illustrious both for the antiquity of their race and for their deeds, relied on their own resources. And so the two most powerful peoples of Greece, equal in the laws instituted by Solon and Lycurgus, rushed into war out of rivalry of strength. For Lycurgus, when he had succeeded his brother Polybiates as king of the Spartans, and could have claimed the kingdom for himself, restored the kingdom with the highest good faith to Charillus, his son, who had been born after his father's death, when the boy had reached adulthood, so that everyone might understand how much the laws of piety count for among good men, more than all wealth. Meanwhile, while the infant grew up and he administered his guardianship, he instituted laws for the Spartans, who had none. He was more distinguished for his example than for the invention of the laws: he enacted nothing by any law upon others which he had not first given proof of in himself. He bound the people to obedience to their princes, and the princes to justice in their commands. He persuaded all to thrift, since the small labour of soldiering would be made easier by a constant habit of frugality. He ordered that single items be bought not with money but by exchange of goods, and he abolished the use of gold and silver, as the material of all crimes.

units.la: 3 Administrationem reipublicæ per ordines diuisit: Regibus potestatem bellorum; magistratibus indicia, & annuos successores; Senatui custodiam legum; populo sublegendi Senatum, vel creandi quos
units.tr: 3 He divided the administration of the commonwealth into orders: to the kings, the power over wars; to the magistrates, the judicial inquiries and annual successors; to the Senate, the custody of the laws; to the people, the choosing of the Senate, or of whichever magistrates

units.la: {d} Optimus legislator Lycurgus. veuet magistratus, potestatem, permisit. Fundos omnium æqualiter inter omnes diuisit, vt æquata patrimonia neminem potentiorem altero redderent.
units.tr: {d} Lycurgus, the best of lawgivers, granted them the power to create whichever magistrates they wished. He divided the lands of all equally among everyone, so that equal patrimonies would make no one more powerful than another.

units.la: 20 Conuiuari omnes publice iussit, ne cuius diuitiæ, vel luxuria in occulto essent. Iuuenibus non amplius vna veste vti toto anno permissum, nec quemquam cultius quam alterum progredi, nec epulari opulentius, ne imitatio in luxuriam verteretur. Pue-
units.tr: 20 He ordered that everyone should dine in public, so that no one's wealth or luxury might lie hidden. Young men were not permitted to wear one garment for the whole year, nor for anyone to go more elegantly dressed than another, nor to feast more lavishly, lest imitation turn into luxury. Boys

units.la: 25 ros puberes non in forum, sed in agrum deduci præcepit, vt primos annos non in luxuria, sed in opere, & in laboribus agerent. Nihil eos somni causa substernere, & vitam sine pulmento degere, neq; prius in vrbem redire, quam viri facti essent, statuit.
units.tr: 25 on reaching puberty he ordered to be led not into the forum but into the countryside, so that they would spend their early years not in luxury but in labour and toil. He decreed that they should not spread bedding for sleep, and should live without a relish, and should not return to the city before they had become men.

units.la: 30 Virgines sine dote nubere iussit, vt uxores eligerentur, non pecunia; feeuerisque matrimonia sua viri coercerent, cum nullis dotis frenis tenerentur. Maximum honorem non diuitum & potentium, sed pro gradu aetatis fenum esse voluit. Nec sane vsquam terrarum locum honoratiorem senectus habet. Hec quoniam primo solutis antea moribus, dura videbat esse, & auctorem eorum Apollinem Delphicum singi, & inde se ea ex praecepto numinis detulisse, vt consuescendi tadium metus religionis vincat. Dein vt aternitatem legibus suis daret, iureiurando obligat ciuitatem, nihil eos de eius legib. mutaturos, priusquam reuerteretur: & simulat se ad oraculum Delphicum proficisci, consulturum quid addendum, mutandumq, legibus videretur. Proficisci tamen Cretam, & ibi, perpetuum exilium egit, abiicq, in mare offa sua morieus iuslit, ne relatis Lacedaemonem, solutos se Spartani religione iurisiurandi in dissoluendis legibus arbitrarentur.
units.tr: 30 He ordered that virgins marry without dowry, so that wives would be chosen for their character, not for money, and that husbands would restrain their own marriages, since they were held by no dowry bridles. He wished the greatest honour to belong not to the rich and powerful, but to age, according to the degree of years; and indeed nowhere on earth does old age have a more honoured place. Since these laws seemed harsh to a people whose morals had previously been loose, he feigned that their author was Apollo of Delphi, and that he had brought them back from the command of the god, so that the fear of religion might overcome the weariness of habit. Then, to give his laws permanence, he bound the state by oath that they would change nothing of his laws before he returned. He pretended to set out for the oracle at Delphi, to consult about what seemed to be added or changed in the laws. He did set out, but for Crete, and there he lived in perpetual exile. Dying, he ordered his bones to be cast into the sea, lest, if they were carried back to Lacedaemon, the Spartans, freed from the religion of their oath, should think themselves free to dissolve the laws.

units.la: 4 Hi igitur moribus ita breui ciuitas conualuit, vt cum Messenii propter stupratas virgines suas, in solemni Messeniorum sacrificio bellum intulissent, grauissima se execrratione obstrinxerunt, non prius quam Messenii expugnassent, reuersuros tantum sibi vel de viribus suis, vel de fortuna spondentes. Quae res initium dissensionis Graeciae, & inter Sinti belli causa & origo. Iustus rigo fuit. Itaq; cum contra praesumptionem suam annis decem in obsidione urbis tenerentur, & querelis vxorū post tam longam viduitatem renocarentur: veriti, ne bac perfecuratia belli, grauius sibi quam Messenii nocerent: qnippe illis quantum iuuentutis bello intercidat, mulierum fecunditate suppleri, sibi & belli damna asidua, & fecunditatem vxorum, absentibus viris, nullam esse legitimam Spartani in qui post iusiurandum in supplementum venerant, quibus Spartam remissis promissos omnium feminarum concubitus permissos uxorum futuram conceptionem rati, si eam singulæ per plures viros experirentur. Ex hu nati, ob notam materni pudoris, Parthenia vocati, qui cum ad annos 30. peruenissent, metu inopia, nulli enim pater exisstebat, cuius in patrimonium successio speraretur, ducem Palantum assumunt, filium Araci, qui auctor Spartanis fuerat, iuuentutis ad generandam subolem domum remittendæ: vt sicuti dudum patrem eius nasci auctorem habuissent, sic ipsum spei ac dignitatis suæ haberent. Itaq; nec salutatis matribus, è quarum adulterio infamiam collegisse videbantur, ad sedes inquirendas proficiscuntur; diuq; & per varios casus iactati, tandem in Italiam defluuntur; & occupata arce Tarentinorum, expugnatis veteribus incolis, sedes ibi cōstituunt. Sed post annos plurimos dux eorum Palantus, per seditionem in exilium proturbatus, Brundusium se contulit, quo expulsi sedibus suis veteres Tarentini concesserant: Is moriens persuadet, vt offa sua, postremasq; reliquias conterant, & tacite sparge in foro Tarentinorum curent: hoc enim modo reuerti posse illos patriam suam posse Apollinem Delphis cecinisse. Illi arbitrantes eum in vltionem sui, ciuium fata prodidisse, præceptis paruere: sed oraculi diuersa sententia fuerat: perpetuitatem enim vrbis, non amissionem hoc facto promiserat. Ita ducis exulis consilio, & hostium ministerio, possessio Tarentina Parthenis in æternum fundata: ob cuius beneficij memoriam Palanto diuino honores decreuere.
units.tr: 4 By these morals the state grew strong in a short time, so that when the Messenians had waged war upon them, because of their raped virgins, during a solemn Messenian sacrifice, the Spartans bound themselves by the most grave execration not to return until they had conquered the Messenians, pledging only that they would return with their own strength or fortune intact. This was the beginning of the dissension of Greece, and the cause and origin of the war between them. The war was just. So when, contrary to their expectation, they were held for ten years in the siege of the city, and their wives' complaints recalled them after so long a widowhood, they feared that this prolonged war would harm them more than the Messenians. For the Messenians' loss of youth in war was made up by the fecundity of their women, but the losses of the Spartans in war were constant, and the fecundity of their wives, with their husbands absent, was no legitimate remedy. The Spartans who had come as reinforcements after the oath were sent back to Sparta, and were permitted the promised intercourse with all the women, thinking that the wives' future conceptions would be theirs if each of the women tried it with several men. Those born from this, marked by the stain of maternal shame, were called Parthenians. When they reached thirty years of age, fearing poverty, since no father existed whose inheritance could be hoped for, they took as their leader Palantus, son of Aracus, who had been the author for the Spartans of the plan of sending youths home to generate offspring, so that just as they had had his father as the author of their birth, so they might have him as the hope and dignity of their own. Thus, neither greeting their mothers, from whose adultery they seemed to have gathered infamy, they set out to seek settlements. Tossed about for a long time and through various misfortunes, they at last drifted into Italy, and, having occupied the citadel of the Tarentines and conquered the old inhabitants, they established their seats there. But after many years their leader Palantus, driven into exile by sedition, withdrew to Brundisium, whither the old Tarentines, expelled from their seats, had retired. Dying, he persuaded them to crush his bones and last remains to dust, and to take care to scatter them secretly in the forum of the Tarentines: in this way, he said, they could return to their homeland, as Apollo had foretold at Delphi. They, thinking that he had betrayed the fates of his citizens out of revenge for himself, obeyed his precepts; but the oracle's meaning had been different, for by this deed it had promised the perpetuity of the city, not its loss. Thus, by the counsel of the exiled leader and the service of their enemies, possession of Tarentum was founded for the Parthenians forever; and in memory of this benefit they decreed divine honours to Palantus.

units.la: 5 Interea Messenij cum virtute non possent, per infidias expugnantur. Dein cum per annos 80. grauia seruitutis verbera, plerunq; & vincula, ceteraq; capta ciuitatis mala perpessi essent, post longam pœnarum patientiam, bellum reflaurant. Lacedæmonij quoq; eo conspiratius ad arma concurrunt, quo aduessus seruos
units.tr: 5 Meanwhile the Messenians, being unable to prevail by valour, were overcome by treachery. Then, after suffering for eighty years the harsh lashes of slavery, often also chains and the other evils that come with a captured state, and after a long endurance of punishment, they renewed the war. The Lacedaemonians too rushed to arms all the more readily because they seemed about to fight with slaves.

units.la: dimicaturi videbantur. Itaq; cum binciniuria, inde indignitas animos acueret, Lacedemonij de belli euen-
units.tr: So, since the wrong was doubled and the indignity sharpened their spirits, the Lacedaemonians consulted the oracle at Delphi about the outcome of the war,

units.la: tu oraculo Delphis confulto, inuentur ducem belli ab Atheniensibus petere. Porro Athenienses cum repon-
units.tr: After the oracle at Delphi had been consulted, they were told to seek a leader for the war from the Athenians.

units.la: sum cogneuiffent, in contemptum Spartanorum Tyrteum poetam claudum pedemijere: qui tribus praliis
units.tr: When the Athenians learned this reply, they sent Tyrtaeus, a lame poet, to the Spartans as a mark of contempt.

units.la: fusus, eo vfq; desperationis Spartanos adduxit, vt ad supplementum exercitus, seruos suos manumitterent,
units.tr: He was defeated in three battles, but he brought the Spartans to such despair that, to make up the army's numbers, they freed their slaves

units.la: hoc, interfectorum matrimonia pollicerentur, vt non numero tantum amissurum ciuium, sed & dignitati succederent. Sed reges Lacedemoniorum, ne contra
units.tr: and promised the wives of the slain to them, so that they would not only replace the citizens they had lost in number but would also succeed to their rank. But the kings of the Lacedaemonians, lest Tyrtaeus should prove ineffective,

units.la: fortunam pugnando maiora detrimenta ciuitati infundarent, reducere exercitum voluerunt, ni interue-
units.tr: When the kings saw the army so inspired, they took care to announce the matter to the enemy.

units.la: niffet Tyrtæus, qui composita carmina exercitui pro concione recitauit, in quibus hortamenta virtutis, da-
units.tr: had him recite before the assembly the poems he had composed for the army, in which he had brought together exhortations to courage, consolations for losses, and counsels of war.

units.la: mnorum felatia, belli consilia conferipferat. Itaq; tantum ardorem militibus iniecit, vt non de salute, sed de sepultura foliciti, teferas, infeulptis suis & pa-
units.tr: So he kindled such ardour in the soldiers that, anxious not for their lives but for their burial, they tied tokens inscribed with their own and their fathers' names to their right arms,

units.la: trum nominibus, dextro brachio deligarent: vt fi omnes aduersum prelium confumpfijfet, & temporis spatio confusa corporum linteamenta effent, ex in-
units.tr: so that if they all fell in an adverse battle, and the features of the bodies were confused with the passing of time, they could still be given burial by the evidence of the inscriptions.

units.la: dicio titulorum tradi sepultura possent. Cum sic animatum reges exercitum viderent, curant rem hofli-
units.tr: When the kings saw the army so inspired, they took care to have word of this carried to the enemy.

units.la: bus nunciare. Meffeniis autem non timorem res, sed emulationem mutuam dedit. Itaque tantis animis concursum est, vt raro vnquam cruentius prelium
units.tr: But the matter gave the Messenians not fear but a rivalry of their own. So the two sides met with such spirit that the battle was rarely any bloodier.

units.la: fuerit: Ad postremum tamen victoria Lacedemoniorum fuit,
units.tr: In the end, however, the victory went to the Lacedaemonians.

units.la: 6 Interiectio tempore tertium quoq; bellum Messenij reparauerc: in cuius auxilium Lacedemonij, inter reliquos socios etiam Athenienses adhibuere sepiorum
units.tr: 6 After an interval, the Messenians renewed a third war as well. To aid against it the Lacedaemonians called in, among their other allies, the Athenians too. But when they came to suspect their loyalty, pretending they were superfluous, they dismissed them from the war.

units.la: fidem cum suspectam habuerunt, superuacaneos fimulantes, à bello eosdem dimiserunt. Hanc rem Athenien- sis. fes grauiter ferentes, pecuniam quae erat in stipendium Perfici belli ab vniuersa Graecia collata, à Deo Athenas transferunt, ne deficientibus à fide societatis Lacedaemoniis, praeda ac rapina esset. Sed nec Lacedaemonij
units.tr: 5 This the Athenians took badly, transferring the money that had been collected from all Greece for the Persian war from Delos to Athens, so that if the Lacedaemonians fell away from the alliance there would be no plunder and spoil. But the Lacedaemonians

units.la: 5 quieuere: qui cum Messeniorum bello occupati essent, Peloponnenses immisere, qui bellum Atheniensibus facerent. Parua tunc temporis, classe in AEgyptum missa, vires Atheniensibus erant: Itaque nauali prœlio dimicantes, facile superantur. Interiecto deinde
units.tr: did not keep quiet: though occupied with the Messenian war, they sent in Peloponnesians to wage war on the Athenians. At that time the Athenians had little strength, having sent a small fleet to Egypt; so, fighting a sea battle, they were easily overcome. Then, after an interval

units.la: 10 tempore, post reditum suorum aucti, & classis, & militum robore, prœlium reparauere. Iam & Lacedaemonij, omisso Messeniis, aduersus Athenienses arma verterant. Diu varia victoria fuit: ad postremum aequo Marte vtrinque discessum. Inde reuocati Lacedaemonij ad Messeniorum bellum, ne medium tempus otium Atheniensibus relinquerent, cum Thebanis pactifcuntur, vt Boeotiorum imperium his restituerent, quod temporibus Perfici belli amiserant, vt illi Athenienfium bella fuscciperent. Tantus furor Spartanorum erat, vt duobus bellis implicit, suscipere tertium non recusarent, dummodo inimicis suis hostes acquirerent. Igitur Athenienses, aduersus tantam tempestatem belli, duos duces deligunt, in Periclem spectatae virtutis virum, & Sophoclem scriptorem tragoediarum: qui dimisso exercitu, & Spartanorum agros vastauerunt, & multas Achaiae ciuitates Atheniensium imperio adiecerunt.
units.tr: 10 a time passed, and after their men returned the Athenians grew in strength both in fleet and in soldiers, and renewed the battle. Now the Lacedaemonians too, having dropped the Messenians, had turned their arms against the Athenians. The victory swung back and forth for a long time, and in the end they parted on equal terms. Then the Lacedaemonians were called back to the Messenian war, but lest they leave the Athenians a breathing space in the meantime, they made a treaty with the Thebans to restore to them the rule of Boeotia, which they had lost in the time of the Persian war, on condition that the Thebans take up the Athenians' wars. Such was the madness of the Spartans that, though entangled in two wars, they did not refuse a third, provided they could gain enemies for their enemies. Therefore the Athenians, facing so great a storm of war, chose two generals: Pericles, a man of proven courage, and Sophocles, the writer of tragedies. They dismissed the army, laid waste the fields of the Spartans, and added many states of Achaia to the rule of Athens.

units.la: 7 Hus malis fracti Lacedaemonij, in annos 30. pepigerunt pacem: sed tam longum otium inimicitiae non tulerunt. Itaq; quintodecimo anno rupto foedere cum contemptu deorum hominumq;, fines Atticos populantur: Et ne praedam potius, quam pugnam expetisse viderentur, hostes ad proelium provocant. Sed Athenienses, consilio Pericli ducis, populationis iniuriam differunt in tempus vltionis, (superuacuam pugnā existimantes, cum vlcisci bostem sine periculo possent. Deinde interiectis diebus naues conscendunt, & nihil sentientibus Lacedæmoniis, totam Spartam depradantur, multoq; plura auserunt, quam amiserant. Prorsus vt in comparatione damnorum, longe sluris suerit vltio, quam iniuria. Clara quidem hæc Periclis expeditio habita; sed multo clarior priuati pa.r.moni contemptus fuit. Huius agros, in populatione ceterorum eum, intactos hostes reliquerant, sperantes acquirere ei illi posse, aut periculum ex inuidia, aut ex suspitione proditionis infamiam: Quod anteprospiciens Pericles & futurum populo prædixerat;u & ad inuidiæ impetum declinandum, agros ipsos dono reipublicæ dederat. Atq; ita unde periculum quæsitum fuerat, ibi maximam gloriam inuenit. Post hæc interiectis diebus, nauali prælio dimicatum est: victi Lacedæmonij fugerunt. Nec cessatum deinceps est, quin aut terra, aut mari varia præliorum fortuna inuicem se trucidarent. Deniq; sesi tot malis, pacem in annos quinquaginta fecere, quam non nisi sex annis seruauerunt. Nam induitias quas proprio nomine condixerant, ex sociorum persona rumpebant: quippe quasi minus periurij contrahèrent: si ferentes socis auxilia, potius quam si aperto prælio dimicassent. Hinc bellum in Siciliam translatum: quod priusquam exponam, de Siciliæ situ pauca dicenda sunt.
units.tr: 7 Broken by these disasters, the Lacedaemonians made peace for thirty years. But such a long rest their hatred could not bear. So in the fifteenth year they broke the treaty in contempt of gods and men and ravaged Attica, and, lest they seem to have sought plunder rather than battle, they challenged the enemy to fight. But the Athenians, on the advice of their general Pericles, deferred the wrong of the raid to a time of vengeance, judging a battle unnecessary when they could punish the enemy without danger. Then, after a few days, they embarked on their ships, and while the Lacedaemonians suspected nothing they plundered all of Sparta and carried off far more than they had lost. Indeed, when the losses were compared, the vengeance was far more notable than the injury. This expedition of Pericles was held in high renown, but the contempt shown for his private property was much more famous. The enemy had left his fields untouched while they ravaged the rest, hoping either to win him over to their side, or to bring him into danger through envy, or into infamy through suspicion of treachery. Pericles, foreseeing this and having also predicted it to the people, had given those very fields as a gift to the state, to blunt the assault of envy. And so, where danger had been sought, there he found the greatest glory. After this, a few days later, a sea battle was fought, and the defeated Lacedaemonians fled. From then on there was no let-up, and by land or by sea, with changing fortune in battle, they kept slaughtering one another. At last, worn out by so many disasters, they made a peace for fifty years, which they kept for only six. For they broke the truces that they had agreed in their own name, through the persons of their allies, since they thought they would incur less perjury by bringing aid to allies than by fighting in open battle. Hence the war was transferred to Sicily; but before I set this out, a few things must be said about the position of Sicily.

units.la: IN LIB. III. IVSTINI SCHOLIA THEOPHILI Cangiseri.
units.tr: On Book III of Justin: Scholia of Theophilus Cangiserus.

units.la: Artabanus praefectus eius] Diodorus eum vocat regiorum stipatorum principem.
units.tr: Artabanus, his prefect] Diodorus calls him the chief of the royal bodyguard.

units.la: Nam amicitia iure semper illi patebat] Idem Diod. narrat lib. 11. Artabanum opera Mithridatis Eunuchi & cubicularii regii noctu clam intra cubiculum regis admissum esse.
units.tr: For friendship at all times gave him access to the king] Diodorus also relates, in book 11, that Artabanus was secretly brought by night into the king's bedchamber through the work of Mithridates, a eunuch and royal chamberlain.

units.la: Filios eius] Qui eo tempore tres adhuc erant superstites: Darius natu maior & Artaxerxes, in aula regia; & Hystaspes, qui tum erat apud Bactrianos. Diod. lib. 11. qui paulum variat ab iis, quae apud nostrum auctorem sequuntur.
units.tr: His sons] Three of them were still alive at that time: Darius, the elder, and Artaxerxes, at the royal court; and Hystaspes, who was then among the Bactrians. See Diodorus, book 11, who differs slightly from what our author follows.

units.la: Spartanis] qui antea κακοτροπωτάτοις ἁπάντων τῶν Ἑλλήνων, ex omnibus Graecis pessime morati erant. Herod. lib. 1.
units.tr: To the Spartans] who were formerly the worst-behaved [κακοτροπωτάτοις ἁπάντων τῶν Ἑλλήνων] of all the Greeks. Herodotus, book 1.

units.la: Leges instituit] Quod factum esse annis centum ante primam Olympiadem scribit Eusebius lib. 10. de praeparat. Euangel. cap. 3 Hisce legibus se opponens Alcandero Lycurgo auctori alterum oculum excussit, eumque fecit μονόφθαλμον, Pausan Lacon. Lycurgum vocat Heroodotus δἰκαιότατον ἀνδρῶν τῶν Σπαρτιατῶν virum inter Spartanos probatum.
units.tr: He established laws] Eusebius, in book 10 of the Preparation for the Gospel, chapter 3, writes that this happened a hundred years before the first Olympiad. In opposing these laws, Alcander knocked out one of Lycurgus' eyes, making him one-eyed [μονόφθαλμον]. Pausanias, in the Laconica. Herodotus calls Lycurgus the most just [δἰκαιότατον ἀνδρῶν τῶν Σπαρτιατῶν] of the Spartan men, a man approved among the Spartans.

units.la: Auctorem eorum Apollinem Delphicum fingit] Val. Max. lib. 1 cap. 34. sed iuxta Plutarchum in Lyc & Strabonem lib. 10. haec non ficta, sed acta sunt. Et Herod. lib. 1. recitat versus Pythiae ad Lycurgum scisscitandi oraculi ergo adventantem.
units.tr: He pretends that Apollo of Delphi was their author] Valerius Maximus, book 1, chapter 34. But according to Plutarch in the Life of Lycurgus and Strabo, book 10, these things were not invented but actually done. Herodotus, book 1, also quotes the verses of the Pythia to Lycurgus, who came to consult the oracle.

units.la: Ἥκεις ὦ Λυκοῦργε ἐμὸν θεοῖς δίαν ἐπὶ πλούτῳ δ' ἁμαρτάνουσιν ἔχυρῳ, &c.
units.tr: You have come, Lycurgus, to my temple, dear to the gods; but they err who put their trust in wealth [Ἥκεις ὦ Λυκοῦργε ἐμὸν θεοῖς δίαν ἐπὶ πλούτῳ δ' ἁμαρτάνουσιν ἔχυρῳ], etc.

units.la: Etsi idem adferat cum Paulania in Laconicis, quod non nulli harum legum non Lycurgum, sed Minoem auctorem atque a Cretensibus eas ad Spartanos per Lycurgum translatas existimant.
units.tr: Although the same author, with Pausanias in the Laconica, reports that some think these laws were not from Lycurgus but from Minos, and were carried over to the Spartans from the Cretans through Lycurgus.

units.la: Ibique perpetuum exilium egit, abiicique] Differunt de loco mortis ac sepulturae apud Plutarchum Apollothemis, Timaeus, Aristoxenus.
units.tr: And there he spent a perpetual exile, and was cast out] Apollothemis, Timaeus and Aristoxenus differ about the place of his death and burial, as reported by Plutarch.
D b Bel.

units.la: B. Illum intulissent] Nonæ Olympiadis anno altero, secundum Pisan. Mæssen. De hoc bello vide præter citatos à Bong. Lactantium. lib. 1. cap. 20. qui nonnihil variat.
units.tr: B. They had brought that war upon him] In the second year of the ninth Olympiad, according to Pisanus and Messenius. Concerning this war, see besides those cited by Bongarsius, Lactantius, book 1, chapter 20, who differs somewhat.

units.la: Ducem Palantum] Strabo lib. 6. auctor est, eos cum seruis Helotibus in Spartanorum ciuium necem hoc modo, vt simularent; in foro pilei lacænici tolerentur, impressio fieret in ciues cœgregatos, & vrbs occuparetur. Quo decreto consilio Parthenię (ita enim legendum esse recte Bongarsius monuit, & apud Strabonem dicuntur παρθενίαι) vitam fuga redemerunt.
units.tr: Leader Palantus] Strabo, book 6, reports that they, with the Helot slaves, planned to murder the Spartan citizens in this way: they would pretend to be tolerated in the forum wearing Laconian caps, make an attack on the citizens gathered together, and seize the city. When this plan was decided, the Parthenians (for so Bongarsius rightly observed that the text should read, since in Strabo they are called Parthenians [παρθενίαι]) saved their lives by flight.

units.la: Tyrtæum] Qui elegiaco carmine id bellum descripsit, vt liquet è Pausania, qui aliquot eius versus narrationi suæ interseruit.
units.tr: Tyrtaeus] Who described that war in elegiac verse, as is clear from Pausanias, who inserted several of his verses into his narrative.

units.la: Peloponnenses] Hæc igitur ἀφορμὴ prima exstitit belli Peloponnesiaci, quod Thucydides 8. libris persequitur, vetustate proximus ab Herodoto, lectuque multis nominibus vtilissimus.
units.tr: Peloponnesians] This, then, was the first pretext [ἀφορμὴ] of the Peloponnesian War, which Thucydides pursues in eight books; he is the nearest in age to Herodotus, and is most useful to read in many respects.

units.la: Periclem] Anaxagoræ philosophi discipulum, qui dicendo fulgurare, tonare, permiscere Græciam ait in oratore Cic ex Aristophane. Alia ipsius encomia vide apud Thucyd. lib. 2. & Plutarchum Periclē.
units.tr: Pericles] A disciple of the philosopher Anaxagoras, who, as Cicero says in the Orator, following Aristophanes, said that he thundered and lightened and threw Greece into confusion when he spoke. For his other encomia see Thucydides, book 2, and Plutarch's Life of Pericles.

units.la: Et ad invidiam impetum declinandum] Simile exemplum Livius de Hannibale & Fabio Max. dictatore commemorat lib. 2 decad. 3.
units.tr: And to deflect the odium and attack] Livy records a similar example concerning Hannibal and Fabius Maximus, the dictator, in book 2 of the third decade.

units.la: POMPEII TROGI EPI- TOMA HISTORIARVM. LIBER IV.
units.tr: The Epitome of the Histories of Pompeius Trogus. Book IV.
SUMMARY.

units.la: 1 Siciliæ insulæ situs, fontes, ignes Ætnæ montis, Scyllæ, Charybdis mirabile, rerum naturam; item & Charybdis mirabilium. 2 Nomina, incolæ veteres, imperium Siciliæ ambiunt, & pro-
units.tr: 1 The situation of the island of Sicily, its springs, the fires of Mount Etna, the marvel of Scylla and Charybdis, and the nature of things; likewise the wonders of Charybdis. 2 Its names and ancient inhabitants; they seek the rule of Sicily, and the tyrants of Sicily,

units.la: tyrannis Siciliæ, cui Carthaginenses inhiant. 3 Rheginenses ab Himeræ ranis oppressi. Athenienses & profequeagunt initio. 4 In incepto pergentes, po Lacedæmoniorum duSyracusam Lacedæmonios ce terra marique fraugunaccersunt. fit Græcorú con- tur, ductibus Demosthene 5 cursu, & bellum in Siciliam & Nicia indecoro fato subtransferrunt. lartis.
units.tr: for which the Carthaginians lust. 3 The Rhegians, oppressed by the men of Himera. The Athenians also pursue the war at the start. 4 Proceeding with their undertaking, they attack Syracuse by land and sea, and the Lacedaemonians summon the Greeks. The war is carried over into Sicily under the leadership of Demosthenes and Nicias, by an ignominious fate.

units.la: ICILIAM ferunt angustis quondam fauctibus Italiæ adhæsisse; direptam, velut à corpore, maiore impetu superi maris, quod toto undarũ onere illuc vehitur. Est autem ipsa terra tenuis ac fragilis; & cauernis quibusdam fistulisq; ita penetrabilis, vt ventorum tota ferme flatibus pateat; necnon & ignibus generandis nutriendisq;, soli ipsius naturalis materia: quippe intrinsecus stratum sulphure & bitumine traditur quæ res facit, vt spiritu cum igne inter interiora luctante, frequenter & compluribus locis nunc flammas, nunc vaporem, nunc fumum eructet. Inde deniq; AEtnæ montis per tot secula durat incendium. Et vbi acrior per spiramenta cauernarum ventus incubuit, harenarum moles egerûtur. Proximum Itaæ promontorium, b Rhegium dicitur, ideo quia Græce abrupta hoc nomine pronuntiantur. Nec mirum si fabulosa est loci huius antiquitas, in quem res tot coiere mira. Primum quod nusquam alias tam torrens flictū, nec solum citato impetu, verumetiam sæuo; neq; experientibus modo terribile, verumetiam procul videntibus: Vndarum porro in se concurrentium tantapugna est, vt alias veluti tergit dantes in imum desidere, alias quasi victrices in sublime ferri videas: nunc hic frenitū ferueniis æstus, nunc illic gemitum in voraginem desidentis exaudias. Accedunt vicini, & perpetui AEt- nae montis ignes, & insularu AEolidum, veluti ipsis vndu alatur incedium. Neq; enim in tã angustis terminis
units.tr: Sicily, they say, was once joined to Italy by a narrow strait, and was torn away, as if from the body, by the greater force of the upper sea, which is carried there with its whole weight of waves. The land itself is thin and fragile, and so penetrated by caverns and pipes that almost all of it lies open to the blasts of the winds. It is also a natural source of material for generating and feeding fires. For it is said to be layered beneath with sulphur and bitumen, which causes the wind, struggling with fire among the inner parts, often to belch out now flames, now steam, now smoke, at many places. Hence the fire of Mount Etna has burned for so many ages. Where a fiercer wind presses through the vents of the caverns, masses of sand are thrown out. The nearest headland of Italy is called Rhegium, because the Greeks call broken-off places by this name. Nor is it surprising that the antiquity of this place is full of fable, since so many wonders have gathered there. First, nowhere else does the sea beat so violently, not only with rapid onset but with savage force, terrifying not only those who experience it but also those who watch from afar. Moreover, the battle of the colliding waves is so fierce that you may see some sink to the bottom as if giving way, and others carried aloft as if victorious. Here you hear the roaring of the boiling tide, there the groaning of the waters sinking into the abyss. Add the neighbouring and unceasing fires of Mount Etna and of the Aeolian islands, as if the fire were fed by the very waves. For in so narrow a space so great a fire could not have lasted through so many ages unless it were nourished by the sustenance of moisture.

units.la: {b} aliter durare tot seculis tantus ignis potuisset, nisi humoris nutrimentis aleretur. Hinc igitur fabulae Scyllam & Charybdim peperere; hinc latratus auditus; hinc monstri credita simulacra, dum nauigantes magnis vorticibus pelagi desidentis exterriti, latrare putant vndas, quasi sorbentis æstus vorago conlidit. Ea dem causa etiam Ætnæ montis perpetuos ignes facit. Nam aquarum ille concursus, raptum secum spiritum in imum fundum trahit, atq; ibi suffocatum tamdiu tenet, donec per spiramenta [terra diffusus, nutrimento] ignis incendat. Iam ipsa Italia, Siciliaq; vicinitas, quantum nunc admirationis, tantum antiquis terroris dederit; credentibus, cōcuntibus in se promontoriis, ac rursum discedentibus, solida intercapi abfumiq; nasigia. Neq; hoc ab antiquis in dulcedinem fabulae compositum, sed metu & admiratione transeuntium. Ea est enim procul inspicientibus natura loci, vt finum maris, non transitum putes; quo cum acceferis, discedere, ac seiungi promontoria, quae antea iuncta fuerat, arbitrere.
units.tr: Hence the fables of Scylla and Charybdis were born; hence the barking that was heard; hence the believed images of the monster, since sailors, terrified by the great whirlpools of the sinking sea, think the waves are barking, as the chasm of the swallowing tide crashes together. For the same reason it also keeps the perpetual fires of Etna burning. That concourse of waters drags the air it has seized down to the bottom, and holds it there suffocated for so long, until it kindles the fire [spreading through the earth by the vents, with nourishment]. Now Italy itself and the nearness of Sicily, as much as they now excite wonder, once gave terror to the ancients, who believed that the headlands, coming together and then drawing apart again, cut off solid land and swallowed up the straits. Nor was this invented by the ancients for the pleasure of a tale, but arose from the fear and amazement of travellers. For the nature of the place is such that, to those looking from afar, you would think it a gulf of the sea and not a passage; but when you approach, you judge that the headlands, once joined, are separating and parting.

units.la: 2 Siciliae primo Trinacria nomen fuit; postea Sicania cognominata est. Hac a principio patria Cyclopum fuit: quibus extinctis, Cocalus regnum infulae occupavit: post quem singulae ciuitates in tyrannorum imperium concesserunt, quorum nulla terra feracior fuit. Horum ex numero Anaxilaus iustitia cum ceterorum crudelitate certabat, cuius moderationis haud mediocrem fructum tulit: Quippe decedens cum filios paruulos reliquisset, tutelamq; eorum Micalo, spectata fidei feruo, commissit; tantus amor memoriae eius apud omnes fuit; vt parere feruo, quam deferre regis filios mallet, principesq; ciuitatis obliti dignitatis suae, sua, regni maiestatem administrari per seruum paterentur.Imperium Siciliæ etiam Carthaginenses tentauere,diuq; varia victoria cum tyrannis dimicatum. Ad postremum amisso Hamilcare imperatore cum exercitu,aliquantisper quieuere, victi.
units.tr: Sicily was at first called Trinacria; afterwards it was named Sicania. From the beginning it was the homeland of the Cyclopes. When they were destroyed, Cocalus seized the kingdom of the island. After him the individual cities submitted to the rule of tyrants, and no land was more fertile than theirs. Among these, Anaxilaus competed in justice with the cruelty of the others, and he reaped no small fruit of his moderation. When he died, leaving small sons, he committed their guardianship to Micalus, a slave of proven loyalty. So great was the love for his memory among all that they preferred to obey a slave rather than hand over the king's sons, and the leading men of the city, forgetting their own dignity, allowed the majesty of the kingdom to be administered by a slave. The Carthaginians also attempted to seize the rule of Sicily, and for a long time they fought with the tyrants with varying success. At last, with their commander Hamilcar and his army lost, they were defeated and rested for a while.

units.la: 3 Medio tempore cum Rhegini discordia laborarēt, ciuitasq; per dissensionem diuisa in duas partes esset, veterani ex altera parte ab Himera in auxilium vocati, pulsis ciuitate, contra quos implorati fuerant; & mox cæsis,quibus tulerant auxilium, vrbem cum coniugibus & liberis sociorum occupauere; ausi facinus nulli tyranno comparandum: quippe vt Rheginis melius fuerit vinci,quam vicisse. Nam siue victoribus captiuitatis iure seruissent,siue amissa patria exulare necesse habuissent,non tamen, inter aras & patrios lares trucidati,crudelissimis tyrannis patriam cum coniugibus ac liberis prædam reliquissent. Catinienses quoq; cum Syracusanos graues paterentur, diffisi viribus suis, auxilium ab Atheniensibus petiuere: qui seu studio magnitudinis imperij, quod Asiam Græciamq; penitus occupauerant; seu metu factæ pridem à Syracusanis classis, ne Lacedæmoniis illæ vires accederet, Lamponium ducem cum classe in Siciliam misere, vt sub specie ferendi Catinienfibus auxilij,tentaret Siciliæ imperium. Et quoniam prima initia, frequenter cæsis hostibus, prospera fuerant; maiore denuo classe, & robustiore exercitu, Lachete & Cariade ducibus,Siciliam petiuere:sed Catinienses siue metu Atheniensium,siue tædio belli, pacem cum Syracusanis, remissis Atheniensium auxilis, fecerant.
units.tr: 3 Meanwhile the Rhegians were troubled by internal discord, and their city, divided by faction into two parts, was torn apart. The veterans from Himera, called in as auxiliaries from one side, drove out the citizens against whom they had been summoned for help. Soon, after slaughtering those whom they had come to aid, they seized the city together with the wives and children of their allies. They dared a deed comparable to no tyrant's: it would have been better for the Rhegians to be conquered than to have conquered. For whether they had been enslaved by the victors under the law of capture, or had been forced to go into exile after losing their homeland, they would not at least have left their country, their wives and their children as plunder to the cruellest tyrants, after being slaughtered between their altars and their ancestral hearths. The Catinians too, since they were heavily oppressed by the Syracusans and distrusted their own strength, sought help from the Athenians. The Athenians, either from eagerness for the greatness of their empire, since they had long since occupied Asia and Greece thoroughly, or from fear of the fleet the Syracusans had built some time before, lest those forces should join the Lacedaemonians, sent Lamachus? no, rather Lamponius, as commander with a fleet to Sicily. Under the pretext of bringing help to the Catinians, he was to try to seize the rule of Sicily. And since the first beginnings had been successful, with the enemy often cut down, they then sought Sicily again with a larger fleet and a stronger army, under the commanders Laches and Charieades. But the Catinians, either from fear of the Athenians or from weariness of war, had made peace with the Syracusans, the Athenian help being dismissed.

units.la: 4 Interiecto deinde tempore , cum fides pacis à Syracusanis non seruaretur, denuo legatos Athenas miserunt, qui sordida veste,capillo barbaq; promissis, & omni squaloris habitu ad misericordiam commouēndam acquisito, concionem deformes adeunt; adduntur precibus lacrymæ: & ita, misericordem populum supplices mouent, vt damnarentur duces, qui ab his auxilia deduxerant. Igitur classis ingens d?crnitur, creantur duces {5}Nicias, & Alcibiades, & Lamachos; tantiq; viribus Sicilia repetitur, vt ipsis terrori essent, in quorum auxilia mittebantur. Brevi post tempore, reuocato ad reatum Alcibiade, duo prælia pedestria secunda Nicias & Lamachos fecerunt: multitudinibus deinde circundatis, hostes etiam maximis commeatibus in vrbe clausos {10} intercludunt. Quibus rebus fracti Syracusani, auxilioum à Lacedæmoniis petierunt. Ab his mittitur Gylippus, solus, sed [in] quo instar omnium auxiliorum erat. Is audito genere belli, iam inclinato statu, auxilio {15} partim in Gracia, partim in Sicilia contractis, opportuna bello loca occupat. Duobus deinde prœlis victus, congressus tertio, occiso Lamacho & hostes in fugam compulit, & socios obsidione liberauit. Sed cum Athe-
units.tr: 4 Some time later, when the Syracusans did not keep the faith of the peace, they again sent envoys to Athens. With squalid clothing, hair and beards neglected, and every sign of mourning assumed to move pity, they approached the assembly in a wretched state. Tears were added to their prayers, and so the suppliants moved the merciful people to such a degree that the commanders who had led help away from them were condemned. Therefore a huge fleet was decreed, and Nicias, Alcibiades and Lamachus were appointed commanders; and Sicily was attacked with such forces that they were a terror to those in whose aid they were being sent. Shortly afterwards, Alcibiades was recalled to answer the charge, and Nicias and Lamachus fought two successful land battles. Then, surrounding the crowds, they cut off the enemy, who were shut up in the city, from even the largest supplies. Broken by these events, the Syracusans sought aid from the Lacedaemonians. From them Gylippus was sent, alone, but he was in himself equal to all the reinforcements. Having heard the nature of the war, now that the state of affairs was turning against them, he gathered help partly in Greece and partly in Sicily, and occupied places suitable for the war. Then, after two battles, having been defeated, he engaged a third time, killed Lamachus, drove the enemy into flight, and freed his allies from the siege.

units.la: nienses à bello terrestri in nauale se transtulissent, Gy- 20 lippus classem Lacedæmone cum auxiliis arcesit: quo cognito, & ipsi Athenienses in locum amissi ducis Demosthenem & Eurymedonta cum supplemento copiarum mittunt: Peloponnesii quoq; communi ciuitatium decreto, ingentia Syracusanis auxilia misere; & quasi 25 Græcia bellum in Siciliam translatum esset, ita ex utraq; parte summis viribus dimicabatur.
units.tr: But when the Athenians had turned from a land war to a naval one, Gylippus summoned a fleet with reinforcements from Lacedaemon. When this was learned, the Athenians themselves sent Demosthenes and Eurymedon, with a supplement of troops, to replace the lost commander. The Peloponnesians too, by common decree of their cities, sent great reinforcements to the Syracusans. And as if the war of Greece had been transferred to Sicily, they fought with the utmost strength on both sides.

units.la: § Prima igitur congressione nauali certaminis, Athenienses vincuntur. Castra quoq; cum omni publica ac priuata pecunia amittunt. Super hæc mala, cum 30 etiam terrestri prœlio victi essent, nunc Demosthenes censere cœpit, vt abirent Sicilia, dum res, quamuis afflicta, nondum tamen perdita forent; neq; in bello male auspiauspicato amplius perseuerandum esse; domi graniora, & forsitan infeliciora bella, in quae feruare hos vrbis apparatus oporteat. Nicias seu pudore male actae rei, seu metu deflituta spei ciuium, seu impellente fato manere contendit. Reparatur igitur nauale bellum, & animata prioris fortuna procella, ad spem certaminis renouantur: sed inscitia ducum, qui inter angustias maris tuentes se, Syracusanos aggressi fuerant facile vincuntur. Eurymedon dux in prima acie fortissime dimicans, primus cadit: triginta naues quibus praesuerat, incenduntur. Demosthenes & Nicias, & ipsi victi, exercitum in terram deponunt: tutiorem fugam rati itinere terrestri. Ab his reliquas centum triginta naues Gylippus inuasit; ipsos deinde insequitur, fugientes partim capit, partim cadit. Demosthenes amissio exercitu, a captiuitate, gladio, & voluntaria morte se vindicat: Nicias autem ne Demosthenis quidem exemplo, vt sibi consuleret admonitus, cladem suorum auxit & dedecore captiuitatis.
units.tr: § In the first encounter of the sea battle, therefore, the Athenians were defeated. They also lost their camp with all their public and private money. Over and above these disasters, when they had also been beaten in a land battle, Demosthenes now began to advise that they should leave Sicily, while their affairs, though shaken, were not yet lost; and that they should no longer persevere in a war begun under bad omens. At home there were heavier and perhaps more unlucky wars, for which they ought to keep the resources of the city. Nicias, whether from shame at the bad outcome, or from fear because the hope of his citizens was failing, or because fate impelled him, insisted on staying. So the naval war was resumed, and the fortune of the earlier storm being revived, they renewed their hopes of battle. But through the incompetence of the commanders, who fought in the narrows of the sea and attacked the Syracusans, they were easily defeated. Eurymedon, fighting most bravely in the front line, was the first to fall, and the thirty ships he commanded were burned. Demosthenes and Nicias, themselves defeated, landed their army on the shore, thinking a land march the safer flight. Gylippus attacked the remaining hundred and thirty ships, then pursued the fugitives, capturing some and cutting down others. Demosthenes, having lost his army, saved himself from captivity by the sword and by voluntary death. But Nicias, although reminded by Demosthenes' example to look to his own safety, increased the ruin of his men and the disgrace of their capture.
ON BOOK IV OF JUSTIN.
THE NOTES OF THEOPHILUS CANGISERUS.

units.la: 2 Siciliam ferunt] Eius descriptio prolixior hisque temporibus conuenientior petenda est è Geographia Marii Aretii eo in volumine, quod eruditos aliquot retum sicularum scriptores continet, atque ante non multos annos Francofurdi Vuechelianis typis excusum est.
units.tr: 2 They say Sicily] Its description should be sought in more detail, and better suited to these times, in the Geography of Marius Aretius, in that volume which contains several learned writers on Sicilian affairs and which was printed at Frankfurt by the Wechel press not many years ago.

units.la: b Rhegium] Suid. Vnde Sicilia Straboni est abrupta & auulsa pars continentis.
units.tr: b Rhegium] Suidas. Hence Sicily is, for Strabo, a part broken off and torn away from the mainland.

units.la: c Sicania cognominata est] Thucydidi, vt habet Plinius lib. 3. cap. 8.
units.tr: c It was called Sicania] Thucydides, as Pliny has it, book 3, chapter 8.

units.la: Cyclopum Ita nuncupatorum, quod vnum tantum κύκλος hoc est circularem oculum habérent in fronte. Horum neque genus, neque vnde venerint, neque quo abierint, nolle se Thucydides profiteri initio lib. 6.
units.tr: Of the Cyclopes So called because they had only one circular [kyklos] eye in the forehead. Thucydides, at the beginning of book 6, professes that he is unwilling to say anything about their race, where they came from, or where they went.

units.la: Nicias & Alcibiades Quorum hic magnopere & suasit expeditionem, ille dissuasit. Utriusque orationes vide ap. Thucid. lib. 6. obtinuit autem Alcibiadis sententia κατακρίνοντος ἤδη ωλησ... qui in multitudinis animos verbis Ipei plenis ante corruperat, quam ea de re in concione ageretur. Plut. Nicia.
units.tr: Nicias and Alcibiades Of whom the former strongly urged the expedition and the latter dissuaded it. See the speeches of both in Thucydides, book 6. But the opinion of Alcibiades prevailed [κατακρίνοντος ἤδη ωλησ...], since he had already won over the minds of the crowd with his own rousing words before the matter was debated in the assembly. Plutarch, Life of Nicias.

units.la: Pudore male actaret Metuensiudicia & calumnias Atheniensium, dicit ap. Plutarch. μᾶλλον αἰςχύνην τὸν ὑπὸ τῶν πολιτῶν θάνατον, ἢ τὸν ὑπὸ τῶν πολιτῶν, malle se ab hostibus, quam civibus suis interfici.
units.tr: Fearing shame Fearing the judgments and slanders of the Athenians, he says in Plutarch that he would rather be put to death by enemies than by his fellow citizens [μᾶλλον αἰσχύνην τὸν ὑπὸ τῶν πολιτῶν θάνατον, ἢ τὸν ὑπὸ τῶν πολιτῶν].

units.la: Dedecore captisuitaris Supplex Gylippo factus inq; catceiem coniectus: vbi vna cum Demosthene cuiusdam custodis opera violentas sibi manus intulit, vt refert è Timaeo Plutarchus.
units.tr: The disgrace of captivity Having become a suppliant to Gylippus, he was thrown into prison. There, together with Demosthenes, with the help of a certain jailer, he laid violent hands on himself, as Plutarch reports from Timaeus.
{g} The disgrace of captivity.
TRANSLATION OF POMPEIUS TROGUS'S PHILIPPIC HISTORIES, EPITOMIZED.
BOOK V. SUMMARY.

units.la: 1 Alcibiades siculi belli concitor in exilium conie- cit Alcibiades, deinde classe Lacedæmonios ad bel- lum Atheniensibus inferendum impellit. Huic bello rex Persarum accedit socius Lacedæmoniis.
units.tr: 1 Alcibiades, the instigator of the Sicilian war, is driven into exile; then he urges the Lacedaemonians with a fleet to make war on the Athenians. The king of the Persians joins the Lacedaemonians as an ally in this war.

units.la: 2 Res gestę Alcibiadis in patriam. Lacedæmoniis su- spectus, negotium illis fa- cessit Tissaferuis opera.
units.tr: 2 The exploits of Alcibiades on returning to his country. Suspected by the Lacedaemonians, he is brought into trouble through the agency of Tissaphernes.

units.la: 3 Statum reipublicę mutauit, deinde classe instructa in bellum pergit aduersus Lacedæmonios.
units.tr: 3 He changes the constitution of the commonwealth, then, with a fleet equipped, proceeds to war against the Lacedaemonians.

units.la: 4 Nauales pugna, & præclara de Lacedæmoniis victoria, reportata ab Alcibiade. Is desideratus ciuibus suis Athenas reuersus, sumina cum omnium lætitia excipitur.
units.tr: 4 Naval battles and a splendid victory over the Lacedaemonians, won by Alcibiades. Longed for by his fellow citizens, he returns to Athens and is received with the joy of all.

units.la: 5 Lacedæmonii Persarum freti auxilio,exercitum A'henienfium in Asia spar.sum opprimunt. Alcibiades 5 ob rem male gestam, veritus populi impetum,denuo in voluntarium exilium proficiscitur.
units.tr: 5 The Lacedaemonians, relying on the help of the Persians, crush the Athenian army that was scattered in Asia. Alcibiades, because of the badly conducted affair and fearing the rage of the people, again sets out into voluntary exile.

units.la: 6 Conon, Alcibiadis 10 successor,inualidos & nouos milites nactus, infeliciter rem gerit, & nauali prælio superatus concedit ad Euagoram.
units.tr: 6 Conon, successor of Alcibiades, having obtained weak and new soldiers, conducts the war unsuccessfully; defeated in a naval battle, he withdraws to Evagoras.

units.tr: 7 The pusillanimity of the Athenians, broken by so many disasters,
