Eo in pugna ca mutat Lysander : inde interfecto, decē millia Grætriginta tyranni, & cædes corum,inuictis barbaris viAlcibiadis, ctoribus patriâ repetunt.
units.tr: 8 The Lacedaemonians, victorious, take possession of Athens after its surrender, and Lysander changes the constitution. Then the Thirty tyrants, and the slaughter they carried out, ... in that battle, Cyrus having been killed, the ten thousand Greeks, though unconquered by the barbarians, seek their homeland again.

units.la: 9 Tyrannorū vnus Thc- ramenes, vir moderatus, à collegis interficitur. Thra- sybulus rempub. collapsam restituit,& præelio commis- so 30. tyrannorum sæuissi- mos Critiam & Hippolo- chum mactat.
units.tr: 9 One of the tyrants, Theramenes, a moderate man, is killed by his colleagues. Thrasybulus restores the fallen commonwealth and, in a battle joined, slays Critias and Hippolochus, the most savage of the Thirty tyrants.

units.la: 10 Populares fugientes placide reuocat Thrafybu- lus: superstites tyrannos vr- be pellit, qui dum bellum reparare student, compre- hensi trucidantur,discordi- arum oblitione inter ciues sancita.
units.tr: 10 Thrasybulus calmly recalls the fugitive citizens. He drives the surviving tyrants from the city; while they try to renew the war, they are seized and slaughtered. An amnesty for discords is sanctioned among the citizens.

units.la: 11 Bellu inter fratres Ar- taxerxem Cyrum Darii fi- lios ... {a}VM Athenienses in Sicilia bellum per biennium cupidius, quam felicius gerunt,interim concitor & dux eius Alcibiades absens Athenis insimulatur, mysteria Cereris initiorum sacra,nullo magis quam silentio solemnia, {b}enuntiauisse. Reuocatus a bello ad iudicium, siue conscientiam, siue indignitatem rei non ferens, tacitus in exilium Elidem profectus est. Inde vbi non damnatum se tantum, verumetiam diris per omnium sacerdotum religiones deuotum cognouit, Lacedæmona se contulit:ibi regem Lacedæmoniorum impellit,turbatis Atheniensibus aduerso Siciliæ prælio vltro bellum inferre. Quo facto, omnia
units.tr: 11 War between the brothers Artaxerxes and Cyrus, sons of Darius ... The Athenians wage war in Sicily for two years, more eagerly than successfully. Meanwhile their leader Alcibiades, absent, is accused at Athens of having divulged the sacred mysteries of the initiation rites of Ceres, which are celebrated above all in silence. Recalled from the war for trial, unable to bear either his conscience or the indignity of the charge, he silently departed into exile at Elis. From there, when he learned that he had been not only condemned but also cursed by the religious rites of all the priests, he betook himself to Lacedaemon. There he urged the king of the Lacedaemonians to make war on the Athenians of his own accord, while they were thrown into confusion by the adverse battle in Sicily. Having done this, all

units.la: {a} Omnē moucret lapidem, vt suos ciues affligat. omnia Græcia regna, velut ad extinguendum commune incendium, concurrunt. Tantum odium Athenienses immoderati imperij crudelitate contraxerant. Darius quoq; rex Persarum, memor paterni auitiq; in hanc vrbem odij, facta cum Lacedæmoniis per Tissafernem præfectum Lydiæ societate omnem sumptum belli pollicetur. Et erat hic quidem titulus cum Græcis coëundi: re autem vera timebat, ne victis Athenien sibus ad se Lacedamonij arma transferrent. Quis igitur miretur, tam florentes Athenien sium opes ruisse, cum ad 10 opprimendam vnam vrbem totius Orientis vires concurrerent? Non tamen inerti, neq; incruento cecidere bello, sed praeliati ad vltimum, victores etiam interdum, consumpti magis fortuna varietate, quam victi sunt. Principio belli omnes ab his etiam socij defciue- 15 rant, vt fit. Quo se fortuna, eodem etiam fauor hominum inclinat.
units.tr: He stirs every stone to afflict his own citizens; all the kingdoms of Greece run together, as if to extinguish a common conflagration. So great was the hatred the Athenians had incurred by the cruelty of their immoderate rule. Darius also, king of the Persians, mindful of the hatred of his father and grandfather against this city, promises every expense of the war, through an alliance made with the Lacedaemonians by Tissaphernes, governor of Lydia. The pretext indeed was to unite the Greeks; but in truth he feared that, with the Athenians defeated, the Lacedaemonians would turn their arms against him. Who then would wonder that the so flourishing resources of the Athenians collapsed, when the forces of the whole East came together to overwhelm one city? Yet they did not fall in an idle or bloodless war; they fought to the end, even sometimes as victors, and were worn down more by the changing of fortune than defeated. At the beginning of the war all their allies, as is usual, had deserted them. Where fortune leans, there also the favour of men inclines.

units.la: 2 Alcibiades quoq; motum aduersus patriam bellum, non gregarij militis opera, sed imperatorijs virtutibus adiuuat. Quippe acceptis quinq; nauibus in Afi- 20 am contendit; & tributarias Atheniensium ciuitates auctoritate nominis sui, ad defectionem compellit. Sciebant enim domi clarum, nec exilio videbant factum minorem; nec tam ablatum Atheniensibus duce, quam Lacedaemonijs traditum; parataq; cum amicis imperia 25 pensare. Sed apud Lacedaemonios virtus Alcibiadis plus inuidiae quam gratiae contraxit. Itaq; cum principes velut emulum gloriae suae interficiendum insidiis mandaffent, cognitare Alcibiades per vxorem Agidis regis, quam adulterio cognouerat, ad Tiffafernem praefectum 30 Darij regis profugit; cui se celeriter officij comitate, & obsequendi gratia insinuauit: erat enim & aetatis flore, & c forme veneratione, nec minus eloquentia etiam inter Athenienses insignis; sed in conciliandis amicitiarum studiis, quam in retinendis vir melior: quia morum vitia sub umbra eloquentia primo latebant. Igitur persuadet Tissaferni, ne tanta stipendia classi Lacedæmoniorum præberet. Vocandos enim in portionem muneris Ionios, quorum pro libertate, cum tributa Athenien-sibus penderent, bellum suscep-tum sit. Sed nec auxiliis nimis enixe Lacedæmonios iuuandos; quippe memorem esse debere alienam se victoriam, non suam instruere. Et eatenus bellum sustinendum, ne inopia deferatur. Nam regem Persarum, differentibus Græcis, arbitrum pacis ac belli fore; & quos suis non posset, ipsorum armis victurum: perfecto autem bello, statim ei cum victoribus dimicandum.
units.tr: 2 Alcibiades also, once war was launched against his country, aided it not as a common soldier but by the virtues of a commander. Indeed, taking five ships, he hastened to Asia, and by the authority of his name he compelled the tributary cities of the Athenians to revolt. For they knew he was distinguished even among the Athenians, and they saw that his exile had made him no less; that the Athenians had lost a leader, and the Lacedaemonians had gained one, and that he was ready to weigh commands together with friends. But among the Lacedaemonians the virtue of Alcibiades drew more envy than favour. So when their leaders, regarding him as a rival to their glory, had commissioned his killing by ambush, Alcibiades learned through the wife of King Agis, whom he had seduced, and fled to Tissaphernes, governor of King Darius. To him he quickly insinuated himself by the courtesy of service and eagerness to comply; for he was in the bloom of youth and of striking appearance, and in winning the pursuits of friendship he was a better man than in keeping them, because the faults of his character were at first hidden under the cover of his eloquence. So he persuaded Tissaphernes not to furnish such large pay to the Lacedaemonian fleet. The Ionians, he said, should be called to share the burden, since the war had been undertaken for their liberty, though they paid tribute to the Athenians. Nor should the Lacedaemonians be helped too eagerly; they should remember that they were building another's victory, not their own. The war should be sustained only so far as to avoid being abandoned for lack of money. For the king of the Persians, while the Greeks were divided, would be the arbiter of peace and war; and whom he could not conquer with his own forces, he would conquer with their arms. But once the war was finished, he would have to fight immediately against the victors.

units.la: 15 Domesticis itaque bellis Græciam obterendam, ne externis vacet; exaquandasque vires partium, & inferiores auxilio leuandos. Non enim quieturos post hanc victoriam Spartanos, qui vindices se libertatis Græcia professi sunt. Grata oratio Tissaferni fuit.
units.tr: 3 Therefore Greece should be worn down by civil wars, lest it be free for foreign ones; the strength of the parties should be evened out, and the weaker should be relieved with aid. For the Spartans, who had professed themselves avengers of Greek liberty, would not be quiet after this victory. Tissaphernes welcomed this speech.

units.la: 20 Itaque commeatus maligne præbere; classem regiam non totam mittere; ne aut victoriam daret, aut necessitatem deponendi belli imponeret.
units.tr: And so they supplied provisions grudgingly; they did not send the whole royal fleet, lest they either give victory or force the Greeks to abandon the war out of necessity.

units.la: 3 Interea Alcibiades hanc operam ciuibus venditabat: ad quem cum legati Athenien-sium venissent, 25 pollicetur his amicitiam regis, si respub. a populo transla-ta ad senatum foret; speraus ut aut concordante civitate, dux belli ab omnibus legeretur; aut discordia inter ordines facta, ab altera parte in auxilium vocaretur. Sed Athenien-sibus imminente periculo belli, maior 30 salutis quam dignitatis cura fuit. Itaq; permittente populo, imperium ad senatum transfertur: qui cum insita genti superbia crudeliter in plebem consuleret, singulis tyrannidis sibi impotentiam vindicantibus, ab exercitu Alcibiades exul revocatur, duxq; classi confituitur. Statim igitur Athenas mittit, ex continenti se cum exercitu venturum, recepturumq; à quadringentis iura populi, ni ipsi redderent. Hac denuntiatione optimates territi, primo urbem prodere Lacedæmoniis tentauere: dein cum id nequiuissent, in exilium prosectifunt. Igitur Alcibiades inteslino malo patria libera-ta. summa cura classem instruxit; atq; ita bellum aduersus Lacedæmonios pergit.
units.tr: 3 Meanwhile Alcibiades was offering this service to his fellow citizens. When envoys of the Athenians came to him, he promised them the king's friendship if the commonwealth were transferred from the people to the senate; he hoped that either, with the city in harmony, a leader of the war would be chosen by all, or, if discord arose between the orders, he would be called in to help by one side. But with the danger of war threatening, the Athenians cared more for safety than for dignity. So, with the people's consent, power was transferred to the senate; which, with the pride innate in the nation, dealt cruelly with the common people, while individuals claimed for themselves the arrogance of tyranny. Then Alcibiades, the exile, was recalled by the army and made commander of the fleet. He at once sent word to Athens that he would come immediately with his army, and would restore the rights of the people from the Four Hundred, unless they gave them back themselves. Frightened by this warning, the optimates first tried to betray the city to the Lacedaemonians; then, when they could not, they went into exile. Therefore Alcibiades, with his country freed from internal evil, equipped the fleet with the greatest care, and so pursued the war against the Lacedaemonians.

units.la: 4 Iam Mindarus & Pharnabazus Lacedæmoniorum duces, instructis nauibus expectabant: prælio commisso, victoria penes Athenienses fuit. In eo bello maior pars exercitus, & omnes ferme hostium duces caesi; naues 80. capta. Interiectis quoq; diebus, cum bellum Lacedæmonij à mari in terram transtulissent, iterato vincuntur. His malis fracti, pacem petierunt: quam ne acciperent, opera eorum effectum est, quibus ea res quaesiit præbebat. Interea & Syracusanorum auxilia, illatum à Carthaginiensibus Siciliæ bellum, domum revocauit: quibus rebus destitutis Lacedæmoniis, Alcibiades cum classe victrici Asiam vastat; multis locis prælia facit; victor recipit civitates quæ defecerant; nonnullas capit, & imperio Athenien-sium addicit: atq; ita prisca navali gloria vindicata, adiecta etiam laude terrestris belli, desideratus civibus suis Athenas revertitur. His omnibus prælis ducenta naues hostium, & prœda ingens capta. Ad hunc redeuntis exercitus triumphum, effusa omnis multitudo obviam procedit: & universos quidem milites, præcipue tamen Alcibiadem mirantur: in hunc oculos civitas universa, in hunc suspensa ora conuertit: hunc quasi de caelo missum, & ut ipsam victoriam contuentur; laudant quæ pro patria, nec minus admirantur quæ exul contra gesserit, excusantes ipsi, iratum prouocatumq; fecisse. Enimuero tantum in vno viro fuisse momenti, vt maximi imperij subuersi, & rursum recepti auctor esset; & unde laetitiffet, eo se victoria transferret: fieretq; cum eo mira quaedam fortuna inclinatio. Igitur omnibus non humanis tantum, verum & diuinis eum honoribus onerant: certant secu ipsi, vtrum contumeliosius eum expulerint, an reuocauerint honoratius. Ipsos illi deos gratulantes tulere obutam, quorum exsecrationibus erat devotus. Et cui paulo ante omnem humanam opem interdixerant, eum, si queant, in coelo posuisse cupiunt. Explent contumelias honoribus, detrimenta muneribus, exsecrationes precibus. Non Siciliae illis aduersa pugna in ore est, sed Graciae victoria; non classes per illum amissae, sed acquisitae; nec Syracusarum, sed Ioniae, Hellespontiq; meminerunt. Sic Alcibiades nunquam mediocribus, nec in offensa, nec in fauore studiis suorum exceptus est. -
units.tr: 4 Now Mindarus and Pharnabazus, commanders of the Lacedaemonians, were waiting with their ships equipped. Battle being joined, victory lay with the Athenians. In that engagement the greater part of the army and almost all the enemy commanders were slain, and eighty ships were captured. After some days, when the Lacedaemonians had moved the war from sea to land, they were again defeated. Broken by these misfortunes, they sought peace; they did not obtain it, the effort being made by those for whom that matter was profitable. Meanwhile the Syracusan auxiliaries, called home because the Carthaginians had brought war to Sicily, also withdrew. With the Lacedaemonians thus deserted, Alcibiades with his victorious fleet ravaged Asia; he fought battles in many places; as victor he recovered the cities that had revolted, captured some, and added them to the empire of the Athenians. And so, with ancient naval glory vindicated and praise for land warfare added, he returned to Athens, longed for by his fellow citizens. In all these battles two hundred enemy ships and immense booty were taken. At the triumph of the returning army, the whole multitude poured out to meet him; they admired all the soldiers, but Alcibiades above all. The whole city turned its eyes and its attentive gaze upon him; they looked on him as if sent from heaven, and on the victory itself as if it were his doing. They praised what he had done for his country, and no less admired what he had done in exile, excusing themselves on the ground that he had acted angered and provoked. Indeed, so much weight had lain in one man that he was the author both of the overthrow and of the restoration of a very great empire; wherever he turned, victory turned with him, and a strange change of fortune went with him. So they loaded him with honours not only human but divine. They vied with one another as to whether they had expelled him more insultingly or recalled him more honourably. They even went out to meet him, rejoicing, with the gods themselves, though he had been devoted to them by curses. And he, to whom a little before they had denied all human help, they now wished, if they could, to have placed in heaven. They fill their insults with honours, their losses with gifts, their curses with prayers. The defeat in Sicily is not on their lips, but the victory for Greece; not the fleets lost through him, but those gained; they remember not Syracuse but Ionia and the Hellespont. Thus Alcibiades was never received by his people with moderate feeling, whether in hostility or in favour.

units.la: 5 Dum haec aguntur, & a Lacedaemoniis Lysander classi bellog. praeficitur, & in locum Tissaphernus, Darius rex Persarum filium suum Cyrum Ioniae Lydiaeq; praeposuit: qui Lacedaemonios auxiliis opibusq; ad spe fortunae prioris erexit. Auctoritate igitur viribus, Alcibiadem cum centum nauibus in Asiam profectum, dum agros longa pace diuites, securus populatur, & prædæ dulcedine sine insidiarum metu sparsos milites habet, repentino adventu oppressere: tantaq; cædes palantium fuit, ut plus vulneris eo prælio Athenienses acciperent, quam superioribus dederant: & tanta desperatio apud Athenienses erat, ut ex continenti Alcibiadem ducem Conone mutarent: arbitrantes victos se non fortuna belli, sed fraude imperatoris: apud quem plus prior offensa valuisset quam recentia beneficia. Vicisse autem eum priore bello ideo tantum, ut oţedcret hostibus, quem ducem spre-
units.tr: 5 While these things were happening, the Lacedaemonians placed Lysander in command of the fleet in place of Tissaphernes, and Darius, king of the Persians, set his son Cyrus over Ionia and Lydia. Cyrus encouraged the Lacedaemonians with auxiliaries and resources, raising their hopes of their former fortune. Therefore, with their authority and forces, they fell upon Alcibiades, who had set out for Asia with a hundred ships. While he was plundering the fields, rich from a long peace, and his soldiers were scattered through the booty without fear of ambush, they attacked him by surprise. The slaughter of the straggling men was so great that the Athenians suffered more wounds in that battle than they had inflicted in earlier ones. The despair among the Athenians was so great that they at once exchanged Alcibiades for Conon as their commander. They believed they had been defeated not by the chance of war but by the treachery of their general, against whom earlier offence had counted for more than recent services. He had won the previous war only so that the enemy would regret having despised him as their leader, and so that he might sell them the victory more dearly.

units.la: 25 Longa pax, opes, prædæ, dulcedo, securitas Alcibiadis opprobrium, exercitui Athenien-sium exitium creant. spreuissent, & vt carius eis ipsam victoriam venderet. Omnia enim credibilia in Alcibiade, vigor ingenÿ, & morum luxùria faciebat. Veritus itaq; multitudinis impetum, denuo in voluntarium exilium proficiscitur.
units.tr: 25 Long peace, wealth, booty, pleasure and security brought Alcibiades disgrace and brought ruin upon the Athenian army. For everything about Alcibiades was believable, since the vigour of his talent and the luxury of his manners made it so. Therefore, fearing the rush of the crowd, he set out again into voluntary exile. spreuissent, and so that he might sell them the victory more dearly.

units.la: 6 Itaq; f Conon Alcibiadi suffectus, habens ante oculos cui duci successisset, classe maxima industria exornat: sed nauibus exercitus deerat, fortissimis quibusq; in Asiæ populatione amissis. Armantur tamen senes, aut impubres pueri, & numerus militum sine 10 exercitus robore expletur. Sed non magnam bello moram ætas fecit imbellis: caduntur passim, aut fugientes capiuntur; tantaq; strages, aut occisorum, aut captiuorum fuit, vt Atheniensium deletum non imperium tantum, verum etiam nomen videretur. Quo prælio perditis & desperatis rebus, ad tantam inopiam rediguntur, vt consumpta militari ætate, peregrinis ciuitatem, seruis libertatem, damnatis impunitatē darent. Eaq; in colluuione hominum, domini antea Græcia, conscripto exercitu, vix libertatem tuebantur. Iterum tamen fortunam maris experiendam decernunt. Tanta virtus animorum erat, vt cum paulo ante salutem desperauerint, nunc non desperent victoriam. Sed neq; is miles erat, qui nomen Atheniensium tuercetur; neq; ea vires, quibus vincere confuerant, neq; ea scientia militaris in his, quos vincula, non castra continuerant.
units.tr: 6 So Conon, who was substituted for Alcibiades and had before his eyes the commander whom he had succeeded, equipped a fleet with the greatest diligence. But the army lacked sailors, since the bravest men had been lost in the plundering of Asia. Nevertheless the old men and the unfit boys were armed, and the number of soldiers was filled up without the strength of an army. But their unwarlike age did not delay the war for long: they were cut down everywhere or captured as they fled. The slaughter, of the dead and the captured alike, was so great that the power of the Athenians seemed destroyed, and even their name. After this battle, with their affairs lost and in despair, they were reduced to such poverty that, with their military age used up, they gave citizenship to foreigners, liberty to slaves, and impunity to the condemned. In this mixed rabble of men, they who had once been masters of Greece could hardly defend their freedom, even after raising an army. Yet they resolved to try the fortune of the sea again. Such was the courage of their spirits that, though they had recently despaired of their safety, they now did not despair of victory. But they were not the soldiers who could uphold the name of the Athenians, nor did they have the strength by which they had been accustomed to conquer, nor that military skill, in men whom chains, not camps, had held.

units.la: Itaq; omnes aut capti, aut occisi: cum dux Conon eo prælio superfuisset, solus crudelitatem ciuium metuens cum octo nauibus ad regem Cyprium concedit Euagoras.
units.tr: Therefore all were either captured or killed. When the commander Conon had survived that battle, he alone, fearing the cruelty of his citizens, went with eight ships to Evagoras, the Cypriot king.

units.la: 7 At dux Lacedæmoniorum rebus feliciter gestis, fortunæ hostiū insultat; captiuas naues cum præda bellica, in triumphi modum ornatas, mittit Lacedæmona; ac tributarias Atheniensium civitates, quas metus dubia belli fortuna in fide tenuerat, voluntarias recepit; nec aliud ditionis Atheniensium praeter vrbem ipsamreliquit. Quae cuncta cum Athenis nuntiata effent, omnes relictis domibus, per vrbem discurrere pauidi; a5 lius alium scitari;auctorem nuntii requirere: non pueros imprudentia, non senes debilitas; non mulieres fexus imbecillitas domi tenet: adeo ad omnem aetatemtanti mali sensus penetrauerat. In foro deinde coeunt, 10 atque ibi perpeti nocte fortunam publicam questibusiterant. Alii fratres, aut filios, aut parentes deflent, cognatos alij, alij amitos cognatis cariores, & cumpriuatis casibus querelam publicam miscent: iam feipsos, iam ipsam patriam perituram, miserioremq; 15 incolumium, quam amissorum fortunam iudicantes: sibi quisq; ante oculos obsidionem, famem, & superbum victoremq; hostem praponentes: iam ruinam vrbis & incendia, iam omnium captiuitatem & mise-rimam seruitutem recordantes: feliciores prorsus prio20 res vrbis ruinas ducentes, quae incolumibus filiis parentibusq;, tectorum tantum ruina taxatae sint. Nunc autem non classem, in quam, sicuti pridem, confugiant, superesse; non exercitum, cuius virtute seruati pulchriora possent moenia extruere.
units.tr: 7 But the commander of the Lacedaemonians, having achieved success, insulted the enemy's fortune. He sent the captured ships with the spoils of war, decked out in the manner of a triumph, to Lacedaemon. He also recovered the tributary cities of the Athenians, which fear of the uncertain fortune of war had kept loyal, and left the Athenians no dominion besides the city itself. When all these things were reported at Athens, everyone, leaving their houses, ran about the city in terror; they asked one another, and sought the author of the news. Neither the boys' thoughtlessness, nor the old men's weakness, nor the weakness of the female sex kept anyone at home; so far had the sense of so great an evil penetrated to every age. Then they gathered in the forum, and there they spent the whole night repeating the public misfortune with complaints. Some wept for brothers, or sons, or parents, others for kinsmen, others for uncles dearer than kinsmen, and mixing public lament with private misfortunes, they judged that they themselves, and the fatherland itself, were about to perish, and that their fortune was more wretched than that of those who had been lost, since they were still safe. Each set before his own eyes the siege, famine, and a proud and victorious enemy. Now they recalled the destruction of the city and the fires, now the captivity of all and most wretched slavery. They thought the earlier ruins of the city more fortunate, since they had been limited to the collapse of houses while sons and parents were unharmed. But now there remained no fleet in which they might take refuge, as before, and no army by whose courage they might have been saved and built finer walls.

units.la: 8 Sic defleta ac prope perdita vrbi hostes superue25 niunt, & obsidione circundata obsessos fame vrgent. Sciebant enim neq; ex aduetiis copiis multum superesse,& ne noua aduchi possent prouiderant: quibus malis rebus Athenienses fracti,post longam famem, & af30 fidua suorum funera, paccem petiuere: quae an dari deberet diu inter Spartanos, sociosq; deliberatum. Cummulti delendu Atheniensium nomen vrbemq, incendioconsumenda censerent, negarut se Spartani, & ex duobus GreGracia oculis alterum eruturos: pacem polliciti, si demissa Pyreum versus muri bracchia deiceret; naues, quæ reliquæ forent, traderet; resq; publica ex semetipsis 30. rectores acciperet. In has leges traditam sibi vrbem, Lacedæmonij formandam Lysandro tradiderunt. In signis hic annus expugnatione Athenarum, & morte Darij regis Persarum, & exilio Dionysii Siciliæ tyranni fuit. Mutato statu Athenarum, etiam ciuium conditio mutatur. Triginta rectores reipublicæ constituuntur, qui fiunt tyranni: quippe à principio tria millia sibi satellitum statuunt, quatum ex tot cladibus prope nec ciuium superfuerat: & quasi paruus hic ad continendâ ciuitatem exercitus esset, septingentos milites à victoribus accipiunt. Cædes deinde ciuium ab Alcibiade auspicantur, ne iterum rempublicam sub obtentu liberationis innaderet. Quem cum profectum ad Artaxerxe Persarum regem comperissent, citato itinere miserunt, qui eum interciperent: à quibus occupatus, cum occidi aperte non posset, vinus in cubiculo in quo dormiebat, crematus est.
units.tr: 8 So the enemy came upon the city, already mourned and nearly lost, and, surrounding it with a siege, pressed the besieged with famine. For they knew that little remained of their own forces, and they had made provision so that new troops could not be brought in. Worn down by these evils, the Athenians, after a long famine and the constant deaths of their people, sought peace. The Spartans and their allies deliberated for a long time whether it ought to be granted. When many advised that the name and city of the Athenians be destroyed and consumed by fire, the Spartans refused, saying that they would not tear out one of the two eyes of Greece. They promised peace on condition that the Athenians tear down the arms of the wall leading toward the Piraeus, hand over whatever ships were left, and accept back their state with thirty rulers chosen from among themselves. The Lacedaemonians handed the city, surrendered on these terms, over to Lysander to be shaped. This year was marked by the capture of Athens, the death of Darius, king of the Persians, and the exile of Dionysius, tyrant of Sicily. With the condition of Athens changed, the condition of the citizens also changed. Thirty rulers of the state were appointed, who became tyrants. Indeed, at the beginning they set up three thousand armed guards for themselves, although after so many disasters scarcely any citizens were left. As if this small force were enough to hold the city, they received seven hundred soldiers from the victors. Then they began the slaughter of citizens with Alcibiades, lest he again seize the state under the pretext of liberation. When they learned that he had set out for Artaxerxes, king of the Persians, they sent men in haste to intercept him. Seized by them, and unable to be killed openly, he was burned alive in the bedchamber where he was sleeping.

units.la: 9 Liberati hoc vltoris metu tyranni, miseras vrbis reliquias cædibus & rapinis exhauriunt. Quod cum dispicere vni ex numero suo Therameni didicissent, ipsum quoq; ad terrorem omnium interficiunt. Fit igitur ex vrbe pasim omnium fuga; repletur, Gracia Athenienses exulibus: quod etiam ip sum auxilium vnicum cum miseris eriperetur, nam Lacedæmoniorum edicto, ciuitates exules recipere prohibebatur, omnes se Argos & Thebas contulere: ibi non solum tutum exilium egerunt, verumetiam spem recuperandæ patriæ receperunt. Erat inter exules Thrasybulus vir strenuus, & domi nobilis, qui audedum aliquid pro patria & pro salute communi, etiam cum periculo ratus, adunatis exulibus castellum Phylen Atticorum finium occupat: nec deerat quarundam ciuitatium tam crudelis casus miserantium fauor. Itaq; Ismenias Thebanorum princeps, etsi publicis non poterat, priuatis ta-
units.tr: 9 Freed by fear of this avenger, the tyrants drained the wretched remains of the city by slaughter and plunder. When one of their own number, Theramenes, learned of this and protested, they killed him as well, to terrify everyone. Thus there was a general flight from the city everywhere, and Greece was filled with Athenian exiles. Even the one remaining help was taken from the wretched people, for by an edict of the Lacedaemonians, cities were forbidden to receive the exiles. All went to Argos and Thebes. There they not only lived in safe exile but also regained hope of recovering their fatherland. Among the exiles was Thrasybulus, a vigorous man and noble at home, who thought that something ought to be attempted for the fatherland and the common safety even at risk. Gathering the exiles together, he seized the fort of Phyle, on the borders of Attica. Nor was the favour of certain cities lacking, pitying so cruel a fate. Therefore Ismenias, the leader of the Thebans, although he could not help publicly, aided them with private resources. And Lysias the Syracusan orator, then an exile, sent five hundred soldiers, equipped at his own expense, to help his common fatherland with his eloquence. So a fierce battle was fought. While the one side fought with all its strength for the fatherland, and the other for the domination of others with less security,

units.la: 5 men viribus adiuuabat: & Lysias Syracusanus orator, exul tunc, quingentos milites stipendio suo instructos, in auxilium patriæ communis eloquentiæ misit. Fit itag, asperum prælium: sed cum hinc pro patria summis viribus, inde pro aliena dominatione securius pugna-
units.tr: 5 the tyrants were defeated. Beaten, they fled back into the city, which they had already drained of its people by slaughter, and they despoiled it also with arms. Then, since they regarded all Athenians as suspected of treason, they ordered them to leave the city and to live in the arms of the wall that had been torn down, while foreign soldiers upheld their rule.

units.la: 10 retur, tyranni vincuntur: victi in vrbem refugerunt, quam exhaustam cædibus suis, etiam armis spoliant. Deinde cum omnes Athenienses proditionis suspectos habērent, demigrare eos ex vrbe iubent, & in brachiis muri, quæ diruta fuerant, habitare, extraneis militi-
units.tr: ...fought out to the end: the tyrants are defeated. Beaten, they fled back into the city, which they had already drained by their own slaughter, and now they strip it of its arms as well. Then, since all the Athenians were regarded as suspected of treachery, they ordered them to leave the city and to live in the ruins of the wall that had been destroyed, while foreign soldiers upheld their rule.

units.la: 15 bus imperium tuentes. Post hæc Thrasybulum corrumpé, imperij societatem pollicentes, conātur: quod cum non centigisset, auxilia à Lacedæmoniis petiuere: quibus accitis, iterato prœliantur. In eo bello Critias & Hippolochus omnium tyrannorum sæuissimi, cadunt.
units.tr: After this they tried to win over Thrasybulus by promising him a share in their power. When that did not succeed, they sought help from the Lacedaemonians, and with these men summoned, they fought again. In that war Critias and Hippolochus, the cruellest of all the tyrants, fell.

units.la: 20 10 Ceteris victis cum exercitus eorum, ex quibus maior pars Atheniensium erat, sugeret, magna voce Thrasybulus exclamat: Cur se victorem fugiant, potius quam vt vindicem communis libertatis adiuuent? Ciuitium illam meminerint aciem, non hostium esse; necse
units.tr: When the rest had been defeated and their army, most of which was Athenian, was retreating, Thrasybulus cried out in a loud voice: why do they flee from a victor rather than help the avenger of common liberty? Let them remember that the battle line they face is made up of citizens, not enemies. He had not taken up arms in order to strip the defeated of anything, but to restore what had been taken away; he was waging war on the masters, not on the state.

units.la: 25 ideo arma cepisse, vt aliqua victis adimat, sed vt ademptâ restituat; se dominis, non ciuitati bellum inferre. Admonet deinde cognationis, legum, sacrorum: tum veteres per tot bella commilitij: orat misereantur exulum ciuium, si tam patienter ipsi serniant: reddant sibi
units.tr: He then reminded them of their kinship, their laws and their sacred rites, and then of the old comradeship they had shared through so many wars. He begged them to pity their exiled fellow citizens, if they themselves were serving so patiently: let them give their country back to these men and receive liberty themselves.

units.la: 30 patriam, accipiant libertatem. His vocibus tātum promotum est, vt reuersus in vrbem exercitus, 30. tyrannos emigrare Eleusina iuberet, substituturis decem qui rempub. regeret: qui, nihil exemplo prioris dominationis tcrterriti, eandem viam crudelitatis aggressi sunt. Dum hac aguntur, nuntiatur Lacedemone, in bellum Athenienses exarsisse: ad quod comprimendum, Paufanias rex mittitur: qui misericordia exulis populi permotus, patriam miseris ciuibus restituit, & decem tyrannos ex vrbe Eleusina migrare ad ceteros iubet. Quibus rebus cum pax statura esset, interiectis diebus, repente tyranni non minus restitutos exules, quam se in exilium actos indignantes, quasi vero aliorum libertas sua seruitus esset; bellum Atheniensibus inferunt: sed ad colloquium veluti dominationem recepturi, progressi, per insidias comprehensi, vt pacis victima trucidantur: populus quo emigrare iusserant, in vrbem reuocatur. Atq; ita per multa membra ciuitas diuipata, in vnum tandem corpus redigitur; & ne qua differsio ex ante actis nasceretur, omnes iureiurando obstringuntur P discordiarum obliuionem fore. Interea Thebani, Corinthii, legatos ad Lacedemonios mittit; qui ex manubiis, portionem prædæ communis belli periculo, peterent: quibus negatis, non quidem aperte bellum aduersus Lacedæmonios decernunt, sed tacitis animis tantam iram concipiunt, vt subesse bellum intelligi posset.
units.tr: (30) to their country, and receive their liberty. Through these words so much was achieved that the army, on returning to the city, ordered the thirty tyrants to emigrate to Eleusis, where ten men were to be set up to govern the state. But these, not at all daunted by the example of the earlier despotism, took up the same path of cruelty. While these things were going on, word came from Lacedaemon that the Athenians had flared up into war; to put this down King Pausanias was sent. Moved by pity for the exiled people, he restored the country to the wretched citizens and ordered the ten tyrants to leave the city and go to Eleusis with the rest. When peace was about to be settled, after a few days the tyrants, indignant that the exiles had been restored no less than that they themselves had been driven into exile, as if the freedom of others were their own slavery, made war on the Athenians. But when they went forward to a conference, as though about to resume their domination, they were seized by an ambush and butchered as the sacrifice of the peace. The people, whom they had ordered to emigrate, were recalled into the city. And so the state, torn apart in many limbs, was brought back into one body at last; and so that no dissension might arise from the past, all were bound by oath that the discords would be forgotten. Meanwhile the Thebans and Corinthians sent envoys to the Lacedaemonians, asking that they receive a share of the spoils, a portion of the common danger of the war; when this was refused, they did not openly decree war against the Lacedaemonians, but they conceived such anger in their silent hearts that it could be understood that war was lurking beneath.

units.la: 11 Eodem forte tempore Darius rex Persarum morte ritur, Artaxerxe & Cyro filiis reliquit: Regnum Artaxerxi, Cyro ciuitates, quarum præfectus erat, tefamieto legauit. Sed Cyro iudicium patris iniuria videbatur. Itaq; occulte aduersus fratrem bellum parabat; quod cum nuntiatum Artaxerxi esset, arcessitum ad se fratrem, & innocentiam dissimulatione belli simulantem, compedibus aureis vinxit: interfecitq;, ni mater prohibuisset. Dimisso igitur Cyrus, iam non occulte bellum, sed palam; nec per dissimulationem, sed aperta profes-sione parare cepit: auxilia vndiq; contrahit. Lacedæ{ }cedemony memores Atheniensi bello exixe fe eius opera adiutos;vel ignorantes contra quem bellum pararetur, decernunt auxilia Cyro mittenda, vbi res eius exegifset:quarentes apud Cyrum gratiam, & apud Artaxerxem,si vicisset,venie patrocinia,cum nihil aduersus eū aperte decreuissent. Sed cum in bello fors proelij virtū, fratrem pugnæ obtulisset, prior Artaxerxes à fratre vulneratur,quem cum equi fuga periculo subtraxisset, Cyrus à cohorte regia oppressus,interfectus : sic victor 10 Artaxerxes,&predafraterni belli,&exercitu potitur. In eo proelio decem millia Graecorum in auxilio Cyri fuerc:quæ & in cornu,in quo steterat, vicerunt; & post mortem Cyri, neq; armis à tanto exercitu vinci, neq; dolo capi potuerunt; reuertentesq; inter tot indomitas 15 nationes, & barbaras gentes, per tanta itineris spacia virtute se ysq; terminos patriæ defenderunt.
units.tr: (11) At about the same time King Darius of the Persians died, leaving two sons, Artaxerxes and Cyrus. By his will he bequeathed the kingdom to Artaxerxes and to Cyrus the cities of which he was governor. But Cyrus thought his father's judgment unjust. So he secretly prepared war against his brother; when this was reported to Artaxerxes, he summoned his brother to himself and, since Cyrus pretended innocence by disguising the preparation of war, bound him in golden fetters, and would have killed him had not their mother prevented it. Cyrus was therefore released, and he began to prepare war no longer in secret but openly, and no longer by dissimulation but by an avowed declaration; he gathered auxiliaries from every side. The Lacedaemonians, mindful that they had been aided by Cyrus in the Athenian war, or ignorant against whom the war was being prepared, decreed that auxiliaries be sent to Cyrus wherever his affair should require, seeking his favour, and with Artaxerxes, should Cyrus win, their protection and pardon, since they had decreed nothing openly against him. But when in the battle chance offered the brothers to each other, Artaxerxes was wounded first by his brother; Cyrus, who had drawn him away from his horse at risk to himself, was overwhelmed by the royal bodyguard and killed. Thus Artaxerxes, the victor, got possession both of the spoils of his brother's war and of his army. In that battle there were ten thousand Greeks in Cyrus' aid; they defeated the wing in which they had stood; and after Cyrus' death they could be neither conquered by arms by so great an army nor captured by treachery; and returning, through so many untamed nations and barbarous peoples, across such great distances of the journey, by their courage they defended themselves and the borders of their homeland.
ON BOOK V OF JUSTIN
SCHOLIA OF THEOPHILUS CANGISER.

units.la: ᵃ Enuntiauisse ] Æm. Probus in Alcibiade,propterea cum accusatum esse dicit, quod domi suæ mysteria celebrasset.Nam id Athenienses non ad religionem sed coniurationem pertinere arbitrabantur.
units.tr: a Enuntiavisse: Aemilius Probus, in his Alcibiades, says that he was accused because he had celebrated the mysteries in his own house. For the Athenians held that this concerned not religion but conspiracy.

units.la: ᵇ Denotum ] Et bonis exsutum. Denotionis exemplum , quo testatior esset memoria , in pila lapidea incisum atque in publico positum esse ait Probus Alcibiad.
units.tr: b Denotum: and stripped of his goods. Probus, in the Alcibiades, says that an example of the denunciation was cut into a stone pillar and set up in public, so that the memory of it would be more lasting.

units.la: ᶜ Formæ generatione,nec minus eloquentia ] Tanta erat commedatio oris atq; orationis, vt nemo ei dicendo posset resistere. Idem Probus.
units.tr: c Formae generatione, nec minus eloquentia: His personal charm and eloquence were so great that no one could resist him when he spoke. Probus again.

units.la: ᵈ Quia mori Vitia ] Refert inter alia Plutarch.dominatain eo esse τὸ φιλόνικον κ φιλάςρολον,deqipsius ingenio
units.tr: d Quia mori Vitia: Plutarch relates, among other things, that the love of victory and the love of preeminence [τὸ φιλόνικον καὶ φιλόπρωτον] predominated in his nature and character; and that the Homeric verse about the land of Egypt was customarily applied to him.
E

units.la: ac moribus vsurpari solitum fuisse illum Homeri versum de agro Ægyptiorum: ὁ ἀπὸ τῆς ἐξ Ἄλλα μέρος μὲν ἐστιν ἁ-ἀπὸ δὲ ἀπὸ Λυκεὰ. Et Probus, Constat, inquit, inter omnes, qui de eo memoriæ prodiderunt, nihil illo fuisse excellentius, vel in vitiis, vel in virtutibus.
units.tr: and that verse of Homer about the land of Egypt was customarily applied to his character and conduct [ὁ ἀπὸ τῆς ἐξ Ἄλλα μέρος μὲν ἐστιν ἁ-ἀπὸ δὲ ἀπὸ Λυκεὰ]. And Probus says: It is agreed, he says, among all who have handed down memories of him, that nothing was more outstanding than he, whether in vices or in virtues.

units.la: Alcibiadem mirantur] Ionantes cum aureis cneisqs coronis. Quod antea nemini praeterquam Olympiæ victoribus vsu euenerat. Prob.
units.tr: Alcibiadem mirantur: They ran with golden and purple crowns. Before this, such a thing had happened to no one except the victors at Olympia. Probus.

units.la: Cæson] De hoc lege præter Plutarchum & Probum, orationem Demosthenis aduersus Leptinem: vbi res gestæ Cononis præcipuæ commemorantur. Prudentem rei militaris & diligentem imperatorem vocat Probus.
units.tr: Cæson: On this man, read, besides Plutarch and Probus, Demosthenes' speech against Leptines, where the principal exploits of Conon are recounted. Probus calls him a prudent and diligent commander in military affairs.

units.la: Ex duobus Græcia oculis] Ne illa fieret ἐπιφθ. Quidere Apollo quoque consultus respondit, ... Æliano teste lib. 4.
units.tr: Ex duobus Græcia oculis: Lest that come about through envy [ἐπιφθ.]. For even Apollo, when consulted, gave the response ..., as Aelian testifies, book 4.

units.la: Deinc. ni] Quæ demolitus est Lysander ad tibiarum cantum. Xenoph. 2. Polyb. lib. 1.
units.tr: Deinc. ni: Which Lysander tore down to the sound of the flutes. Xenophon, book 2; Polybius, book 1.

units.la: Infigniis hic annus] à condito mundo termillesimus quingentesimus quadragesimus septimus. Olymp. 94.
units.tr: Infigniis hic annus: This year is notable: the 3547th from the creation of the world. Olympiad 94.

units.la: Morte Darii] à qua incipit Xenoph. de expeditione Cyri minoris.
units.tr: Morte Darii: From this point Xenophon begins his account of the expedition of Cyrus the Younger.

units.la: Qui fuerunt tyranni] De horum nefaria crudelitate legε Diod. lib. 14. & X-noph. lib. 2.
units.tr: Qui fuerunt tyranni: For the nefarious cruelty of these men, read Diodorus, book 14, and Xenophon, book 2.

units.la: Virum in cubiculo, in quo dormiebat, crematus est] non vivus, sed mortuus iam & barbarorum telis transfixus, iuxta Probum, cuius hæc verba sunt in Alcib: Illi(qui ad necandum eum missi erant) cum ferro aggredi non auderent, nō&tu ligna contulerunt circa Samiaeam, in qua quiescebat, eamque succenderunt, ut incendio conficeretur, quem manu superari posse dissidebant. Ille autem, ut sonitu flammæ est excitatus, etsi gladiusei erat subductus, familiaris tamen sui subalare telum arripuit. Hunc sequi seiuber, & vestimentis in ignem eiectis flammæ vim transfiir. Quem ut barbari incendium effugisse emisus viderunt, telis mittis interfecerunt, caputque eius ad Phrasnabazum retulerunt. At mulier, quæ cum eo vixerat confuerat, muliebri sua veste contectum ædificii incendio mortuum cremauit, quod ad viuum interimendum erat comparatum.
units.tr: Virum in cubiculo, in quo dormiebat, crematus est: He was not burned alive but was already dead and pierced with barbarian weapons, according to Probus, whose words in the Alcibiades are these: "Those who had been sent to kill him did not dare to attack him with the sword, so they piled wood around the Samiaean house in which he was resting and set it alight, since they despaired of overcoming him by hand. But he, roused by the crackling of the flames, though his sword had been removed, seized the short spear that belonged to his companion. He rushed out, threw his garments into the fire, and made his way through the flames. When the barbarians saw that he had escaped the fire, they killed him with a volley of missiles and carried his head to Pharnabazus. But the woman who had lived with him wrapped him in her own womanly dress and burned him, dead, in the fire of the building that had been prepared to destroy him while alive."

units.la: Interficiunt] Accusatore Critia tyrannorum omnium 40 cruerudelissimo, cum hausisset venenum de manu carnificis in loco publico. Vide Cic. 1 Tusc.
units.tr: Interficiunt: With Critias, the most cruel accuser of all the tyrants, when he had drunk the poison from the executioner's hand in a public place. See Cicero, Tusculan Disputations, book 1.

units.la: ° Thrasybulus Vir strenuus] Hunc Pausan. in Att. vocat ἀνδρα τῶν π ὑγιεον, καὶ ὅσοι πρὸ αὐτοῦ γεγόνασιν ἀλλὰ ἀθηναίοις γόνιμοι, τὰ πάντα ἀρισ-τον, virum omnium qui post & ante eum ab Athenien-sibus nati sunt longe praestantissimum. Etin eius vita Æm. Probus. Si per se virtus sine fortuna ponderanda sit: dubito, an hunc primum omnium poaam, illi sine dubio neminem praefero fide, 10 constantia, magnitudine animi, in patriam amore.
units.tr: ° Thrasybulus Vir strenuus: Pausanias, in the Attica, calls him a man by far the most outstanding of all who were born at Athens before and after him, the best in every respect [ἀνδρα ... τὰ πάντα ἄριστον]. And Aemilius Probus writes of his life. If virtue is to be weighed apart from fortune, I doubt whether I should put him first of all; but without hesitation I prefer no one to him in loyalty, steadfastness, greatness of spirit, and love of country.

units.la: P Di(cordiarum oblivionem fore] ἀμνησίαν: Quam Probus legem oblivionis vocat. Ejus meminit Cic. in 1. Philip. & Plato in Polit. ·
units.tr: P Discordiarum oblivionem fore: amnesty [ἀμνησίαν]. Probus calls this the law of oblivion. Cicero mentions it in the first Philippic, and Plato in the Politics.

units.la: 9 Cyro] Qui cognomento minor dicitur: de quo vide 15 Orof. lib. 2 cap. 18. Plut. in Artoxerxe, Xenoph. lib. 1. ἀναβασ. Qui ei & militavit & familiaris fuit. Cicero ei laudem agriculturae tribuit in Catone maiore.
units.tr: 9 Cyro: He is called the Younger by surname; see Orosius, book 2, chapter 18; Plutarch, in the Artaxerxes; and Xenophon, book 1 of the Anabasis. He both served as a soldier under him and was his friend. Cicero attributes to him the praise of agriculture in the Cato Maior.

units.la: r A cohorte regis oppressus interficitur] anno M. ter milles. quingentesimo, septuagesimo primo, secundum 20 alios septuages. Olymp. 95.
units.tr: r A cohorte regis oppressus interficitur: in the year 3571 from the creation, according to others 3570. Olympiad 95.
The Epitome of the Histories of Pompeius Trogus
Book VI. Summary

units.la: 1 Lacedemonii Asiae impugnant bellum viâtimoquent. Rex Persarum Athenienfibus per Cononem auxilium concedit. | 4 Inclinatio fortunae Lacedaemoniorum, quam Athenienses Iphicrates... gesilai fortitudo sustentat.
units.tr: 1 The Lacedaemonians make war on Asia and provoke a conflict. The king of the Persians grants help to the Athenians through Conon. | 4 The decline of the Lacedaemonians' fortune, which the Athenians under Iphicrates... and the courage of Agesilaus sustains.

units.la: 2 Ducem exercitui Agesilaum Lacedaemonii praefi-ciunt. Cononis prudenter & fortiter gesta. | 5 Athenienses Iphicra-tem & Cononem Lacedae-moniis opponunt. ex Lacedaemoniorum spoliis Athe-nae instauruntur.
units.tr: 2 The Lacedaemonians place Agesilaus in command of the army. Conon's prudent and brave deeds. | 5 The Athenians set Iphicrates and Conon against the Lacedaemonians. From the spoils of the Lacedaemonians, Athens is restored.

units.la: LACEDAEMONII more ingenij humani, quo plura habent, eo ampliora cupientes, non contenti accessione Atheniensium opum vires sibi duplicatas, totius Asiæ imperium affectare cœperunt : sed maior pars sub regno Persarum erat. Itaque Hercyllidas dux in hanc militiam electus, cum videret sibi aduersus duos præfectos Artaxerxis regis, Pharnabazum & Tissaphernem, maximarum gentium viribus succinctos, dimicandum, pacificandum cum altero statuit. Aptior visus Tissaphernes, vir & industria potior, & militibus Cyri quondam regis instruction in colloquium vocatur, & statutis conditionibus, ab armis dimittitur. Hanc rem Pharnabazus apud communem regem criminatur, vt Lacedæmonios A-...
units.tr: Being driven by the nature of human beings, who, the more they have, the more they desire, the Lacedaemonians, not content with the addition of the Athenian resources, which doubled their strength, began to aspire to the empire of all Asia. But the greater part of it was under the kingdom of the Persians. Therefore Hercyllidas, chosen as commander for this campaign, seeing that he would have to fight against the two governors of King Artaxerxes, Pharnabazus and Tissaphernes, who were girded with the forces of very great peoples, resolved to make peace with the one and fight the other. Tissaphernes seemed the more suitable, a man more powerful in energy; he was called to a conference, and, with the soldiers of the former king Cyrus instructed, on agreed conditions is dismissed from arms. Pharnabazus accuses this matter before the common king, that the Lacedaemonians A-

units.la: fiam ingressos non repulcrit armis, sed impensis regiis alucrit; merceturque ab his vt differant bella, quam gerant, tanquam non ad vnius summam imperiį detrimentum omne perueniat. Indignum ait bella non perfici, sed redimi; hostem precio, non armis summoueri. His vocibus regem Tiffaferni alienatum hortatur, vt in locum eius, nauale belli ducem eligat Conona Athenien-sem, qui amissa bello patria Cypri exulabat: quippe Athenien-sibus, etsi fracta sint opes, nauare tamen nauale vsum, nec si eligendus sit ex vniuersis, meliorem alium esse. Accepti igitur quingentis talentis, iussus est Conona classi praficere.
units.tr: ...who had entered Asia were not repulsed by arms but were nourished with royal funds; and he buys from them a postponement of the wars they wage, as if the whole loss would not fall on the sum of one empire. He says it is shameful for wars not to be fought out but bought off; an enemy is removed by money, not by arms. By these words the king, alienated from Tissaphernes, is urged to choose in his place as commander of the naval war Conon the Athenian, who, having lost his homeland in war, was living in exile on Cyprus. For the Athenians, though their resources were broken, still retained naval experience, and even if one had to be chosen from all, there was no better man. Therefore, having received five hundred talents, he was ordered to put Conon in charge of the fleet.

units.la: 2 His cognitis, Lacedamonij & ipsi a rege AEgypti Hercynione auxilia nauali belli per legatos petunt, a quo centum triremes, & sexcenta millia modium frumenti missa: a ceteris quoque sociis ingentia auxilia contracta sunt. Sed tanto exercitui, & contra tantum ducem deerat dignus imperator. Itaque postulantibus sociis Agesilaum ducem, regem tunc Lacedæmoniorum: propter responsum oraculi 10 Delphici, diu Lacedæmonij, an eum summæ rei præponerent, deliberauerunt: quibus futurus imperij finis denuntiabatur, cum regium claudicasset imperium: erat enim pede claudus. Ad postremum statuerunt, melius esse incessu regem, quam imperio regnum claudicare. Postquam Agesilaum cum ingentibus copiis in Asiam misere: non facile dixerim quod aliud par ducum tam bene comparatum fuerit: quippe ætas, virtus, consilium, sapientia utrinque prope vna; 20 gloria quoque rerum gestarum eadem: quibus cum paria omnia fortuna dederit, inuictum tamen ab altero utrunque seruauit. Magnus igitur amborum apparatus belli, magnæ res gestæ fuerunt. Sed Cononem seditio militum inuadit, quos præfecti regis fraudare stipendio soliti erant, eo instantius debita poscentibus, quo grauiorem sub magno duce militiam præsumebant. Itaque Conon diu rege per epistolas sustra fatigato, ad postremum ipse ad eum pergit: a cuius aspectu & colloquio prohibitus est, quod eum more Persarum adorare nollet: agit tamen cum eo per 30 internuntios, & queritur opulentissimi regis bella inopia delabi, & qui exercitum parem hostibus habeat, pecunia vinci, qua præfert, inferioremque eum ea parte virium inueniri, qua longe superior sit: postulat dari sibi ministrum impensè, quia plurimus sit mandare perniciosum sit: Dato sperdio, ... remittitur: nec moram agendus rebus facit: ... titer, multa feliciter agit: agros hostiles ... expugnat; & quasi tempestas quaedam ... nit. Quibus rebus territi Lacedaemonii ... dium, revocandum ab Asia Agesilaum ...
units.tr: 2 When this was known, the Lacedaemonians also sought naval aid through envoys from the king of Egypt, Hercynion, who sent a hundred triremes and six hundred thousand measures of grain; great auxiliary forces were also gathered from their other allies. But such an army, and against such a commander, lacked a worthy general. So, at the request of the allies, they chose Agesilaus, then king of the Lacedaemonians. Because of an oracle's response from Delphi, the Lacedaemonians long deliberated whether to place him at the head of so important a matter, since the end of their rule had been announced for when the royal power should limp: for he was lame in one foot. In the end they decided it was better for the king to limp in his gait than for the kingdom to limp in its rule. After they sent Agesilaus into Asia with huge forces, I could hardly say that any other pair of commanders was so well matched: their age, courage, judgement and wisdom were nearly the same, and their glory from deeds was equal. Fortune gave them everything in equal measure, yet each kept the other unconquered. Great, therefore, was the war preparation of both, and great the deeds done. But a mutiny attacked Conon's men, whom the king's governors were accustomed to defraud of their pay, and they demanded their dues the more insistently the heavier they expected their service under a great commander to be. So Conon, having wearied the king for a long time with letters, at last went to him in person. He was kept from his sight and conversation because he refused to adore him in the Persian manner. He nevertheless dealt with him through intermediaries, and complained that the wars of the most wealthy king were collapsing for lack of money, and that a man who has an army equal to the enemy's is beaten by money, in that part of his forces in which he is inferior, while he is far superior in the rest. He asked that a minister be assigned to him at once, since it was harmful to delay the handling of affairs... Given this, he was sent back, and he did not delay the business... he succeeded in many things: he attacked hostile fields... and, like a kind of storm, he... Terrified by these events, the Lacedaemonians... decided that Agesilaus should be recalled from Asia...

units.la: 3 Interim Pisandrus ab Agesilao profectus ... tria relictus, ingentem classem iuniorum virtutum ..., fortuna belli tentaturus. Nec non & Conon ... cum hostium exercitu concursurus, ... natos suos. Summa igitur non tam ducum ... quam militum aemulatio fuit. Nam & ... non non tam Persis, quam patriae studebat; & sicut ... {15}flictis Atheniensium rebus, auctor animisque dominationis fuerat, sic volebat idem haberi reddita, patriam, velcendo recipere, quam vistus amiserat: eo spectosius, quod ne ipsorum quidem Atheniensium sed alieni imperij viribus dimicet; pugnaturus periculo regis, visuurus premio patria, gloriamq; diuersis artibus, quam priores ciuitatis suae duces consecuturus: quippe illos vincendo Persas, patriam defendisse; se Persas viͤores faciendo, restituturum patriam esse. Porro Pisandrus pro coniunctione Agesilai, etiam virtutum amulator erat; contendebatq;, ne a rebus gestis eius, & gloria splendore decederet; neue tot bellis ac seculis quaeistum imperium, breuis momenti culpa subuerteret. Eadem [militum] & omnium regum cura erat, quos maior solicitudo cruciabat, non tam ne ipsi quaesitas opes amitterent, quam ne pristinas Athenienses reciperent. Sed quanto {30} maius prælium fuit, tanto & clarior victoria Cononis. Victi Lacedæmonij fugam ca-pesserunt; præsidia hostium Athenis deducuntur; populo restituta dignitate condiditio seruilis eripitur ; multa quoque ciuitates recipiautur.
units.tr: 3 Meanwhile Pisander, having set out from Agesilaus... leaving behind... a huge fleet of young men of tried courage, to try the fortune of war. Nor did Conon... to meet the army of the enemy... their sons. The contest was therefore not so much between the leaders as between the zeal of the soldiers. For... was intent not so much on the Persians as on his country; and just as he had been the originator and inspiration of Athenian domination when their affairs were broken, so he wished the same to be held: to recover by his own victory the homeland he had lost. It was all the more splendid because he fought not with the forces of the Athenians themselves but with those of a foreign empire, about to risk his life at the king's peril, about to see his country as his reward, and to win glory by different arts from those of the earlier leaders of his city. For they had defended their country by conquering the Persians; he, by making the Persians victors, would restore his country. Moreover Pisander, in alliance with Agesilaus, was also a rival in virtue. He contended that he must not fall short of his glory and splendour in deeds, nor should the fault of a brief moment overturn an empire acquired over so many wars and ages. The same care was felt by all the kings, whom greater anxiety tormented, not so much lest they themselves lose the wealth they had acquired, as lest the Athenians recover their former power. But the greater the battle, the brighter the victory of Conon. The defeated Lacedaemonians took to flight; the enemy garrisons were withdrawn from Athens; the people's dignity was restored, and servile condition was snatched away; many cities were also recovered.

units.la: 4 Hoc initium Atheniensibus refumeda potentia, & Lacedemoniis habende finis fuit. Namq; velut cum 5 imperio etiam virtutem perdidissent, contemni a finitimis coepere. Primi igitur Thebanj auxiliantibus Atheniensibus, Lediam bis intulereque ciuitas ex infimis incrementis, virtute Epaminonde ducis, ad spem impery Graecia erecta est. Fit itaq; terrestre prelium, eadem 10 Lacedemoniorum fortuna, qua pugnatum aduersus Conona nauali prelio fuerat. In eo bello Lyfander, quo duce Athenienses victi a Lacedemoniis fuerant, interficitur. Paufanias quoq; alter dux Lacedemoniorum proditionis accusatus, in exilium abiit. Igitur Thebani potiti victoria, vniuersum exercitum ad vrbem Lacedemoniorum ducut facilem expugnationem rati, quoniam deserti a sociis omnibus erant : quod metuentes Lacedemonij, regem suum Agefilaum ex Asia, qui ibi magnas res gerebat, ad defensionem patriæ arcessunt.
units.tr: 4 This was the beginning of the Athenians' recovery of power and of the end of the Lacedaemonians' dominion. For, as if they had lost their virtue along with their empire, they began to be despised by their neighbours. First, therefore, the Thebans, with the Athenians helping, twice attacked the Lacedaemonians, and their state, raised from the lowest beginnings by the virtue of its leader Epaminondas, was lifted up to hope of empire. So a land battle was fought, and the Lacedaemonians met the same fortune that they had met against Conon in the naval battle. In that war Lysander, under whose leadership the Athenians had been defeated by the Lacedaemonians, was killed. Pausanias, the other Lacedaemonian leader, was accused of treason and went into exile. Therefore the Thebans, having gained the victory, led their whole army against the city of the Lacedaemonians, thinking it an easy capture since they had been deserted by all their allies. Fearing this, the Lacedaemonians summoned their king Agesilaus from Asia, where he was achieving great things, for the defence of the homeland.

units.la: 20 Occiso enim Lyfandro, nullius alterius fiduciam ducis habebant. Cuius quoniam ferus adventus erat, conseripto exercitu, obuiam hosti procedunt. Sed victis, aduersus paulo ante victores, nec animus, neq; vires pares suere. Prima igitur congressione funduntur. Deletis iam 25 suorum copijs, superuenit rex Agefilaus, qui restituto prelio, non difficulter, recenti & multis expeditionibus indurato milite, hostibus victoriam eripuit, ipse tamen graviter sauciatur.
units.tr: For with Lysander dead, they had no confidence in any other leader. Since his arrival was slow, they raised an army and went out to meet the enemy. But the defeated, facing those who had been victors a little before, had neither spirit nor strength equal to theirs. So in the first encounter they were routed. With their forces already destroyed, King Agesilaus arrived. Renewing the battle, he snatched victory from the enemy without difficulty, since his soldiers were fresh and hardened by many campaigns, though he himself was seriously wounded.

units.la: 5 Quibus rebus cognitis, Athenienses verentes ne, 30 iterum Lacedemoniis victoribus, in pristinam fortem seruitutis redigerentur, exercitum contrahunt, cumq; in auxilium Bæotiorum per Iphicratem, viginti quidem annos natum, sed magnæ indolis iuvenem, duci iubent. Huius adolescentis supra aetatem virtus admirabilis fuit; nec vnquam ante eum Athenienses, inter tot tantosq; duces, aut spei maioris, aut indolis maturioris imperatorem habuerunt, in quo non imperatoriae tantum, verum & oratoriae artes fuere. Conon quoq; audito reditu Agesilai, & ipse ex Asia ad depopulandos Lacedæmoniorum agros reuertitur: atque ita, vndiq; belli formidine circumstrepente, clausi Spartani, ad summam desperationem redigùntur. Sed Conon vastatis hostium terris, Athenas pergit: vbi magno civium gaudio exceptus, plus tamen tristitiae ipse ex incendiâ, & diruta à Lacedæmoniis patria, quam laetitiae ex recuperata post tantum temporis, cepit. Itaq; quae incensa fuerant, prædarum sumptu & exercitu Persarum restituit; quae diruta, reficit. Fatum illud Athenarum fuit, vt ante à Persis cremata, manibus eorum; & nunc à Lacedæmoniis diruta, ex spoliis Lacedæmoniorum restituerentur: versa quoq; vice, haberent nunc socios, quos tunc hostes habuerant; & hostes nunc paterentur, cum quibus iunċti tunc arctissimis societatis vinculis fuerant.
units.tr: 5 When these things were known, the Athenians, fearing that, if the Lacedaemonians were victorious again, they would be brought back into their former slavery, raised an army and ordered it led to the aid of the Boeotians under Iphicrates, a young man of twenty years, yet of great promise. The courage of this youth, beyond his years, was admirable; and never before him had the Athenians, among so many great leaders, had a commander of greater promise or more mature talent, in whom there were not only military but also oratorical skills. Conon too, on hearing of Agesilaus's return, came back from Asia to lay waste the fields of the Lacedaemonians. Thus, with the dread of war sounding on every side, the Spartans, shut in, were reduced to utter despair. But Conon, having laid waste the enemy lands, made his way to Athens, where, received with great joy by the citizens, he felt more grief at the burning and destruction of his homeland by the Lacedaemonians than joy at its recovery after so long a time. Therefore what had been burned he restored with the cost of spoils and the Persian army; what had been destroyed, he rebuilt. Such was the fate of Athens: once burned by the Persians at their hands, and now destroyed by the Lacedaemonians, it was restored from the spoils of the Lacedaemonians. The tables were also turned: they now had as allies those whom they had then had as enemies, and now suffered as enemies those with whom they had then been joined by the closest bonds of alliance.

units.la: 6 Dum hæc gererentur, Artaxerxes rex Persarum legatos in Græciam mittit, per quos iubet omnes ab armis discedere; qui aliter fecissent, eum se pro hoste habiturum; ciuitatibus libertatem, suaq; omnia restituit: quod non Græcia laboribus, assiduisq; bellorum internecinis odiis consulens fecit; sed ne occupato sibi Ægyptio bello, quod propter auxilia, aduersus præfectos suos Lacedæmoniis missa, susceperat, exercitus sui in Græcia detinerentur. Fefi igitur tot bellis Græci, cupide parere. Hic annus non eo tantum insignis fuit, quod repente pax tota Græcia facta est; sed etiam eo quod eodem tempore vrbs Romana à Gallis capta est. Sed Lacedæcedæmonij securis insidiantes, absentiam Arcadum speculati, castellum eorum expugnant, occupatoq; præsidium imponunt. Itaq; armato instructoq; exercitu, Arcades adhibitis in auxilium Thebanis; amissa lello repetunt. In eo prælio Archidamus dux Lacedæmoniorum vulneratur: qui cum cadi suos iam vt victos videret, per præconem corpora interfectorum ad sepulturam poscit. Hoc est enim signum apud Græcos victoriæ tradita. Qua confessione contenti Thebani, signum parcendi dedere.
units.tr: 6 While these things were happening, Artaxerxes, king of the Persians, sent envoys into Greece, ordering all the states to lay down their arms. Whoever did otherwise, he said, he would regard as an enemy. He restored liberty to the cities and all their property. He did this not out of concern for Greece, worn down by labours and the deadly hatreds of constant wars, but so that his armies would not be kept in Greece while he was occupied with the Egyptian war, which he had undertaken because of the auxiliaries the Lacedaemonians had sent against his governors. So the Greeks, worn out by so many wars, eagerly obeyed. This year was remarkable not only because general peace was suddenly made throughout Greece, but also because at the same time the city of Rome was captured by the Gauls. But the Lacedaemonians, lying in wait with treacherous intent and watching for the Arcadians to be absent, stormed their fortress and, once they had taken it, set a garrison in it. So the Arcadians, with their army armed and drawn up, took the Thebans in as allies and recovered it, though they lost the battle. In that battle Archidamus, the Lacedaemonian general, was wounded. When he saw his men already falling as though defeated, he asked through a herald for the bodies of the slain for burial, for among the Greeks this is the sign of a surrender. The Thebans, content with this admission, gave the signal to spare.

units.la: 7 Paucis deinde post diebus, neutris quicquam hostile facientibus, cum quasi tacito consensu indutia essent, Lacedæmoniis alia bella aduersus finitimos gerentibus, Thebani Epaminonda duce, occupanda vrbis eorum spem ceperunt. Igitur principio noctis, taciti Lacedæmona proficiscuntur: non tamen aggredi incautos potuerunt. Quippe senes, & cetera imbellis ætas, cum aduentum hostium præsensissent, in ipsis portarum angustiis armati occurrunt; & aduersus quindecim millia militum, non amplius centum iam effœta ætatis viri, pugna se se offerunt: tantum animorum viriumq; patriæ, & penatium conspectus submiserat; tantoq; præsentia, quam recordatione sui, maiores spiritus largiuntur. Nam vt videre inter quæ, & pro quibus staŕent, aut vincendum sibi, aut moriendum censuerunt. Pauci igitur sustinuere senes aciem, cui par ante diem vniuersa iuuentus esse non potuit. In eo prælio duo duces hostium cecidere. Cum interim, Agesilai aduentu nuntiato, Thebani recessere: nec bellum diu dilatum: siquidem Spartanorum iuuentus, senum virtute & gloria incensa, teneri nō potuit, quin ex continenti acie decerneret. Cū victoria Thebanorum esset, Epaminondas dū nō duis tantū, verumetiā fortissimi militis officio fungitur, gitur, grauiter vulneratur. Quo audito, bis ex dolore metus,& illis ex gaudio stupor iniicitur, atq; veluti ex placito consensu a praelio discedituir.
units.tr: 7 A few days later, with neither side doing anything hostile and a truce existing by a kind of tacit agreement, while the Lacedaemonians were waging other wars against their neighbours, the Thebans under Epaminondas conceived hope of seizing their city. So at the beginning of the night they set out silently for Lacedaemon, but they could not attack them unawares. For the old men and the rest of the unwarlike age, having sensed the enemy's approach, rushed armed to meet them in the very narrows of the gates. Against fifteen thousand soldiers, no more than a hundred men, now worn out with age, offered battle. So much courage and strength did the sight of their country and household gods supply, and so much greater spirit did their presence, rather than their memory, give them. For, seeing among what and for what they were fighting, they decided they must either conquer or die. So a few old men sustained the battle line, which the whole young generation had not been able to match the day before. In that battle two enemy leaders fell. Meanwhile, Agesilaus' arrival was announced, and the Thebans withdrew. Nor was the war long delayed, for the youth of Sparta, fired by the courage and glory of the old men, could not be restrained from deciding the matter at once in the line of battle. When the victory went to the Thebans, Epaminondas, performing not only the duty of a general but also that of the bravest soldier, was gravely wounded. On hearing this, fear seized the one side and stupor the other, from grief and from joy respectively, and as if by agreed plan they withdrew from the battle.

units.la: 8 Post paucos deinde dies Epaminondas decedit, cū quo vires quoq; reipub. ceciderunt: Nam sicuti telo si primam aciem perfregeris, reliquo ferro vim nocendi sustuleris; sic illo velut mucrone teli ablato duce Thebanorum,vei quoq; publicæ vires bebetatæ sunt: vt non tam illum amisisse, quam cum illo interisse omnes viderentur. Nam neq; hunc ante ducem vllum memorabile bellum gessere; nec postea virtutibus, sed cladibus insignes fuere: vt manifestum fit,patriæ gloriam & nomen extinctam cum eo fuisse. Fuit autem incertū, vir melior,an dux esset: nam & imperium nō sibi sed patriæ quæsuit: & pecuniæ adeo parcus fuit, vt sumptus funeri defuerit;gloria quoq, non cupidior quā pecuniæ:quippe recusanti,omnia imperia ingesta sunt: honoresq; ita gesit, vt ornamentum non accipere, sed dareipsi dignitati videretur: 4 Iam litterarum studium,iam philosophiæ doctrina tanta,vt mirabile videtur, vnde tam insignis militiæ scientia hominiū inter literas nato. Neq; ab hoc vita proposito mortis ratio differfit. Nam vt relatus in castra Semianimis, vocem spiritumq; collegit, id vnum a circumstantibus requisiuit,num cadenti sibi scutum ademisset hostis: quod vt seruatum audiuit, allatumq;, velut laborum gloriaq; socium osculatus est. Iterum quæsiuit vtri viciissent: vt audiuit Thebanos, Bene habere se rem, dixit: atq; ita velut gratulabundus patriæ,exspirauit.
units.tr: 8 A few days later Epaminondas died, and with him the strength of the commonwealth also declined. For just as, if you break through the first line with a weapon, you take away the power to harm from the rest of the iron, so with the leader of the Thebans removed, as if the point of the weapon had been taken away, the public strength was also blunted, so that they seemed not so much to have lost him as to have perished along with him. For they waged no memorable war under any leader before him, and afterwards they were distinguished not by virtues but by defeats; so it is plain that the glory and name of the homeland were extinguished together with him. It was uncertain whether he was the better man or the better general. For he sought power not for himself but for his country, and he was so sparing with money that there was not enough for his funeral expenses. He was no more eager for glory than for money: though he refused, all commands were thrust upon him, and he held honours in such a way that he seemed not to receive an ornament but to bestow dignity upon it. 4 Moreover, his devotion to letters and his training in philosophy were so great that it seems remarkable that such outstanding military skill came from a man so devoted to learning. Nor did his manner of death differ from his way of life. When he was carried back into camp half-alive, he gathered his voice and breath and asked only one thing of those standing around: whether the enemy had taken his shield from him as he fell. When he heard that it had been saved and brought back, he kissed it as a companion of his labours and glory. Again he asked which side had won; when he heard that the Thebans had, he said, "It is well with us," and so, as if rejoicing for his country, he breathed his last.

units.la: 9 Huius morte etiam Atheniensium virtus interit: cidit:siquidem amisso cui emulari consueuerant,in fegnitiam,torporemq; resoluti,non vt olim in classem & exercitus, sed in dies sestos, apparatuq; ludorum reditum publipublicos effundunt; & cum aćtoribus nobilißimis poë-tæ theatra celebrant, frequentius scenam quam castravisentes; versificatoresq; melliores, quam duces laudantes. Tunc vectigal publicum, quo antea milites & re-
units.tr: 9 With his death the courage of the Athenians also perished. Having lost the one whom they had been accustomed to emulate, they dissolved into sloth and torpor, and no longer poured public money into fleets and armies but into festival days and the preparations of games; with the most noble actors the poets filled the theatres, frequenting the stage more than the camp and praising versifiers more than generals. Then the public revenue, by which the soldiers and

units.la: § miges alebantur, cum vrbano populo diuidi cœptum est. Quibus rebus effećtum est, vt inter etia Græcorum, sordidum & obscurum antea, Macedonum nomen emergeret. Et Philippus obses triennio Thebis habitus, Epaminōnda & Pelopida virtutibus eruditus, regnum10 Macedoniæ, Græciæ, & Asiæ ceruicibus, velut iugum seruitutis imponeret.
units.tr: § rowers were fed, began to be divided among the urban populace. As a result of these things, the name of the Macedonians, formerly obscure and contemptible even among the Greeks, began to rise. Philip, held as a hostage for three years at Thebes and educated in the virtues of Epaminondas and Pelopidas, would lay the kingdom 10 of Macedonia, Greece and Asia upon their necks, as a yoke of servitude.
IN LIB. IVSTINI V- I.
SCHOLIA THEOPHILI Cangiseri.

units.la: a Agesilaum] Cuius laudes peculiari libro celebrat Xenophon ipsi familiarissimus.
units.tr: a Agesilaus: his praises are celebrated in a separate book by Xenophon, who was very intimate with him.

units.la: 20 b Erat enim pede claudus] Hic tantus vir (ait Probus in eius vita) vt naturam fautricem habuerat in tribuendis animi virtutibus, sic maleficam naćtus est in corpore exiguo & claudus altero pede. Quæ res etiam nonnulla adferebat deformitatem: atque ignoti faciem eius cum intuerentur, contemnebant: qui autem virtutem nouerant, non poterant admirari fatis.
units.tr: 20 b For he was lame in one foot. This great man (says Probus in his life of him) had nature as a kind mother in bestowing the virtues of the mind, but in his small body and lame in one foot she was as a harsh stepmother. This also added some deformity, and when strangers looked upon his face they despised him; but those who knew his virtue could not admire him enough.

units.la: 25 c Graviter Gulneratur] Apud Mantineam. Probus cum in ipso prælio ex vulnere mortuum esse ait, cum ferrum, quod ex hastili in corpore remanserat, vsque eo retinuisset, quoad renunciatum ipsi esset de victoria Bœotiorum. Id postquam audiuit, Satis, inquit, vixi: inuićtus enim motior, & ferro extrećto confećtum examinatus est. Mirę parsimoniæ ac frugalitatis exemplum est, quod de ipso Frontin. prodidit lib. 4. strategem. quod præter venum ahenum & vnum vero in sua suppellećtile non habuerit.
units.tr: 25 c Seriously wounded: at Mantinea. Probus says that he died of the wound in the battle itself, the iron head that had stayed in his body from the shaft being held in until news was brought to him of the victory of the Boeotians. When he heard this, "Enough," he said, "I have lived"; for he was carried away unconquered, and once the iron was drawn out he breathed his last. It is an remarkable example of thrift and frugality, which Frontinus records about him in book 4 of his Stratagems: that he had in his household furniture nothing but a bronze vessel and only one wooden one.
d Now

units.la: In quo praeceptorem habuit Lysiam Tarentinum Pythagoream, cui quidem sic fuit deditus cupiditate discendi, ut adolescens tristem ac severum senem omnibus aequalibus suis in familiaritate anteponeret, nec prius ab eo discederet, quam doctrina omnes commilitones suos superaret. Probus.
units.tr: Under him he had as teacher Lysias of Tarentum, a Pythagorean, to whom he was so devoted in his eagerness to learn that, as a young man, he preferred the stern old man to all his companions in intimacy, and would not leave him until he surpassed all his fellow soldiers in learning. Probus.

units.la: Quae incidit in annum M. termilles. sexcent. nonfm, Olympiadem vero quattam & centesimam. Moriens, teste Xenophonte, dixit, se, licet caeleb decedat, duos tamen filios relinquere victoriam Leuctricam & Mantineam. Atque hic subsistit historia Xenophontis, qui propter elegantiam dicendi ac suavitatem apis Atticae cognomentum meruit, cuiusque orationem ipsas finxisse gratias olim exilii matum est.
units.tr: This falls in the year (the figures are garbled in the scan, "M. termilles. sexcent. nonfm"), in the hundred and fourth Olympiad. Dying, according to Xenophon, he said that, although he died unmarried, he left behind two sons, the victory at Leuctra and the victory at Mantinea. Here Xenophon's history ends; he earned the surname "Attic Bee" for the elegance and sweetness of his style, and it is recorded that the Graces themselves once fashioned his oratory while he was in exile.
