units.la: ACEDONIA ante nomine Emathionis regis, cuius prima virtutis experimenta in illis locis extant, Emathia cognominata est. Huius sicuti incrementa modica, ita termini perangusti scre. Populus Pelasgus, regio Bœotia dicebatur. Sed postea virtute regum, & gĕtis industria, subactis primo finitimis, mox populis, nationibusq; imperium s extremos Orientis terminos prolatum.
units.tr: MACEDONIA was formerly named Emathia, after King Emathion, whose first proofs of courage are still found in those places. As its increases were modest, so its boundaries were very narrow. The Pelasgian people; the region was called Boeotia. But afterwards, through the valour of its kings and the industry of its people, the empire was extended by subduing first the neighbouring peoples, then the nations further off, until it reached the farthest limits of the East.

units.la: In regione Paeonia, quae nunc portio est Macedonia, regnasse fertur Telegonus pater Asteropaei, cuius Troiano bello, inter clarissimos vindices vrbis, nomen accepimus. Ex alio latere in Europa regnum Europus nomine tenuit. Sed & Caranus cum magna multitudine Grecorum, sedes in Macedonia responso oraculi iussus quaerere, cum in Emathiam venisset, vrbem Aedessam non sentientibus oppidanis, propter imbrium & nebulae magnitudinem, gregem caprarum, imbrem fugientiũ, secutus occupauit: reuocatusq; in memoriam oraculi, quo iussus erat, ducibus capris imperium quaerere, regni sedem statuit: religioseq; postea obseruauit, quocunq; agmen moueret, ante signa easdem capras habere, capptorum duces habiturus, quas regni habuerat auctôres. Vrbem Aedessam ob memoriam muneris Aegeas, populum Aegeadas, vocauit. Pulso deinde Mida (nam quoq; portionem Macedonia tenuit) aliusq; regibus pulsis, in locum omnium solus successit; primusq; adunatis gentibus variorum populorum, b veluti vnum corpus Macedonia fecit; crescentiq; regno, valida incrementorum fundamenta constituit.
units.tr: In the region of Paeonia, which is now part of Macedonia, Telegonus is said to have reigned, the father of Asteropaeus, whose name we have learned as one of the most famous defenders of the city in the Trojan War. On the other side, in Europe, a king named Europus held the realm. Caranus also, with a great multitude of Greeks, was ordered by an oracle's response to seek a seat in Macedonia. When he came into Emathia, he occupied the city of Aegae, which the townspeople did not notice, because of the heavy rain and the thick mist. He followed a flock of goats fleeing the storm. Recalling the oracle that had ordered him to seek a kingdom with goats as his guides, he established the seat of his rule there. Afterwards he scrupulously kept the custom that whenever his army moved, the same goats went before the standards, since he intended to have as leaders of his troops the goats that had been the authors of his kingdom. In memory of this gift he called the city Aegae and the people Aegeadae. Then, after Midas was driven out (for he too held a part of Macedonia), and other kings were likewise driven out, he alone succeeded to the place of them all. He was the first to unite the tribes of various peoples, and he made Macedonia like one body. As the kingdom grew, he laid firm foundations for its expansion.

units.tr: 2 After him Perdiccas reigned, whose life was distinguished and whose final days were memorable, as if they had been foretold by an oracle. For when he was dying as an old man, he [instructed] Argeus, his son,

units.la: monstrauit locum,quo condi vellet, ibiq; non sua tantum, sed & succedentium sibi regum ossa poni iussit, prefatus, quoad ibi condita posterorum reliquiae forent, regnum in familia mansurum: credunt q; hac superstitione extinctam in Alexandro sirpem, quia locum secundam pulturae mutauerit. Argaus moderate, & cum amore popularium administrato regno, successorem filium Philippum reliquit: qui immatura morte raptus, Europum paruulum admodum instituit heredem. Sed Macedonibus assidua certamina cum Thracibus & Illyriis fuere: quorum armis veluti quotidiano exercitio indurati, gloria bellica laudis finitimos terrebant. Igitur Illyrij infantiam regis pupilli contemnentes, bello Macedonas aggrediuntur: qui prælio pulsi, rege suo in cunis prolato, & pone aciem posito; acrius certamen repetierunt: tanquam ideo victi fuissent antea, quod bellantibus sibi regis sui auspicia defuisset; futuri vel propterea victores, quod ex superstitione animum vincendi ceperant: simul & miseratio eos infantis tenebat, quem si victi forent, captiuum de lege facturi videbantur.Coferto itaq; prælio, magna cæde Illyrios fudere, offendentes, hostibus suis, priore bello regem Macedonibus, non virtutem defuisse. Huic Amyntas succedit, & propria virtute, & Alexandri filij egregia indole inter clarus: cui Alexandro tanta omnium virtutum natura ornamenta extitere, vt etiam Olympio certamine vario ludicrorum genere contenderit.
units.tr: showed him the place where he wished to be buried, and ordered that there should be laid not only his own bones but also those of the kings who would succeed him. He added that the kingdom would remain in the family as long as the remains of his descendants were buried there. They believe that the line was extinguished in Alexander by this superstition, because he changed the place of burial for the second time. Argaeus administered the kingdom moderately and with the affection of his people, and he left his son Philip as successor. Philip was snatched away by an early death and left Europus, still a small child, as heir. But the Macedonians had constant wars with the Thracians and the Illyrians. Hardened by their arms, as if by daily exercise, they struck fear into their neighbours by their military glory. So the Illyrians, despising the infancy of the boy king, attacked the Macedonians in war. The Macedonians, beaten in battle, brought their king out in his cradle and placed him behind the battle line, and they renewed the contest more fiercely. They reasoned that they had been defeated before because they had lacked the auspices of their king in the fighting, and that they would be victorious now for the same reason, since they took courage from this superstition. At the same time, pity for the infant held them, for they seemed likely to make him a captive by law if they were defeated. So the battle was joined, and they routed the Illyrians with great slaughter, showing their enemies that in the earlier war the Macedonians had lacked a king, not courage. Amyntas succeeded him, distinguished both by his own virtue and by the outstanding character of his son Alexander. Alexander had such natural gifts of every virtue that he even competed at Olympia in a varied kind of athletic contest.

units.la: 3 Cum interim Darius rex Persarum, turpi ab Scythia fuga sumimotus, ne vbiq; deformis militia damnis haberetur, mittit cum parte copiarum Megabazum ad subigendam Thraciam, ceteraq; eius tractus regna: quibus pro ignobili momento erat accessura Macedonia. Qui breui tempore exsecuto regis imperio, legatis ad Amyntam regem Macedoniæ misit, obsides in pignus futuræ pacis dari sibi postulabat. Sed legati benigne excepti, inter epulas ebrietate crescente, rogant Amyntam vt apparatui epularum adiiciat ius familiæ
units.tr: 3 Meanwhile Darius, king of the Persians, roused by a shameful flight from Scythia, and anxious that his military failure should not be regarded as disgraceful everywhere, sent Megabazus with part of the forces to subdue Thrace and the other kingdoms of that region, to which Macedonia would be added as a minor part. Megabazus carried out the king's order in a short time and sent envoys to Amyntas, king of Macedonia, demanding that hostages be given as a pledge of future peace. But the envoys were received kindly, and while they were at the feast, with drunkenness increasing, they asked Amyntas to add to the banquet the right of family intimacy, having his sons and wives brought to his table; among the Persians, they said, this was held to be a pledge and bond of hospitality.

units.tr: When the women and boys came in, the Persians handled them rather wantonly. Alexander, Amyntas' son, asked his father, in view of his own age and dignity, to withdraw from the banquet, promising that he himself would restrain the guests' jokes.

He enlarged his kingdom no less by his own valour than by the generosity of the Persians. Then, in order,

units.tr: 30 and Philip, father of Alexander the Great of Macedon, and a daughter, Eurynoe. By Cynane he had Archelaus, Arrhidaeus and Menelaus. Then he waged serious wars with the Illyrians and the Olynthians. But he was nearly overwhelmed by the plot of his wife Eurydice, who had agreed with her son-in-law to kill her husband and hand the kingdom over to an adulterer, had not his daughter revealed her mother's adultery and the plans of her crime. Having survived so many dangers, the old man died, leaving the kingdom to Alexander, the eldest of his sons.

units.la: & Philippum Alexandri Magni Macedonis patrem, & filiam Euryonem: Ex Cygnaea autem Archelaum, Archideum, Menelaum. Cum Illyriis deinde, & cum Olynthiis grauia bella gesit. Infidus autem Eurydices uxoris, quae nuptias generi pacta, occidendum virum, regnumq; adultero tradendum susceperat, occupatus fuisset, ni filia pellicatum matris & sceleris consilia prodidisset. Functus itaq; tot periculis, senex decessit, regno maximo ex filiis Alexandro, tradito.
units.tr: Philip, the father of Alexander the Great of Macedon, and the daughter Euryone. From Cygnaea came Archelaus, Archideus and Menelaus. Afterwards he waged serious wars against the Illyrians and the Olynthians. He was seized by treachery from his wife Eurydice, who had agreed with her lover to marry her son-in-law, to kill her husband and to hand the kingdom over to her adulterer. He would have been caught had his daughter not revealed the mother's unchastity and her plots of crime. So, having survived so many dangers, he died as an old man, leaving the kingdom to his eldest son Alexander.

units.la: § Igitur Alexander inter prima initia regni, bellum ab Illyriis pacta mercede, & Philippo fratre dato obside, redemit. Interfecto quoq; tempore per eundem obsidem cum Thebanis gratiam pacis reconciliat: quae res Philippo maxima incrementa egregiae indolis dedit. Siquidem Thebis triennio obses habitus, prima pueritia rudimenta, in urbe seueritatis antiqua, & in domo Epaminondae, summi & philosophi & imperatoris, depositus. Nec multo post Alexander infidus Eurydices matris appetitus occumbit: cui Amyntas in scelere dcprebensæ, propter communes liberos, ignarus eisdem quandog₃ exitiosam fore, pepercerat. Frater quoq₃ eius Perdiccas pari insidiarum fraude circumcipitur. Indignum propsus libidinis causa liberos a matre vita privatos, quam scelerum suorum supplicijs liberorum contemplatio vindicauerat. Perdicca hoc dignior cædes videbatur, quod ei apud matrem misericordiam nec paruulus quidem filius coœiliauerat. Itaq₃ Philippus diu non regem, sed tutorem pupilli egit. At vbi grauiora bella imminebant, serumq₃ auxilium in exspectatione infantis erat, compulsus à populo, ᵉregnum suscepit.
units.tr: § Early in his reign Alexander bought off a war with the Illyrians with a payment and redeemed it by giving his brother Philip as a hostage. Later, through the same hostage, he reconciled the peace with the Thebans. This affair gave Philip great opportunities to show his outstanding character. For Philip was held as a hostage at Thebes for three years, and there he laid down the first rudiments of his boyhood, in a city of ancient strictness and in the house of Epaminondas, a man both philosopher and commander of the highest rank. Not long afterwards, Alexander, who had fallen to the lust of his mother Eurydice, died. Amyntas, who had been caught in the crime, had been spared by Alexander because of their common children, not knowing that these children would one day be a deadly danger. His brother Perdiccas was likewise caught in a similar snare of treachery. It was unworthy that children should be deprived of life by their mother for the sake of lust, a mother whom the punishment of her own crimes had been meant to restrain, through regard for her children. The killing of Perdiccas seemed the more deserved because even his little son had not moved his mother to pity. So Philip for a long time acted not as king but as guardian of the boy. But when more serious wars threatened, and help was too slow while they waited for the infant, he was compelled by the people and took up the kingship.

Primum illi cum secta. Atheniensibus certamen fuit: quibus per insidias victis, metu belli grauioris, cum interficere omnes posset, incolumes sine pretio dimisit. units.tr: 6 As soon as he entered upon the rule, everyone had great hopes of him, and not without reason. Both his character, which promised a great man, and the old destiny of Macedonia encouraged this hope. The oracles had foretold that under one of the sons of Amyntas the state of Macedonia would flourish most of all, and the crime of this man's mother had made this hope doubtful. At the beginning of his reign, when the unworthy murders of his brothers on one side, the great number of enemies on another, fear of plots on a third, and the scarcity of a continuous war and an exhausted kingdom pressed upon him, a youth not yet mature, and when wars were gathering from various places as if by a certain conspiracy to crush Macedonia, he judged that he could not face them all at once. So he divided them up: he settled some by interposing a treaty, and he bought off others. He attacked the easiest first, so that their victory would strengthen the frightened spirits of his soldiers and remove their contempt for the enemy. His first contest was with the Athenians. He defeated them by stratagem, and, fearing a more serious war, although he could have killed them all, he dismissed them unharmed and without ransom. After this he turned the war against the Illyrians, and many thousands of the enemy fell. He captured the most famous city of Larissa. From there he attacked Thessaly unexpectedly. He was not driven by greed for plunder, but because he eagerly wished to add the strength of the Thessalian cavalry to his army; the Thessalians, fearing war least of all, were taken by surprise. He made the foot soldiers and the cavalry into one body, the forces of an unconquered army. With these successes going well, he married Olympias, the daughter of Neoptolemus, king of the Molossians. Her brother, the king of the Molossians, Arrybas, arranged the marriage, and he hoped to gain through his cousin's marriage to Philip the sister of Olympias, Troas. But Arrybas was deprived of his own kingdom by Philip and spent his life in exile. After these achievements Philip, no longer content merely to ward off wars, even attacked peaceful peoples of his own accord. When he was besieging the city of Methone, an arrow shot from the walls at a man passing by struck the king's right eye and destroyed it.

units.la: Quo vulnere nec segnior in bellum, nec iracundior aduersus hostes factus est: adeo vt interiectis diebus, pacem deprecantibus dederit; nec moderatus tantum, verumetiam mitis aduersus victos fuerit.
units.tr: He was not made more sluggish in war by this wound, nor more angry against his enemies. So much so that, a few days later, he granted peace to those who begged for it; and he was not only moderate but even merciful towards the conquered.

units.la: ᵉ Dextrum oculum regis effodit] Plutarchus refert, eum oculo priuatum esse, cum per ostii rimam Deum conspicaretur cum Olympiade vxore concumbentem.

units.tr: The defeat of Greece under Philip of Macedon. The Thebans contend with one another over who should crush the Phocians, and the Phocians wage civil war. The Athenians look to the public safety as far as each man can. Philip, on the other hand, cunningly deceives them. He tears Greece apart, joins Cappadocia to Macedonia, and reduces the Phocians and the remaining Greeks to slavish obedience. He practises robbery in various ways. He establishes a monarchy by the greatest injustice. Athenians, Thessalians, Boeotians and Phocians...

units.tr: While the Greek cities each wanted to rule alone, they all lost their power. Rushing headlong into mutual destruction without limit, they came to feel what each had lost only when they were already crushed. Philip, king of Macedon, watching as from a kind of lookout and betraying the liberty of all, fed their quarrels while lending aid to the weaker side. He forced both the defeated and the victors alike to submit to royal slavery. The cause and origin of this evil were the Thebans. When they gained control of affairs, they bore their good fortune with a weak spirit. They proudly accused the Lacedaemonians and the Phocians, whom they had defeated in arms, before the common council of Greece, as though the Lacedaemonians and Phocians had paid only small penalties for their murders and plunder. The Lacedaemonians were charged with having seized the Theban citadel during a truce, and the Phocians with having laid waste Boeotia. It was as if, after arms and war, they had left no room for laws. Since judgment was given at the pleasure of the victors, such huge fines were imposed that they could not be paid. Therefore the Phocians, stripped of their fields, children and wives, and despairing, under a certain Philomelus as leader, seized the very temple of Apollo at Delphi, as if defying the gods. From there, rich in gold and money, they hired mercenary soldiers and made war on the Thebans. The Phocians' deed, although everyone condemned it for sacrilege, nevertheless brought more hatred on the Thebans, by whom they had been driven to this necessity, than on the Phocians themselves. So auxiliaries were sent to them both by the Athenians and by the Lacedaemonians. In the first encounter Philomelus drove the Thebans from their camp. In the next battle he fell fighting in the front ranks of the thickest of the fray, and he paid the penalty for sacrilege with his impious blood. Onomarchus was made leader in his place.

units.la: 2 Aduersus quem Thebani Thessalig, non ex ciuibus suis, ne victoris potentiam ferre non possent, sed Philippum Macedoniæ regem ducem eligunt; & externa dominationi, quam in suis timuerunt, spõnte succedunt. Igitur Philippus quasi sacrilegy, non Thebanorum vltor esset, omnes milites coronas laureas sumere iubet, atq; ita veluti deo duce, in prælium pergit. Phocenses insignibus dei conspectis, conscientia delictorum territi abiectis armis fugam capessunt, pœnasq; violatæ religionis sanguine & cædibus suis pendunt. Incredibile quantum ea res apud omnes nationes Philippo gloriæ dedit. Illum vindicem sacrilegij, illum vltorem religionum, quod orbis viribus expiari debuit, solum qui piacula exigeret extitisse dignum. Itaq; à diis proximus habebatur, per quem deorum maiestas vindicata fit. Sed Athenienses audito belli euentu, ne inGræciam Philippus transiret, angustias Thermopylarum pari ratione sicuti antea aduenientibus Persis:occupaueré; sed nequaquam simili aut virtute, aut causa. siquidem tunc pro libertate Græcia, nunc pro sacrilegio publico, tunc à rapina hostium templa vindicaturi, nunc aduersus vindices, templorum raptores defensuri: agitq; propugnatores sceleris, cuius turpe erat alios vindices suisse: immemores prorsus, quod in dubiis rebus suis, illo deo etiá consiliorum auctore vsi fuerant; quod illo duce tot bella victores inierant; tot vrbes auspicato condiderant; tantum imperium terra mariq; quasicrant; quod nihil sine maiestate numinis eius aut priuata vnquam, aut publica rei gesserant. Tantum facinus admisisse ingenia omni doctrina exculta, pulcherrimis legibus institutisq; formata, vt quid posthac succensere iure barbaris 5 possent, non haberent.
units.tr: Against him the Thessalians, not choosing one of their own citizens lest they be unable to bear the power of a victor, but choosing Philip, king of Macedon, as their leader, and willingly yielding to foreign rule what they feared under their own. So Philip, as though he were avenging sacrilege rather than the Thebans, ordered all his soldiers to take laurel crowns, and thus, as if with a god as leader, he advanced into battle. When the Phocians saw the emblems of the god, terrified by their guilty conscience, they threw down their arms and took to flight, and they paid the penalty for their violated religion with their own blood and slaughter. It is incredible how much glory this deed brought Philip among all nations. He alone seemed worthy to be the avenger of sacrilege, the punisher of religious wrongs, which the strength of the whole world ought to have expiated, and the one who exacted the atonement. So he was regarded as second only to the gods, through whom the majesty of the gods was vindicated. But the Athenians, when they heard the outcome of the war, so that Philip might not cross into Greece, occupied the narrow pass of Thermopylae, in the same way as they had once done against the Persians as they advanced. Yet it was by no means the same in courage or in cause. For then they were defending Greek liberty, but now they defended public sacrilege; then they were going to protect temples from the plunder of enemies, now they were defending the temple-robbers against avengers. They were champions of a crime, when it was shameful for them to be avengers of others; utterly forgetful that in their own doubtful affairs they had used that very god as the author of their counsels; that under his leadership they had waged so many wars as victors, had founded so many cities under auspicious omens, had acquired such an empire by land and sea; that they had never done anything, public or private, without regard to the majesty of his divinity. Minds cultivated by every learning, formed by the finest laws and institutions, had committed so great a crime that they no longer had any right to be angry with barbarians.

units.la: 3 Sed nec Philippus melioris fidei aduersus socios fuit: quippe veluti timens ne ab hostibus sacrilegij scelere vinceretur, ciuitates quarum paulo ante dux fuerat,qua sub auspiciis eius militauerant, qua gratulate 10 illi,sibique victoriam fuerant, hostiliter occupatas diripuit: Coniuges liberosque omnium sub corona venudidit: non deorum immortalium templis, non aedibus sacris, non dis penatibus publicis priuatisque, ad quos paulo ante ingressus hospitaliter fuerat,pepercit: prorsus vt non tam sacrilegij vltor extitisse, quam sacrile15 giorum licentiam quasisse videretur. Inde veluti rebus egregie gestis, in Cappadociam traiicit: vbi bello pari perfidia gesto, captisque per dolum & occisis finitimis regibus, vniuersam prouinciam imperio Macedonia adiungit. Deinde ad abolendam inuidiae famam,qua in-20 signis praeter cateros tum temporis habebatur, per regna mittit,&opuletissimas ciuitates,qui opinione sererent, regem Philippi magna pecunia locare,& muros per ciuitates, & fana,& templa facieda; & vt per pracones 25 suscepto res solicitarent;qui cum in Macedoniam venissent, variis dilationibus frustrati, vim regia maiestatis timeres,taciti proficiscebantur.d Post hac Olynthios ag-greditur: Receperant enim per misericordia post cadem vnius,duos fratres eius,quos Philippus ex nouerca geni30 tos, veluti participes regni interficere gestiebat, Ob hac igitur causam vrbem antiquam & nobilem exscindit;& fratres olim destinato supplicio tradit;praedaq; ingenti, pariter & parricidij voto fruitur. Inde quasi omnia,
units.tr: But Philip was no more faithful toward his allies. As though fearing lest he be defeated by the enemy's sacrilege, he plundered with hostile hand the cities over which he had lately been leader, cities that had served under his auspices, and that had congratulated him and themselves on their victory. He sold the wives and children of everyone under the spear. He spared neither the temples of the immortal gods, nor the sacred buildings, nor the public and private household gods, into whose shrines he had lately entered as a guest. He seemed to be not so much an avenger of sacrilege as a seeker of license for sacrilege. Then, as if he had accomplished great deeds, he crossed into Cappadocia, where, after waging war with equal treachery, and having captured by stratagem and killed the neighboring kings, he joined the whole province to the Macedonian empire. Then, to remove the reputation for hatred, in which he was then notoriously regarded above all others, he sent men through the kingdoms, and to the wealthiest cities, to spread the rumour that King Philip was hiring out large sums of money, and that walls, shrines and temples would be built throughout the cities. And that they should stir up the business by heralds. When these men came to Macedonia, they were cheated by various delays, and, fearing the power of royal majesty, they departed in silence. After this he attacked the Olynthians. For they had received, out of pity, after the murder of one man, two brothers of his, whom Philip, born of a stepmother, was eager to kill as sharers in the kingdom. For this reason he destroyed the ancient and noble city, and handed over the brothers to a punishment long ago decided upon; and he enjoyed the great booty together with the fulfilment of his vow of parricide. Then, as though everything he had planned were permitted to him, he seized the gold mines in Thessaly and the silver mines in Thrace. And so that he might leave no law or right unviolated, he also set about practising piracy.

units.la: d Ex Ioanne Verhaus. qua agitasset animo, ei licerent, auraria in Thessalia, argenti metalla in Thracia occupavit. Et ne quod ius vel fas inuiolatum praetermitteret, piraticam quoq; exercere instituit. His ita gestis, forte euenit, vt cum fratres duo, reges Thraciae, non contemplatione iustitiae eius, sed inuicem metuentes ne alterius viribus accederet, disceptationum suarum iudicem eligerent. Sed Philippus more ingenij sui, ad iudicium veluti ad bellum, inopinantibus fratribus, instructo exercitu superuenit: & regno vtrunq; non iudicij more, sed fraude latronis ac scelere spoliauit.
units.tr: d From Johannes Verhaus. When these things had been done, it happened by chance that two brothers, the kings of Thrace, chose Philip as judge of their disputes, not out of respect for his justice, but because each feared lest the other's forces should come to the other's side. But Philip, true to his nature, came upon them, as if for a battle rather than a judgment, with his army drawn up, while the brothers suspected nothing; and he stripped both of their kingdoms, not in the manner of a judgment, but by the fraud and crime of a robber.

units.la: 4 Dum haec aguntur, legati Atheniensium petentes pacem ad eum venerunt. Quibus auditis, & ipse legatos Athenas cum pacis conditionibus misit: ibiq; ex commodo vtrorumq; pax facta. Ex ceteris quoq; Graeciae ciuitatibus, non pacis amore, sed belli metu legationes venere. Siquidem crudescente ira, Thessali, Boeotiique orant, vt profligatum aduersum Phocenses ducem Graeciae exhibeat: tanto odio Phocensium ardentes, vt obliti cladium suarum, perire ipsi, quam non perdere eos praeoptarent; expertamq; Philippi crudelitatem pati, quam parcere hostibus suis mallent. Contra Phocensium legati, adhibitis Lacedaemoniis & Atheniensibus, bellum deprecabantur, cuius ab eo dilationem ter iam emerant. Fœdum prorsus, miserandumq; spectaculum, Græciam etiam nunc & viribus, & dignitate orbis terrarum principem; regum certe gentiumq; semper victricem, & multarum adhuc vrbium dominam, alienis excusare sedibus; aut rogantem bellum aut deprecantem, in alterius ope omnem spem posuisse orbis 30 terrarum vindices; eoq; discordia sua, ciuilibusq; bellis redactos, vt adulentur vltro sordidam paulo ante clientelæ suæ partem: & hac potissimum facere Thebanos, Lacedæmoniosq; antea inter se imperij, nunc Gracie imperatis æmulos. Philippus, venditatione gloriæ suæ, tantarum vrbium fastidium agitat; atq; vtros potius dignetur,æstimat. Secreto igitur auditis vtrisq; legationibus,his veniam belli pollicetur,iureiurando adactis, 5 responsum nemini prodituros; illis contra venturum se,auxiliumq; laturum : Vtrosq; vetat parare bellum, aut metuere.Sic variato resposo securis omnibus,Thermopylarum angustias occupat.
units.tr: While these things were happening, envoys of the Athenians came to him seeking peace. When he had heard them, he too sent envoys to Athens with the terms of peace, and there peace was made on terms advantageous to both sides. Embassies also came from the other Greek cities, not out of love of peace but out of fear of war. For as anger grew hot, the Thessalians and Boeotians begged that he should hand over the leader of Greece against the Phocians, now defeated. They burned with such hatred of the Phocians that, forgetting their own disasters, they preferred to perish themselves rather than fail to destroy them; and they preferred to suffer the cruelty of Philip, which they had already experienced, rather than spare their enemies. On the other side the envoys of the Phocians, with the Lacedaemonians and Athenians as helpers, pleaded against war, the postponement of which they had already bought from him three times. It was a shameful and pitiable spectacle: Greece, still the leader of the world in strength and dignity, the one that had always been the conqueror of kings and nations and still the mistress of many cities, was seeking excuses from foreign powers, begging for war or begging against it, placing all her hope in another's help, the avengers of the whole world, reduced by her own discord and civil wars to flattering, of her own accord, a part of her clientele that had lately been contemptible. And the Thebans and Lacedaemonians, who had earlier been rivals for empire among themselves, were now doing this above all, when they had been ordered to command Greece. Philip, pursuing the display of his own glory, scorned so many cities and weighed which of them he should deign to favour. So, having heard both embassies in secret, he promised pardon for war to the one side, binding them by oath not to reveal his answer to anyone; to the other he said that he would come and bring aid. He forbade both to prepare for war or to fear it. With his answer thus varied, and everyone off guard, he seized the narrow pass of Thermopylae.

units.la: 5 Tunc primum Phocenses captos se fraude Philippi animaduertentes, trepidi ad arma confugiunt. Sed 10 neq; spatium erat instruendi belli, nec tempus ad contrahenda auxilia : & Philippus excidium minabatur, ni fieret deditio. Victi igitur necessitate, ᶜ pacta salute se dederunt. Sed pactio eius fidei fuit, cuius antea fuerat deprecati belli promisto. Igitur caduntur passim rapiunturq;, non liberi parentibus, non coniuges ma- 15 ritis,non deorum simulacra templis suis relinquuntur: Vnum tantum miseris solatium fuit, quod cum Philippus portione prædæ socios fraudasset, nihil rerū suarum apud inimicos viderunt : Reuersus in regnum, vt pecora pastores nunc in hibernos,nunc in æstiuos saltus 20 traiiciunt, sic ille populos & vrbes,vt illi vel replenda, vel derelinquenda quæq; loca videbantur , ad libidinem suam transfert. Miseranda vbiq; facies , & excidio similis erat:Non quidem pauor ille bostilis,nec discursus per vrbem militum erat; non tumultus armorum; non bonorum atq; hominum rapina: sed tacitus mæror & luctus,verentibus nē ipse lacryme pro contumacia baberentur. Crescit dissimulatione ipsa dolor , hoc altius 30 demissus,quo minus profiteri licet . Nunc sepulcra maiorum,nunc veteres penates,nūc tecta, in quibus geniti erant,in quibus genuerant,considerabant: miserâtes F nunc vicem suam, quod in eam diem vixissent; nunc filiorum, quod non post eam diem nati essent.
units.tr: Then for the first time the Phocians, realizing that they had been trapped by Philip's treachery, fled in alarm to arms. But there was neither time to array the battle nor opportunity to gather help, and Philip threatened destruction unless they surrendered. Therefore, overcome by necessity, they gave themselves up on the promise of safety. But the terms were kept in the same faith as the promise of peace in war they had earlier sought to avoid. So people were cut down and seized everywhere; children were not left to their parents, wives not to their husbands, and the images of the gods were not left in their temples. Their only consolation in their wretchedness was that, since Philip had cheated his allies of their share of the plunder, they saw none of their own goods among the enemy. Returning to his kingdom, as shepherds drive their flocks now to winter pastures and now to summer pastures, so he moved peoples and cities at his pleasure, to whatever places seemed to him to need filling or emptying. Everywhere the sight was pitiable and resembled a ruin. There was not that hostile panic, nor did soldiers rush about the city; there was no tumult of arms, no plundering of goods and men; but there was silent grief and mourning, for they feared that their very tears would be taken as defiance. Grief grows by the very concealment, sinking the deeper the less it is permitted to be expressed. Now they gazed upon the tombs of their ancestors, now upon their old household gods, now upon the roofs under which they had been born and under which they had begotten children; now they pitied their own lot, that they had lived up to that day, and now the lot of their sons, that they had not been born after that day.

units.la: 6 Alios populos in finibus ipsis hostibus opponit; alios in extremis [regni terminis] statuit; quosdam bello captos in supplementis urbium divisit. Atque, ita ex multis gentibus, nationibusque unum regnum populumque constituit. Compositis ordinatisque in Macedonia rebus, Dardanos, ceterosque finitimos fraude captos expugnat. Sed nec à proximis manus abstinet. Siquidem Arrybam regem Epiri, uxori suæ Olympiadi arctissima cognatione iunctum, pellere regno statuit; atque Alexandrum priuignum eius uxoris Olympiadis fratrem, puerum honestæ pulchritudinis, in Macedoniam nomine sororis arcessit, omnique studio solicitatum spe regni, simulato amore ad stupri consuetudinem perpulit, maiora in eo obsequia habituru, sine conscientiæ pudore, sine regni beneficio. Cum igitur ad viginti annos peruenissent, ereptum Arrybæ regnum puero admodum tradit; scelestus in utroque; nam nec in eo ius cognationis seruauit, cui ademit regnum; & eum cui dedit, impudicum fecit ante quam regem.
units.tr: 6 He placed some peoples on the very borders with his enemies, some at the extremities [of the kingdom's boundaries], and divided others, taken in war, among the populations of his cities as reinforcements. Thus from many nations and peoples he made one kingdom and one people. Having put affairs in order in Macedonia, he overcame the Dardanians and the other neighbouring peoples by treachery. Nor did he keep his hands off his own kin. For he resolved to drive Arybbas, king of Epirus, from his kingdom, a man closely related by marriage to his wife Olympias. He summoned to Macedonia, in the name of his sister, Alexander, Olympias's stepson and her brother, a boy of remarkable good looks. Stirring him with every effort by the hope of a kingdom, and feigning love, he drove him into a habit of debauchery, expecting greater compliance from him, without shame of conscience and without any kingdom to reward it. So when they had reached twenty years of age, he handed the kingdom, taken from Arybbas, over to the boy, who was by then quite grown. He was wicked in both respects: he did not keep the claim of kinship in the case of the man from whom he took the kingdom, and he made the one to whom he gave it a debauched man before he made him a king.

units.la: Philippi Alexandrum polluentis, Arrybam spoliantis, iniustitia summa.
units.tr: Philip's injustice was supreme: he defiled Alexander and despoiled Arybbas.

units.la: IN LIB. VIII. IVSTINI scholia Theophili Cangiseri.
units.tr: Scholia on Book 8 of Justin, by Theophilus Cangiserus.

units.la: Apud commune Græcia concilium] Amphictyonicum appellatum ab Amphictyone Deucalionis filio, qui primus illud instituit, vide Pausaniam Phocicis, vbi numerum Amphictyonum & populos Græciæ, qui concilii huius participes fuerunt, & alia copiosè explicat.
units.tr: Before the common council of Greece] Called the Amphictyonic council, after Amphictyon, son of Deucalion, who first established it. See Pausanias in the Phocica, where he explains at length the number of the Amphictyons, the peoples of Greece who took part in this council, and other matters.
{b} Bcl.

units.la: Bellum Thebanis intulerunt] Initium belli sacri, quod incidit in Olympiadis centesimæ quintæ annum quartum ac durauit integrum decennium, teste Pausania.
units.tr: They made war on the Thebans] The beginning of the Sacred War, which fell in the fourth year of the 105th Olympiad and lasted a full ten years, according to Pausanias.

units.la: Dimicans cecidit] iuxta Diodorum aliquot accepti s vulneribus cum in locum angustum inclusus esset, è quo elabi facile non posset, inde se dedit præcipitem, hostium supplicia metuens, si ab eis comprehenderetur.
units.tr: Fighting, he fell] According to Diodorus, some say that he had received several wounds, and that, shut into a narrow place from which he could not easily escape, he threw himself headlong, fearing the punishments of the enemy if he were captured.

units.la: Post hæc Olynthios aggreditur] Olymp. 107. Hinc tres illæ, quæ adhuc extant, orationes Olynthiacæ Demosthenis, quibus hortatur Athenienses, ut Olynthiis contra Philippum ferant suppetias. Sequente anno, quo Philippus Olynthum solo æquauit, Plato mortuus est, de quo vide Laertium lib. 3. & 5. Athen. libro 5, Senecam epist. 18.
units.tr: Afterwards he attacks the Olynthians] In the 107th Olympiad. Hence those three Olynthiac orations of Demosthenes which still survive, in which he urges the Athenians to bring aid to the Olynthians against Philip. In the following year, when Philip razed Olynthus to the ground, Plato died; on him see Diogenes Laertius, books 3 and 5, Athenaeus, book 5, and Seneca, letter 18.

units.la: Pacta salute se dederunt] Ita huic decennali bello impositus est finis. Diodorus lib. 16. Pausan. Phoc. anno quarto olymp. CIIX. Quo anno Demosthenes oratione nem περὶ παραπρεσβείας [scripsit, sed non habuit: in qua suadet, ut Athenienses paciantur Philippum victorem locum Phoceosium occupare in conuentu Amphictyonico. Id quod euenit.
units.tr: They surrendered on terms of safety] Thus an end was put to this ten-year war. Diodorus, book 16; Pausanias, Phocica; in the fourth year of the 108th Olympiad. In that year Demosthenes wrote the speech "On the Embassy" [περὶ παραπρεσβείας], but it was not delivered. In it he urges the Athenians to allow Philip, as victor, to occupy the Phocian seat in the Amphictyonic assembly. This came to pass.
POMPEIUS TROGUS, EPITOME OF THE PHILIPPIC HISTORIES
Book IX. Summary.

units.tr: 1 On the subjugation of Greece. Philip, pursuing his plans in various ways, is thwarted, so he takes up arms, and the booty is carried off. He besieges Byzantium, but in vain. 3 The Triballi strip Philip of his booty. The Athenians and the Thebans he crushes in battle.

units.la: 2 A Scytharum rege va-Thebanos pœlio atterit.
units.tr: 2 He is harassed by the king of the Scythians, and he defeats the Thebans in battle.

units.la: 4 Victoria moderate v- niquo iudice exigens, titur: Sæuit in Thebanos, 7 Olympiade & Alexanqui fortiter se gerunt. dro conscius Philippus in-
units.tr: 4 Victory, moderately used, though the judge is unfair, and the Thebans, who fought bravely. He rages against the Thebans, 7 and Philip, aware of the plot of Olympias and Alexander, is killed.

units.la: 5 Græciam pacare stu- terficitur, det, vt Persas bello adoria- 8 Philippi elogium , etur. iufdemque cum Alexandro
units.tr: 5 He seeks to pacify Greece so that he may attack the Persians in war; 8 Philip's eulogy, and his comparison with his son and successor Alexander.

units.la: 6 Paufanias Philippum filio & successore comparaobtruncat, vltionem ab i- tio.
units.tr: 6 Pausanias cuts down Philip, taking vengeance for the injury.

units.la: N Græciam Philippus cum venisset, folicitatus paucarum ciuitatium direptione; & ex preda modicarum vrbium, quanta opes vniuersarum effent animo prospiciens, bellum toti Græciæ inferre statuit. Ad cuius emolumentum egre-
units.tr: When Philip had come to Greece, stirred up by the plundering of a few cities, and considering in his mind from the booty of small towns how great the resources of all the cities were, he resolved to make war on all Greece.

units.la: gie pertinere ratus, fi Byzantium, nobilem & maritimam vrbem, receptaculum terra maris, copiis suis suturum, in potestatem redegisset. Eandem claudentem sibi portas, obsidione cinxit. Hac namq; vrbs condita primo a Paufania rege Spartanorum, & per 7. annos possessa fuit: deinde variante victoria, nuncLacedæmoniorum, nunc Atheniensium iuris habita est. Quæ incerta possessio effecit, vt nemine quasi suam auxilio iuuante, libertatem constantius tueretur. Igitur Philippus longa obsidionis mora exhaustus, pecunia commercium depiratica mutuatur. Captis itaq; centu feptuaginta nauibus mercium, & distractis, anhelantem inopiam paululum recreauit. Deinde, ne vnius vrbis oppugnatione tantus exercitus tereretur, profeCtus cum fortissimis, multas Cherfonenfium vrbes expugnat, Filiumq; b Alexandrum decem & octo annos natum, vt sub militia patris tyrocinij rudimenta deponeret, ad fe arcessit. In Scythiam quoq; prædandi causa profectus est, more negotiantium, impensas belli alio bello refe- rturus.
units.tr: He thought it would be greatly to his advantage if he could bring Byzantium, a noble maritime city and the receptacle of land and sea, under his power with his forces. He surrounded with siege the city, which was closing its gates against him. This city was first founded by Pausanias, king of the Spartans, and was held for seven years; then, as victory shifted, it was held at one time under the rule of the Lacedaemonians and at another under that of the Athenians. This uncertain possession meant that no city, having no one to help it as its own, defended its liberty more steadfastly. So Philip, worn out by the long delay of the siege, borrowed money from pirates against their trade. Having therefore captured and sold a hundred and seventy ships of merchandise, he relieved his gasping want for a little while. Then, so that so great an army would not be worn down by the attack on a single city, he set out with his strongest troops, took many cities of the Chersonesus, and summoned to him his son Alexander, eighteen years old, so that he might lay down the first rudiments of soldiering under his father's command. He also set out against Scythia for the sake of plunder, like a trader, intending to recover the expenses of one war by another.
b

units.la: 2 Erat eo tempore rex Scytharum Atheas,qui cum bello Istrianorum premeretur,auxilium à Philippo per Apollinensis petit, in successionem eum regni Scythiæ adoptaturus. cum interim Istrianorum rex decedens,
units.tr: 2 At that time the king of the Scythians was Atheas, who, being hard pressed by a war with the Istrians, sought help from Philip through the men of Apollonia, intending to adopt him as successor to the kingdom of Scythia; but meanwhile the king of the Istrians died,

units.la: 5 & metu belli,& auxiliorum necessitate Scythas soluit. Itaq; Atheas remisit Macedonibus renuntiari Philippo iubet, neq; auxilium eius se petisse, neq; adoptionem mandasse. Nam neq; vindicta Macedonum egere Scythas,quibus meliores forent: neq; heredem sibi incolu-
units.tr: 5 and the fear of war and the need for help released the Scythians. So Atheas ordered word to be sent back to the Macedonians for Philip: that he had neither asked for his help nor commissioned an adoption. For the Scythians had no need of Macedonian vengeance, being the better men, nor did he lack an heir while his son was alive.

units.la: 10 mi filio deesse. His auditis Philippus legatos ad Atheam mittit,iumpense obsidionis portionem petentes, ne inopia deferere bellum cogatur. Quod eo promptius cum facere debere, quod mifus à se in auxilium eius militibus, ne sumptum quidem viæ, non modo officij pretia
units.tr: 10 When Philip heard this, he sent envoys to Atheas, demanding a share of the expenses of the siege, so that he would not be forced by want to abandon the war. He ought to do this the more readily, they said, since the soldiers he had sent to his aid had not received even the cost of the journey, let alone the reward for their service.

units.la: 15 dederit. Atheas inclementiam cœli, & terræ sterilitatem causatus , quæ non patrimoniis ditet Scythas, sed vix alimentis exhibeat, respondit nullas sibi opes esse, quibus tantum regem expleat;& turpius putare paruo defungi,quam totum abnuere: Scythas autem virtute
units.tr: 15 Atheas pleaded the harshness of the sky and the barrenness of the land, which does not enrich the Scythians with wealth but scarcely supplies them with food. He replied that he had no resources with which to satisfy so great a king, and that it was more shameful to pay a small sum than to refuse altogether. The Scythians, he said, are valued for courage of spirit and hardness of body, not for wealth.

units.tr: 25 which he said he had come to set up at the mouth of the Ister, asking for a peaceful approach to the worship of the god, and promising to come himself as a friend to the Scythians. Atheas, if Philip wished to fulfil his vow, ordered that a statue of Philip himself be set up; he promised not only that it would be protected but that it would remain inviolate. But he refused to let the army enter his borders. And if Philip set up the statue against the will of the Scythians, he would carry it away when Philip withdrew and turn it into the points of arrows.

units.la: 30 tis Scythis statuam ponat,eo digresso sublaturum;versurumq; es statuæ in aculeos sagittarum. His vtrimq;, irritatis animis, prælium committitur. Cum virtute & animo præstarent Scythæ, astu Philippi vincuntur. Viginti millia puerorum ac feminarum capta, pecora magna vis, auri argenti, nihil. Ea fides primum ingenii Scythicae fuit. Viginti millia nobilium equarum ad genus faciendum in Macedoniam missa.
units.tr: 30 With the minds of both sides provoked, battle was joined. Although the Scythians excelled in courage and spirit, they were conquered by the cunning of Philip. Twenty thousand boys and women were taken, a great quantity of cattle, and little gold or silver. This was the first proof of the Scythian character. Twenty thousand noble mares were sent to Macedonia to breed a race.

units.la: 3 Sed reuertenti ab Scythia, Triballi Philippo occurrunt; negant se transitum daturos, ni portionem praedae accipiant: Hinc iurgium, & mox praelium; in quo ita in femore vulneratus est Philippus, ut per corpus eius equus interficeretur. Cum omnes occisum putarent, praeda amissa est. Ita Scythica, velut deuota, spolia pene luctuosa Macedonibus fuere. Vbi vero ex vulnere primum convaluit, diu dissimulatum bellum Athenienfibus infert: quorum causa Thebani se iunxere, metuentes ne vicitis Atheniensibus, veluti vicinum imcendiū belli ad se transfiret. Facta igitur inter duas palo ante infestissimas ciuitates societate, legationibus Graeciam fatigant, communem hostem putat communibus viribus summouendum: neq; enim cessaturum Philippum, si prosperè prima successerint, nisi omnem Graciam dominerit. Mox quaedam ciuitates Athenienfibus se iungunt: quaedam autem ad Philippū belli metus traxit. 6 Praelio commisso, cum Athenienses longe maiore militum numero praestarent, assiduis bellis indurata virtute Macedonum vincuntur, nō tamen immemores pristina gloria cecidere: quippe aduersis vulneribus, omnes loca quae tuenda a ducibus acceperant, morientes corporibus texerunt. Hic dies vniuerse Gracia & gloriam dominationis, & vetustissimam libertatem finiuit.
units.tr: 3 But as he was returning from Scythia, the Triballi met Philip and refused to let him pass unless they received a share of the booty. From this came a quarrel, and soon a battle, in which Philip was wounded in the thigh so badly that the horse under him was killed by the wound passing through his body. When everyone thought he was dead, the booty was lost. Thus the Scythian spoils, as if accursed, were nearly fatal to the Macedonians. But when Philip first recovered from his wound, he launched war against the Athenians, which he had long put off. The Thebans joined them for their sake, fearing that if the Athenians were defeated, the fire of war, as if from a neighbouring house, would spread to them. So an alliance was made between two cities that had long been most hostile to each other, and they wearied all Greece with embassies. Philip judged that a common enemy must be driven off by common forces, for he would not cease, if his first successes went well, until he had dominated all Greece. Soon some cities joined the Athenians, while others were drawn to Philip by fear of war. 6 When battle was joined, the Athenians, who had a far greater number of soldiers, were defeated by the courage of the Macedonians, which war had hardened; yet, not forgetful of their former glory, they fell, for with their wounds in front they covered with their bodies all the places which they had received from their commanders to defend, and died there. That day ended for all Greece both the glory of its supremacy and its most ancient liberty.

units.la: 4 Huius victoria callide d dissimulata laetitia est. Denique, non solita sacra Philippus illa die fecit; non in conuiuio risit; non ludos inter epulas adhibuit; non coronas aut vngueta sumpsit; & quantum in illo fuit ita vicit,vt victorem nemo sentiret: Sed nec regē se Gracia sed ducem appellari iußit. Atqa ita inter tacitā latitiam & dolorem hostiū temperauit, vt neq; apud suos exultasse,neq; apud victos infultasse videretur. Atheniensi5 bus, quos passus infestissimos fuerat, & captiuos gratis remisit;& bello consumptorū corpora sepultura reddidit;reliquiasq; funerū vt ad sepulchra maiorum deferrent,vltro hortatus est. Super hac Alexandrū filium cū amico Antipatro,qui pacē cum his amicitiamq; iunge10 ret, Athenas misit. Thebanorū porro non solum captiuos,verumetiā interfectorum sepulturā vendidit:Principes ciuitatis alios securi percussit,alios in exiliū redegit, bonaq; omnium occupauit. Pulsos deinde per iniuriam, in patriam restituit; ex horum num. 300. exules 15 iudices,rectoresq; ciuitati dedit:apud quos cū potentissimi quiq; sei eius ipsius criminis postularetur,quod per iniuriam se irexiliū egissent,huius constantiafuerunt, vt omnes se auctores fateretur, melius, cum republica actum cū damnati essent,quam cum restituti cōtende20 ret. Mira prorsus audacia:de iudicibus vita necisq; sua, quemadmodū possunt,sententiā ferunt,contemnunt q, absolutionem quam dare inimici possunt: & quoniam rebus nequeunt vlcisci, verbis vsurpant libertatem.
units.tr: 4 Philip concealed his joy over this victory shrewdly. He did not perform the customary sacrifices that day; he did not laugh at the feast; he did not bring in games among the banquets; he did not take up garlands or perfumes; and so far as lay in him he conquered in such a way that no one would perceive him as the victor. He ordered himself to be called not the king of Greece but its leader. Thus he tempered his silent joy and his grief for the enemy so that he seemed neither to have exulted among his own people nor to have insulted the vanquished. He released without ransom the Athenians, whom he had suffered as most hostile, and he restored the bodies of those who had fallen in the war for burial, and urged them to carry the remains of the dead to the tombs of their ancestors. Besides this, he sent his son Alexander, with his friend Antipater, to Athens, to make peace and to forge friendship with them. As for the Thebans, he sold not only the prisoners but also the burial of the dead. He beheaded some of the leaders of the state, drove others into exile, and seized the property of all. Then he restored to their homeland, by unjust means, those who had been expelled, and from among these he appointed three hundred exiles as judges and rulers of the state. When the most powerful of them were charged with the very crime of having driven others into exile unjustly, they showed such constancy that all of them confessed to being the authors of it, and they preferred to argue that the state had fared better when they were condemned than when they were restored. A truly remarkable audacity! They pronounce sentence on their judges with their own lives and deaths, as far as they can, and they despise the acquittal which their enemies can grant; and since they cannot avenge themselves by deeds, they claim their liberty in words.

units.la: 5 Compositis in Gracia rebus, Philippus omniū ci25 uitatium legatos ad formandum rerū prasentium statum euocari Corinthum iubet.Ibi pacis legem vniuersa Gracia pro meritis singularum ciuitatiū statuit;conciliumq; omnium,veluti vnum senatum,ex omnib. elegit.
units.tr: 5 When affairs in Greece had been settled, Philip ordered envoys from all the cities to be summoned to Corinth to fix the state of the present affairs. There he laid down the law of peace for all Greece according to the merits of each city, and from all of them he chose a council, like a single senate.

units.la: Soli Lacedæmonij,& regem,& leges conseruerunt:ser30 uitutem non pacem rati,quæ non ipsis ciuitatibus conueniret,sed à victore ferretur. Auxilia deinde singularum ciuitatium describuntur,siue adiuuandus ea manu rex oppugnante aliquo foret,seu duce illo bellū infe- renrendum : neq; enim dubium erat, imperium Persarum bis apparatibus peti. Summa auxiliorum duecenta millia peditum fuere, & equitum quindecim millia. Extra hanc summam & Macedonia exercitus erat, & confinis domitarum gentium barbaries. Initio veris tres duces in Asiam Persarum iuris pramittit, Parmenionem, Amyntam, & Attalum, cuius sororem nuper expulsa Alexandri matre Olympiade propter stupri suspicionem, in matrimonium receperat.
units.tr: Only the Lacedaemonians preserved both their king and their laws, judging that it was slavery and not peace, one that did not suit the cities themselves but was imposed by the victor. Then the auxiliary forces of the individual cities were listed, whether the king should be aided with that force when he was attacking someone, or whether war was to be waged under that leader; for there was no doubt that the empire of the Persians was being sought with these preparations. The total of the auxiliaries came to two hundred thousand foot soldiers and fifteen thousand horsemen. Beyond this total there was also the army of Macedonia and the barbarian tribes of the neighbouring conquered peoples. At the beginning of spring he sent three commanders ahead into Asia, under Persian rule: Parmenion, Amyntas, and Attalus, whose sister he had recently taken in marriage after Alexander's mother Olympias had been driven out on suspicion of adultery.

units.la: 6 Interea dum auxilia à Graecia coëunt, nuptias Cleopatrae filiae, & Alexandri, quem regem Epiri secerat, celebrat. Dies erat pro magnitudine duorum regum, & collocantis filiam, & vxorem ducentis, apparatibus insignis. Sed nec ludorum magnificentia decerat: ad quorum spectaculum Philippus cum fine cusledibus, medius inter duos Alexandros filium generumq; contenderet, rem aegre ferens Pausanias, querelam Philippo saepe detulerat. Cum variis frustrationibus non fine risu differretur, & honoratum insuper ducatu aduersarium cerneret, iram in ipsum Philippum vertit; vltionemq; quā ab aduersario non poterat, ab iniquo iudice exegit.
units.tr: 6 Meanwhile, while auxiliary forces were gathering from Greece, he celebrated the wedding of his daughter Cleopatra to Alexander, whom he had made king of Epirus. The day was remarkable for its preparations, fitting the rank of the two kings, the one giving away his daughter and the other taking a wife. Nor was there any lack of splendour in the games. At their spectacle Philip walked with only a few guards between his two Alexanders, son and son-in-law. Pausanias, taking this badly, had often brought his complaint to Philip. When the matter was put off with various excuses, not without laughter, and he saw his rival even honoured with a command, he turned his anger against Philip himself. The vengeance he could not take from his rival he exacted from an unjust judge.

units.la: 7 Creditum est etiam immissum ab Olympiade matre Alexandri fuisse; nec ipsum Alexandrum ignarum paterna cadis extitisse: quippe non minus Olympiapiadem repudium, & pralatam sibi Cleopatram, quā fluprum raufaniam doluisse. Alexandrum quoque, regni emulum fratrem [ex nouerca susceptum timuiffe: eoq; actum, vt in conuiuio antea primum cum Attalo, mox cum ipso patre iurgaret; adeo vt etiam stristo gladio eum Philippus consectatus fit , agreq; a filij cæde amicorum precibus exoratus. Quamobrem Alexander ad auunculum fe in Epirum cum matre, inde ad regem Illyriorum contulerat: vixq; reuocanti mitigatus est patri, precibusque cognatorum agre redire compulsus: Olympias quoq; fratrem suum Alexandrū Epiri regem in bellum subornabat, peruiciffetq; ni filia nuptijs pater generum occupaffet. His stimulis irarum vtriq; Paufaniam de impunitate stupri sui querentem, ad tantum facinus impulisse creduntur: Olympias terte fugienti percussori, equos quoq; præparatos habuit.] Ipsa deinde audita regis nece, cum titulo officij ad exequias cucurrisset, in cruce pendentis Paufaniæ capiti, eadem nocte qua venit, coronam auream imposuit: quod nemo alius audere, nisi hæc, superstite Philippi filio potuisset. Paucos deinde post dies, refixum corpus interfectoris super reliquias mariti cremauit; & tumulum ei eodem fecit in loco, parentariq; eodem quotannis, incussa populo superstitione, curauit. Post hac Cleopatram, à qua pulsa Philippi matrimonio fuerat, in gremio eius prius filia interfecta finire vitam suspendio coegit, spectaculoq; pendentis vltionem potita est, ad quam per parricidium festinauerat. Nouissime gladium, quo rex percussus est, Apollini sub nomine Myrtalis consecrauit: Hoc enim nomen ante Olympiadis paruula fuit. Quæ omnia ita palam facta sunt, vt timuiffe videatur ne facinus ab ea commissum, non probaretur.
units.tr: 7 It is also believed that Olympias, Alexander's mother, set him on, and that Alexander himself was not ignorant of the plot against his father. For Olympias grieved no less at her repudiation, and at Cleopatra being preferred to her, than Pausanias grieved at his debauching. Alexander too feared his rival for the kingdom, his half-brother born of the stepmother. Hence it came about that at a banquet he first quarrelled with Attalus, and soon afterwards with his father himself. So far did it go that Philip pursued him with a drawn sword, but the king, calmed, was persuaded by the prayers of friends not to kill his son. Therefore Alexander withdrew with his mother to his uncle in Epirus, and from there to the king of the Illyrians. He was only with difficulty softened when his father recalled him, and he was compelled by the entreaties of his relatives to return. Olympias too was inciting her brother, Alexander king of Epirus, to war, and would have succeeded had the father not secured the son-in-law by marriage to his daughter. By these goads of anger on each side, they are believed to have driven Pausanias, complaining of the impunity of his debauchery, to so great a deed. Olympias also had horses ready for the fleeing assassin. [When the news of the king's death was heard, she hurried to the funeral under the pretext of duty, and on the very night of her arrival she placed a golden crown on the head of Pausanias hanging on the cross. No one else would have dared to do this, except one who survived Philip's son.] A few days later she had the body of the murderer taken down and burned over the remains of her husband, and built a tomb for him in the same place, and saw to it that he was honoured with yearly funeral rites there, having instilled superstition into the people. Afterwards she forced Cleopatra, by whom she had been expelled from Philip's marriage, to end her life by hanging, after her daughter had first been killed in her lap. By the spectacle of the hanging she obtained the vengeance for which she had hurried through parricide. Lastly she consecrated the sword with which the king was struck to Apollo under the name Myrtalis, for this had been her own name as a little girl, before she was called Olympias. All these things were done so openly that she seems to have feared the deed committed by her would not be approved.

units.la: Olympiadis in Philippum & quæ Philippo chara fuerunt, imanitas.
units.tr: The savagery of Olympias towards Philip, and towards those things which were dear to Philip.
8 Philip died in his forty-seventh year, having reigned

units.la: nis 15. regnasset. Genuit ex Lariffæa saltatrice filium Aridæum, qui postea Alexandrum regnauit. Habuit & alios multos ex variis matrimonii regio more fusceptos, qui partim fato, partim ferro periere. Fuit rex armorum quam conuiuiorum apparatibus studiosior; cuius maxima opes erant instrumenta bellorum: diuitiarum quæstu, quam custodia folertior. Itaq; inter quotidianas rapinas semper inops erat. Misericordia in eo & perfidia pari iure dilecta. Nulla apud eum turpis ratio vincendi: blandus pariter, & insidiosus alloquio; qui plura promitteret, quam præstaret: in feria & iocos artifex. Amicitias vtilitate, non fide colebat. Gratiam fingere in odio, instruere inter concordantes odia, apud vtrumq; gratiam quærere, solemnis illi consuetudo. Inter hæc eloquentia, & insignis oratio, acuminis & folertiæ plena; vt nec ornatui facilitas, nec facilitati
units.tr: for 15 years. He begot by the dancer Larissaea a son Arrhidaeus, who afterwards reigned as Alexander. He had many other children by various marriages, taken in the royal manner, who perished partly by fate and partly by the sword. He was a king more devoted to the equipment of war than to the splendour of banquets; his greatest resources were the instruments of war. He was more skilled at getting wealth than at keeping it, so that amid his constant plunder he was always short of money. Mercy and treachery were equally dear to him. No base method of winning was beneath him: he was as charming in conversation as he was deceitful, and he promised more than he would perform, skilled in jests and in tricks. He cultivated friendships for advantage, not for loyalty. To feign favour amid hatred, to stir up enmities between those who were in agreement, and to seek favour with both sides, was his customary practice. Besides these, he had eloquence and a remarkable oratory, full of sharpness and cleverness, so that his ease of speech lacked no ornament, nor his ornament lacked ease in invention.

units.la: inuentionum deesset ornatus. Huic Alexander filius suacessit, & virtute & vitiis patre maior. Itaq; vincendi ratio vtriq;, diuersa: Hic aperte, ille artib. bella tractabat. Deceptis ille gaudere hostibus, hic palam fusis. Prudentior ille consilio, hic animo magnificentior. Iram pater dissimulare, plerumq; etiam vincere, hic vbi exarsit, nec delatio vltionis, nec modus erat. Vini nimis vulpinæ, mis wergauidus, sed ebrietatis diuersa vitia. Patri mos erat etiam de coniuio in hostem procurrere, periculis se temere offerre: Alexander non in hostem, sed in suos sæuiebat. Quamobrem Philippum sepe vulneratum præliaremisere; hic amicorum interfectore conuiuio frequenter excessit. Regnare ille cum amicis nolebat, hic in armicos regna exercebat. Amari pater malle, hic metui. Litterarum cultus vtriq; similis. Solertia pater maior, hic fidei. Verbis atq; oratione Philippus, hic rebus modes-
units.tr: Alexander, his son, succeeded him, greater than his father both in virtue and in vices. So the methods of conquering were different for each: the one waged war openly, the other by artifice. The one rejoiced in deceiving his enemies, the other in defeating them outright. The one was more prudent in counsel, the other more magnificent in spirit. The father used to conceal his anger and often even master it; the son, once it flared up, had neither restraint in taking revenge nor any measure. Both were given to wine, but the vices of their drunkenness were different. It was the father's custom to rush from the banquet against the enemy and rashly expose himself to danger; Alexander raged not against the enemy but against his own men. Therefore battles often sent Philip home wounded, while the son often left the feast after killing friends. The one did not want to rule with his friends, the other exercised his power against his friends. The father preferred to be loved, the son to be feared. Devotion to letters was similar in both. The father was greater in cleverness, the son in good faith. In words and oratory Philip was more restrained,

units.la: moderatior. Parcendi vitiis filio animus & promptior, & bonefiior. Frugalitati pater, luxuriæ filius magis deditus erat. Quibus artibus orbis imperij fundamenta pater iecit, operis totius gloriam filius consummauit.
units.tr: and in deeds the son was more moderate. The son's mind was readier and more inclined to pardon vices, and more beneficent. The father was more devoted to thrift, the son to luxury. By these arts the father laid the foundations of the empire of the world; the son brought the glory of the whole work to completion.

units.la: ² Obsidione cinxit] Ad opem Byzantiis ferendam Demolithenes hortatur Atheniensis Philippica oratione quarta.
units.tr: He surrounded it with a siege] Demosthenes, in his fourth Philippic oration, urges the Athenians to bring help to the Byzantines.

units.la: ᵇ Alexandri ums decem & octo annos natum] Cum effer in lucem editus anno primo centesimæ sextæ Olymp. qui est annus mundi tertmilles. sexcentesimus decimus sextus. Die ipsius natali, ut refert Plutarchus in Alexandro Dianæ Ephesiæ conflagrauit. Quo incendio Magi, quotquot Ephesi tum fuerunt; perterriti faciem pugnis cecederunt, clamaruntque, ingentem illud cladem ac prænimiam vniuersæ Asiæ portendere.
units.tr: Alexander, now eighteen years old] He was born in the first year of the 106th Olympiad, which is the year of the world 3616. On the day of his birth, as Plutarch relates in his Life of Alexander, the temple of Diana at Ephesus burned down. At that fire, all the Magi then at Ephesus beat their faces with their fists, crying out that this great disaster foretold a great calamity for the whole of Asia.

units.la: ᶜ Prælio commisso] Ad Chæroneam vrbem PœFuit hoc olymp. CX. anno tertio. à M. C. termicentesimo trigesimo quarto. Hac clade cognita ille ad tes inedia quatridui seipse necauit, cum Athenas quàm tum ab hoste occupatas adspiceret se posse negare, vt Plu- tarchus prodidit in vitis Rhetorum.
units.tr: The battle having been joined] This took place at the town of Chaeronea in the third year of the 110th Olympiad, in the year 334 before Christ. When this defeat became known, Demosthenes starved himself to death over four days, since he could not bear to see Athens, then occupied by the enemy, as Plutarch reports in his Lives of the Orators.

units.la: ᵈ Dissimulata lætitia est] In causa fuit Demadis oratoris παρρησία, qui regi ob victoriam petulantius exsultanti; mores theriscos in Agamemnonis persona ex- probrasse dicitur. Ea libertate mitigatus Philippus, cum oratorem vinculis liberari iussit, tum ea, quam Iustinus hic describit, laudabili erga victos clementia & moderatione vsus fuit: cum antea multo repletus mero, per mediam captiuorum turbam saltare, ac suas illis calamitates obiicere non erubuisset. Diod. lib. 16. sub. an. 23.
units.tr: His joy was concealed] The cause was the frankness (παρρησία) of the orator Demades, who is said to have reproached Philip, who was exulting too insolently over his victory, with having the character of a Thersites in the role of Agamemnon. Philip was moderated by this frankness, and ordered the orator to be freed from his chains. Then he showed that praiseworthy clemency and moderation towards the defeated that Justin describes here, although before this, filled with much wine, he had not been ashamed to dance through the middle of the crowd of captives and to throw their misfortunes in their faces. Diodorus, book 16, under the year 23.

units.la: ᵉ Paulanias nobilis adolescens] Vnus è stipatoribus regii corporis. Cædis causam Diod. paulo aliter exponit; extremo libro 16. vbi dicit inter alia, Paulaniam magis esse incitat ad facinus ab Hermocrate Sophista, qui ei sciscitanti, qua ratione celebris euasurus esset, respondit: εἰ τὰ μίγιστα πεῖξαντα ἀνίλοι, si eum, qui res maximas gessisset, è medio tolleret.
units.tr: The noble youth Pausanias] He was one of the bodyguards of the royal person. Diodorus explains the cause of the murder a little differently, at the end of book 16, where he says among other things that Pausanias was urged to the deed by the sophist Hermocrates, who, when Pausanias asked how he might become famous, answered: [εἰ τὰ μέγιστα πράξαντα ἀνέλοι] if he should remove the man who had accomplished the greatest deeds.

units.la: Incidit mors Philippiin annum mundi ter milles.sexcentesimum, trigesimum sextum,
units.tr: Philip's death fell in the year of the world 3636.

units.la: Perfidia] Πίσιν πλιμπε μάλισα ἀνθρώπων. Fides nulli mortalium minori curæ fuit Paufan. Achaicis & Stoboeo referente, cum hostibus dixit agendum esse ἢ δόλῳ ἢ βίᾳ: ἢ ἀμφαδὸν, ἢ κρυβηδὸν: dolus, an virtus quis in hoste requirat.
units.tr: Faithlessness] [πίστιν πλεῖστα μάλιστα ἀνθρώπων] He cared least of all men for good faith. Pausanias, in his Achaica, and Stobaeus, citing him, report that he said enemies must be dealt with either by guile or by force, either openly or in secret: whether one seeks cunning or courage in an enemy.

units.la: Nulla apud eum turpis ratio vincendi] Valerius eum non victorem, sed mercatorem Græciæ ait fuisse maiori ex parte, nec à Philippo, sed Philippi auro Græciam suisse superatam.
units.tr: He had no shameful method of conquering] Valerius says that for the most part he was not a conqueror of Greece but its merchant, and that Greece was overcome not by Philip but by Philip's gold.

units.tr: 1 Artaxerxes' sons conspire against their father. Ochus rages against his sons. His accession fills the royal house with the slaughter of his kinsmen and princes.

units.la: 2 Causa parricidii,ex mul- pum strage regiam replet. tiplici libidine nata. Persicæ monarchiæ finis.
units.tr: 2 The cause of the parricide arose from manifold lust. The end of the Persian monarchy.

units.la: ARTAXERXES regi Persarum ex pellicibus 115. filij fuere,sed tres tantum iusto matrimonio suscepti Darius,Ariarates,& Ochus. Ex his Darium contra morem Persarum, apud quos rex non nisi morte mutatur, per indulgentiam pater regem viuus fecit; nihil sibi ablatum existimans, quod in filium contulisset, sinceriusq; gaudium ex procreatione capturus, si insignia maiestatis sua vi- uus in filio conspexisset. Sed Darius post nouá paterna pietatis exempla, interficiendi patris consilium cepit. Sceleratus, si solus parricidium cogitasset; tanto scelera5 tior, quod in societatem facinoris assumptos, quinquaginta fratres fecit parricidas. Ostenti prorsus genus, vbi in tanto populo non solum sociari, verumetiam sileri parricidium potuit; vt ex quinquaginta liberis nemo inuentus fit, quem aut paterna maiestas, aut vene10 ratio fenis, aut indulgentia patris, à tanta immanitate renocaret. Adeone vile paternum nomen apud tot numero filios fuit, vt quorum praesidio tutus etiam aduersus hostes esse debuerat, eorum insidiis circumuentus, tutior ab hostibus, quam à filiis fuerit?
units.tr: Artaxerxes had 115 sons by concubines, but only three born of a lawful marriage: Darius, Ariarates and Ochus. Contrary to the custom of the Persians, among whom a king is changed only by death, their father out of indulgence made Darius king while he was still alive. He thought he lost nothing of his own by what he had bestowed on his son, and he expected a purer joy from his offspring if he saw the marks of his majesty in his son while he himself still lived. But after these new examples of paternal kindness, Darius resolved to kill his father. He would have been wicked enough had he planned the parricide alone; but he was more wicked still, because he took fifty brothers into partnership in the crime and made them all parricides. It was truly a monstrous thing, where among so great a people the parricide could not only be shared but also kept silent; for among the fifty sons no one was found whom either their father's majesty, or reverence for his years, or his indulgence should call back from such great savagery. Was a father's name so cheap among so many sons that he, who ought to have been safe even against enemies by their protection, was surrounded by their plots and was safer from enemies than from his sons?

units.la: 2 Causa parricidij sceleratior ipso parricidio fuit. Occiso quippe Cyro fraterno bello, cuius mentio supra habita est, Asp asiam pellicem eius rex Artaxerxes in matrimonium receperat. Hanc patrem cedere sibi, sicut regnum, Darius postulauerat: qui pro indulgentia 20 sua in liberos, primo facturum se dixerat; mox poenitentia ductus, vt honeste negaret, quod temere promiserat, Solis eam sacerdotio praefecit, quo perpetua illi ab omnibus viris pudicitia imperabatur. Hinc exacerbatus iuuenis, in iniuria primo patris erupit; mox facta 25 cum fratribus coniuratione, dum patri insidias parat, deprehensus cum sociis, poenas parricidij diis paternæ maiestatis vltoribus dedit. Coniuges quoq; omnium cū liberis, ne quod vestigium tanti sceleris extaret, intersecta. Post hac Artaxerxes morbo ex dolore contracto 30 decedit; rex quam pater felicior.
units.tr: 2 The cause of the parricide was more wicked than the parricide itself. For after Cyrus was killed in the civil war, mentioned above, King Artaxerxes had taken Aspasia, Cyrus' concubine, as his wife. Darius had demanded that his father give her to him, as he had given him the kingdom. At first, from his indulgence towards his children, the father said he would do it; but afterwards, moved by regret, and in order to refuse honourably what he had rashly promised, he placed her in the priesthood of the Sun, by which she was bound to perpetual chastity from all men. The young man, enraged by this, at first broke out in complaints against his father for the wrong done to him; then, having formed a conspiracy with his brothers, while he was preparing a plot against his father, he was caught with his accomplices and paid the penalty for parricide to the gods, the avengers of paternal majesty. The wives of them all, together with their children, were also put to death, so that no trace of so great a crime might remain. Afterwards Artaxerxes died of a illness brought on by grief; a king more fortunate than his father.

units.la: Libri duo, qui sequuntur, Alexandri M. res gestas continent: quibus percensendis in Diodori quoque bibliotheca liber 17. totus consumitur. Eas olim tum alii complures, tum Callisthenes Aristotelis discipulus, & Aristobulus & Ptolemæus, qui adsidui regis comites rerumque omnium ὑπομνήματα fuerunt, litteris ac memoriæ prodiderunt. Quorum scripta tamen nobis hominü ac temporum iniquitas iamdudum eripuit. Soli adhuc superfuntde Græcis quidem præter Diodorum, Plutarchus & Arrianus: Quorum ille & vitam eius descripsit in parallelis, & duos de ipsius fortuna peculiares libros cō-posuit: hic vniuersam eius historiam elegantí ac planè Xenophonteo dicendi genere libris octo persecutus est. De Latinis vero adhuc reliquus est Quintus Curtius Rufus bonus inprimis scriptor & argutus, sed ἀξιόλογος.
units.tr: The two books that follow contain the deeds of Alexander the Great, which in Diodorus' library also fill the whole of book 17. Many others recorded them in writing and in memory, and so did Callisthenes, a pupil of Aristotle, and Aristobulus and Ptolemy, who were the king's constant companions and wrote the records [ὑπομνήματα] of all his affairs. Yet the wickedness of men and the passing of time have long since snatched their writings from us. Among the Greeks, apart from Diodorus, only Plutarch and Arrian survive. Plutarch described his life in his Parallel Lives and composed two separate books on his fortune; Arrian pursued his whole history in eight books, in an elegant and plainly Xenophontean style. Of the Latin writers there remains Quintus Curtius Rufus, a good writer above all and clever, but [ἀξιόλογος] ...

units.la: Galterus etiam poeta non contemnendus argumentum hoc peculiari poemate tractauit, quod ille ad exemplum Maronis & Statii nominat Alexandreida. Vitra commemoratos Orosius, Zosimus, Valerius Maximus, Plinius, Cicero, Apuleius aliique multi hinc inde de Alexandro Magno alius alia in litteras retulerunt. Quos & ipsos qui volet, cum volet, adeat.
units.tr: Galterus, too, a poet not to be despised, treated this subject in a special poem, which he calls the Alexandreis after the model of Maro and Statius. Besides those already mentioned, Orosius, Zosimus, Valerius Maximus, Pliny, Cicero, Apuleius and many others have written here and there about Alexander the Great, each in a different way. Whoever wishes may consult them too, whenever he likes.

units.la: Sed ne vlterius hoc Scholiorum quasi filum pertexā, festinatione Typographorum impedior. Quæ tamen Scholia, vbi denuo liber typis mandabitur, benevolo lectori, tum in hos decem tum in cæteros insequentes libros & pleniora & accuratiora promittimus. Nam hæc, quæ nunc edimus, tumultuario (vt cum Apuleio loquar) intra pauculos dies & inter alias occupationes confecta sunt.
units.tr: But lest I spin this thread of scholia any further, I am hindered by the printers' haste. Yet when the book is printed again, we promise the kind reader scholia both fuller and more accurate, on these ten books and on the following ones. For these notes which we now publish were put together hurriedly (to use Apuleius' words) within a few days and among other occupations.

units.la: POMPEII TROGI EPI- TOMA HISTORIARVM LIBER XI.
units.tr: THE POMPEIUS TROGUS EPITOME OF THE HISTORIES, BOOK XI.
SUMMARY.

units.tr: 1 Philip is killed, and Alexander keeps the Macedonians in obedience. | 6 He organises military discipline. With a small force he undertakes great enterprises and defeats the Persians in battle.
