units.la: N exercitu Philippi,sicuti varia gen- tes erant, ita eo occiso, diuersi motus animorum fuere. Alij quippe iniusta 15 seruitute oppressi, ad spem se libertatis erigebant; alij tædio longinqua militiæ vemissam sibi expeditionem gaudebant; nonnulli facem nuptiis filia accésam, rogo patris subditam
units.tr: Among the army of Philip, as the peoples were various, so with his death the movements of minds were diverse. Some, oppressed by unjust servitude, raised themselves to hope of freedom; others, weary of the long campaign, rejoiced that the expedition had been called off for them; some grieved that the torch kindled for a daughter's wedding had been turned to her father's funeral pyre.

units.la: 20 dolebant. Amicos quoq;tam subita mutatione rerum, haut mediocris metus ceperat, reputantes nunc prouocatam Asiam; nunc Europam nondum perdomitam; nunc Illyrios & Thracas, & Dardanos, ceterasq; barbaras gentes fidei dubiæ, & mentis infidæ: qui omnes
units.tr: Their friends too, by so sudden a change of affairs, were seized by no small fear, reflecting that Asia had now been provoked, that Europe was not yet thoroughly subdued, that the Illyrians, Thracians, Dardanians and the other barbarian peoples were of doubtful loyalty and faithless mind; and if all these peoples rebelled together, that they could in no way be resisted.

units.la: 25 populi si pariter deficiant,resisti nullo modo posse. Quetis rebus, veluti medela quædam interuentus Alexandri fuit;qui pro concione,ita vulgus omne consolatus,hortatusq; pro tempore est, vt & metum timentibus demeret,& in spem omnes impelleret. Erat hic annos 20,
units.tr: At such a time, as if by a kind of remedy, Alexander intervened. He addressed the assembly, consoling and encouraging the whole crowd as the occasion required, so as both to remove fear from the frightened and to drive all towards hope. He was twenty years old,

units.la: 30 natus; in qua ætate ita moderate de se multa pollicitus est,vt appareret plura eum experimetis reseruare,Macedonibus in munitatem cunctarum rerum,præter militiæ vacationem dedit:quo facto tantum sibi fauorem omnium conciliauit, vt corpus hominis, non virtutem
units.tr: at an age in which he promised so much about himself with such moderation that it appeared he was keeping most of his plans for experience. He granted the Macedonians immunity from all burdens except military service. By this act he won over the goodwill of all so completely that they said it was the body of the man, rather than the spirit of the king,
that had changed.

units.la: 2 Prima illi cura paternarum exequiarum fuit: in quibus ante omnia, cædis cõscios ad tumulum patris occidi iussit: soli Alexandro Lyncestarum fratri pepercit, seruans sane auspicium dignitatis sue; nam regem eum primus salutauerat. Æmulum quoq; imperii Caranum fratrem ex nouerca suscepto, interfici curauit. Inter initia multas gentes rebellantes compescuit; orientes nonnullas seditiones extinxit. Quibus rebus erectus, citato gradu in Græciam contendit: vbi exemplo patris Corinthum euocatis ciuitatibus, dux in locum eius substituitur. Inchoatum deinde à patre Persicum bellum aggreditur, in cuius apparatu occupato nuntiatur Athenienses, & Lacedæmonios ab eo ad Persas defecisse, auctoremq; eius defectionis, magno auri pondere a Persis corruptum, Demosthenem oratorem extitisse; qui Macedonum deletas omnes cum rege copias à Triballis affirmauerit, producto in concionem auctore, qui in eo prælio, in quo rex ceciderit, se quoq; vulneratum diceret. Qua opinione mutatos omnium ferme ciuitatium animos esse; præsidia Macedonum obsideri. Qui- bus motibus occursurus tanta celeritate instructo paratoq; exercitu Græciam oppressit, vt quem venire non senserant, videre se vix crederent.
units.tr: 2 His first concern was his father's funeral rites. In these, before all else, he ordered the accomplices in the murder to be killed at the father's tomb. He spared only Alexander, brother of the Lyncestians, preserving indeed the privilege of his rank, for he had been the first to greet him as king. He also saw to it that Caranus, his stepmother's son and his rival for the throne, was put to death. Early in his reign he subdued many rebellious peoples and crushed several seditions that were springing up. Encouraged by these successes, he hastened into Greece. There, following his father's example, he summoned the states to Corinth and was made commander in his father's place. Then he took up the Persian war that his father had begun. While he was busy with its preparations, it was reported that the Athenians and Lacedaemonians had revolted from him to the Persians, and that the author of this revolt was the orator Demosthenes, who had been bribed by the Persians with a great weight of gold. Demosthenes had asserted that all the Macedonian forces had been destroyed together with the king by the Triballi, producing before the assembly a witness who said that he too had been wounded in the battle in which the king had fallen. By this report the minds of almost all the states had been changed, and the Macedonian garrisons were being besieged. To meet these disturbances, he moved with such speed, his army being equipped and ready, that he overwhelmed Greece; those who had not known he was coming could scarcely believe they saw him.

units.la: 3 In transitu hortatus Thessalos fuerat; beneficiorumq; Philippi patris, maternaq; sua cum his sub AEacidarum gente necessitudinis admonuerat. Cupide hac Thessalis audientibus, exemplo patris dux universæ gentis creatus erat; & vectigalia omnia, redditusq; suos ei tradiderant. Sed Athenienses, sicuti primi defecerant, ita primi pænitere cœperunt; contemptum hostis in admirationem vertentes, pueritiamq; Alexandri spretam antea, supra virtutem veterum ducum extollentes. Misis itaq; legatis, bellum deprecantur: quibus audita & grauiter increpatis, Alexander bellum remisit. Inde Thebas exercitum conuertit, eadem indulgentia vsurus, si parem poenitentiam inuenissent. Sed Thebani armis, non precibus nec deprecatione vsi sunt.
units.tr: 3 On the march he had encouraged the Thessalians, and had reminded them of his father Philip's benefits and of his own mother's kinship with them under the house of the Aeacids. The Thessalians heard this eagerly, and following his father's example they created him leader of the whole nation, and handed over to him all their revenues and their own resources. But the Athenians, who had been the first to revolt, were also the first to repent. They turned their contempt of the enemy into admiration and exalted Alexander, whose youth they had previously despised, above the courage of the ancient generals. So they sent envoys to beg for peace. Alexander heard them, rebuked them severely, and then laid down the war. Then he turned his army towards Thebes, intending to show the same indulgence if they found an equal repentance. But the Thebans relied on arms, not on prayers or entreaties.

units.la: 5 Itaq; victi, grauissima quaq; supplicia miserrima capitis experti sunt. In consilio cum de excidio vrbis deliberaretur, Phocenses, & Plataenses, & Thespienses, & Orchomenij, Alexandri socij, victoriaq; participes, excidia vrbium suarum, crudelitatem; Thebanorum 10 referebant, studia in Persas non praesentia tantum, verum & vetera aduersus Graecia libertatem increpantes. Quamobrem odium eos omnium populorum esse; quod vel ex eo manifestari, quod iureiurando se omnes obstrinxerint, vt victis Persis Thebas diruerent. Adii- 15 ciunt & scelerum priorum fabulas, quibus omnes scenas repleuerunt, vt non praesenti tantum perfidia, verum & vetere infamia inuisi forent.
units.tr: 5 Therefore, having been defeated, they suffered the most severe punishments and the most wretched fates. When the council deliberated on the destruction of the city, the Phocians, Plataeans, Thespians and Orchomenians, allies of Alexander and sharers in his victory, recounted the destruction of their own cities and the cruelty of the Thebans. They denounced their zeal not only in the present against the Persians but also in the past against the liberty of Greece. Therefore, they said, all peoples hated them; this was made plain by the fact that all of them had bound themselves by oath to destroy Thebes once the Persians were defeated. They added stories of earlier crimes with which the Thebans had filled every stage, so that they were hated not only for their present treachery but also for their old infamy.

units.la: 4 Tunc Cleadas vnus ex captiuis data potestate. dicendi, non a rege defecisse, quem interfectum audie- 20 rint, sed a regis heredibus; quicquid in eo fit admissum, crudelitatis, non perfidiae culpam esse, cuius tamen iam magna se supplicia pependisse: deleta iuuentute, nunc fenum feminarumq;, sicuti infirmum, ita innoxium reliquare vulgus, quod ipsum stupris contumeliisq;, ita ve- 25 xatum esse, vt nihil amarius vmquam sint passi: nec iam pro ciuibus se, qui tam pauci remanserint orare; sed pro innoxio patria solo, & pro vrbe, quae non viros tantum, verum & deos genuerit. Priuata etiam regem supersitione deprecatur, geniti apud ipsos Herculis, 30 vnde originem gens Aeacidarum trahat; atq; Thebis a patre eius Philippo pueritia: rogat vrbi parcat, qua maiores eius partim apud se genitos, deos adoret; partim educatos summa maiestatis reges viderit.
units.tr: 4 Then Cleadas, one of the captives, being given the chance to speak, said that the Thebans had not revolted from the king, whom they had heard was dead, but from the king's heirs. Whatever wrong had been committed in this, was the fault of cruelty, not of treachery; yet they had already paid heavy penalties for it. Their youth had been destroyed, and now the old men and women, being feeble, had been spared as harmless, while the common people, who were harmless, had been so harassed with dishonour and insult that they had suffered nothing more bitter ever. Nor did he now plead for them as citizens, since so few remained, but on behalf of the innocent native soil and the city which had produced not only men but gods. He also begged the king by his private devotion, by Hercules, who had been born among them and from whom the Aeacid race traces its origin, and by Thebes where his father Philip had spent his boyhood. He asked him to spare the city in which his ancestors had been born, worshipped their gods, and seen the kings educated there in the highest dignity.

units.la: Sed potentior fuit ira, quam preces. Itaq; vrbs diruitur, agri inter victores diuiduntur; captiui sub corona venduntur, quorum pretium non ex ementium commodo, sed ex inimicorum odio extenditur. Miseranda res Atheniensibus visa. Itaq; portas refugiis profugorum cōtra interdictum regis aperuere. Quam rem ita grauiter tulit Alexander, vt secunda legatione denuo bel- lum deprecantibus, ita demum remiserit, vt oratores & duces, quorum fiducia toties rebellent, sibi dedātur: paratiq; Atheniensibus, ne cogantur subire bellum, eo res deducta est, vt retentis oratoribus, duces in exilium agerentur: qui ex continenti ad Darium profecti, non mediocre momentum Persarum viribus accessere.
units.tr: But anger was more powerful than prayers. So the city was razed, and its lands were divided among the victors; the captives were sold under the spear, and their price was set not by the convenience of the buyers but by the hatred of the enemies. The matter seemed pitiful to the Athenians, so they opened their gates to the refugees, against the king's prohibition. Alexander took this so badly that when envoys pleaded for peace a second time, he relented only on condition that the orators and generals, on whose confidence they had so often rebelled, should be handed over to him. The Athenians, prepared not to be forced into war, were brought to such a point that, the orators being detained, the generals were sent into exile. They went straight from there to Darius and added no small strength to the Persian forces.

units.la: § Proficiscens ad Persicum bellum, omnes nouerca suæ cognatos, quos Philippus in excelsiorem dignitatis locum proueheńs imperiis præfecerat, interfecit: sed nec suis, qui apti regno videbantur, pepercit, ne qua materia seditionis, procul se agente, in Macedonia remaneret: & regis stipendiarios conspectioris ingenij, ad commilitium secum trahit; segniores ad tutelam regni relinquit. Adornato deinde exercitu naues onerat: vnde conspecta Asia, incredibili ardore mentis accensus, duodecim aras deorum in belli vota statuit. Patrimonium omne suum, quod in Macedonia Europaq; habebat, amicis diuidit sibi Asiam sufficere prasatus. Priusquam vlla nauis littore excederet, bostias cædit, petens victoriam bello, quo toties a Persis petita Gracia vltor electus sit: quibus longa iam fatis, & matura imperia cotigisse, quorum maq; tempus esse vices excipere melius a- Ambitio Ale- sturos. Sed nec exercitus eius alia, quam regis animo- xandri, aua- rum præsumptio fuit: quippe obliti omnes coniugum, titia Alexan- liberorumq;, & longinqua domo militia, Persicum au- dri exercitū impellit, rum, & totius Orientis opes, iam quasi suam prædam ducebant: nec belli periculorum q;, sed diuitiarum meminerant. Cum delati in continentem essent, primus Alexander iaculum velut in hostilem terram iecit; armatusq; de nauí tripudianti similis prosiluit; atq; ita hostias cadit, precatus ne se regem illa terra inuita accipiant. In Ilio quoq; ad tumulos eorum, qui Troiano bello cecederant,parentauit.
units.tr: § As he set out for the Persian war, he killed all his stepmother's relatives whom Philip had raised to high office and placed in command. Nor did he spare his own kin who seemed fit for kingship, so that no source of sedition might remain in Macedonia while he was far away. He took with him the king's soldiers of more conspicuous ability as companions in arms, and left the less vigorous ones to guard the kingdom. Then, with his army readied, he loaded the ships. When Asia came into view, he was seized with incredible ardour of mind and set up twelve altars to the gods as vows for the war. He divided among his friends all his patrimony that he had in Macedonia and Europe, saying that Asia would be enough for himself. Before any ship had left the shore, he sacrificed victims, praying for victory in a war in which Greece, so often attacked by the Persians, might be avenged. Long ago, he said, the fates had granted these empires and their time was ripe; it was better for others to take up their turn. But his army's presumption was no less than the king's ambition: all of them forgot their wives and children and their distant homes in the military campaign. They already were counting the Persian wealth and the riches of the whole East as their own booty, and did not remember the dangers of war, only the riches. When they had been brought to the mainland, Alexander first cast his javelin, as though onto hostile soil, and leaping armed from the ship like one dancing, sacrificed victims, praying that the land would receive him as its king even against its will. At Ilium, too, he made offerings at the tombs of those who had fallen in the Trojan War.

units.tr: 6 From there he marched against the enemy. He forbade his soldiers to plunder Asia, telling them to spare their own property and not to destroy what they had come to possess. His army had 30,000 foot, 4,500 horse and 182 ships. With so small a force it is uncertain whether it was more admirable that he conquered the whole world or that he dared to attack it, for he chose for so dangerous a war

units.la: sum bellum exercitum legeret, non iuuenes robustos, nec primum florem atatis sed veteranos;plerosq; etiam emerita militia,qui cum patre, patriusq; militauerat, elegit:vt non tam milites quam magistros militiae electos putares. Ordines quoq; nemo nisi sexagenarius duxit: vt si principia castrorum cernerec, senatum te alicuius prisca reipub. videre diceres. Itaq; nemo in prœlio fugam, sed victoriam cogitauit; nec in pedibus cuiquā spes, sed in lacertis fuit. Contra rex Persarum Darius, fiducia virium,nil astu agere,affirmans suis occulta cō-
units.tr: not strong young men nor men in the prime of life, but veterans, most of them discharged from service, who had served under his father and grandfather. You would have thought them not so much soldiers as chosen masters of war. No one but men of sixty commanded the companies, so that if you saw the headquarters of the camp you would say you were looking at the senate of some ancient commonwealth. Therefore no one in battle thought of flight but of victory, and no one placed his hope in his feet but in his arms. Darius, king of the Persians, on the other hand, trusting in his strength, did nothing by cunning. He declared that secret plans did not suit a victory won by stealth, and that the enemy should not be kept off the borders of the kingdom but admitted into its heart, for he thought it more glorious to repel war than not to admit it.

units.la: filia victoriae furtiuae non conuenire; nec hostem regni finibus arcere,sed in intimum regnum accipere:gloriosius ratus repellere bellum, quam non admittere.Prima igitur congressio in campo Adrasti fuit.In acie Persarum sexcenta millia militum fuere, qua non minus
units.tr: The first encounter therefore took place in the plain of Adrastus. In the Persian line there were six hundred thousand soldiers, and they turned their backs, overcome no less by Alexander's skill than by the valour of the Macedonians.

units.la: arte Alexandri quam virtute Macedonum superata terga verterunt. Magna itaq; cades Persarum fuit. De exercitu Alexandri nouem pedites, centum viginti equites cecidere, quos rex impense ad ceterorum exem- plum plum humatos, statuis equestribus donauit, cognatis eorum immunitates dedit. Post victoriam maior pars Asiae adeum defecit. Gessit & plura bella cum praefectis Darij, quos iam non tam armis, quam terrore nominis sui vicit. §
units.tr: There was great slaughter of the Persians. Of Alexander's army nine foot soldiers and 120 horsemen fell. The king buried them lavishly, as an example to the rest, honoured them with equestrian statues, and granted immunities to their kinsmen. After the victory most of Asia went over to him. He also waged further wars with the prefects of Darius, whom he now conquered not so much by arms as by the terror of his name. §

units.la: 7 Dum haec aguntur, interim indicio captiui ad eum defertur, insidias ei ab Alexandro Lyncestarum, genero Antipatri, qui praepositus Macedoniae erat, parari. Ob quam causam timens, ne quis interfecto eo in Macedonia motus oriretur, in vinculis eum habuit. 10
units.tr: 7 While these things were happening, word was brought to him by a captive that the Lyncestian, Antipater's son-in-law, who was governor of Macedonia, was plotting against him. Fearing that if he killed him some disturbance might arise in Macedonia, he kept him in chains. 10

units.la: Post hac Gordien urbem petit, quae posita est inter Phrygiam maiorem & minorem: cuius urbis potiunda non tam propter praedam cupido eum cepit, sed quod audierat in ea urbe in templo Iouis iugum Gordy positum; cuius nexum fiquis soluisset, eum tota Asia regnaturum, antiqua oracula cecinisse. Huius rei causa & origo illa fuit. Gordius cum in his regionibus bubus conductis araret, aues eum omnis generis circumuolare coeperunt: profectus ad consulendos augures vicinae urbis, obuiam in porta habuit virginem eximiae pulchritudinis; percontatus eam, quem potissimum augurem consuleret: illa audita causa consulendi, gnara artis ex disciplina parentum, regnum ei portendi, re-
units.tr: After this he made for the city of Gordium, which lies between Greater and Lesser Phrygia. His desire to take the city was driven less by greed for booty than by what he had heard: that in the temple of Jupiter in that city stood the yoke of Gordius, and that the ancient oracles had declared that whoever untied its knot would rule all Asia. The cause and origin of this was as follows. Gordius, while ploughing in these regions with hired oxen, was circled by birds of every kind. Setting out to consult the augurs of a neighbouring city, he met at the gate a girl of extraordinary beauty. He asked her which augur he should consult. She, having heard the reason for his consulting, and being skilled in the art from her parents' teaching, foretold him a kingdom,

units.la: spondit: pollicetur, se & matrimonij, & spei sociam. Tam pulchra conditio, primaregni felicitas videbatur. Post nuptias, inter Phrygas orta seditio est. Consulentibus de fine dissidiarum, oracula responderunt, regem discordiis opus esse. Iterato quaerentibus de persona regis, iubentur eum regem obseruare, quem reuersi primum in templum Iouis euntem plaustro reperissent. 30
units.tr: and replied that she offered herself as partner both in marriage and in hope. Such a fine match seemed the first happiness of his reign. After the wedding a sedition arose among the Phrygians. When they consulted about an end to the dissensions, the oracles answered that the kingdom needed a king for its discords. Asking again about the person of the king, they were told to acclaim as king the man whom they should first find on their return, going to the temple of Jupiter in a wagon.

units.la: Obuius illis Gordius fuit, flatimq; eum regem consalutant: ille plaustrum, quo vehenti regnum delatum fuerat, in templo Iouis positum, maiestati regia conse-
units.tr: Gordius met them, and they at once hailed him as king. He dedicated the wagon in which he had been riding when the kingship was brought to him, placing it in the temple of Jupiter as a token of royal majesty.

units.la: ¹ 3 6 ⁴ crauit. Post hunc filius Mida regnauit, qui ab Orpheo sacrorum solemnibus initiatus, Phrygiam religionibus implenit: quibus tutior omni vita, quam armis fuit.
units.tr: ¹ 3 6 ⁴ After him his son Midas reigned. He was initiated into the sacred rites by Orpheus and filled Phrygia with religious observances, and by these he was safer all his life than he was by arms.

units.la: Igitur Alexander capta vrbe cum in templum Iouis veniffet, iugum plaustri requisiuit: quo exhibito, cum capita loramentorum intra nodos abscondita reperire nō posset, violentius oraculo vsus, gladio loramenta cedit: atque ita resolutis nexibus, latentia in nodis capita inuenit.
units.tr: So when Alexander, after taking the city, came to the temple of Jupiter, he asked for the yoke of the wagon. When it was shown to him, he could not find the ends of the thongs, which were hidden inside the knots. Using the oracle more violently, he cut the thongs with his sword, and so, the knots being undone, he found the hidden ends.

units.la: 8 Haec illi agenti, nuntiatur Darium cum ingenti exercitu aduentare. Itaque timens angustias, magna celeritate Taurum transcendit; in qua festinatione quingenta stadia cursu fecit. Cum Tarsum venisset, captus Cydni fluminis amœnitate, per mediam vrbem influentis, proiectis armis, plenus pulueris, ac sudoris, in praefrigidam vndam se proiecit. Tum repente tantus neruos eius occupauit rigor, vt interclusa voce non spes modo remedij, sed nec dilatio periculi inueniretur. Vnus erat ex medicis, nomine Philippus, qui solus remedium pollicetur: sed & ipsum, Parmenionis pridie à Cappadocia missa epistola, suspectum faciebant: qui ignarus infirmitatis Alexandri scripserat, à Philippo medico cauerct: nam corruptum illum à Dario ingenti pecunia esse. Tutius tamen est ratus, dubia se fidei me-dici credere, quam indubitato morbo perire. Accepto igitur poculo, epistolas medico tradidit; atq; ita inter bibendum oculos in vultum legentis intendit. Vt fecurum conspexit, latior factus est, sanitatem quarta die recepit.
units.tr: 8 While he was doing this, word came that Darius was approaching with a huge army. Fearing the narrow passes, he crossed the Taurus with great speed; in this haste he covered five hundred stadia at a run. When he came to Tarsus he was captivated by the pleasantness of the river Cydnus, which flows through the middle of the city. Full of dust and sweat, he threw down his arms and plunged into its very cold water. Then suddenly such a stiffness seized his sinews that, his voice cut off, there was found no hope of a remedy, nor even any delay of the danger. There was one of the physicians, named Philip, who alone promised a cure. But Alexander was made suspicious even of him by a letter, sent the day before from Cappadocia by Parmenion, who, ignorant of Alexander's illness, had written that he should beware of the physician Philip, for he had been bribed by Darius with a huge sum of money. Yet he judged it safer to entrust himself to the doubtful faith of the physician than to die of a certain disease. So, having received the cup, he handed the letters to the doctor, and while drinking he kept his eyes fixed on the face of the reader. When he saw that the man was unmoved, he grew more cheerful, and on the fourth day he recovered his health.

units.la: 9 Interea Darius cum quadringentis millibus peditum, ac centum millibus equitum in aciem procedit. Mouebat hac multitudo hostium, respectu paucitatis suae, Alexandrum: sed interdum reputabat, quātas res s cum ista paucitate gesisset; quantosq; populos fudisset. Itaq; cum spes metum vinceret, periculosius differre bellum ratus, ne desperatio suis cresceret, circuectus suos, singulas gentes diuersa oratione alloquitur, Illyrios & Thracas opum ac diuitiarum ostentatione; Graecos veterum bellorum memoria, interneciuiq; cum Persis odij accendebat: Macedones autem nunc Europa victa admonet, nunc Asiae expetitae; nec inuentos illis toto orbe pares viros gloriatur. Ceterum & laborum finem hunc, & gloriae cumulum fore. Atq; inter haec identidem conspicere aciem iubet, ut hac mora consuescant oculus turbam hostium sustinere. Nec Darij segnis opera in ordinanda acie fuit. Quippe omisso ducum officiis, ipse omnia circumire, singulos hortari, veteris gloriae Persarum, imperiiq; perpetuae a diis immortalibus datae posses-sionis admonere.Post haec praelium ingentibus animis
units.tr: 9 Meanwhile Darius advanced into the field with 400,000 foot and 100,000 horse. The sheer number of the enemy troubled Alexander, given how few his own men were. But at times he reflected how great the things were that he had done with so small a force, and how many peoples he had routed. So, when hope overcame fear, and judging it more dangerous to put off the war lest despair grow among his men, he gathered his troops around him and addressed each nation in a different speech. He inflamed the Illyrians and Thracians by showing them the wealth and riches of the enemy; the Greeks by the memory of old wars and their hatred of the Persians, which was bound up with slaughter; and the Macedonians he reminded now of Europe conquered, now of Asia to be won, boasting that no equal men could be found for them anywhere in the world. Moreover, he said, this would be the end of their labours and the crown of their glory. Meanwhile, again and again he ordered them to look at the enemy's battle line, so that by this delay they might grow accustomed to bearing the sight of the enemy's crowd. Nor was Darius idle in arranging his line. Leaving the duties of the commanders aside, he went round everything himself, encouraging individuals and reminding them of the old glory of the Persians and of the lasting possession of empire given them by the immortal gods. After these things the battle was joined with great spirit

units.la: Aliud stratagema. Darii vigilantia, & admonitio ad milites. committitur. In eo vterq; rex vulneratur: tamen diu certamen anceps fuit, quoad fugeret Darius. Exinde cædes Persarum secuta est. Cæsa sunt peditum unum & sexaginta millia, equitum decem millia; captā quadraginta 20 millia. Ex Macedonibus cecidere pedestres 130. equites 150. In castris Persarum multum auri, ceterarumq; opum inventum. Inter captiuos castrorum, mater, & vxor eademq; soror, & filia duæ Darij fuere. Ad quas visendas hortandasq; cum Alexander venisset, confpe25 ctis armatis inuicem se amplexæ, veluti statim morituræ complorationem ediderunt. Prouoluta deinde genubus Alexandri, non mortem, sed dum Darij corpus sepeliant, delationem mortis deprecantur. Motus tanta mulierum pietate Alexander, & Darium viuere dixit; 30 & timentibus mortis metum dempsit; easq; haberi, vt reginas præcepit: Filias quoq; non sordidius dignitate patris sperare matrimonium iußit.
units.tr: Another stratagem: Darius's vigilance, and his exhortation to the soldiers. on both sides. In this battle both kings were wounded, yet the struggle was long doubtful, until Darius fled. After that the slaughter of the Persians followed. Sixty-one thousand foot and ten thousand horse were slain, and forty thousand were taken. Of the Macedonians 130 foot and 150 horse fell. In the Persian camp much gold and other wealth was found. Among the captives of the camp were the mother of Darius, his wife, who was also his sister, and his two daughters. When Alexander came to visit and encourage them, they embraced one another, as if about to die at once, and raised a lament. Then, prostrating themselves at Alexander's knees, they begged not for death but for the postponement of their death until they could bury Darius's body. Alexander, moved by such devotion of the women, said that Darius was alive, and removed the fear of those who dreaded death. He ordered that they be treated as queens, and he directed that the daughters should look for marriages no less dignified than their father's rank.

units.la: 10 Post hac opes Darij, diuitiarumque apparatum contemplatus, admiratione tantarum rerum capitur. Tunc primum luxuriosa conuiuia, & magnificentiam epularum sectari, tunc Barsenen captiuam diligere
units.tr: 10 After this, having surveyed the wealth of Darius and the store of his riches, he was seized with admiration for such great things. Then for the first time he pursued luxurious banquets and the magnificence of feasts. Then, too, he began to love Barsine, a captive, for the beauty of her form.

units.la: 5 propter formae pulchritudinem coepit. A qua postea sufceptum puerum Herculem vocauit. Memor tamen adhuc Darium viuere, Parmenionem ad occupandam Persicam classem, aliosque amicos ad recipiendas Asiae ciuitates misit: quae statim audita fama victoriae, ipsis
units.tr: 5 Afterwards he called the son he had by her Hercules. Still mindful that Darius was alive, he sent Parmenion to seize the Persian fleet, and other friends to recover the cities of Asia. As soon as the report of victory was heard, these cities

units.la: 10 Darij praefectis cum auri magno pondere tradentibus se, in potestatem victorum venerunt. Tunc in Syriam proficiscitur: vbi obuios cum infulis multos Orientis reges habuit. Ex his pro meritis singulorum alios in societatem recepit; aliis regnum ademit, suffectis in loca eorum nouis regibus. Insignis praeter ceteros fuit Abdalonimus, rex ab Alexandro Sidoniae constitutus. Quem Alexander, cum operas oblocare ad puteos exhauriendos, hortosque irrigandos solitus esset, miserere vitam exhibentem, regem fecerat, spretis nobilibus, ne generis id,
units.tr: 10 and the prefects of Darius themselves, handing over their charges together with great weight of gold, came into the power of the victor. Then he set out for Syria, where he met many kings of the East, wearing their fillets. Of these, according to the merits of each, he took some into alliance; from others he took away their kingdoms, new kings being set up in their places. Outstanding beyond the rest was Abdalonimus, whom Alexander had made king of Sidon. Alexander, who had been used to having him labour at drawing water from wells and watering gardens, made him king when he showed himself patient in enduring poverty, disregarding the nobles, lest they should think it was a matter of birth

units.la: 20 non dantis beneficium putarent. Tyriorum ciuitas cum coronam aureum magni ponderis per legatos in titulum gratulationis Alexandro misisset, grate munere accepto, Tyrum se ire velle ad vota Herculi reddenda, dixit. Cum legati rectius id eum in Tyro vetere & antiquiore templo facturum dicerent, deprecantes eius introitum, ita exarsit, vt vrbi excidium minaretur. Confestim, exercitu insulae applicato, non minus animosis Tyriis fiducia Carthaginensium, bello excipitur.
units.tr: 20 not as the gift of a benefactor, they would think. When the city of the Tyrians sent Alexander, through envoys, a golden crown of great weight as a token of congratulation, he accepted the gift gladly and said he would go to Tyre to fulfil his vows to Hercules. When the envoys said he would do this more properly in old Tyre, the more ancient temple, and begged him not to enter the city, he flared up so that he threatened the city with destruction. At once he brought his army to the island, and the Tyrians, no less spirited and relying on the Carthaginians, met him in war.

units.la: Augebat enim Tyrios animos Didonis exemplum, quae 30 Carthagine condita, tertiam partem orbis quaesiisset; turpe ducentes, si feminis suis plus animi fuisset in imperio quaerendo, quam sibi in tuenda libertate. Amota igitur imbelli aetate Carthaginem, & arcessitis mox auxiliis, non magno post tempore per proditionem capiuntur.
units.tr: For the example of Dido spurred the Tyrians' spirits. She had founded Carthage and then sought a third part of the world. They thought it shameful if their women had had more courage in seeking empire than they themselves had in defending their liberty. Therefore, having removed the men unfit for war to Carthage, and soon summoning help, they were taken after no long time by treachery.

units.la: 11 Inde Rhodum Alexander, Aegypti, Ciliciamq; fine certamine recepit. Ad Iouem deinde Hammonem pergit, consulturus & de eventu futurorum, & de origine sua. Namq; mater eius Olympias confessa viro suo Philippo fuerat, Alexandrū non ex eo sed ex serpente ingentis magnitudinis concepisse. Denig; Philippus vltimo prope vita sua tempore, filium suum non esse palam praedicauerat: Qua ex causa Olympiadem, velut stupri compertam, repudio dimisserat. Igitur Alexander cupiens originē diuinitatis acquirere, simul & matrem infamia liberare, per praemissos subornat antiquites, quid sibi respondere vellet. Ingredienti templum, statim antistites ut Hammonis filium salutant. Ille letus dei adoptione, hoc se patre censeri iubet. Rogat deinde, an omnes interfectores paretis sui fit vltus: respondetur patre eius nec posse interfici, nec mori; regis Philippi peractam pene vltionem esse. Tertiam interrogationem poscenti, victoriam omnium bellorum, possit fionemq; terrarum dari respondetur. Comitibus quoque suis respondum, vt Alexandrum pro deo, non pro rege colerent. Hinc illi aucta insolentia, simulq; animo increvit tumor, exempta comitate, quam & Graecorum literis, & Macedonum institutis didicerat. Reuersus ab Hammone Alexandriam condidit, & coloniam Macedonum caput esse Aegypti iubet.
units.tr: 11 From there Alexander received Rhodes, Egypt and Cilicia without any contest. He then went on to Jupiter Ammon, intending to consult both about the outcome of future events and about his own origin. For his mother Olympias had confessed to her husband Philip that she had conceived Alexander not by him but by a serpent of huge size. Finally, Philip, almost at the end of his life, had openly declared that his son was not his, and for this reason he had divorced Olympias as one found guilty of adultery. Therefore Alexander, wishing to acquire a divine origin and at the same time to free his mother from infamy, sent ahead men to bribe the priests as to what answer they should give him. As he entered the temple, the priests at once greeted him as the son of Ammon. Glad at the god's adoption, he ordered that he be reckoned as the son of this father. He then asked whether all the murderers of his father had been avenged. He was told that his father could neither be killed nor die, and that the vengeance on King Philip had been almost completed. When he asked a third question, he was told that victory in all wars and dominion over the lands of the earth could be given to him. They also answered his companions that they should worship Alexander as a god, not as a king. From this his arrogance grew, and at the same time his mind swelled with pride; he laid aside the courtesy which he had learned both from Greek literature and from Macedonian custom. On returning from Ammon he founded Alexandria and ordered that the Macedonian colony be the capital of Egypt.

units.la: 12 Darius cum Babyloniam profugisset, per epistolas ad Alexandrum precatur, redimendarum sibi captiuarum potestatem faciat, inq; eam rem magnam pecuniā pollicetur. Sed Alexander in pretium captiuarum regnum omne, non pecuniam petit. Interiecto tempore, alia epistola Darij Alexandro reddunt, quibus filia matrimonium & regni portio offertur: sed Alexander sua sibi dari rescripsit; iuísitq; supplicem venire, & regni arbitria victori permittere. Tum spe pacis amissa, bellum Darius reparat: cum quadringentis millibus peditum, & centum millibus equitum obuiam vadit Alexandro.In itinere nuntiatur vxorem eius ex collisione abiecti partus decessisse, eiusq; mortem illacrymatum Alexandrum, exequiasq; benigne prosecutum, idq; eum non amoris, sed humanitatis causa fecisse: Nam semel tantum eam Alexándro visam esse, cum matrem filiasq; eius paruulas frequenter consolaretur. Tunc se ratus vere victum, cum post tot prælia, etiam beneficiis ab hoste superaretur; gratumq; sibi esse, si vincere nequeat, quod à tali potissimum vinceretur. Scribit itaque & tertias epistolas, & gratias agit, quod nihil in suos hostile fecerit. Offert deinde maiorem partem regni vsq; flumen Euphraten, & alteram filiam vxorem; pro reliquis captiuis triginta millia talentum.Ad hæc Alexander gratiarum actionem ab hoste superuacaneam esse respondit; nec à se quicquam factum in hostis adulationem, nec quod in dubios belli exitus, aut in leges pacis sibi lenocinia quaereret: sed animi magnitudine, quæ didicerit aduersus vires hostium, non aduersus calamitates contendere; polliceturque præstaturum se ea 25 Dario, si secundus sibi, non par haberi velit. Ceterum neque mundum posse duobus solibus regi, neque orbem summa duo regna sulno stato terrarum habere: propterea aut deditionem ea die, aut in posterum, aliem parent; nec polliceatur sibi aliam, quam sit expertus victoriam.
units.tr: 12 When Darius had fled to Babylon, he begged Alexander by letter to grant him the power of ransoming his captives, and promised a large sum of money for this. But Alexander demanded in exchange for the captives not money but the whole kingdom. After an interval, Darius's men brought Alexander another letter, offering a daughter in marriage and a share of the kingdom. Alexander wrote back that his own terms should be given; and he ordered Darius to come as a suppliant and to leave the decision about the kingdom to the victor. Then, hope of peace lost, Darius renewed the war: he advanced to meet Alexander with four hundred thousand foot and a hundred thousand horse. On the march it was reported that his wife had died from a miscarriage caused by a collision, and that Alexander had wept at her death and honoured her funeral kindly; and that he had done this out of humanity, not love, for he had seen her only once, while he frequently comforted her mother and little daughters. Then Darius thought himself truly beaten, since after so many battles he was overcome by his enemy even in acts of kindness; and he said it was a gratification to him, if he could not conquer, to be conquered by such a man in particular. So he wrote a third letter too, and thanked Alexander for having done nothing hostile to his family. He then offered the greater part of the kingdom up to the river Euphrates, and his other daughter as a wife, and thirty thousand talents for the remaining captives. To this Alexander replied that thanks from an enemy were superfluous. He had done nothing to flatter the enemy, nor did he seek inducements in doubtful outcomes of war or in the terms of peace. He had contended with the greatness of spirit that he had learned to show against the strength of enemies, not against a marriage and a portion of the kingdom are offered: but Alexander wrote that his own terms should be given, and ordered him to come as a suppliant; he contended against calamities; he promised to grant Darius these things, if he wished to be held second, not equal. Moreover, the world cannot be ruled by two suns, nor can the earth have two supreme kingdoms. Therefore Darius should either surrender that day or prepare for another battle in future, and he should not promise himself any victory other than the one he had already experienced.

units.la: 13 Postera die aciem producunt: tum repente ante prælium, confectum curis Alexandrum somnus arripuit. Cum ad pugnam solus rex deesset, à Parmenione egre ægre excitatus, quærentibus somni causas omnibus inter pericula, cum etiam in otio semper parcior fuerit: Magno se æstu liberatum ait, somnum q; sibi à repentina securitate datum, quod liceat cum omnibus Darij copiis confligere; veritum se longau belli moram, si Persæ exercitum diuisissent. Ante prælium vtraq; acies hostibus spectaculo fuit. Macedones multitudinem hominum, corporum magnitudinem, armorumq; pulchritudinem mirabantur: Persæ à tam paucis victa suorum tot millia, stupebant. Sed nec duces circumire suos cessabant. Darius vix denis armatis singulos hostes, si diuisio fieret, euenire dicebat: Alexander Macedonas monebat, ne multitudine hostium, ne corporum magnitudine, vel coloris nouitate mouerentur: tantum meminisse iubet, cum iisdem se tertio pugnare; nec meliores factos putarent fuga, cum in aciem secum tam triste memoriam cadium suarum, & tantum sanguinis duobus praeliis fusi ferrent: & quemadmodum Dario maiorem turbam hominum esse, sic virorum sibi. Hortatur spernant illam aciem auro & argento fulgentem, in qua plus prada, quam periculi sit; cum victoria non armorum decore, sed ferri virtute quaeratur.
units.tr: 13 On the following day they drew up their battle line. Then suddenly, before the battle, sleep seized Alexander, who was worn out with cares. When the king alone was missing for the fight, he was roused with difficulty by Parmenion; when men asked the causes of his sleep, though among dangers he was always more sparing of it even in leisure, he said that he was freed from great anxiety, and that the sleep given him by sudden security was because he might fight with all of Darius's forces at once; he feared a long delay in the war if the Persians had divided their army. Before the battle both armies were a spectacle to the enemy. The Macedonians marvelled at the multitude of men, the size of their bodies and the beauty of their arms; the Persians were astonished that so many thousands of their own had been conquered by so few. Nor did the leaders cease going round their men. Darius said that if the battle were divided, scarcely ten armed men would fall to each enemy. Alexander warned the Macedonians not to be moved by the multitude of the enemy, nor by the size of their bodies, nor by the novelty of their colours. He bade them only to remember that they were fighting with the same men for the third time, nor should they think them better for having fled, since they bore in their line such a sad memory of their slaughter and so much blood shed in two battles; and just as Darius had a greater crowd of men, so he had more men of valour. He urges them to scorn that line glittering with gold and silver, in which there is more booty than danger, since victory is sought not by the splendour of arms but by the courage of iron.

units.la: 14 Post hac praelium committitur. Macedones in ferrum cum contemptu toties a se victi hostis ruebant: contra Persa mori, quam vinci praeoptabant. Raro ullo proelio tantum sanguinis fusum est. Darius cum vinci suos videret; mori voluit & ipse; sed a proximis fugere compulsus est. Suadentibus deinde quibusdam, ut pons Cydni fluminis, ad iter hostium impediendum, intercluderetur; non ita se saluti suae velle consultum ait, ut tot millia sociorum hosti obiiciat; debere & aliis fuga viam patere, quae patuerit sibi. Alexander autem periculosissima quaeque aggrediebatur; & ubi confertissimos hostes
units.tr: 14 After this the battle was joined. The Macedonians rushed upon the iron with contempt for an enemy so often beaten by them; the Persians preferred to die rather than be conquered. Rarely in any battle was so much blood shed. Darius, seeing his men being beaten, wished to die himself too; but he was compelled to flee by those nearest him. Then some advised that the bridge over the Cydnus river, to hinder the enemy's march, should be cut; but he said he did not wish his safety to be looked after in such a way as to expose so many thousand allies to the enemy; others should also have a way of flight open, as it had been open to him. Alexander, however, attacked whatever was most perilous, and wherever he saw the enemies fighting most fiercely in dense ranks, he always threw himself there; he wanted his own peril, not that of his soldiers.

units.la: Praelium commissum. hostes acerrime pugnare conspexisset, eo se semper immergebat; periculaq; sua esse, non militum volebat. Hoc praelio Asiae imperium rapuit, quinto post acceptum regnum anno; cuius tanta felicitas fuit, ut post hoc neNote
units.tr: The battle joined: by this battle he seized the empire of Asia, in the fifth year after he had received the kingdom. Such was its good fortune that after this no one dared to rebel, and the Persians, after the empire of so many years, patiently accepted the yoke of servitude.

units.la: 5 mo rebellare ausus fit: patienterq; Persae post imperium tot annorum, iugum servitutis acceperint. Donatis refectisq; militibus 34. diebus prædam recognouit. In urbe deinde clausa 40. millia talentum inuenit. Expugnat & Persepolim, caput Persici regni, urbem multis
units.tr: 5 After he had given gifts to and refreshed his soldiers, he spent thirty-four days reviewing the booty. Then, in the city which had been closed, he found forty thousand talents. He also stormed Persepolis, the capital of the Persian kingdom, a city

units.la: 10 annis illustrem; refertamq; orbis terrarum spoliis, quae interitu eius primum apparuere. Inter haec 800. admodum Graeci occurrunt Alexandro, qui poenam captiuitatis truncata corporis parte tulerant; rogates ut, sicuti Graeciam, se quoq; ab hostium crudelitate vindicaret.
units.tr: 10 famous for many years, and full of the spoils of the whole world, which first came to light at its destruction. Meanwhile about eight hundred Greeks, who had suffered the punishment of captivity with a part of their body cut off, came to meet Alexander, begging him to avenge them against the cruelty of the enemy, as he had avenged Greece.

units.la: 15 Data potestate redeundi, agros accipere maluerunt, ne non tam gaudium parentibus, quam detestandum sui conspectum reportarent.
units.tr: 15 When the power of returning home was granted, they preferred to receive fields, lest they bring back to their parents not so much joy as a sight of themselves which was to be detested.

units.la: Interea Darius in gratiam victoris a cognatis suis aureis compedibus, catenisq; in vico Parthoru Thara vincitur. Credo ita diis immortalibus vindicantibus, ut in terra eorum, qui successuri imperio erant, Persarum regnum finiretur. Alexander quoque citato cursu postera die superuenit: ibique cognouit Darium clauso vehiculo per noctem exportatum. Inde itaq; exercitu subsequi, cum 6. millibus equitum, fugientem insequitur: in itinere multa & periculosa praelia facit.
units.tr: Meanwhile Darius, to win the victor's favour, was bound in golden fetters and chains by his own kinsmen in the village of the Parthians, Thara. I believe the immortal gods so avenged it that the Persian kingdom should end in the land of those who were to succeed to the empire. Alexander also came up the next day at swift pace, and there learned that Darius had been carried off through the night in a closed carriage. Thence he followed with his army and six thousand horse, pursuing the fleeing man; on the march he fought many dangerous battles.

units.la: Emensus deinde multa millia passuum, cum nullum Darij indicium reperisset, respirandi equis data potestate, vnus ex militibus dum ad fontem proximum state, pergit, in vehiculo Darium multis quidem vulneribus confossum, sed spirantem adhuc inuenit: qui applicito captiuo cum ciuem ex voce cognouisset, id saltem praesentis fortuna solatium habere se dixit, quod apud intelleƈturum locuturus effet, nec incassum postremas voces emissurus. Perferri hac Alexandro iubet, si nullus eum meritorum officiis, maximorum illi debitorem mori, quod in matre liberisq; suis regium eius, non hostilem animum expertus, felicius hostem quam cognatos sortitus sit: quippe matri & liberis suis ab eodem hoste vitam datam; sibi a cognatis ereptam, quibus & vitam, & regna dederit: Quamobrem gratiam illis eam futuram, quam ipse victor volet. Alexandro referre se, quam solam moriens potest gratiam; precari superum inferumque numina, & regales deos, uti illi terrarum omnium victori contingat imperium: pro se iustam magis, quam gravem sepultura veniam orare. Quod ad ultionem pertineat, iam non suam, sed exemplì, communemque omnium regum esse causam, quam negligere, illi & indecorum & periculosum esse: quippe cum in altero iustitiæ eius, in altero etiam utilitatis causa versetur. In quam rem unicum pignus fidei regiæ dexteram se ferendam Alexandro dare. Post hac porrecta manu exspirauit. Qua ubi Alexandro nuntiata sunt, viso corpore defuncti, tam indignam illo fastigio mortem lacrymis prosecutus est; corpusque regio more sepeliri, & reliquias eius maiorum tumulis inferri iußit.
units.tr: After he had covered many miles and found no trace of Darius, and the horses had been given a chance to catch their breath, one of the soldiers, hurrying on to the nearest spring, found Darius in the carriage, pierced with many wounds but still breathing. Darius took the captive's hand, and on recognizing from his voice that the man was a fellow countryman, he said that this at least was some comfort in his present misfortune, that he would be speaking to someone who could understand him and would not be uttering his last words in vain. He bade them report this to Alexander: though he had received no service from him that earned it, he was dying as Alexander's debtor for the greatest kindness, because in the case of his mother and children he had found Alexander's conduct royal, not hostile, and had been more fortunate in meeting an enemy than in having kinsmen. For his mother and children had had their lives granted by that same enemy, while his own life had been taken by his kinsmen, to whom he had given both life and kingdoms. Therefore, he said, the favour shown to them would be whatever the victor himself wished. He said that he could return Alexander only the one thanks that a dying man could give; he prayed the gods above and below, and the gods of the royal house, that rule over all the lands might fall to Alexander as victor. For himself, he asked a pardon that was just rather than burdensome: burial. As for vengeance, he said, the cause was no longer his own but one of example and common to all kings; for Alexander to neglect it would be both unseemly and dangerous, since it touched on his justice in one respect and on his advantage in another. For this purpose he gave his right hand to be carried to Alexander as the sole pledge of royal faith. After this he stretched out his hand and expired. When this was reported to Alexander, he went to see the dead body and wept over a death so unworthy of that rank; and he ordered that the body be buried in royal fashion and its remains be placed in the tombs of his ancestors.
POMPEIUS TROGUS' EPITOME OF THE HISTORIES.
BOOK XII. SUMMARY.

units.la: 1 Alexandri in retinendo militare folertia. Bellum Græci abscente Alexandro repa-rant.
units.tr: 1 Alexander's skill in keeping his soldiers under control. With Alexander absent, the Greeks renew the war.

units.la: 2 Epiri rex Alexander I. taliam turbat, & tandem in pugna cadit. Scythę Alexandri præfectum & exercitum internecione delent.
units.tr: 2 Alexander, king of Epirus, disturbs Italy and at last falls in battle. The Scythians destroy Alexander's prefect and his army to a man.

units.la: 3 Alexandri simulatio, ambitio, cum Thalestri coubitus, luxus & profusio-nes.
units.tr: 3 Alexander's pretence and ambition; his intercourse with Thalestris; his luxury and extravagance.

units.la: 4 Qua ratione Macedones tumultuantes in officio continet.
units.tr: 4 By what means he keeps the rioting Macedonians in obedience.

units.la: 5 In domesticos suos sesrum stringit, & noua ratione aduersarios vlciscitur. Populos multos subigit, & Belsum Darii interfectorem de medio tolli curat.
units.tr: 5 He thrusts his sword into his own household and avenges his enemies in a novel way. He subdues many peoples and takes care to remove Bessus, the murderer of Darius.

units.la: 6 In cōiuuio mactat Clitum amicum, quem srustra incidit.
units.tr: 6 At a banquet he kills his friend Clitus, whom he afterwards
regrets, moved by belated repentance for his crime.

units.la: 7 Ad ingenium reuersus in prudentes consiliarios seuit. ad Orientem statuit imperii limites. Bacchi vestigiis delectatur, Herculisque ge-sta superare contendit.
units.tr: 7 Returning to his natural temper, he rages against his prudent counsellors. He sets the limits of his empire in the East. He delights in the footsteps of Bacchus and strives to surpass the deeds of Hercules.

units.la: 8 Porum prælio supera-tum regie excipit & dimittit. Multis populis expugnatis quietem exercituiconcedere velle videtur.
units.tr: 8 He receives Porus, defeated in battle, with royal honour and releases him. Having conquered many peoples, he seems willing to grant his army rest.

units.la: 9 Bellum instaurat. In Sugambrorum vibe de vita ceiıat &periclitatur,ab amicis periculo ereptus.
units.tr: 9 He renews the war. In the city of the Sugambri he fights for his life and is imperilled, rescued from danger by his friends.

units.la: 10 Oceanum lustrat, terminos imperii statuit. Præ-sectos vita priuat, & ad nu-ptias applicat animum.
units.tr: 10 He surveys the Ocean and sets the boundaries of his empire. He deprives his prefects of life and turns his mind to marriage.
11 His liberality, munificence and severity.

units.la: 12 Qua ratione Macedo-nes seditiosos ad officium reuocauerit. Ephæstionis o-bitus & tumulus.
units.tr: 12 By what means he brought the seditious Macedonians back to duty. The death and tomb of Hephaestion.

units.la: 13 Dum Occidentales prouinciæ manus porrigunt, Alexander Babylonem per-gens in lethalem morbum incidit.
units.tr: 13 While the Western provinces stretch out their hands, Alexander, pressing on to Babylon, falls into a deadly sickness.
14 Alexander is killed with poison through the arts of Antipater.
15 Alexander's last words as he lay dying.

units.la: 16 Magni huius Mace-donis, annos triginta tres nati quum decessit, elo-gium.
units.tr: 16 Eulogy of this great Macedonian, who died at the age of thirty-three.

units.la: ALEXANDER in persequēdo Dario, amissos milites magnis funerum impensis extulit; reliquis expeditionis eius sociis, tredecim millia talentum diuisit. Equorum maior pars ęstu amissa, inutilesque etiam qui superfuerant, facti. Pecunia omnis centum nonaginta millia talentum Ecbatana nuper congesta, eiq; Parmenio praepositus. Dum haec aguntur, epistolae Antipatri Macedonia ei redduntur, quibus bellum Agidis regis Spartanorum in Graecia; bellum Alexandri regis Epiri in Italia; bellum Sopyrionis praefecti eius in Scythia, continebatur. Quibus varie affectus, plus tamē laetitiae cognitis mortibus duorum aemulorum regum, quam doloris amissi cum Sopyrione exercitus suscepit. Namq; post profectionem Alexandri, Graecia ferme omnis in occasionem recuperandae libertatis, ad arma concurrerat, auctoritatem Lacedæmoniorum secuta, qui Philippi Alexandriq, pacem soli præuerant, & leges resp uerant. Dux huius belli Agis rex Lacedæmoniorum fuit; quem motum Antipater contractis militibus, in ipso ortu oppressit. Magna tamen utrinque cædes fuit. Agis rex cum suos terga dantes videret, dimissis satellitibus, ut Alexandro felicitate non virtute inferior videretur, tantam stragem hostium edidit, ut agmina interdum fugaret. Ad postremum, & si a multitudine victus, gloria tamen omnes vicit.
units.tr: Alexander, in pursuing Darius, buried the soldiers he had lost with great funeral expenses; he divided thirteen thousand talents among the remaining companions of his expedition. Most of the horses had perished from the heat, and even those that survived were rendered useless. All the money, one hundred and ninety thousand talents recently gathered at Ecbatana, was entrusted to Parmenio. While these things were being done, letters from Antipater were delivered to him in Macedonia, reporting the war of Agis, king of the Spartans, in Greece; the war of Alexander, king of Epirus, in Italy; and the war of Sopyrion, his prefect, in Scythia. Affected in various ways by them, he felt more joy at the deaths of his two rival kings than grief at the loss of the army with Sopyrion. For after Alexander's departure, almost all of Greece had rushed to arms in the hope of recovering its liberty, following the authority of the Lacedaemonians, who alone had resisted the peace of Philip and Alexander and had rejected their laws. The leader of this war was Agis, king of the Lacedaemonians; Antipater, having gathered his soldiers, crushed him at the very outset. Yet there was great slaughter on both sides. King Agis, seeing his men turning their backs, dismissed his bodyguards, so that he might seem not inferior to Alexander in good fortune, if not in courage, and he inflicted such slaughter on the enemy that at times he routed their ranks. At last, although overcome by the multitude, he conquered them all in glory.

units.la: 2 Porro Alexander rex Epiri, in Italiam a Tarentinis, auxilia aduersus Brutios deprecantibus, solicitatus, ita cupide profectus fuerat, veluti in diuisione orbis terrarum, Alexandro Olympiadis fratris sue filio Oriens, sibi Occidens forte contigisset; non minorem rerum materiam in Italia, Africa, Siciliaq, quam ille in Asia, & in Persis habiturus. Huc accedebat, quod sicut
units.tr: 2 Next, Alexander, king of Epirus, had been solicited by the Tarentines, who sought auxiliaries against the Bruttians, to make war in Italy. He had set out so eagerly, as if in a division of the lands of the world the East had fallen by chance to Alexander the son of his sister Olympias and the West to himself, and he expected to find no less material for deeds in Italy, Africa and Sicily than the other would have in Asia and Persia. Moreover, this too was a factor: just as

units.la: Alexandro Magno Delphica oracula insidias in Macedonia, ita huic responsum Dodonei Iouis vrbem Pandosiam, amnemq; Acherusium praedixerat. Quae vtraq; cum in Epiro essent, ignarus eadem & in Italia esse, ad declinanda fatorum pericula peregrinam militiam cupidius elegerat. Igitur, cum in Italiam venisset, primum illi bellum cum Appulis fuit: quorum cognito vbus fato; breui post tempore pacem & amicitiam cum rege eorum fecit. Erat namq; tunc temporis vrbs Appulis Brundusium, quam AEtoli sequuti tum fama rerum in Troia gestarum clarissimum ac nobilissimum ducem Diomedem, condiderant: sed pulsi ab Appulis, consulentes oracula responsum acceperant, locum quem repetissent, perpetuo possessuros. Hac igitur ex causa, per legatos cum belli comminatione, restitui sibi ab Appulis vrbem postulauerant. Sed vbi Appulis oraculum innotuit, interfectos legatos in urbe sepelierant, perpetuam ibi sedem habituros. Atq; ita defuncti responso, diu urbem possederunt. Quod factum cum cognouisset Alexander, antiquitatis fata veneratus, bello Appulorum abstinuit. Gessit & cum Brutiis Lucanisq; bellum; multasque urbes cepit: tum & cum Metapontinis, & Pediculis, & Romanis foedus, amicitiamque fecit. Sed Brutij Lucanig, cum auxilia a finitimis contraxissent, acrius bellum repetiuere. Ibi rex iuxta urbem Pandosiam & flumen Acheronta, non prius fatalis loci cognito nomine quam occideret, interficitur; moriensq;non in patria fuisse sibi periculosam mortem, propter quam patriam fugerat, intellexit. Corpus eius Thurij publice redemptum sepulturae tradiderunt. Dum haec aguntur in Italia, Sopyrion quoq;, praefectus Ponti ab Alexandro Magno relictus, otiosum se ratus, si nihil & ipse gessisset, adunato 30. millium exercitu, Scythis bellum intulit;
units.tr: for Alexander the Great the Delphic oracles had foretold plots in Macedonia, so for him the response of Dodonean Jupiter had foretold the city of Pandosia and the river Acheron. Although both were in Epirus, not knowing that they were also in Italy, he had more eagerly chosen a foreign campaign to avoid the perils of fate. So when he came to Italy, his first war was with the Apulians; having learned the place of his doom, shortly afterwards he made peace and friendship with their king. For at that time the Apulian city of Brundisium, which the Aetolians, following the fame of the deeds done at Troy, had founded under the most famous and noble leader Diomedes, was held by the Apulians. But when the Aetolians had been driven out, they consulted the oracles and received the answer that they would possess forever the place which they had sought to recover. For this reason they had demanded through envoys, with threats of war, that the city be restored to them by the Apulians. But when the oracle became known to the Apulians, they buried the slain envoys in the city, so that they would have a lasting seat there. And so, having been dead in accordance with the response, they held the city for a long time. When Alexander learned of this deed, reverencing the fate of antiquity, he abstained from war with the Apulians. He also waged war with the Bruttians and Lucanians and captured many cities; then he also made a treaty and friendship with the Metapontines, the Peucetians and the Romans. But the Bruttians and Lucanians, having gathered auxiliaries from their neighbours, renewed the war more fiercely. There the king, near the city of Pandosia and the river Acheron, not recognising the name of the fatal place until he was about to die, was killed; and dying, he understood that the death he had fled his homeland to escape was not in his homeland but dangerous to him there. His body was ransomed publicly by the people of Thurii and given to burial. While these things were being done in Italy, Sopyrion also, prefect of Pontus, left behind by Alexander the Great, thinking himself idle if he did nothing, assembled an army of thirty thousand and made war on the Scythians;
He pursues the Bruttians and Lucanians.

units.la: Tandem in loco fatali pugnans interficitur. tulit: Cafusq; cum omnibus copiis, poenas temere illati belli genti innoxiæ, luit.
units.tr: At last, fighting in the fatal place, he is killed; and having fallen with all his forces, he paid the penalty for the rashly waged war against an innocent people.

units.la: 3 Hac cum nuntiata in Parthis Alexandro essent, simulato mærore, propter Alexandri cognationem, exercitui suo triduum luctum indixit. Omnibus deinde velut perpetrato bello, reditum in patriam exspectantibus, coniugesque ac liberos suos animo iam quodammodo complectentibus, ad concionem exercitum vocat: ibi nihil actum tot egregiis prœliis ait, si incolumis Orientalis barbaria relinquatur; nec se corpus, sed regnum Darij petisse; persequendosque esse eos, qui a regno defecerint. Hac oratione velut ex integro incitatis militum animis, Hyrcaniam, Mardosque subegit.
units.tr: 3 When this was announced to Alexander among the Parthians, he feigned grief because of his kinship with Alexander and declared three days of mourning for his army. Then, as if the war had been completed and the soldiers were awaiting their return home, already embracing in spirit their wives and children, he summoned the army to an assembly. There he said that nothing had been achieved by so many distinguished battles if the Eastern barbarians were left unharmed; that he had sought not merely the body but the kingdom of Darius; and that those who had defected from the kingdom must be pursued. With the soldiers' spirits, as if renewed from the beginning, stirred up by this speech, he subdued Hyrcania and the Mardi.

units.la: Ibi ei occurrit Thalestris siue Minithæa Amazonum regina cum 300. mulieribus, 25. dierum inter confertissimas gentes itinere confecto, ex rege liberos quaesitura: cuius conspectus adueniusque admirationi omnibus fuit, & propter insolitum feminis habitum, & propter expetitum concubitum. Ob hoc tredecim diebus otio a rege datis, ut visa est vterum implesse, discessit. Post hac Alexander habitum regum Persa- rum, & diadema insolitum antea regibus Macedonicis, velut in leges eorum quos vicerat transfiret, assumit. Quae ne inuidiosius in se vno conspicerentur, amicos quoque suos longam vestem auratam, purpureamque 25 sumere iubet, vt luxum quoque, sicuti cultum Persarum imitaretur. Inter pellicum regiarum greges electa pulchritudinis, nobilitatisque noctium vices diuidit. His rebus ingentes epularum apparatus adiicit, ne ieiuna & destructa luxuria videretur, conuiuiumque 30 iuxta regiam magnificentiam ludis exornat: immemor prorsus tantas opes amitti his moribus, non quaeri solere.
units.tr: There Thalestris, or Minithaea, queen of the Amazons, met him with three hundred women, having completed a journey of twenty-five days through most crowded nations, in order to seek children from the king. Her sight and arrival were a wonder to everyone, both because of the women's unusual dress and because of the desired intercourse. For this, after thirteen days' leave given by the king, when she was seen to have conceived, she departed. After this, Alexander assumed the dress of the Persian kings and a diadem, unusual before for Macedonian kings, as if he were passing over into the customs of those he had conquered. Lest these things should be seen as too invidious on himself alone, he ordered his friends also to wear long, golden, purple robes, so that he might imitate the luxury as well as the dress of the Persians. Among the herds of royal concubines he divided the nights into turns among the chosen beauties and noble women. To these things he added huge preparations of banquets, lest his indulgence seem meagre and dismantled, and he adorned the feast with games worthy of royal magnificence, quite forgetting that such great wealth is lost by these habits and not acquired.

units.la: 4 Inter haec indignatio omnium totis castris erat, à Philippo illum patre tantum degenerauisse, vt etiam patriae nomen eiuraret, moresq; Persarum assumeret, quos propter tales mores vicerat. Sed ne solus vitiis eorum, quos armis subegerat, succubuisse videretur; militibus quoq; suis permisit, si quarum captiuarum consuetudine tenerentur, ducere vxores: existimans minorem in patriam reditus cupiditatem futuram, habentibus in castris imaginem quandam lariim, ac domesticae sedis: simul & laborem militiae molliorem fore dulcedine vxorum. Insuper supplementa quoque militum, minus exhauriri posse Macedoniam, si veteranis patribus tyrones filij succederent, militaturi in vallo, in quo essent nati, constantioresq; futuri, si non solum tyrocinia, verum & incunabula in ipsis castris posuissent: quae consuetudo in successoribus quoq; Alexandri manfit. Igitur & alimenta pueris statuta; & instrumenta armorum, equorumq; iuuenibus data; & patribus, pro numero filiorum, praemia statuta: Si quorum patres occidissent, nihilominus pupilli stipendia patrum trahebant; quorum pueritia inter varias expeditiones, militia erat. Itaq; à paruula aetate periculis laboribusq; indurati, inuictus exercitus fuere: neque castra aliter quam patriam, neque pugnam aliud vnquam, quam victoriam duxere. Hac suboles nomen habuit Epigoni. Parthis deinde domitis, praefectus his statuitur ex nobilibus Persarum Andragoras: inde postea origo Parthorum reges habuere.
units.tr: 4 Meanwhile there was indignation throughout the whole camp that he had so degenerated from his father Philip that he renounced even the name of his country and adopted the customs of the Persians, whom he had conquered on account of such customs. But lest he seem alone to have yielded to the vices of those he had subdued by arms, he also allowed his soldiers, if they were held by the company of any captive women, to take them as wives. He reasoned that there would be less desire to return home among those who had in the camp a kind of image of children and a household, and that the toil of soldiering would be made softer by the sweetness of wives. Moreover, the supply of soldiers could be drawn less heavily from Macedonia if young sons succeeded their aged fathers, to serve in the camp where they had been born; and they would be steadier if they had placed in the camp itself not only their training but their cradles. This custom remained also among Alexander's successors. Therefore rations were set for the boys, arms and horses were given to the young men, and rewards were set for the fathers according to the number of their sons. If any fathers had died, the orphans nonetheless drew their fathers' pay; their childhood was spent in military service amid various expeditions. Thus, hardened from tender age by dangers and labours, they became an unconquered army; they regarded the camp no differently than their homeland, and never regarded battle as anything other than victory. This offspring had the name Epigoni. Afterwards, when the Parthians had been subdued, Andragoras, one of the Persian nobles, was set over them as prefect; from him the kings of the Parthians later took their origin.

units.la: 5 Interea Alexander non regio, sed hostili odio seuire in suos coepit. Maxime indignabatur carpi se sermonibus suorum, Philippi patris, patriaque mores subuertisse. Propter quae crimina, Parmenion quoque senex, dignitate regi proximus, cum Philota filio, de utroq; {a}vtroq; prius quaestionibus habitis, interficitur. Fremere itaq; omnes vniuersis castris coepere, innoxij fenis filiiq; casum miserantes; interdum se quoq; non debere melius sperare dicentes. Quae cum nuntiata Alexandro essent, verens ne haec opinio etiam in Macedoniam diuulgaretur, & ne victoriae gloria sauitiae maculam infuscaretur, simulat se ex amicis quosdam in patriam victoriae nuntios misisse. Hortatur milites suis scribere, variorem habituros occasionem, propter militiam remotiorem. Datos fasces epistolarum tacite ad se deferri iubet: ex quibus cognito de se singulorum iudicio, in unam cohortem eos qui de rege durius opinati fuerant, contribuit, aut consumpturus eos, aut in ultimis terris in colonias distributurus. Inde Drancas, Eucrgetas, Paryamas, Parapammenos, Adaspios, ceterosq; populos, qui in radice Caucasi morabantur, subegit. Interea vnus ex amicis Darij Bessus, vinctus perducitur, qui regem non solum prodiderat, verum & interfecerat. Quem in vltionem perfidiae excruciandum fratri Darij tradidit; reputans non tam hostem suum fuisse Darium, quam amicum eius, a quo esset occisus. Et vt his terris nomen relinqueret, vrbem Alexandriam super amnem Tanaim condidit, intra diem septimumdecimum muro 6. millium passuum consummato, translatis eo trium ciuitatium populis, quas Cyrus condiderat. In Bactrianis quoq; Sogdianisque 12. vrbes condidit, distributis bis, quoscunq; in exercitu seditiosos habebat.
units.tr: 5 Meanwhile Alexander began to rage against his own people, not with royal dignity but with hostile hatred. He was especially indignant at being criticised in conversation by his men for having departed from the customs of his father Philip and of his homeland. On account of these alleged crimes, Parmenion, an old man second in rank to the king, was put to death along with his son Philotas, after each had first been examined under questioning. Then all the soldiers in the whole camp began to murmur. They pitied the innocent old man and his son, and some said that they too should not expect better treatment. When this was reported to Alexander, fearing that this opinion would spread to Macedonia, and that the glory of his victory would be stained by the stigma of cruelty, he pretended that he had sent some of his friends home with news of the victory. He urged the soldiers to write to their families, saying that they would have a more convenient opportunity, since the army was so far away. He ordered the bundles of letters to be brought to him secretly. From them he learned each man's opinion of himself. He gathered into a single cohort those who had judged the king too harshly, intending either to destroy them or to scatter them as colonists in the most distant lands. From there he subdued the Drangae, Eucergetae, Paryami, Parapamisadae, Adaspii and the other peoples who dwelt at the foot of the Caucasus. Meanwhile Bessus, one of Darius' friends, was brought to him in chains. Bessus had not only betrayed the king but had also killed him. Alexander handed him over to the brother of Darius to be tortured in punishment for his treachery, reasoning that Darius had been not so much his enemy as the friend by whom he had been murdered. And so that he might leave his name upon these lands, he founded a city named Alexandria on the river Tanais. He completed its wall, six thousand paces in circuit, within seventeen days, and transferred to it the peoples of three cities which Cyrus had founded. He also founded twelve cities among the Bactrians and Sogdians, and he distributed among them all the seditious men he had in his army.

units.la: 6 His ita gestis sollemni die amicos in conuiuium vocat. Vbi orta inter ebrios rerum a Philippo gestarum mentione, praeferre se patri ipse, rerumq; suarum magnitudinem extollere caelo tenus coepit, assentante maiore conuiuarum parte. Itaque cum vnus e senibus Clitus, fiducia amicitiae regiae, cuius palmam tenebat, memo-
units.tr: 6 Having done these things, on a festival day he invited his friends to a banquet. There, among the drunken guests, the deeds of Philip were mentioned, and Alexander began to prefer himself to his father and to raise the greatness of his own achievements to the skies, while most of the guests agreed with him. So when one of the old men, Clitus, relying on the confidence of the royal friendship, whose hand he held, began to defend the memory of Philip and praise his deeds,
mo-

units.la: {a} Viros de se optime meritos obtruncat.
units.tr: He cuts down men who had deserved best of him.

units.la: moriam Philippi tueretur, laudaretque eius res gestas; adeo regem offendit, vt telo à satellite rapto, eundem in conuiuio trucidauerit. Qua cæde exultans, mortuo patrocinium Philippi, laudabat paterna militia obiecta5 bat. Postquam satiatus cæde animus conquieuit, & in iram locum successit existimatio, modo personam occisi, modo causam occidendi considerans, pigere eum facti cœpit: quippe paternas laudes tam iracunde accepisse se, quam nec conuitia debuisset; amicumque senem & innoxium à se occisum, inter epulas & pocula, dolebat.
units.tr: the memory of Philip, and praised his achievements; so greatly did he offend the king that, snatching a spear from a bodyguard, he slew him at the banquet. Exulting in this slaughter, and mocking the dead man's defence of Philip, he reproached him with his father's campaigns.5 But when his spirit, sated with slaughter, grew calm, and anger gave way to judgement, considering now the person of the dead man and now the cause of the killing, he began to regret the deed. Indeed, he had received his father's praises as angrily as if they had been insults, which he ought not to have done; and he grieved that he had killed an old friend who was innocent, in the midst of feasting and drinking.

units.la: Eodem igitur furore in pœnitentiam, quo pridem in iram versus, mori voluit. Primum in fletus progressus, 10 amplexari mortuum, vulnera tractare, & quasi audienti confiteri dementiam; arreptum telum in se vertit:
units.tr: Therefore, with the same frenzy with which he had lately turned to anger, he turned to repentance, and wished to die. At first he gave way to tears, embraced the corpse, handled the wounds, and, as if the dead man could hear him, confessed his madness. Then he seized a weapon and turned it against himself.

units.la: peregisset, facinus, nisi amici interuenissent. Mansit hac voluntas moriendi etiam sequentibus diebus. Acceßerat enim poenitentia nutricis suae, & sororis Cliti recordatio; cuius absentiseum maxime pudebat: tam foedam illi alimentorum suorum mercedem redditam, ut in cuius manibus pueritiam egerat, huic iuuenis, & victor, pro beneficiis funera remitteret. Reputabat deinde, quantum in exercitu suo, quantum apud deuictas gentes fabulárum atq; inuidiae, quantum apud ceteros amicos metuim & odium sui fecerit; quam amarum & triste reddiderit conuiuium suum, non armatus in acie, quam in conuiuio terribilior. Tunc Parmenion & Philotas, tunc Amyntas consobrinus, tunc nouerca fratresque interfecti: tunc Attalus, Eurylochus, Paufanias, aliique Macedoniae extincti principes occurrebant. Ob haec illi quattriduo perseuerata inedia est, donec exercitus vniuersi precibus exoratus est, precantis ne ita morte vnius doleat, vt vniuersos perdat, quos in vltimam deductos Barbariam, inter infestas, & irritatas bello gentes, deflituat. Multum profuere Callisthenis philosophi preces, condiscipulatu apud Aristotelem familiaris illi, & tunc ab ipso rege ad prodenda memoria acta eius accitus. Revocato igitur ad bella animo, Chorasinos & Dahas in deditionem accepit.
units.tr: he would have completed the deed, had his friends not intervened. This wish to die remained for the following days as well. For repentance had come upon him, together with the memory of his nurse and of Clitus' sister; her absence especially shamed him. It was so foul a return for the nourishment he had received, that he, a young man and a victor, should repay with death the one in whose hands he had spent his childhood. He then reflected how much hatred and fear of himself he had created among his army, how much rumour and resentment among the conquered peoples, and how much dread and hatred among his other friends; how bitter and gloomy he had made his banquets, and that he was more terrible at the table than he had ever been unarmed in battle. Then Parmenion and Philotas came before him, then Amyntas his cousin, then his stepmother and brothers, all put to death. Then Attalus, Eurylochus, Pausanias and the other leading men of Macedonia who had been killed rose up before him. Because of these thoughts he persisted in fasting for four days, until the whole army, entreating him, persuaded him, begging that he should not grieve so much for the death of one man as to ruin them all, whom he would abandon, having led them into the furthest barbarian lands, among hostile peoples who were roused to war. The prayers of the philosopher Callisthenes, who had been his fellow pupil under Aristotle and was intimate with him, and who had then been summoned by the king himself to record his deeds, were of great help. So, with his spirit recalled to war, he received the Chorasini and the Dahae into surrender.

units.la: 7 Deinde quod primo ex Persico superbia regia more difsulerat, ac omnia pariter inutidiosiora essent, non salutari, sed adorari se iubet. Accrimus inter recusantes Callisthenes fuit. Quae res & illi, & multis principibus Macedonum exitio fuit: siquidem sub specie insidiarum omnes interfecti. Retentus tamen est a Macedonibus mos salutandi regis, explosa adoratione.
