Post hac Indiam petit, ut Oceano, ultimoq; Oriente Imperii finiret imperium. Cui gloriae, ut etiam exercitus ornamenta conucnirent, phalerας equorum, & armia militum argento inducit; exercitumque suum, ab argenteis clypeis, Argyraspidas appellauit. Cum ad Nysam vrbem venisset, oppidanis non repugnantibus, fiducia religionis Liberi patris, a quo condita vrbs erat, parci iussit: laetus non militiam tantum, verum & vestigia se dei sequutum. Tunc ad spectaculum sacri montis duxit exercitum, naturalibus bonis, vite, hederaq; non aliter vestiti, quam si manu cultus, colentiumque induitria exornatus esset. Sed exercitus eius, vbi ad montem accessit, repentino impetu mentis, in sacros dei vlulatus influxerunt, cum stupore regis, sine noxia difcurrit: vt intelligeret, non tam oppido se parcendo, quam exercitui suo consuluisse. Inde montes Dadalos, regnaque Cleofidis regnum petit. Quae cum se dedidissit ei, concubitu redemptum regnum ab Alexandro recepit; illecebris consecuta, quod virtute non potuerat: filiumque ab eo genitum, Alexandrum nominauit, qui postea
units.tr: 7 Then, because he had at first put off the Persian custom of royal pride, and because all things were becoming more envious, he ordered that he be not greeted but worshipped. Callisthenes was the fiercest of those who refused. This matter proved fatal both to him and to many leading Macedonians, for under the pretext of plots they were all put to death. Nevertheless the Macedonians retained the custom of greeting the king, the worship having been rejected. After this he made for India, so that by the Ocean he might bring his empire to an end at the furthest East. To add splendour to this glory, and so that the army too might be adorned, he had the trappings of the horses and the arms of the soldiers made of silver, and he called his army the Argyraspides, from their silver shields. When he came to the city of Nysa, and the townspeople did not resist, he ordered them spared, trusting in the religion of Father Liber, by whom the city had been founded. He rejoiced that he had followed not only the military exploits but also the footsteps of the god. Then he led the army to a view of the sacred mountain, clothed with natural goods, ivy and vine, dressed in no other way than if he had been adorned by the hand and industry of its worshippers. But when his army came to the mountain, with a sudden impulse of mind they rushed into the sacred revelry of the god, shouting, and ran about without harm, to the king's astonishment, so that he understood he had consulted not so much for the town by sparing it as for his own army. From there he sought the Dadali mountains and the kingdom of Cleophis. When she surrendered to him, he recovered his kingdom from Alexander, which she had bought with her favours; she had gained by allurements what she had not been able to gain by valour. She named the son born to her by him Alexander, who afterwards

units.la: Redit ad ingenium prin-ceps ambiti-osus: & in consiliarios prudentes sæuit crude-liter.
units.tr: He returns to his character: an ambitious prince, and he raged cruelly against prudent counsellors.
He sought to end his empire at the farthest East.
He follows the footsteps of Bacchus.
The Macedonian army runs riot like Bacchants.

units.la: Scorto regiō regnum con-cedit Alexandr. postea regnum Indorum potitus est. Cleofis regina, propter profstratam pudicitiam, scortum regium ab Indu cxinde appellata est. Peragrata India, cum ad saxu mire aspexitatis & altitudinis, in quod multi populi confugerant, peruenisset, cognoscit Herculem ab expugnatione eiusdem saxi terramotu prohibitum: Captus itaq; cupidine, Herculis acta superare, cum summo labore ac periculo potitus saxo, eius omnes loci gentes in deditionem accipit.
units.tr: Alexander grants the kingdom to the royal courtesan. afterwards obtained the kingdom of the Indians. Cleophis the queen, because her chastity had been overthrown, was called after the Indus, a royal courtesan. Having traversed India, when he reached a rock wonderful for its steepness and height, into which many peoples had fled, he learned that Hercules had been prevented by an earthquake from storming that same rock. Seized therefore with desire to surpass the deeds of Hercules, he gained possession of the rock with great toil and danger, and received into surrender all the peoples of that region.

units.la: 8 Vnus ex regibus Indorum fuit, Porus nomine, viribus corporis, & animi magnitudine pariter insignis, qui bellum iampridem, audita Alexandri opinione, in aduentum eius parabat. Commisso itaque prœlio exercitum suum Macedonas innadere iubet; sibi regem eorum priuatum hostem deposcit. Nec Alexander pugna moram fecit: sed prima congressione vulneratu equo, cum praeceps ad terram decidisset, concursu satellitum seruatur. Porus multis vulneribus obrutus capitur. Qui victum se adeo doluit, vt cum veniam ab hoste accepisset, neque cibum sumere voluerit; neque vulnera curari passus fit, aegreque fit ab eo obtentum, vt vellet viuere. Quem Alexander ob honorem virtutus, incolumem in regnum remisit. Duas ibi vrbes condidit, vnam Nicaeam; alteram ex nomine equi Buce-
units.tr: 8 There was one of the kings of the Indians, named Porus, remarkable alike for the strength of his body and the greatness of his spirit, who had long been preparing war against Alexander's coming, having heard of his reputation. So, when battle was joined, he ordered his army to attack the Macedonians, and he demanded that their king be given to him as a private enemy. Alexander did not delay the fight. But in the first encounter his horse was wounded, and when he fell headlong to the ground, he was saved by the rush of his bodyguards. Porus, overwhelmed by many wounds, was taken. He grieved so much at being defeated that, although he had received pardon from his enemy, he would neither take food nor allow his wounds to be treated, and it was with difficulty obtained from him that he should wish to live. Alexander, for the honour of his courage, sent him back unharmed into his kingdom. There he founded two cities, one called Nicaea, and the other, from the name of his horse, he called Buce-

units.la: phalen vocauit. Inde Adrestas, Gesleanos, Prosidas, Gangaridas, caesis eorum exercitibus, expugnat. Cum ad Cuphites venisset, vbi eum hostium ducenta millia equitum opperiebantur, exercitus omnis non minus victoriarum numero, quam laboribus fessus, lacrymis
units.tr: -phalen, he called it. Thence he stormed the Adrestae, Gesleani, Prosidae and Gangaridae, after their armies had been cut down. When he came to Cuphites, where two hundred thousand enemy horsemen awaited him, the whole army, worn out no less by the number of its victories than by its labours, with tears

units.la: cum deprecatur, finem tandem belli faceret; aliquando patriae, reditusque meminisset; respiceret militum animos, quibus vix aetas ad reditum sufficeret: osteнdere alios canicium, alios vulnera, alios aetate con- sumsumpta corpora, alius cicatricibus exhausta: solos se esse qui duorum regum, Philippi Alexandrique, continuam militiam pertulerint. Tandem orare, ut reliquias saltem suas paternis sepulcris reddat, quorum non tam studiis deficiatur, quam annis: Ac si non militibus, vel ipse sibi parcat, ne fortunam suam nimis onerando fatiget. Motus his tam iustis precibus, velut in finem victoriae, castra solito magnificentiora fieri iussit, quorum molitionibus & hostis terreretur, & posteris admiratio sui relinqueretur. Nullum opus milites latius fecere. Itaque, caesis hostibus, cum gratulatione in eadem reverterunt.
units.tr: begged him that he would at last make an end of the war; that he would sometimes remember his homeland and his return; that he would consider the spirits of his soldiers, for whom their age hardly sufficed for the journey home. They showed some their grey hair, others their wounds, others bodies worn out by the passing of years, others bodies exhausted by scars. They alone, they said, were the ones who had endured the continuous military service of two kings, Philip and Alexander. Finally they begged that he at least restore their remnants to their fathers' tombs, for whom it was not so much zeal that failed as years; and if not for the soldiers' sake, that he at least spare himself, lest by overloading his fortune he wear it out. Moved by these so just prayers, as if at the end of the victory, he ordered the camp to be built more magnificently than usual, by whose construction both the enemy might be terrified and admiration for himself be left to posterity. The soldiers never built any work more extensively. And so, having cut down the enemy, they returned with rejoicing to the same place.

units.la: 9 Inde Alexander ad amnem Accesinem pergit: per hunc in Oceanum deiicitur. Ibi Hiacensanas Sileosque, quos Hercules condidit, in deditionem accepit. Hinc in Ambros & Sugambros navigat. Quae gentes cum armatis 80. millibus peditum, & 60. millibus equitum excipiunt. Cum proelio victor esset, exercitum ad urbem eorum ducit. Quam desertam a defensoribus, cum de muro, quem primus ceperat, animadvertisset, in urbis planiciem sine vllo satellite desiliit. Itaq; cum eum hostes solum conspexissent, clamore edito, vndiq; concurrunt, si possint in vno capite orbis bella finire, & vltionem tot gentibus dare. Nec minus Alexander constanter restitit, & vnus aduersus tot millia praeliatur. Incredibile dictu est, vt eum non multitudo hostium, non vis magna telorum, non tantus lacessentium clamor terruerit; solus tot millia cecideritac fugauerit. Vbi vero obrui multitudine se vidit, trunco se, qui tum propter murum stabat, applicuit: cuius auxilio tutus, cum diu agmen sustinuisset, tandem cognito periculo eius, amici ad eum desiliunt; ex quibus multi caesi: praelium tamdiu anceps fuit, quoad omnis exercitus, muris deiectis; lectis, in auxilium venirent. In eo prælio sagitta sub mamma traiectus, cum sanguinis fluxu deficeret, genu posito tamdiu prœliatus est, donec eum, à quo vulneratus suerat, occideret. Curatio vulneris grauior ipso vulnere fuit.
units.tr: 9 Then Alexander made for the river Accesines, down which he was carried into the Ocean. There he received the Hiacensani and the Sileans, whom Hercules had founded, into surrender. From here he sailed against the Ambri and the Sugambri. These peoples met him with 80,000 armed infantry and 60,000 cavalry. When he had won the battle, he led his army to their city. Seeing it deserted by its defenders, he leapt down from the wall, which he had been the first to seize, into the open square of the city, without any attendant. When the enemy caught sight of him alone, they raised a shout and ran together from every side, as if they could end the wars of the whole world in one man and avenge so many nations. Alexander resisted no less steadfastly, and alone he fought against many thousands. It is incredible to relate: neither the multitude of enemies, nor the great force of missiles, nor the enormous clamour of those attacking him frightened him; alone he slew and routed many thousands. But when he saw himself being overwhelmed by the crowd, he pressed his back against a tree trunk that stood beside the wall at that time. Protected by its help, he held off the column for a long time. At last, when his danger was recognised, his friends leapt down to him, and many of them were slain. The battle hung in the balance until the whole army came to help, the walls having been breached and the picked men brought up. In this fight he was struck by an arrow under the breast, and as he was failing from loss of blood, he fought on kneeling until he killed the man by whom he had been wounded. The treatment of the wound was more grievous than the wound itself.

units.la: Io Itaq; ex magna desperatione tandem saluti redditus, Polypercthonta cum exercitu Babyloniam mittit, ipse cum lectissima manu nauibus consconsensis, Oceani littora peragrat. Cum veniset ad vrbem Ambigeri regis, oppidani inuictum ferro audientes, sagittas veneno armant: atq; ita gemino mortis vulnere, hostem à muris summouentes, plurimos interficiunt. Cum inter multos vulneratus etiam Ptolemæus esset, moriturusq; iam iam videretur, per quietem regi monstrata in remedia veneni herba est; qua in potu accepta, statim periculo liberatus est, maiorq; pars exercitus hoc remedio seruata. Expugnata deinde vrbe, reuersus in naues, Oceano libamenta dedit, prosperum in patriam reditum precatus, ac veluti curru circa metam acto; positis imperii terminis, quia sinus aut terrarum solitudines prodire passe sunt, aut mare nauigabile fuit, secundo æstu ostio fluminis Indi inuehitur. Ibi in monumenta verum à se gestarum, vrbem Barcen condidit, arasque statuit, relicto ex numero amicorum, littoralibus Indis præfecto. Inde iter terrestre facturus, cum arida loca medij itineris dicerentur, puteos opportunis locis fieri præcipit, quibus ingenti dulci aqua inuenta, Babyloniam redit. Ibi multa deuicta gentes, præfectos suos accusauerunt; quos sine respectu amicitiæ, Alexander in conspectu legatorum necari iussit. Filiam post hæc Darij regis, Statiram in matrimonium recepit: sed & optimis Macedonum lectas ex omnibus gentibus nobi-lissimas virgines tradidit, ut communi facto crimen regis leniretur.
units.tr: 10 Therefore, after great despair, he was at last restored to health. He sent Polyperchon with the army to Babylon, while he himself, with a chosen band in ships that had been assembled, traversed the shores of the Ocean. When he came to the city of King Ambiger, the townsmen, hearing that he could not be conquered by iron, armed their arrows with poison, and so, inflicting a double deadly wound and driving the enemy from the walls, they killed very many. Among the many wounded was also Ptolemy, who seemed about to die at any moment. A herb was revealed to the king in a dream as the remedy for the poison; when it was taken in drink, he was at once freed from danger, and the greater part of the army was saved by this remedy. Then, the city having been taken, he returned to the ships and made libations to the Ocean, praying for a prosperous return to his homeland, as if he had driven a chariot round the turning-post. Since the boundaries of his empire were fixed, because the gulfs or the desolate lands allowed passage, or the sea was navigable, he was carried by the second tide into the mouth of the river Indus. There, as a memorial of the deeds he had done, he founded the city of Barce and set up altars, leaving behind, from among his friends, a governor for the coastal Indians. Then, about to make the journey by land, since the middle stretch of the route was said to be arid, he ordered wells to be dug at suitable places, and abundant sweet water was found; and he returned to Babylon. There the many subjugated nations accused their governors, and Alexander, without regard for friendship, ordered them to be put to death in the sight of the envoys. After this he took Statira, the daughter of King Darius, in marriage; but he also gave the most noble virgins, chosen from all nations, to the best of the Macedonians, so that the king's offence might be softened by a common act.

units.la: 11 Hinc ad concionem exercitus vocat: & promittit se as alienum omnium propria impensa soluturum, vt praedam praemiaq; integra domos ferat. Insignis haec munificentia non summa tantum, verumetiam titulo muneris fuit, nec à debitoribus magis, quam à creditoribus gratius excepta: quoniam vtrisq; exactio pariter ac solutio difficilis erat. 20. millia talentum in hos sumptus expensa. Dimissis veteranis, exercitum iuvenibus supplet. Sed retenti veteranorum discessum agre ferentes, misionem & ipsi flagitabant, nec annos, sed stipendia sua numerari iubebant; pariter in militiam lectos, pariter sacramento solui aequum censentes: nec iam precibus, sed conuitio agebant, iubetes eum solum cum patre suo Hammone inire bella, quatinus milites suos fastidiat. Contra ille nunc castigare milites, nunc lenibus verbis monere, ne gloriosam militiam seditionibus infuscarent. Ad postremum cum verbis nihil proficeret, ad corripiendos seditionis auctores, e tribunali in concionem armatam inermis ipse desiliit, & nemine prohibente, 13. correptos, manu sua ipse ad supplicia duxit: tantam vel illis moriendi patientiam metus regis, vel huic exigendi supplicij constantiam disciplina militaris dabat.
units.tr: 11 From here he called the army to an assembly and promised to pay all their debts from his own funds, so that they might carry home their booty and rewards intact. This remarkable generosity was notable not only for its size but also for the manner of the gift, and it was welcomed no more gladly by the debtors than by the creditors, since both the collecting and the paying were equally difficult. Twenty thousand talents were spent on these expenses. Having discharged the veterans, he made up the army with young men. But the veterans who were kept back, resenting their departure, also demanded their discharge. They ordered that their service be counted not by years but by campaigns, thinking it fair that those enlisted together should be released from the oath together. Now they spoke not with entreaties but with insults, bidding him wage wars alone with his father Hammon, so that he might do without his soldiers. In reply he sometimes rebuked the soldiers and sometimes admonished them with gentle words, lest they stain glorious service with mutiny. At last, when words achieved nothing, in order to seize the ringleaders of the sedition, he leapt unarmed from the tribunal into the armed assembly, and with no one hindering him he himself led thirteen seized men to execution with his own hand. Such patience in dying was given to them by fear of the king, and such steadiness in carrying out the punishment was given to him by military discipline.

units.la: 12 Inde separatim auxilia Persarum in concione alloquitur. Laudat perpetuam illorum tum in se, tum in priscinos reges fidem; sua in illos beneficia commemorat; vt numquam quasi victos, sed veluti victoriae socios habuerit; denique se in illorum, non illos in gentis sua morem transfisse, affinitatibus connubiorum victos victoribus miscuisse: Nunc quoque ait, custodiam corporis sui non Macedonibus tantum se, verum & illis crediturum. Atque ita mille ex his iuvenes in numerum satellitum legit; auxiliorum quoque portionem nem, formatam in disciplinam Macedonum, exercitui suo miscet. Quam rem agre Macedones tulerunt, iactantes hostes suos in officium suum a rege subiectos. Tunc vniuersi flentes, regem adeunt, orant supplicis suis potius saturet se, quam contumeliis. Qua modestia obtinuerunt, vt vndecim millia militum veterano-rum exauctoraret. Sed & ex amicis dimissi senes Polyperchon, Clytus, Gorgias, Polydamas, Amadas, Antigenes. Dimisso his, Craterus præponitur, iussus præesse Macedonibus in Antipatri locum; Antipatrumque cum supplemento tyronum in locum eius euocat: stipendia reuertentibus, veluti militantibus, data. Dum hæc aguntur, vnus ex amicis eius Ephæ-stion decedit, dotibus primo forme pueritiaque, mox obsequiis regi percarus: quem contra decus regium, Alexander diu luxit; tumulumque ei duodecim millium talentum fecit; eumq; post mortem, coli vt deum iussit.
units.tr: 12 Then he addressed the Persian auxiliaries separately in an assembly. He praised their constant loyalty, both towards himself and towards the earlier kings. He recalled his own benefits to them, saying that he had never treated them as conquered men but as partners in victory. Finally, he said that he had gone over to their customs, not they to his, and that by marriage alliances he had mixed the defeated with the victors. Now too, he said, he would entrust the guard of his body not only to the Macedonians but also to them. And so he chose a thousand of these young men into the number of his bodyguards, and he also mixed a portion of the auxiliaries, trained in Macedonian discipline, into his army. The Macedonians took this badly, complaining that their enemies had been set by the king over their own duty. Then all of them, weeping, approached the king and begged him to satisfy himself with his suppliants rather than with insults. By such moderation they prevailed, so that he discharged eleven thousand veteran soldiers. Among his friends too, the old men Polyperchon, Clytus, Gorgias, Polydamas, Amadas and Antigenes were dismissed. After these were dismissed, Craterus was put in charge, ordered to command the Macedonians in place of Antipater, and Antipater was summoned back with a supply of recruits to take his place. Pay was given to those returning as if they were still serving. While these things were being done, one of his friends, Hephaestion, died. He had been most dear to the king first for the endowments of beauty and boyhood, and later for his services. Alexander mourned him for a long time, contrary to royal dignity, and made him a tomb costing twelve thousand talents; and he ordered that after death he be worshipped as a god.

units.la: 13 Ab vltimis litoribus Oceani Babyloniam reuertenti, nuntiatur legationes Carthaginensium, ceterarumq; Africæ ciuitatium, sed & Hispaniarum, Siciliæ, Galliæ, Sardiniæ, nonnullas quoque ex Italia eius aduentum Babylonia opperiri. Adeo vniuersum terrarum orbem nominis eius terror inuaserat, vt cuncta gentes, veluti destinato sibi regi adulantur. Hac igitur ex causa Babyloniam festinanti, velut conuentum terrarum orbis actturo, quidam ex magis predixit, ne vrbem intraret, testatus hunc locum ei fatalem fore. Ob hoc omissa Babylonia, in Burfiam vrbem trans Eufraten, desertam olim, concessit. Ibi ab Anaxarcho philosopho compulsus est rursum magorum predicta contemnere, vt falsa & incerta; & si fatis constent, ignota mortalibus; at si natura debeatur, immutabilia.
units.tr: 13 As he was returning to Babylon from the farthest shores of the Ocean, it was reported that embassies from the Carthaginians and the other cities of Africa, and also from Spain, Sicily, Gaul and Sardinia, and some even from Italy, were awaiting his arrival at Babylon. So completely had the terror of his name overrun the whole orb of the earth that all nations flattered him as if he were a king already destined for them. Therefore, as he hastened to Babylon, as if about to hold an assembly of the whole world, a certain magus foretold that he should not enter the city, declaring that this place would be fatal to him. On account of this he passed by Babylon and withdrew to the city of Borsippa beyond the Euphrates, which had long been deserted. There the philosopher Anaxarchus persuaded him to scorn again the predictions of the magi as false and uncertain; and if they agree with fate, they are unknown to mortals, but if they are due to nature, they are unchangeable.

units.la: Reuersus igitur Babyloniam, multis diebus otio datis, intermissum olim conuiuium sollemniter instituit; totusq; in latitiam effusus, cum digi noctem peruigilem iunxisset, recedentem iam è conuiuio medicus Theffalus, instaurata comessatione, & ipsum & sodales eius inuitat. Accepto poculo, media potione repente veluti telo confixus, ingemuit: elatusq; è conuiuio semianimis tanto dolore cruciatus est, vt ferrum in remedia posceret, taCtumq; hominum velut vulnera indolesceret. Amici causas morbi, intemperiem ebrietatis dissemina- 10 uerunt. Re autem vera insidiæ fuerunt, quarum infamiam successorum potentia oppresit.
units.tr: Returning therefore to Babylon, and after many days had been given to leisure, he solemnly revived a banquet that had long been interrupted. Being wholly given over to merriment, he joined a sleepless night to the day. As he was already leaving the banquet, a Thessalian physician renewed the revelry and invited both him and his companions. He took the cup, and in the middle of drinking he suddenly groaned, as if struck by a missile. Carried out of the banquet half-dead, he was tormented by such pain that he demanded iron as a remedy, and the touch of men made his wound ache as if it were fresh. His friends put the cause of the illness down to the intemperance of drunkenness. In truth, however, it was a plot, whose infamy the power of his successors suppressed.

units.la: 14 Auctor insidiarum Antipater fuit, qui cum carissimos amicos eius interfectos videret; Alexandrum Lynciestarum generum suum occisum; se magni rebus 15 in Græcia gestis, non tam gratum apud regem, quam inuidiosum esse; à matre quoq; eius Olympiade variis se criminationibus vexatum. Huc accedebat ante paucos dies, supplicia in præfectos deuictarum nationum crudeliter habita. Ex quibus rebus se quoq; à Macedonia nō ad societatem militia, sed ad pœnam euocatum arbitrabatur. Igitur ad occupandum regem, Cassandrum filium dato veneno subornat, qui cum fratribus Philippo & Iolla ministrare regi solebat: cuius veneni tanta vis fuit, vt non ære, non ferro, non testa contineretur, nec aliter ferri, nisi in vngula equi potuerit: praemonito filio, nè alij quam Thessalo, & fratribus crederet. Hac igitur ex causa, apud Thessalum paratum, repetitumq; conuiuium est. Philippus & Iollas pręgustare ac temperare potum regis soliti, in aquafrigida venenum habuerunt, quam pręgustata iam potioni su- permiserunt.
units.tr: 14 The author of the plot was Antipater. He saw his dearest friends killed, and his son-in-law Alexander of Lyncestis slain; he reasoned that he himself, great for his deeds in Greece, was not so much pleasing to the king as hateful to him, and that he was harassed by various accusations from the king's mother Olympias. To this was added the cruel punishments inflicted a few days earlier on the governors of the conquered nations. From these things he also believed that he had been summoned from Macedonia not to share the military command but to be punished. Therefore, to get rid of the king, he secretly prepared poison through his son Cassander, who used to serve the king together with his brothers Philip and Iollas. The poison was so potent that it could not be held in bronze, iron or earthenware, and could be carried only in a horse's hoof. The son had been warned not to trust anyone but the Thessalian and his brothers. For this reason the banquet was prepared and repeated at the Thessalian's house. Philip and Iollas, who were accustomed to taste the king's drink beforehand and mix it, put the poison in cold water, and after tasting it they added it to the drink.

units.la: 15 Quarto die Alexander indubitatam mortem sentiens, agnoscere se fatum domus maiorum suorum ait: nam plerosque AEacidarum intra trigesimum annum defunctos. Tumultuantes deinde milites, insidiis que perire regem suspicantes, ipse se sedavit; eoque omnes cum
units.tr: 15 On the fourth day, Alexander, sensing that his death was beyond doubt, said that he recognised the fate of his forefathers' house, for most of the Aeacidae had died before their thirtieth year. Then the soldiers began to riot and suspected that the king was being killed by treachery, but he himself calmed them, and with that all of them wept and mourned for him.

units.la: prolatus in editissimum urbis locum esset, ad conspectum suum admisit, osculandamque dextram suam flentibus porrexit. Cum lacrymarent omnes, ipse non sine lacrymis tantum, verumetiam sine ullo tristioris mentis argumento fuit, ut quosdam impatientius dolentes consolatus sit, quibus mandata ad parentes eorum dedit: adeo sicut in hostem, ita et in mortem inuictus animus fuit. Dimissis militibus, amicos circumstantes percontatur, videturne similem sibi reperturi regem? Tacentibus cunctis, tum ipse, ut hoc nesciat, ita illud scire, vaticinarique se, ac pene oculis videre dixit, quantum sit in hoc certamine sanguinis fusura Macedonia; quantis cadibus, quo cruore, mortuo sibi parentaturā. Ad postremum, corpus suum in Hammonis templo condi iubet. Cum deficere eum amici viderent, quaerunt quem imperii faciat haeredem: Respondit, Dignissimum. Tanta illi magnitudo animi fuit, ut cum Herculem filium, cum fratrem Aridaeum, cum Roxanen uxorem praegnantem relinqueret; oblitus necessitudinum, dignissimum nuncuparet haeredem. Prorsus quasi nefas esset, viro forti alium quam virum fortem succedere; aut tanti regni opes aliis, quam probatis relinqui. Hac voce veluti bellicum inter amicos cecinisset, aut malum discordiae misisset, ita omnes in aemulationem confurgunt, et ambitione vulgi tacitum favorem militum quaerunt. Sexta die praeclusa voce, exemptum digito anulum Perdicca tradidit: quae res glisccentem amicorum dissensionem sedavit. Nam etsi non voce nuncupatus haeres, indicio tamen electus esse videbatur.
units.tr: When he had been carried out to the highest place in the city, he admitted them to his sight and held out his right hand for them to kiss as they wept. While they all wept, he himself wept too, yet showed no sign of a sad spirit beyond those tears. He consoled some who were grieving too impatiently, and gave them messages for their parents. So unconquered was his spirit in death, just as it had been against an enemy. When the soldiers had been dismissed, he asked the friends standing around him whether they thought they would find a king like him again. When everyone was silent, he said, as if he did not know this but did know that, and as if he were prophesying, that he could almost see with his own eyes how much blood Macedonia would shed in this contest, what slaughters, and what gore there would be to pay funeral rites to him once he was dead. Finally, he ordered that his body be buried in the temple of Hammon. When his friends saw him failing, they asked whom he would make heir to his empire. He replied, "The most worthy." Such was the greatness of his spirit that, although he was leaving behind his son Hercules, his brother Aridaeus, and his pregnant wife Roxane, he forgot his family ties and named the most worthy as heir. It was as if it were wrong for any man of courage to be succeeded by anyone but a man of courage, or as if it were wrong for the wealth of so great a kingdom to be left to anyone but proven men. With these words, as if he had sounded a battle-trumpet or sent out the seed of discord, all the friends rose up in rivalry and, through ambition, sought the silent favour of the common soldiers. On the sixth day, when his voice had failed, he took the ring from his finger and handed it to Perdiccas. This act calmed the growing dissension among his friends, for although he had not named an heir aloud, he seemed to have chosen one by a sign.

units.la: 16 Decessit Alexander, mensem vnum, annos tres & triginta natus; vir supra humanam potentiam magnitudine animi praeditus. Qua nocte eum mater Olympias concepit, visa per quietem est cum ingenti serpente volutari: nec decepta somnio est: nam profecto 5 maius humana mortalitate opus vtero tulit: quam cum AEacidarum gens ab vltima saeculorum memoria, & regna patris, fratris, mariti, ac deinceps maiorum omnium illustrauerint, nullius tamen nomine, quam filij, clarior fuit. Prodigia magnitudinis eius in 10 ipso ortu nonnulla apparuere: nam ea die qua natus est, duae aquilae tota die prope supra culmen domus patris eius sederunt, omen duplicis imperij, Europae Asiaeque praeferentes: eadem quoq; die nuntium pater eius duarum victoriarum accepit; alterius belli Illyrici, 15 alterius certaminis Olympici, in quod quadrigarum currus miserat: quod omen vniuersarum terrarum victoriam infanti portendebat. Puer acerrimis litterarum studiis eruditus fuit. Exacta pueritia per quinquennium sub Aristotele doctore inclyto omnium phi- 20 losophorum, creuit. Accepto deinde imperio, regem se terrarum omnium ac mundi appellari iussit: tantamq; fiducia𝑚 sui militibus fecit, vt illo præsente nullius hostis arma, nec inermes, timuerint. Itaq; cum nullo hostium vmquam congressus est, quem non vicerit; nullam gentem adiit, quam non calcauerit. Victus denique ad postremum est, non virtute hostili, sed insidiis suorum, & fraude ciuili.
units.tr: 16 Alexander died in the thirty-third year of his age, after one month, a man endowed with a greatness of spirit beyond human power. On the night he was conceived, his mother Olympias dreamed that she saw a huge serpent coiling about her, and the dream did not deceive her, for she certainly bore in her womb a work greater than mortal human nature. Although the race of the Aeacidae and the kingdoms of his father, his brother, his husband, and in turn all his ancestors had shone from the earliest memory of the ages, none was more famous by name than her son. Several marvels of his greatness appeared at his very birth. On the day he was born, two eagles sat almost the whole day above the roof of his father's house, presaging a double empire, of Europe and Asia. On the same day his father also received news of two victories: one in the Illyrian war, the other in the Olympic contest, to which he had sent a chariot team. This omen foretold to the infant the victory over all lands. The boy was educated in the most eager studies of letters. After his boyhood had run its course, he grew up for five years under Aristotle, the famous teacher of all philosophers. When he received the empire, he ordered that he be called king of all lands and of the world, and he inspired such confidence in his soldiers that, while he was present, they feared no enemy's arms, not even when they were unarmed. Thus he never met an enemy whom he did not defeat, and he never approached a nation that he did not trample. At last he was finally overcome, not by hostile valour but by the treachery of his own people and by civil fraud.

units.la: POMPEII TROGI EPI- TOMA HISTORIARVM LIBER XIII.
units.tr: THE HISTORIES OF POMPEIUS TROGUS, EPITOMISED BY JUSTIN, BOOK 13
SUMMARY

units.la: 1 Lucius post Alexandri excessum. Macedonum ambitio, gratitudo, ducum ambitio, militumque auaritia. | 5 Bellum pro Graecia libertate, ab Athenien sibus & Aetolis reparatum. Demosthenis pro patria labore.
units.tr: 1 After Alexander's death. The ambition of the Macedonians, their gratitude, the ambition of the commanders, and the greed of the soldiers. | 5 The war for Greek liberty, renewed by the Athenians and Aetolians. Demosthenes' labour for his country.

units.la: 2 De Alexandri successorum exercitus sena tentiq pugnantes, | 6 Perdicca a Cappadoces prælio fatigat. Bellum inter Antigonum & Perdiccam. Ptolemaei foliersindustria.
units.tr: 2 The armies and senates of Alexander's successors fight one another. | 6 Perdiccas fights the Cappadocians in battle. War between Antigonus and Perdiccas. Ptolemy's cunning industry.

units.la: 3 Perdiccæ sententiæ rem clamant pedires; unde tumultus & seditio, cui Perdicca prudenter medetur. | 7 De origine urbis Cyrenes digressio.
units.tr: 3 Perdiccas' opinion is rejected by the foot soldiers; hence tumult and sedition, which Perdiccas wisely remedies. | 7 A digression on the origin of the city of Cyrene.

units.la: 4 Aridæo rege designato, Perdicca & alii duces seu Principes prouincias diuiserunt. | 8 Ptolemæus bellum parat in Perdiccam. Eumenes fortiter & feliciter gesta.
units.tr: 4 With King Aridaeus designated, Perdiccas and the other commanders or leaders divide the provinces. | 8 Ptolemy prepares war against Perdiccas. Eumenes' brave and successful exploits.

units.la: XTINCTO in ipso ætatis, ac victoriarum flore Alexandro Magno, triste apud omnes, tota Babylone silentium fuit. Sed nec deuicta gentes fidem nuntio habuerunt, quod ut viuictum regem, ita immortalem esse crediderant: recordantes, quoties præsenti morte ereptus esset; quam sæpe pro amisso, repente se non sospitem tantum suis, vemetiam victorem obtulisset. Vt vero mortis eius fides adfuit, omnes barbaræ gentes paulo ante ab eo devicta, non vt hostem, sed vt parentem luxerunt. Matter quoque Darij regis, quam amisso filio, à fastigio tanta maiestatis in captiuitatem redactam, indulgentia victoris, in eâ diem vita non pœnituerat, audita
units.tr: When Alexander the Great was extinguished in the very bloom of his age and victories, there was a grim silence throughout Babylon, shared by all. Yet the conquered nations did not believe the messenger, for they had believed that the king, as he was unconquered, was also immortal. They recalled how often he had been snatched from imminent death, and how often, when given up for lost, he had suddenly presented himself to his men not merely safe but victorious. But when the report of his death was confirmed, all the barbarian peoples, lately conquered by him, mourned him not as an enemy but as a father. The mother of King Darius too, who after losing her son had been reduced from the height of such majesty to captivity, and had not repented of living to that day because of the victor's kindness, on hearing of Alexander's death killed herself.

units.la: morte Alexandri, mortem sibi ipsa conscivit; non quod hostem filio praeferret, sed quod pietate filij in eo, quem vt hostem timuerat, experta esset. Contra Macedones versa vice, non vt ciuem, ac tanta maiestatis regem, verum vt hostem amissum, gaudebant; seueritatem nimiam, & assidua belli pericula execrantes. Huc accedebat, quod principes regnum & imperia, vulgus militum thesauros, & grande pondus auri velut inopinatam predam,spectabant: illi successionem regni, bi opum, ac diuitiarum hereditatem cogitantes. Erant enim in thesauris quinquaginta millia talentum, & inannuo vectigali tributo, tricena millia. Sed amici Alexandri fuftra regnum spectabant; nam eius virtutis ac venerationis erant, vt singulos reges putares. Quippe ea forma pulchritudo, & proceritas corporis, & virium ac sapientia magnitudo in omnibus fuit, vt qui eos ignoraret, non ex vna gente, sed ex toto terrarum orbe electos iudicaret: neq; enim vmquam ante Macedonia, vel vlla gens alia, tam clarorum virorum prouentu floruit: quos primo Philippus, mox Alexander tanta cura legerat, vt non tam ad societatem belli, quam in successionem regni, electi viderentur. Quis igitur miretur, talibus ministris, orbem terrarum victum, cum exercitus Macedonum tot, non ducibus, sed regibus regeretur? quinumquam sibi reperiffent pares, si non inter se concurriffent: multosque Macedonia pro vno Alexandros habuisset, nisi fortuna eos aemulatione virtutis in perniciem mutuam armasset.
units.tr: She did not do so because she preferred an enemy to her son, but because she had experienced the kindness of Alexander, whom she had feared as an enemy. The Macedonians, by contrast, rejoiced at the turn of events: not that they had lost a fellow citizen and a king of such majesty, but that they had lost an enemy; they cursed his excessive severity and the constant dangers of war. Moreover, the princes looked to the kingdom and the commands, and the common soldiers to the treasures and the great weight of gold, as an unexpected prize; the one thinking of the succession to the kingdom, the other of the inheritance of wealth and riches. For there were fifty thousand talents in the treasuries, and an annual revenue of thirty thousand talents in tribute. But Alexander's friends were vainly looking to the kingdom, for they were of such virtue and reputation that each of them might be taken for a king. Indeed, such beauty of form, stature of body, and greatness of strength and wisdom were found in all of them, that anyone who did not know them would judge them chosen not from one nation but from the whole world. For never before had Macedonia, or any other nation, flourished with such a supply of distinguished men; these Philip first, and then Alexander, had selected with such care that they seemed chosen not so much as comrades in war as successors to the kingdom. Who then would wonder that the world was conquered by such ministers, when so many Macedonian armies were ruled not by commanders but by kings? Indeed, they would never have found their equals had they not been pitted against one another; and Macedonia would have had many Alexanders in place of one, had not fortune armed them, through rivalry in virtue, for their mutual destruction.

units.la: 2 Ceterum occiso Alexandro, non vt lati ita & fecuri fuere, omnibus vnum locum competentibus: nec minus milites quam inuicem se timebant, quorum & libertas solutior & fauor incertus erat. Inter ipsos vero . aequalitas discordiam augebat, neminem tantum ceteros . exceexcedente, vt ei aliquis se summitteret Armati itaq; in regiam coeunt, ad firmandum rerum praesentium sta-
units.tr: 2 Moreover, after Alexander was killed, they were not as happy and secure as they had been; since not all could occupy the same place, the soldiers feared one another no less than they feared the commanders, for their freedom was rather loose and their favour uncertain. Among the leaders themselves, equality increased the discord, since no one so far surpassed the others that anyone would submit himself to him. Therefore they came armed into the palace, to secure the present state of affairs.

units.la: tum. Perdicca censet Roxanis exspectari partum, quae exacto mense octauo, matura iam ex Alexandro erat;
units.tr: Perdiccas advised that they should await the birth of Roxana's child, for in the eighth month, her child by Alexander was now ripe for birth.

units.la: 5 & si puerum peperisset, hunc dari successorem patri. Meleager negat differendum in partus dubios, consiliumq; expectandum dum reges nascerentur, cum iam genitis uti liceret: seu puer illis placeat, esse Pergami filium Alexandri natum ex Barsine, nomine Herculem;
units.tr: 5 And if she bore a son, he should be given as successor to his father. Meleager denied that decisions should be postponed for doubtful births, and that they should wait for kings to be born when they could use those already born. Whether they preferred a boy, he said, there was a son of Alexander born at Pergamum to Barsine, named Hercules;

units.la: 10 seu mallent iuuenem, esse in castris fratrem Alexandri Aridæum comem, & cunctis non suo tantum, verum & patris Philippi nomine acceptissimum. Ceterum Roxanem esse originis Persicæ, nec esse fas, vt Macedonibus ex sanguine eorum, quorum regna deleuerint,
units.tr: 10 or whether they preferred a young man, there was in the camp Alexander's brother Aridaeus, pleasing to all, and most acceptable not only by the name of his father but also by that of Philip. Moreover, Roxana was of Persian origin, and it was not right that kings should be set up for the Macedonians from the blood of those whose kingdoms they had destroyed,

units.la: 15 reges constituantur: quod nec ipsum Alexandrum voluisse dicit. Denique morientem nullam de eo mentionem habuisse. Ptolemaeus recusabat regem Aridæum, non propter maternas modo sordes, quod ex Lariffæo scorto natus esset, sed etiam propter valitudinem maiorem,
units.tr: 15 which, he said, Alexander himself had not wished either. Finally, he had made no mention of her when dying. Ptolemy refused King Aridaeus, not only on account of his maternal baseness, since he had been born of a Larisaean harlot, but also on account of the greater illness from which he suffered;

units.la: 20 quam patiebatur; ne ille nomen regis, alius imperium teneret: melius esse ex his legi, qui pro virtute regi suo proximi fuerint, qui provincias regant, quibus bella mandentur, quam sub persona regis indignorum subiiciantur imperio. Vicit Perdiccæ sententia, consensu vniuersorum. Placuit itaq; Roxanis expectari partum; & si puer natus fuisset, tutores Leonatum & Perdiccam, & Crateron, & Antipatrum constituunt; consestim͏ in tutorum obsequia iurant.
units.tr: 20 lest the one should hold the name of king while another held the power: it was better that they should choose from those who were nearest to their king in virtue, to rule the provinces and to whom wars might be entrusted, than that they should be subjected to the rule of unworthy men under the title of king. Perdiccas' opinion prevailed, with the consent of all. It was therefore decided that Roxana's child should be awaited; and if a son were born, they appointed as guardians Leonnatus, Perdiccas, Craterus and Antipater; and at once they all swore obedience to the guardians.

units.la: 3 Cum equites quoq; idem fecissent, pedites indignati, nullas sibi consiliorum partes relictas, Aridæum Alexandri fratrem regem appellant, satellitesq; illi ex tribu sua legunt, & nomine Philippi patris vocari iubent. Quæ cum nuntiata equitibus essent, legatos ad mitigandos eorum animos, duos ex proceribus, Attalum & Meleagrum mittunt, qui potentiam ex vulgi adulatione quaerentes, omissa legatione, militibus consentiunt. Statim & seditio creuit, vbi caput & confilium habere coepit. Tunc ad delendum equitatum cunctri armati in regiam irrumpunt: quo cognito, equites trepidi ab vrbe discedunt, castris, positis, & ipsi pedites terreri coeperunt. Sed nec procerum inter se odia cessabant. Attalus ad interficiendum Perdiccam ducem partis alterius, mittit: ad quem armatum, & vltro vocantem, cum accedere percussores ausi non fuissent; tanta constantia Perdicca fuit, vt vltro ad pedites venire, & in concionem vocatos edoceret quod facinus molirentur, reprehicerent contra quos arma sumpsissent: non illos Persas, sed Macedonas; non hostes, sed cives eorum, plerosque, etiam cognatos eorum, certe commilitones, eorundem castrorum ac periculorum socios: edituros deinde egregium hostibus suis spectaculum, vt quorum armis victos se doleant, eorum mutuis caedibus gaudeant, parentaturosque, sanguine suo manibus hostium a se interfectorum.
units.tr: 3 When the cavalry had done the same, the foot soldiers, indignant that no share of the counsels was left to them, proclaimed Aridaeus, Alexander's brother, king, and chose bodyguards for him from their own tribe, and ordered that he be called by the name of his father Philip. When this was reported to the cavalry, they sent two of the nobles, Attalus and Meleager, to calm their spirits. But these men, seeking power through the flattery of the common people, abandoned their embassy and sided with the soldiers. At once the sedition grew, once it began to have a head and a plan. Then, to destroy the cavalry, all the leaders in arms burst into the palace; when this became known, the cavalry in alarm left the city and pitched their camp, and the foot soldiers themselves began to be terrified. Nor did the hatred among the nobles cease: Attalus sent men to kill Perdiccas, the leader of the opposing party. But when he, armed and even calling them to him, was approached by assassins who dared not come near, Perdiccas showed such constancy that he went of his own accord to the foot soldiers, and summoned them to an assembly and explained what crime they were planning, and what they were reproaching and against whom they had taken up arms: not Persians, but Macedonians; not enemies, but their own citizens, many of them even their kinsmen, and certainly their fellow soldiers, comrades of the same camp and dangers; and that they would then provide an excellent spectacle for their enemies, so that they who grieve at having been conquered by their arms should rejoice at their mutual slaughter, and that they would make funeral offerings with their own blood to the shades of those slain by the hands of their enemies.

units.la: 4 Hac cum pro singulari facundia sua Perdicca peroraffet, adeo mouit pedites, vt probato consilio eius dux ab omnibus legeretur. Tum equites in concordiam reuocati, in Aridaeum regem consentiunt. Seruata est portio regni Alexandri filio, si natus esset. Hac agebant, posito in medio corpore Alexandri, vt maiestas eius testis decretorum esset. His ita compositis, Macedonia & Graecia Antipater praeponitur: Regia pecunia custodia Cratero traditur: Castrorum, & exercitus, & rerum cura Meleagro, & Perdicca assignatur: iubeturque Aridaeus rex, corpus Alexandri in Hammonis templum deducere. Tunc Perdicca infensus seditionis auctori
units.tr: 4 When Perdiccas had spoken at length with his singular eloquence, he moved the foot soldiers so greatly that, approving his plan, they chose him as their leader by common consent. Then the cavalry, recalled to harmony, agreed to have Aridaeus as king. A portion of the kingdom was preserved for Alexander's son, if he should be born. They did these things with Alexander's body placed in their midst, so that his majesty might be a witness to their decrees. With these matters settled, Antipater was placed over Macedonia and Greece; the royal treasure was entrusted to Craterus; the care of the camp, the army, and affairs was assigned to Meleager and Perdiccas; and King Aridaeus was ordered to convey the body of Alexander to the temple of Hammon. Then Perdiccas, hostile to the author of the sedition, ...

units.la: {y} Aridaeus Antipater obtinet. ftoribus, repête ignaro collega, lustrationem castrorum propter mortem regis, in posterum edicit. Postquam armatum exercitum in campo constituit, consentientibus vniuersis, euocatos dum transit, de singulis manipulis seditiosos, supplicio tradi occulte iubet. Reuersus inde, inter principes prouincias diuidit, simul vt & remoueret æmulos, & munus imperij, beneficij sui faceret. Primo Ptolemæo Ægyptus, & Africa, Arabiaque pars forte venit, quem ex gregario milite Alexander virtutis causa prouexerat: cui ad tradendam prouinciam Cleomenes, qui Alexandriam ædificauerat, datur. Confinem huic prouinciæ Syriam Laomedon Mityleneus, Ciliciam Philotas, Philo Illyrios accipiunt. Media maiori Acropatos, minori socer Perdicca præponitur. Sufiana gens Scyno, Phrygia maior Antigono Philippi filio assignatur. Lyciam & Pamphiliam Nearchus, Cariam Cassander, Lydiam Menander sortíuntur. Leonato minor Phrygia euenit; Thracia & regiones Pontici maris Lysimacho: Cappadocia cum Paphlagonia Eumeni data. Summus castrorum tribunatus Seleuco Antiochi filio cessit. Stipatoribus regis satellitibusque Cassander filius Antipatri præficitur. In Bactriana vlteriore, & India regionibus, priores præsecti retenti. Terras inter amnes Hydaspem & Indum, Taxiles habebat. In coloniis in Indis conditas, Pithon Agenoris filius mittitur. Parapamenos, fines Caucasi montis, Extarches accepit. Aracosii Gedrosiqúe Sibyrtio tradunt̃: Dranca & Arei Statanori: Bactrianos Amyntas sortitur, Sogdianos Scythæus, Nicanor Parthos, Philippus Hyrcanos, Phratasernes Armenios, Tleptolemus Persas, Peucestes Babylonios, Archos Pelasgos, Arcesilaus Mosopotamiam. Cum hæc diuisio, veluti fatale munus singulis contigisset,
units.tr: Antipater holds Aridaeus. Without the knowledge of his colleague, he ordered a purification of the camp because of the king's death, to be done in future. After he had drawn up the armed army on the plain, with the consent of all, he secretly ordered that, as they were called out one by one as he passed, the seditious men from each company be handed over to punishment. Returning from there, he divided the provinces among the leading men, both to remove his rivals and to make the office of government a gift of his own kindness. To Ptolemy fell by chance Egypt, Africa, and part of Arabia, whom Alexander had promoted from a common soldier for his valour; to him Cleomenes, who had built Alexandria, was given to hand over the province. Laomedon of Mytilene received Syria, which borders this province; Philotas Cilicia; Philo Illyria. Atropates was placed over Media Major, and Perdiccas' father-in-law over Media Minor. Scynus received the Susian people, and Antigonus, son of Philip, was assigned Greater Phrygia. Nearchus obtained Lycia and Pamphylia, Cassander Caria, and Menander Lydia. Lesser Phrygia fell to Leonnatus; Thrace and the regions of the Pontic sea to Lysimachus; Cappadocia with Paphlagonia was given to Eumenes. The chief tribunate of the camp passed to Seleucus, son of Antiochus. Cassander, son of Antipater, was placed in charge of the king's attendants and bodyguards. In Further Bactria and the regions of India, the former prefects were retained. Taxiles held the lands between the rivers Hydaspes and Indus. Pithon, son of Agenor, was sent to the colonies founded in India. Extarchus received Parapamisus, the borders of Mount Caucasus. Sibyrtius was handed Arachosia and Gedrosia; Stasanor Drangiana and Areia; Amyntas obtained the Bactrians, Scythaeus the Sogdians, Nicanor the Parthians, Philip the Hyrcanians, Phrataphernes the Armenians, Ptolemy son of Lagus the Persians, Peucestes the Babylonians, Archon the Pelasgians, and Arcesilaus Mesopotamia. When this division had fallen to each of them like a fated gift,

units.la: ita magna incrementorum materia plurimis fuit. Si quidem non magno post tempore, quasi regna, non praesecturas diuisissent; sic reges ex praefectis facti, magnas opes non sibi tantum parauerunt, verumetiam posteris reliquerunt.
units.tr: Thus the great source of increase was given to many. For not long afterwards they divided the provinces as if they were kingdoms rather than governorships, so that the governors became kings. They gained great wealth, not only for themselves but also for their descendants.

units.la: Dum haec in Oriente aguntur, in Gracia Athe- niens, & AEtoli bellum, quod iam viuo Alexandro mouerant, summis viribus instruebant. Causa belli erant, quod reuer-sus ab India Alexander, epistolas in Graciam scripserat, quibus omnium ciuitatium exules, praeter cadis damnati, reflituebantur. Qua recitata praesente vniuersa Gracia, in mercatu Olympiaco, magnos motus fecerunt; quod plurimi non legibus pulsi patria, sed per factionem principum fuerant, verentibus iisdem principibus, ne revocati potentiores in republica fierent. Palam igitur iam tunc multa ciuitates, libertatem bello vindicandam fremebant. Principes tamen omnium Athenienses, & AEtoli fuere. Quod cum nuntiatum Alexandro effet, mille naues longas focis imperari praeceperat, quibus in Occidente bellum gereret; excurfurusq; cum valida manu fuerat ad Athenas delendas. Igitur Athenienses, contracto 30. millium exercitu, & 200. nauibus, bellum cum Antipatro, cui Gracia forte euenerat, gerunt; eumq; detrectantem prælium, & Heraclea vrbis moenibus tuentem se, obsidione cingunt. Eodem tempore, Demosthenes Athenien- sis orator, pulsus patria, ob crimen accepti ab Harpalo auri, qui crudelitatem Alexandri fugerat, quod ciuitatem in eiufdem Alexandri bellum impelleret, forte Megaris exulabat: qui vt missum ab Atheniensibus Hyperidem legatum cognouit, qui Peloponnenses in societatem armorum solicitaret, sequutus eum Sicyona, Argos & Corinthum, ceterasq; ciuitates, eloquentia sua Athenienfibus iunxit. Ob quod factum, missa ab Athenien sibus obuiam naue, ab exilio reuocatur. Interim in obsidione Antipatri, Leosthenes dux Athenien sium, telo è muris in transeuntem iacto, occiditur. Quae res tantum animorum Antipatro dedit, vt etiam vallum rescindere auderet. Auxilium deinde à Leonato per legatos petit : qui cum venire cum exercitu nuntiatus esset, obuij ei Athenienses cum instructis copiis fuere, ibique equestri prælio, graui vulnere ictus extinguitur. Antipater, tametsi auxilia sua videret victa, inorte tamen Leonati letatus est: quippe & æmulum sublatum, & vires eius accessisse sibi gratulabatur. Statim igitur exercitu eius recepto, cum par hostibus etiam prælio videretur, solutus obsidione, in Macedoniam concessit. Gracorum quoque copiae, finibus Græciæ hoste pulso, in vrbes dilapsæ.
units.tr: While these things were happening in the East, the Athenians and the Aetolians in Greece were busily preparing with all their strength a war that they had begun to plan while Alexander was still alive. The cause of the war was this. On returning from India, Alexander had written letters to Greece ordering that the exiles of every city be restored, except those condemned for murder. When these letters were read aloud before all Greece at the Olympic assembly, they caused great agitation. Most of those exiled had been driven from their homeland not by law but by the factions of the leading men, who feared that if the more powerful exiles were recalled they would gain control of the state. Openly, then, many cities were already murmuring that liberty must be defended by war. The chief leaders of this movement were the Athenians and the Aetolians. When this was reported to Alexander, he gave orders that a thousand warships be built in the ports, intending to wage war in the West, and he had set out with a strong force to destroy Athens. The Athenians therefore raised an army of 30,000 men and 200 ships and waged war against Antipater, to whom Greece had fallen by lot. Antipater refused to fight and defended himself within the walls of Heraclea, and the Athenians besieged him there. At the same time, Demosthenes, the Athenian orator, who had been driven from his country on the charge of having accepted gold from Harpalus, who had fled from Alexander's cruelty, and of having urged the state into war against that same Alexander, was living in exile at Megara. When he learned that Hyperides had been sent by the Athenians as envoy to win the Peloponnesians to a military alliance, he followed him to Sicyon, Argos and Corinth and the other cities, and by his eloquence he won them over to the Athenians. Because of this deed, a ship was sent by the Athenians to meet him, and he was recalled from exile. Meanwhile, during the siege of Antipater, Leosthenes, the Athenian commander, was killed when a missile was thrown from the walls at him as he passed by. This event gave Antipater such courage that he dared to tear down the rampart. Next he sought help from Leonnatus through envoys. When it was announced that Leonnatus was coming with an army, the Athenians met him with their forces drawn up, and there in a cavalry battle he was struck by a grievous wound and died. Antipater, although he saw his own auxiliaries defeated, nevertheless rejoiced at the death of Leonnatus, for he congratulated himself that a rival had been removed and that his forces had been increased. Therefore, having taken back his army, and since the battle seemed to be even with the enemy, he lifted the siege and withdrew into Macedonia. The Greek forces too, once the enemy had been driven from the borders of Greece, scattered into their cities.

units.la: 6 Interea Perdicca, bello Ariaratni regi Cappadocum illato, prælio, victor, nihil præmij præter vulnera, & pericula retulit. Quippe hostes ab acie in vrbem recepti, occisis coniugibus, & liberis, domos quisque suas cum omnibus copiis incenderunt. Eodem congestis etiam seruitiis, & semetipsos præcipitant, vt nihil hostis victor suarum rerum, præter incendij spectaculo fuerit. Inde, vt viribus auctoritatem regiam acquireret, ad nuptias Cleopatræ sororis Alexandri Magni, & alterius Alexandri quondam vxoris, non aspernante Olympiade matre eius, intendit: sed prius Antipatrum, sub affinitatis obtentu, capere cupiebat. Itaque fingit se in matrimonium filiam eius petere, quo facilius ab eo supplementum tyronū ex Macedonia obtineret. Quem dolum prasentiente Antipatro, dum duas eodem tempore vxores quarit, neutram obtinuit. Post hæc bellum inter Antigonum & Perdiccam oritur, Antigono Cra-
units.tr: 6 Meanwhile Perdiccas, having waged war on Ariarathes, king of the Cappadocians, won the battle but gained nothing from it except wounds and dangers. For the enemy, retreating from the line into their city, slew their wives and children and then each man set fire to his own house with all his possessions. Then, having piled up their slaves as well, they threw themselves into the flames, so that the victorious enemy got nothing of their property except the spectacle of the fire. Then, to strengthen his power with royal authority, he aimed at marrying Cleopatra, the sister of Alexander the Great and former wife of another Alexander, and Olympias, the mother of Alexander, did not object. But first he wished to seize Antipater under the pretext of kinship, so he pretended that he was asking for Antipater's daughter in marriage, so that he could more easily obtain from him a supply of recruits from Macedonia. Antipater, aware of this trick, while Perdiccas sought two wives at the same time, obtained neither. After this a war arose between Antigonus and Perdiccas,

units.la: Cappadoces bello aggreditur, & cineres pro præmio referunt.
units.tr: The Cappadocians he attacked in war, and they brought back ashes as their reward.

units.la: Cleopatræ nuptias ambit, & Antipatro parat insidias.
units.tr: He sought the marriage with Cleopatra, and he prepared plots against Antipater.

units.la: Bellum inter Antigonu & Perdiccam. terus & Antipater auxilium ferebant; qui facta cum Atheniensibus pace, Polyperchonta Gracia & Macedonia praponunt. Perdicca, alienatis rebus, Aridaum, & Alexandri Magni filium in Cappadocia, quorum cura illi mandata fuerat, de summa belli in consilium adhibet. 5 Quibusdam placebat bellu in Macedoniam transferri, ad ipsum fontem & caput regni, vbi & Olympias effet mater Alexandri, non mediocre momentum partium, & ciuium fauor, propter Alexandri, Philippique nomina: sed in rem visum est ab AEgypto incipere, ne in Macedoniam profectis, Asia à Ptolemaeo occuparetur. Eumeni, praeter prouincias quas acceperat, Paphlagonia, & Caria, & Lycia, & Phrygia adiiciuntur. Ibi Craterum & Antipatrum opperiri iubetur: adiutores ei dantur cum exercitibus frater Perdicca Alcetas, & Neoptolemus: Clito cura classis traditur: Cilicia Philota adempta, Philoxeno datur; ipse Perdicca AEgyptum cum ingenti exercitu petit. Sic Macedonia, in duas partes discurrentibus ducibus; in sua viscera armatur; ferrumque ab hostili bello in ciuilem sanguinem vertit, exemplo furentium, manus ac membra sua ipsa cæsura. Sed Ptolemæus in Ægypto, sollerti industria, magnas opes parabat: quippe & Ægyptios insigni moderatione in fauorem sui solicitauerat; & reges finitimos beneficiis, obsequisque deuinxerat; terminos quoque imperij, acquisita Cyrene vrbe, ampliauerat; factusque iam tantus erat, vt non tam timeret hostes, quam timendus ipse hostibus esset.
units.tr: War between Antigonus and Perdiccas. Craterus and Antipater were giving aid to Antigonus. Having made peace with the Athenians, they placed Polyperchon in charge of Greece and Macedonia. Perdiccas, with affairs now estranged, consulted Aridaeus and the son of Alexander the Great, whom he had left in Cappadocia under their care, about the conduct of the war. Some thought the war should be transferred to Macedonia, to the very source and head of the kingdom, where Olympias, the mother of Alexander, was, and where the name of Alexander and Philip carried no small weight with the party and the favour of the citizens. But it seemed better to begin with Egypt, lest, if they set out for Macedonia, Asia would be seized by Ptolemy. To Eumenes, in addition to the provinces he had received, Paphlagonia, Caria, Lycia and Phrygia were added. He was ordered to wait there for Craterus and Antipater; his helpers were given with their armies: Perdiccas's brother Alcetas and Neoptolemus. The command of the fleet was entrusted to Clitus; Cilicia was taken from Philotas and given to Philoxenus. Perdiccas himself made for Egypt with a huge army. Thus Macedonia, with its commanders running in two directions, armed itself against its own vitals, and turned the sword from a foreign war to civil bloodshed, like madmen who cut off their own hands and limbs. But Ptolemy in Egypt, by skilful diligence, was building up great resources. Indeed, by his remarkable moderation he had won over the Egyptians to his side, and by benefits and favours he had bound the neighbouring kings to himself. He had also enlarged the borders of his realm by acquiring the city of Cyrene, and he had become so powerful that he feared his enemies less than he was feared by them.

units.la: 7 Cyrene autem condita fuit ab Aristæo, cui nomen Battus propter linguæ obligationem fuit. Huius pater Cirnus, rex Theramenis insulæ, cum ad oraculum Delphos, propter dedecus adolescentis filij nondum loquentis, deum deprecaturus venisset, responsum accepit, quo iubebatur filius eius Battus Africam petere, & vrbem Cyrenem condere, vsum lingua ibi accepturus. Cum responsum ludibrio simile videretur, propter foli-
units.tr: 7 Cyrene was founded by Aristaeus, who was called Battus because of an impediment of his tongue. His father, Cyrnus, king of the island of Thera, went to the oracle at Delphi to beseech the god, because of the shame of his son who could not yet speak, and he received a response ordering that his son Battus should go to Africa and found the city of Cyrene, where he would receive the use of his tongue. Since the response seemed like a mockery, because of the desolation of the island of Thera, from which the colonists were ordered to set out to found a city in so vast a region of Africa, the matter was dropped.

units.la: 5 tudihem Theramenis insula, ex qua coloni ad vrbem condendam in Africam tam vaste regionis, proficisci iubebantur, res omissa est. Interiecto deinde tempore, velut contumaces, pestilentia Deo parere compelluntur: quorum tam insignis paucitas fuit, vt vix vnam
units.tr: 5 After an interval, as if they were rebellious, they were compelled by a pestilence to obey the god. Their number was so small that they could scarcely fill one ship.

units.la: 10 nauem complerent. Cum venissent in Africam pulsis accolis, montem Cyran, & propter amoenitatem loci, & propter fontis vbertatem occupauere. ibi Battus dux eorum, lingua nodis solutis, loqui primum coepit: quae res animos eorum, ex promissis dei iam parte percepta,
units.tr: 10 When they had come to Africa, having driven out the inhabitants, they occupied the mountain of Cyrene, both for the pleasantness of the place and for the richness of its spring. There Battus, their leader, with his tongue loosed from its knots, began first to speak. This event, since part of the god's promises had now been fulfilled, kindled their hope for the rest, namely the founding of the city.

units.la: 15 in reliquam spem condenda vrbis accendit. Positis igitur castris opinionem veteris fabulae accipiunt, Cyrenem eximie pulchritudinis virginem, à Theffalia monte Pelio ab Apolline raptam, perlatamque in eiusdem montis iuga, cuius collem occupauerant, à deo
units.tr: 15 Having pitched their camp, they adopted the story of an old legend: that Cyrene, a maiden of extraordinary beauty, had been carried off from Mount Pelion in Thessaly by Apollo, and had been brought to the ridges of that same mountain, of which the hill they had occupied formed part, and that there she bore four sons:

units.la: 20 repletam, quatuor pueros peperisse, Nomium, Ariftaeum, Authocum, Argaeum: missos à patre Speo rege Theffalia, qui perquirerent virginem, loci amoenitate captos in iisdem terris cum virgine resedisse. Ex his pueris tres adultos in Theffaliam reuersos, auita re-
units.tr: 20 Nomius, Aristaeus, Autochthon and Argaeus. These boys were sent by their father, Aristaeus, king of Thessaly, to search for the maiden, but captivated by the pleasantness of the land, they settled there with the maiden. Of these boys, three, when grown up, returned to Thessaly and seized the ancestral kingdom.

units.la: 25 gna cepisse. Ariftaeum in Arcadia late regnaffe, eumque primum, & apium, & mellis vsum, & lactis ad coagula hominibus tradidisse, solstitialisque ortus fideriis primum inuenisse. Quibus auditis, Battus virginis nomine ex responsis aguito, vrbem Cyrenem condidit.
units.tr: 25 Aristaeus was said to have ruled widely in Arcadia, and he was the first to teach men the use of bees and honey, and of milk for curdling, and he was the first to discover the rising of the Dog Star at midsummer. When these things had been heard, Battus, taking the name of the maiden from the responses, founded the city of Cyrene.
30 He founded it.

units.la: 8 Igitur Ptolemaeus huius vrbis auctus viribus, bellum in aduentum Perdicca parabat. Sed Perdicca plus odium arrogantia, quam vires hostium nocebant, quam exosi etiam socij, ad Antipatrum gregatim profugiebant. Neoptolemus quoque in auxilium Eumeni relictus, non solum transfugere, verumetiam prodere partium exercitum voluit. Quam rem cum prafensisset Eumenes, cum proditore decernere prælio necesse habuit: victus Neoptolemus, ad Antipatrum & Polyperchonta profugit; hisq; persuadet, ut cotinuatis mansionibus lato ex victoria & securo fuga sua, Eumeni superueniant. Sed res Eumenem non latuit: Itaq; infidiæ in insidiatores versæ; & qui securum aggressuros putabant, securis in itinere, & peruigilio noctis fatigatis occursum est. In eo prælio Polyperchon occiditur. Neoptolemus quoq; cum Eumene congressus, diu mutuis vulneribus acceptis, colluctatus est; in summa victus, occumbit. Victor igitur duobus prœliis continuis Eumenes, afflictas partes transitione sociorum paulum sustentauit. Ad postremum tamen Perdicca occiso, ab exercitu bostilis cum Phytone, & Illyrio, & Alceta fratre Perdicce appellatur: bellumq; aduersus eos Antigono decernitur.
units.tr: 8 Therefore Ptolemy, strengthened by the resources of this city, was preparing for war against the coming of Perdiccas. But Perdiccas was more harmed by his own hatred and arrogance than by the strength of his enemies, and even his allies, whom he had come to hate, fled in droves to Antipater. Neoptolemus too, who had been left to aid Eumenes, not only wished to desert but also to betray the army of his party to the enemy. When Eumenes perceived this, he was forced to decide the matter by battle with the traitor. Neoptolemus was defeated and fled to Antipater and Polyperchon, and he persuaded them to come upon Eumenes, who would be off his guard, by making continuous marches, relying on the glory of his victory and on his flight being unknown. But Eumenes did not miss this: the snares were turned back upon the ambushers, and those who thought they would attack a man off his guard were met on the march, weary from their night watch and sleepless. In that battle Polyperchon was killed. Neoptolemus too, when he met Eumenes, struggled for a long time, wounding each other in turn, and in the end, defeated, he fell. Eumenes, victor in two successive battles, held up for a while the broken party, supported by the desertion of its allies. At last, however, after Perdiccas had been killed, the army proclaimed as its leaders Pithon, Illyrius and Alcetas, the brother of Perdiccas, and war was decreed against them with Antigonus.
POMPEII TROGI EPITOMA HISTORIARVM
Book XIV. SUMMARY.

units.la: 1 Eumenisin bello aduersus Antigonum prudentia & fortitudo: 2 Prælio victus obsidetur, hostium virtute superantur: liberatur, ad Argyraspidas vnde in Eumenem coniuratio confugit, eosque ad suas partes.
units.tr: 1 Eumenes' prudence and courage in the war against Antigonus. 2 Defeated in battle, he is besieged; though his enemies overcome him by their valour, he is rescued and takes refuge with the Argyraspides, whom he wins over to his side, away from the conspiracy against Eumenes.
3 While the Argyraspides scorn Eumenes' orders,

units.la: 4 Eumenis captiui ad Ar- gerens Græciæ ciuitates oppugnspidas oratio, qua petit primit, & in Macedoniam vt sibi inter eos mori liceat. aduersus Olympiadem proPetitione frustratus, prodi- ficiscitur.
units.tr: 4 Eumenes, a captive, makes a speech to the Argyraspides, asking that he be allowed to die among them; frustrated in this petition, he sets out. Polyperchon, attacking the cities of Greece, sets out against Olympias.

units.la: 5 totū capita dcuouet,& An- 6 Olympias fugit,obsidētigono vinctus traditur. tur, victori Cassādro se tra- 5 Cassander Aridei vices dit, cuius iussu interficitur.
units.tr: 5 He curses their heads and is handed over, bound, to Antigonus. Olympias flees and is besieged; she surrenders to the victor Cassander, and on his orders is put to death. Cassander takes the place of Arrhidaeus.

units.la: VMENES, vt Perdiccam occisum, se hostem à Macedonibus iudicatum, bellumq, Antigono decretum cognoscit; vltro ea militibus suis indicauit, ne fama aut rem in maius extolleret; ne fama aut rem in maius extolleret; aut militum animos rerum nouitate terreret; simul, vt circa se animati essent, cognosceret, sumpturus consilium ex motu vniuersorum. Constanter tamen præfatus est, si cui hæc terrori essent, habere eum discedendi potestatem. Quā voce adeo cunctos in studium partium suarum induxit, vt vltro illum omnes hortarentur, resciscerentque se ferro decreta Macedonum affirmarent.
units.tr: When Eumenes learned that, with Perdiccas dead, he had been judged an enemy by the Macedonians and that war had been decreed against Antigonus, he made this known to his soldiers of his own accord, so that they would not magnify the rumour or the matter, nor terrify the spirits of the soldiers by the novelty of the situation. At the same time he wished to learn how spirited they were around him, so that he could take counsel from the feeling of them all. Yet he declared firmly that if anyone was frightened by this, he was free to leave. By these words he so won all of them to the cause of his party that they all urged him on, and they affirmed that they would uphold with the sword the decrees of the Macedonians.

units.la: 20 Tunc exercitu in AEtoliam promoto, pecuniās ciuitatibus imperat; recusantes dare, hostiliter diripit. Inde Sardis profectus est ad Cleopatram, sororem Alexandri Magni, vt eius voce centuriones, principesq, confirmarentur, exist imaturos ibi maiestatem regiam verti, vnde soror Alexandri staret. Tanta veneratio magnitudinis Alexandri erat, vt etiam per vestigia mulierum, fauor sacrati eius nominis quaerentur. Cum reuersus in castra esset, epistolæ totis castris abiectæ inueniuntur: quibus iis, qui Eumenis caput ad Antigonum detulissent, magna præmia definiebantur. His cognitis, Eumenes vocatis ad concionem militibus, primo gratias egit, quod nemo inuentus esset, qui sphem cruenti premij fidei sacramento anteponeret: deinde callide subnectit, confictas has à se epistolas ad experiundos
units.tr: 20 Then, with the army advanced into Aetolia, he ordered the cities to pay money; those who refused to pay he plundered as enemies. From there he set out for Sardis, to Cleopatra, sister of Alexander the Great, so that by her voice the centurions and leaders would be encouraged, since they would think that royal majesty ought to turn toward wherever Alexander's sister stood. So great was the reverence for the greatness of Alexander that people even sought the favour of that consecrated name by following the footsteps of a woman. When he had returned to the camp, letters were found thrown about the whole camp, in which great rewards were promised to those who had brought Eumenes' head to Antigonus. When this was learned, Eumenes called the soldiers to an assembly. First he thanked them, because no one had been found who would put the reward of a bloody prize before the sacred oath of loyalty; then he cleverly added that these letters had been fabricated by himself, to test the spirits of his men.

units.la: K suosuorum animos esse. Ceterum salutem suam in omnium potestate esse; nec Antigonum, nec quemquam ducum sic velle vincere, vt ipse in se exemplum pessimum slatuat. Hoc facto, & in præsenti labantium animos deterruit; & in futurum prouidit, vt siquid simile accidisset, non se ab hoste corrumpi, sed ab duce tentari arbitrarentur. Omnes igitur operam suam certatim ad custodiam salutis eius offerunt.
units.tr: Otherwise, he said, his safety lay in the power of all of them; neither Antigonus nor any of the commanders wished to conquer him in such a way that he himself would set the worst example. By this act he both calmed the minds of the wavering men for the present, and provided for the future, so that if anything similar should happen, they would think that they were being tempted by the commander, not corrupted by the enemy. All therefore vied with one another in offering their service for the safeguarding of his life.

units.la: 2 Cum interim Antigonus cum exercitu siperuenit, castrisq; positis, postera die in aciem procedit. Nec Eumenes moram prælio fecit: qui victus, in munitum quoddam castellum confugit: vbi cum videret se fortunam obsidionis subiturum, maiorem exercitus partem dimisit, ne aut consensu multitudinis hosti traderetur, aut obsidio ipsa multitudine grauaretur. Legatos deinde ad Antipatrum, quod solus par Antigoni viribus videbatur, supplices mittit: à quo cum auxilia Eumeni missa Antigonus didicisset, ab obsidione recessit. Erat quidem solutus ad tempus metu mortis Eumenes; sed nec salutu, dimisso exercitu, magna spes erat. Omnia igitur circumspicienti, optimum visum est, ad Alexandri Magni Argyraspidas inuictum exercitum, & tot victoriarum præfulgentem gloria, decurrere. Sed Argyraspides post Alexandrum omnes duces fastidiebant, sordidam militiam sub aliis post tanti regis memoriam existimantes. Itaq; Eumenes blandimentis agere; suppliciter singulos alloqui; nunc commilitones suos, nunc patronos appellans, periculorum Orientalium socios; nunc refugia salutis suæ, & vnica præsidia commemorans: solos esse quorum virtute Oriens sit domitus; solos qui militiam Liberi patris, qui Herculis monumenta superarint: per hos Alexandrum magnum factum; per hos diuinos honores, & immortalem gloriam cõsequu-tum: tum: orat vt non tam ducem se, quam commilitonem recipiant, vnumq; ex corpore suo esse velint. Receptus hac lege, paulatim imperium, primum monendo singulos, mox qua perperam facta erant blande corrigendo, vsurpat: nihil in castris sine illo agi, nihil administrari sine solertia illius poterat.
units.tr: Meanwhile Antigonus arrived with his army, pitched camp, and the next day advanced into battle line. Nor did Eumenes delay the fight; defeated, he fled into a certain fortified stronghold. There, seeing that he would have to undergo the fate of a siege, he dismissed the greater part of the army, lest it be handed over to the enemy by the agreement of the multitude, or the siege itself be burdened by the multitude. Then he sent suppliant envoys to Antipater, since he alone seemed a match for the forces of Antigonus; when Antigonus learned from him that auxiliaries were being sent to Eumenes, he withdrew from the siege. Eumenes was indeed freed for the time being from the fear of death; but with the army dismissed, there was no great hope of safety. Therefore, looking around at everything, he thought it best to run to the invincible army of Alexander the Great's Argyraspides, shining with the glory of so many victories. But the Argyraspides, after Alexander, scorned all commanders, thinking it a squalid kind of soldiering to serve under others after the memory of so great a king. And so Eumenes used flattery; he addressed each of them humbly, now calling them his fellow soldiers, now his patrons, the companions of his dangers in the East; now recalling the refuges of his safety and their only protection: that they alone were the men by whose valour the East had been subdued; they alone who had surpassed the military feats of Father Liber and the monuments of Hercules; through them Alexander the Great had been made great, through them had attained divine honours and immortal glory. He begged them to receive him not so much as a commander as a fellow soldier, and to wish him to be one of their body. Received on this condition, he gradually seized power: first by advising individuals, then by gently correcting what had been done amiss; nothing could be done in the camp without him, nothing could be managed without his shrewdness.

units.la: 3 Ad postremum cum Antigonum venire cum exercitu nuntiatum esset, compellit eos in aciem descendere. Ibi dum ducis imperia contemnunt, bellum vitute superantur. In prælio non gloriam tantum tot bellorum, cum coniugibus & liberis, sed & præmia longa militia parta, perdiderunt. Sed & Eumenes, qui auctor cladis erat, nec aliam spem salutis reliquam habebat, victos hortabatur: Nam & virtute eos superiores fuisse affirmabat: quispe ab his quinq; millia hostium capta; & si in bello perstent, vltro hostes pacem petituros.
