Damna, quibus se victos putent, duo millia mulierum & paucos infantes, & seruitia esse, quæ melius vincendo posint reparare; quam decerendo victoriam. Porro Argyraspides neq; fugam se tentaturos dicunt, post damna matrimoniorum, & post coniuges amissus, neque bellum gesturos contra liberos suos, vtroque eum conuitiis agitant, quod se post tot annos emeritorum stipendiorum, redeuntes domum cum præmiis tot bellorum, ab ipsa missione rursus in nouam militiam, immensaque bella reuocauerit, & a laribus iam quodammodo suis, & ab ipso limine patriæ abductos, inanibus promissis deceperit: nunc quoque amissis omnibus felicitatis militiæ quaslibus, ne victos quidem in misera & inopi senecta quiescere sinat. Ignaris deinde ducibus, confessim ad Antigonum legatos mittunt, petentes vt sua reddi iubeat. Is reddituum se pollicetur, si Eumenem sibi tradant. Quibus cognitis, Eumenes cum
units.tr: At last, when it was announced that Antigonus was coming with his army, he compelled them to go down into battle. There, while they scorned the orders of their commander, they were conquered by the enemy's valour. In the battle they lost not only the glory of so many wars, together with their wives and children, but also the long-won rewards of military service. But Eumenes, who was the cause of the disaster and had no other hope of safety left, exhorted the defeated men: for he asserted that they had been superior in valour, since five thousand of the enemy had been taken by them; and if they persevered in the war, the enemy would of their own accord seek peace. The losses by which they thought themselves defeated were two thousand women and a few infants, and slaves, which by conquering they could make good more easily than by yielding the victory. Moreover, the Argyraspides said that they would not attempt flight, after the loss of their marriages and their wives, nor would they wage war against their own children; and they reviled him in both ways: that after so many years of completed service, returning home with the rewards of so many wars, he had recalled them from the very discharge into new service and immense wars, and, having drawn them away from their household gods, and as it were from the very threshold of their homeland, had deceived them with empty promises; and now, with all the fruits of their fortunate military service lost, he did not even allow them, conquered as they were, to rest in a wretched and destitute old age. Then, with the commanders ignorant of it, they at once sent envoys to Antigonus, asking that he order their property to be restored to them. He promised that it would be restored, if they handed over Eumenes to him. When this became known, Eumenes, with a few men, tried to flee; but he was dragged back, and when, his affairs despaired of, a crowd had gathered, he asked that he be allowed to address the army one last time.

units.la: K pauci fugere tentauit : sed retractus, desperatis rebus, cum concursus multitudinis factus esset, petit vt postremum sibi alloqui exercitum liceret.
units.tr: Eumenes tried to flee with a few men, but was dragged back; and when, his affairs despaired of, a crowd had gathered, he asked that he be allowed to address the army one last time.

units.la: 4 Iussus ab vniuersis dicere facto silentio, laxatisq; vinculis, protalatam, sicut erat catenatus, manuum ostentat dit : Cernitis milites, inquit, habitum atq; ornamenta ducis vestri, quae mihi nō hostium quisquam imposuit : nam hoc etiam solatio foret. Vos me ex victore victum, vos me ex imperatore captiuum fecistis ; quater intra hunc annum in mea verba iureiurando obstricti estis, & ista omitto: Neq; enim miseros conuitia decent. Vt num oro, si propositorum Antigoni in meo capite summa consistit, inter vos me velitis mori. Nam neq; illius interest, quemadmodum aut vbi cadam ; & ego fuero ignominia mortis liberatus. Hoc si impetro soluo vos iureiurando ; quo toties vos sacramento mihi deuouistis. Aut si ipsos pudet roganti vim adhibere, ferrum huc date ; & permittite quod vos facturos pro imperatore iuraftis, imperatorem pro vobis sine religione iuriiurandi facere. Cum non obtineret, preces in iram vertit. At vos, ait, devota capita, respiciant dij periuriorum vindices; talesq; vobis exitus dent, quales vos ducibus vestris dedistis. Nempe vos iidem paulo ante & Perdiccę sanguine estis aspersi, & in Antipatrum eadem moliti. Ipsum denique Alexandrum, si fas fuisset eum mortali manu cadere, interemptuti; quod maximum erat, seditionibus agitastis. Vltima nunc ego perfidorum victima, has vobis diras atq; inferias dico ; vt inopes extorresq; omne euum in hoc castrensi exilio agatis, desorentq; vos arma vestra, quibus plures vestros, quam hostium duces absumpsistis. Plenus deinde ira, custodes suos praecedere ad Antigoni castra coepit. Sequitur exercitus prodito imperatore suo, & ipse captiuus, triumphumq; de se ipso ad victoris sui castra ducit omnia auspicia regis Alexandri, & tot bellorum palmas, laureasq; vna secum victori tradentes: & nequid deesset pompae, elephanti quoq;, & auxilia Orientalia subsequuntur. Tanto pulchrior hac Antigono, quam Alexandro tot victoriae fuerunt; vt cum ille Orientem vicerit, hic etiam eos a quibus Oriens victus fuerat, superauerit. Igitur Antigonus domitores illos orbis, exercitui suo diuidit, redditis eorum quae in victoria ceperat. rat. Eumenem vero verecundia prioris amicitiae, in conspectum suum venire prohibitum, asignari custodibus praecepit.
units.tr: 4 Ordered by all to speak, with silence made and his chains loosened, he showed his hands, which were still bound, as he had been fettered: "You see, soldiers," he said, "the dress and the insignia of your commander, which none of the enemy has put upon me; for that would at least have been a consolation. You have made me from a victor a vanquished man, you have made me from a commander a captive; four times within this year you have bound yourselves to me by oath, and these things I pass over. For abuse does not become the wretched. Yet I beg you, if the purpose of Antigonus rests entirely on my head, that you wish me to die among you. For it is of no concern to him how or where I fall, and I shall have been freed from the disgrace of death. If I obtain this, I release you from the oath by which you have so often devoted yourselves to me. Or if you are ashamed to use force against a man who asks, give me the iron here, and permit me, without the sanction of an oath, to do what you swore to do for your commander on his behalf." When he did not obtain this, he turned his prayers into anger. "But you," he said, "accursed heads, may the gods, the avengers of perjuries, look upon you, and may they give you such an end as you gave to your commanders. Indeed, you were the same men who a little while ago were stained with the blood of Perdiccas, and who plotted the same against Antipater. Finally, you even killed Alexander himself, if it had been lawful for him to fall by a mortal hand; and what was greatest of all, you troubled him with mutinies. Now I, the last victim of the faithless, pronounce these curses and these funeral offerings upon you: that you may live out your whole lives destitute and exiled in this military exile, and that the arms with which you have destroyed more of your own commanders than of the enemy's may desert you." Then, full of anger, he began to go before his guards to the camp of Antigonus. The army followed, having betrayed its commander, and he himself, a captive, led a triumph over himself to the camp of his conqueror, carrying with him the auspices of King Alexander and the palms and laurels of so many wars, handing them all over to the victor together; and so that nothing should be lacking to the procession, elephants and the Eastern auxiliaries followed as well. So much more splendid were these victories to Antigonus than to Alexander: that while the latter had conquered the East, the former had also surpassed those by whom the East had been conquered. Therefore Antigonus distributed those conquerors of the world among his own army, with the spoils of their victory restored to them. But Eumenes, out of regard for their former friendship, he ordered to be forbidden to come into his sight and to be assigned to guards.

units.la: 5. Interea Eurydice, vxor Aridaei regis, vt Polyperchonta a Graecia redire in Macedoniam cognouit, & abeo arcesitam Olympiadem, muliebri aemulatione perculsa, abutens valitudine viri, cuius officia sibi vindicabat, scribit regis nomine Polyperchonti, Cassandro exercitum tradat, in quem regni administrationem rex transtulerit: eadem & in Asiam Antigono per epistolas nuntiat. Quo beneficio deuinctus Cassander, nihil non ex arbitrio muliebris audaciae gerit. Deinde profectus in Graeciam, multis civitatibus bellum infert; quarum excidio, veluti vicino incendio territi Spartani, vrbem quam semper armis, non muris defenderant, tum contra responsa fatorum & veterum maiorum gloriam, armis diffisi, murorum praesidio includunt. Tantum eos degenerasse a maioribus, vt cum multis saeculis murus vrbi ciuium virtus fuerit, tunc cives salvos se fore non existimauerint, nisi intra muros latherent. Dum haec aguntur, Cassandrum a Graecia turbatus Macedoniae status domum reuocavit. Namque Olympias mater Alexandri Magni regis, cum ab Epiro in Macedoniam, prosequente AEacida rege Molossorum,
units.tr: 5. Meanwhile Eurydice, the wife of King Aridaeus, learned that Polyperchon was returning from Greece to Macedonia and that Olympias had been summoned from there. Stirred by a woman's rivalry, and taking advantage of her husband's poor health, whose duties she was claiming for herself, she wrote in the king's name to Polyperchon, ordering him to hand over the army to Cassander, to whom the king had transferred the administration of the kingdom. She also sent word of the same thing by letter to Antigonus in Asia. Bound by this favour, Cassander did nothing except at the bidding of the woman's audacity. Then, setting out for Greece, he waged war on many cities. At their destruction the Spartans, terrified as if by a nearby fire, shut themselves up behind walls, having lost confidence in arms, contrary to the oracles of the fates and the glory of their forefathers, a city they had always defended with arms, not walls. So far had they degenerated from their ancestors that, although for many centuries the courage of its citizens had been the city's wall, they now thought themselves safe only if they lay hidden within walls. While these things were happening, the troubled state of Macedonia called Cassander home from Greece. For Olympias, the mother of King Alexander the Great, when she was coming from Epirus into Macedonia, escorted by Aeacides, king of the Molossians, was prevented by Eurydice and King Aridaeus from entering the borders;

units.la: veniret, prohibería, finibus ab Eurydice & Aridaeo rege capisset; seu memoria mariti, seu magnitudine filij, & indignitate rei moti Macedones, ad Olympiadem transfiere: cuius iussu & Eurydice, & rex occiditur, sex annis post Alexandrum potitus regno.
units.tr: Either out of remembrance of her husband, or out of regard for her son's greatness and the outrage of the affair, the Macedonians went over to Olympias; by her order both Eurydice and the king were put to death, six years after Alexander had gained the kingdom.

units.la: 6 Sed nec Olympias diu regnauit. Nam cum principum passim cades, nuliebri magis, quam regio more fecisset fauorem sui in odium vertit. Itaq; audito Cassandri aduentu, diffisa Macedonibus, cum nuru Roxane, & nepote Hercule, in Pydnam urbem concedit. Prosificiscenti Deidamia Aeacide regis filia, & Thessaloniceprivigna, & ipsa clara Philippi patris nomine, multaq; alia principum matrona, speciosus magis quam virtus grex, comites fuere. Hac cum nuntiata Cassandro essent, statim citato cursu Pydnam venit, & urbem obsidione cingit. Cum fame, ferroq; vrgeretur Olympias, longae obsidionis tædio, pacta salute, victori se tradidit.
units.tr: 6 But Olympias did not reign long either. For when the slaughter of the leading men was everywhere, and she had done this more in a woman's fashion than in a royal manner, she turned the people's favour toward herself into hatred. Therefore, on hearing of Cassander's approach, she lost the trust of the Macedonians and withdrew with her daughter-in-law Roxane and her grandson Hercules to the city of Pydna. Accompanying her as she set out were Deidamia, daughter of King Aeacides, and Thessalonice, stepdaughter of Philip, who was herself famous for her father's name, along with many other noblewomen, a company more showy than virtuous. When these things were reported to Cassander, he came at once to Pydna at full speed and surrounded the city with a siege. As Olympias was pressed by famine and the sword, wearied by the long siege, she surrendered herself to the victor on terms of safety for her life.

units.la: Sed Cassander ad concionem vocato populo, sciscitatus quid de Olympiade fieri velint, subornat parentes interfectorum, qui sumpta lugubri veste, crudelitatem mulieris accusarent; a quibus accensi Macedones, sine respectu pristinae maiestatis, occidendam decernunt: immemores prorsus, quod per filium eius, virumque, non solum vitam ipsi inter finitimos tutam habuissent, verumetiam tantas opes imperiumq; orbis quassissent.
units.tr: But Cassander called the people to an assembly, and asking what they wished to be done about Olympias, he induced the parents of the slain, who had put on mourning garments, to accuse the woman's cruelty; the Macedonians, inflamed by these men, with no regard for her former majesty, decreed that she should be put to death, utterly forgetful that through her son and her husband they had not only had a safe life among their neighbours but had also shaken the empire and wealth of the world.

units.la: Sed Olympias vbi obstinatos venire ad se armatos vidit, vestę regali, duabus ancillis innixa, vltro obuiam procedit. Qua visa, percussores attoniti fortuna maiestatis prioris, & tot in ea memoriae occurrentibus rerum suorum nominibus substiterunt; donec à Cassandro missi sunt, qui eam confoderent, non refugientem gladium, nec vulnera: aut muliebriter vociferantem; sed virorum more fortium, pro gloria veteris prosapiae morti succumbentem, vt Alexandrum posses etiam in moriente matre cognoscere. Insuper expirans, capillis & veste crura contexisse fertur, nequid posset in corpore eius indecorum videri. Post hac Cassander Thessalonicen, regis Aridaei filiam, vxorem ducit: filium Alexandri cum matre, in arcem Amphipolitanam custodiendos mittit.
units.tr: But when Olympias saw the men coming against her armed and resolute, she went out to meet them of her own accord, dressed in royal robes and leaning on two maidservants. At the sight of her the executioners, dumbfounded by the fortune of her former majesty and by the many memories of her achievements that came to mind, stopped short; until Cassander sent men who would stab her, and she did not flee the sword nor the wounds, nor did she cry out womanishly, but, in the manner of brave men, she submitted to death for the glory of her ancient lineage, so that one could recognise Alexander even in his mother as she died. Moreover, as she expired, it is said that she covered her legs with her hair and her garment, lest anything indecorous might appear on her body. After this Cassander married Thessalonice, daughter of King Aridaeus; he sent the son of Alexander with his mother to be kept in the citadel of Amphipolis.
The Epitome of the Histories of Pompeius Trogus
BOOK XV. SUMMARY.

units.la: 1 Antigoni bellum aduersus socios, in quo Demetrius F. proelio superatur. 4 Nouus hostis Antigoni accedit, nempe Seleucus, cuius origo & res gestae prosperi successus in subiiciuntur. Antigonus in proelio occumbit.
units.tr: 1 The war of Antigonus against his allies, in which Demetrius, his son, is defeated in battle. 4 A new enemy of Antigonus appears, namely Seleucus, whose origin and deeds, with their prosperous outcome, are set out below. Antigonus falls in battle.

units.la: 2 Cassandri in familiam Alexandri M. saeuitia. Anticus, cuius origo & res gestae bello.
units.tr: 2 The cruelty of Cassander against the family of Alexander the Great. Antiochus, whose origin and deeds in war are described.

units.la: ERIDICCA, & fratre eius, Eumene ac Polyperchonte ceterisque ducibus diuersae partis occisis, finitum certamen inter successores Alexandri Magni videbatur, cum repente inter ipsos victores vata discordia est: quippe postulantibus Ptolemaeo, & Cassandro, & Lysimacho, vt pecunia in praeda capta, prouinciaq; diuiderentur; Antigonus uerbum gauit se in eius belli praemia socios admissurum, in cuius periculum solus descenderit. Et vt bonestiu aduersus suscipit, sociós socios bellum suscipere videretur, diuulgat fe Olympiadis mortem a Cassandro interfecta, vtcunque velle, & Alexandri regis sui filium cum matre obsidione Amphipolitana liberare. His cognitis, Ptolemæus & Cassander, inita cum Lysimacho & Seleuco societate, bellum 5 terra mariq; eneixe instruunt. Tenebat Ptolemæus AEgyptum cum Africa parte maiore, & Cypro, & Phœnice. Cassandro parebat Macedonia cum Græcia. Asiam & partem Orientis occupauerat Antigonus, cuius filius Demetrius, prima belli congressione, a Ptolemæo apud 10 Galatam vincitur. In quo prælio maior Ptolemæi moderationis gloria, quam ipsius victoria fuit. Siquidem & amicos Demetrij non solum cum suis rebus, vestrumetiam additis insuper muneribus, dimisit & ipsius Demetrij priuatum omne instrumentum, ac familiam 15 reddidit, adiecto honore verborum, non se propter prædam, sed propter dignitatem inisse bellum; indignatum quod Antigonus deuictis diuersa factionis ducibus, solus communis victoria premia corripuisset.
units.tr: When Eridicca, with his brother Eumenes, Polyperchon and the other leaders of the opposing side, had been killed, the struggle among the successors of Alexander the Great seemed to be over. Suddenly, however, discord arose among the victors themselves. Ptolemy, Cassander and Lysimachus demanded that the money taken as booty and the provinces be divided, but Antigonus replied that he would admit his allies to the rewards of this war, though he alone had faced its danger. To make his conduct appear more honourable, so that he seemed to be taking up the war on behalf of his allies, he spread the report that Olympias had been killed by Cassander, and that he wished by any means to free the son of his king, Alexander, and his mother from the siege of Amphipolis. When this was known, Ptolemy and Cassander, having entered into alliance with Lysimachus and Seleucus, prepared the war by land and sea. Ptolemy held Egypt with the greater part of Africa, and Cyprus and Phoenicia. Macedonia and Greece obeyed Cassander. Antigonus had occupied Asia and part of the East, and his son Demetrius, in the first encounter of the war, was defeated by Ptolemy near Gaza. In this battle Ptolemy won more glory for his moderation than for his victory. He sent back Demetrius' friends not only with their belongings but with added gifts, and he returned all of Demetrius' private equipment and servants, adding honourable words: he had entered the war not for plunder but for the sake of dignity, and he was indignant that Antigonus, having defeated the leaders of the opposing faction, had alone seized the rewards of the common victory.

units.la: 2 Dum hæc aguntur, Cassander ab Apollonia reediens, incidit in Abderitas, qui propter variarum mutiriumq; multitudinem relicto patria solo, sedes quærebant: veritus ne Macedoniam occuparent, factaque pactio20 ne, in societatem eos recepit; agrosq; iis vltrin.es Macedonia assignat. Deinde, ne Hercules Alexandri filius, qui fere annos quatuordecim excesserat, fuore paterni nominis in regnum Macedoniae vocaretur, occidi eum tacite cum matre Barsine iubet, corpora eorum in terra obrui, ne cades sepultura proderetur: & quasi parum facinoris in ipso primum rege, mox in matre eius Olympiade, ac filio admisset, alterum quoq; filium cum matre Roxane pari fraude interficit; scilicet quasi regnum Macedoniae, quod affectabat, aliter consequi,
units.tr: 2 While these things were happening, Cassander, returning from Apollonia, met the Abderites, who, because of the great number of mixed peoples among them, had left their homeland and were seeking new settlements. Fearing they might seize Macedonia, he made a pact, received them into alliance, and assigned them lands beyond Macedonia. Then, lest Hercules, the son of Alexander, who was now nearly fourteen, be called to the kingdom of Macedonia on the strength of his father's name, he ordered him secretly killed together with his mother Barsine, and their bodies buried in the earth so that the deed would not be betrayed by a public burial. As if he had committed too little crime by first killing the king, then his mother Olympias and her son, he killed the other son with his mother Roxane by the same treachery; plainly he believed he could not otherwise obtain the kingdom of Macedonia, which he coveted, except by crime.

units.la: quam scelere non posset. Interea Ptolemaeus cum Demetrio nauali proelio iterato congreditur; & amissa classe, hostiq; concessa victoria, in AEgyptum refugit, Demetrius filium Ptolemaei Leontiscum, & fratrem Menelaum, amicosq; eius cum priuati instrumenti ministerio, pari prouocatus antea munere AEgyptum remittit: & vt apparerent eos non odij, sed dignitatis gloria accensos, donis, muneribusq; inter ipsa bella contendebant. Quo honestius tunc bella gerebantur, quam nunc animo ... ... Hac victoria elatus Antigonus, regem se cum Demetrio filio appellari a populo iubet. Ptolemaeus quoq; ne minoris apud suos auctoritatis haberetur, rex ab exercitu cognominatur. Quibus auditis, Cassander & Lysimachus, & ipsi regiam sibi maiestatem vindicaverunt. Huius honoris ornamentum tamdiu omnes abstinuerunt, quamdiu filij regis sui superesse potuerunt. Tanta in illis verecundia fuit, vt cum opes regias haberent, regnum tamen nominibus aequo animo caruerint, quoad Alexandro iustus heres fuit.
units.tr: Meanwhile Ptolemy engaged Demetrius in a second naval battle. Having lost his fleet and conceded victory to the enemy, he fled to Egypt. Demetrius, who had been challenged before to a similar exchange of gifts, sent back to Egypt Ptolemy's son Leontiscus, his brother Menelaus, and their friends, together with their private equipment and servants. And so that they might appear to be moved not by hatred but by a zeal for honour, they vied with one another in gifts and kindnesses even in the midst of war. How much more honourably wars were waged then than now... Elated by this victory, Antigonus ordered that he and his son Demetrius be called kings by the people. Ptolemy too, lest he be held of lesser authority among his own, was named king by the army. When this was heard, Cassander and Lysimachus also claimed royal majesty for themselves. All of them had abstained from this mark of honour for as long as the sons of their king could survive. There was such modesty in them that, although they had royal resources, they bore calmly the lack of royal titles, for as long as Alexander's rightful heir was alive.

units.la: Sed Ptolemaeus & Cassander, ceteriq; factionis alterius duces, cum carpi se singulos ab Antigono viderent, dum primatum singulorum, non commune vniuersorum bellum ducunt, nec auxilium ferre alter alteri volunt, quasi victoria vnius, non omnium foret; per epistolas se inuicem confirmantes, tempus, locum coeundi conditionem, bellumque communibus viribus instruunt. Cui cum Cassander interesse propter finitimum bellum non posset, Lysimachum cum ingentibus copiis, in auxilium sociis mittit.
units.tr: But Ptolemy and Cassander, and the other leaders of the second faction, seeing that Antigonus was picking them off one at a time, conducted their war for individual supremacy rather than as a common war of all. They would not bring help to one another, as if the victory of one were not the victory of all. Yet, by letters confirming one another, they arranged the time, the place and the terms of their meeting, and prepared the war with combined forces. Since Cassander could not take part in it himself because of a war on his border, he sent Lysimachus with large forces to aid the allies.

units.la: 3 Erat hic Lysimachus illustri quidem Macedonia loco natus, sed virtutis experimentis omni nobilitate clarior; quae tanta in illo fuit, vt animi magnitudine, philosophia ipsa, viriumque gloria omnes, per quos Orientis riens domitus est, vicerit. Quippe cum Alexander Magnus Callisthenem philosophum, propter salutationis Persicæ interpellatum morem, insidiarum, quæ sibi parata fuerant, conscium fuisse iratus finxisset; eumque truncatis crudeliter omnibus membris, abscisisque auribus, ac naso, labiisque, deforme ac miserandum spectaculum reddidisset; insuper cum cane in cauea clausum, ad metum ceterorum circumferret: tunc Lysimachus audire Callisthenem, & præcepta ab eo virtutis accipere solitus, miseratus tanti viri, non culpæ, sed libertatis pœnas pendentis, venenum ei in remedia calamitatum dedit. Quod adeo agre Alexander tulit, ut eum obici ferocissimo leoni iuberet: Sed cum ad conspectum eius concitatus leo impetum fecisset, manum amiculo inuolutam Lysimachus in os leonis immersit, arreptaque lingua, feram exanimauit. Quod cum nuntiatum regi esset, admiratio in satisfactionem cessit; cariorem eum propter constantiam tanta virtutis habuit. Lysimachus quoq; magno animo, regis, veluti parentis contumeliam tulit. Denique, omni ex animo huius facti memoria exturbata, postea in India insectanti regi quosdam palantes hostes, cum a satellitum turba, equi sui celeritate desertus esset, solus ei per immensas harenarum moles comitatus fuit. Quod idem antea Philippus frater eius cum facere voluisset inter manus regis exspirauerat. Sed Lysimachum desiliens equo Alexander, hasta cuspide ita in fronte vulnerauit, ut sanguis aliter cludi non posset, quam diadema sibi demptum rex, alligandi vulneris causa, capiti eius imponeret. Quod auspicium, primum regalis maiestatis Lysimacho fuit. Sed & post mortem Alexandri, cum inter successores eius provincia diuiderentur, ferocissima gentes, quasi omnium fortissimo assignatae sunt: adeo etiam consensu vniuersi nerforum palmam virtutis inter cateros tulit.
units.tr: 3 This Lysimachus was born of a distinguished Macedonian family, but he was more famous for proofs of his courage than for any nobility. His virtue was so great that in greatness of spirit, in philosophy itself, and in the glory of his strength, he surpassed all those through whom the East was subdued. When Alexander the Great, angered, had accused the philosopher Callisthenes of knowing about plots against him, because he had objected to the Persian custom of prostration, he cruelly mutilated all his limbs, cut off his ears, nose and lips, and made him a deformed and pitiable spectacle. Moreover, he carried him about in a cage with a dog, to terrify the others. Then Lysimachus, who used to listen to Callisthenes and receive precepts of virtue from him, pitied so great a man, who was suffering punishment not for guilt but for his freedom, and gave him poison as a remedy for his calamities. Alexander took this so badly that he ordered Lysimachus thrown to a fierce lion. But when the lion, roused, charged at the sight of him, Lysimachus thrust his hand, wrapped in his cloak, into the lion's mouth, seized its tongue and killed the beast. When this was reported to the king, admiration gave way to approval; he held him dearer for the constancy of such great virtue. Lysimachus too bore the king's rebuke, as a parent's, with great spirit. Finally, when all memory of this deed had been driven from his mind, in India, when the king was pursuing some scattered enemies and had been left by his retinue because of the speed of his horse, Lysimachus alone accompanied him across the vast mounds of sand. His brother Philip had tried to do the same and had died in the king's arms. But Alexander, leaping from his horse, wounded Lysimachus in the forehead with the point of a spear, so that the blood could not be stopped except by the king taking off his own diadem and placing it on Lysimachus' head to bind the wound. This was the first omen of royal majesty for Lysimachus. Also after Alexander's death, when the provinces were divided among his successors, the most fierce peoples were assigned to him, as to the bravest of all. So greatly did the consent of all grant him the palm of virtue over the others, even over the Thracians.

units.la: 4 Priusquam bellum inter Ptolemaum, sociosque eius, aduersus Antigonum committeretur, repente ex Asia maiore digressus Seleucus, nouus Antigono hostis acceßerat. Huius quoque & virtus clara, & origo admirabilis fuit. Siquidem mater eius Laudice, cum nupta esset Antiocho, claro inter Philippi duces viro, visa est sibi per quietem ex concubitu Apollinis concepisse, grauidamque factam, munus concubitus, anulum à 5 deo accepisse, in cuius gemma ancora sculpta esset: iussaque donum filio, quem peperisset, dare. Admirabilem fecit hunc visum & anulus, qui postera die, eiusdem sculptura, in lecto inuentus est; & figura ancora, qua in femore Seleuci nata cum ipso paruulo fuit. Quamobrem Laudice anulum Seleuco cunti cum Alexandro 10 Magno ad Persicam militiam, edocto de origine sua, dedit. Vbi post mortem Alexandri, occupato regno Orientis, vrbem condidit, ibique gemina originis memoriam consecrauit. Nam & vrbem ex Antiochi patris nomine: Antiochiam vocauit; & campos vicinos vrbi, Apollini dicauit. Originis eius argumentum etiam in posteris mansit: Siquidem filij, nepotesq; eius ancoram in femore, veluti notam generis naturalem habuere. Multa in Oriente, post diuisionem inter socios regni Macedonici, bella gesit. Principio Babyloniam cepit: inde auctis ex victoria viribus, Bactrianos expugnauit. Transitum deinde in Indiam fecit, quae post mortem Alexandri, veluti ceruicibus iugo seruitutis excusso, praefectos eius occiderat. Auctor libertatis Sandrocotus fuerat, sed titulum libertatis post victoriam in seruitutem verterat. Siquidem occupato regno, populum quem ab externa dominatione vindicauerat, ipse seruitio premebat. Fuit hic quidem humili genere natus, sed ad regni potestate maiestate numinis impulsus. Quip‐ pe cum procacitate sua Alexandrum regem offendi‐set, interfici à rege iussus, salutem pedum celeritate quasierat: ex qua fatigatione,cum somno captus iace‐ ret, leo ingentis forma ad dormientem accęsit, sudo‐ remq; profluentem linguae ei detersit, expergefactumq; blande reliquit. Hoc prodigio primum ad spem regni impulsus, contractis latronibus, Indos ad nouitatem regni solicitauit. Molienti deinde bellum aduersus præ‐sectos Alexandri,elephantus ferus infinita magnitudi‐ nis vltro se obtulit, & veluti domita mansuetudine, eum tergo excepit; duxque belli, & præditor insignis fuit. Sic acquisito regno, Sandrocottus ex compestate, qua Seleucus futuram magnitudinis suæ fundamenta iacie‐ bat, Indiam possidebat: cum quo factaq; pactione Seleu‐ cus, compositisq; in Orientę rebus, in bellum Antigoni descendit. Adunatis igitur omnium sociorum copiis, prœlium committitur: in eo Antigonus occiditur; De‐ metrius filius eius in fugam vertitur, Sed sociį profli‐ gato hostili bello,denuo in semetipsos arma verterunt: & cum de prœda non conuenirent, iterum in duas fa‐ctiones deducuntur. Seleucus Demetrio,Ptolemaus Ly‐ simacho iunguntur. Cassandro defuncto Philip‐ pus filius succedit. Sic,quasi ex integro, noua Macedonia bella na‐ scuntur.
units.tr: 4 Before the war between Ptolemy and his allies against Antigonus was joined, Seleucus suddenly departed from Asia Minor and became a new enemy of Antigonus. His valour was famous, and his origin remarkable. His mother Laudice, having married Antiochus, a distinguished man among Philip's commanders, seemed to herself in a dream to have conceived from intercourse with Apollo. Being pregnant, she received from the god, as a gift for the union, a ring on which an anchor was engraved, and she was told to give the gift to the son she would bear. The vision was made remarkable also by the ring, which was found on her bed the next day with the same engraving, and by the figure of an anchor, which was born on the thigh of Seleucus together with the infant himself. Therefore Laudice gave the ring to Seleucus when he went with Alexander the Great on the Persian campaign, having told him of his origin. After Alexander's death, when he had seized the kingdom of the East, he founded a city and there consecrated a memorial of his double origin. He named the city after his father Antiochus, calling it Antioch, and he dedicated the fields near the city to Apollo. Evidence of his origin remained in his descendants, for his sons and grandsons had an anchor on the thigh, as a natural mark of their race. After the division among the allies of the Macedonian kingdom, he waged many wars in the East. First he took Babylon; then, his strength increased by victory, he conquered Bactria. Next he crossed into India, which, after Alexander's death, had thrown off the yoke of servitude from its neck and killed his prefects. The author of its liberty had been Sandrocottus, but after the victory he turned the title of liberty into slavery. For once he had seized the kingdom, he himself oppressed with servitude the people he had rescued from foreign rule. He was of humble birth, but was driven to royal power by a sense of divine majesty. When by his insolence he had offended King Alexander, and was ordered by the king to be killed, he sought safety by the speed of his feet. Exhausted from that flight, he lay down and fell asleep, when a lion of huge size approached the sleeper, licked off the sweat flowing from him with its tongue, and left him gently when he woke. Driven first to hope of kingship by this portent, he gathered robbers and stirred up the Indians to the novelty of a new kingdom. Then, when he was planning war against Alexander's prefects, a wild elephant of infinite size offered itself of its own accord, and, as if its ferocity had been tamed, received him on its back; he became a leader in war and a notable commander. Thus, with the kingdom acquired, Sandrocottus held India, in the very plain where Seleucus was laying the foundations of his future greatness. A pact was made with him, and when affairs in the East had been settled, Seleucus went down into the war against Antigonus. With the forces of all the allies united, battle was joined; in it Antigonus was killed, and his son Demetrius was put to flight. But the allies, the hostile war having been brought to an end, turned their arms against one another again; and when they could not agree about the booty, they split once more into two factions. Seleucus joined Demetrius, and Ptolemy joined Lysimachus. When Cassander died, his son Philip succeeded him. Thus, as if from the beginning, new wars over Macedonia were born.

units.la: POMPEII TROGI EPI- TOMA HISTORIARVM LIBER XVI.
units.tr: THE EPITOME OF POMPEIUS TROGUS' PHILIPPIC HISTORIES, BOOK XVI.
SUMMARY

units.la: 1 Antipater Cassandri filius, machi. De Heraclae origine, fit parricida. Demetrius necstatu digressio.
units.tr: 1 Antipater, son of Cassander, plots, and becomes a parricide. Digression on the origin of Heraclea and on Demetrius' situation.

units.la: 10 Alexandrum Cassandri F. interfecit & Macedoniam vsurpat. 4 Clearchi tyranni Heraclensis artes luculenter descriptae.
units.tr: 10 He kills Alexander, son of Cassander, and seizes Macedonia. 4 The arts of Clearchus, tyrant of Heraclea, vividly described.

units.la: 2 Demetrius proelio susus fugatus. Antipater parricida fœde perit. In Cassandri familiam Numinis vindicta. Ptolemaei placidum fatum. 5 Tyrannidem quibus rationibus firmauerit Clearchus, tandem à Chione & Leonide iuuenibus nobilissimis obtruncatus. Post Clearchi supplicium Heraclea conditio.
units.tr: 2 Demetrius is defeated in battle and put to flight. Antipater, the parricide, perishes shamefully. Divine vengeance on the family of Cassander. The peaceful fate of Ptolemy. 5 By what means Clearchus strengthened his tyranny, until at last he was cut down by the young nobles Chion and Leonides. After Clearchus' execution, the condition of Heraclea.
3 The war of Pyrrhus and Lysimachus.

units.la: OST Cassandri regis, filiisque eius Philippi continuas mortes, Thessalonice regina vxor Cassandri, non magno post tempore, ab Antipatro filio, cum vitam etiam per vbera materna deprecaretur, occiditur. Causa parricidii fuit, quod post mortem mariti, in diuisione inter fratres regni, propensior fuisse pro Alexandro videbatur. Quod facinus eo grauius omnibus visum est, quod nullum matern-ae fraudis vestigium fuit. Quamquam in parricidio, nulla satis iusta causa ad sceleris patrocinia pratexi potest. Ob hac igitur Alexander in vltionem materna necis, gesturus cum fratre bellum, auxilium a Demetrio petit: nec Demetrius, spe inuadendi Macedonici regni, moram fecit. Cuius aduentum verens Lysimachus, persuadet genero suo Antipatro, vt malit cum fratre in gratiam reuerti, quam paternum hostem in Macedoniam admitti: Inchoatam igitur inter fratres reconciliationem cum præsentisset Demetrius, per insidias Alexandrum interfecit; occupatoque Macedoniæ regno, eadem apud exercitum excusaturus, in concionem vocat. Ibi priorem se petitum ab Alexandro allegat; nec fecisse se, sed occupasse insidias. Regem autem se Macedoniæ vel ætatis experimentis, vel causis iustiorem esse.
units.tr: After the continual deaths of King Cassander and of his sons Philip and others, Queen Thessalonice, Cassander's wife, was killed, not long afterwards, by her son Antipater, though she begged for her life even by pointing to her mother's breasts. The cause of the parricide was that, after her husband's death, in the division of the kingdom between the brothers, she seemed more inclined to favour Alexander. The crime seemed all the more grievous to everyone because there was no trace of any deceit on her part. Yet for parricide no sufficiently just cause can be pleaded in its defence. Therefore Alexander, intending to wage war on his brother in revenge for his mother's murder, sought help from Demetrius; and Demetrius, hoping to seize the Macedonian kingdom, made no delay. Lysimachus, fearing his arrival, persuaded his son-in-law Antipater that he should rather be reconciled with his brother than admit a hostile father into Macedonia. When Demetrius learned that a reconciliation between the brothers had begun, he killed Alexander by treachery. Having seized the kingdom of Macedonia, he called an assembly in order to make the same excuse to the army. There he alleged that Alexander had attacked him first; he had not done so himself, but had only forestalled the plot. He said that he was the more rightful king of Macedonia, both by the proof of his age and by the justice of his cause.

units.la: Patrem enim suum & Philippo regi, & Alexandro Magno socium in omni militia fuisse; liberorum deinde Alexandri ministrum, & ad persequendos defectores ducem extitisse. Contra Antipatrum auum horum adolescētium amariorem semper ministrū regni, quam ipsos reges fuisse. Cassandrum vero patrem extinctorem regiæ domus, non feminis, non pueris pepercisse, neccessasse, quoad omnem stirpem regiæ subolis deleret. Horrum scelerum vltionem, quia nequisset ab ipso Cassandro exigere, ad liberos eius translatam. Quamobrem etiam Philippum, Alexandrumq;(siquis manium suis est) non interfectores suos, ac stirpis suæ, sed vltores eorum Macedoniæ regnum tenere malle. Per hæc mitigato populo, rex Macedoniæ appellatur. Lysimachus quoq; cum bello Doricetis regis Thracum premeretur; ne eodem tempore & aduersus eum dimicare necesse haberet, tradita ei altera parte Macedoniæ, quæ Antipatro eius genero obuenerat, pacem cum eo fecit.
units.tr: For his father had been a companion of King Philip and of Alexander the Great in every campaign; afterwards he had served as minister to Alexander's children and had become leader in hunting down deserters. Antipater, their grandfather, on the other hand, had always been a more bitter minister of the kingdom than the kings themselves. Cassander, the father of these men, had been the destroyer of the royal house: he had spared neither women nor boys, and had persisted until he wiped out every shoot of the royal stock. Since he could not exact vengeance for these crimes from Cassander himself, it had been transferred to his children. Therefore, if Philip and Alexander have any feeling among the dead, they would prefer that the kingdom of Macedonia be held not by their killers and the destroyers of their line, but by their avengers. By these arguments the people were pacified, and he was called king of Macedonia. Lysimachus too, being hard pressed in war by Doricetis, king of the Thracians, and not wanting to be forced to fight against him at the same time, handed over to Demetrius the other part of Macedonia, which had fallen to his son-in-law Antipater, and made peace with him.

units.la: 2 Igitur Demetrius, toti Macedoniæ regni viribus instructus, cum Asiam occupare statuisset, iterato Ptolemæus, Seleucus; & Lysimachus experti priore certamine quanta vires essent concordia, pactaq; societ ate adunatuque exercitibus, bellum aduersus Demetrium transferunt in Europam. His comitem se, & belli socium iungit Pyrrhus rex Epiri, sperans non difficilius Demetrium amittere Macedoniam posse, quam acquisierat. Nec spes frustra fuit: quippe exercitu eius corrupto, ipsoque in fugam acto, regnum Macedonia occupauit.
units.tr: 2 Therefore Demetrius, equipped with all the forces of the Macedonian kingdom, decided to seize Asia. Ptolemy, Seleucus and Lysimachus, who had learned in the earlier struggle how much strength lay in concord, made a pact of alliance, joined their armies, and transferred the war against Demetrius into Europe. King Pyrrhus of Epirus joined them as companion and ally, hoping that Demetrius could lose Macedonia no less easily than he had acquired it. Nor was his hope in vain: for when Demetrius' army was corrupted and he himself driven into flight, Pyrrhus occupied the kingdom of Macedonia.

units.la: 5 Dum haec aguntur, Lysimachus generum suum Antipatrum, regnum Macedoniae ademptum sibi socerufraudi de querentem, interfecit; filiamque suam Eurydicen quelarum sociam, in custodiam tradit: atque ita universa Caßandri domus Alexandro Magno, seu necis ipsius, seu
units.tr: 5 While these things were happening, Lysimachus killed his son-in-law Antipater, who was complaining to him that the kingdom of Macedonia had been taken from him by deceit, and handed over his daughter Eurydice, the companion of his complaints, into custody. And so the whole house of Cassander paid the penalty to Alexander the Great, for his death or for the extinction of his line, partly by slaughter, partly by execution, partly by parricide.

units.la: stirpis extinctae poenas partim caede, partim supplicio, partim parricidio luit. Demetrius quoque a tot exercitibus circumuentus, cum posset honeste mori, turpiter se dedere Seleuco maluit. Finito bello, Ptolemaeus cum magna rerum gestarum gloria moriturus, contra
units.tr: Demetrius too, surrounded by so many armies, when he could have died honourably, preferred to surrender shamefully to Seleucus. The war being over, Ptolemy, about to die with the great glory of his achievements, contrary

units.la: 15 ius gentium, minimo natu ex filiis, ante infirmitatem, regnum tradiderat, eiusque rei populo rationem reddiderat: cuius non minor fauor in accipiendo, quam patris in tradendo regno fuerat. Inter cetera patris & filij mutua pietatis exempla, etiam ea res amorem populi 20 iuueni concilauerat, quod pater regno ei publice tradito, priuatus officium regi inter satellites fecerat, omnium regno pulchrius regis esse patrem duxerat.
units.tr: 15 to the law of nations, handed the kingdom, before his illness, to the youngest of his sons, and had given the people an account of that decision. The people's approval on receiving the kingdom was no smaller than the father's readiness in handing it over. Among the other examples of mutual affection between father and son, this action had also won the young king the love of the people: the father, having publicly handed the kingdom to him, had taken a private position and served the king among his bodyguards, judging that the father of a king was more splendid than any kingdom.

units.la: 3 Sed inter Lysimachum & Pyrrhum regem, socios paulo ante aduersus Demetrium, Asiduum inter pares 25 discordia malum, bellum mouerat. Victor Lysimachus, pulso Pyrrho Macedoniam occupaucrat. Inde Thraciae, ac deinceps Heracleae bellum intulerat: cuius urbis & initia & exitus admirabiles fuere; quippe Boeotiis pestilentia laborantibus, oraculum Delphis responderat, co-
units.tr: 3 But between Lysimachus and King Pyrrhus, who had been allies a little before against Demetrius, the constant evil of discord between equals stirred up war. Victorious Lysimachus, having driven Pyrrhus out, had occupied Macedonia. From there he had made war on Thrace and then on Heraclea. The beginnings and the outcome of that city were remarkable. For when the Boeotians were suffering from pestilence, an oracle at Delphi had answered that they should found a colony in the region of Pontus, sacred to Hercules.

units.la: 30 loniam in Ponti regione sacram Herculi conderet. Cum propter metum longe ac periculosae nauigationis, morantem in patria omnibus praeoptantibus, res omissa esset, bellum his Phocenses intulerunt: quorum cum aduersa prælia paterentur, iterato ad oraculum decurrunt; responsum, idem belli quod seditionis remedium fore. Igitur conscripta colonorum manu in Pontum delati, vrbem Heraclceam condiderunt. Et quoniam fatorum auspiciis in eas sedes delati erant, breui tempore magnas opes parauere. Multa deinde huius vrbis aduersus finitimos bella, multa etiam domestica dissensiones fuere. Inter cetera magnifica, vel præcipue illud memorabile fuit. Cum rerum potirentur Athenienses, victisque Persis, Græciæ & Asiæ tributum in tutelam classis descripsissent, omnibus cupide ad præsidium salutis sue conserentibus; soli Heraclienses ob amicitiam regum Persicorum, collationem abnuerant. Missus itaque ab Atheniensibus Lamachus cum exercitu ad extorquendum quod negabatur, dum relictis in littore nauibus, agros Heracliensium populatur, classem cum maiore parte exercitus, naufragio repentinæ tempestatis amisit. Itaque cum nec mari posset amissis nauibus, neque terra aduerteret, cum parua manu inter tot ferocissimas gentes, reuerti; Heraclienses honestiorem beneficij, quam vltionis occasionem rati, instructos commeatibus, auxiliisque dimittunt: bene agrorum suorum populationem impensam exististimantes, si quos hostes habuerant, amicos reddidissent.
units.tr: 30 Because of the fear of a long and dangerous voyage, and since everyone preferred to remain in his homeland, the matter was dropped. Then the Phocaeans made war on them. When they suffered defeats, they ran again to the oracle, and the answer was that the remedy for war would be the same as the remedy for sedition. So they enrolled a band of colonists, were carried to Pontus, and founded the city of Heraclea. And since they had been brought to those seats under the auspices of fate, in a short time they gained great wealth. Afterwards this city fought many wars against its neighbours and suffered many domestic dissensions. Among its other splendid episodes, this one was especially memorable. When the Athenians held power, and after the Persians had been defeated, they drew up a tribute for Greece and Asia for the protection of the fleet, and everyone eagerly contributed to the safeguarding of their security. Only the Heracleans, because of their friendship with the Persian kings, refused the contribution. So Lamachus was sent by the Athenians with an army to extort what was refused. While he left his ships on the shore and plundered the fields of the Heracleans, a sudden storm wrecked his fleet, and with it most of his army. Since he could neither go back by sea, with his ships lost, nor make headway on land, with a small force among so many fierce peoples, he withdrew. The Heracleans, judging the occasion more honourable for a kindness than for vengeance, sent him away provided with supplies and auxiliaries. They considered the plundering of their fields well spent, if they had made friends of those who had been enemies.

units.la: 4 Pœsi sunt inter plurima mala, etiam tyrannidem: siquidem cum plebs etiam nouas tabulas, & diuisionem agrorum diutius impotenter flagitaret, diu re in senatu tractata, cum exitus rei non inueniretur, ad postremum aduersus plebem nimio otio lasciuientem, auxilia a Timotheo Atheniensium duce, mox ab Epaminonda Thebanorum petiuere. Vtrisque negantibus, ad Clearchum, quem ipsi in exilium egerant, decurrunt: tanta calamitatis necessitas fuit, ut cui patriam inter-
units.tr: 4 Among the very many evils they also suffered tyranny. For when the common people for a long time violently demanded the cancellation of debts and a division of the lands, and the matter had been debated for a long time in the senate without any resolution being found, at last, against the plebs running wild in excessive idleness, they sought help first from Timotheus, the Athenian commander, and then from Epaminondas of the Thebans. When both refused, they ran to Clearchus, whom they themselves had driven into exile. So great was the necessity of the calamity that the man whom they had denied a place in their country

units.la: interdixerant,eum ad tutelam patriæ revocarent. Sed Clearchus exilio facinorosior redditus,& dissensionem populi occasionem inuadenda tyrannidis existimans, primo tacitum cum Mithridate ciuium suorum hoste colloquitur; & inita societate paciscitur, vt revocatus
units.tr: they recalled to the defence of the fatherland. But Clearchus, made more villainous by exile, and thinking that dissension among the people was an opening for seizing tyranny, first held a secret talk with Mithridates, the enemy of his fellow citizens, and formed an alliance, agreeing that, once recalled to his country,

units.la: 5 colloquitur; & inita societate paciscitur, vt revocatus in patriam prodita ei vrbe, prefectus eius constitueretur. Postea autem insidias, quas ciuibus parauerat, in ipsum Mithridatem verterat. Namq; cum velut arbiter ciuilis discordiæ, de exilio reuersus esset, statuto tempore, quo vrbem Mithridati traderet, ipsum cum amicis suis cepit;captumq;,accepta ingenti pecunia.dimisit. Atque vt in illo subitum se ex socio fecit hostem, sic ex defensore senatoriæ causæ,repente patronus plebis euasit; & aduersus auctores potentiæ suæ, à quibus revocatus in patriam, per quos in arce collocatus fuerat, non solum plebem accendit, verumetiam nefandissima quæq; tyrannica crudelitatis exercuit. Igitur populo ad concionem vocato,neq; se affuturum amplius grassanti in populum senatui,ait;intercessurum etiam si in priuata 20 stina seuitia perseueret: quod si pares se crudelitati senatorum arbitrarentur, abiturum cum militibus suis, neque ciuilibus discordiis interfuturum; sin vero dissidant viribus propriis, vindicta se ciuium non defuturum. Proinde consulant sibiipsis, vbeant abire se, si malint,vel causæ populari socium remanere. His verbis solicitata plebs,summum ad eum imperium defert; & dum senatus potentiæ ira scitur,in seruitutem se tyrannica dominationis cum coniugibus & liberis tradit. Itaque Clearchus 6o.senatores comprehensos(nam ceteri 30 in fugam dilapsi erant) in vincula compingit. Latari plebs, quod à duce potissimum senatorum ,senatus delerctum versaq, vice, auxilium eorum in exitium conuersum esse. Quibus dum mortem passim omnibus mi-
units.tr: 5 with the city betrayed to him, he should be made its prefect. Afterwards, however, he turned the ambush he had prepared for the citizens against Mithridates himself. For when he had returned from exile as arbiter of the civil discord, at the appointed time when he was to hand the city over to Mithridates, he seized him with his friends, and, having taken a huge sum of money, released him. Just as in that case he changed from ally into enemy, so from defender of the senatorial cause he suddenly became champion of the plebs. Against the authors of his power, by whom he had been recalled to his country and through whom he had been placed in the citadel, he not only stirred up the plebs but also practised every most nefarious act of tyrannical cruelty. So, calling the people to an assembly, he declared that he would no longer be present while the senate raged against the people; he would intervene even if they persisted in their private savagery. But if they thought themselves equal to the cruelty of the senators, he would depart with his soldiers and take no part in the civil discord; but if they distrusted their own strength, he would not fail to avenge the citizens. Let them therefore consult their own interests, and order him to leave if they preferred, or to remain as an ally of the popular cause. Moved by these words, the plebs conferred supreme power on him, and while the anger of the senate's power was still felt, they handed themselves over, with their wives and children, into the slavery of tyrannical rule. Thus Clearchus threw sixty senators who had been seized into chains (for the rest had scattered in flight). The plebs rejoiced that the senate had been chosen by its own leader, and that by a turn of fortune their help had been turned to their ruin. While death was being threatened indiscriminately to all of them,

units.la: natur, cariora eorum pretia facit: siquidem Clearchus magna pecunia (quasi minus populi occulte eos subtracturus) accepta, spoliatos fortunis, vita quoq; spoliauit.
units.tr: While he threatens death to all alike, he raises their ransoms. Clearchus, having taken large sums of money (as though he would secretly take less from the people), stripped them of their fortunes and then of their lives.

units.la: 5 Cognito deinde, quod bellum sibi ab iis qui profugerant, misericordia in auxilium solicitatis ciuitatibus, pararetur, seruos eorum manumittit. Et nequid mali afflictis honestissimis domibus deesset; vxores eorum, filiasq; nubere seruis suis, proposita recusantibus morte, compellit; vt eos sibi fidiores, & dominis infestiores redderet. Sed matronis tam lugubres nuptiae, gratiores repentinis funeribus fuere. Itaq; multae se ante nuptias, multae in ipsis nuptiis, occisis primum novis maritis, interficiunt, & se tam funestis calamitatibus, virtute ingenui pudoris, eripiunt. Prælium deinde 15 committitur: quo victor tyrannus captiuos senatores in triumphi modum per urbem trahit. Reuersus in urbem, alios vincit, torquet alios, alios occidit; nullus locus urbis a crudelitate tyranni vacat. Accedit seuitia insolentia, crudelitati arrogantia: interdum enim ex 20 successu continuae felicitatis obliuiscitur se hominem, interdum Iouis filium dicit. Eunti per publicum, aurea aquila velut argumentum generis praeferebatur: vestem purpurea, & cothurnos regum tragicorum, & aurea corona vtebatur: filium quoq; suum Ceraunon vocat, vt deos non mendacio tantum, verumetiam nomi-
units.tr: Then, learning that a war was being prepared against him by those who had fled, and that the cities were being roused to help them out of pity, he set their slaves free. And so that no evil should be lacking to these most honourable households, he compelled their wives and daughters to marry his slaves, with death threatened for those who refused, so as to make the slaves more loyal to him and more hostile to their masters. But to the matrons these dismal weddings were more welcome than sudden funerals. So many of them killed themselves before their weddings, and many during the weddings themselves, having first killed their new husbands, and by the courage of free-born modesty they snatched themselves from such deadly calamities. Then battle was joined, in which the victorious tyrant dragged the captured senators through the city in the manner of a triumph. Returning to the city, he conquered some, tortured others, and killed others; no place in the city was free from the tyrant's cruelty. To his savagery was added insolence, and to his cruelty arrogance: sometimes, through the success of his continued good fortune, he forgot that he was a man, and sometimes he called himself a son of Jupiter. When he went through the public square, a golden eagle was carried before him as a token of his descent; he wore a purple robe, the buskins of tragic kings, and a golden crown. He also called his son Ceraunos, so that he mocked the gods not only with lies but even with their names.

units.la: nibus illudat. Hac illum facere, duo nobilissimi iuuenes Chion & Leonides indignantes, patriam liberaturi in necem tyranni conspirant. Erant hi discipuli Platonis philosophi; qui virtutem, ad quam quotidie praeceptis magistri erudiebantur, patriae exhibere cupientes, quinquaginta cognatos, veluti clientes, in insidiis locat. Ipsi more iuvantium, ad tyrannum veluti ad regem 30 gem in arcem contendunt, qui iure familiaritatis admissi, dum alterum priorem dicentem intentus audit tyrannus, ab altero obtruncatur. Sed & ipsi socii tardius auxilium ferentibus, a satellitibus obruuntur. Quare factum est, ut tyrannus quidem occideretur, sed patria non liberaretur. Nam frater Clearchi Saturus eadem via tyrannidem invadit; multisque annis, per gradus successionis, Heraclienses sub regno tyrannorum fuere.
units.tr: Indignant at these things, two most noble young men, Chion and Leonides, resolved to conspire against the tyrant's life in order to liberate their country. They were disciples of the philosopher Plato, and, wishing to display in practice the virtue in which they had been daily trained by their teacher's precepts, they posted fifty of their kinsmen in ambush, as though they were clients. They themselves, in the manner of men coming to offer help, hastened to the tyrant in the citadel as to a king. Admitted by right of their familiarity, they struck while the tyrant listened intently to the one who spoke first, and the other cut him down. But the accomplices themselves, who were bringing help too slowly, were overwhelmed by the guards. Hence it came about that the tyrant was indeed killed, but the country was not freed. For Clearchus's brother Satyrus seized the tyranny by the same route, and for many years, through successive generations, the Heracleots remained under the rule of tyrants.
POMPEII TROGI EPITOMA HISTORIARUM
BOOK XVII.
SUMMARY.

units.la: ER idem ferme tempus in Hellesponti & Chersonesi regionibus terraemotu fuit: maxime tamen Lysimachia ı̄ vb sante duos & viginti annos a Lysimacho rege condita, euersa est. Quod portentum dira Lysimacho, strip·q, eius, ac regni ruinam, cum clade vexatarum regionum portendebat. Nec ostentis fides defuit: nam brevi post tempore, Agathoclem filium suum, quem in successionem regni ordinauerat, per quem multa bella prosperè gesserat, non solum patrium, verumetiam humanum ultra morem perosus, ministra Arsinoë novercae, veneno interfecit. Hec illi prima mali
units.tr: At about the same time there was an earthquake in the regions of the Hellespont and the Chersonese. Most of all, Lysimachia, founded twenty-two years earlier by King Lysimachus, was overthrown. This portent foretold dire misfortune for Lysimachus himself, for his children and for his kingdom, and the ruin of the stricken regions along with it. Nor was the omen without fulfilment. For a short time later, he poisoned, through the agency of his stepmother Arsinoe, his son Agathocles, whom he had designated as successor to the kingdom and through whom he had successfully waged many wars. He hated him beyond the ordinary measure, not only as a father but as a man. This was the first stain of evil, the beginning of the ruin that was coming.

units.la: {1} Lysimacho rege condita: i.e. Lysimachia, ut dicitur.
units.tr: {1} Founded by King Lysimachus: that is, Lysimachia, as it is called.

units.la: mali labes, hoc initum impendentis ruinæ fuit. Nam parricidium, principum sequuta cædes sunt, luentium supplicia quod occisum iuuenem dolebant. Itaq; & hi qui cædibus superfuerant, & hi qui exercitibus præerant, certatim ad Seleucum deficiunt; eumque pronum iam ex æmulatione gloriæ, bellum Lysimacho inferre compellunt. Vltimum hoc certamen commilitonum Alexandri fuit, & velut ad exemplum fortunæ par reseruatum. Lysimachus quatuor & 70. annos natus erat. Seleucus septem & 70. Sed in hac ætate vtriq; animi iuuenileserant, imperiiq; cupiditatem insatiabilem gerebant. Quippe cum orbem terrarum duo soli tenerent, angustiis sibimet inclusi videbantur, vitaque finem non annorum spatio, sed imperij terminis metiebantur.
units.tr: For parricide was followed by the slaughter of the leading men, who paid the penalty because they had grieved over the young man's killing. And so both those who had survived the murders and those who commanded the armies eagerly deserted to Seleucus, and their rivalry for glory drove him, already inclined, to make war on Lysimachus. This final contest was between companions of Alexander, and it was as if fortune had kept an equal match in reserve for the sake of the pattern. Lysimachus was seventy-four years old, Seleucus seventy-seven. But at this age both men still had youthful spirits and an insatiable desire for power. Since the two of them alone held the whole world, they seemed hemmed in by narrow bounds, and they measured their lives not by the span of years but by the limits of their empire.
The ambition of each of the two princes.

units.la: 2 In eo bello Lysimachus amissis ante variis casibus 15. liberis, non in strenue moriens, postremus domus suae ruinae cumulus accessit. Latus tanta victoria Seleucus, & quod maius victoria putabat, solum se de cohorte Alexandri remansisse; victoremq; victorum extitisse, 20 non humanum esse opus, sed divinum mutuo gloriatur: ignarus prorsus, non multo post, fragilitatis humanae ipsum exemplum futurum. Quippe post menses admodum septem a Ptolemaeo, cuius sororem Lysimachus in matrimonio habuerat, per insidias circumuentus occiditur; regnumq; Macedoniae, quod Lysimacho eripuerat; cum vita pariter amittit. Igitur Ptolemaeus cum & in gratiam memoriae magni Ptolemaei patris, & in favorem ultionis Lysimachi ambitiosus apud populares esset, primo Lysimachi filios conciliare sibi statuit; 25 nuptiasq; Arsinoes sororis suae matris eorum petit, pueror-um adoptione promissa, ut cum in locum patris eorum succedissent, nihil illi moliri, vel verecundia matris, vel appellatione patris auderent. Fratris quoque regis AEgypti concordiam per epistolas deprecatur; professus deponere fe offensam erepti paterni regni,neq, amplius à fratre quaesiturum, quod honestius à paterno hoste perceperit. Omnia arte adulatur Eumeni,& Antigono Demetrij filiis, Antiocho filio Seleuci, cum quibus bellum habituru s erat, ne tertius sibi hosti accederet.
units.tr: In that war Lysimachus, having previously lost fifteen children through various misfortunes, died not bravely, and the final heap of ruin was added to his house. Seleucus, elated by so great a victory, and by what he thought greater than the victory, that he alone had remained of Alexander's companions, boasted, in a mutual exchange of praise, that he had become the conqueror of conquerors, a feat not human but divine. He was utterly unaware that, not long afterwards, he himself would become the very example of human frailty. For about seven months later he was trapped by treachery and killed by Ptolemy, whose sister Lysimachus had married; and he lost the kingdom of Macedonia, which he had taken from Lysimachus, together with his life. Ptolemy, ambitious among the people both out of regard for the memory of his father, the great Ptolemy, and out of a desire to avenge Lysimachus, first decided to win over Lysimachus' sons. He sought the marriage of Arsinoe, his sister and their mother, promising to adopt the boys, so that when they succeeded to their father's place they would not dare to attempt anything against him, out of respect for their mother or the name of their father. He also sought by letters the goodwill of the brother of the king of Egypt, declaring that he would lay aside his resentment over the seizure of his father's kingdom and would no longer demand from his brother what he had received more honourably from a hostile father. He flattered by every means Eumenes and Antigonus, sons of Demetrius, and Antiochus, son of Seleucus, with whom he was going to have to fight, so that a third enemy should not join them against him.

units.la: Sed nec Pyrrhus rex Epiri omissus, ingens momentum futurus, vtri parti socius accessisset, qui & ipse spoliare 10 singulos cupiens,omnibus fe partibus venditabat. Itaq; Tarentinis aduersus Romanos laturus auxilium, ab Antigono naues, ad exercitum in Italiam deportandum,mutuo petit; ab Antiocho pecuniam; qui opibus quam militibus instructior erat; a Ptolemaeo Macedo15num militum auxilia. Sed Ptolemaeus, cui nulla dilationis ex infirmitate virium venia effet, quinq; millia peditum, equitum quatuor millia, elephantos quinquaginta,non amplius, quam in bieny vsum dedit. Ob hac Pyrrhus, filia Ptolemei in matrimonium accepta, vindicem eum regni reliquit: ne abducta in Italiam 20 iuuentute,predam hostibus regnum relinqueret.
units.tr: Nor was Pyrrhus, king of Epirus, overlooked, though he was going to be of great importance to whichever side he joined. He too, wishing to plunder each party in turn, offered himself to all sides. So, intending to bring help to the Tarentines against the Romans, he asked Antigonus for ships to transport his army to Italy, and asked Antiochus for money, since Antiochus was better supplied with wealth than with soldiers, and asked Ptolemy for an auxiliary force of Macedonian soldiers. But Ptolemy, who could not excuse any delay on the ground of weakness of his forces, gave him no more than five thousand foot, four thousand horse and fifty elephants, for use in this one war. Pyrrhus, having taken Ptolemy's daughter in marriage, left him as guardian of his kingdom, so that the kingdom would not be left as prey for enemies, with its young men carried off to Italy.

units.la: 3 Sed quoniam ad Epiri mentionem ventum est, de origine regni eius pauca narranda sunt.Molossorum primum in ea regione regnum fuit.Post Pyrrhus Achil25lis filius, amisso per absentiam [ Troianis temporibus ] paterno regno,in his locis conjedit, qui Pyrrhida primo,postea Epirota dicti sunt. Sed Pyrrhus cum in templum Dodonei Iouis ad consulendum venisset, ibi Laa nassam neptem Herculis rapuit: ex cuius matrimonio 30 octo liberos sustulit. Ex his nonnullas virgines nuptum finitimis regibus tradidit, opesq, affinitatium auxilio magnas parauit:atque ita Heleno filio Priami regis,ob industriam singularem,regnum Chaonum,& Andro- mamachen Hectoris, quam & ipse matrimonio suo in di–uisione Troiana prædæ acceperat, uxorem tradidit: breuiq; post tempore, Delphis insidiis Orestæ filij Agamemnonis, inter altaria dei interiit. Successor huic Pialis filius fuit. Per ordinem deinde, regnum ad Arrybâ descendit: cui, quoniam pupillus & unicus ex gente nobili superesset, intentiore omnium cura seruandi eius, educandi, publice tutores constituuntur: Athenas quoq; eruditionis gratia missus, quanto doctior maioribus suis, tanto & gratior populo fuit. Primus itaq; leges, & senatum, annuosq; magistratus, & reipub. formam composuit: & vt à Pyrrho sedes, sic vita cultior populo ab Arrybâ statuta. Huius filius Neoptolemus fuit: ex quo nata est Olympias, mater Alexandri Magni, & Alexander, qui post eum regnū Epiri tenuit; & in Italia bello gesto, in Bruttiis interiit. Post eius mortem frater AEacides regno successit, qui assiduis aduersus Macedonas bellorum certaminibus populum fatigando, offensam ciuium contraxit, ac propterea in exilium actus, Pyrrhum filium suum, admodum paruulum in regno reliquit: qui & ipse cum à populo propter odium patris ad necem quæreretur, furtim subtractus in Illyrios defertur; traditusq; est Beroæ, Glauci regis uxori nutriendus, quæ & ipsa generis AEacidarum erat. Ibi eum seu miserecordia fortuna eius, seu infantilibus blandimentis inductus, rex aduersum Cassandrū Macedoniæ regem, qui eum sub belli comminatione deposcebat, diu protexit, addito in auxilium etiam adoptionis officio. Quibus rebus moti Epirotæ, odio in miserecordia uerso, annorum xi. eum in regnū reuocauerunt, datis tutoribus, qui regnū usq; ad adultæ eius ætatem tuerentur. Adulescens deinde multa bella gessit, tantusq; rerum successu haberi cœptus est, vt Tarentinos aduersus Romanos tueri posse videretur.
units.tr: But since mention has been made of Epirus, a few things must be told about the origin of its kingdom. The first kingdom in that region was that of the Molossians. Afterwards Pyrrhus, son of Achilles, having lost his father's kingdom through his absence [in the times of the Trojan War], settled in these places, and those people were called first Pyrrhidae, later Epirotes. But when Pyrrhus came to the temple of Dodonaean Jove to consult the oracle, he there carried off Lanassa, granddaughter of Hercules, and from this marriage he had eight children. Some of these daughters he gave in marriage to neighbouring kings, and so he gained great resources through the help of these alliances. Thus he gave the kingdom of the Chaonians to Helenus, son of King Priam, for his singular diligence, and gave Andromache, widow of Hector, whom he himself had received as his share of the Trojan spoils, to him as wife. Shortly afterwards, at Delphi, he perished among the altars of the god, through an ambush laid by Orestes, son of Agamemnon. His successor was Pialus, his son. Then in order the kingdom passed to Arybas. Since Arybas was a ward and the only surviving male of a noble line, the public appointed guardians for him, with the greatest care of all for his protection and upbringing. He was also sent to Athens for education, and the more learned he became than his ancestors, the more pleasing he was to the people. Thus he was the first to draw up laws, a senate, annual magistrates and the form of the commonwealth; and just as Pyrrhus had established their seats, so Arybas established a more civilised way of life for the people. His son was Neoptolemus, and from him was born Olympias, mother of Alexander the Great, and Alexander, who held the kingdom of Epirus after him, and who perished in the Bruttian country while waging war in Italy. After his death his brother Aeacides succeeded to the kingdom. He wore out the people with constant wars against the Macedonians, and so drew upon himself the hatred of his citizens. For this reason he was driven into exile, leaving his son Pyrrhus, a very little boy, in the kingdom. The people, because of their hatred of the father, sought the boy's death as well; but he was secretly taken away and carried off to the Illyrians, and was handed over at Beroea, to be brought up by the wife of King Glaucias, who was herself of the Aeacid line. There, either moved by pity for his fortune or drawn by his infantile charms, the king long sheltered him against Cassander, king of Macedonia, who demanded him under threat of war, adding also the service of adoption to his protection. Moved by these things, the Epirots, their hatred turned into pity, recalled him to the kingdom when he was eleven years old, appointing guardians who would protect the kingdom until he came of age. The young man then waged many wars, and he came to be regarded with such success in his undertakings that he seemed able to defend the Tarentines against the Romans.
The Epitome of the Histories of Pompeius Trogus

units.la: 1 Pyrrho Tarentinis aduersus Romanos suppetias ferendi Valerius Læuinus occurrit: unde prœlia & strages.
units.tr: 1 Valerius Laevinus meets Pyrrhus, who has come to bring help to the Tarentines against the Romans; battles and slaughter follow.

units.tr: 2 The Romans send back the Carthaginian auxiliaries. Peace is made with Pyrrhus. The Romans hold ... (a).

units.tr: 3 A digression on the origin of the Carthaginians and their early inhabitants, including the founders of Sidon and Tyre.

units.la: 4 Noui incolæ Tyri, inter quos Elissa, quæ a Pygmalione fratre recedit, vt illus.
units.tr: 4 The new inhabitants of Tyre, among whom Elissa, who withdraws from her brother Pygmalion, as follows.

units.la: 5 Elissa, agnomine Dido, Cyprum appellit, deinde in sinum Africæ defertur, & Carthaginem condit.
units.tr: 5 Elissa, also called Dido, lands on Cyprus, is then carried into a bay of Africa, and founds Carthage.

units.la: 6 Propter Hiarbæ voluntum Elissa sibi vim infert, Carthaginiensium crudelis superstitio.
units.tr: 6 For the sake of Hiarbas' will, Elissa does violence to herself; the cruel superstition of the Carthaginians.

units.la: 7 Cladesque Carthaginiensium in Sardinia. Superstites in exilium pulsi patriam armis recuperare niruntur, unde Malei patris in Cartalonem filium seuericas, & paulo post cruentius intergerunt.
units.tr: 7 The Carthaginians' defeats in Sardinia. The survivors, driven into exile, strive to recover their homeland by arms, and afterwards with severe and then even bloodier fighting against Malchus' son, the son of the father.

units.la: GITVR Pyrrhus rex Epiri, cum iteraratatarentinorum legatione, additis Samnitium & Lucanorum precibus, & ipsis auxilio aduersus Romanos indigentibus, fatigaretur, non tam supplicum precibus, quam spe inuadendi Italiæ imperij inductus, venturum se cum exercitu pollicetur. In quam rem inclinatum semel animum, præcipitem agere coeperant exempla maiorum: ne aut inferior patruo suo Alexandro videretur, quo defensore iidem Tarentini adversus Bruttios vsi fuerant; aut minores animos Magno Alexandro habuisse, qui tam longa à domo militia Oriẽ-
units.tr: Therefore Pyrrhus, king of Epirus, when he was worn down by the embassy of the Tarentines, together with the prayers of the Samnites and Lucanians, who also needed help against the Romans, was moved not so much by the entreaties of suppliants as by the hope of invading the empire of Italy, and promises that he will come with an army. Once his mind was inclined to this, the examples of his forefathers began to drive him headlong: lest he seem inferior to his uncle Alexander, under whose leadership the same Tarentines had used arms against the Bruttians; or lest he be thought to have smaller spirit than Alexander the Great, who through so long a campaign far from home subdued the East.

units.la: Vana spe inuadendi Italiæ imperii Pyrrhus, auxilium Tarentinis aduersus Romanos polliceretur.
units.tr: Pyrrhus' vain hope of invading the empire of Italy leads him to promise help to the Tarentines against the Romans.

units.la: Ambitio cæca miserum principem cuerit. tem subegit. Igitur relicto custode regni filio Ptolemaeo, annos 15.nato, exercitum in portu Tarentino exponit, duobus parvulis filiis, Alexandro & Heleno, in solatia longinquae secum expeditionis adductis. Cuius audito aduentu, Consul Romanus Valerius Laevinus festinans, ut prius cum eo congrederetur quam auxilia sociorum conuenirent, exercitum in aciem educit: Nec rex, tamen etsi numero militum inferior esset, certamini moram fecit. Sed Romanos vincentes iam, inusitata ante elephantorum forma stupere prioris, mox cedere praelio coegit, victoresque iam noua Macedonum monstra repente vicerunt. Nec hostibus incruenta victoria fuit: nam & ipse Pyrrhus graviter vulneratus est, & magna pars militum eius caesa; maioremque gloriam eius victoria, quam laetitiam habuit. Huius pugnae eventum multa civitates secutae, Pyrrho se tradunt. Inter ceteras civitam Locri, prodito praesidio Romano, ad Pyrrhum defecerunt. Ex ea praeda Pyrrhus 200. captivos milites Romanam gratis remisit, ut cognita virtute eius, Romani cognoscerent etiam liberalitatem. Interiectis deinde diebus, cum sociorum exercitus superveniset, iterato praelium cum Romanis facit, in quo par fortuna priori bello fuit.
units.tr: Blind ambition drove the unhappy prince on. Leaving his son Ptolemy, aged fifteen, as guardian of the kingdom, he landed his army in the harbour of Tarentum, taking with him his two young sons, Alexander and Helenus, as comfort during the long expedition. When his arrival was heard of, the Roman consul Valerius Laevinus hurried to engage him before the forces of the allies could join, and led his army out into battle line. The king, although he was inferior in number of soldiers, did not delay the contest. But when the Romans were already winning, the unfamiliar shape of the elephants, which they had never seen before, astonished them; soon he forced them to give ground, and the Macedonian new monsters suddenly overcame the victors. Nor was the victory bloodless for the enemy: Pyrrhus himself was seriously wounded, and a large part of his soldiers were slain; the victory brought him more glory than joy. Many cities followed the outcome of this battle and surrendered to Pyrrhus. Among the rest, the city of Locri, after its Roman garrison had been betrayed, revolted to Pyrrhus. From that booty Pyrrhus sent back to the Romans, without ransom, two hundred captured soldiers, so that the Romans, having learned of his courage, might also learn of his generosity. Then, after some days had passed and the army of the allies had come up, he fought a second battle with the Romans, in which the fortune was equal to the first.

units.la: 2. Interea Mago, dux Carthaginiensium, in auxilium Romanorum cum 120. navibus missus, senatum adiit, aegre tulisse Carthaginienses, affirmans, quod bellum in Italia a peregrino rege paterentur: Ob quam causam missum se, ut quoniam externo hoste oppugnarentur, externis auxiliis iuuarentur. Gratia a senatu Carthaginiensibus acta, auxiliaque remissa. Sed Mago Punico ingenio, post paucos dies tacitus, quasi pacificator Carthaginiensium, Pyrrhum adiit speculaturus filia eius de Sicilia, quo eum arcessiri fama erat. Nam
units.tr: 2. Meanwhile Mago, commander of the Carthaginians, who had been sent with 120 ships to help the Romans, approached the senate and declared that the Carthaginians were grieved that they were suffering war in Italy from a foreign king. For this reason, he said, he had been sent: since they were attacked by a foreign enemy, they should be aided by foreign help. The senate gave thanks to the Carthaginians, and the auxiliaries were sent back. But Mago, with Punic cunning, after a few days, quietly, as though he were the peacemaker of the Carthaginians, approached Pyrrhus, to spy out the rumour, which was current, that Pyrrhus was being summoned from Sicily. For

units.la: Romanis eadem causa mittendi auxilij Carthaginienfibus fuerat, vt Romano bello, ne in Siciliam transire posset Pyrrhus, in Italia detineretur. Dum hac aguntur, legatus a senatu Romano Fabricius Lufcinus mif- 5 sus, patem cum Pyrrho composuit. Ad quam confirmandam, Cyneas Romam cum ingentibus a Pyrrho donis missus, neminem, cuius domus muneribus pateret,innuenit, Huic continentia Romanorum simile exemplum, iisdem ferme temporibus fuit. Nam missi a 10 senatu in AEgyptum legati, cum ingentia sibi a Ptolemaeo rege missa munera spreuissent, interiectis diebus ad cænam inuitatis, aurea corona misse sunt, quas illi honoris causa receptas,postera die statuis regis imposuerunt. Igitur Cyneas cum turbatam cum Romanu pa15 cem ab Appio Claudio renuntiaffet, interrogatus a Pyrrho,qualis Roma effet,respondit, Regum vrbem sibi visam.
