Post hæc legati Siculorum superueniunt, tradentes Pyrrho totius infulæ imperium, quæ assiduis Carthaginiensium bellis vexabatur,Itaq; relicto Locris 20 Alexandro filio,firmatisq, sociorum ciuitatibus valido præfidio,in Siciliam exercitum traiecit,
units.tr: the Romans had the same reason for sending help to the Carthaginians: so that, while the Romans were at war, Pyrrhus might not be able to cross into Sicily but would be kept in Italy. While these things were being done, Fabricius Luscinus was sent as legate by the Roman senate and made peace with Pyrrhus. To confirm this, Cyneas was sent to Rome with great gifts from Pyrrhus, and he found no one whose house was open to bribes. A similar example of Roman self-restraint occurred at about the same time. For when the legates sent by the senate to Egypt had rejected the great gifts sent to them by King Ptolemy, they were invited to dinner a few days later and sent golden crowns; they accepted these as a mark of honour and on the next day placed them on the king's statues. Therefore, when Cyneas reported that the peace with the Romans had been disturbed by Appius Claudius, Pyrrhus asked him what Rome was like, and he replied that it seemed to him a city of kings. After this, ambassadors of the Sicilians arrived, handing over to Pyrrhus the rule of the whole island, which was harassed by the constant wars of the Carthaginians. So, leaving his son Alexander at Locri, and securing the cities of the allies with a strong garrison, he led his army across into Sicily.

units.la: 3 Et quoniam ad Carthaginiensium mentionem ventum est,de origine eorum pauca dicenda sunt,repetitis Tyriorum paulo altius rebus, quorum casus etiam 25 dolendi fuerunt. Tyriorum gens condita a Phœnicibus fuit,qui terramotu vexati,relicto patria solo,Assyrium stagnum primo, mox mari proximum littus incoluerunt, conditaibi vrbe,quam a piscium vbertate,Sidona appellauerunt: nam piscem Phœnices fidon vocant.
units.tr: 3. And since mention has been made of the Carthaginians, a few things must be said about their origin, going back somewhat further into the history of the Tyrians, whose misfortunes also deserve lamentation. The Tyrian people was founded by the Phoenicians, who, troubled by an earthquake, left their native soil, first settling by the Assyrian lake, and afterwards the shore nearest the sea. There they founded a city, which they named Sidon from the abundance of fish, for the Phoenicians call a fish "fidon."

units.la: 30 Post multos deinde annos a rege Afcaloniorum expugnati,nauibus appulsi,Tyron vrbem ante annum Troiana cladis condiderunt:ibi Persarum bellis diu,varieq, fatigati, victores quidem fuere; sed attritis viribus, a feruis suis multitudine abundantibus, indigna suppli& shy;cia perpessi sunt: qui conspiratione facta, omnem libe& shy;rum populum cum dominis interficiunt; atq; ita potiti vrbe, lares dominorum occupant, rempub. invadunt, coniuges ducunt, & quod ipsi non erant, liberos pro­creant. Vnus ex tot millibus seruorum fuit: qui miti ingenio, senis domini, parvulig; filij eius fortuna mo& shy;ueretur; dominosq; non truci feritate, sed pia misericordia humanitate respiceret. Itaq; cum velut occisos ali enaffet, scrutiq; de statu reipub. deliberantibus placuif­set regem ex suo corpore creari, eumq; potissimum quasi acceptissimum diis, qui solem Orientem primus vidif& shy;set, rem ad Stratonem (hoc enim ei nomen erat) domi& shy;num occulte latentem detulit. Ab eo formatus, cum medio noctis omnes in vnum campum processissent, ce­teris in Orientem spectantibus, solus Occidentis regio& shy;nem intuebatur. Id primum alij viderunt furor, in Occi­dente solis ortum quaerere: vbi vero dies adventare coe& shy;pit, editissimisq; culminibus vrbis oriens splendere, ex& shy;spectantibus alijs, vt ipsum solem aspicerent, hic primus omnibus fulgorem solis in summo fastigio ciuitatis o­stendit. Non seruilis ingenij ratio visa, requirentibusq; auctorem, de domino confitetur. Tunc intellectum est: Quantum ingenua seruilibus ingenia praestarent; malitiaq; seruos, non sapientia, vincere. Igitur venia se­ni filioq; data est; & velut humine quodam reserua& shy;tos arbitrantes, regem Stratonem creauerunt. Post cuius mortem regnum ad filium, ac deinde ad nepotes transfiit. Celebre hoc seruorum facinus, metuendumq; exemplum toto orbe terrarum fuit. Itaque Alexander Magnus, cum interiecto tempore in Oriente bellum gereret, velut vtfor publica securitatis, expugnata eo& shy;rum vrbe, omnes qui proelio superfuerant, ob memoriam riam veteris cadis crucibus affixit; genus tantum Stratonis inuiolatum seruauit, regnumq; stirpi eius restituit, ingenuis & innoxiis incolis insulæ attributis, vt, exstirpato seruili germine, genus vrbis ex integro conderetur.
units.tr: Many years later, having been expelled by the king of the Ascalonites, they landed by ship and founded the city of Tyre before the Trojan disaster. There, worn out for a long time and variously harassed by the wars of the Persians, they were indeed victorious, but with their strength exhausted, they suffered unworthy punishments at the hands of their slaves, who were abundant in number. By a conspiracy they killed all the free people along with their masters; and so, having seized the city, they took possession of their masters' household gods, invaded the state, married their wives, and begot children, which they themselves were not. Only one of the many thousands of slaves was different: gentle by nature, he pitied the fortune of the old master and his little son, and looked upon his masters not with savage cruelty but with pious kindness and humanity. So when they had believed that the free people had been killed, and the slaves were deliberating about the condition of the state, it was decided that a king should be created from their own body, and especially one who was most acceptable to the gods, namely the one who had been the first to see the rising sun. This man secretly reported the matter to Strato (for that was his name), who was hiding at home. Trained by him, when at midnight they had all gone out into one open plain, while the others were looking towards the East, he alone was gazing at the region of the West. The others first thought this madness, to seek the rising of the sun in the West; but when the day began to draw near and the East began to shine over the highest roofs of the city, while the others waited to see the sun itself, he alone showed the brightness of the sun on the highest point of the city. His reasoning did not seem servile, and when they asked him for the author of it, he confessed about his master. Then it was understood how much free-born minds surpass servile ones, and that slaves conquer by malice, not by wisdom. Therefore pardon was granted to the old man and his son; and, thinking them as if restored from some kind of death, they made Strato king. After his death the kingdom passed to his son, and then to his grandsons. This deed of slaves was famous and a fearful example throughout the whole world. And so Alexander the Great, when some time later he was waging war in the East, as an avenger of public security, after capturing their city, fixed all who had survived the battle to crosses, in memory of the ancient crime; only the family of Strato he kept unharmed, and restored the kingdom to his line, assigning the free and innocent inhabitants of the island to the city, so that, the servile seed having been wiped out, the people of the city might be founded afresh.

units.la: 4 Hoc igitur modo Tyrij Alexandri auspiciis conditi, parcimonia & labore quærendi cito conualuere. Ante cladem dominorum cum & opibus, & multitudine abundarent, missa in Africam iuuentute, Vticam condidere: cum interim rex Tyro decedit, filio Pygmalione, & Elissa filia, insignis formæ virgine, heredibus instituto. Sed populus Pygmalioni admodum puero regnum tradidit. Elissa quoq;, Acerbæ auunculo suo, sacerdoti Herculis, qui honos secundus ærege erat, nubit.
units.tr: 4. In this way, therefore, the Tyrians were founded under the auspices of Alexander, and by thrift and industry in acquiring wealth they soon grew strong. Before the destruction of their masters, when they abounded both in resources and in population, they sent their young men into Africa and founded Utica. Meanwhile the king died at Tyre, leaving his heirs, his son Pygmalion, who was quite a boy, and his daughter Elissa, a virgin of remarkable beauty. The people handed the kingdom over to Pygmalion, though he was still very young. Elissa too married Acerbas, her uncle, who was priest of Hercules and held the second office in the kingdom.

units.la: 15 Huic magna, sed dissimulate opes erant; aurumq; metu regis non tectus, sed terræ crediderat: quam rem etsi hominess ignorabant, fama tamen loquebatur. Qua incensus Pygmalion, oblitus iuris humani, auunculum suum, cundemq; generum, sine respectu pietatis occidit.
units.tr: She had great wealth, but it was hidden; for out of fear of the king she had entrusted her gold not to a secure place but to the earth. Although people did not know this, rumour nevertheless spoke of it. Inflamed by this, Pygmalion, forgetting human right, killed his uncle, who was also her husband, without any regard for piety.

units.la: 20 Elissa diu fratrem propter scelus auersata, ad posterum dissimulato odio, mitigatoq;, interim vultu fugam tacito molitur, assumptis quibusdam principibus in societatem, quibus par odium in regem esse, eandemque sugiendi cupiditatem arbitrabatur. Tunc fratrem dolo aggreditur, fingit se ad eum migrare velle, ne amplius ei mariti domus, cupide obliuionis, grauem luctus imaginem renouaret, neue vltra amara admonitio oculis eius occurrat. Non inuitus Pygmalion verba sororis audiuit, exitiamas cum ea & aurum Acerbæ ad se venturum. Sed Elissa ministros migrationis ærege missos, nauibus cum omnibus opibus suis prima vespera imponit, proueftaq, in altum, compellit eos onera harena pro pecunia inuolucris inuoluta, in mare deiicere. Tunc defiens flens ipsa, lugul´riq; voce Acerbam ciet; orat, vt libens opes suas recipiat, quas reliquerat; habeatq; inferias, quas habuerat causam mortis. Tunc ipsos ministros aggreditur: sibi quidem ait optatam olim mortem,sed illis acerbos cruciatus, & dira supplicia imminere, qui Acerbæ opes, quarum spe parricidium rex fecerit, auaritiæ tyranni subtraxerint. Hoc metu omnibus iniecto, comites fugæ accepit. Iunguntur & senatorum in eam noctem præparata agmina; atq; ita sacris Herculis, cuius sacerdos Acerbas fuerat, repetitis, exilio sedes quarunt.
units.tr: For a long time Elissa, having turned away from her brother because of his crime, kept quiet. Then, setting aside her hatred and softening her expression for the time being, she secretly planned her flight. She took into partnership certain leading men whom she judged to have an equal hatred of the king and the same desire to escape. Then she approached her brother by trickery, pretending that she wished to move to him, so that the house of her husband, which craved oblivion, would not renew the heavy image of grief, and bitter reminders would no longer meet his eyes. Pygmalion heard his sister's words not unwillingly, thinking that Acerbas would come to him with all his wealth. But at the first evening Elissa loaded the ships with all her wealth and with the king's envoys who had been sent to escort the migration. Once they were out at sea, she ordered them to throw into the water sacks wrapped up and filled with sand instead of money. Then, weeping and lamenting, she herself called on Acerbas with a mournful voice, praying that he would willingly receive back the wealth she had left behind, and accept as offerings what had been the cause of his death. Then she turned on the ministers themselves. She said that death had long been her own wish, but that bitter torments and dreadful punishments hung over them, who had taken from the tyrant's greed the wealth of Acerbas, for the hope of which the king had committed the murder. With this fear instilled in all of them, she took the companions of her flight. Bands of senators, prepared for that same night, joined her. So, having repeated the sacred rites of Hercules, whose priest Acerbas had been, they sought a home in exile.

units.la: 5 Primus illis appulsus terra, Cyprus infula fuit: vbi sacerdos Iouis, cum coniuge & liberis, deorum monitu, comitem se Elissæ sociumq; præbuit, pastus sibi posterisque perpetuum honorem sacerdotij: Conditio pro manifesto omne accepta. Mos erat Cypriis, virgines ante nuptias statutis diebus dotalem pecuniam quæsituras, in quæstum ad littus maris mittere, pro reliqua pudicitia libamenta Veneri soluturas. Harum igitur ex numero 80. admodum virgines raptas nauibus imponi Elissa iubet; vt & iuuentus matrimonia, & vrbs subolem habere posset. Dum hæc aguntur, Pygmalion cognita sororis fuga, cum impio bello fugientem persequi pararet; ægre precibus matris, & deorum minis victus, quieuit: cui cum inspirati vates canerent, non impune laturum: si incrementa vrbis toto orbe auspicatissimæ interpellasset, hoc modo spatium respirandi snigentibus datum. Itaq; Elissa delata in Africæ sinum, incolas loci eius, aduentu peregrinorum, mutuarumq; rerum commercio gaudentes, in amicitiam solicitat: deinde empto loco, qui corio bouis tegi posset, in quo sessos longa nauigatione soiios, quoad proficisceretur, resicere posset; corium in tenuissimas partes secari iubet, atq;
units.tr: Their first landfall was the island of Cyprus, where a priest of Jupiter, by the warning of the gods, joined Elissa as her companion and partner, with his wife and children. He was granted, for himself and his descendants, the perpetual honour of the priesthood; this condition, accepted as certain, was agreed. It was the custom of the Cypriots that, before marriage, their virgins should be sent to the shore on appointed days to earn their dowry money by prostitution, and to pay offerings to Venus for the chastity they had left. Elissa therefore ordered that eighty of these girls, seized, be placed on board the ships, so that the young men might have wives and the city might have offspring. While these things were happening, Pygmalion, having learned of his sister's flight, prepared to pursue the fugitive with impious war. Scarcely overcome by the prayers of his mother and the threats of the gods, he held back. When inspired seers foretold that he would not go unpunished if he interfered with the growth of a city destined to be most auspicious throughout the world, a breathing space was granted in this way to the fugitives. So Elissa, carried into the bay of Africa, sought friendship with the inhabitants of that region, who rejoiced at the arrival of strangers and at the exchange of goods. Then, having bought a plot of land which could be covered by an ox-hide, on which she might refresh the sailors weary from their long voyage, she ordered the hide to be cut into very thin strips, and

units.la: Locum, cui à facto nomen Byrsa, emit. arg̃, ita maius loci spacium quam petierat, occupat: unde postea ei loco Byrsa nomen fuit. Confluentibus deinde vicinis locorum, qui spe lucri multa hospitibus venalia inferebant; sedesq̃ ibi statuentibus, ex frequentia hominum velut instar civitatis effectum est. Vticensium quoq̃ legati, dona ut cōsanguineis attulerunt; hortatiq̃ sunt, urbem ibi conderent, ubi sedes sortiti essent. Sed & Afros detinendi adventas amor cepit. Itaq̃ consentientibus omnibus, Carthago conditur, statuto annuo vectigali pro solo urbis. In primis fundamentis caput bubulum inventum est: quod auspicium quidem fructuosæ terræ, sed laboriosæ, perpetuoque servæ urbis fuit : propter quod in alium locum vrbs translata. Ibi quoq; equi caput repertum, bellicosum potentemq; populum futurum significans, vrbi auspicatam sedem designit. Tunc ad opinionem noua vrbis concurrentibus gentibus, breui & populus, & ciuitas magna facta.
units.tr: she bought the place which, from the deed, was named Byrsa. By means of the strips she enclosed a larger space than she had asked for, and for this reason the place was later called Byrsa. Then the neighbouring peoples gathered there, who, hoping for profit, brought many goods for sale to the newcomers and settled there themselves, and from this crowd of people something like a city came into being. Envoys of the Uticans also brought gifts, as to kinsmen, and urged them to found the city in the place where they had obtained their seats. But the love of the Africans also held the newcomers there. So, with everyone agreeing, Carthage was founded, with an annual tax fixed on the ground of the city. In the first foundations an ox's head was found. This was an omen of a land that would be fruitful but laborious, and of a city that would always be enslaved, on account of which the city was later moved to another site. There too a horse's head was found, signifying a warlike and powerful people to come, and it marked out an auspicious seat for the city. Then, as the peoples flocked to the reputation of the new city, soon both a population and a great state had come into being.

units.la: ö Cum successu rerum florentes Carthaginis opes essent, rex Maxitanorum Hiarbas decem Poenorum principibus ad se arcessitis, Elissæ nuptias sub belli denuntiatione petit : quod legati regina referre metuentes, Punico cum ea ingenio egerunt ; nuntiantes regem aliquem poscere, qui cultiores vitus eum, Afrosq; perdoceat : sed quem inueniri posse, qui ad Barbaros & ferarum more viuentes transfire a consanguineis velit ?
units.tr: When the wealth of Carthage was flourishing with success, King Hiarbas of the Maxitani summoned ten Punic chiefs to himself and demanded Elissa's marriage under threat of war. The envoys, fearing to report this to the queen, dealt with her in the Punic manner. They announced that the king was asking for someone who could instruct him and the Africans in more civilized ways of life. But who could be found, they asked, who would be willing to pass over from his kinsmen to barbarians who lived like wild beasts?

units.la: Tunc a regina castigati, si pro salute patria asperiorem vitam recusarent, cui etiam ipsa vita, si res exigat, debeatur : regis mandata aperuere, dicentes, quae praecipiat aliis, ipsi facienda esse, si velit vrbi consultum esse. Hoc dolo capta, diu Accerbe viri nomine cum multis lacrymis & lamentatione flebili inuocato, ad postremum ituram se quo suae vrbis fata vocarent, respondit. In hoc trium mesium sumpto spatio, pyra in ultima parte
units.tr: Then the queen rebuked them: if they refused a harder life for the safety of their country, to which even life itself is owed if the situation demands it. They then disclosed the king's orders, saying that what he commanded others, they themselves ought to do, if she wished the city to be provided for. Caught by this trick, after long invoking the name of her husband Acerbas with many tears and mournful lamentation, she finally answered that she would go wherever the fates of her city called her. Having taken three months for this, a pyre was built in the farthest part of the city, as though to appease her husband's shade. About to send offerings before the marriage, she slaughtered many victims, and taking up a sword she mounted the pyre. And so, looking back at the people, she said that she would go to her husband as they had instructed, and ended her life

units.la: vrbis exstructa, velut placatura viri manes, inferias, ante nuptias missura, multas hostias cadit, & sumpto gladio pyram conscendit; atque ita ad populum respicieus, ituram se ad virum, sicut praeceperant, dixit, vitamque gladio finiuit. Quandiu Carthago inuicta fuit, pro dea cultaest. Condita est vrbs haec 72. annis ante quam Roma; cuius virtus sicut bello clara fuit, ita domi status variis discordiarum: casibus agitatus est. Cum inter cetera mala, etiam peste laborarent, cruenta sacrorum religione, & scelere pro remedio vsi fuerunt. Quippe homines, vt victimas, immolabant; & impuberes (quae aetatis etiam hostium misericordiam pronocat) Jaris admonebant, pacem deorum sanguine eorum expiscentes, pro quorum vita dij rogari maxime solent.
units.tr: with the sword. While Carthage remained unconquered, she was worshipped as a goddess. The city was founded seventy-two years before Rome. Its valour was as famous in war as it was buffeted at home by the various chances of civil discord. Since, among its other troubles, they also suffered from plague, they used bloody religious rites and crime as a remedy. Men were sacrificed as victims, and children (an age which even the mercy of enemies spares) were offered to Saturn, seeking to appease the peace of the gods with their blood, though it is usually for the lives of children that the gods are entreated.

units.la: 7 Itaq; aduersus tato scelere numinibus, cum in Sicilia diu feliciter dimicassent, translato in Sardiniam bello, amissa maiore exercitus parte, graui praelio victi sunt. Propter quod ducem suum Maleum, cuius auspiciis & Siciliae parte domuerant, & aduersus Afros magnas res gesserat, cum parte exercitus, quae superfuerat, exulare iusserunt. Quam rem aegre ferentes milites, legatos Carthaginem mittunt, qui redditu primo, veniaque infelicis militiae petant; tum denuntient, quod precibus nequeant, armis se consecuturos. Cum & preces & mina legatorum spreta esset, interiectis diebus, conscensis nauibus, armati ad vrbem veniunt: ibi deos, homines que testari non se expugnatum, sed recuperatum patriam venire; ostensurosque ciuibus suis, non virtutem sibi priore bello, sed fortunam defuisse. Prohibitis commeatibus, obsessaque vrbe, in summam desperationem Carthaginienses adduxerunt. Interea Cartalo Malei exsulis dutis filius, cum praeter castra patris a Tyro, quo decimas Herculis ferre, ex praeda Sicilienfi; quam pater eius ceperat; perat, à Carthaginiensibus missus fuerat, reuerteretur, arcesitusq; à patre esset, prius publice se religionis ossicia exsecuturum quam priuate pietatis, respondit: Quam rem & si indigne ferret pater, non tamen vim afferre religioni ausus est: Interiectis deinde diebus, Cartalo petito commeatu à populo, cum reuersus ad patrem esset, ornatusq; purpura, & infulis sacerdotij, omnium se oculis ingereret, tunc in secretum abducto pater ait, Aususne es, nefandissimum caput, ista purpura ornatus, in conspectum tot miserorum ciuium venire? & maesta ac lugentia castra circumfluentibus quietæ felicitatis insignibus, velut exultabundus intrare? Nusquamne te alii iactare potuisti? Nullus locus aptior, quam sordes patris, & exilij infelicis arumnæ fuerunt? Quid, quod paulo ante vocatus non dico patrem, ducem certe ciuium tuorum superbe strenuisti? quid porro in purpura ista coronisq; aliud, quam victoriarum mearum titulos geris? Quoniam igitur tu in patre nihil nisi exsulis nomen agnoscis: ego quoq; imperatorem me magis, quam patre indicabo, statuamq; in te exemplum, ne quis posthac infelicibus miseris patris illudat. Atqui ita eum ornatu suo, in altissimam crucem in conspectu urbis suffigi iussit. Post paucos deinde dies Carthaginem capit: evocatoq; populo ad concionem, exilij iniuriam queritur: belli necessitatem excusat: contentum o victoria sua, punitis auctoribus miserorum civium, iniuriosi exilij omnibus se veniam dare dicit. Atq; ita decem senatoribus interfectis, urbem legibus suis reddidit. Nec multo post ipse affectati regni accusatus, duplicis & in filio & in patria parricidij panas dedit. Huic Mago imperator successit, cuius industria, & opes Carthaginiensium, & imperij fines, & vetustae gloria laudes creverunt.
units.tr: Therefore, having fought happily for a long time in Sicily against the gods offended by such a crime, when the war was transferred to Sardinia and the greater part of their army was lost, they were defeated in a heavy battle. For this reason they ordered their leader Malchus, under whose auspices they had subdued part of Sicily and had achieved great deeds against the Africans, to go into exile with that part of the army which had survived. The soldiers, taking this badly, sent envoys to Carthage, who first asked for their return and pardon for their unlucky campaign, and then threatened that what they could not obtain by prayers they would obtain by arms. When both the prayers and the threats of the envoys were spurned, after some days the soldiers boarded ships and came armed to the city. There they called gods and men to witness that they came not as conquerors but as recoverers of their country, and that they would show their fellow citizens that in the earlier war it had been fortune, not courage, that had failed them. With supplies cut off and the city besieged, they brought the Carthaginians to utter despair. Meanwhile Cartalo, son of the exiled Malchus, who had been sent by the Carthaginians to Tyre to carry the tithes of Hercules from the Sicilian booty his father had captured, was returning. When his father summoned him, he replied that he would first perform the public duties of religion, and only then those of private piety. Though his father took this badly, he did not dare to use force against religion. Some days later, Cartalo, having asked leave of the people, returned to his father and presented himself to the eyes of all, adorned with purple and the fillets of the priesthood. His father then led him aside in private and said: "Have you dared, most abominable head, to come before the sight of so many wretched citizens dressed in this purple? Have you dared to enter the mourning and lamenting camp, flaunting the insignia of happy fortune as if exulting? Could you not show off elsewhere? Was there no place more fitting than your father's squalor and the unhappy hardships of exile? And what of the fact that a little while ago, when summoned, you proudly acted as if you were not merely a father but at least the leader of your citizens? What else do you bear in that purple and those garlands, except the titles of my victories? Since you recognise in your father nothing but the name of an exile, I too will declare myself a commander rather than a father, and I will make you an example, so that no one henceforth mocks wretched exiles for their father." And so he ordered him to be fixed, in his finery, to a very high cross in full view of the city. A few days later he captured Carthage. Calling the people to an assembly, he complained of the injury of exile and excused the necessity of war. Content with his victory, with the authors of the citizens' misery punished, he said he granted pardon to all for the unjust exile. So, with ten senators killed, he restored the city to its own laws. Not long afterwards, accused of aspiring to kingship, he paid the penalty for a double parricide, against both his son and his country. Mago succeeded him as commander, and under his diligence the wealth of the Carthaginians, the bounds of their empire and the praise of their ancient glory increased.

units.la: POMPEII TROGI EPI- TOMA HISTORIARVM. LIBER XIX.
units.tr: THE HISTORIES OF POMPEIUS TROGUS, EPITOMISED. BOOK XIX.
SUMMARY:

units.la: 1 Magoni Carthaginen- exercitus Carthaginiénsis in sium imperatori, succedunt Siciliæ: Hasdrubal & Hamilcar. In 3 Imilco, Dux huius exSardinia Hasdrubal perit. ercitus, Carthaginem reInde Siculum bellū & Per- ueitus, spe omni abiecta, sarum legatio. mortem sibi infert.
units.tr: 1 Mago, general of the Carthaginians, is succeeded by Hasdrubal and Hamilcar. Hasdrubal perishes in Sardinia. Imilco, leader of the army in Sicily, returns to Carthage, abandons all hope, and takes his own life. The Sicilian war and the Persian embassy.

units.la: 2 Horum filii, & clades MAGO Carthaginiensium imperator, cum primus omnium ordinata disciplina militari, imperium Poenorum condidisset, viresq; ciuitatis non minus bellandi arte quam virtute firmasset, diem fungitur, relictis duobus filiis Hasdrubale & Hamilcare: qui per vestigia paterna virtutis decurrentes, sicuti generi, ita & magnitudini patris successerunt. His ducibus Sardiniae bellum illatum: aduersus Afros quoq; vectigal pro solo vrbis multorum annorum repetentes, dimicatum: sed Afrorum sicuti causa iustior, ita & fortuna superior fuit; bellumq; cum his solutione pecuniae non armis finitum. In Sardinia quoq; Hasdrubal graviter vulneratus imperio Hamilcari fratri tradito interiit: cuius mortem, cum luctus ciuitatis, tum & dictatura vndecim, & triumphi quatuor insignem fecere: hostibus quoq; creuere animi, veluti cum duce vires Poenorum cecidissent. Itaq; Siciliae populis propter assiduas Carthaginiensium iniurias, ad Leonidam fratrem regis Spartanorum concurrentibus, graue bellum natum: in quo & diu, & varia victoria prœliatu fuit. Dum hæc aguntur, legati à Dario Persarum rege Carthaginem venerunt, afferentes edictum, quo Pœni humanas hostias immolare, & canina vesci prohibebantur; mortuorumq; corpora cremare potius, quam terra obruere à rege iubebantur: petentes simul auxilia adversus Græciam, cui illaturus bellum Darius erat. Sed Carthaginienses auxilia negantes, propter assidua finitimorum bella, ceteris, ne per omnia contumaces viderentur, cupide paruere.
units.tr: 2 Mago, general of the Carthaginians, was the first to establish a disciplined military order and to build up the power of the Carthaginians, and he strengthened the strength of the state no less by the art of war than by courage. He died, leaving two sons, Hasdrubal and Hamilcar. Following their father's footsteps in courage, they succeeded to his position as well as to his greatness. Under these leaders war was waged on Sardinia, and they also fought against the Africans, who were demanding tribute for the land of the city over many years. But the Africans' cause was as much more just as their fortune was greater, and the war with them was ended by payment of money, not by arms. In Sardinia too, Hasdrubal was severely wounded and died after handing command to his brother Hamilcar. His death was made remarkable by the grief of the state, by his eleven dictatorships and four triumphs, and it also made the enemy bolder, as if the strength of the Carthaginians had fallen with their leader. So it was that the peoples of Sicily, angered by the constant wrongs done by the Carthaginians, flocked to Leonidas, brother of the king of the Spartans, and a grave war arose, in which fighting lasted a long time with varying success. While these things were going on, envoys came to Carthage from Darius, king of the Persians, bringing an edict by which the Carthaginians were forbidden to sacrifice human victims and to eat dog's flesh, and were ordered by the king to burn their dead rather than bury them in the earth. At the same time they asked for help against Greece, which Darius was about to attack. But the Carthaginians refused the aid, because of the constant wars with their neighbours, yet to avoid seeming wholly defiant they eagerly complied with the rest.

units.la: 2 Interea Hamilcar bello Siciliensi interficitur, relictis tribus filiis, Imilcone, Hannone, Gisco ne. Hasdrubali quoq; par numerus filiorum fuit, Annibal & Hasdrubal, & Sapphio. Per hos res Carthaginiensium ea tempestate gerebantur. Itaq; & Mauris bellum illatum, & aduersus Numidas pugnatum, & Afri compulsi stipendium urbis condita Carthaginiensibus remittere. Deinde tum familia tanta imperatorum grauis libera ciuitati esset, omniaq; ipsi agerent simul & iudicarent, centum ex numero senatorum iudices deliguntur, qui reuersis a bello ducibus, rationem rerum gestarum exigerent, ut hoc metu ita in bello imperia cogitarent, vt domi iudicia legesq; repeterent. In Sicilia in locum Hamilcaris, imperator Imilco succedit: qui cum nauali terrestriq; bello secunda prælia fecisset, multasq; ciuitates cepisset, repente pestilentis syderis vi exercitum amisit. Qua res cum nuntiata Carthagini esset, mœsta ciuitas fuit; o- mnes ut vlulatibus, non secus ac si vrbs ipsa capta esset, personabant; clausa priuata domus, clausa deorum templa, intermissa omnia sacra, omnia priuata officia damnata; cunctiq; deinde ad portam congregantur, egredientesq; paucos è nauibus, qui cladi superfuerant, de suis percontantur. Vt vero dubia antea spe, & suspenso metu, incerta orbitatis exspectatione, casus suorum miseris eluxit, tunc toto littore plangentium gemitus, tunc infelicium matrum vlulatus, & flebiles querelae audiebantur.
units.tr: 2 Meanwhile Hamilcar was killed in the Sicilian war, leaving three sons: Imilco, Hanno and Gisco. Hasdrubal also had as many sons: Hannibal, Hasdrubal and Sapphio. Through these men the affairs of the Carthaginians were conducted at that time. So the Mauri were attacked, the Numidians were fought against, and the Africans, when compelled, remitted to the Carthaginians the tribute imposed on the city. Then, since so great a family of generals was a burden on the free state, and since they themselves both conducted affairs and judged them, one hundred judges were chosen from the number of the senators, who, when the generals returned from war, were to call them to account for their conduct, so that, under this fear, they would plan their commands in war in such a way that they would be bound to restore judicial process and laws at home. In Sicily, the general Imilco succeeded in place of Hamilcar. Although he had won successes in naval and land battles and had captured many cities, he suddenly lost his army to the violent force of a pestilential star. When this was reported at Carthage, the city was plunged into mourning. Everyone wailed as if the city itself had been taken. Private houses were shut, temples of the gods were closed, all sacred rites were suspended, and all private business was forbidden. Then everyone gathered at the gate and questioned the few men who had survived the disaster and had come off the ships about their own people. But when the hope that had been uncertain until then, and the fear that had hung in suspense, and the uncertain expectation of being bereft at last, shone out as the miserable fate of their kinsmen, then the groans of mourners were heard along the whole shore, and the howling of unhappy mothers and tearful complaints.

units.la: 3 Inter hæc procedit inops è naui sua imperator, fordida seruiliq; tunica discinctusque ad cuius conspectu plangentium omnia iunguntur. Ipse quoq; manus ad cœlum tendens, nunc fortem suam, nunc publicam fortunam deflet, nunc deos accusat, qui tanta belli decora, & tot ornamenta victoriarum, quæ ipsi dederant, abstulerint; qui captis tot urbibus, totiesq; hostib. terrestri nauali; prælio victis, exercitum victorem nō bello, sed peste deleuerint: deferre se tamen ciuibus suis non modica solatia, quod malis eorū hostes gaudere, nō gloriari possent.
units.tr: 3 In the midst of this the general came forth destitute from his ship, dressed in filthy slave's clothing and with his belt undone. At the sight of him, all who were mourning joined in lamentation. He too, stretching his hands to heaven, now bewailed his own fortune and now the fortune of the state; now he accused the gods, who had taken away such glorious honours of war and so many trophies of victory, which they themselves had given him; who, after so many cities had been taken and so many enemies defeated in land and sea battles, had destroyed an army that had conquered, not by war but by plague. Yet, he said, he could bring his fellow citizens no small consolation: that their enemies could not rejoice at their misfortunes, nor boast of them.

units.la: Quippe cum neq; eos qui mortui sunt, à se occisos; neq; eos qui reuersi sunt, à se fugatos posse dicere. Pradam quam relictis à se castris abstulerint, nō esse talem, quā velut spolium victi hostis ostētent: sed quam possessione vacua, fortuitis dominorū mortibus, sicuti caduca occuparint. Quod ad hostes pertinet, victores se recessisse; quod ad pestem, victos: nihil tamē se grauius ferre, quā quod inter fortissimos viros mori nō potuerit, cruatusq; sit non ad vitæ iucunditatem, sed ad ludibriū calamitatis: Quamquā vbi miseras copiarū reliquias Carthaginē reduxerit, se quoq; sequuturū commilitones suos; ostēsurumq; patriæ, non ideo se in eam diē vixisse, quoniā velit viuere; sed ne hos, quibus nefanda lues peperceratinter hostiū exercitus relictos, morte sua proderet.
units.tr: For neither could they say that the dead had been killed by him, nor that the survivors had been put to flight by him. The booty they had carried off from the camps they had left behind was not such that they could display it as the spoils of a defeated enemy; rather, they had seized it like windfalls from an empty possession, through the chance deaths of its owners. As for the enemy, they had withdrawn as victors; as for the plague, they had been defeated. Yet, he said, he bore nothing more grievously than that he had not been able to die among the bravest men, and that he had been spared not for the pleasure of life but as a plaything of calamity. Still, when he had brought the wretched remnants of the forces back to Carthage, he would follow his fellow soldiers too, and he would show his country that he had not lived up to that day because he wished to live, but so that he would not betray by his death those whom the unspeakable pestilence had spared, left behind among the enemy's armies.

units.la: Tali vociferatione per vrbē ingressus, vt ad limina domus sua venit, prosecutam multitudinē velut postremo alloquio dimisit; obseratiq; foribus, ac nemine ad se, nec filiis quidem admissis, mortem sibi conscivit.
units.tr: Having entered the city with such an outcry, when he came to the threshold of his house, he dismissed the crowd that had followed him, as if with a final address. Then, having shut the doors and admitted no one to himself, not even his sons, he took his own life.
THE EPITOME OF THE HISTORIES OF POMPEIUS TROGUS.
BOOK XX. SUMMARY.

units.la: 1 Dionysius Siciliæ tyrannus Graciæ magnæ incolas bello aggreditur.
units.tr: 1 Dionysius, tyrant of Sicily, attacks the inhabitants of Magna Graecia in war.
2 The origin and fortunes of the Metapontines.
3 The wars of the Crotoniates and the Locrians.

units.la: 4 Pythagoras Philosophus Crotonienses ad frugalitatis cultum revocat.
units.tr: 4 Pythagoras the philosopher recalls the Crotoniates to the practice of frugality.

units.la: 5 Dionysius victis Locrensibus Crotonienses aggreditur, quos relinquit, ab Hannone retractus, & tandem suorum insidiis opprimitur.
units.tr: 5 Dionysius, after defeating the Locrians, attacks the Crotoniates. He leaves them when recalled by Hanno, and is at last overwhelmed by the plots of his own men.

units.la: IONYSIVS è Sicilia Carthaginiensibus pulsis, occupatoq; totius insulæ imperio, graue otium regno suo periculosamq; desidiam tanti exercitus ratus, copias in Italiam traiecit: simul vi militum vires continuo labore acuerentur, & regni fines proferrentur. Prima illi militia aduersus Græcos, qui proxima Italici maris littora tenebat, fuit: quibus deuictis, finitimos quosq; aggreditur, omnesque Græci nominis Italiam possidentes, hostes sibi destinat: quæ gentes non partem, sed vniuersam ferme Italiæ ea tempestate occupauerant. Deniq; multæ vrbes adhuc post tantam vetustatem vestigia Græci moris ostentant. Namq; Thuscorum populi, qui oræ inferi maris possident, à Lydia venerunt: & Venetos, quos incolas superi maris videmus, capta & expugnata Troia, Antenore duce, misit: Adria quoq; Illyrico mari proxima, quæ & Adriatico mari nomen dedit, Græca vrbs est: Arpos Diomedes excisio Ilio, naufragio in ea loca delatus, condidit. Sed &
units.tr: Dionysius, after the Carthaginians had been driven from Sicily and dominion over the whole island secured, judged that a heavy idleness and a dangerous inactivity was no good for so great an army, and so he transported his forces into Italy. At the same time, the strength of his soldiers was sharpened by constant labour, and the boundaries of his kingdom were extended. His first campaign was against the Greeks who held the coast nearest the Italian sea. Having defeated them, he attacked the neighbouring peoples and marked out as enemies all who held Italy under the Greek name. These races had occupied at that time not part but almost the whole of Italy. Even now, after so great an antiquity, many cities still show traces of Greek custom. For the Tuscan peoples who hold the lower coast of the sea came from Lydia. The Veneti, whom we see as the inhabitants of the upper sea, were sent by Antenor as leader after Troy was captured and stormed. Adria too, near the Illyrian sea and which gave its name to the Adriatic, is a Greek city; Diomedes, after the destruction of Ilium, was shipwrecked and carried to those places, and founded Arpi. But also

units.la: Pisæ in Liguribus Græcos auctores habent: & in Thuscis, Tarquinij à Thessalis & Spinábris: Perusini quoq; originem ab Achais ducunt. Quid Ceren vrbem dicam? Quid Latinos populos, qui ab Aenea conditi videntur? Iam Falisci, Nolani, Abelani, nonne Chalcidensium coloni sunt? Quid tractus omnis Campaniæ? Quid Brutij, Sabiniq;? Quid Samnites? Quid Tarentini? quos Lacedæmone profectos, Spuriosq; vocatos accepimus? Thurinorum vrbem condidisse Philoctetem ferunt, ibiq; adhuc monumentum eius visitur; & Herculis sagitta in Apollinis templo, quæ fatum Troiæ fuere.
units.tr: Pisa among the Ligurians is held to have Greek founders, and among the Tuscans Tarquinii is said to have been founded by Thessalians and Spinabrians. The Perusians too trace their origin to the Achaeans. Why should I speak of the city of Caere? Why of the Latin peoples, who seem to have been founded by Aeneas? Are not the Faliscans, the Nolans and the Abellans already colonists of the Chalcidians? What of the whole district of Campania? What of the Bruttians and the Sabines? What of the Samnites? What of the Tarentines, whom we have learned set out from Lacedaemon and were called Spurii? They say that Philoctetes founded the city of the Thurians, and his monument is still visited there; and Hercules' arrow, which was the fate of Troy, is kept in the temple of Apollo.

units.la: 2 Metapontini quoq; in tēplo Minervæ ferramenta, quibus Epeus, à quo conditi sunt, equum Troianum fabricauit, ostentant: propter quod omnis illa pars Italiæ, maior Græcia appellata est. Sed principio originum Metapontini cum Sybaritanis & Crotoniensibus pelleve ceteros Græcos Italia statuerunt. Cum primum vrbem Sirim cepissent, in expugnatione eius quinquaginta iuuenes amplexos Mincrua simulacrum, sacerdotem, dea velatum ornamentis, inter ipsa altaria truci-dauerunt. Ob hæc cum pestę & seditionibus vexarentur, priores Crotonienses Delphicum oraculum adierunt. Responsum his est, finem mali fore, si violatum Minervæ numen, & interfectorum manes placassent.
units.tr: 2 The Metapontines also show, in the temple of Minerva, the iron tools with which Epeus, their founder, built the Trojan horse. On account of this, that whole part of Italy was called Greater Greece. At the beginning of their history the Metapontines, together with the Sybarites and Crotoniates, resolved to drive the other Greeks out of Italy. When they first took the city of Siris, in its storming they butchered, between the very altars, fifty young men who had clasped the image of Minerva, and a priest veiled with the goddess's ornaments. Because of these deeds, when they were troubled by plague and seditions, the elder Crotoniates went to the Delphic oracle. The response was that the evil would end if they appeased the violated majesty of Minerva and the shades of the slain.

units.la: Itaq; cum statuas iuuenibus iusta magnitudinis, & in primis Minervæ fabricare cœpissent, Metapontini cognito oraculo deorum, occupandam manium & deæ pacem rati, iuuenibus modica & lapidea simulacra ponunt, & deam panificiumplacant. Atque ita pestis vtrubiq; sedata est, cum alteri magnificentia, alteri velocitate certassent. Recuperata sanitate, non diu Crotonienses quieuere. Itaq; indignantes in oppugnatione Siris auxilium contra se à Locrensibus latum, bellum bis intulerunt. Quo metu territi Locrenses, ad Spartanos decurrunt; auxilium supplices deprecantur. Illi longinqua militia grauati, auxilium à Castore & Polluce petere eos iubent. Neq; legati responsum sociis urbis præuerunt: profectiq; in proximum templum, sacrificio sacrificio; auxilium deorum implorant, litatis hostiis, obtentoq;, vt rebantur, quod petebant, haud secus læti, quam si deos ipsos secum aduecturi essent; puluinaria in naui componunt, faustisq; profecti ominibus, solatia suis pro auxiliis deportant.
units.tr: Therefore, when they had begun to make statues of the young men of proper size, and especially of Minerva, the Metapontines, having learned the oracle of the gods, reckoned that the peace of the shades and of the goddess must be secured. They set up small statues of stone for the young men and appeased the goddess with an offering of bread. And so the plague was calmed in both places, while the one party vied in magnificence and the other in speed. Once health was restored, the Crotoniates did not stay quiet for long. Indignant that the Locrians had brought aid against them at the siege of Siris, they made war on them twice. Terrified by this, the Locrians ran to the Spartans and begged for help as suppliants. The Spartans, burdened by a distant campaign, told them to seek aid from Castor and Pollux. Nor did the envoys wait to report the answer to their allies. They went to the nearest temple, sacrificed, and implored the help of the gods; the victims were propitiously offered, and they obtained, as they believed, what they sought. They were no less glad than if the gods themselves were going to come with them. They set up couches on the ship, and setting out under auspicious omens, they brought back comfort for their people instead of help.

units.la: 3 Hiscognitis, Crotonienses & ipsi legatos ad oraculum Delphos mittunt, victoriae facultatem, bellique prosperos euentus deprecantes: responsum, prius votis hostes, quam armis vincendos. Cum vouissent Apollini decimas prada, Locrenses & voto hostium, & responso dei cognito, nonas vouerunt; tacitamque eam rem habuere, ne votis vincerentur. Itaq; cum in aciem processissent, & Crotonienfium centum viginti millia armatorum constitissent, Locrenses paucitatem suam circumspicientes (nam sola quindecim millia militum habebant) omissa spe victoriae, in desperatam mortem conspirant; tantusq; ardor ex desperatione singulos cepit, vt victores se putarent, si non inulti moreretur. Sed dum mori honeste quaerunt, felicitèr vicerunt: Nec alia causa victoriae fuit, quam quod desperauerunt. Pugnantibus Locris, aquila ab acie nunquam recessit, eosq; tamdiu circumuolauit, quoad vincerent. In cornibus quoq; duo iuuenes diuerso à ceteris armorum habitu, eximia magnitudine, & albis equis, & coccineis paludamentis, pugnare visi sunt, nec vltra apparuerunt, quam pugnatum est. Hanc admirationem auxit incredibilis fama velocitas. Nam eadem die, qua in Italia pugnatum est, & Corintho, & Athenis, & Lacedæmone nuntiata est victoria.
units.tr: 3 When this was known, the Crotoniates too sent envoys to the oracle at Delphi, asking for the power of victory and a prosperous outcome of the war. The response was that enemies must be conquered by vows before they are conquered by arms. They vowed to Apollo a tenth of the booty. The Locrians, having learned of the enemy's vow and the god's response, vowed a ninth, and kept the matter quiet, lest they be overcome by vows. So when they had advanced into battle, and the Crotoniates had drawn up 120,000 armed men, the Locrians, looking round at their own small numbers (for they had only 15,000 soldiers), gave up hope of victory and conspired to die desperately. Such ardour from despair seized each man that they thought themselves victors if they did not die unavenged. But while they sought to die honourably, they fortunately conquered; nor was there any other cause of victory than that they had despaired. While the Locrians fought, an eagle never left the battle line, and flew around them for as long as they were winning. On the wings too, two young men of extraordinary size, with armour different from the others, on white horses and in scarlet cloaks, were seen fighting, and they appeared no longer than the fighting lasted. This wonder was increased by the incredible speed of the news. For on the same day that the battle was fought in Italy, the victory was announced at Corinth, at Athens and at Lacedaemon.

units.la: 4 Post hac Crotoniẽsibus nulla virtutis exercitatio, nulla armorum cura fuit. Oderant enim quæ infeliciter sumpserant; mutassentq; vitam luxuria, ni Pythagoras philosophus fuisset. Hic Sami Demarato locuplete negotiatore natus, magnisq; sapientiæ incrementis ornatus, AEgyptum primo, mox Babylonian ad perdiscendos siderum motus, originemq; mundi speƈtandâ profectus, summam scientiam consequutus erat. Inde regressus, Cretam & Lacedæmona ad cognoscendas Minoïs & Lycurgi inclitas ea tempestate leges, contenderat. Quibus omnibus instructus, Crotonam venit, populumq; in luxuriam lapsum, auƈtoritate sua ad vsum frugalitatis reƈocauit. Laudabat quotidie virtutem, &
units.tr: 4 After this, the Crotoniates had no exercise of virtue and no care for arms. For they hated the things they had taken up unhappily, and they would have changed their life into luxury, had not Pythagoras the philosopher been there. Born at Samos, the son of Demaratus, a wealthy merchant, and adorned with great increases of wisdom, he first set out for Egypt and then for Babylon, to learn thoroughly the motions of the stars and the origin of the world, and gained the highest knowledge. Returning from there, he hastened to Crete and Lacedaemon to study the laws of Minos and Lycurgus, famous at that time. Equipped with all of these, he came to Croton and, by his authority, recalled the people, who had slipped into luxury, to the practice of frugality. He praised virtue every day, and

units.la: vitia luxuriæ, cæsusq; ciuitatium ea peste perditarum enumerabat; tantumq; studium ad frugalitatem multitudinis pronocauit, vt aliquos ex his luxuriatos incredibile videretur. Matronarum quoq; seperatam à viris doctrinam, & puerorum à parentibus frequenter habuit. Docebat nunc has pudicitiam, & obsequia in viros; nunc illos modestiam, & litterarum studium. Inter hac velut Genitricem virtutum frugalitatem omnibus ingerebat, confecutusq; disputationum assiduitate erat, vt matronæ auratas vestes, ceteraq; dignitatis suæ ornamenta, velut instrumenta luxuriæ deponerent, eaq; omnia delata in Iunonis ædem ipsi deæ conserrent, prædicentes, Vera ornamenta matronarum pudicitiam, non vestes esse. In iuuentute quoq; quanti ũ profligatum sit, victi feminarũ contumaces animi manifestant. Sed 300. ex iuuenibus cum sodalitij iure sacramento quodam nexi, separatam à ceteris ciuibus vitam exercerent, quasi cœtum clandestina coniurationis haberent, ciuitatē in se conuerterunt, quae eos, cum in vnam domū conuenissent, cremare voluit. In quo tumultu 60. ferme periere, ceteri in exilium profecti. Pythagoras autem cum annos 20. Crotonae egisset, Metapontum migrauit, ibiq; decessit: cuius tanta admiratio fuit, vt ex domo eius templum facerent; eumq; pro deo colerent.
units.tr: denounced the vices of luxury. He counted up the ruin of cities destroyed by that plague, and he stirred up such zeal for frugality among the multitude that some who had been luxurious seemed incredible. He also often gave lessons to the matrons apart from their husbands, and to the boys apart from their parents. Now he taught the women chastity and obedience to their husbands; now he taught the men modesty and the study of letters. Among these lessons he impressed upon everyone frugality, the mother of the virtues, and by constant disputation he brought it about that the matrons laid aside their gilded clothes and their other ornaments of dignity, as instruments of luxury. All these things were brought together and dedicated in the temple of Juno to the goddess herself, the women declaring: "The true ornaments of matrons are chastity, not clothes." How far discipline had collapsed among the young men too, the stubborn spirits of the defeated show plainly. But 300 of the young men, bound by a certain oath under the law of a fellowship, lived a life separate from the other citizens, as if they had a secret conspiracy. They turned the city against themselves, and it wished to burn them when they had gathered in one house. In this uproar about sixty perished, and the rest went into exile. Pythagoras, however, after he had lived twenty years at Croton, migrated to Metapontum and died there. Such was the admiration for him that they made a temple of his house and worshipped him as a god.

units.la: Igitur Dionysius tyrannus, quem supra à Sicilia exercitu in Italiam traiecisse, bellumq; Graecis intulisse memoramus, expugnatis Locris, Crotoniē ses vix vires lōgo otio ex prioris belli clade resumētes, aggreditur: qui fortius cū paucis tanto exercitu eius, quā antea cū tot millibus Locrēsiū paucitati refliterunt. Tantū virtutis paupertas aduersus insolentes diuitias habet, tantoq; insperata interdum sperata victoria certior est. Sed Dionysium gerētem bellum, legati Gallorum, qui ante menses Romā incenderāt, societatem, amicitiāq;, petētes adeunt: gentē suam inter hostes eius positā esse, magnoq; vsui ei futurā vel in acie bellanti, vel de tergo intentis in praelii hostibus affirmāt. Grata legatio Dionysio fuit, Ita pacta societate, & auxiliis Gallorū auctus, bellū velut ex integro reflaurat. Iis autē Gallis causa in Italiā veniendi, sedesq; nouas quaerēdi intestina discordia, & assidua domi dissensiones fuere: quarū tædio, cū in Italia venissent, sedibus Thufcos expulerunt, & Mediolanum, Comum, Brixiā, Veronam, Vergamū, Tridentum, Vicentiam condiderunt. Thufci quoq;, duce Rhetō, auitis sedibus amissis, Alpes occupauere: & ex nomine ducis gentes Rhetorū condiderunt. Sed Dionyfium in Siciliam aduetus Carthaginiensiū revocavit: qui reparato exercitu, bellū quod lue deseruerāt, auctis viribus repetebant. Dux belli Hanno Carthaginiensis erat: cuius inimicus Suniatus potentissimus ea tempe-state
units.tr: Therefore Dionysius the tyrant, whom we have recorded above as having transported his army from Sicily into Italy and made war on the Greeks, having taken the Locrians, attacks the Crotoniates, who had scarcely recovered their strength after the defeat of the earlier war through long idleness. They resisted more bravely, with few men against his so great army, than before they had against so many thousands of Locrians. So much does poverty of virtue weigh against insolent riches, and so at times a victory unhoped for is surer than one hoped for. But envoys of the Gauls, who had burned Rome some months earlier, approach Dionysius while he is waging war, seeking alliance and friendship. They affirm that their people, placed among his enemies, would be of great use to him, whether fighting in the battle line or attacking the enemy from behind. The embassy was welcome to Dionysius. Having made the alliance and been strengthened by Gallic aid, he renews the war as if from the beginning. The reason these Gauls came to Italy and sought new seats was internal discord and constant dissensions at home. Weary of these, when they had come to Italy they drove the Tuscans from their seats and founded Milan, Como, Brescia, Verona, Bergamo, Trento and Vicenza. The Tuscans too, under their leader Rhaetus, having lost their ancestral seats, occupied the Alps, and from their leader's name founded the Rhaetian peoples. But the arrival of Dionysius in Sicily recalled the Carthaginians, who, with their army restored, sought again with increased strength the war they had abandoned through pestilence. The leader of the war was Hanno the Carthaginian, and his enemy Suniatus, the most powerful of the Carthaginians at that time

units.la: state Pœnorum, cum odio eius, Græcis litteris Dionysio aduentum exercitus, & segnitiem ducis familiariter prænunciasset, comprehensis epistolis proditionis damnatur: facto senatusconsulto, nequis postea Carthaginiensis, aut litteris Græcis, aut sermoni studeret, ne aut loqui cum hoste, aut scribere sine interprete posset. Nec multo post Dionysius, quem paulo ante non Sicilia, [non Italia] capiebat, assiduis belli certaminibus victus, fractusque, insidiis ad postremum suorum interficitur.
units.tr: Suniatus, the most powerful Carthaginian of that time, was condemned. Out of hatred for him, the Carthaginians' Greek letters had informed Dionysius of the army's arrival and of the commander's sluggishness, and when the letters of treachery were intercepted, Suniatus was condemned. A decree of the senate was passed that no Carthaginian should thereafter study Greek letters or the language, lest he be able either to speak with the enemy or to write without an interpreter. Not long after, Dionysius, whom shortly before neither Sicily nor [non Italia] could contain, was worn down and broken by constant battles, and at last was killed by an ambush of his own men.

units.la: POMPEII TROGI EPI- TOMA HISTORIARVM LIBER XXI.
units.tr: POMPEII TROGI EPITOMA HISTORIARUM LIBER XXI.
SUMMARY.

units.la: 1 Dionysii iunioris arcem Carthagini occupare tentes tyrannicè describuntur. | tantis tragœdia. 20
units.tr: 1 The tyrannical attempts of the younger Dionysius to seize the citadel of Carthage are described. | Such a tragedy. 20

units.la: 2 Eiusdem luxuria, crudelitas, doli, exilium, tyrannis in Locrenses. | 5 Dionysius iunior Sicilia eiectus Corinthi moratur. 25
units.tr: 2 The luxury, cruelty, deceits, exile, and tyranny of Dionysius against the Locrians. | 5 The younger Dionysius, expelled from Sicily, lingers at Corinth. 25

units.la: 3 Callido commeto Locrenses spoliat & obtruncat, ac Syracusas per proditionem recipit. | 6 Hamilcarem, cognominé Rhodanum, Alexandri consilia speculatum, ingrati Carthaginienses interficiunt.
units.tr: 3 By a clever stratagem he plunders and slaughters the Locrians, and recovers Syracuse by treachery. | 6 Hamilcar, surnamed Rhodanus, who spied on the plans of Alexander, is killed by the ungrateful Carthaginians.
4 The tyranny of Hanno |

units.la: XTINCTO in Sicilia Dionysio tyranno; in locum eius milites maximum natu ex filiis eius, nomine Dionysium, suffecere; & naturam eius secuti, & quod firmius futurum esse regnum, si penes vnum remansisset, quam si portionibus inter plures filios diuideretur, arbitrabantur. Sed Dionysius inter initia regni, auunculos fratrum suorum, velut aemulos imperij sui, hortatoresque puerorum ad diuisionem regni, tollere gestiebat. Quare paulisper dissimulatum animum prius ad fauorem popularium conciliandum intendit; excusatius facturus quod statuerat, si probatus ante omnibus foret. Igitur nexorum tria millia e carcere dimisit; tributa populo per trienium remisit; & quibuscumque delinimentis poterat, animos omnium solicitat. Tunc ad destinatum facinus conuersus, non cognatos tantum fratrum, sed etiam ipsos fratres interfecit: vt quibus consortium regni debebat, ne spiritus quidem consortium relinqueret, tyrannidem in suos prius quam in exteros aspicatus.
units.tr: When the tyrant Dionysius died in Sicily, the soldiers set in his place the eldest of his sons, also named Dionysius, and followed his character, believing that the kingdom would be more secure if it remained in the hands of one man than if it were divided into shares among several sons. But Dionysius, in the early days of his reign, eagerly sought to remove his uncles, whom he regarded as rivals to his power and as encouragers of the boys to divide the kingdom. Therefore he first concealed his purpose for a time, intending to win the favour of the common people; he would be more excused for what he had decided if he were first approved by everyone. Accordingly he released three thousand prisoners from jail, remitted taxes to the people for three years, and by whatever flatteries he could, he courted the goodwill of all. Then, turning to the crime he had planned, he killed not only his brothers' kinsmen but the brothers themselves, so that those who ought to have shared the kingdom with him were not even left a share of life, since he looked upon tyranny over his own family before tyranny over foreigners.

units.la: Sublatis deinde aemulis, in segnitiam lapsus, saginam corporis ex nimia luxuria, oculorumque valitudinem contraxit; adeo vt non solem, non puluerem, non deniq; splendorem ferre lucis ipsius posset. Propter quadam contemni se putat, sauitia grassatur; nec vt pater carcerem nexis, sed cadibus ciuitatem replet: ob quam non contemptior omnibus, quam inuisior fuit. Itaque cum bellum aduersus eum Syracusani decreuissent, diu dubitauit, imperium deponeret, an bello resisteret:
units.tr: Then, having removed his rivals, he sank into sloth, and from excessive luxury he gained a bloated body and a weakness of the eyes, so that he could not bear the sun, nor the dust, nor even the brightness of the light itself. Because he thought that he was despised by certain people, he raged with cruelty; and not like his father with prisons and chains, but he filled the city with rods. On account of this he became not less contemptible to all than he was hateful. And so, when the Syracusans had decided on war against him, he long hesitated whether to lay down his power or to resist with arms.

units.la: sed a militibus pradam & vrbis direptionem sperantibus, descendere in prœlium cogitur. Victus, cum iterato non felicius fortunam tentasset, legatos ad Syracusanos mittit; spondens se depositurum tyrannidem, si mitterent ad eum quibus cum sibi de pace conueniret.
units.tr: But the soldiers, hoping for plunder and the sacking of the city, forced him to go down into battle. Defeated, and having tried his fortune again without better success, he sent envoys to the Syracusans, promising that he would give up the tyranny if they sent to him men with whom he could come to terms about peace.

units.la: In quam rem missos primores, in carcere retinet; atque ita incautis omnibus, nec quicquam hostile metuentibus, exercitum ad delendam ciuitatem mittit. Fit igitur in ipsa vrbe anceps prœlium: in quo oppidanis multitudo... titudine superantibus, Dionysius pellitur: qui cum obsidionem arcis timeret, cum omni regio apparatu in Italiam profugit tacitus. Exul à Locrensibus sociis exceptus, velut iure regnaret, arce occupat; solitamq; sibi saevitiam exercet: Coniuges principum ad fluprum rapi iubebat; virgines ante nuptias abducebat, sfluprata-sq; sponsis reddebat, locupletissimos quosq; aut civitate pellebat, aut occidi imperabat, bonaq; eorum inuadebat.
units.tr: He kept the leading men whom they sent for this purpose in prison; and so, while everyone was unguarded and feared nothing hostile, he sent an army to destroy the city. Thus a doubtful battle took place within the city itself, in which the townsfolk, superior in numbers, drove Dionysius out. Fearing a siege of the citadel, he fled secretly to Italy with all his royal equipment. Received as an exile by the Locrians, his allies, he seized the citadel as if he ruled by right, and resumed his accustomed savagery. He ordered the wives of the leading men to be dragged off to debauchery; he carried off virgins before their weddings, and returned them deflowered to their betrothed; he drove the wealthiest men from the city or ordered them to be killed, and seized their goods.

units.la: 3 Dein cum rapina occasio deesset, vniuersam ciuitatem callido commento circumuenit. Cum Rheginorum tyranni Leophronis bello Locrenses premerentur, vouerant, si victores forent, vt die festo Veneris virgines suas proflituerent. Quo voto intermisso, cum aduersa bella cum Lucanis gerentur, in concionem eos Dionysius vocat; hortatur vt vxores filiasq;, suas in templum Veneris, quam possint ornatissimas mittant: ex quibus forte ducta centum, voto publico fungantur, religionisq; gratia, vno flent in lupanari mense, omnibus ante inuratis viris, ne quis vllam attaminet: Quae res ne virginibus, voto ciuitatem soluentibus fraudi esset, decretum facerent, nequa virgo nuberet, priusquam illa maritis traderentur. Probato consilio, quo & superstitioni & pudicitia virginum consulebatur, certatim omnes feminae impensius exornata, in templum Veneris conueniunt: quas omnes Dionysius immissis militib. spoliat, ornamentaque matronarum in praedam suam vertit.
units.tr: 3 Then, when there was no opportunity for plunder, he deceived the whole city by a clever stratagem. When the Locrians were hard pressed in war by Leophron, the tyrant of Rhegium, they had vowed that, if they were victorious, they would prostitute their virgins on a festival day of Venus. This vow was put off, and when a difficult war with the Lucanians was being waged, Dionysius called them to an assembly and urged them to send their wives and daughters to the temple of Venus, as richly adorned as they could. From these, a hundred were chosen by lot to fulfil the public vow, and for the sake of religious observance they were to remain for one month in a brothel, with all the men beforehand kept away so that none would touch any of them. And so that this would not be a disadvantage to the virgins, who were fulfilling the city's vow, he had a decree passed that no virgin should marry before those women had been given to their husbands. The plan was approved, since it provided for both the superstition and the chastity of the virgins; all the women, vying with one another, came together at the temple of Venus, dressed up more lavishly. Dionysius sent in soldiers who stripped them all, and turned the matrons' ornaments into his own booty.

units.la: Quarundam viros ditiores interficit, quasdam ad prodendas virorum pecunias torquet. Cum his artibus per annos sex regnasset, conspiratione Locrorum ciuitate pulsus, in Siciliam redit. Ibi Syracusas securis omnibus, post longam interca pedinem pacis per proditionem recepit. 4 Dum hac in Sicilia geruntur, interim in Africa princeps Carthaginiensium Hanno opes suas, quibus vires reipub. superabat, ad occupandā dominationem intendit, regnumq; inuadere, interfecto senatu, conatus est. Cui sceleri sollemne nuptiarum diem filia sua legit, ut religione votorum, nefanda comenta facilius tegerentur. Itaq; plebi epulas in publicis porticibus, senatui in domo sua parat, ut poculis veneno infectis, secretius senatum, & sine arbitris interficeret, orbamq; rempub. facilius inuaderet. Qua re magistratibus per ministros prodita, scelus declinatum, non vindicatum est, ne in viro tam potenti plus negotii faceret res cognita, quam cogitata. Contenti itaq; cohibuisse, decreto modum nuptiarum sumptibus statuunt; idq; obseruari non ab vno, sed ab uniuersis iubent, ne persona defiguata, non vitia correcta viderentur. Hoc consilio praeuentus, iterum seruitia cōcitat, statutaq; rursus cadium diem, cum denuo se producitur videret, timens iudicium, munitum quoddam castellum cum viginti millibus seruorum armatis occupat. Ibi dum Afros, regemq; Maurorum concitat, capitur, virgisq; caesus, effossis oculis, & manibus cruribusq; fractis, velut a singulis membris poena exigerentur, in conspectu populi occiditur; corpus verberibus lacerum in crucem figitur. Filij quoq;, cognatiq; omnes, etiam innoxij, supplicio traduntur, ne quisquam aut ad imitandum scelus, aut ad mortem vlciscendam, ex tam nefaria domo superesset.
units.tr: Some of their husbands who were wealthier he killed, and some women he tortured to reveal their husbands' money. After he had ruled for six years by these arts, he was driven from the city by a conspiracy of the Locrians and returned to Sicily. There, after a long interval of peace, he recovered Syracuse by treachery, when all were unsuspecting. 4 While these things were happening in Sicily, meanwhile in Africa Hanno, the leader of the Carthaginians, set his mind on seizing the sovereignty by means of his wealth, by which he surpassed the strength of the commonwealth, and attempted to seize the kingdom by killing the senate. For this crime he chose the solemn day of his daughter's wedding, so that the sacredness of the vows might more easily cover his unspeakable schemes. Therefore he prepared feasts for the common people in the public colonnades, and for the senate in his own house, so that he might kill the senate more secretly, with poisoned cups and without witnesses, and seize the leaderless commonwealth more easily. The plot was betrayed to the magistrates through their agents, and the crime was prevented rather than avenged; lest the matter, once known, should cause more trouble with a man so powerful than it had caused when merely planned. Therefore, content with having restrained him, they fixed by decree a limit to the expense of weddings, and ordered that this be observed not by one man but by everyone, so that the man would not seem singled out while the faults themselves went uncorrected. Forestalled by this measure, Hanno again stirred up the slaves; and when he saw that the day he had set for slaughter had been postponed again, fearing judgment he seized a certain fortified stronghold with twenty thousand armed slaves. There, while he was stirring up the Africans and the king of the Moors, he was captured, scourged with rods, his eyes gouged out, his hands and legs broken, and was put to death in the sight of the people, as if punishment were being exacted for each of his limbs; his body, torn by the lashes, was fixed to a cross. His sons, kinsmen, and all, even the innocent, were handed over to execution, so that no one from so wicked a household should survive either to imitate the crime or to avenge the death.

units.la: 5 Interea Dionysius Syracusis receptus, cum gravior crudeliorq; in dies ciuitati esset, iterata conspiratione obsidetur. Tunc depos ito imperio, arcem Syracusanis cum exercitu tradidit; receptoq; priuato instrumento, Corinthum in exilium profectus est. Ibi humilima quaq; tutissima exististimas, in sordidissimum vitae genus descendit: non contentus in publico vagari, sed potare; nec conspici in popinis, lupanaribusq; sed totis diebus defidere; cum perditissimo quoq; de minimis rebus disceptare, pannosusq; & squalidus incedere; risum libentius prabere, quam captare; in macello perstare; quod emere non poterat, oculis devorare; apud Aediles aduersus lenones iurgari; omniaq; ita facere, vt contemnendus magis, quam metuendus videretur. Nouissime, ludimagistrum professus, pueros in triuio docebat, vt aut à timentibus semper in publico videreretur, aut à non timentibus facilius contemneretur. Nam licet tyrannicis vitiis semper abundaret, tamen simulatio hac vitiorum, non natura erat; magisq; hac arte, quam amisso regali pudore faciebat, expertus quam inuisa tyrannorum forent etiam sine opibus nomina. Laborabat itaq; inuidiam praeteritorum contemptu praesentium demere; neq; honesta, sed tuta consilia circunspiciebat. Inter has tamen dissimulationis artes, insimulatus est affectatae tyrannidis; nec aliter quam dum contemnitur liberatus est,
units.tr: 5 Meanwhile Dionysius, received at Syracuse, becoming heavier and crueler to the city day by day, was besieged by a renewed conspiracy. Then, laying down his power, he handed over the citadel to the Syracusans with his army; and, taking back his private property, he set out into exile at Corinth. There, thinking the most humble things the safest, he sank into the most abject way of life: not content to wander in public, he also drank; he was seen not in taverns and brothels but sat about all day; he argued over trifles with the most worthless men, walked about in rags and filth; he was more willing to provide laughter than to seek it; he lingered in the market and devoured with his eyes what he could not buy; he brawled with the aediles against the pimps; and he did everything in such a way that he seemed more to be despised than feared. Finally, professing to be a schoolmaster, he taught boys at the crossroads, so that he would either be seen in public always by those who feared him, or be more easily despised by those who did not fear him. For although he always abounded in tyrannical vices, yet this pretence of vices was not his nature; and he did it more by this art than by a loss of royal shame, having learned by experience how hateful even the names of tyrants are, even without power. He therefore laboured to remove the hatred of past deeds by the contempt of present ones, and he looked around for not honourable but safe counsels. Nevertheless, among these arts of dissimulation, he was accused of aiming at tyranny again; and he was freed from this charge only while he was held in contempt.

units.la: 6 Inter haec Carthaginienses tanto successu rerum Alexandri Magni exterriti, verentes ne Persico regno & Africam vellet adiungere, mittunt ad speculandos eius animos Hamilcarem, cognomento Rhodanum, virum solertia facundiaque prater ceteros insignem. Augebant enim metum & Tyrus vrbs, auctor originis suae, capta, & Alexandria aemula Carthaginis, in terminis Africae & AEgypti condita, & felicitas regis, apud quem nec cupiditas, nec fortuna vllo modo terminabantur. Igitur Hamilcar per Parmenionem aditu regis obtento, profugisse se ad regem expulsum patria fingit, militemq; se expeditionis offert. Atque ita consilijs eius exploratis, in tabellis ligneis, vacua desuper cera inducta, ciui-
units.tr: 6 Meanwhile the Carthaginians, terrified by the great success of Alexander the Great, fearing that he would wish to add Africa to the Persian kingdom, sent Hamilcar, surnamed Rhodanus, a man distinguished above others for skill and eloquence, to spy out his intentions. For the city of Tyre, the originator of their own origin, had been taken, and Alexandria, a rival of Carthage, founded on the borders of Africa and Egypt, increased their fear, as did the good fortune of the king, by whom neither desire nor fortune was in any way limited. Therefore Hamilcar, having obtained access to the king through Parmenion, pretended that he had fled to the king as one expelled from his homeland, and offered himself as a soldier for the expedition. And so, having explored his plans, he wrote down everything for his fellow citizens on wooden tablets, with wax spread over their empty surfaces, ...

units.la: 1. civibus suis omnia perscribebat. Sed Carthaginienses post mortem regis reuersum in patriam, quasi urbem regi venditasset, non ingrato tantum, verumetiam & crudeli animo, necauerunt.
units.tr: 1. ...to his fellow citizens. But the Carthaginians, after the king's death, when he had returned to his homeland, put him to death, not only with ungrateful but also with cruel spirit, as if he had sold the city to the king.
POMPEIUS TROGUS, EPITOME OF THE HISTORIES
BOOK XXII. SUMMARY.

units.la: 1 Agathoclis Siciliae tyranni otigo, pueritia, adolescentia, misera conditio. 2 Felicitas bellica, artes, noua dignitas, perfidia, crudelitas, tyrannis. 3 Carthaginienses in Hamilcarem proditorem taciturn suffragia ferunt. Bella Agathoclis. 4 Syracusis à Carthaginiensibus obsessis Agathocles audaci consilio bellum in Africam infert. 5 Expositio in litore Africæ exercitu, giaui oratione suos ad pugnam accendit. 6 Discussa superstitionis Carthaginiensibus. nebula, & nauibus incensis, Carthaginienses prælio superat, & urbes nobilissimas recepit. 7 Siciliam Carthaginienses relinquere coguntur, & infeliciter cum Agathocle pugnantin Africa, fatum acerbum Aphellæ & Bomilcaris. 8 Totius Siciliæ imperium occupat Agathocles: In Africam reuertitur, infeliciter pugnat, castra deserit: unde militum defectio, filiorum Agathoclis mors cruenta, & Agathoclis pax inita cum Carthaginiensibus.
units.tr: 1 The origin of Agathocles, tyrant of Sicily: his boyhood, youth and wretched condition. 2 His success in war, his arts, his new dignity, his treachery, cruelty and tyranny. 3 The Carthaginians pass votes in silence against Hamilcar the traitor. The wars of Agathocles. 4 Besieged by the Carthaginians at Syracuse, Agathocles with a bold plan carries the war into Africa. 5 Having landed his army on the African shore, he rouses his men to battle with a stirring speech. 6 The superstitious fear of the Carthaginians is dispelled; he burns his ships, defeats the Carthaginians in battle, and recovers the most noble cities. 7 The Carthaginians are forced to leave Sicily; fighting unsuccessfully with Agathocles in Africa, the bitter fate of Aphelas and Bomilcar. 8 Agathocles seizes the rule of all Sicily; he returns to Africa, fights unsuccessfully, and deserts his camp. Hence the defection of his soldiers, the bloody death of Agathocles' sons, and the peace made by Agathocles with the Carthaginians.

units.la: GATHOCLES Siciliæ tyrannus, qui magnitudini prioris Dionysij successit, ad regni maiestatem ex humili & sordido genere peruenit. Quippe in Sicilia patre figulo natus, non honestiorem pueritiam, quam principia originis habuit. Siquidem forma, & corporis pulchritudine egregius, diu vitam stupri patientia exhibuit. Annos deinde pubertatis egressus, libidinem à viris ad feminas transtulit. Post hæc apud virum quondam sexum famosus, vitam latrociniis mutavit. Interiecto tempore, cum Syracusas concessisset, accitusque in civitatem inter incolas esset, diu sine fide fuit; quoniam nec in fortunis quod amitteret, nec in verecundia quod inquinaret habere videbatur: in summa gregariam militiam sortitus, nō minus tunc seditiosa, quam antea turpi vita, in omne facinus promptissimus erat. Nam & manu strenuus, & in concionibus perfacundus habebatur. Breui itaq; centurio, ac deinceps tribunus militum factus est. Primo bello aduersus Aetneos magna experimenta [sui Syracusanis dedit. Sequenti Campanorum, tantam de se spem omnibus fecit, vt in locum [demortui ducis Damasconis sufficeretur. Cuius vxorem adulterio cognitam, post mortem viri in matrimonium recepit. Nec contentus quod ex inope repente dives factus esset, piraticam aduersus patriam exercuit. Saluti ei fuit, quod socij capti tortiq;, de illo negauerunt. Eis occupare imperium Syracusanorum voluit; bis in exilium actus est.
units.tr: Agathocles, tyrant of Sicily, who succeeded the greatness of the earlier Dionysius, rose to royal majesty from a humble and lowly family. Born in Sicily to a potter for a father, he had no more honourable a boyhood than the beginnings of his origin would suggest. For being outstanding in beauty of form and body, he long endured a life of submitting to lust. Then, passing the years of puberty, he transferred his desire from men to women. After this, notorious among men for his sexual conduct, he changed his life for brigandage. After an interval, when he had come to Syracuse and been received as a citizen among the inhabitants, he was for a long time without credit, since he seemed to have nothing in his fortunes to lose and nothing in his reputation to soil. At length he was assigned to common soldiering, and no less seditious then than he had been dissolute before, he was most ready for any crime. For he was reckoned both vigorous with his hands and exceedingly eloquent in the assemblies. Thus in a short time he was made a centurion, and then a military tribune. In his first war against the Aetnaeans he gave the Syracusans great proofs of himself; in the next, against the Campanians, he gave everyone such hope of himself that he was appointed in place of the dead commander Damasco. He married Damasco's wife, whom he had known in adultery, after her husband's death. Nor was he content that from being poor he had suddenly become rich; he turned to piracy against his own country. It saved him that his captured and tortured accomplices denied anything about him. He wished to seize the rule of the Syracusans, and was twice driven into exile.

units.la: 2 A Murgantinis apud quos exulabat, odio Syracusanorum primo prator, mox dux creatur.
