In eo bello & vrbem Leontinorum capit, & patriam suam Syracusas obsidere coepit: ad cuius auxilium Hamilcar dux Pœnorum imploratus, depositis hostilibus odiis, prasidia militum mittit. Ita vno eodemq; tempore Syracusae, & ab hoste, ciuili amore defensae; & a ciue, hostili odio impugnatae sunt. Sed Agathocles, cum videret fortius defendi vrbem quam oppugnari, precibus per intercessionem Hamilcarē exorat, vt inter se & Syracusanos pacis arbitria suscipiat, peculiaria in ipsum officia sua repromittens. Qua spe impletus Hamilcar, societatem cum eo metu potentiae eius iungit: ut quantum virium Agathocli aduersus Syracusanos dedisset, tantum ipse ad incre-
units.tr: 2 Among the Murgantines, where he was in exile, he was first made praetor and soon general, through hatred of the Syracusans. In that war he took the city of the Leontines and began to besiege his own country, Syracuse. To help against this, Hamilcar, commander of the Carthaginians, was implored; laying aside their hostile hatreds, he sent troops for their defence. Thus at one and the same time Syracuse was defended by an enemy out of civic affection, and attacked by a citizen out of hostile hatred. But Agathocles, seeing that the city was being defended more stoutly than it could be assailed, by prayers through Hamilcar's intercession begged him to undertake the arbitration of peace between himself and the Syracusans, promising special services to Hamilcar in return. Hamilcar, filled with this hope, joined an alliance with him from fear of his power, so that as much strength as he gave Agathocles against the Syracusans, so much he himself would recover for the increase of his own domestic power.

units.la: menta domesticae potentiae reciperaret. Igitur non pax tantum Agathocli conciliatur, verum etiam praetor Syracusis constituitur. Tunc Hamilcari expositus ignibus cereis txctusq; in obsequia Poenorum iurat. Deinde acceptis ab eo quinq; millibus Afiorum, potentissimos quosq; ex principibus interfecit: atq; ita veluti reipub. statum formaturus, populum in theatrum ad concionem vocari iubet, contracto in gymnasio senatu, quasi quaedam prius ordinaturus. Sic compositis rebus, immissis militibus populum obsidet; senatum trucidat: cuius peracta cade, ex plebe quoq; locupletissimos & promptissimos interfecit.
units.tr: Accordingly, not only was peace secured for Agathocles, but he was also appointed praetor at Syracuse. Then, having been exposed to Hamilcar's [...] he swore an oath in the service of the Carthaginians. Next, having received from him five thousand Africans, he killed the most powerful of the leading men; and so, as if about to shape the state of the commonwealth, he ordered the people summoned to the theatre for an assembly, while the senate was gathered in the gymnasium, as though he were first going to set some things in order. With matters thus arranged, he sent in soldiers, besieged the people, and slaughtered the senate. When that butchery was finished, he also killed the wealthiest and most energetic men from the common people.

units.la: 3 His ita gestis, militem legit, exercitumq; conscribit: quo instructus, finitimas ciuitates nihil hostile metuentes, ex improuiso aggreditur. Poenorum quoq; socios permittente Hamilcare, foede vexat: propter quod querelas Carthaginem socij non tam de Agathocle, quam de Hamilcare detulerunt: hunc vt dominum & tyrannum, illum vt proditorem arguentes: à quo infestissimo hosti fortunæ sociorū, interpositā pactione, donatæ sint;
units.tr: 3 With these things done, he levied soldiers and enrolled an army. Equipped with it, he attacked the neighbouring cities without warning, which feared no hostility. With Hamilcar allowing it, he also cruelly harassed the allies of the Carthaginians. On account of this, the allies brought their complaints to Carthage, accusing not so much Agathocles as Hamilcar: the one as lord and tyrant, the other as traitor, by whose agreement the fortunes of the allies had been handed over, by a treaty, to the most hostile enemy.

units.la: sicut ab initio Syracusæ in pignus societatis sint traditæ, vrbs semper Poenis infesta, & de imperio Siciliæ Carthaginis æmula; nunc insuper ciuitates sociorum eidem titulo pacis addictas. Denuntiare igitur se, haec breui ad ipsos redundatura, ac propediem sensuros quantum malum non Siciliæ magis, quam ipsi Africæ attulerint. His querelis senatus in Hamilcarem accenditur. Sed quoniam in imperio esset, tacita de eo suffragia tulerunt; & sententias priusquam recitarentur, in vnam coniectas obsignari iusserunt, dum alter Hamilcar Gisgonis filius, à Sicilia reuerteretur. Sed hac callida commenta Poenorum, & sententias, inaudita mors Hamilcaris praeuenit; liberatusque est fati munere, quem sui per iniuriam ciues inauditum damnauerant. Qua res Agathocli aduersus Poenos occasionem mouendi belli dedit. Prima igitur illi cum Hamilcare Gisgonis filio, praelij congressio fuit: à quo victus, maiori mole reparaturus bellum, Syracusas concessit. Sed secundi certaminis eadem fortuna, qua & prioris fuit.
units.tr: Just as Syracuse had been handed over at the start as a pledge of alliance, a city always hostile to the Carthaginians and a rival for the rule of Sicily, so now the cities of the allies had been given over to the same man under the name of peace. They declared that these things would soon rebound upon the Carthaginians themselves, and that they would shortly feel how great an evil they had brought not so much to Sicily as to Africa itself. At these complaints the senate was inflamed against Hamilcar. But since he was in command, they passed their votes against him in secret, and before the verdicts were read out they had them gathered into one and ordered them sealed, until the other Hamilcar, son of Gisgo, should return from Sicily. But the unexpected death of Hamilcar anticipated both these shrewd schemes of the Carthaginians and their verdicts; and he was freed by the gift of fate from the men who, by their injustice, had condemned him without a hearing. This event gave Agathocles an occasion to begin war against the Carthaginians. The first engagement was therefore with Hamilcar, son of Gisgo; defeated by him, Agathocles withdrew to Syracuse, intending to renew the war with greater force. But in the second contest his fortune was the same as in the first.

units.la: 4 Cum igitur victores Poeni Syracusas obsidione cinxissent, Agathocles cum se neque viribus parem, neque ad obsidionem ferendam instructum videret: super hac & sociis crudelitate eius offensis, destitus esset, statuit bellum in Africam transferre: mira prorsus audacia, ut quibus in solo urbis sua par non erat, eorum urbi bellum inferret; & qui sua tueri non poterat, impugnaret alienam; victusque victoribus insultaret. Huius consilij non minus admirabile silentium, quam commentum fuit, populo hoc solum professus, inuenisse se victoriae viam: animos illi tantum in breuem obsidionis patientiam firmarent, vel si cui status praesentis fortuna displiceret, dare se ei discedendi liberam potestatem. Cum mille fexcenti discessissent, ceteros obsidionis necessitate frumento & stipendio instruit: quinquaginta tantum secum talenta ad praesentem vsum aufert, cetera ex hoste melius, quam ex sociis parature. Omnes deinde seruos, militaris aetatis, libertate donatos sacramento adegit, eosque & maiorem partem ferme militum naquibus imponit, ratus exaquata viriusque ordinis conditione, mutuam inter eos virtutis aemulationem futuram; ceteros omnes ad tutelam patriae reliquit.
units.tr: 4 Accordingly, when the victorious Carthaginians had encircled Syracuse with a siege, Agathocles, seeing that he was neither a match for them in strength nor equipped to endure a siege, and being also abandoned by his allies, who were offended at his cruelty, resolved to carry the war over into Africa. It was a truly remarkable audacity: to bring war against the city of those whom he could not match on his own soil, and to attack another's home while being unable to defend his own, and, being defeated, to insult the victors. Not less admirable than the plan itself was his silence about it. He declared to the people only this, that he had found a way to victory; he merely asked that they strengthen their spirits for a short endurance of the siege, or, if anyone was dissatisfied with the present state of fortune, he would give them free leave to depart. When one thousand six hundred had gone away, he provided the rest with grain and pay for the siege's necessity; he took with him only fifty talents for immediate use, intending to obtain the rest more readily from the enemy than from his allies. Then he bound all the slaves of military age, who had been granted freedom, by oath, and placed them, together with nearly the greater part of his soldiers, on the ships, reckoning that with the condition of both classes made equal, there would be a mutual rivalry in courage between them; all the others he left to guard the homeland.

units.la: 5 Septimo igitur imperij anno, comitibus duobus adultis filiis, Archagatho & Heraclida, nullo militum sciente quo veheretur, cursum in Africam dirigit. Cum omnes aut in Italiam prædatum fe, aut in Sardiniam ituros crederent, tum primum, exposito in Africa litore exercitu, consilium suum omnibus aperit. Quo in loco Syracusæ positæ sint, ostendit: quibus aliud nullum auxilium fuperceffet, quam vt hostibus faciant, quæ ipsi patiantur. Quippe aliter domi, aliter foris bella tractari. Domi ea sola auxilia esse, quæ patriæ vires subministrent; foris hostem etiam suis viribus vinci deficientibus socijs, & odio diuturni imperij externa auxilia circumspicientibus. Huc accedere, quod vrbes, caftellaq; Africæ non muris cinctæ; non in montibus positæ sint, sed in planis campis, fine vllis munimentis iacent: quas omnes metu excidij facile ad belli societatem perlici posse.
units.tr: 5 Accordingly, in the seventh year of his rule, with his two grown sons, Archagathus and Heraclides, as companions, and without any of the soldiers knowing where he was being carried, he directed his course to Africa. While all believed they were going to plunder Italy or would sail to Sardinia, then for the first time, when the army was landed on the African shore, he revealed his plan to them all. He showed in what position Syracuse had been placed, for which no other help remained except that they should do to the enemy what they themselves were suffering. For wars were waged in one way at home and in another abroad. At home the only help was what the strength of the homeland supplied; abroad the enemy could be conquered even by his own strength, when allies fail and, from hatred of a long rule, look around for foreign help. Moreover, the cities and fortresses of Africa were not walled, nor placed on mountains, but lay on open plains without any defences; all of them could easily be enticed into an alliance in war by fear of destruction.

units.la: Maius igitur Carthaginiensibus, ab ipsa Africa, quam ex Sicilia exarfurû bellum, coituraq; auxilia omnium adueríus vnam vrbem, nomine quam opibus amplioriem, & quas non attulerit vires, inde sumpturum. Nec in repentino Pœnorum metu, modicum momentum victoriæ fore, qui tanta audacia hostium perculsi, trepidaturi sint. Accessura & villarū incendia, castellorum, vrbiumq; contumacium direptionem, tum ipsius Carthaginis obsidionem. Quibus omnibus non sibi tantum in alios, sed & aliis in fe sentient patere bella. His non solum Pœnos vinci, sed & Siciliam liberari posse. Nec enim moraturos in eius obsidione hostes, cum sua vrgeantur. Nusquam igitur alibi facilius bellum, sed nec prædam vberiorem inueniri posse. Nam capta Carthagine, omnem Africam Siciliamq;, præmium victorum fore. Gloriam certe tam honesta militia tantam in omnem æuum futuram, vt terminari nullo tempore obliuione possit; vt dicatur eos solos mortalium esse, qui bella, qua domi ferre non poterant, ad hostes transfulerint, victiq; victores insecuti sint, & obsessores urbis suae obsederint. Omnibus igitur forti ac laeto animo bellum ineundum, quo nullum aliud possit aut praemium victoribus uberius, aut victis monumentum illustrius dare.
units.tr: Therefore the war would blaze more fiercely against the Carthaginians in Africa itself than it had in Sicily, and the aid of all would converge against one city, which they would take from its wealth, which is greater in name than in resources, and they would draw from there whatever strength they did not bring. Nor would the victory be of small moment against the sudden fear of the Carthaginians, who would be struck down by such audacity of the enemy and thrown into confusion. There would also come the burning of farms, the plundering of fortresses and of stubborn cities, and then the siege of Carthage itself. From all these things they would feel that war was open not only to them against others, but also to others against them. By these means they could not only conquer the Carthaginians but also free Sicily; for the enemy would not linger in its siege when their own affairs were pressing. Nowhere else, therefore, could a war be easier, nor could a richer booty be found; for once Carthage was taken, all Africa and Sicily would be the prize of the victors. And certainly such an honourable campaign would bring glory to all future ages, so that it could never be erased by any lapse of time; it would be said that they alone of mortals had transferred to the enemy the wars which they could not bear at home, and, once defeated, had pursued the victors, and had besieged those who were besieging their own city. Therefore all should undertake the war with a brave and cheerful spirit, since no other war could give either a richer reward to the victors or a more glorious memorial to the vanquished.

units.la: 6 His quidem adhortationibus animi militum erigebantur; sed terrebat eos portenti religio, quod navigantibus eis, sol defecerat. Cuius rei rationem non minore cura rex, quam belli reddebat, affirmans, si prius quam proficiscerentur factum esset, creditypum aduersum profecturos prodigium esse: nunc quia egressis accidderat, illis ad quos eatur portendere. Porro defectus naturalium siderum semper praesentem rerum statum mutare, certumq; esse florentibus Carthaginiensium opibus, adversisque rebus suis commutationem significari. Sic 15 consolatis militibus, universas naves conscientes exercitu incendi iubet, ut omnes sciren t, auxilio fuga adempto, aut vincendum, aut moriendum esse. Deinde cu omnia, quacunq; ingrederentur, prosternerent, villas castellaq; incenderent, obuius eis fuit cum 30. millibus Pœnorum Hanno, sed prælio commisso, duo de Siculis, tria millia de Pœnis cum ipso duce cecidere. Hac victoria & Siculorum animi eriguntur, & Pœnorum franguntur. Agathocles victus hostibus, vrbes castellaq; expugnat, prædas ingetes agit, hostium multa millia truncidat. Castra deinde quinto lapide à Carthagine statuit, vt damna carifimarum rerum, vastitatemque agrorum, & incendia villarum, de muris ipsius vrbis specularentur. Interea ingens tota Africa deleti Pœnorum exercitus fama, occupatarumque vrbium diuulgatur.
units.tr: 6 These exhortations raised the spirits of the soldiers, but they were troubled by the scruple of a portent: while they were sailing, the sun had been eclipsed. The king explained the omen with as much care as he had given to planning the war. If the eclipse had happened before they set out, he argued, it would have been a prodigy portending disaster for those about to sail; but since it came after they had departed, it portended those against whom they were going. Moreover, eclipses of the heavenly bodies always alter the present state of affairs, and it was certain that they signified a change in the flourishing resources of the Carthaginians and in their own adverse circumstances. Having thus comforted the soldiers, he ordered the ships that had carried the army to be burned, so that everyone would know that, with flight taken away as a help, they must either conquer or die. Then, as they overran everything in their path and burned villages and fortresses, Hanno met them with thirty thousand Carthaginians. In the battle that followed, two of the Sicilians and three thousand Carthaginians fell, together with the commander himself. This victory raised the spirits of the Sicilians and broke those of the Carthaginians. Agathocles, having defeated the enemy, stormed their towns and fortresses, drove off huge booty, and cut down many thousands of the enemy. He then pitched camp five miles from Carthage, so that the Carthaginians could look down from the city walls upon the ruin of their dearest possessions, the devastation of their fields and the burning of their villas. Meanwhile the report of the destruction of the great Carthaginian army and of the cities taken spread throughout all Africa.

units.la: Stupor itaq; omnes & admiratio incessit, vnde tanto imperio tam subitum bellum, præsertim ab hoste iam victo: admiratio deinde paulatim in contemptum Pœnorum vertitur. Nec multo post non Afri tantum, vetustissimam Carthaginiensium nobilissima nouitatem sequuta, ad Agathoclem defecere; frumentoq; & stipendio victorem instruxere.
units.tr: Astonishment and wonder seized everyone: how could such a sudden war come against so great an empire, and especially from an enemy already beaten? Then this wonder gradually turned into contempt for the Carthaginians. Soon afterwards, not only the Africans but also the most ancient and noble allies of the Carthaginians went over to Agathocles, and they supplied the victor with grain and pay.

units.la: 7 His Poenorum malis etiam deletus in Sicilia cum imperatore exercitus, velut quidam arumnarum cumulus accessit. Nam post profectionem à Sicilia Agathoclis, in obsidione Syracusarum Poeni segniores reditti, ab Antandro fratre regis Agathoclis occidione caesi nuntiabantur. Itaq; cum domi, foris, eadem fortuna Carthaginiensium esset, iam non tributaria tantum ab his urbes, verumetiam socij reges deficiebant, amicitiarum iura non fideiussa successu ponderantes. Erat inter ceteros rex Cyrenarum Aphellas, qui spe improba, regnum totius Africae amplexus, societatem cum Agathocle per legatos iunxerat; pactusq; cum eo fuerat, ut Siciliae illi, sibi Africae imperium victis Carthaginiensibus, cederet. Itaq; cum ad belli societatem cum ingenti exercitu ipse venisset, Agathocles blando alloquio, & humili adulatione, cum saepius simul cenassent; adoptatusq; filius eius ab Aphellae esset, incautum interficit: occupatoque exercitu eius, iterato Carthaginiensibus omnibus viribus bellum cientes, magno utriusq; exercitus sanguine, graui proelio superat. Hoc certaminis dimicatione tanta desperatio illata Poenis est, ut nisi in exercitu Agathoclis orta seditio fuisset, traditurus ad eum Bomilcar, rex Poenorum, cum exercitu fuerit. Ob quam noxam in medio foro à Poenis patibulo suffixus est: ut idem locus monumentum supplicium eius esset, qui ante fuerat ornamentum honorum. Sed Bomilcar magno animo crudelitatem civium tulit; adeo ut de summa cruce, veluti de tribunali, in Poenorum scelera concionaretur: obiectans illis, nunc Hannonem falsa affectati regni inuidia circumuentum; nunc Gis- gonis innocentis exilium;nunc in Hamilcarem patruū suum tacita suffragia, quod Agathoclem socium illis facere, quam hostem maluerit. Hac cum in maxima populi concione vociferatus esset,expirauit.
units.tr: 7 To these Carthaginian disasters there was added, like a heap of further calamities, the destruction of the army in Sicily together with its commander. For after Agathocles had left Sicily, the Carthaginians who had been left behind in the siege of Syracuse were reported to have been cut down by Antander, the brother of King Agathocles. And so, since the Carthaginians' fortune was the same at home and abroad, not only tributary cities but even allied kings now began to desert them, weighing the obligations of friendship not by security given but by success. Among the others was Aphellas, king of the Cyrenaeans, who, with a wicked hope of seizing the whole of Africa, had formed an alliance with Agathocles through envoys. He had agreed with him that Agathocles should have Sicily and that he himself should have the empire of Africa once the Carthaginians were defeated. So when Aphellas came in person to join the war with a huge army, Agathocles, with a friendly manner and humble flattery, dined with him several times; then, after Aphellas's son had been adopted by him, he killed him off his guard. Having seized his army, he again turned all his forces against the Carthaginians and defeated them in a severe battle, with great bloodshed on both sides. This struggle brought such despair upon the Carthaginians that, had a mutiny not arisen in Agathocles' army, Bomilcar, the king of the Carthaginians, would have gone over to him with his army. For this crime he was fixed to a gibbet in the middle of the forum by the Carthaginians, so that the same place which had been the ornament of his honours became the monument of his punishment. But Bomilcar bore the cruelty of his fellow citizens with great courage, so much so that from the top of the cross, as if from a tribunal, he harangued them about the crimes of the Carthaginians. He reproached them: now for having let Hanno be circumvented by false envy, on the charge of aiming at kingship; now for the exile of the innocent Gisgo; now for giving silent votes against Hamilcar, his uncle, because Hamilcar had preferred to make Agathocles their ally rather than their enemy. When he had shouted these things before a very large assembly of the people, he died.

units.la: 8 Interea Agathocles profligatis in Africa rebus, tradito Archagatho filio exercitu,in Siciliam recurrit; nihil actum in Africa existimans, si amplius Syracusa obsiderentur. Nam post occisum Hamilcarem, Gisgonis filium,nouus eo a Poenis missus exercitus fuerat.Statim 10 igitur primo aduentu eius, omnes Siciliae vrbes auditis rebus,quas in Africa gesserat,certatim se ei tradiderunt:atq; ita pulsis e Sicilia Poenis, totius insulae imperium occupauit. In Africam deinde reuersus, seditione militum excipitur.Nam stipendiorum solutio in aduentum pa15 tris dilata a filio fuerat. Igitur ad concionem vocatos, blandis verbis permulsit stipendia illis non a se flagitandaesse,sed ab hoste quarenda, communem victoriam, communem pradam futuram:paulum modo anniterētur,dum belli reliquiae peraguntur,cum sciant Carthaginem captam spes omnium expleturam. Sedato militari tumultu, interiectis diebus, ad castra hostium exercitum ducit: ibi inconsultius prelium committendo maiorem partem exercitus perdidit. Cum itaq; in castris cum filio profugit. fuga fugisset, verfamq; in se inuidiam temere commisi 25 belli videret,pristinamq;offensam non depensi stipendij metueret,cōcubia nocte solus a castris cum Archagatho filio profugit. Quod vbi milites cognouere, haud secus quam si ab hoste capti essent, trepidauere: Bis se a rege suo in mediis hostibus relictos esse proclamantes;salu- 30 temq; suam desertam ab eo esse, quorum ne sepultura quidem relinquenda fuerit. Cum persequi regem velent,a Numidis exceptis, in castra reuertuntur; comprehensō. henso tamen reductoq; Archagatho, qui à patre noctis errore discesserat. Agathocles autem nauibus, quibus reuersus à Sicilia fuerat, cum custodibus earumdem Syracusas defertur. Exemplum flagitij singulare, rex exercitus sui defertor, filiorumq; pater proditor. Interim in Africa post fugam regis, milites pactione cum hostibus facta, interfectis Agathoclis liberis, Carthaginiensibus se tradidere. Archagathus cum occideretur ab Archesilao amico antea patris, rogauit eum quidnam liberis eius facturum Agathoclem putet, per quem ipse liberis careat? Tunc respondit, satis habere se, quod superstites eos esse Agathoclis liberos sciat. Post hac Pœni ad persequendum belli reliquias, duces in Siciliam miserunt, cum quibus Agathocles pacem æquis conditionibus fecit.
units.tr: 8 Meanwhile Agathocles, with affairs in Africa ruined, handed over the army to his son Archagathus and hurried back to Sicily, thinking nothing had been accomplished in Africa so long as Syracuse was still under siege. For after Hamilcar, son of Gisgo, had been killed, the Carthaginians had sent a new army there. So at his first arrival, all the cities of Sicily, having heard of what he had done in Africa, eagerly surrendered to him; and so, with the Carthaginians driven out of Sicily, he seized control of the whole island. Then he returned to Africa, where he was met by a mutiny of his soldiers, for their pay had been postponed by his son until his father's return. So he summoned them to an assembly and soothed them with soft words: their pay was not to be demanded from him but to be sought from the enemy; victory and booty would be shared in common; they need only hold on a little while longer, until the remnants of the war were finished, since they knew that the capture of Carthage would fulfil everyone's hopes. When the military tumult had subsided, after some days he led the army to the enemy camp. There, joining battle too rashly, he lost the greater part of his army. And so, having taken refuge in the camp with his son, and seeing that the hatred aroused by his rashly joined battle was turning against him, and fearing the old resentment over unpaid wages, he fled alone from the camp at midnight with his son Archagathus. When the soldiers learned of this, they panicked no less than if they had been captured by the enemy, crying out that their king had twice left them in the midst of enemies, and that he had abandoned their safety, when he ought not even to have left them without burial. When they wanted to pursue the king, they were intercepted by the Numidians and turned back to the camp; yet Archagathus, who had been separated from his father in the confusion of the night, was seized and brought back. Agathocles, meanwhile, was carried back to Syracuse in the ships in which he had returned from Sicily, with their guards. A singular example of shameful conduct: a king who deserted his army, and a father who betrayed his sons. Meanwhile in Africa, after the king's flight, the soldiers made a pact with the enemy, killed the children of Agathocles, and surrendered themselves to the Carthaginians. When Archagathus was being killed by Archesilaus, a former friend of his father, he asked him what he thought Agathocles would do to his children, seeing that through Agathocles he himself was deprived of his children. Archesilaus replied that it was enough for him to know that the children of Agathocles were still alive. After this the Carthaginians sent generals to Sicily to pursue the remnants of the war, and Agathocles made peace with them on equal terms.
POMPEII TROGI EPITOMA HISTORIARUM
LIBER XXIII. BREVIARIUM.

units.la: 1 Agathocles transit in Agathoclis in Ægyptū pelItaliam aduersus Bruttios, lunt, Agathoclis obitus. quorum origo & potentia 3 Pyrrhi Epiroti bella & paucis perstricta. res gestæ tum in Sicilia, tum
units.tr: 1 Agathocles passes over into Italy against the Bruttians, and the death of Agathocles is recorded. Their origin and power, the wars of Pyrrhus of Epirus, and his deeds, are briefly outlined, both in Sicily and in Italy.
2 Worn down by the force of disease, Agathocles dies in Italy.

units.la: Agathocles in Siciliam reuertitur, vbi turbæ domesti-4 Hieronis Siciliæ princicipis laudatissimi dignitas cæ, quæ vxorem & liberos & virtutes.
units.tr: Agathocles returns to Sicily, where domestic disturbances arise concerning his wife and children. 4 The dignity and virtues of Hiero, the most praised prince of Sicily.

units.la: GATHOCLES rex Siciliæ pacificatus cum Carthaginiensibus, partem ciuitatium àse a se fiducia virium diffidentem armis subegit. Dein quasi angustiis insula terminis clauderetur, cuius imperij partem primus incrementis ne sperauerat quidem, in Italiam transcendit; exemplum Dionysij secutus, qui multas ciuitates Italiae subegerat. Primi igitur Bru- 5 ttes illi Bruttij fuere, qui et fortissimi tum, et opulentissimi videbantur, simul et ad iniurias vicinorum prompti: Nam multas ciuitates Graeci nominis Italiae expulerant: auctores quoque suos Lucanos bello vicerant, et pacem cum his aequis legibus fecerant. Tanta feritas 10 animorum erat, ut nec origini suae parcerent. Namque Lucani iisdem legibus liberos suos, quibus et Spartani, instituere soliti erant. Quippe ab initio pubertatis, in silvis inter pastores habebantur, sine ministerio servili, sine veste quam induerent, vel cui incubarent; ut a pri- 15 mis annis duritia, parcimoniaque, sine ullo usu urbis, afsuescerent: Cibus his praeda venatica, potus aut lacte, aut fontium liquor erat. Sic ad labores bellicos indurabantur. Horum igitur ex numero quinquaginta primo ex agris finitimorum praedari soliti, confluente deinde 20 multitudine, solicitati praeda, cum plures facti effent, infestas regiones reddebant. Itaque fatigatus querelis sociorum Dionysius Siciliae tyrannus, sexcentos Afros ad compescendos eos miserat, quorum castellum proditum sibi per Bruttiam mulierem, expugnauerunt; ibique ci- 25 uitatem, concurrentibus ad opinionem novae urbis pastoribus, statuerunt; Bruttiosque se ex nomine mulieris vocauerunt. Primum illis cum Lucanis, originis suae auctoribus, bellum fuit. Qua victoria erecti, cum pacem aequo iure fecissent, ceteros finitimos armis subegerunt; 30 tantaque opes brevi consecuti sunt, ut perniciosi etiam regibus haberentur. Deinde Alexander rex Epiri, quum in auxilium Graecarum civitatum, cum magno exercitu, in Italiam venisset, cum omnibus copiis ab his deletus est. Quare feritas eorum successu felicitatis incen- sa, diu terribilis finitimis fuit. Ad postremum imploratus Agathocles, spe amplianti regni, à Sicilia in Italiam traiecit.
units.tr: AGATHOCLES, king of Sicily, having made peace with the Carthaginians, subdued by arms some of the cities that distrusted his strength. Then, as if the island were closed in by narrow boundaries, he crossed over into Italy, though he had never even hoped for an increase of the part of his realm that he had first gained. He followed the example of Dionysius, who had subdued many cities of Italy. The first of the Italian peoples to be attacked were the Bruttians, who then seemed both the bravest and the wealthiest, and at the same time quick to take offence at their neighbours. For they had driven many Greek cities out of Italy; they had also defeated their own founders, the Lucanians, in war, and had made peace with them on equal terms. Such was the fierceness of their spirit that they did not spare even their own origin. For the Lucanians used to bring up their children by the same laws as the Spartans. From the beginning of puberty they were kept among the herdsmen in the woods, without servants, without any clothing to wear, or any bed to lie on, so that from their earliest years they grew accustomed to hardship and frugality, with no experience of the city. Their food was the game they hunted, their drink milk or spring water. Thus they were hardened for the labours of war. Of these, fifty of the youths at first used to raid the fields of their neighbours; then, as a crowd gathered and they grew more numerous, drawn on by plunder, they made the regions around them hostile. Therefore Dionysius, tyrant of Sicily, worn out by the complaints of his allies, sent six hundred Africans to restrain them. These men took by storm a stronghold that had been betrayed to them by a Bruttian woman. There, as herdsmen flocked to the notion of a new city, they founded a town and named themselves Bruttians after the woman's name. Their first war was with the Lucanians, the authors of their origin. Elated by this victory, when they had made peace on equal terms, they subdued their other neighbours by arms; and they gained such wealth in a short time that they were regarded as dangerous even to kings. Then Alexander, king of Epirus, when he came into Italy with a great army to help the Greek cities, was destroyed with all his forces by them. Therefore their savagery, kindled by this success, long remained a terror to their neighbours. At last, invoked by the Italian Greeks, Agathocles, in hope of enlarging his kingdom, crossed over from Sicily into Italy.

units.la: 2 Principio aduentus opinionis eius concussi, legatos ad eum, societatem amicitiamq; petentes miserunt. Quos Agathocles ad cœnam inuitatos, ne exercitum traiici viderent, in posterum statuta his die, conscensis navibus fruistratus est. Sed fraudis haud latus euentus fuit: siquidem reuerti eum in Siciliam, interiectu paucis diebus, vis morbi coëgit, quo toto corpore comprehensus, per omnes neruos articulosq; humore peltifero grassante, velut intestino singulorum membrorum bello impugnabatur. Ex qua desperatione bellum inter filium nepotemq; eius, regnum iam quasi mortui vindicantibus, oritur: occiso filio, regnum nepos occupauit. Igitur Agathocles, cum morbi cura, & aegritudo grauiores essent, & inter se alterum alterius malo cresceret, desperatis rebus, vxorem suam Texenam, genitosq; ex ea duos paruulos, cum omni pecunia, & familia, regaliq; instrumento, quo praeter illum nemo regum ditior fuit, nauibus impositos Aegyptum, unde vxorem acceperat, remittit; timens ne praedonem regni sui, bostem paterentur. Quamquam vxor diu, ne ab aegro diuellerètur, deprecata est, ne discessus suus adiungi nepotis parricidio posset; & tam cruente hanc deseruisse vi-rum, quam ille impugnasse auum videretur; Nubendo se non prospera tantum, sed omnis fortuna iniisse societatem: nec inuitam periculo spiritus sui empturam, vt extremos viri spiritus exciperet; & exsequiarum officium, in quod, profecta se, nemo fit successurus, obsequio debitae pietatis impleret. Discedentes N paruuli, flebili vlulatu amplexi patrem tenebant. Ex altera parte vxor maritum non amplius visura, osculis fatigabat. Nec minus senis lacryma miserabiles erant, Flebant morientem patrem, ille exules liberos; hi defcessu suo solitudinem patris, agri senis; ille in spem regni susceptos relinqui in egestate lugebat. Inter haec regia omnis assistentium fletibus tam crudelis discidij implebta, resonabat. Tandem finem lacrymis necessitas prosessionis imposuit, & mors regis proficiscentes filios insequuta est. Dum haec aguntur, Carthaginienses cognitis quae in Sicilia agebantur, occasionem totius insulae occupandae datam sibi existimantes, magnis viribus eo traiiciunt; multasq; ciuitates subigunt,
units.tr: 2 At first the rumour of his coming alarmed them, and they sent envoys to him seeking alliance and friendship. Agathocles invited them to a dinner, and, so that they would not see his army being transported, he set a day for them to return, and then, when the ships were boarded, he deceived them. But the outcome of the treachery was not unhappy for him. For a sickness soon forced him to return to Sicily, after only a few days. Seized by it throughout his whole body, and with a watery humour spreading through all his sinews and joints, he was assailed as if by a civil war within each of his limbs. From this despair a war broke out between his son and his grandson, who were both claiming the kingdom as though he were already dead: the son was killed, and the grandson seized the kingdom. Therefore Agathocles, since the care of his illness and his sorrow were both more grievous, and since each man's misfortune increased the other's, despaired of his affairs. He sent back to Egypt, from which he had taken his wife, his wife Texena, and the two little children born of her, together with all his money, his household, and the royal equipment, of which no king was richer except himself, all loaded onto ships. He feared that they would suffer from the plunderer of his kingdom, his enemy. Although his wife for a long time begged not to be torn away from her sick husband, so that her departure might not be joined to the parricide of her grandson, and she seemed to have deserted her husband as cruelly as he had attacked his grandfather, she pleaded that by marrying him she had entered into partnership not only in prosperity but in every fortune; that she would not, unwilling, risk her life to receive her husband's last breath; and that she would fulfil the duty of funeral rites, which no one else would perform once she had gone away, with the devotion of due piety. As they departed, the little children clung to their father, weeping with wailing cries. On the other side, the wife, who would no longer see her husband, wore him out with kisses. The tears of the old man were no less pitiful: he wept for his dying father, and the children were lamenting their exile; these grieved for the loneliness of their father, an old man in his fields; he, in the hope of a kingdom, mourned that his children were left behind, taken up in poverty. Meanwhile the whole royal household was filled with weeping from those standing by, and the sad parting echoed through the palace. At last the necessity of departure set an end to the tears, and the death of the king followed the departing sons. While these things were going on, the Carthaginians, learning what was happening in Sicily, and thinking that an opportunity had been given them to seize the whole island, crossed over with great forces, and subdued many cities.

units.la: Eo tempore & Pyrrhus aduersus Romanos bellum gerebat, qui imploratus à Siculis in auxilium, sicuti dictum est, cum Syracusas venisset, multasq; ciuitates subegisset, rex Siciliae, sicut Epiri appellabatur. Quarum rerum felicitate laetus, Heleno filio Siciliae, velut auitum (nam susceptus ex filia Agathoclis regis erat) Alexandro autem Italiae regnum destinat. Post haec multa secunda praelia cum Carthaginiensibus facit. Interiecto deinde tempore, legati ab Italicis sociis venerunt, nuntiantes Romanis resisti non posse, deditionemq; futuram, nisi subueniat. Anxius tam ambiguo periculo, incertusq; quid ageret, vel quibus primum subueniret, in vtrumq; pronus consultabat. Quippe instantibus hinc Carthaginiensibus, inde Romanis, periculosum videbatur, exercitum in Italiam non traiicere, periculosius à Sicilia deducere; ne aut illi non lata ope, aut hi deserti amitterentur. In hoc astu periculorum, tutissimus portus consiliorum visus est, omnibus viribus decernere in Sicilia: & profligatis Carthaginiensibus, victorem exercitum transponere in Italiam. Itaque conferto prœlio,cum superior fuisset,quoniam tamen à Si-
units.tr: At that time Pyrrhus was also waging war against the Romans. Having been invoked by the Sicilians for help, as has been said, he had come to Syracuse and subdued many cities, and he was called king of Sicily, just as he was of Epirus. Delighted by the good fortune of these affairs, he destined the kingdom of Sicily for his son Helenus, as an inheritance from his grandfather (for Helenus had been born of Agathocles' daughter), and the kingdom of Italy for Alexander. After this he fought many successful battles against the Carthaginians. Then, after an interval of time, envoys came from the Italian allies, announcing that the Romans could not be resisted and that surrender would follow unless he came to their aid. Anxious at such a doubtful peril, and uncertain what to do or to which side to bring help first, he deliberated, inclining now to one side and now to the other. For since the Carthaginians pressed him on one side and the Romans on the other, it seemed dangerous not to cross the army into Italy, and more dangerous to withdraw it from Sicily; for fear of losing one or the other, either these would not receive his help or those would be abandoned. In this maze of dangers the safest harbour of plans seemed to be to resolve with all his forces upon Sicily, to defeat the Carthaginians, and then to transfer the victorious army into Italy. Accordingly, the battle was joined, and though he was victorious, yet because he left Sicily he seemed to have fled as one defeated; and for that reason his allies deserted him, and he lost the rule of Sicily as quickly as he had gained it. But he did not fare better in Italy, and he returned to Epirus. The fate of both enterprises was remarkable and served as an example. For just as before, when fortune was flowing beyond his wishes, it had brought him the rule of Italy and Sicily and so many victories over the Romans, so now, showing adversity as if to display the frailty of human affairs, it overthrew what it had heaped up: it added to the wreck of Sicily the shipwreck of the sea, a shameful battle against the Romans, and a disgraceful departure from Italy.

units.la: cilia abiret, pro victo fugere visus est : ac propterea socij ab eo defecerunt; & imperium Siciliæ tam cito amisit, quam facile quæsierat. Sed nec in Italiam melior felici- 5 tate vsus, in Epirum reuertitur. Admirabilis vtriusq; rei casus, in exemplum fuit. Nam sicut ante secunda fortuna, rebus supra vota fluentibus, Italiæ Siciliæque imperium, & tot de Romanis victorias adstruxerat; ita nunc aduersa, velut in ostentatione fragilitatis hu- 10 mana, destruens quæ cumulauerat, Siciliæ ruinæ naufragium maris, & fœdam aduersus Romanos pugnam, turpemq; ab Italia discessum adiecit.
units.tr: ...he seemed to flee as one defeated, since he had left Sicily. Consequently his allies deserted him, and he lost the rule of Sicily as quickly as he had won it. Nor, having experienced a better fortune in Italy either, did he return to Epirus. The reversal of both affairs was a remarkable example. For just as before, when his fortune was favourable and affairs flowed beyond his hopes, he had secured for himself the rule of Italy and Sicily and so many victories over the Romans, so now adversity, as if to display the frailty of human affairs, overturned what it had heaped up: it brought upon him the wreck of Sicily, a shameful battle against the Romans, and a disgraceful departure from Italy.

units.la: 4 Post profectionem à Sicilia Pyrrhi, magistratus Hiero creatur: cuius tanta moderatio fuit, vt consenti-
units.tr: 4 After Pyrrhus' departure from Sicily, Hiero was made magistrate. His moderation was so great that, with the favour of all the cities in agreement, he was first made commander against the Carthaginians and soon afterwards king.

units.la: 15 ente omnium ciuitatium fauore, dux aduersus Carthaginienses primum, mox rex crearetur. Huius futura maiestatis, ipsa infantis educatio quasi prænuntia fuit: quippe genitus erat patre Hieroclyto, nobili viro, cuius origo à Gelo, antiquo Siciliæ tyranno, manabat: sed
units.tr: 15 entium of all the cities' favour, he was made commander first against the Carthaginians, and soon after king. The very upbringing of the infant was, as it were, a foretelling of his future greatness. For he had been born to the father Hieroclytus, a nobleman, whose descent ran back to Gelo, the ancient tyrant of Sicily; but his mother's family was lowly and indeed shameful.

units.la: 20 maternum illi genus sordidum, atq; adeo pudibundum fuit: nam ex ancilla natus, ac propterea a patre, velut dehonestamentum generis, expositus fuerat. Sed paruulum, & humanæ opis egentem, apes, congesto circa iacentem melle, multis diebus aluere. Ob quam rem re-
units.tr: 20 For he had been born of a slave-woman, and for that reason was exposed by his father, as a disgrace to the family. But the little boy, needing human help, was nourished for many days by bees, which gathered honey around him as he lay there.

units.la: 25 sponso arusp icum admonitus pater, qui regnum infanti portendi canebant, paruulum recolligit, omniq; studio ad sphem maiestatis, quæ promittebatur, instituit. Eidem in ludo inter coæquales discenti, lupus tabulam, in turba puerorum repente conspectus, eripuit. Adole-
units.tr: 25 On account of this, the father, warned by the soothsayers who declared that a kingdom was foretold for the child, took the little boy back and brought him up with every care for the dignity of the greatness that was promised. When he was learning at school among his equals, a wolf suddenly appeared in the crowd of boys and snatched away his writing tablet. As he grew up and began his first wars, an eagle settled on his shield and an owl on his spear.

units.la: 30 scenti quoq; prima bella ineunti, aquila in clypeo, noctua in hasta consedit. Quod ostentum & consilio cautum, & manu promptum, regnq; futurum significabat. Deniq; aduersus prouocatores sæpe pugnauit, semperg, victoriam reportauit. A Pyrrho rege multis militaribus donis donatus est. Pulchritudo ei corporis mirifica, vires quoque in homine admirabiles fuere: In alloquio blandus, in negotio iustus, in imperio moderatus, prorsus vt nihil ei regium deesse, praeter regnum videretur.
units.tr: 30 As he was growing up and entering on his first wars, an eagle settled on his shield and an owl on his spear. This portent, which signified both caution in counsel and readiness in hand, also foretold that he would be king. In the end he often fought against challengers and always won the victory. King Pyrrhus honoured him with many military gifts. He had a remarkable beauty of body, and his strength was likewise wonderful in a man: pleasant in conversation, just in business, moderate in command, so that nothing seemed lacking to him in kingly qualities except the kingdom itself.
POMPEII TROGI EPITOMA HISTORIARUM
BOOK XXIV. SUMMARY.

units.la: VM hac in Sicilia geruntur, interim in Graecia dissidentibus inter se bello Ptolemaeo Cerauno, & Antiocho, & Antigono regibus; omnes ferme Graeciae ciuitates, ducibus Spartanis velut occasione data, ad spem libertatis erectæ, missis inuicem legatis, per quos in societatis fœdera alliganetur, in bellum prorumpunt: & ne cum Antigono, sub cuius regno erant, bellum cepisse viderentur, socios eius Aetolos aggrediuntur, causas belli prætendentes, quod consensu Græciæ sacratum Apollini Cirræum campum, per vim occupassent. Huic bello ducem delegunt Arean; qui adunato exercitu, vbes, satag, in his campis posita, depopulatur; quæ auferri non poterant, incendit. Quod cum è mœstibus consp̄icati Aetolorum pastores essent, congregati admodum quingenti, sparsos hostes, ignorantes quanta manus esset, quoniam cospectum illis metus & incendiorum fumus abstulerat, consectantur, trucidatisq; admodum nouem millibus, prædones in sugam verterunt. Reparantibus deinde Spartanis bellum, auxilium multæ ciuitates negauerunt, existimantes, dominationem eos, non libertatem Græciæ, quærere. Interea inter reges bellum finitur: nam Ptolemæus pulso Antigono cum regnum totius Macedoniæ occupasset, pacem cum Antiocho facit; affinitatemq; cum Pyrrho, data ei in matrimonium filia sua, iungit.
units.tr: Meanwhile these things were happening in Sicily, and in Greece the kings Ptolemy Ceraunus, Antiochus and Antigonus were at war with one another. Almost all the states of Greece, with the Spartans as leaders, seeing what looked like an opportunity, were roused to hope of liberty. They sent envoys back and forth by whom they might be bound in alliances, and they broke out into war. So that they might not seem to have begun war against Antigonus, under whose rule they stood, they attacked his allies, the Aetolians, putting forward as the cause that the Aetolians had seized by force the Cirrhaean plain, which by the agreement of Greece was consecrated to Apollo. For this war they chose Areus as leader. He assembled an army and laid waste the towns that lay on those plains, and whatever could not be carried off he set on fire. When the Aetolian herdsmen saw this from the hills, about five hundred of them gathered and went after the scattered enemy. They did not know how large a force it was, since fear and the smoke of the fires had hidden it from their view. They slaughtered almost nine thousand men and put the robbers to flight. When the Spartans then renewed the war, many states refused their aid, believing that they sought domination rather than the liberty of Greece. Meanwhile the war between the kings was brought to an end: for Ptolemy, having driven out Antigonus and taken possession of the whole kingdom of Macedonia, made peace with Antiochus and joined himself in marriage alliance with Pyrrhus, giving him his daughter in marriage.

units.la: 2 Exinde externo metu depositio, impium & faciinorosum animum ad domestica scelera conuertit, insidiasq; Arsinoæ sorori suæ instruit: quibus & filios eius vita, & ipsa Cassandrea vrbis possessione priuaret. Primus ei dolus fuit, simulato amore, sororis matrimonium petere: aliter enim ad sororis filios, quorum regnum occupauerat, quam concordia fraude peruenire non poterat. Sed nota scelerata Ptolemæi voluntas sorori erat. Itaq; non credenti, mandat velle se cum filiis eius regni consortium iungere: cum quibus non ideo se armis contedisse, quoniam eripere his regnum; sed quod id facere sui muneris vellet, In hoc mitteret arbitrū iurisiurandi: quo
units.tr: 2 Then, freed from fear of foreign enemies, he turned his impious and criminal mind to domestic crimes, and he laid plots against his sister Arsinoe, by which he would deprive her of her sons' lives and of the possession of the city of Cassandrea. His first trick was to seek his sister's hand in marriage under a pretence of love, for he could not otherwise gain, by agreement without deceit, the sons of his sister whose kingdom he had seized. But Ptolemy's wicked intention was known to his sister. So, since she did not believe him, he sent word that he wished to share the kingdom with her sons, and that he had not gone to war against them in order to snatch their kingdom from them, but because he wished to do this as a duty; he would send, as a witness to an oath, one before whose presence, by whatever oaths she wished, in the sight of the ancestral gods, he would bind himself.

units.la: Ptolemæi in sororem cōspiratio. quo praesente apud deos patrios, quibus vellet obsecrati‑ onibus, se obligaret. Incerta Arsinoë quid ageret: si mit‑ teret, decipi periurio; si non mitteret, provocare rabiem fraterna crudelitatis timebat. Itaq; plus liberis, quam sibi timens, quos matrimonio suo protecturam se arbi‑ trabatur, mittit ex amicis suis Chodionem: quo perdu‑ cto in sanctissimum Iouis templum, veterrimaMacedo‑ num religionis, Ptolemaeus sumptis in manus altaribus, contingens ipsa simulacra, & puluinaria deorum, in‑ auditis, vltimisq; execrationibus adiurat, se sincera fide matrimonium sororis petere; nuncupaturumque se eam reginam; neq; in contumeliam eius se aliam vxo‑ rem, aliosve, quam filios eius liberos habituram. Arsi‑ noë postquam & spe impleta est, & metu soluta, ipsa cum fratre colloquitur; cuius vultus, & blandientes oculi, cum fidem non minorem, quam iusiurandum pro‑ mitterent, reclamante Ptolemaeo filio fraudem subesse, in matrimonium fratris concedit.
units.tr: The conspiracy of Ptolemy against his sister. Arsinoe did not know what to do. If she sent someone, she feared being deceived by perjury; if she did not send, she feared provoking the fury of her brother's cruelty. So, fearing more for her children than for herself, whom she believed her marriage would protect, she sent Chodion, one of his friends. When he had been led into the most holy temple of Jupiter, the most ancient object of Macedonian religion, Ptolemy, laying his hands on the altars and touching the images and couches of the gods, swore with unheard-of and extreme curses that he sought his sister's hand in marriage in sincere good faith; that he would acknowledge her as queen; and that he would have no other wife, nor any other children than her sons, so as not to insult her. When Arsinoe, her hope fulfilled and her fear dispelled, met with her brother in person, his face and his flattering eyes promised no less faith than the oath did, although her son Ptolemy protested that treachery lay beneath it. She consented to marry her brother.

units.la: 3 Nuptia magno apparatu, laetitiaq; omnium ce‑ lebrantur. Ad concionem quoq; vocato exercitu, capitisororis diadema imponit, reginamque eam apppellat. Quo nomine in laetitia effusa Arsinoë, quia quod morte Lysimachi prioris mariti amiserat, recepisset; vltro virum in urbem suam Cassandream inuitat, cuius urbis cupiditate fraus struebatur. Pragresca igitur virum, diem festum urbi in aduetum eius indicit; domos, tem‑ pla, ceteraq; omnia exornari iubet; aras vbiq;, hostias, dispone; filios quoq; suos, Lysimachum sexdecim annos natum, Philippum triennio minorem, vtrumq; formainfignem, coronatos occurrere iubet. Quos Ptolemaeusad celandam fraudem, cupide & vltra modum vetæ af‑sectionis amplexus, oculis diu fatigat. Vbi ad portam ventum est, occupari arcem iubet; pueros interfici. Qui cum ad matrem confugissent, in gremio eius, inter ipsa oscula trucidantur. Proclamante Arsinoë, quod tantum nefas aut nubendo, aut post nuptias contraxisset, pro filiis saepe se percussoribus obtulit: frequenter corpore suo 5 puerorum corpora amplexata protexit; vulneraque, excipere quae liberis intendebantur, voluit. Ad postremum etiam spoliata funeribus filiorum, scissa veste, & crinibus sparsis, cum duobus servulis ex urbe protracta, Samothraciam in exilium abiit; eo miserior, quod mori 10 cum filiis ei non licuit. Sed nec Ptolemaeo inulta scelera fuerunt. Quippe diis immortalibus tot periuria, & tam cruenta parricidia vindicantibus, breui post à Gallis spoliatus regno, captusque, vitam ferro, vt meruerat, amisit.
units.tr: 3 The wedding was celebrated with great display and the joy of all. He also summoned the army to an assembly, placed the diadem on his sister's head, and hailed her as queen. Arsinoe, overflowing with joy because she had recovered by this name what she had lost through the death of her former husband Lysimachus, of her own accord invited her husband to her city of Cassandrea, the desire for which city was the cause of the plot. Ptolemy therefore set out, and for his arrival he proclaimed a festival day for the city; he ordered houses, temples and all other things to be decorated, altars and victims to be set up everywhere; and he ordered her sons, Lysimachus, sixteen years old, and Philip, three years younger, both handsome in appearance, to come out to meet him crowned. Ptolemy, to conceal his treachery, eagerly and beyond measure embraced them with a show of affection and wearied his eyes with gazing at them for a long time. When they came to the gate, he ordered the citadel to be seized and the boys to be killed. When they had fled to their mother, they were slaughtered in her lap, in the midst of her kisses. Arsinoe cried out that so great a crime had been committed either by her marriage or after the wedding; she often offered herself to the murderers in place of her sons, and frequently she protected the bodies of the boys by embracing them with her own body; she wished to receive the wounds that were aimed at her children. At last, stripped of her sons' corpses, her clothing torn and her hair dishevelled, she was dragged out of the city with two servants and went into exile at Samothrace; she was the more wretched because she was not allowed to die with her sons. But Ptolemy's crimes did not go unpunished. For the immortal gods, avenging so many perjuries and such bloody parricides, soon after this he was deprived of his kingdom by the Gauls, was captured, and lost his life by the sword, as he had deserved.

units.la: 4 Namque Galli abundanti multitudine, cum eos non caperent terra quae genuerant, trecenta millia hominum ad sedes novas quaerendas, velut ver sacrum miserunt. Ex his portio in Italia consedit, quae & urbem Romanam captam, incendit; & portio Illyricos sinus, 20 ducibus auibus (nam augurandi studio Galli prae ceteros callent) per strages Barbarorum penetrauit, & in Pannonia consedit: gens aspera, audax, bellicosa, quae prima post Herculem, cui ea res virtutis admirationem & immortalitatis fidem dedit, Alpium inuicta iuga, 25 & frigore intractabilia loca transcendit: ibi domitis Pannoniis per multos annos cum finitimis varia bella gesserunt. Hortante deinde successu, diuisis agminibus, alij Graeciam; alij Macedoniam, omnia ferro proterentes, petiere. Tantusque terror Gallici nominis erat, vt 30 etiam reges non lacessiti; vltro pacem ingenti pecunia mercarentur. Solus rex Macedoniae Ptolemaeus, aduentum Gallorum intrepidus audiuit; hisque cum paucis & incompositis, quasi bella non difficilius, quam scelera patrapatrarentur, parricidiorum furiis agitatus, occurrit. Dardanorum quoq; legationem, viginti millia armatorum in auxilium offerentem,spreuit; addita insuper contumelia,actum de Macedonia dicens, si cum totum Orientem foli domuerint, nunc in vindictam finium Dardanis egeant;milites se habere filios eorum,qui sub Alexandro rege stipendia, toto orbe terrarum victores, fecerint. Quæ vbi Dardano regi nuntiata sunt, inclytum illud Macedoniæ regnum breui immaturi iuuenis temeritate casurum dixit.
units.tr: 4 For the Gauls, with their population grown so large that the lands that had given them birth could not hold them, sent out three hundred thousand men to seek new homes, like a sacred spring. Part of them settled in Italy, and they captured and burned the city of Rome. Another part, led by birds (for the Gauls are more skilled than others in the art of augury), made their way through the slaughter of the barbarians into the Illyrian gulf, and settled in Pannonia. It is a harsh, bold, warlike people, which, after Hercules (to whom that feat gave admiration for his valour and assurance of immortality), first crossed the unconquered ridges of the Alps and regions unfit for habitation because of the cold. There, having subdued the Pannonians, they waged various wars for many years with their neighbours. Then, encouraged by success, they divided their army into bands, and some made for Greece and others for Macedonia, laying everything waste with the sword. So great was the terror of the Gallic name that even kings, not attacked, bought peace from them with huge sums of money. Only Ptolemy, king of Macedonia, heard of the coming of the Gauls without fear. He went to meet them with a few men, poorly arranged, as if wars were no more difficult than the crimes they had committed, driven on by the furies of parricide. He also scorned the embassy of the Dardanians, who offered him twenty thousand armed men in aid; and he added an insult, saying that Macedonia was done for if the Dardanians needed to defend their borders now, when the Gauls had only just conquered the whole East; he said that he had soldiers who were the sons of those men who had served under King Alexander and made the whole world their conquest. When this was reported to the Dardanian king, he said that that famous kingdom of Macedonia would soon fall through the rashness of a young man who was not yet ripe.

units.la: § Igitur Galli, duce Belgio, ad tentandos Macedonum animos,legatos ad Ptolemæum mittunt, offerentes pacem, si emere velit: sed Ptolemæus inter suos, belli metu pacem Gallos petere gloriatus est; nec minus fecit, rociter se legatus, quam inter amicos iactauit; aliter se pacem daturum negando,nisi principes suos obsides dederint,& arma tradiderint:non enim fidem se,nisi inermibus habituram Renuntiata legatione,riere Galli, vndiq;acclamantes, breui sensurum, sibi an illi consulentes ,pacem obtulerint. Interiectis diebus, prælium conseritur; victique Macedones caduntur: Ptolemæus multis vulneribus sauciùs capitur; caput eius amputatum; & lancea fixum tota acie ad terrorem hostium circumfertur: Paucos ex Macedonibus fuga seruauit; ceteri aut capti,aut occisi.Hæc cum nuntiata per omnè Macedoniam effent, porta vrbium clauduntur; luctu omnia replentur: nunc orbitatem amissorum filiorum dolebant; nunc excidia vrbium metuebant; nunc Alexandri,Philippiq;regum suorum nomina,sicuti numina, in auxilium vocabant, sub illis se non solum tutos, verumetiam victores orbis terrarum extitisse: vt tuerentur patriam suam, quam gloriam rerum gestarum cælo proximam reddidissent; vt opem afflictis ferrent, quos furor & temeritas Ptolemaei regis perdidisset, orabant. Desperantibus omnibus, non votis agendum, Sosthenes unus de Macedonum principibus, ratus, contra Gallos iuuentute, & Gallos victoria exultantes compescuit, & Macedoniam ab hostili populatione defendit. Ob quae virtutis beneficia, multis nobilibus reguntur Macedonia affectantibus, ignobilis ipse praeponitur: & cum rex ab exercitu appellatus esset, ipse non in regis, sed ducis nomen iurare milites compulit.
units.tr: § So the Gauls, under their leader Belgius, sent envoys to Ptolemy to test the spirit of the Macedonians, offering peace if he were willing to buy it. But Ptolemy boasted among his own people that the Gauls were seeking peace out of fear of war; and he acted no less boldly than he had boasted among his friends. He replied to the envoys that he would not grant peace unless their chiefs gave hostages and surrendered their arms, for he would trust them only when they were unarmed. When the embassy had reported back, the Gauls laughed and shouted from every side that he would soon learn whether they or he had been wiser in offering peace. After a few days, battle was joined; the Macedonians were defeated and cut down. Ptolemy, badly wounded, was captured; his head was cut off, fixed on a spear and carried all round the line to terrify the enemy. A few Macedonians escaped by flight; the rest were either captured or killed. When these events were reported throughout Macedonia, the gates of the cities were shut and everything was filled with grief. Some lamented the loss of their sons; others feared the destruction of their cities; others called upon the names of Alexander and Philip, their kings, as if they were gods, to come to their aid. Under them, they said, they had become not only safe but masters of the whole world; they begged that they would defend their country, which they had made famous by their deeds, closer to heaven than any other, and bring help to those whom the madness and rashness of King Ptolemy had destroyed. When all despaired, and said that prayers were not enough, Sosthenes alone, one of the leading Macedonians, reckoned that the Gauls must be checked by youth against them, and against the Gauls exulting in victory, and he defended Macedonia from hostile plundering. For these services of valour, many noblemen who aspired to the kingdom of Macedonia were passed over, and he, a man of no noble birth, was put in front of them; and when the army had hailed him as king, he compelled the soldiers to swear allegiance not in the name of king but of general.

units.la: 10 Interea Brennus, quo duce portio Gallorum in Graeciam se effuderat, audita victoria suorum, qui Belgio duce Macedones vicerant: indignatus parta victoria opimam praedam, & Orientis opulis onustam tam facile relictam esse, ipse adunatis 150 millibus peditum, 15 & 15. millibus equitum, in Macedoniam irrumpit. Cum agros villasque popularetur, occurrit ei cum instructo exercitu Macedonum Sosthenes; sed pauci a pluribus, trepidi a valentibus facile vincuntur. Itaque, cum victi se Macedones intra muros urbium condidissent, 20 victor Brennus, nemine prohibente, totius Macedoniae agros depraedatur. Inde quasi terrena iam spolia sordescent, animum ad deorum immortalium templa convertit, scilicet locupletes deos largiri hominibus oportere. Statim igitur Delphos iter vertit, praedam religioni, aurum offerens deorum immortalium praeferens; quos nullis opibus egere, ut qui eas largiri hominibus solent, affirmabat. Templum autem Apollinis Delphis positum est in monte Parnaso, in rupe undique impendente: ibi civitatem frequentia hominum 30 facit: qui ad affirmationem maiestatis undique concurrentes, in eo saxo consedere: atque ita templum & civitatem non muri, sed praecipitia; nec manu facta, sed naturalia praesidia defendunt: prorsus ut incertum sit, virum vtrum munimentum loci, an maiestas dei plus hic admirationis habeat. Media saxi rupes in formam theatri recessit. Quamobrem & hominum clamor, & si quando accidit tubarum sonus, personantibus & respondentibus inter se rupibus, multiplex audiri, ampliorg, quam editur resonare solet. Qua res maiorem maiestatis terrorem ignaris rei, & admirationem, stupentibus plerumq, affert. In hoc rupis anfractu, media ferme montis altitudine, planicies exigua est; atque in ea profundum terra foramen, quod in oracula patet: ex quo frigidus spiritus, vi quadam velut vento in sublime expulsus, mētes vatum in vecordiam vertit; impletasq, deo, responsa consulentibus dare cogit. Multa igitur ibi & opulenta regum populorumque visuntur munera; quaq, magnificentia sui reddentium vota, gratam voluntatem, & deorum responsa manifestant.
units.tr: 10 Meanwhile Brennus, under whose leadership a part of the Gauls had poured into Greece, heard of the victory of his men, who under the leadership of Belgius had defeated the Macedonians. Indignant that so rich a prize, laden with the wealth of the East, had been left behind so easily, he gathered 150,000 infantry and 15,000 cavalry and burst into Macedonia. As he was ravaging the fields and farmsteads, Sosthenes met him with his army drawn up for battle. But few are easily beaten by many, and the timid by the strong. So when the defeated Macedonians had shut themselves within the walls of their cities, the victorious Brennus, with no one to stop him, plundered the fields of all Macedonia. Then, as earthly spoils now seemed sordid, he turned his mind to the temples of the immortal gods, reasoning that wealthy gods ought to bestow their riches on men. He therefore at once set out for Delphi, offering the plunder to religion and preferring gold to the immortal gods, who, he declared, had no need of any wealth, since they were accustomed to give it to men. The temple of Apollo at Delphi stands on Mount Parnassus, on a rock overhanging on every side. There people gather in great numbers to affirm its majesty, and they have settled on that rock, so that the temple and city are protected not by walls but by precipices, and by natural defences rather than by human hands. It is thus uncertain whether the strength of the place or the majesty of the god inspires more wonder here. In the middle, the rock recedes in the form of a theatre. Hence the shouting of men, and whenever the sound of trumpets is heard, echoes back and forth between the answering cliffs, and returns manifold and louder than the sound that produced it. This brings greater terror of majesty to those who do not know the place, and often astonishment. In this hollow of the rock, at about the middle height of the mountain, there is a small level space, and in it a deep opening in the earth, which stands open for the oracles. From it a cold breath, driven upward by a certain force as if by wind, turns the minds of the prophetesses to frenzy, and, filled by the god, compels them to give answers to those who consult them. Therefore many rich gifts of kings and peoples are to be seen there, and the magnificence of those who render their vows reveals their gratitude and the responses of the gods.

units.la: 7 Igitur Brennus cum in conspectu haberet templi, diu deliberauit, an confessim rem aggrederetur: an verofessis via militibus, noctis spatium ad resumendas vires daret. Emanus & Thessalorus duces, qui se ad pra-de societatem iunxerant, amputari moras iubent, dum imparati hostes, & recens aduentus sui, terrori esset: interiecta nocte & animos hostibus sorsitan & auxilia accessura, & vias qua tunc pateant, obstructum iri. Sed Gallorum vulgus ex longa inopia, vbi primum vino, ceterisq, commeatibus referta rura inuenit, non minus abundantia, quam victoria latum per agros se sparserat; desertisq, signis ad occupanda omnia pro victoribus vagabantur. Qua res dilationem Delphis dedit. Prima namq, opinione aducntus Gallorum prohibiti agrefles oraculis sesuntur, messes, vinaq, villis esferre: cuius rei salutare præceptum non prius intellectum est, quam vini, ceterarumq, copiarum abundantia velut mora Gallis obiecta, auxilia finitimorum conuenere. Prius itaq; urbem suam Delphi, aucti viribus sociorum, permunire, quam Galli vino velut prada incubantes, ad signa reuocarentur. Habebat Brennus lecta ex omni exercitu peditum sexaginta quinq; millia: Delphorum sociorum, non nisi quatuor millia militum erant; quorum contemptu Brennus ad accendos suorum animos: praeda ubertatem omnibus ostendebat, statuasq; cum quadrigis, quarum ingens copia procul visebatur, solido auro susas esse; plusq; in pondere, quam in specie habere praeda affirmabat.
units.tr: 7 Brennus, then, with the temple in view, deliberated for a long time whether to attack at once or to give his soldiers a night's rest to recover their strength. The leaders Emanus and Thessalorus, who had joined him for the sake of plunder, ordered that delay be cut short, while the enemy was unprepared and still terrified by his recent arrival. If night intervened, the enemy might perhaps receive reinforcements, and the roads, which were then open, would be blocked. But the Gallic common soldiers, after a long want, as soon as they found the countryside full of wine and other supplies, spread across the fields, carried away no less by abundance than by victory. Abandoning their standards, they wandered about to seize everything as victors. This gave Delphi a respite. For at first, on the rumour of the Gauls' approach, the country people, warned by the oracle, were carrying away their harvests and wine from the villages. The wholesome counsel of this was not understood until the abundance of wine and other supplies, like a delay placed in the Gauls' way, gathered the aid of the neighbouring peoples. Thus Delphi, strengthened by the forces of its allies, fortified its city before the Gauls, lying over the wine as if over plunder, were recalled to the standards. Brennus had 65,000 infantry picked from the whole army, while the Delphian allies had no more than 4,000 soldiers. To make light of these and to inflame the spirits of his men, Brennus showed everyone the abundance of the booty. He said that statues with their chariots, of which a huge number could be seen from afar, were cast of solid gold, and he asserted that the plunder had more weight than show.

units.la: 8 Hac asseueratione incitati Galli, simul & hesterno mero saucij, sine respectu periculorum in bellum ruebant. Contra Delphi plus in deo, quam in viribus reponentes, cum contemptu hostium resistebant; scandentesq; Gallos e summo montis vertice, partim saxo, partim armis obruebant. In hoc partium certamine, repente vniuersorum templorum antistites, simul & ipsi vates, sparsis crinibus, cum insignibus atq; infulis, pauidi, vecordesque in primam pugnantium aciem procurrunt: aduenisse Deum clamant; cumq; se vidisse delitem in templum per culminis aperta fastigia. Dum omnes opem dei supplicitier implorant; iuuenem supra humanum modum insignis pulchritudinis, comitesq; ei duas armatas virgines, ex propinquis duabus Dianae Mineruaeq; aedibus occurrisse; nec oculis tantum hac se perspexisse, audisse etiam strepitorem arcus, ac strepitum armorum. Proinde ne cunctarentur, diis antesignanis, hostem cadere, & victoriae deorum socios se adiuuagere, summis obsecrationibus monebant. Quibus vocibus incensi, ... certatim in proelium prosiliunt. Praesentia dei & ... terramotu portio montis abrupta ... Galli ... exercitum, & conferti ... cunei non fine vulneribus hostium dissipati ruebant.
units.tr: 8 Roused by this boast, and also wounded by yesterday's wine, the Gauls rushed into battle without regard for the dangers. The Delphians, however, placing more trust in the god than in their own strength, resisted with contempt for the enemy, and as the Gauls climbed from the mountain's summit, they overwhelmed them, partly with stones and partly with weapons. In the midst of this struggle, suddenly the chief priests of all the temples, and the prophets themselves, with dishevelled hair, with their insignia and fillets, pale and frenzied, ran out to the front line of the fighting men. They cried that the god had arrived, and said that they had seen him leap into the temple through the open gable of the roof. While all were humbly imploring the god's help, a youth of more than human beauty appeared, and with him two armed maidens, coming from the two nearby temples of Diana and Minerva. They said that they had not only seen this with their eyes, but had also heard the twang of a bow and the clash of arms. Therefore, they urged with the most fervent entreaties, let them not hesitate: the gods were going before them, the enemy would fall, and they should help as allies in the god's victory. Fired by these words, they leapt eagerly into battle. ... By the presence of the god and an earthquake, a part of the mountain was broken off ... the Gauls ... their army, and the massed wedges, scattered not without wounds inflicted by the enemy, rushed on in disorder.

units.la: Insecuta deinde tempestas est, quæ grandine & frigore, saucios ex vulneribus absumpsit. Dux ipse Brennus cum dolorem vulnerum ferre non posset, pugione vitam finiuit. Alter ex ducibus, punitis belli auctoribus, cum decem millibus sauciorum citato agmine Gracia excedit. Sed nec fugientibus fortuna commodior fuit: siquidem pauidis nulla sub tectis acta nox; nullus sine labore & periculo dies; assidui imbres & gelu, nix concreta, & fames, & lassitudo, & super hac maximum peruigilia malum, miseras infelicis belli reliquias obterebant. Gentes quoq;, nationesq;, per quas iter habebant, palantes velut prædam sectabantur. Quo pacto euenit, vt nemo ex tanto exercitu, qui paulo ante fiducia virium etiam aduersus deos contendebat, vel ad memoriam tantæ cladis, superesset.
units.tr: Then a storm followed, which by hail and cold carried off the wounded through their injuries. The leader Brennus himself, unable to bear the pain of his wounds, ended his life with a dagger. The other leader, having punished the instigators of the war, left Greece with ten thousand wounded men, marching at speed. But fortune was no kinder to those who fled. For the frightened men had no night passed under shelter, no day without toil and danger. Constant rains and frost, snow piled up, hunger and exhaustion, and above all the greatest evil of sleepless nights, wore down the wretched remnants of the ill-starred war. The peoples and nations through whose territory they passed also hunted them down as they straggled, as if they were prey. As a result, not one man survived of so great an army, which only a little before had marched with confidence in its strength even against the gods, nor was any left to be remembered for so great a disaster.

units.la: POMPEII TROGI EPI- TOMA HISTORIARUM. LIBER XXV.
units.tr: The Epitome of the Histories of Pompeius Trogus. Book 25.
Summary.

units.la: 1 Gallorum in Antigonum Macedoniæ regē conspiratio. 2 Dum ad prædam currunt, prœda fiunt ipsi, & Antigonus pacē obtinet. Nam Gallorum formidabile, & armorum inuicta felicitas.
units.tr: 1 The Gauls' conspiracy against Antigonus, king of Macedonia. 2 While they run after plunder, they themselves become plunder, and Antigonus keeps the peace. For the Gauls were formidable, and their arms had an invincible good fortune.

units.la: 3 Pyrrhus Macedonia potitur, Antigono eiecto. 4 Monarchiam dū Pyrrhus somniat, à Spartanis mulieribus atteritur. 5 Apud Argos occiditur Pyrrhus, cuius elogium & rerum gestarum summam lustinus subiicit.
units.tr: 3 Pyrrhus seizes Macedonia after Antigonus is driven out. 4 While Pyrrhus dreams of a monarchy, he is worn down by the Spartan women. 5 Pyrrhus is killed at Argos; Justin appends his character and a summary of his deeds.

units.la: NTER duos regas, Antigonum & Antiochum statuta pace, cum in Macedoniam Antigonus reuerteretur, novus eidem repente hostis exortus est. Quippe Galli, qui à Brenno duce, cū in Graeciam profecisserentur, ad terminos gentis tuendos relicti fuerant, ne soli destides viderentur, peditum quindecim millia, equitum tria millia armaverunt; fugatisq; Getarum, Triballorumq; copiis, Macedoniæ imminentes, legatos ad regem miserunt, qui pacem ei venalem offerrent, simul & regis castra spectatum rent. Quos Antigonus pro regali munificentia, ingenti apparatu epularum ad cœnam invitavit. Sed Galli expositum grande auri argentiq; pondus admirantes, atq; prædæ vberitate sollicitati; infestiores quam venerant, reuertuntur: Quibus & elephantos ad terrorem, velut inusitatas Barbaris formas, rex ostendi iusserat, & naves onustas copiis demonstrari; ignarus, quod quibus ostentatione virium, metum sè iniicere existimabat, eorum animos vt ad opinionem prædam sollicitabat. Itaq; legati ad suos reuerti, omnia in maius extollentes, opes pariter & negligentiam regis ostendunt: referta auro & argento castra, sed neq; vallo, fossaue munita; & quasi satis munimenti in diuitiis haberent, ita eos omnia officia militaria intermisisse: prorsus quasi ferri auxilio non indigerent, quoniam abundarent auro:
units.tr: Between the two kings, Antigonus and Antiochus, a peace having been agreed, as Antigonus was returning to Macedonia, a new enemy suddenly rose up against him. The Gauls, who under their leader Brennus had set out for Greece but had been left behind to guard the borders of the nation, lest they seem the only idlers, armed fifteen thousand foot and three thousand horse. Having routed the forces of the Getae and Triballi, and threatening Macedonia, they sent envoys to the king offering to sell him peace, and at the same time to view the king's camp. Antigonus, out of royal generosity, invited them to dinner with a lavish display of food. But the Gauls, marvelling at the great weight of gold and silver on show, and tempted by the abundance of plunder, returned more hostile than they had come. The king had ordered elephants shown to them to inspire terror, as forms unusual to barbarians, and ships loaded with troops displayed. He was ignorant that by displaying his strength he was stirring up their minds toward plunder, when he thought he was striking them with fear. So the envoys returned to their people and, magnifying everything, reported the king's wealth and his carelessness: the camp was full of gold and silver, yet it was protected by neither rampart nor ditch; and as if they had enough defence in their riches, they had neglected all military duties, as if they had no need of iron because they abounded in gold.

units.la: 2 Itacrelatione, auida gentis animi satis ad prædam incitabantur. Accedebat tamen & exemplum Belgij; qui non magno ante tempore Macedonum exercitum cum rege trucidauerat. Itaq; consentientibus omnibus, nocte castra legis aggrediuntur: qui præsentiens tātam tempestatem, signum pridie dederat, vt omnibus rebus ablatis in proxima silua taciti se occultarent. Neque aliter seruata castra, quam quod deserta sunt. Siquidem Galli vbi omnia vacantia, nec sine defensoribus modo, verumetiam sine custodibus vident, non fugam hostium, sed dolum arbitrantes, diu intrare portas timuerunt. Ad postremum integris & intactis munimentis, firmiores potius quam diripientes, castra occupauerunt. Tunc ablatis quae innuenerant, ad littus conuertuntur. Ibi dum naues incautius diripiunt, a temigibus, & ab exercitus parte, quae eo cum coniugibus & liberis confugerant, nihil tale metuentes trucidantur: tantaque cædes Gallorum fuit, vt Antigono pacem opinio huius fortitudine victoria,non à Gallis tantum,verumetiam à finitimorum feritate praefiterit. Quaquam Gallorum ea tempestate tanta fecunditatis iuuentus fuit, vt Asiam omnemi velut examine aliquo implerent, Denig, neque reges Orientis fine mercenario Gallorum exercitu vlla bella gesserunt,neq, pulli regno ad alios quam adGallos confugerunt: Tantus terror Gallici nominis,& armorum inuicta felicitas erat, vt aliter neque maiestatem suam tutam,neq, amissam reciperare se posse sine Gallica virtute arbitrarentur.
