Itaq, in auxilium à Bithynia rege inuocati, regnum cum eo parta victoria diuiferunt; eamque regionem Gallograciam cognominā- uerunt.
units.tr: 2 By this report the greedy spirit of the nation was sufficiently roused to plunder. Moreover there was the example of the Belgae, who not long before had slaughtered a Macedonian army together with its king. So with all agreeing, they attacked the camp by night. Antigonus, sensing so great a storm, had given the signal the day before that, everything having been carried off, the men should hide quietly in the nearest forest. The camp was kept safe in no other way than by being deserted. For when the Gauls saw everything empty, and not only without defenders but without guards, thinking it a trick rather than the enemy's flight, they long feared to enter the gates. At last, finding the fortifications intact and untouched, they occupied the camp more as conquerors than as plunderers. Then, carrying off what they had found, they turned to the shore. There, while they plundered the ships too carelessly, they were slaughtered by the rowers and by a part of the army, which had fled there with wives and children, fearing nothing of the kind. The slaughter of the Gauls was so great that Antigonus's peace was judged to have been secured by the reputation of this victory, won not only against the Gauls but against the savagery of the neighbouring peoples. Yet the Gallic youth of that time was so fertile that they filled all Asia as if with a swarm. Indeed, the kings of the East waged no wars without a mercenary Gallic army, and exiled princes fled to no one but the Gauls. Such was the terror of the Gallic name and the invincible good fortune of their arms that men believed they could neither keep their majesty safe nor recover what they had lost without Gallic valour. So, invited to help by the king of Bithynia, they divided the kingdom with him after victory was won, and called that region Gallograecia.

units.la: 3 Dum hęc in Asia geruntur, interim in Sicilia Pyrrhus à Pœnis nauali prælio victus,ab Antigono Macedonia rege supplementum militum per legatos petit: denuntiansmi mittat, redire se in regnum necesse habere,incrementa rerum,quae de Romanis voluerit,de ipsoquasiturum. Quod vbi negatum legati retulerunt, dissimulatis causis, repentinam fingit professionem. Socios interim parare bellum iubet; arcis Tarentinae cuffodiam Heleno filio,& amico Miloni tradit.Reuersus in Epirum,flatim fines Macedoniae innadit:cui Antigonus cum exercitu occurrit;victusq;prælio in fugam vertitur. Atq,ita Pyrrhus Macedoniam in deditionem accipit;
units.tr: 3 While these things were happening in Asia, meanwhile in Sicily Pyrrhus, defeated by the Carthaginians in a naval battle, asked Antigonus, king of Macedonia, through envoys for a supply of soldiers. He declared that he must return to his kingdom, and that he would discuss with Antigonus later the growth of power he wished to achieve against the Romans. When the envoys reported that this had been refused, Pyrrhus concealed his real reasons and feigned a sudden pretext. Meanwhile he ordered his allies to prepare for war, and he entrusted the guard of the citadel of Tarentum to his son Helenus and his friend Milo. Returning to Epirus, he at once invaded the borders of Macedonia. Antigonus met him with an army, but was defeated in battle and turned to flight. And so Pyrrhus received Macedonia in surrender.

units.la: Pyrrhus ab Antigono petit auxilii contra Pœ- nos.
units.tr: Pyrrhus asks Antigonus for help against the Carthaginians.

units.la: Eines Macedoniae inua- dit. accipit; & veluti damna amisse Siciliæ Italiæq, acquisito Macedoniæ regno pensasset, relictum Tarentini filium & amicum arcessit, Antigonus autem cum paucis equitibus, fuga comitibus, repēte fortuna ornamentis destitutus, amissi regni speculaturus euentus, Thessalonicam se recepit; vt inde cum conducta Gallorum mercenaria manu bellum reparet. Rursus à Ptolemæo Pyrrhi filio funditus victus cum septem comitibus sugiens, non iam reciperandi regni spem, sed salutis latebras, ac fugæ solitudines captat.
units.tr: Pyrrhus invades the borders of Macedonia and receives its surrender. As if to make up for the losses of Sicily and Italy by acquiring the kingdom of Macedonia, he summoned the son and friend he had left at Tarentum. Antigonus, however, with a few horsemen as companions in flight, suddenly stripped of the trappings of fortune, withdrew to Thessalonica to watch the outcome of his lost kingdom, so that from there he might renew the war with a hired band of Gallic mercenaries. Again he was utterly defeated by Ptolemy, son of Pyrrhus, and fled with seven companions, seeking no longer any hope of recovering his kingdom, but hiding-places for safety and lonely retreats for flight.

units.la: 4 Igitur Pyrrhus in tanto fastigio regni collocatus, iam nec eo ad quod votis peruenien dum fuerat contentus, Græcia, Asiaq, regna meditatur; neq, illi maior ex imperio, quam ex bello voluptas erat; nec quisquam Pyrrhum, qua tulisset impetum, sustinere valuit. Sed vt ad deuincenda regna inuictus habebatur, ita deuictis acquisitisq, celeriter carebat: tanto melius studebat acquirere imperia, quam retinere. Itaque cum copias Cherroneso transposuisset, legationibus Atheniēsium, & Achæorum, Messeniorumq, excipitur. Sed & Græcia omnis admiratione nominis eius, simul & rerum aduersus Romanos Pœnosq, gestarum gloria attonita, aducentum eius exspectabat. Primum illi bellum aduersus Spartanos fuit: vbi maiore mulierum, quam virorum virtute exceptus, Ptolemæum filium, & exercitus partem robustissimam amisit. Quippe oppugnanti vrbem, ad tutelam patriæ tanta multitudo feminarum concurrit, vt non fortius victus, quam verecundius recederet. Porro Ptolemæum filium eius adeo strenuum, & manu fortem fuisse tradunt, vt vrbem Corcyram cum sexaginta ceperit: item prælio nauali quinqueremem ex scapha cum septem infilmerit, captamq, tenuerit. In oppugnatione quoq, Spartanorum vsq, in mediam vrbem equo procurrerit;ibiq; concursu multitudinis interfectus sit. Cuius corpus vt relatum patri est, dixisse Pyrrhum ferunt, aliquanto tardius cum, quam timuerit ipse, vel temeritas eius meruerit, occisum esse.
units.tr: 4 Therefore Pyrrhus, placed at such a height of power, was no longer content with what he had prayed to reach. He meditated on Greece and Asia as kingdoms. Nor did he take greater pleasure in ruling than in war, and no one could withstand the onslaught he made. But as he was thought unconquered in subduing kingdoms, so after conquering and acquiring them he quickly lost them; he was far keener to acquire empires than to keep them. So when he had transported his forces across the Chersonese, he was received with embassies from the Athenians, the Achaeans and the Messenians. All Greece, astonished by the renown of his name and the glory of his deeds against the Romans and Carthaginians, awaited his coming. His first war was against the Spartans. There, received with more valour from women than from men, he lost his son Ptolemy and the most robust part of his army. For as he attacked the city, so great a crowd of women ran to defend their homeland that he withdrew no less ashamed than defeated. They also report that his son Ptolemy was so brave and vigorous in hand that he took the city of Corcyra with sixty men, and in a naval battle leapt from a skiff onto a quinquereme with seven men and held it when it was captured. In the attack on the Spartans, too, he rode his horse right into the middle of the city, and there he was killed in the press of the crowd. When his body was brought back to his father, Pyrrhus is said to have remarked that he had been killed rather later than he had feared, or than his rashness deserved.

units.la: 5. Repulsus à Spartanis Pyrrhus, Argos petit: ibi dum Antigonum in vrbe clausum expugnare conatur, inter confertissimos violentissime dimicans, saxo de muris ictus occiditur. Caput eius Antigono refertur: qui victoria mitius vsus, filium eius Helenum cum Epirotis sibi deditum, in regnum remisit,eiq; infesulti patris ossa in patriam referenda tradidit. Satis constans inter omnes auctores fama est, nullum nec eius, nec superioris aetatis regem comparandum Pyrrho fuisse; raroq; non inter reges tantum, verum etiam inter illustres viros, aut vita sanctioris, aut iustitia probatioris visum suisse: Scientiam certe rei militaris in illo viro tantam
units.tr: 5 Repulsed by the Spartans, Pyrrhus made for Argos. There, while he tried to storm Antigonus shut up in the city, fighting most fiercely among the thickest ranks, he was struck by a stone from the walls and killed. His head was brought to Antigonus, who, using victory more mildly, restored to the kingdom his son Helenus, who had surrendered to him together with the Epirotes, and handed over to him the bones of his unhappy father to be carried home. It is a fairly settled report among all authors that no king of his own or earlier times was to be compared with Pyrrhus; and it was rarely seen, not only among kings but even among illustrious men, that a life more holy, or justice more approved, had been seen: certainly in that man there was such a knowledge of the military art

units.la: fuisse, ut cum Lysimacho, Demetrio, Antigono, tantis regibus bella gerens, invictus semper fuerit. Illyriorum quoque, Siculorum, Romanorum, & Carthaginiensium bellis, numquam inferior, plerumque etiam victor extiterit: qui patriam certe suam angustam, ignobilemque fama rerum gestarum, & claritate nominis sui, toto orbe illustrem reddiderit.
units.tr: that, waging wars against Lysimachus, Demetrius and Antigonus, such great kings, he was always unconquered. In the wars with the Illyrians, Sicilians, Romans and Carthaginians he never proved inferior, and was mostly even the victor. He rendered his small homeland, obscure in the fame of its deeds, illustrious throughout the whole world by the renown of his name.

units.la: POMPEII TROGI EPI- TOMA HISTORIARUM LIBER XXVI.
units.tr: THE EPITOME OF THE HISTORIES OF POMPEIUS TROGUS, BOOK XXVI.
SUMMARY

units.la: I Peloponnesii per pro- cidåt, deinde Numinis vinditionem Antigono tradû- dicta omnes internecione tur. Epirotas, Ariftotimus delentur. Antigoni varius tyrannus affligit, & Hella- casus. nici prudentia opprimitur. 3 Pyrrhi filius Alexander 2 Antigonus Gallis oc- in regnum teftituitur. Recurrit, qui in furorem versi gni. Cyrenarum turbulencõiuges & liberos suos tru- tus status.
units.tr: The Peloponnesians are handed over to Antigonus by treachery. The Epirots are oppressed by the tyrant Aristotimus, and his rule is brought down by the prudence of Hellanicus. Alexander, son of Pyrrhus, is restored to the kingdom. Antigonus meets the Gauls, who, driven into a frenzy, slaughter their own wives and children. The turbulent state of Cyrene.

units.la: O S T mortem Pyrrhi non in Mace- donia tantum, verumetiam in Asia, Graeciaque, magni bellorum motus fuere: Nam & Peloponnesii per pro- ditionem Antigono traditi; & vari- ante hominum partim dolore, partim gaudio, prout singulae ciuitates aut auxilium de Pyrrho sperauerant, aut metus suffinuerant, ita aut cum Antigono societatem iungebant, aut mutuis inter se odiis in bellum ruebant. Inter hunc turbatarum prouinciarum motum, Epirorum quoq; vrbs ab Ariftotimo principe per tyrannidem occupatur : à quo cum multi ex primoribus occisi, plures in exilium acti: essent, Aetolis per legatos postulantibus,coniuges liberosq; exulum redderet,primo negauit: postea quasi poeniteret, proficiscendi ad suos omnibus matronis potestatem dedit, diemque prosectionis statuit. Ille quasi in perpetuum cum viru exuexulatura, pretiosissima quaq, auferentes cum ad portam quasi vno agmine profectura conuenissent, omnibus rebus exspoliate, in carcerem recluduntur: occisis prius in gremio matrum paruulo liberis, virginibusq, ad fluprum direptis. Ad tam sæuam dominationem stupentibus omnibus, princeps eorum Hellanicus, senex & liberis orbus, vt qui nec etatis, nec pignoris respectu timeret, contractos domum fidissimos amicorum in vindictam patriæ hortatur. Cunctantibus priuato periculo publicum finire, & deliberandi spatium postulantibus, arcessitis ferus subet obseruari fores; tyrannoq; nuntiari, mitteret qui coniuratos apud se comprehenderet: obiectans singulis, se quia liberanda patriæ auctor esse non posset, deferte vltorem futurum. Tunc illi ancipiti periculo circumuenti, honestiorem viam eligentes, coniurant in tyranni necem: atq; ita Aristotimus, quinto postquam tyrannidem occupauerat mense opprimitur,
units.tr: After the death of Pyrrhus great upheavals of war arose, not only in Macedonia but also in Asia and Greece. For the Peloponnesians were handed over to Antigonus by treachery. And as men's feelings varied, some grieving and some rejoicing, according as each state had hoped for help from Pyrrhus or had suffered fear of him, so some formed alliances with Antigonus and others rushed into war with one another out of mutual hatred. Amid this stirring of the troubled provinces, the city of the Epirots was seized by Aristotimus, its leading citizen, who made himself tyrant. Many of the chief men were put to death by him and more were driven into exile. When the Aetolians sent envoys demanding that he return the wives and children of the exiles, he at first refused. Later, as if he had repented, he gave all the matrons the power to leave and join their husbands, and set a day for their departure. They, as if they were to be exiles forever with their husbands, gathered at the gate as one column, carrying their most precious possessions. Then they were stripped of everything and shut up in prison, after their small children had first been slain in their mothers' laps and the young girls had been seized for debauchery. While everyone stood stunned at such savage tyranny, their leader Hellanicus, an old man without children, who feared neither his age nor the claims of his offspring, urged the most faithful of his friends, who had been gathered at his house, to avenge their country. When they hesitated, unwilling to end the public evil at the risk of their own lives, and asked for time to deliberate, he summoned them and had the doors watched. He sent word to the tyrant that he should send men to seize the conspirators gathered in his house. He told each of them that since he himself could not be the author of their country's liberation, they would have a future avenger in whoever betrayed them. Then those men, caught between two dangers, chose the more honourable course and conspired to kill the tyrant. And so Aristotimus was overthrown in the fifth month after he had seized power.

units.la: 2 Interea Antigonus cum multiplici bello, & Ptolemæi regis, & Spartanorum, premeretur, nouusq, illi hostis Gallogræcia exercitus affluxisset, in speciem caftrorum parua manu aduersus ceteros relicta, aduersus Gallos totis viribus proficiscitur. Quibus cognitis, Galli cum & ipsi se prælio parárent, in auspicia pugnæ hostias cadunt; quarum extis cum magna cades, interitusque omnium prædiceretur, non in timorem, sed in furorem versi, speranteisque deorum minas expiari cæde suorum posse, coniuges & liberos suos trucidant, auspicia belli à parricidio incipientes. Tanta rabies feros animos inuaserat, vt non parcerent ætati, cui etiam hostes pepercissent; bellumq, internecium cum liberis, liberorumq, matribus gererent, pro quibus bella suscipi solent. Itaq, quasi scelere vitam, victoriamq, redemissent, sicut erat cruenti ex recenti suorum cæde, in prælium non meliore euentu, quam omine proficiscuntur. Siquidem pugnantes, prius parricidiorum furiæ, quam hostes circumuenere; obuerfantibusq;, ante oculos manibus in-
units.tr: 2 Meanwhile Antigonus was hard pressed by a many-sided war, with King Ptolemy and the Spartans against him. A new enemy, an army of Gallo-Greeks, had also come against him. He left a small force in a show of a camp to face the rest, and set out with all his strength against the Gauls. When the Gauls learned of this, they prepared for battle and, as an omen for the fight, sacrificed victims. When a great slaughter and the destruction of them all was foretold from the entrails, they did not fall into fear but into frenzy. Believing that the wrath of the gods could be appeased by the slaughter of their own people, they butchered their wives and children, beginning their war with parricide as an omen. Such a madness had seized these savage minds that they spared no age, not even the age that enemies had spared. They waged a war of extermination against children and the mothers of children, the very people for whose sake wars are usually fought. And so, as if they had bought their lives and victory with crime, still stained with the fresh slaughter of their own people, they set out to battle with an outcome no better than the omen. For the furies of parricide overcame them before the enemy did, and as they fought, with the hands of the slain standing before their eyes,

units.la: 5 teremptorum omnes occidione cæsi. Tanta strages fuit, vt pariter cum hominibus diis, consensisse in exitium parricidarum viderentur. Post huius pugnæ euentum, Ptolemæus & Spartani, victorem hostium exercitum declinantes, in tutiora se recipiunt. Antigonus quoque 10 vbi eorum discessum videt, recenti adhuc ex priori victoria militum ardore, bellum Athenien-sibus infert. In quo cum occupatus esset, interim Alexander rex Epiri vlcisci mortem patris Pyrrhi cupiens, fines Macedoniæ depopulatur. Aduersus quem cum reuersus à Græcia 15 Antigonus esset, trāsfitione militum destitutus, regnum Macedoniæ cum exercitu amittit. Huius filius Demetrius puer admodum, absente patre, reparato exercitu, non solum amissam Macedoniam recipit, verumetiam Epiri regno Alexandrum spoliat. Tanta vel mobilitas 20 militum, vel fortunæ varietas erat, vt vicissim reges, nunc exules, nunc reges viderentur.
units.tr: all of them were cut down in the slaughter of the slain. So great was the carnage that it seemed the gods themselves had agreed to the destruction of these parricides. After the outcome of this battle, Ptolemy and the Spartans, avoiding the victorious enemy army, withdrew to safer places. When Antigonus also saw their departure, and while the soldiers' ardour from the earlier victory was still fresh, he made war on the Athenians. While he was occupied with this, King Alexander of Epirus, desiring to avenge the death of his father Pyrrhus, laid waste the borders of Macedonia. When Antigonus returned from Greece to deal with him, he was deserted by his soldiers through defection and lost the kingdom of Macedonia along with his army. His son Demetrius, still a boy, while his father was away, rebuilt the army. He not only recovered the lost Macedonia but also stripped Alexander of the kingdom of Epirus. Such was the fickleness of the soldiers, or the variability of fortune, that kings were seen to change places, now exiles, now kings again.

units.la: 3 Igitur Alexander cum exul ad Acarnanas confugisset, non minore Epirotarum desiderio, quam sociorum auxilio, in regnum restituitur. Per idem tempus 25 rex Cyrenarum Agas decessit: qui ante infirmitatem, Beronicen vnicam filiam, ad finienda cum Ptolemæo fratre certamina, filio eius desponderat. Sed post mortem regis, mater virginis Arsinoë, vt inuita se contractum matrimonium sollueretur, misit qui ad nuptias 30 virginis, regnumq;, Cyrenarum, Demetrium fratrem regis Antigoni à Macedonia arcesserent: qui & ipse ex filia Ptolemæi procreatus erat. Sed nec Demetrius moram fecit. Itaq; cum secundate vento celeriter Cyrenas {a}adulasset, fiducia pulchritudinis, qua nimis placere socrui cœperat, statim à principio superbus, regiæ famili-lia, militibusque impotens erat; studiumque placendi à virgine in matrem contulerat. Quæ res suspecta primo virgini, dein popularibus militibusq;, inuisa fuit. Itaq; svestis omnium animis in Ptolemaï filium, insidiæ Demetrio comparantur; cui cum in lectum socrus concessisset, percussores immittuntur. Sed Arsinoë audita voce filiæ, ad fores stantis & præcipientis vt matri parceretur, adulterum paulisper corpore suo protexit. Quo 1{b} interfecto, Beronice, & slupra matris, salua pietate, vlta est, & in matrimonio sortiendo, iudicium patris secuta.
units.tr: 3 Accordingly, when Alexander had fled as an exile to the Acarnanians, he was restored to the kingdom, with no less longing from the Epirots than help from his allies. At about the same time Agas, king of Cyrene, died. Before his illness he had betrothed his only daughter Berenice to the son of Ptolemy, to end the strife with his brother Ptolemy. But after the king's death, the virgin's mother Arsinoe, wishing the arranged marriage to be dissolved against her own will, sent for Demetrius, brother of King Antigonus, from Macedonia, to come for the wedding and the kingdom of Cyrene. He too was born of a daughter of Ptolemy. Demetrius did not delay. And so, when he had quickly reached Cyrene with a favourable wind, relying on his good looks, by which he had begun to please his mother-in-law too much, he was from the start arrogant and overbearing toward the royal household and the soldiers, and he had transferred his zeal for pleasing from the virgin to her mother. This conduct was at first viewed with suspicion by the virgin, then with hatred by the common people and the soldiers. So the feelings of all turned against the son of Ptolemy, and plots were laid against Demetrius; when he had gone to bed with his mother-in-law, assassins were sent in. But Arsinoe, hearing her daughter's voice, who stood at the door and ordered that her mother be spared, shielded the adulterer for a while with her own body. When he was killed, Berenice avenged her mother's dishonour while keeping her filial duty intact, and in choosing a husband she followed her father's judgement.

units.la: POMPEII TROGI EPI- TOMA HISTORIARVM LIBER XXVII.
units.tr: POMPEII TROGI EPITOMA HISTORIARVM LIBER XXVII.
BREVIARIVM.

units.la: 1 Seleucus nouercam & ocho Hierace petit & imfratrem infantē interficit. petrat.
units.tr: 1 Seleucus attacks his stepmother and, with Hierax, kills his infant brother.

units.la: 2 Classe naufragio amissa,ciuitates amissas recipit: Antiochum Hieracem & prælio victus aufugit: auxi- lium noxium à fratre Anti- ocho.
units.tr: 2 With his fleet lost in a shipwreck, he recovers the cities he had lost; defeated in battle by Antiochus Hierax, he flees; he seeks a harmful aid from his brother Antiochus.

units.la: 3 Asiæ lacerus status. In Seleucum Numinis vindi- cta.
units.tr: 3 The wretched state of Asia. Divine vengeance on Seleucus.

units.la: ORTVO Syriæ rege Antiocho,cum in locum eius filius Seleucus succeffisset, hortante matre Laudice, quæ prohibere debuerat, auspicia regni à parricidio cœpit, Quippe Beronicen nouercam suam, sororem Ptolemaei regis Aegypti,cum paruulo fratre ex ea suscepto interficit. Quo facinore perpetrato, & infamia maculam subiit, & Ptolemaei bello se implicuit. Porro Beronice cum ad se interficiendam missos didicisset, Daphne se claudit. Vbi cum obsideri eam cum paruulo filio nuntiatum Asiae ciuitatibus esset, recordatione paterna maiorumq; eius dignitatis, casum tam indignae fortunae miserantes, auxilia ei omnes miserunt. Frater quoq; Ptolemaeus periculo forofinis exterritus, relicto regno, cum omnibus viribus aduolat. Sed Beronice ante aduentum auxiliorum, cum vi expugnari non posset, dolo circumuenta trucidatur.
units.tr: When Antiochus, king of Syria, died, his son Seleucus succeeded him. At the urging of his mother Laodice, who ought to have restrained him, he began his reign with parricide. He killed Berenice, his stepmother, sister of Ptolemy, king of Egypt, together with the little brother she had borne to his father. Having committed this crime, he incurred both infamy and the stain of guilt, and he entangled himself in a war with Ptolemy. Meanwhile Berenice, having learned that men had been sent to kill her, shut herself up in Daphne. When it was reported to the cities of Asia that she was under siege there with her little son, they all sent her aid, remembering her father and the dignity of her ancestors and pitying the fall of so undeserved a fortune. Her brother Ptolemy too, terrified by the danger to his sister, left his kingdom and hurried to her with all his forces. But before the auxiliaries arrived, Berenice could not be overcome by force, and she was betrayed by a trick and put to death.

units.la: Indigna res omnibus visa. Itaq; cum vniuersae ciuitates, quae defecerant, ingentem classem comparassent, repente exemplo crudelitatis exterrita, simul & in vltionem eius, quam defensuri erant, Ptolemaeo se tradunt; qui nisi in Aegyptum domestica seditione reuocatus esset, totum regnum Seleuci occupasset: tantum vel illi odium, parricidiale scelus; vel huic fauorem indigne perempta mors sororis, attulerat.
units.tr: The deed seemed shameful to all. So when all the cities that had revolted had equipped a great fleet, they were suddenly struck with horror at the example of such cruelty, and at the same time, to avenge the one they were about to defend, they surrendered to Ptolemy. Had he not been recalled to Egypt by a rebellion at home, he would have seized the whole kingdom of Seleucus. So great was the hatred that Seleucus' parricidal crime had roused in them, and the favour that the undeserved death of his sister had won Ptolemy.

units.la: 2 Post discessum Ptolemaei, Seleucus cum aduersus ciuitates, quae defecerant, ingentem classem comparasset, repente veluti diis ipsis parricidium vindicantibus, orta tempestate classem naufragio amittit; nec quicquam illi ex tanto apparatu, praeter nudum corpus, & spiritum, & paucos naufragij comites residuos fortuna fecit. Misera quidem res, sed optanda Seleuco fuit: siquidem civitates, quae odio eius ad Ptolemaeum transierant, velut diis arbitris satisfactum sibi esset, repentina animorum mutatione in naufragij misericordiam versae, imperio se eius restituunt. Latus igitur malis suis, & damnis ditior redditus, veluti par viribus bellum Ptolemaeo infert: sed quasi ad ludibrium tantum fortuna natus esset, nec propter aliud opes regni recepisset, quam vt amitteret, victus praelio non multo quam post naufragium comitatior, trepidus Antiochiam confugit. Inde ad Antiochum fratrem literas facit: quibus auxilium eius implorat, oblata ei Asia, inter fines Tauri montis, in pramium lata opis. Antiochus autem cum esset annos 14. natus, supra aetatem regni auidus, occasionem non tam pio animo, quam offerebatur, arripuit. Sed latronis more, totum fratri eripere cupiens, puer scelerata, virilemq; sumit audaciam. Unde Hierax est cognominatus: quia non hominis, sed accipitris ritu, in alienis eripiendis vitam sectaretur. Interea Ptolemaeus cum Antiochum in auxilium Seleuco venire cognouisset, ne cum duobus uno tempore dimicaret, in annos decem cum Seleuco pacem facit: sed pace ab hoste data, interpellatur a fratre; qui conducto Gallorum mercenario exercitu pro auxilio bellum, pro fratre hostem, implorato exhibuit. In eo praelio virtute Gallorum victor quidem Antiochus fuit; sed Galli arbitrantes Seleucum in praelio cecidisse, in ipsum Antiochum arma vertere: liberius depopulaturi Asiam, si omnem sirpem regiam extinxissent. Quod vbi senserit Antiochus, velut a praedonibus, auro se redimit, societatemq; cum mercenariis suis iungit.
units.tr: 2 After Ptolemy's departure, Seleucus had equipped a great fleet against the cities that had revolted. But suddenly, as though the gods themselves were avenging the parricide, a storm arose and he lost the fleet in a shipwreck. Of so great a preparation, fortune left him nothing but his bare body, his breath, and a few companions of the shipwreck who survived. It was a wretched affair, yet it was one to be wished for by Seleucus. For the cities that had passed to Ptolemy out of hatred for him, as if the gods were witnesses and satisfaction had been made to them, were turned by a sudden change of feeling to pity for his shipwreck and restored themselves to his rule. Thus he was lifted up from his misfortunes and, enriched by his losses, he waged war on Ptolemy as if he were his equal in strength. But fortune, as if he had been born only for mockery, and had recovered the resources of his kingdom for no other purpose than to lose them, defeated in battle, with fewer companions than after the shipwreck, fled in alarm to Antioch. From there he wrote to his brother Antiochus, imploring his aid, and offered him Asia, as far as the Taurus mountains, as the reward for his help. Antiochus, then fourteen years old and greedy for royal power beyond his age, seized the opportunity with no pious purpose but as it was offered. Acting like a robber, wishing to snatch the whole kingdom from his brother, the boy took on a wicked and manly boldness. Hence he was surnamed Hierax, because, in the manner of a hawk and not of a man, he pursued life by seizing what belonged to others. Meanwhile Ptolemy, learning that Antiochus was coming to help Seleucus, made peace with Seleucus for ten years, so as not to fight two enemies at once. But when peace was granted by the enemy, Seleucus was attacked by his brother, who, having hired an army of Gallic mercenaries, sought war as aid and enmity against a brother. In that battle Antiochus indeed won the victory, through the valour of the Gauls; but the Gauls, supposing Seleucus had fallen in the battle, turned their arms against Antiochus himself, intending to plunder Asia more freely once the whole royal line was destroyed. When Antiochus perceived this, he bought himself off with gold, as if from pirates, and united himself in alliance with his mercenaries.

units.la: 3 Interea rex Bithyniae Eumenes, sparsis consusis fratribus bello intestina discordia, quasi Vacatem Asiae possessionem inuasurus victorem Antiochum, Gallosq; aggreditur: nec difficile saucios adhuc ex superiore congressione, integer ipse viribus, superat. Ea namque tempestate omnia bella in exitium Asiae gerebantur; vti quisq; fortior fuisset, Asiam velut praedam occupabat. Seleucus & Antiochus fratres bellum, propter Asiam gerebant: Ptolemaeus rex AEgypti, sub specie sororis vlionis, Asia inhiabat. Hinc Bithynus Eumenes, inde Galli (humiliorum semper mercenaria manus) Asiam depopulabantur, cum interea nemo defensor Asiae inter tot praedones inueniebatur. Victo Antiocho, cum Eumenes maiorem partem Asiae occupasset, ne tunc quidem dem fratres perdito praemio, propter quod bellum gerebant, concordare potuerunt; sed omisso externo hoste, in mutuum exitium bellum reparant. In eo Antiochus denuo victus, multorum dierum fuga fatigatus, tandem ad socerum suum Artamenem regem Cappadociae perfugit...
units.tr: 3 Meanwhile Eumenes, king of Bithynia, seeing the brothers divided by civil discord in war, attacked the Gauls, as though he were about to seize the possession of Asia, now left empty by the victorious Antiochus. Nor was it difficult for him to overcome them, still wounded from the earlier encounter, while he himself was fresh in strength. For in that time all the wars were waged to the ruin of Asia; whoever was the stronger seized Asia as plunder. Seleucus and Antiochus, the brothers, fought over Asia; Ptolemy, king of Egypt, under the pretext of avenging his sister, lusted after Asia. On one side Eumenes of Bithynia, on the other the Gauls (always a mercenary band of the lowly) laid Asia waste, while meanwhile no defender of Asia was to be found among so many plunderers. After Antiochus was defeated and Eumenes had occupied the greater part of Asia, the brothers still could not come to agreement even when the prize for which they fought was lost. Neglecting the foreign enemy, they renewed the war to mutual destruction. In that war Antiochus, again defeated and worn out by many days of flight, at last fled to his father-in-law Artamenes, king of Cappadocia...

units.la: uehitur. A quo cum primum benigne exceptus esset, interiectis diebus, cognito quod insidiae sibi pararentur, salutem fuga quaesiit. Igitur cum profugo nusquam tutus locus esset, ad Ptolemaeum hostem, cuius fidem tutiorem quam fratris exist imabat, decurrit; memor vel
units.tr: He was carried away. Once he had been kindly received by him, after some days, learning that plots were being laid against him, he sought safety in flight. Then, since there was nowhere safe for a fugitive, he ran to Ptolemy, his enemy, whose good faith he judged more reliable than his brother's, mindful of what he himself would have done to his brother, and of what he had deserved from him.

units.la: quae facturus fratri esset, vel quae meruisset a fratre. Sed Ptolemaeus non amici debito, quam hostis factus, seruari eum artissima custodia iubet. Hinc quoq; Antiochus opera cuiusdam meretricis adiutus, quam familiarius nouerat, deceptis custodibus elabitur; fugiensq; a latronibus interficitur. Seleucus quoq; iisdem ferme diebus, amisso regno, equo praecipitatus finitur. Sic fratres, quasi & germanis casibus, exules ambo, post regna, sceleru[m] suorum poenas luerunt.
units.tr: But Ptolemy, having become an enemy rather than a friend, ordered him to be kept under the strictest guard. Here too Antiochus, aided by the services of a certain courtesan whom he knew intimately, eluded his guards and escaped; and as he fled he was killed by robbers. Seleucus too, at about the same time, lost his kingdom and died after being thrown from his horse. Thus the brothers, both exiles, as if by a common fate, after their reigns paid the penalties of their crimes.

units.la: Quem frater Seleucus sequitur. In sceleratos fratres Numinis vindicta.
units.tr: Whom his brother Seleucus follows. Divine vengeance on the wicked brothers.

units.la: POMPEII TROGI EPI- TOMA HISTORIARVM LIBER XXVIII.
units.tr: THE EPITOME OF THE HISTORIES OF POMPEIUS TROGUS, BOOK XXVIII.
SUMMARY.

units.la: 1 Olympias Alexandri interfecta, Epirus grauiter Epirotæ vidua Demetrio affligitur. Demetrius Macedoni Ptiam filiam dat cedo vita abit. Huius filii vxorem, unde tragœdia & Philippi Antigonus tutelam bellorum initia. lam suscepit, quam prudenter administrat.
units.tr: 1 Olympias, daughter of Pyrrhus, is killed, and Epirus is grievously afflicted after the death of its widowed queen. Demetrius gives his daughter Phthia to the Macedonian king, and then dies. Antigonus takes up the guardianship of Demetrius's son and the wife of this son, from which come the tragedy and the beginnings of wars. He now assumes the regency of Philip and administers it prudently.

units.la: 2 Ætoli superbe respondent Romanis qui Acarnanis auxilium præbebant, & sus Spartanos, quorum rex arma mouerunt intrepide. Cleomenes viribus attritis
units.tr: 2 The Aetolians answer the Romans haughtily, the Romans who were giving help to the Acarnanians. The war against the Spartans follows, whose king Cleomenes took up arms fearlessly. Cleomenes, his forces worn down,

units.la: 4 Bellū Antigoni aduersus Spartanos, quorum rex arma mouerunt intrepide.
units.tr: 4 The war of Antigonus against the Spartans, whose king took up arms fearlessly.

units.la: 3 Filiis duobus morbo in Ægyptum profugit, vbi sublatus, Olympias non diu interficitur. Antigono moriuntur superuiuit. Laudamia filiæ tuo Philippus regnat.
units.tr: 3 With her two sons she fled into Egypt by way of sickness; there, having been carried off, Olympias was not long afterward killed. Antigonus died; she survived him. Laodamia, daughter of Philip, reigns.

units.la: OLYMPIAS Pyrrhi Epirotæ regis filia, amisso marito, eodem germano fratre Alexandro, cum tutelam filiorum ex eo susceptorum Pyrrhi & Ptolemaei, regni, administrationem in
units.tr: Olympias, daughter of Pyrrhus, king of the Epirots, having lost her husband and her brother Alexander, took upon herself the guardianship of the sons she had had by him, Pyrrhus and Ptolemaeus, and the administration of the kingdom.

units.la: se recepisset, ab Ætolis parteni Acarnaniæ, quam in portionem belli pater pupillorum acceperat, eripere volentibus, ad regem Macedoniæ Demetrium decurrit; eiq; habenti vxorem Antiochi regis Syriæ sororem, filiam suam Ptiam in matrimonium tradit: vt auxilium quod miseri cordia non poterat, iure cognationis obtineret. Fiunt igitur nuptiæ, quibus & noui matrimonij gratia acquiritur, & veteris offensa contrahitur. Nam prior vxor velut matrimonio pulsa, sponte sua ad fratrem Antiochum discedit; eumq;, in mariti bellum impellit. Acarnanes quoq; diffisi Epirotis, aduersus AEtolos auxilium Romanorum implorantes, obtinuerunt à Romano senatu, vt legati mitterentur, qui denuntiarent AEtolis, praesidia ab vrbibus Acarnania deducerent; 5 paterenturque esse liberos, qui soli quondam aduersus Troianos, auctores originis suae, auxilia Graecis non miserunt.
units.tr: When the Aetolians wished to snatch from her the part of Acarnania which her husband had received as his share of the war, she ran to Demetrius, king of Macedonia, and gave her daughter Phthia in marriage to him, though he already had a wife, the sister of Antiochus, king of Syria. She did this so that she might obtain by right of kinship the help which pity could not win her. The wedding therefore took place, by which the favour of a new marriage was gained and the offence of the old one was incurred. For the first wife, as if cast off by the marriage, went of her own accord to her brother Antiochus and urged him to make war on her husband. The Acarnanians, too, distrusting the Epirots and seeking Roman help against the Aetolians, obtained from the Roman senate that envoys be sent to warn the Aetolians to withdraw their garrisons from the cities of Acarnania; 5 and to allow them to be free, since they alone once did not send help to the Greeks against the Trojans, the originators of their own race.

units.la: 2 Sed AEtoli legationem Romanorum superbe audiuere: Poenos illis & Gallos, à quibus tot bellis occidio10 ne cafsint, exprobrantes; dicentesq;, prius illis portas aduersus Carthaginienses aperiendas, quas clauserit metus Punici belli, quam in Graeciam arma transferenda. Meminisse deinde iubent, qui quibus minentur: aduersus Gallos vrbem eos suam tueri non potuisse; ca15 ptamq;, non ferro defendisse, sed auro redemisse: Quam gentem se aliquanto maiore manu Graeciam ingressam, non solum nullis externis viribus sed ne domesticis quidem totis adiutos, vniuersam delesse; sedemq; sepulchrum eorum praebuisse, quam illi viribus, imperioq; suo proposuerant. Contra, Italiam, trepidis ex recti vrbis suae incendio Romanis, vniuersam ferme à Gallis occupatam. Priusigitur illis Gallos Italia pellendos, quam minentur AEtolis; prius q; sua defendenda. Quos autem bonos minesRomanos esse? nempe pastores, qui latrocinio iuslis dominis ademptum solum tenent: qui vxores cum proper originis debonestamenta non inuenirent, vi publica rapuerint: qui denique, vrbem ipsam parricidio condiderint; murorumq; fundamenta fraterno sanguine asperserint. AEtolos autem principes Graciae semper suisse; & sicut dignitate, ita & virtute ceteris praestitisse; socios denique, esse, qui Macedonas imperio terrarum florentes, semper contempserint; qui Philippum regem non timuerint; qui Alexandri Magni post Persus Indosque deuideuictos,cum omnes nomen eius horrerent,edicta spreuerint. Monere igitur se Romanos, contenti sint fortuna præsenti, nec prouocent arma, quibus & Gallos casos, & Macedonas contemptos videant. Sic dimissa legatione Romanorum,ne fortius locuti,quam fecisse viderentur, fines Epiri regni & Acarnaniæ depopulantur.
units.tr: 2 But the Aetolians heard the Roman envoys with arrogance. They reproached the Romans with the Carthaginians and Gauls, by whose wars they had almost been destroyed, 10 and said that the gates should first be opened against the Carthaginians, which the fear of the Punic war had closed, before arms were carried into Greece. Then they bade the envoys remember whom they were threatening: the Romans had not been able to defend their own city against the Gauls, and when it was taken they had not defended it with iron but ransomed it with gold. 15 That same people, having entered Greece with a much larger force, had been wholly destroyed, not only without any outside strength but not even fully aided by their own; and the land which they had meant to seize by their power and command had become their grave. On the other hand, Italy, with the Romans panicked by the burning of their city, had been almost wholly occupied by the Gauls. Therefore the Gauls should first be driven out of Italy, and the Romans should defend their own land before they threaten the Aetolians. And what sort of good men were the Romans, who threatened? Shepherds, surely, who held by robbery land taken from its rightful lords; who, when they could not find wives for lack of noble descent, seized them by public violence; who, finally, founded their city itself with parricide and sprinkled the foundations of its walls with a brother's blood. The Aetolians, on the other hand, had always been the leaders of Greece, and had excelled the others in honour as well as in courage; they were, in short, allies, and had always scorned the Macedonians, who flourished in empire over the lands; they had not feared King Philip; and after Alexander the Great had conquered the Persians and Indians, when all men shuddered at his name, they had spurned his edicts. They therefore warned the Romans to be content with their present fortune and not to provoke arms with which they saw that the Gauls had been overthrown and the Macedonians despised. So, the Roman embassy being dismissed, the Aetolians, lest they seem to have spoken more boldly than they had acted, laid waste the borders of the kingdom of Epirus and of Acarnania.

units.la: 3 Iam Olympias filiis regna tradiderat; & in locum Pyrrhi fratris defuncti Ptolemæus successerat: qui cum hostibus instructo exercitu obuius processisset, infirmitate correptus, in itinere decedit. Olympias quoq; non magno post tempore,gemino funerum vulnere afflicta, ægrum spiritum trahens, non diu filiis superuixit. Cum ex gente regia sola Nereis virgo,cum Laudamia sorore superesset, Nereis nubit Geloni Siciliæ regis filio:Laudamia autem cum in aram Dianæ confugisset, concursu populi interficitur. Quod facinus diy immortales assiduis cladibus gentis, & prope interitu totius populi vindicauerunt. Nam sterilitatem,famemq,passi,&intestina discordia vexati,externis adpostremum 20 bellis pene consumpti sunt: Miloq, Laudamiæ percussor in furorem versus, nunc ferro, nunc saxo, in summa dentibus laceratis visceribus, duodecima die interiit. His in Epiro gestis, interim in Macedonia Demetrius rex, relicto filio Philippo, paruulo admodum, decedit. 25 Cui Antigonus tutor datus, accepta in matrimonium matre pupilli, regem se constitui laborabat. Interiecto deinde tempore; cum seditione minaci Macedonum, clausus in regia teneretur, in publicum sine satellitibus procedit; proiectoque in vulgus diademate ac purpura, 30 dare hæc eos alteri iubet, qui aut imperare illis nesciat, aut cui parere ipsi sciant:se adhuc inuidiosum illud regnum,non voluptatibus,sed laboribus ac periculis sentire.Commemorat deinde beneficia sua: vt defectionem sociorum vindicauerit; vt Dardanos, Theffalosq; exultantes morte Demetrij regis compescuerit; vt denig; dignitatem Macedonum non solum defenderit, verumetiam auxerit. Quorum fi illos pœniteat, deponere imperium, & reddere illis munus suum; ipsi regem quarant, cui imperent. Cum populus pudore motus, recipere eum regnum iuberet, tamdiu recusauit, quoad seditionis auctores supplicio traderentur.
units.tr: 3 Now Olympias had handed over the kingdoms to her sons, and Ptolemaeus had succeeded in place of her brother Pyrrhus, who had died. When he had advanced to meet the enemy with his army drawn up, he was seized by illness and died on the march. Olympias too, not long afterward, struck by a double bereavement of funerals, and drawing her last breath, did not long survive her sons. When only Nereis, a virgin of the royal family, and Laodamia, her sister, were left, Nereis married Gelo, son of the king of Sicily; but Laodamia, having fled to the altar of Diana, was killed by a crowd of people. The immortal gods avenged this deed by the constant disasters of the nation and by the near destruction of the whole people. For, suffering from barrenness and famine, vexed by internal discord, they were at last almost consumed by foreign wars; and Milo, the slayer of Laodamia, driven mad, tore at himself now with iron, now with stone, and at last with his teeth, his entrails torn, and died on the twelfth day. With these things done in Epirus, meanwhile in Macedonia King Demetrius died, leaving his son Philip, still quite a little boy. Antigonus was given to him as guardian, and, having taken the boy's mother in marriage, he strove to have himself made king. Then, after some time, when a threatening sedition of the Macedonians held him shut up in the palace, he came out before the public without bodyguards; and, throwing the diadem and purple among the crowd, he bade them give these to another who either did not know how to rule them or whom they themselves knew how to obey: he said that he himself still felt that kingship, which was hated, not as pleasure but as toil and danger. He then recounted his services: how he had avenged the revolt of the allies, how he had checked the Dardanians and Thessalians, who were exulting at the death of King Demetrius, and how he had not only defended but even increased the dignity of the Macedonians. If they repented of these things, he said, let them lay down his power and return his office to him; they themselves might seek a king to rule over them. When the people, moved by shame, bade him take back the kingdom, he refused for as long as the authors of the sedition were not handed over to punishment.

units.la: 4 Post hac bellum Spartanus infert; qui foli Philippi Alexandriq, bellis, & imperium Macedonum, & omnibus metuenda arma contempserant. Inter duas nobilissimas gentes bellum, summis vtrimq; viribus fuit: cum hi pro vetere Macedonum gloria, illi non solum pro illibata libertate; sed etiam pro salute certarent. Victi Lacedæmonij, non ipsi tantum, sed etiam coniuges, liberiq; magno animo fortunam tulere. Nemo quippe in acie saluti pepercit; nulla amissum coniugem fleuit: filiorum mortem senes laudabant; patribus in acie cæsis filij gratulabantur; suam vicem omnes dolebant, quod non ipsi pro patria libertate cecidissent. Patentibus omnes domibus saucios excipiebant; vulnera curabant, lassos refciebat. Inter hac nullus in vrbe strepitus, nulla trepidatio; magisq; omnes publicam, quam priuatam fortunam lugebant. Inter hæc Cleomenes rex post multas hostium cædes, toto corpore, suo pariter & hostium cruore madens, superuenit; ingressusq; vrbem, non bumi consedit, non cibum aut potum poposcit, non deniq; armorum onus deposuit: sed acclinis parieti, cum quattuor millia sola ex pugna superfuisse conspexisset, hortatur vt se ad meliora reipublicæ tempora reseruarent. Tum cum coniuge & liberis Aegyptum ad Ptolemaeum profecisceretur: a quo honorifice susceptus, diu in summa P digna-
units.tr: 4 After this the Spartans made war; they alone had scorned the arms of Philip and Alexander, and the empire of the Macedonians, which all others feared. Between the two most noble peoples the war was fought with the utmost strength on both sides: the one side contended for the old glory of the Macedonians, the other not only for its unbroken liberty but also for its safety. The defeated Lacedaemonians bore their fortune with great courage, not only they themselves but also their wives and children. Indeed, no one in the battle spared his life; no woman wept for her lost husband; the old men praised the deaths of their sons; the sons congratulated their fathers who had fallen in battle; all lamented that they themselves had not fallen for the liberty of their country. With their houses open, everyone received the wounded, tended their wounds, and restored the exhausted. Meanwhile there was no noise in the city, no panic; all mourned the public fortune more than their private one. In the meantime King Cleomenes arrived, dripping with blood from his whole body, his own and his enemies', after many slaughters of the foe. Having entered the city, he did not sit down on the ground, did not ask for food or drink, and did not even lay down the weight of his arms; but, leaning against a wall, when he saw that only four thousand had survived the battle, he urged them to keep themselves for better times for the commonwealth. Then, with his wife and children, he set out for Egypt to Ptolemaeus, by whom he was received with honour and lived for a long time in the highest regard of the king.
The Spartans then wage war.

units.la: Qui victi, magno animo cladem acceptam fecerunt, patriæ amantes.
units.tr: They mourn not their private fortune but the public one.

units.la: Nec priuatæ, sed publicæ fortunam lugent.
units.tr: They mourn not private but public fortune.

units.la: Horum rex Cleomenes superstites hortatur vt reipub. consulant.
units.tr: Their king Cleomenes, while they survive, urges them to take thought for the commonwealth.

units.la: Ipse in Ægyptum profectus intetficitur. dignatione regis vixit. Postremo post Ptolemaei mortem, à filio eius cum omni familia interficitur. Antigonus autem, caesis occidione Spartanis, fortunam tanta urbis miseratus, à direptione milites prohibuit; veniam quoque his qui superfuerant dedit, praefatus bellum se cum Cleomene, non cum Spartanis habuisse: cuius fuga omnis ira eius finita fit: nec minori sibi gloriae fore, si ab eo seruata Lacedaemon à quo solo capta fit, proderetur. Parcere igitur se solo urbi ac tectis, quoniam homines quibus parceret, non superfuissent. Nec multo post ipse decedit, regnumque Philippo pupillo, annis 14. nato, tradidit.
units.tr: He himself, having gone to Egypt, is killed. He lived in the king's esteem. Finally, after the death of Ptolemaeus, he was killed with his whole family by Ptolemaeus's son. Antigonus, however, when the Spartans had been slaughtered, pitying the fortune of so great a city, forbade his soldiers to plunder it; he also granted pardon to those who had survived, declaring that he had waged war against Cleomenes, not against the Spartans; with Cleomenes' flight, all his anger had ended; and it would be no less glory to him if Lacedaemon, which had been taken by no one but him, were preserved by him. He would therefore spare the city and its buildings only, since there were no people left whom he might spare. Not long afterward he himself died, and handed the kingdom to Philip, his ward, who was fourteen years old.

units.la: POMPEII TROGI EPI- TOMA HISTORIARVM Liber XXIX.
units.tr: Pompeius Trogus, Epitome of the Histories, Book 29.
SUMMARY.

units.la: 1 Orbis multa imperia, nova regum successione mutantur, nominatim in Africa, Aegypto & Macedonia. | 3 Infandam hanc mentem speciosis verbis occultatam.
units.tr: 1 Many empires of the world change through a new succession of kings, especially in Africa, Egypt and Macedonia. | 3 This unspeakable intention, hidden under fair words.

units.la: 2 Philippus rex Macedoniae malo consilio impulsus, Romanis bellum in ferre constituit. | 4 Tandem, apertus hostis apparet, unde cruentum bellum, ipsi Philippo perniciosum simul ac ignominiosum.
units.tr: 2 Philip, king of Macedonia, impelled by an evil plan, resolved to make war on the Romans. | 4 At last he appeared as an open enemy, whence came a bloody war, ruinous to Philip himself and shameful as well.

units.la: [Woodcut initial] ISDEM ferme temporibus prope universi orbis imperia, nova regum successione mutata sunt. Nam & in Macedonia Philippus mortuo Antigono tutore, codemq; vitrico, annorum quatuor decim regnum suscepit; & in Asia intersecto Seleuco, impubes adhuc rex Antiochus constitutus est: Cappadociae quoq; regnum Ariarathi puero admodum pater ipse tradiderat: AEgyptum patre ac matre interfectis, occupauerat Ptolemaeus, cui ex facinoris crimine, cognomentum Philopator fuit. Sed & Spartani in locum Cleomenis substituerunt Lycurgum. Et neque temporibus mutatio deesset, apud Carthaginienses quoque aetate immatura dux Annibal constituitur, non penuria seniorum, sed odio Romanorum, quo imbutum eum a pueritia sciebant. Fatale non tam Romani, quam ipsi Africae malum. His regibus pueris, etsi nulli seniores aetatis rectores erant, tamen in suorum quisq; malorum vestigia intentis, magna indoles virtutis enituit. Solus Ptolemaeus sicut scelestus in occupando regno, ita & segnis in administrando fuit. Philippum Dardani, ceterique omnes finitimi populi, quibus velut immortale odium cum Macedonum regibus erat, contemptu aetatis assidue lacessebant. Contra ille 20 summotis hostibus, non contentus sua defendisse, vltro etiam AEtolis bellum inferre gestiebat.
units.tr: At about the same time, the empires of almost the whole world changed through a new succession of kings. In Macedonia, Philip took up the kingdom at the age of fourteen, after the death of Antigonus, his guardian and stepfather. In Asia, after Seleucus was murdered, the still underage Antiochus was installed as king. In Cappadocia, the father himself had handed the kingdom to his young son Ariarathes. Ptolemy occupied Egypt after his father and mother had been killed, and he received the surname Philopator from the guilt of that crime. The Spartans, too, put Lycurgus in place of Cleomenes. Nor was change lacking elsewhere: among the Carthaginians also, Hannibal was made commander at an immature age, not from any shortage of older men but from hatred of the Romans, in which they knew he had been steeped from boyhood. That was a disaster fated not so much for the Romans as for Africa itself. Although these boy kings had no older guardians, each one, keenly following the footsteps of his own ancestors' misdeeds, showed a great gift for virtue. Only Ptolemy, as wicked in seizing the kingdom as he was slack in governing it, was the exception. The Dardanians and all the other neighbouring peoples, who bore an almost immortal hatred toward the Macedonian kings, kept harassing Philip because of his youth. He, however, drove off his enemies and, not content with merely defending his own lands, was eager to make war on the Aetolians as well.

units.la: 2 Quae agitantem illum Demetrius rex Illyriorum, nuper a Paulo Romano consule victus, supplicibus precibus aggreditur, iniuriam Romanorum querens, qui 25 non contenti Italiae terminis, imperium spe improba totius orbis amplexi, bellum cum omnibus regibus gerant: sic illos Siciliae, sic Sardiniae, Hispaniaeq;, sic denique totius Africae imperium affectantes, bellum cum Poenis & Annibale suscepisse, sibi quoq; non aliam ob causam, 30 quam quod Italiae finitimus videbatur, bellum illatum: quasi nefas esset, aliquem regem iuxta imperij eorum terminos esse: sed & ipsi cauendum esse exemplum, cuius quato promptius nobilitas, fit regni, tanto sit Romanos acriores hostes habiturus. Super hac cedere se illi regno, quod Romani occupauerint profitetur, gratius habiturus, si in possessione imperij sui societum potius, quam hostes videret. Huiusmodi oratione impulit Philippum, vt omissis AEtolis, bellum Romanis inferret, minus negotij exististimantem, quod iam victos ab Annibale apud Trasimenum lacum audierat. Itaq; ne eodem tempore multis bellis detineretur, pacem cum AEtolis facit; non quasi alio bellum translaturus; sed vt Graciae quieti consulturus, quam nunquam in maiori periculo fuisse 10 affirmabat. Siquidem consurgentibus ab Occidente nouis Poenorum & Romanorum imperiis, quibus vna hac a Graecia atq; Asia sit mora, dum inter se bello discrimen imperij faciunt; ceterū statim victoribus transitum in Orientem fore. 15
units.tr: 2 While he was occupied with these plans, Demetrius, king of the Illyrians, recently defeated by the Roman consul Paulus, approached him with urgent pleas. He complained of the injustice of the Romans, who, not content with the bounds of Italy, had embraced an unscrupulous hope of empire over the whole world and were waging war on all kings. In this way, they had undertaken war with the Carthaginians and Hannibal, aiming at the empire of Sicily, of Sardinia, of Spain and finally of all Africa; and war had been brought to him too for no other reason than that he seemed to be a neighbour of Italy, as though it were a crime for any king to exist near the borders of their empire. He warned Philip that he too must take care, for the more readily the Romans could be seen to ennoble a kingdom, the fiercer enemies they would be to it. As for himself, he said he would gladly yield that kingdom, which the Romans had seized, if he could see Philip as an ally rather than an enemy in possession of his own realm. By such an argument he persuaded Philip to abandon the Aetolians and make war on the Romans, thinking it would be a small matter, since he had heard that they had already been defeated by Hannibal at Lake Trasimene. So, to avoid being tied down in many wars at once, he made peace with the Aetolians. He did this not because he intended to shift the war elsewhere, but because he meant to look after the peace of Greece, which he declared had never been in greater danger. For, with the new empires of the Carthaginians and the Romans rising in the West, Greece and Asia were held back only by the one delay, that these powers were fighting each other for mastery; otherwise the victors would at once have a passage into the East.

units.la: .3 Videre se itaq; ait consurgentem in Italia nubem illam, truci & cruenti belli, videre tonantem ac fulminantem ab occasu procellam, quam in quascunq; terrarum partes victoriae tempestas detulerit, magno cruoris imbre omnia foedaturam. Frequenter Graeciam in- 20 gentes motus passam, nunc Persarum, nunc Gallorum, nunc Macedonum bellis; sed omnia illa leuia fuisse existimaturos, si ea quae nunc in Italia concurrat manus, extra terram illam se effuderit. Cernere se quam cru- enta & sanguinaria inter se bella, vtriq; populi & vi- 25 ribus copiarum, & ducum artibus, gerant: quae tabies finiri solo partis alterius interitu, sine ruina finitimorum non possit. Feros igitur animos victorum minus quidem Macedoniae, quam Graeciae timendos, quia & remotior, & in vindictam sui robustior sit: scire tamen 30 se eos qui tantis viribus concurrant; non contentos hos sine victoria fore; metuendum quoque sibi certamen eorum, qui superiores extiterint. Hoc praetextu finito cum AEtolis bello, nihil aliud quam Punorum Romanorumq; bella respiciens, singulorum vires perpendebat. Sed nec Romani, tametsi Pœni & Annibal in ceruicibus erant, soluti metu Macedonico videbatur: quippe terrebat eos & vetus Macedonum deuicti Orientis 5 gloria, & Philippus studio Alexandri aemulationis incensus, quem promptum in bella, industriumq; cognoue- rant.
units.tr: 3 He said, therefore, that he saw that dark cloud of cruel and bloody war gathering in Italy, and saw a storm thundering and flashing from the West, which, wherever the tempest of victory carried it, would stain everything with a great rain of blood. Greece had often suffered great upheavals, now from the wars of the Persians, now of the Gauls, now of the Macedonians; but he thought all those would seem slight if the forces now meeting in Italy poured out beyond that land. He saw how bloody and murderous the wars were that the two peoples waged against each other, with their forces and the skill of their commanders, and how this plague could end only with the destruction of one side, without the ruin of their neighbours. Therefore, the fierce spirits of the victors were to be feared, though less for Macedonia than for Greece, since Macedonia was more remote and stronger for taking revenge. Yet he knew that those who clashed with such great forces would not be content without victory, and that the struggle of those who came out on top was also a thing to fear. Under this pretext, once the war with the Aetolians was ended, he weighed the strength of each side, looking at nothing but the wars of the Carthaginians and the Romans. But the Romans, even though the Carthaginians and Hannibal were at their necks, did not seem free of fear of Macedonia: for they were frightened both by the old glory of the Macedonians, who had conquered the East, and by Philip, who was fired with the zeal of rivalling Alexander, and whom they had come to know as ready for war and diligent.

units.la: 4 Igitur Philippus cum iterato prælio victos à Pœ10 nis Romanos didicisset, aperte hostem se his professus, naues, quibus in Italiam exercitum traiiceret, fabricare coepit. Legatum deinde ad Annibalem, iungenda societatis gratia, cum epistolis mittit: qui comprehensus, & ad senatum perductus, incolumis dimissus est, nō 15 in honorem regis, sed ne dubius adhuc, indubitatus hostis redderetur. Postea vero cum Romanis nuntiatum esset, in Italiam Philippum copias traiecturum, Lauinum pratorem cum instructu nauibus ad prohibendum transitum mittunt. Qui cum in Græciam traiecisset, 20 multis promissis impellit AEtolos bellum aduersus Philippum suscipere. Philippus quoq; Achaeos in Romanorum bella solicitat. Interea & Dardani Macedoniae fines vastare coeperunt, abductiq; 20. millibus captiuorum, Philippum à Romano bello ad tuendum regnum 25 reuocauerunt. Dum haec aguntur, Lauinus Prator, iuncta cum Attalo rege societate, Græciam populatur. Quibus cladibus perculsae ciuitates, auxilium petentes, Philippum legationibus fatigant; necnon & Illyriorum reges lateri eius haeretes, assiduis precibus promissa exi30 gebant. Super haec vastati Macedones, vltionem flagitabant. Quibus tot tantisq; rebus obsessus, cui rei primum occurreret, ambigebat: omnibus tamen propediem auxilia se missurum pollicetur; non quia facere posset
units.tr: 4 Therefore, when Philip learned that the Romans had been defeated by the Carthaginians in a second battle, he openly declared himself their enemy, and began to build ships by which he might carry an army into Italy. Then he sent an envoy with letters to Hannibal to form an alliance. He was captured and brought before the senate, and was released unharmed, not out of honour to the king, but so that the enemy, still doubtful, would not be made certain. Later, when it was reported to the Romans that Philip was going to transport troops into Italy, they sent the praetor Laevinus with a fleet to block the crossing. When he had crossed into Greece, he persuaded the Aetolians with many promises to take up war against Philip. Philip, for his part, tried to stir up the Achaeans to join the Roman wars. Meanwhile the Dardanians began to lay waste the borders of Macedonia, and having carried off twenty thousand captives, they called Philip away from the Roman war to defend his kingdom. While these things were going on, Laevinus the praetor, having joined in alliance with King Attalus, ravaged Greece. The states, shattered by these disasters, sought help and wearied Philip with embassies; the kings of the Illyrians, too, clinging to his side, demanded with constant entreaties the promises he had made. Besides this, the Macedonians, laid waste, were clamouring for vengeance. Beset by so many and so great troubles, he hesitated over which to meet first; yet he promised all of them that he would soon send help, not because he could do what he promised

units.la: posset quæ promittebat, sed vt spe impletos, in societatis iure retineret. Prima tamē illi expeditio aduersus Dardanos fuit: qui absentiam eius occupantes, maiore belli mole Macedoniæ imminebant. Cum Romanis quoque pacem facit, contentus interim bellum Macedonicum dissimulasse: Philopœmeni Achæorum duci, quem ad Romanos, sociorum animos sollicitare didicerat, insidias pratendit. Quibus ille cognitis, vitatisq; discedere ab eo Achæos auctoritate sua coëgit.
units.tr: but so that, sustained by hope, they would remain bound by the law of alliance. His first expedition, however, was against the Dardanians, who, seizing the opportunity of his absence, were threatening Macedonia with a greater force of war. He also made peace with the Romans, content meanwhile to have disguised the Macedonian war. He laid a trap for Philopoemen, the leader of the Achaeans, whom he had learned was trying to win over the allies to the Romans. When Philopoemen discovered this and avoided it, he forced the Achaeans, by his own authority, to withdraw from Philip.
The Epitome of the Histories of Pompeius Trogus
BOOK XXX.

units.la: 1 Ptolemæi Ægyptii regis luxuria, vecordia, parricidia. cipiunt, Philippumq; prius bello reducunt ad humilioremSmentem.
units.tr: 1 The luxury, madness and parricides of Ptolemy, king of Egypt. He takes up the struggle and first brings Philip back to a humbler frame of mind by war.

units.la: 2 Miserrimus Ægypti status sub turpissimo principe, cuius meretrix & lenones crudeli fato pereunt.
units.tr: 2 The most wretched condition of Egypt under a most disgraceful prince, whose mistress and pimps perish by a cruel fate.

units.la: 3 Mortuo Ptolemæo Romani tutelam pupilli aduersus Antiochum Syrum & Philippum Macedonē suf- cipiunt, Philippumq; prius bello reducunt ad humiliorem mentem.
units.tr: 3 After Ptolemy's death the Romans take up the guardianship of the boy against Antiochus the Syrian and Philip the Macedonian. They first bring Philip back to a humbler mind by war.

units.la: 4 Terræmotus ingentes. Romani pacem repudiant. Philippus & Flaminus suos ad pugnam accendunt. Macedonas Romana fortuna vincit, & Philippus spoliatur.
units.tr: 4 Huge earthquakes. The Romans reject peace. Philip and Flamininus rouse their men to battle. Roman fortune conquers the Macedonians, and Philip is stripped of his possessions.

units.la: HILIPPO in Macedonia magnis rebus intento, in Ægypto Ptolemæi diuersi mores erant. Quippe regno parricidio parto, & ad necē utriusq; parentu, cade etiam fratris adiuncta, velut reb. feliciter gestis, luxuriæ se tradiderat; regisque mores omnis sequuta regia erat. Itaque non amici tantū, præfectiq;, verumetiā omnis exercitus depositis militiæ studiis, otio ac desidia corrupti marcebant. Quibus rebus cognitis, Antiochus rex Syriæ, veteri inter se regnorum odio stimulante, repentino bello multas urbes eius oppressit, ipsamq; Aegyptum aggreditur. Trepidare igitur Ptolemæus; legationibus missis, quoad vires pararet, morari Antiochum. Magno deinde in Græcia exercitu & conducto, secundū prælium facit; spoliasset q; regno Antiochum si fortunam virtute iuuisset. Sed contentus recuperatione urbium, quas amiserat, facta pace, auide materiam quietis arripuit, revolutusq; in luxuriam, occisa Eurydice uxore, eademq; sorore sua, Agathoclia merētricis illecebris capitur. Atq; ita omnem magnitudinem nominis, ac maiestatis oblitus, noctes in stupris, dies in conuiuiis consumit. Adduntur Instrumenta luxuriæ, tympana & crepundia; nec iam spectator rex, sed magister nequitiæ, neruorū oblectamenta modulatur. Hæc primo laborantis regiæ tacitæ pestes, & occultæ fuere.
units.tr: While Philip was occupied with great affairs in Macedonia, the conduct of Ptolemy in Egypt was very different. Having obtained the kingdom through parricide, and with the murders of both his parents followed by the killing of his brother, he had given himself over to luxury, as though his affairs had prospered. The whole court followed the king's example. Accordingly not only his friends and prefects but the whole army too, having laid aside their military zeal, grew sluggish and rotted away in idleness and sloth. When these conditions became known, Antiochus, king of Syria, spurred on by the old hatred between the two kingdoms, suddenly made war, overran many of Ptolemy's cities and attacked Egypt itself. Ptolemy was alarmed. He sent embassies and delayed Antiochus while he prepared his forces. Then, with a large army raised and hired in Greece, he fought a successful battle; and he would have stripped Antiochus of his kingdom had he supported fortune with courage. But he was content with recovering the cities he had lost, made peace, and eagerly seized the pretext for rest. Then, sliding back into luxury, after killing his wife Eurydice, who was also his own sister, he was captivated by the allurements of the courtesan Agathoclia. Thus, forgetting all the greatness of his name and majesty, he spent his nights in debauchery and his days at banquets. Instruments of luxury were added, drums and rattles; and the king, no longer a spectator, but a master of wickedness, played the entertainments of stringed instruments himself. These were the first hidden plagues of the crumbling court, secret and unseen.

units.la: 2 Deinde crescente licentia, iam nec parietibus regiæ domus contineri meretricis audacia potest: quam proteruiorem; sociata cum Agathocle fiatre, ambitiosæ pulchritudinis scorto, quotidiana regis stupra faciebat. Accedebat & mater Oenanthe, quæ gemina subolis ui lecebris deuinctum regem tenebat. Itaq; non contenta rege, iam etiam regnum possident, iam in publico visuntur, iam salutantur, iam comitantur. Agathocles regis lateri iunctus, ciuitatem regebat; tribunatus, præfecturas, & ducatus mulieres ordinabat; nec quisquam in suo regno minus, quam ipse rex poterat: cum interim relicto quinquenni ex Eurydice sorore filio, moritur: sed mors eius, dum pecuniam regiam mulieres rapiunt, & imperium inita cum perditißimis societate occupare conantur, diu occultata fuit. Rc tamen cognita, concursu multitudinis & Agathocles occiditur, & multeres in vltionem Eurydicis patibulis suffiguntur. Morte regis, supplicio meretricum velut expiata regni infamia, legatos Alexandrini ad Romanos misere, orantes vt tutelam pupilli susciperent; tuerenturque regnum AEgypti, quod iam Philippum & Antiochum, factaꝫ inter se paćtione, diuisisse dicebant.
units.tr: 2 Then, as licence grew, the courtesan's audacity could no longer be contained even within the walls of the royal house. She became more and more shameless. Allied with Agathocles, her brother, a catamite of ambitious beauty, she committed daily debaucheries with the king. Her mother Oenanthe also joined them, and by the lures of this pair of offspring she held the king in bondage. So, not content with the king, they now possessed the kingdom itself; now they were seen in public, now they were greeted, now they were attended. Agathocles, joined to the king's side, governed the state; the women appointed tribunes, prefects and commanders; and no one in the kingdom had less power than the king himself. Meanwhile he died, leaving a five-year-old son by Eurydice, his sister. But his death was concealed for a long time, while the women plundered the royal treasury and, in league with the most depraved men, tried to seize the power. When the matter became known, Agathocles was killed by a crowd of people, and the women were fastened to gibbets in revenge for Eurydice. With the king's death and the punishment of the courtesans, as if the infamy of the kingdom had been expiated, the Alexandrians sent envoys to the Romans, begging them to take up the guardianship of the boy and to protect the kingdom of Egypt, which, they said, Philip and Antiochus had already divided between them by an agreement.

units.la: 3 Grata legatio Romanis fuit, causam belli aduersus Philippum quaerentibus, qui insidiatus eis temporibus Punici belli fuerat. Huc accedebat, quod Poenis & Annibale superato, nullius magis arma metuebant, reputantibus quantum motum Pyrrhus parua manu Macedonum in Italia fecisset, quantasqz res Macedones in Oriente gessissent. Mittuntur itaqz legati, qui Antiocho & Philippo denuntient regno AEgypti abstineat. Mittitur & M. Lepidus in AEgyptum, qui tutorio nomine regnum pupilli administret. Dum haec aguntur, interim legationes Attali regis, & Rhodiorum, iniurias Philippi querentes, Romam venerunt. Qua res omnem cunćtationem Macedonici belli senatui exemit,
units.tr: 3 The embassy was welcome to the Romans, who were seeking a cause for war against Philip, who had plotted against them during the Punic War. Moreover, with the Carthaginians and Hannibal defeated, they feared no one's arms more, and they considered how great a stir Pyrrhus had caused in Italy with a small force, and what great deeds the Macedonians had performed in the East. Therefore envoys were sent to warn Antiochus and Philip to keep away from the kingdom of Egypt. Marcus Lepidus was also sent to Egypt to administer the kingdom in the name of guardian for the boy. While these things were being done, meanwhile envoys of King Attalus and of the Rhodians, complaining of the wrongs done by Philip, came to Rome. This event removed from the senate all hesitation about the Macedonian war.

units.la: {} Statim igitur titulo ferendi socijs auxilij, bellum ad‑ uersus Philippum decernitur, legionesq; cum consule in Macedoniam mittuntur. Nec multo post tempore, tota Græcia fiducia Romanorum, aduersus Philippum, spe pristinæ libertatis erecta, bellum ei intulit: Atq; ita cum rex vndiq; vrgeretur, pacem petere compellitur. Dein‑de cum exposita conditiones pacis à Romanis essent, re‑ petere sua & Attalus, & Rhodij, & Achai, & AEtoli cœpere. Contra Philippus adduci se posse, vt Romanis pareat, concedebat; ceterum indignum esse, Græcos à Philippo & Alexandro maioribus suis victos, & sub iugum
units.tr: Therefore at once, under the pretext of bringing aid to allies, war was decreed against Philip, and legions were sent into Macedonia with the consul. Not long afterwards, all Greece, trusting in the Romans and roused against Philip by hope of its former liberty, made war on him. And so, since the king was pressed on every side, he was compelled to seek peace. Then, when the terms of peace were set out by the Romans, Attalus, the Rhodians, the Achaeans and the Aetolians began to demand their own back. Philip, on the other hand, conceded that he could be brought to obey the Romans; but he said it was unworthy that Greeks, conquered by Philip and by Alexander, his ancestors, and

units.la: Philippus pacem petere, & quæ aliis damna inferre voluerat, ipse pati compellitur. jugum Macedonici imperij subactos, veluti victores leges pacis sibi dicere, quibus prius sit servitutis ratio reddenda; quam libertas vindicanda. Ad postremum tamen petente eo, indutia duorum mensium data, ut pax qua in Macedonia non conveniebat, Roma a senatu peteretur,
units.tr: Philip was compelled to seek peace, and to suffer himself the losses he had wished to inflict on others. brought under the yoke of the Macedonian empire, should dictate peace terms to him as if they were victors, and that they should first render an account of servitude before liberty was claimed. At last, however, when he petitioned, a truce of two months was granted, so that peace, which was not agreed in Macedonia, might be sought from the senate at Rome.

units.la: 4 Eodem anno inter insulas Theramenem & Therasiam, medio utriusque ripa & maris spatio, terraemotus fuit. In quo, cum admiratione navigantium, pente ex profundo cum calidis aquis insula emerserit. In Asia quoque eadem die idem motus terra Rhodum, multasque, alias civitates graui ruinarum labe concussit; quasdam solidas absorbuit. Quo prodigio territis omnibus, vates cecinere, oriens Romanorum imperium, vetus Gracorum ac Macedonum voraturum. Interim a senatu repudiata pace, Philippus in societatem belli Nabin tyrannum solicitat. Atqui ita, cum in aciem exercitu instructis e diuerso hostibus produxisset, hortari suos coepit, referendo Persas, Bactros, Indosq;, & omnem A- fiam, Orientis finem, à Macedonibus perdomitam, tanto q; fortius hoc bellum quam illa suslinendum, quanto sit libertas imperio carior. Sed & Flamininus Romanus consul, relatione rerum recentissime gestarum, suos stimulabat in prælium, ostendendo hinc Carthaginem
units.tr: 4 In the same year, between the islands of Therasia and Thera, in the middle of the sea and the space between their shores, there was an earthquake. During it, to the amazement of sailors, an island rose up from the deep together with hot waters. In Asia too, on the same day, the same tremor shook Rhodes and many other cities with the heavy collapse of ruins; some it swallowed up entirely. Everyone was terrified by this portent, and seers prophesied that the rising empire of the Romans would devour the ancient power of the Greeks and Macedonians. Meanwhile, the peace having been rejected by the senate, Philip sought to draw Nabis, the tyrant, into an alliance in the war. And so, when he had led his army out into the line of battle with the enemy drawn up opposite, he began to exhort his men, reminding them of the Persians, Bactrians and Indians, and all Asia, the limit of the East, subdued by the Macedonians; and he said that this war must be waged the more bravely, the dearer liberty is than empire. But the Roman consul Flamininus too, by recounting the deeds recently done, roused his men to battle, showing on the one hand Carthage with Sicily conquered by Roman valour, and on the other Italy and Spain subdued;

units.la: cum Sicilia, inde Italiam & Hispaniam Romana virtute perdomitas: nec Annibalem quidem Alexandro Magno postponendum; quo Italia pulso, Africam ipsam tertiam partem mundi superauerint. Sed nec Macedonas veteri fama, sed præsentibus viribus æstimandos: quia non cum Alexandro Magno, quem inuictum audierant, nec cum exercitu eius, qui totum Orientem deuicerat, bellum gerant; sed cum Philippo puero immatura ætate, qui regni terminos aduersus finitimos
units.tr: and that Hannibal was not to be ranked below Alexander the Great, since after he had been driven out of Italy they had conquered Africa itself, the third part of the world. But the Macedonians were not to be judged by their old reputation, but by their present strength: for they were not waging war with Alexander the Great, whom they had heard was unconquered, nor with his army, which had subdued the whole East; they were waging it with Philip, a boy of immature age, who could hardly defend the borders of his kingdom against his neighbours;

units.la: {a}agre defendat; & cum his Macedonibus, qui non ita pridem prædæ Dardanis fuerunt. Illos maiorum decora, se suorum militum commemorare. Non enim alio exercitu Annibalem & Pœnos, & totum ferme Occidentem, sed his ipsis, quos in acie habeat militibus, subactos. His adhortationibus utrimque concitati milites, prælio concurrunt, alteri Orientis, alteri Occidentis imperio gloriantes; ferentesque in bellum, alij maiorum suorum antiquam & obsoletam gloriam, alij virētem recentibus experimentis virtutis florem. Sed Macedonas Romana fortuna vicit. Fractus itaque bello Philippus, pace à Flaminino consule petita, nomen quidem regium retinuit; sed omnibus Græciæ urbibus, velut reliquæ membris extra terminos antiquæ possessionis amissis, solam Macedoniam retinuit. Offensi tamen Ætoli, quod non ex arbitrio eorum Macedonia quoque adempta regi, & data sibi in præmium belli effet, legatos ad Antiochum mittunt, qui eum adulatione magnitudinis, in Romana bella, ipse societatis universæ Græciæ, impellerent.
units.tr: and with those Macedonians who not long before had been plunder for the Dardanians. The Romans, he said, called to mind the glories of their ancestors and their own soldiers. For Hannibal and the Carthaginians, and almost the whole West, had been subdued not by another army, but by these very soldiers whom they had in the line of battle. Roused by these exhortations on both sides, the soldiers rushed into battle, the one boasting of the empire of the East, the other of the West; and they went into war, some carrying the ancient and faded glory of their ancestors, others the flower of courage fresh from recent proofs. But Roman fortune conquered the Macedonians.
