Philip, therefore, broken in war, and having sought peace from the consul Flamininus, kept the royal title; but, with all the cities of Greece lost, like limbs cut off beyond the limits of his ancient possessions, he retained only Macedonia. Nevertheless the Aetolians, offended that Macedonia too had been taken from the king at their own discretion and given to them as a reward for the war, sent envoys to Antiochus, who were to urge him, by flattering his greatness, to go to war with the Romans, and to join himself as leader of the whole alliance of Greece.

units.la: POMPEII TROGI EPI- TOMA HISTORIARVM LIBER XXXI.
units.tr: POMPEII TROGI EPITOMA HISTORIARVM, BOOK XXXI.
SUMMARY.

units.la: 1 Antiochum Syrum legatione coercent Romani. Annibal fugiens ad Antiochum Nabide Græciam libera chum cuiusum dirigit. ri iubent. Annibalis nomen Romanis formidabile.
units.tr: 1 The Romans check Antiochus the Syrian by an embassy. Hannibal, fleeing, makes his way to Antiochus. They order Nabis to free Greece. The name of Hannibal is dreaded by the Romans.

units.la: 2 Romanorum insidias Nabis duobus prœliis fractus, post Romanorum
units.tr: 2 Nabis, broken in two battles by the Romans' snares, takes up arms again after the Romans have departed.

units.la: discessum arma mouet. Annibalis ad Antiochum de opprimedis Romanis consilium. Annibalis sana consilia rident: inde subuersio Antiochi qui terrestri & nauali praelio a Romanis superatur.
units.tr: Hannibal's plan to crush the Romans is presented to Antiochus. His sound counsels are laughed at, and so Antiochus is overthrown, being defeated by the Romans in a land battle and a sea battle.

units.la: 4 Carthaginienses ab Antiocho sollicitari rem Romanis significant, qui politico strategemate Annibalem ab Antiocho diuelluut. 7 Scipiones ducto in Africam exercitu pacis leges Antiocho praescribut, quas ipse repudiat.
units.tr: 4 The Carthaginians, being courted by Antiochus, report the matter to the Romans, who by a shrewd stratagem pull Hannibal away from Antiochus. 7 The Scipios lead an army into Africa and prescribe terms of peace to Antiochus, which he rejects.

units.la: 5 Iterarum Annibalis consilium de bello in Italia inferendo. 8 Bello reparato & punga commissa, caesis quinquaginta Asiaticorum milibus, Antiochus subactus pacem petit & obtinet.
units.tr: 5 Hannibal's plan of carrying the war into Italy again. 8 The war is renewed, a battle is joined, fifty thousand Asiatics are slain, and Antiochus, subdued, seeks peace and obtains it.
6 The flatterers of Antiochus.

units.la: ORTVO Ptolemaeo Philopatore regi AEgypti, contemptaq, paruuli filij eius aetate, qui in spem regni relictus, praeda etiam domesticis erat, Antiochus rex Syriae occupare AEgyptum statuit. Itaque Phoenicem, ceterasque Syriae quidem, sed iuris AEgypti ciuitates cum inuasisset, legatos ad eum Senatus mittit, qui denuntiarent ei, abstineret regno pupilli, postremis patris precibus fidei suae traditi.
units.tr: When Ptolemy Philopator, king of Egypt, had died, and the youth of his little son was held in contempt, the boy having been left with hopes of the kingdom but being even the prey of his own household, Antiochus, king of Syria, resolved to seize Egypt. So, having invaded Phoenicia and the other cities of Syria that were subject to Egypt, he was sent envoys by the Senate, who warned him to keep away from the kingdom of the ward, who had been entrusted to the good faith of the Romans by his father's last prayers.

units.la: Quibus spretis, interiecto tempore alia legatio superuenit, quae omissa pupilli persona, ciuitates, iure belli fallas populi Romani in integrum restitui iubebat. Abuenti, bellum denuntiatum: quod ille facile susceптum, infeliciter gesit.
units.tr: When these warnings were scorned, after an interval another embassy arrived, which, setting aside the person of the ward, ordered that the cities, taken by the right of war, be restored to their former state under the protection of the Roman people. When he refused, war was declared on him; he undertook it readily but conducted it unsuccessfully.

units.la: 25 Eodem tempore & Nabis tyrannus multas Graeciae ciuitates occupauerat. Igitur senatus, ne uno tempore duplici bello Romanae vires detinerentur, scripsit Flaminino, si ei videatur, sicuti Macedonia
units.tr: 25 At the same time the tyrant Nabis had also seized many cities of Greece. Therefore the Senate, so that Roman forces would not be held by a double war at the same time, wrote to Flamininus that, if he thought fit, he should free Greece from Nabis just as he had freed Macedonia from Philip.

units.la: 30 a Philippo, ita Graeciam a Nabide liberet, Ob quam causam imperium ei prorogatum est. Terribile quippe Antiochi bellum Annibalis nomen faciebat, quem aemuli eius occultis mandatis, cum Antiocho iniisse socie-
units.tr: 30 For this reason his command was prorogued. For the name of Hannibal made the war with Antiochus a terrifying one, and his rivals accused him among the Romans, by secret instructions, of having entered into an alliance with Antiochus.

units.la: tatem apud Romanos criminabantur: negantes eum æquo animo sub legibus viuere, assuetum imperio, & immoderata licentia militari; semperque tadio quietis vrbana, nouas belli causas circumspicere: quæ etsi falsa nuntiata fuissent, apud timentes tamen pro veris habebantur.
units.tr: They asserted that he could not live calmly under laws, being accustomed to command and to unbridled military license, and that, always weary of the quiet of the city, he was looking about for new causes of war. Even if these charges were falsely reported, they were nonetheless held as true by the fearful.

units.la: 2 Denique senatus metu perculsus, ad speculandos actus Annibalis, legatum in Africam Gnæum Seruilium mittit: eique tacitis mandatis præcipit, si posset, eum per emulos eius interficeret, metuque inuisi nominis, tandem populum Romanum liberaret. Sed res Annibalem non diu latuit, virum ad prospicienda cauendaque pericula peritum; nec minus in secundis aduersa, quam in aduersis secunda cogitantem. Igitur cum tota die in oculis principum, legatique Romani, in foro Carthaginiensium obuersatus in supremum fuisset, appropinquante vespere, equum conscendit; & rus vrbanum, quod propter littus maris habebat, ignaris seruis, iusso, ad portam reuertentem opperiri, contendit. Habebat ibi naues cum remigibus occulto sinu littoris abscondita: Erat & grandis pecunia in eo agro præparata, vt cum res exegisset, nec facultas fugam, nec inopia moraretur.
units.tr: 2 Finally the Senate, struck with fear, sent Gnaeus Servilius to Africa as legate to watch Hannibal's actions, and with secret instructions ordered him, if he could, to have Hannibal killed through his rivals, so that the Roman people might at last be freed from the fear of a hated name. But the matter did not long escape Hannibal, a man skilled at foreseeing and guarding against dangers, who thought no less of adversity in prosperity than of prosperity in adversity. So, having spent the whole day in the sight of the leaders and the Roman legate in the forum of the Carthaginians, as evening approached he mounted a horse and, ordering his slaves, who knew nothing, to wait for him at the gate on his return, he made for his country house, which he had by the seashore. There he had ships with rowers hidden in a secret inlet of the shore. A large sum of money was also prepared on that estate, so that, when the matter demanded it, neither lack of means for flight nor poverty would delay him.

units.la: Lecta igitur feruorum iuuentute, quorum copiam Itacorum captiuorum numerus augebat, nauem conscendit, cursumque ad Antiochum dirigit. Postera die ciuitas principem suum, ac tum temporis consulem, in foro exspectabat. Quem vt profectum nuntiatum est, non aliter quam si vrbs capta esset, omnes trepidauere, exitio famæque sibi fugam eius ominati sunt. Legatus vero Romanus quasi bellum iam illatum Italiæ ab Annibale esset, tacitus Romam regreditur, trepidumque nuntium refert.
units.tr: Therefore, having chosen the young men among his slaves, whose number was increased by the captive Itacans, he boarded the ship and directed his course to Antiochus. The next day the city waited in the forum for its leader, who was then also consul. When it was announced that he had departed, everyone trembled as if the city had been captured, and they took his flight as an omen of ruin and famine for themselves. The Roman legate, however, as if Hannibal had already brought war upon Italy, returned to Rome in silence and reported the frightened news.

units.la: 3 Interim in Graciam Flamininus, iuncta cum quibusdam ciuitatibus societate, Nabidem tyrannum duobus continuis prœliis subegit; & grauiter fractum velut exsanguem in regno reliquit. Sed libertate Gracia restituta, eductisq; ab vrbibus præsidiis, cum Romanus exercitus in Italiam reportatus esset, velut vacuarursus possessione solicitatus, multas ciuitates repentino bello inuasit. Quibus rebus exterriti Achai,ne vicinum Romalum etiam ad se perferet,bellum aduersus Nabidem decernunt, ducemq; prætorem suum Philopœmenem, insignis industriæ virum, constituunt: cuius in eo bello tanta virtus eniluit, vt opinione omnium Flaminino Romano imperatori compararetur. Eodem tempore Annibal cum ad Antiochum peruenisset, velut deorum munus excipitur:tantusque eius aduentu ardor animi regis accessit, vt non tam de bello, quam de præmiis victoriæ cogitaret, Sed Annibal, cui nota Romana virtus erat, negabat opprimi Romanos nisi in Italia posse. Ad hoc sibi centum naues, & decem millia peditum, & mille equites poscebat: promittens hac manu non minus bellum, quam gesserit, Italiæ restauraturum; & in Asiam regi cedenti, aut victoriam de Romanis, aut aequas pacis conditiones relaturum: quippe & Hispanis bello flagrantibus, ducem tantum deesse; & Italiam notiorem sibi nunc, quam pridem fuisse; sed nec Carthaginem quieturam, sociamque se ei sine mora præbituram.
units.tr: 3 Meanwhile in Greece Flamininus, having joined with some cities in alliance, subdued the tyrant Nabis in two successive battles, and left him heavily broken, as if drained of blood, in his kingdom. But Greece was restored to liberty, the garrisons were withdrawn from the cities, and when the Roman army had been brought back to Italy, Nabis, as if stirred by the vacated possession, suddenly attacked many cities with war. Alarmed by these events, the Achaeans, lest the Romans, being their neighbours, should also reach them, decreed war against Nabis and appointed as their praetor leader Philopoemen, a man of remarkable industry. In that war his valour shone so brightly that in the opinion of all he was compared to the Roman commander Flamininus. At the same time Hannibal, having arrived at Antiochus, was received as if he were a gift of the gods, and such ardour came into the king's spirit by his arrival that he thought less of the war than of the rewards of victory. But Hannibal, who knew Roman valour, denied that the Romans could be crushed except in Italy. Besides, he demanded for himself a hundred ships, ten thousand foot soldiers and a thousand horsemen, promising that with this force he would renew the war in Italy no less than he had waged it, and would bring back to the king, who was staying in Asia, either victory over the Romans or fair terms of peace. For the Spaniards too were blazing with war and only a leader was lacking; Italy was now better known to him than it had been long before; and Carthage would not remain quiet and would without delay show itself his ally.

units.la: 4 Cum regi consilia placuissent,mittitur Carthaginem vnus ex comitibus Annibalis, qui in bellum cupidos hortetur, Annibalemque cum copiis affuturum nuntiet:nihil,dicat partibus, nisi animos Carthaginiensium deesse, Asiam & vires belli, & sumptum præbituram. Hac cum relata Carthaginem essent, nuntius ipse ab inimicis Annibalis comprehenditur, & perductus in senatum, cum interrogaretur, ad quem missus esset, Punico ingenio respondit, se ad vniuersum senatum missum: Nec enim hoc opus singulorum, sed vniuersorum esse. Dum multis diebus deliberant, an eum Romam ad purgandam publicam conscientiam mittant, tacitus conscensa nanque ad Annibalem reuertitur: quo cognito, Carthaginienses vltro rem Romam per legatum deferunt. Romani quoque ad Antiochum legatos misere, qui sub specie legationis, & regis apparatu specularentur, & Annibalem aut Romanis mitigaret, aut assiduo colloquio suspectum inimicumque regi redderent. Itaq; legati cum Ephesi conuenissent ad Antiochum, mandata et senatus tradunt. Dum respondsum exspectant, omnibus diebus assidui circa Annibalem fuere: dicentes, timide eum a patria recessisse, cum pacem Romani non tam cum republica eius, quam cum eo statuerunt, summa fide custodiant; nec bella eum Romanorum magis odio, quam patriae amore gessisse, cui abopiso quoque etiam spiritus ipse debeatur: has enim publicas inter populos, non priuatas inter duces, bellandi causas esse: inde res gestas eius laudare. Quorum sermone latus, sapius, cupidiusque cum legatis colloquebatur, ignarus quod familiaritate Romana, odium sibi apud regem crearet. Quippe Antiochus tam assiduo colloquio, reconciliatam eius cum Romanis gratiam eximias, nihil ad eum sicuti solebat referre; expertemque totius consilij, veluti hostem proditoremque suum, odisse coepit. Qua res tantum apparatum belli, cessante imperatoria arte, corrupit. Senatus mandata fuerant, vt contentus terminis Asiae esset, ne ipsis ingrediendi Asiam necessitatem imponeret: Quibus spretis, non accipiendum bellum, statuit, sed inferendum.
units.tr: 4 When these plans pleased the king, one of Hannibal's companions was sent to Carthage to urge on those eager for war, and to announce that Hannibal would come with his forces. He said that nothing was lacking to the cause except the spirit of the Carthaginians, and that Asia would supply both the forces for war and the expense. When this was reported at Carthage, the messenger himself was seized by Hannibal's enemies and led into the Senate. When asked to whom he had been sent, he answered in the Punic manner that he had been sent to the whole Senate, since this business belonged not to individuals but to all. While for many days they debated whether to send him to Rome to purge the public conscience, he silently boarded a ship and returned to Hannibal. When this became known, the Carthaginians of their own accord referred the matter to Rome through a legate. The Romans also sent envoys to Antiochus, who, under the pretext of an embassy and the king's splendour, were to spy out the situation, and either to soften Hannibal toward Rome or, by constant conversation, to make him suspect and hostile to the king. So when the legates met Antiochus at Ephesus, they handed over the Senate's instructions. While they awaited the reply, they were every day constantly around Hannibal, saying that he had withdrawn timidly from his fatherland, since the Romans had made peace not so much with his state as with him, and kept it with the utmost good faith. Nor had he waged wars out of hatred of the Romans more than out of love for his country, to which he owed even the very breath of his life from birth; for these were public causes of war between peoples, not private quarrels between leaders, and so they praised his exploits. Elated by their talk, he conversed with the legates more often and more eagerly, unaware that by his familiarity with the Romans he was creating hatred for himself with the king. For Antiochus, seeing such constant conversation, began to resent the reconciled favour between Hannibal and the Romans; he no longer referred anything to him as he used to, and, being excluded from all counsel, he began to hate him as an enemy and traitor. This matter ruined so great a preparation for war, the art of command ceasing. The Senate's instructions had been that Antiochus should be content with the bounds of Asia, so that they would not be forced to enter Asia themselves. Scorning these, he resolved not to await war but to bring it on.

units.la: 5 Dicitur quum frequenter de bello consilii habuiffet, remoto Annibale, tandem eum vocari iussisse, non vt ex sententia eius aliquid ageret, sed ne per omnia eum spreuisse videretur: omnibus perrogatis postremum interrogasse. Quo ille animaduerso, intelli5 gere se professus est, non quia egeat consilio, sed ad supplendum numerum sententiarum se vocatum; tamen & odio Romanorum, & amore regis, apud quem solum tutum sibi exilium relictum fit, se viam gerendi belli edisserturum. Veniam deinde libertati prefatus, nihil 10 se aut consiliorum, aut captorum prefentium, probare ait; neque sedem belli Græciam sibi placere, cum Italia vberior materia sit: quippe Romanos vinci non nisi armis suis posse; nec Italiam aliter, quam Italicis viribus subigi: siquidem diuersum ceteris mortalibus esse illud 15 & hominum & belli genus. Aliis bellis plurimum momenti habere, priorem aliquam cepisse occasionem loci, temporisq; agros diripuisse, vrbes aliquas expugnasse: cum Romano seu occupaueris prior aliqua, seu viceris, tum etiam cum victo & iacente luctandum esse. 20 Quamobrem si quis eos in Italia lacessat, suis eos opibus, suis viribus, suis armis posse vincere, sicut ipse secerit. Sin vero quis illis Italia velut fonte virium cesserit, perinde falli, acsi quis amnes non ab ipsis fontium primordiis deriuare, sed concretis iam aquarum molibus 25 auertere vel exsicare velit. Hac & secreto se censuisse, vtroq; ministerium consilij sui obtulisse; & nunc presentibus amicis ideo repetisse, vt scirent omnes rationem cum Romanis gerendi belli; eosque foris inuictos, domi fragiles esse. Nam prius illos vrbe quam imperio 30 prius Italia quam prouinciis exui posse: quippe & à Galli captos, & à se prope deletos esse: neq; se vmquam victum prius, quam terris eorum cesserit. Reuerso Carthaginem, statim cum loco fortunam belli mutatam.
units.tr: 5 It is said that, when he had often held councils about the war, Hannibal having been set aside, at last he ordered him to be summoned, not so that he might act according to his opinion, but lest he seem to have despised him entirely; and, all the others having been asked, he asked him last. Noticing this, Hannibal declared that he understood he had been summoned not because the king needed counsel but to fill out the number of opinions; nevertheless, both from hatred of the Romans and from love of the king, with whom alone a safe exile had been left to him, he would set out his way of conducting the war. Then, prefacing his words with a plea for indulgence for his frankness, he said that he approved neither of the present counsels nor of the commanders. Nor did Greece please him as the seat of war, since Italy offered richer material: for the Romans could be conquered only by their own arms, and Italy could not be subdued except by Italian forces, that kind of war and of men being different from all others. In other wars it matters a great deal to have seized some earlier opportunity of place and time, to have plundered fields, to have stormed some cities; but against the Romans, whether you have occupied some position first or have conquered, you must still struggle with the defeated and the fallen. Wherefore, if anyone attacks them in Italy, he can beat them with their own resources, their own forces and their own arms, just as he himself had done. But if anyone yields Italy to them as the fount of their strength, he is as mistaken as one who would divert or drain rivers not at their very springs but when their masses of water are already gathered. He said that he had held this view in secret and had offered his counsel to both; and now, with friends present, he had repeated it so that everyone might know his plan for waging war with the Romans, who were invincible abroad but fragile at home. For they could be stripped of the city before the empire, and of Italy before the provinces: both had been captured by the Gauls and nearly destroyed by himself, and he had never been beaten before he yielded his own lands. Once he had returned to Carthage, the fortune of war at once changed along with the place.

units.la: 6 Huic sententiæ obtrectatores amici regis erant: non vtilitatem rei cogitantes, sed verentes, ne probato consilio eius, primum apud regem locum gratiæ occuparet. Et Antiocho non tam consilium, quam auctor displiciebat, ne gloria victoriæ Annibalis, non sua esset. Omnia igitur variis assentationum adulationibus corrumpebantur; nihil consilio vel ratione agebatur. Rex ipsē per hiemem in luxuriam lapsus, novis quotidie nutritus ptiis deditus erat. Contra Acilius Romanus consul, qui ad hoc bellum missus erat, copias, arma, cæteraque bello necessaria, summa industria parabat; ciuitates sociās confirmabat, dubias illiciebat: nec alius exitus belli, quam apparatus vtriusque partis fuit: Itaq; prima belli congressione, cum cedentes suos rex cerneret, non laborantibus auxilium tulit; sed fugientibus se ducem præbuit, castraq; ditia victoribus reliquit. Deinde cum in Asiam, præda Romanis occupatis, fugiendo peruenisset; pænitere neglecti consilij cœpit; reuocatoq; in amicitiam Annibale, omnia ex sententia eius agere. Interim nuntiatur AEmilium Romanum ducem cum octoginta rostratis nauibus, in bellum nauale à senatu missum, aduentare: quæ res illi spem restituendæ fortunæ dedit. Itaq; priusquam socia ciuitates ad hostes deficerent, decernere nauali prælio statuit, sperans cladem in Gracia acceptam, noua posse victoria aboleri. Traditaque igitur Annibali classe prælium committitur: sed nec Asiani milites Romanis, neq; naues eorum pares rostratis nauibus fucre; minor tamen clades ducis folertia fuit. Romam nondum opinio victoriæ venerat, & idcirco in consulibus creandis suspensa ciuitas erat.
units.tr: 6 The king's friends were opposed to this view. They were not weighing the advantage of the plan but feared that if his counsel were approved, the man who proposed it would win the first place in the king's favour. Antiochus disliked not so much the plan as its author, lest the glory of the victory belong to Hannibal and not to himself. Everything was therefore corrupted by various flatteries and fawning; nothing was done by counsel or reason. The king himself, over the winter, sank into luxury and, nourished daily by new pleasures, gave himself up to them. Acilius, the Roman consul who had been sent for this war, on the other hand prepared with the greatest diligence troops, arms and everything else the war required. He strengthened the allied cities and won over the wavering ones. The outcome of the war was nothing other than the preparations of each side. Thus, at the first clash, when the king saw his men giving way, he did not bring help to those who were struggling but showed himself a leader to those who were fleeing, and left his camp, rich in plunder, to the victors. Then, when he had reached Asia in flight, with the spoils taken by the Romans, he began to repent of the counsel he had neglected. He recalled Hannibal into his friendship and did everything according to Hannibal's opinion. Meanwhile it was reported that Aemilius, the Roman commander, was coming with eighty beaked ships, sent by the senate for a naval war; this news gave Antiochus hope of restoring his fortune. Therefore, before the allied cities revolted to the enemy, he resolved to decide the matter by a sea battle, hoping that the defeat suffered in Greece could be wiped out by a new victory. So the fleet was handed over to Hannibal and battle was joined. But neither the Asian soldiers were a match for the Romans, nor their ships for the beaked warships; the loss was nonetheless smaller because of the general's skill. The report of victory had not yet reached Rome, and so the city was in suspense about the election of consuls.

units.la: 7 Sed aduersus Annibalem ducem quis melior quam Africani frater crearetur, cum vincere Pænos opus Scipionum esset? Creatur igitur Consul Lucius Scipio: eiq; datur
units.tr: 7 But against the general Hannibal, who could be a better choice to be created than the brother of Africanus, since defeating the Carthaginians was the task of the Scipios? Therefore Lucius Scipio is created consul, and to him is given

units.la: Ducis folertia minorem cladē efficit. Scipiones in Africam ducunt exercitum. datur legatus frater Africanus, vt intelligeret Antiochus,nō maiorem fiduciam se in Annibale victo, quam Romanos in victore Scipione habere. Traiicientibus in Asiam Scipionibus exercitum, iam vtrubiq; profligatum bellum nuntiatum esset; victumq; Antiochum terrestri, Annibalem nauali bello inuenerunt. Primo igitur aduentu eorum, legatos pacem petentes ad eos Antiochus mittit, peculiare donum Africano ferentes ipsius filium, quem rex parvo nauigio traiicientem ceperat. Sed Africanus priuata beneficia a rebus publicis secreta esse dixit; aliaq; esse patris officia, alia patriæ iura, quæ non liberis tantum, verumetiam vitæ ipsi proponantur: proinde gratum se munus accipere, priuatoq; impendio munificentia regis responsurum. Quod ad bellum patemq; pertineat, nihil neq; gratia dari, neq; de iure patriæ decidi posse, respondit. Nam neq; de redimendo filio vmquam tractauit, nec senatum de eo agere permisit; sed vt dignum maiestate eius erat, armis fereceptu rum filium dixerat. Post hac leges pacis dictauit: vt Asia Romanis cederet; contentus Syria regno esset; naues vniuersas, captiuos & transfugas traderet, sumptumq; omnem belli Romanis restitueret. Quæ cum nuntiata Antiocho essent, nondum ita victum se esse respondit, vt spoliari se regno pateretur, belliq; ea irritamenta, non pacis blandimenta esse.
units.tr: The general's skill makes the defeat smaller. The Scipios lead the army into Asia. His brother Africanus is given to him as legate, so that Antiochus might understand that the Romans had no greater confidence in Scipio the victor than he had in Hannibal, defeated. When the Scipios were transporting the army into Asia, the war was already announced as finished everywhere, and they found Antiochus defeated in a land battle and Hannibal in a naval one. So at their first arrival, Antiochus sent ambassadors to them seeking peace, bringing as a special gift to Africanus his son, whom the king had captured when the boy was crossing in a small boat. But Africanus said that private kindnesses must be kept apart from public affairs, and that the duties of a father are one thing, the rights of the homeland another, rights that are set before not only children but life itself. Therefore he said he would accept the gift gladly and would respond to the king's generosity with a private recompense. As to what pertained to the war and to the homeland, he replied that nothing could be given by favour or be settled by a change of right. For he never discussed the ransoming of his son, nor did he allow the senate to deal with the matter; he said that his son would be recovered by arms, as was worthy of the majesty of the Roman people. After this he dictated the terms of peace: that Asia should yield to the Romans; that Antiochus should be content with the kingdom of Syria; that he should hand over all his ships, the prisoners and the deserters, and restore to the Romans the whole cost of the war. When these terms were reported to Antiochus, he replied that he was not yet so defeated as to suffer himself to be stripped of his kingdom, and that these were incentives to war, not enticements to peace.

units.la: 8 Igitur cum ab vtrisq; bellum parauretur, ingressiq; Asiam Romani Ilion venissent; mutua gratulatio [Iliensium ac Romanorum fuit:] Ilienfibus AEncam, ceterosq; cum eo duces à se profectos, Romanis se ab his proacreatos referentibus. Tantaque latitia omnium fuit, quanta esse post longum tempus inter parentes & liberos solet. Iuuabat Ilienses; nepotes suos, Occidente & Africa domita, Asiam vt auitum regnum vindicare, Q. opta-
units.tr: 8 So, since both sides were preparing for war, and the Romans had entered Asia and come to Ilion, there was mutual rejoicing [of the Ilians and the Romans]: the Ilians were reminded that Aeneas and the other leaders who had set out from them, and the Romans reported that they had been born of them. Such joy was felt by all as is usual between parents and children after a long time. It pleased the Ilians that their descendants, having subdued the West and Africa, were now claiming Asia as their ancestral kingdom, Q. opta-
Antiochus and Scipio

units.la: Africano filium captum remittit. optabilem Troiæ ruinam fuisse dicentes, vt tam feliciter renasceretur. Contra Romanos, auitos lares, & incunabula maiorum, templaque ac deorum simulacra, inexplebile desiderium videndi tenebat. Profectus ab Iulio Romanis, Eumenes rex cum auxiliis occurrit: nec multo post prælium cum Antiocho commissum. Cum in dexteriore cornu pulsa legio Romana, maiore dedecore, quam periculo ad castra fugeret, M. Æmilius tribunus militum ad tutelam castrorum relictus, armare se milites suos, & extra vallum progredi iubet, strictoque gladio fugientibus minari, morituros dicens, nisi in prælium reuertantur, infestioraque sua, quam hostium castra inuenturos. Attonita tam ambiguo periculo legio, comitantibus commilitonibus qui fugere eos prohibuerant, in prælium reuertitur, magnaque edita, initium victoriæ fuit. Caesa hostium quinquaginta millia, capta 11. Antiocho pacem petenti, nihil ad superiores conditiones additum, Africano prædicante, neque Romanis, si vincantur, animos minui, neque si vincant, secundis rebus insolescere. Captas ciuitates inter socios diuisere Romani, aptiorem gloriam, quam possessiones voluptarias indicantes. Quippe victoriæ gloriam Romano nomini vindicandam, opum luxuriam sociis relinquendam.
units.tr: Antiochus sends the captured son back to Africanus. They said that the ruin of Troy had been a desirable thing, so that it might be reborn so happily. On the other hand, the Romans were held by an insatiable longing to see their ancestral household gods, the cradles of their forefathers, and the temples and images of the gods. Eumenes the king, having set out from Julius, came to meet the Romans with auxiliary troops, and not long after a battle was joined with Antiochus. When the Roman legion on the right wing was driven back and was fleeing to the camp with greater disgrace than danger, Marcus Aemilius, a military tribune left to guard the camp, ordered his soldiers to arm themselves and to advance outside the rampart; drawing his sword, he threatened the fleeing men, saying they would die unless they turned back to the fight, and that they would find their own camp more hostile than the enemy's. The legion, astonished at such an uncertain danger, accompanied by fellow soldiers who had stopped them from fleeing, turned back into the battle, and with a great shout it was the beginning of victory. Fifty thousand of the enemy were slain and 11 [thousand?] taken. When Antiochus sought peace, nothing was added to the earlier terms, Africanus declaring that the Romans' spirit would not be lessened if they were defeated, nor would they grow proud in prosperity if they conquered. The Romans divided the captured cities among their allies, pointing out that the glory was the more fitting share, while the pleasant possessions were the luxury of wealth. For the glory of victory was to be claimed for the Roman name, and the luxury of wealth left to the allies.
The battle fought with Antiochus.

units.la: M. Æmilii virtute legio fugiens denuo pugnat, & victoriæ præclaræ faciit initium.
units.tr: By the courage of Marcus Aemilius the fleeing legion fights again and makes the beginning of a splendid victory.

units.la: Scipionis nobile dictum, & Romanorum virtus ac eximia laus.
units.tr: Scipio's noble saying, and the courage and outstanding praise of the Romans.
The Epitome of the Histories of Pompeius Trogus
BOOK XXXII.
SUMMARY.

units.la: 1 Ætoli libertate spoliantur. Bellum inter Messenios & Achaeos. Philopoemen captus & veneno interemtus, unde Messenio rum clades.
units.tr: 1 The Aetolians are stripped of their liberty. War between the Messenians and the Achaeans. Philopoemen is captured and killed by poison, which brings about the defeat of the Messenians.

units.la: 2 Antiochus Syrus, dum sacrilegio sibi prouidere putat, interficitur. Seriatus Romanus Philippo parcit, cita, Romani Annibalem ob Demetrii filii virtutem, persequuntur. Is hausto veneno Perseus frater inuidet, & Demetrium impiis artibus tollit de medio.
units.tr: 2 Antiochus the Syrian, while he thinks he is providing for himself by sacrilege, is killed. Servilius the Roman spares Philip. The Romans quickly pursue Hannibal on account of the valour of Demetrius, son of Philip. Hannibal, after drinking poison, is envied by his brother Perseus, who removes Demetrius by impious arts.
3 The death of Philip and the war.

units.la: ETOLI qui Antiochum in bella Romana impulerant, victo eodem, soli aduersus Romanos & viribus impares, & omni auxilio destituti remanserunt: Nec multo post victi, libertatem quam illibatam aduersus dominationem Atheniensium & Spartanorum, inter tot Graecia ciuitates soli retinuerant, amiserunt. Quae conditio tanto amarior illis, quanto serior fuit, reputatibus tempora illa, quibus tantis Persarum opibus, domesticis viribus refiterat; quibus Gallorum violentia, Asia, Italiaque, terribilem, Delphico bello fregerant. Quae gloriosa recordatio, maius desiderium libertatis augebat. Dum haec aguntur, medio tempore inter Messenios & Achaos
units.tr: The Aetolians, who had urged Antiochus into the Roman war, remained alone, unequal in strength and without any help, when he was defeated. Soon afterwards they were conquered, and they lost the liberty which, unimpaired, they alone among the many states of Greece had kept against the domination of the Athenians and Spartans. Their condition was all the more bitter for them the later it came, when they reflected on those times in which they had resisted the great power of the Persians with their own strength, and in the Delphic war had broken the violence of the Gauls, a terror to Asia and Italy. This glorious memory increased their longing for liberty. While these things were happening, in the meantime, between the Messenians and the Achaeans...
Restless and foolish, the Aetolians lose their liberty.
Fools grow wise too late.

units.la: Messenii & Achaei non fiunt alieno periculo cautiores. Achaeos de principatu primo dissensio, mox bellum ortum est. In ea nobilis Achaeorum Philopœmenes imperator capitur: non quia pugnando vita pepercerit, sed dum suos in præalium reuocat, in trafitu fossa equo præcipitatus, a multitudine hostium oppressus est. Quem iacentem Meffenij fcu metu virtutis, vel verecundia diguitatis, interficere ausi non fuerunt. Itaq; velut in illo omne bellum confecissent, captiuum per vniuersam ciuitatem, in modum triumphi circumduxerunt, effuso obuiam populo, ac fi suus, non hostium imperator aduentaret: nec victorem Achaei auidius vidissent, quam victum hostes viderunt. Igitur eundem in theatrum duci iusserunt, vt omnes contuerentur, quem potuisse capi incredibile singulis videbatur. Inde in carcerem ducto, verecundia magnitudinis eius, venenum dederunt: quod ille latus, ac fi vicisset, accepit; quæsito prius, an Ligortas præfectus Achaorum, quem secundum a fe esse scientia rei militaris sciebat, incolumis effugisset.Quem vt accepit euasisse, non in totum dicens consulum male Achaeis, exspirauit. Nec multo post, reparato bello, Meffenij vincuntur; pœnasq; interfecti Philopœmenis pependerunt.
units.tr: The Messenians and Achaeans do not become more cautious at another's peril. Among the Achaeans, first a dispute over leadership and then war arose. In it the noble Achaean commander Philopoemen was captured. This was not because he spared his life in fighting, but while he was calling his men back to battle, his horse plunged into a ditch he was crossing, and he was overwhelmed by a crowd of enemies. The Messenians, either out of fear of his valour or out of respect for his dignity, did not dare to kill him as he lay there. So, as if they had finished the whole war in him, they led him captive through the entire city, in the manner of a triumph. The people poured out to meet him, as if their own commander, not an enemy's, were arriving. The Achaeans had never seen their victor more eagerly than the enemy saw their defeated general. They then ordered him to be led into the theatre, so that all might gaze upon the man whom, it seemed incredible to each one, could have been taken. Then he was led into prison, and out of respect for his greatness they gave him poison. He took it cheerfully, as if he had won, after first asking whether Lycortas, the prefect of the Achaeans, whom he knew to be second to himself in military skill, had escaped unharmed. When he heard that he had got away, he said that the Achaeans had not been wholly unfortunate, and he breathed his last. Not long afterwards, when the war was renewed, the Messenians were defeated, and they paid the penalty for the killing of Philopoemen.

units.la: 2 Interea in Syria rex Antiochus cum graui tributo pacis a Romanis victus oneratusq; effet, seu inopia pecuniæ compulsus, seu auaritia folicitatus, qua sperabat fe, sub specie tributaria necessitatis, excusatius facrilegia commissurum, adhibito exercitu, nocte templum Didymai Iouis aggreditur. Qua re prodita, concursu infularum, cum omni militia interficitur. Romæ cum multa Græcia ciuitates, questum de iniuriis Philippi regis Macedonum venissent, & disceptatio in fenatu inter Demetrium Philippi filium, quem pater ad satisfaciendum senatui miserat, & legatos ciuitatium effet turba querelarum confusus adolescens, repente obticuit. Tunc senatus verecundia eius motus, quae probata etiam antea, cum obses Romae esset, omnibus fuerat, causam illi donauit: atque ita modestia sua Demetrius veniam patri, non iure defensionis, sed patrocinio pudoris obtinuit, quod ipsum decreto senatus significatum esset, ut appareret non tam absolutum regem, quam donatum filio patrem. Quae res Demetrio non gratiam legationis, sed odium obtrectationis comparauit. Nam apud fratrem Perseum aemulatio illi inuidiam contraxit; & apud patrem nota absolutionis causa, offensae fuit, indignante Philippo, plus momenti apud senatum personam filii, quam auctoritatem patris; ac dignitatem regiae maiestatis habuisse. Igitur Perseus perfidia patris agritudine, quotidie absentem Demetrium apud eum criminari; & primo inuisum, post etiam suspectum reddere; nunc amicitiam Romanorum, nunc proditionem ei patris obiectare. Ad postremum, insidias sibi ab eo paratas confingit: ad cuius rei probationem immittit indices, testes subornat, & facinus quod obiicit, admittit: Quibus rebus compulso ad parricidium patre, funestam omnem regiam facit.
units.tr: 2 Meanwhile in Syria King Antiochus, having been defeated by the Romans and burdened with a heavy tribute for peace, was driven either by lack of money or stirred by greed, since he hoped that under the pretext of the necessity of paying tribute he could commit sacrilege more excusably. With an army he attacked by night the temple of Jupiter at Didyma. The plot was revealed, and at the gathering of the priests he was killed with all his soldiers. At Rome, when many Greek states had come to complain of the wrongs done by Philip, king of the Macedonians, and a hearing was being held in the senate, Demetrius, son of Philip, whom his father had sent to satisfy the senate, was confused by the uproar of the envoys' complaints and suddenly fell silent. Then the senate, moved by his modesty, which had also been approved earlier when he was a hostage at Rome and was known to all, granted him the cause. And so by his modesty Demetrius obtained pardon for his father, not by the right of defence but by the protection of shame. This was made known by a decree of the senate, so that it might appear that the king was not so much acquitted as a father given back to his son. This act won Demetrius not thanks for his embassy but the hatred of jealousy. For with his brother Perseus rivalry drew envy upon him, and with his father the cause of his acquittal became a mark of offence, Philip being indignant that the person of the son carried more weight with the senate than the authority of the father, and that he had held the dignity of royal majesty. Therefore Perseus, taking advantage of his father's irritation, daily accused Demetrius, who was absent, before him. First he made him hateful, then suspect, and now he charged him with friendship with the Romans, now with betrayal of his father. At last he invented a plot prepared against himself by Demetrius; to prove it he sent in informers, suborned witnesses, and admitted the crime he laid to his brother's charge. By these means he drove his father to the murder of his son, and made the whole royal house a house of mourning.

units.la: 3 Occiso Demetrio, sublatoque aemulo non negligentior tantum Perseus in patrem, verumetiam contumacior erat; nec haeredem regni, sed regem fegerebat. His rebus offensus Philippus, impatientius in dies mortem Demetrij dolebat, tuncque insidiis circumuentum supplicari, testes indicesque torquere. Atque ita cognita fraude, non minus scelere Persei, quam innoxia Demetrij morte cruciabatur; peregisset atque ultionem, nisi morte praeuentus fuisset. Nam breui post tempore, morbo ex agritudine animi contracto, decessit, relicto magno belli apparatu aduersus Romanos: quo postea Perseus usus est:
units.tr: 3 With Demetrius killed and his rival removed, Perseus became not only less respectful towards his father but even more insolent; he did not treat him as heir to the kingdom but as a king. Offended by this, Philip grieved over the death of Demetrius more and more impatiently each day, and he began to ask that those who had been entrapped by the plot be tortured, and the witnesses and informers too. And so, when the fraud was discovered, he was tormented no less by the crime of Perseus than by the innocent death of Demetrius. He would have taken vengeance had he not been forestalled by death. For shortly afterwards he died of an illness contracted from his mental distress, leaving behind a great war preparation against the Romans, which Perseus later used.

units.la: nam & Gallos Scordiscos ad belli societatem perpulerat : fecissetque Romanis graue bellum, nisi decessisset. Namq; Galli bello aduersus Delphos infeliciter gesto, in quo maiorem vim numinis, quam hostium senserant, amisso Brenno duce, pars in Asiam, pars in Thraciam extorres fugerant. Inde per eadem vestigia, qua venerant, antiquam patriam repetiuere. Ex his manus quaedam in confluente Danubij & Sabi consedit, Scordisci, cosq; se appellari voluit. Tectosagi autem cum in antiquam patriam Tolosam venissent, comprehensi, pestifera lue essent, non prius sanitatem recuperauere, quae aruspicum responsis moniti, aurum argentumq; bellis sacrilegiisq; quaesitum, in Tolosensem lacum mergerent. Quod omne magno post tempore Capio Romanus consul abstulit. Fuere autem argenti pondo centum decem millia; auri pondo quinquies decies centum millia. Quod sacrilegium causa excidij Capioni, exercituique eius postea fuit. Romanos quoque Cimbrici belli tumultus, velut vltor sacrae pecuniae, insecutus est. Ex gente Tectosagorum non mediocris populus praeda dulcedine Illyricum repetiuit, spoliatusq; Istris, in Pannonia consedit. Istrorum gentem fama est originem a Colchis ducere, missos ab Aeta rege ad Argonautas, raptoresq; filia persequendos: qui vt a Ponto intrauerunt Istrum, alueo Sabi fluminis penitus inuecti, vestigia Argonautarum insequentes, naues suas humeris per iuga montium, vsq; ad littus Adriatici maris transtulerunt; agnito quod Argonautae, idem propter magnitudinem nau is priores fecissent: quos vt auectos Colchi non reperiunt, sine metu regis, sine tedio longa nauigationis; iuxta Aquileiam consedere; Istriq; ex vocabulo amnis, quo a Istro appelli conceperant, appellati. Daci quoq; suboles Getarum sunt: qui, cum Oiole rege aduersus Bastarnas
units.tr: For he had also won over the Gallic Scordisci to join the war, and he would have caused the Romans a grievous war had he not died. For after the Gauls had waged an unlucky war against Delphi, in which they had felt a greater power of the divinity than of their enemies, and Brennus their leader had been lost, one part fled as exiles into Asia and another into Thrace. Thence, by the same tracks by which they had come, they sought their ancient homeland again. Of these a certain band settled at the confluence of the Danube and the Save, and wished to be called Scordisci after themselves. The Tectosages, however, when they had come back to their ancient homeland at Tolosa, were seized by a deadly plague, and did not recover their health until, warned by the responses of the soothsayers, they sank in the lake of Tolosa the gold and silver that had been got by wars and sacrileges. All this was carried off a long time afterwards by Caepio, the Roman consul. There were a hundred and ten thousand pounds of silver, and five hundred thousand pounds of gold. This sacrilege was the cause of Caepio's ruin and that of his army afterwards. The tumult of the Cimbric war, like an avenger of the sacred money, also pursued the Romans. A not inconsiderable people of the Tectosages, driven by the sweetness of plunder, sought Illyricum again, and after plundering the Istrians settled in Pannonia. It is said that the race of the Istrians derives its origin from the Colchians, who were sent by King Aeetes to pursue the Argonauts and the abductress of his daughter. When they entered the Istros from the Pontus, they sailed far up the channel of the river Save, following the tracks of the Argonauts, and carried their ships over the mountain ridges on their shoulders as far as the shore of the Adriatic Sea, recognising that the Argonauts had done the same before them because of the size of their ships. When the Colchians, having been carried off, could not find them, they settled near Aquileia, without fear of their king and without weariness from the long voyage; and they were named Istrians from the name of the river by which they had conceived the idea of being called after the Istros. The Dacians too are a offspring of the Getae. When they had fought badly against the Bastarnae under King Oeolus, they were compelled by the king's command, as a punishment for their cowardice, to place their heads on stones instead of their feet while they slept, and to perform for their wives the menial services which they themselves had previously been accustomed to do for them. Nor were these things changed until they wiped out the disgrace received in war by their courage.

units.la: male pugnassent, ad vltionem segnitia, capturi somnū capita loco pedum ponere iussu regis cogebantur; ministeriaq; vxoribus, quae ipsis antea fieri solebant, facere. Neq; hac ante mutata sunt, quam ignominiam bello acceptam virtute delerent.
units.tr: Because they had fought badly, they were punished for their sloth: when they were about to take their sleep, the king's order compelled them to put their heads where their feet should be, and to perform for their wives the menial services that had formerly been done for them. Nor were these conditions changed until they wiped out the disgrace they had incurred in the war by their courage.

units.la: 4 Igitur Perseus, cum imperio Philippi patris successisset, omnes has gentes aduersus Romanos in societatem belli solicitabat. Interim inter Prusiam regem, ad quem Annibal post pacem Antiocho à Romanis datam, profugerat, & Eumenem bellum ortum est, quod Prusias Annibalis fiducia rupto foedere, prior intulit. Namq; Annibal, cum ab Antiocho Romani inter ceteras conditiones pacis deditionem eius deposcerent, admonitus à rege, in fugam versus Cretam defertur; Ibi cum diu quietam vitam egisset, inuidiosumque se propter nimias opes videret, amphoras plumbo repletas in templo Diana, quasi fortunae suae praesidia deponit: atq; ideo nihil de illo solicita ciuitate, quoniam velut pignus opes eius tenebat, ad Prusiam contendit, auro suo in statuis, quas secum portabat infuso, ne conspectae opes vita nocerent. Dein cum Prusias terrestri bello ab Eumene victus esset, & proelium in mare transtulisset, Annibal nouo commento auctor victoriae fuit. Quippe omne serpentium genus in fictiles lagenas coniici iussit, medioque proelio in naues hostium mittit. Id primum Ponticis ridiculum visum fictilibus dimicare, qui ferro nequeant. Sed vbi serpentibus repleri naues coepere, ancipiti periculo circumuenti, hosti victoriam cessere. Quae vbi Romam nuntiata sunt, missi a senatu legati sunt, qui virumque regem in pacem cogerent, Annibalemque deposcerent. Sed Annibal re cognita, sumpto veneno, legationem morte praeuenit. Infignis hic annus trium toto orbe maximorum imperatorum rum mortibus fuit, Annibalis, & Philopœmenis, & Scipionis Africani. Ex quibus constat Annibalem, nec tum cum Romano tonantem bello Italia contremuit, nec cum reuersus Carthaginem summum imperium tenuit, aut cubantem cœnasse, aut plus quam sextario vini indulsisse; pudicitiamq; eum tantam inter tot captiuas habuisse, vt in Africa natum quiuis negaret: Moderationis certe eius fuit, vt cum diuersarum gentium exercitus rexerit, neq; misdiis suorum militum fit petitus vmquam, neq; fraude proditus, quum vtrumq; hostes sæpe tentassent.
units.tr: 4 Therefore Perseus, when he had succeeded his father Philip in the kingdom, urged all these peoples into an alliance for war against the Romans. Meanwhile between King Prusias, to whom Hannibal had fled after the peace which the Romans had granted Antiochus, and Eumenes a war broke out, which Prusias, relying on Hannibal, began first by breaking the treaty. For when the Romans, among other conditions of peace, demanded Hannibal's surrender from Antiochus, he was warned by the king and fled to Crete. There, after he had lived quietly for a long time, and seeing that he was hated because of his excessive wealth, he deposited in the temple of Diana amphorae filled with lead, as if they were the protection of his fortune. Therefore the state, not disturbed about him, since it held his wealth as a kind of pledge, he made his way to Prusias, having poured his gold into the statues which he carried with him, lest the sight of his riches should harm his life. Then, when Prusias had been defeated in a land battle by Eumenes and had carried the fight out to sea, Hannibal was the author of victory by a novel device. For he ordered every kind of serpent to be put into earthen jars, and in the middle of the battle sent them into the enemy's ships. This first seemed ridiculous to the Pontic men, that they should fight with earthen pots, which could not hurt them with iron. But when the ships began to be filled with serpents, they were surrounded by a double danger and gave the victory to the enemy. When this was announced at Rome, the senate sent envoys to force both kings into peace and to demand Hannibal. But Hannibal, learning the situation, took poison and forestalled the embassy by death. This year was remarkable for the deaths of three of the greatest commanders in the whole world: Hannibal, Philopoemen, and Scipio Africanus. From these it is established that Hannibal, neither when he thundered in Italy against the Romans in war did Italy tremble, nor when he returned to Carthage and held supreme power did he dine reclining, or indulge in more than a sextarius of wine; and that he kept such chastity among so many captive women that anyone would deny he was born in Africa. Certainly it was a mark of his moderation that, though he ruled armies of different peoples, he was never attacked by the plots of his own soldiers, nor betrayed by treachery, although his enemies had often tried both.
The Epitome of the Histories of Pompeius Trogus
BOOK XXXIII. SUMMARY.

units.la: 1 Macedonicum bellum, nes fusi fugati. Perseus & fiPersei, & consulum Roma- lii capti in fuga. Macedonia norum animus. in prouinciam redacta, &
units.tr: 1 The Macedonian war. Perseus and his sons, and the consuls, routed and put to flight, and captured in flight. Macedonia reduced into a province, and the spirit of the Macedonians.

units.la: 2 Pugna in qua Macedo- Ætoli oppressi.
units.tr: 2 The battle in which the Macedonians and the Aetolians were crushed.

units.la: INORE quidem rerum motu Romani Macedonicum, quam Punicum bellum gesserunt; sed tanto clarius, quanto nobilitate Macedones Pœnos antecesserunt. Quippe cum gloria Orientis domiti, tum & auxiliis omnium regum iuuabantur. Itaq; Romani & legiones plures numero conscripserunt; & auxilia à Masinissa rege Numidarum, ceterisq; sociis omnibus accuerunt; & Eumeni regi Bithythynia denuntiatum, vt bellum summis viribus iuuaret : Perseo prater Macedonicum inuicta opinionis exercitum,decennis belli sumptus,à patre paratus,in thefauris & horreis erat:quibus rebus inflatus,oblitus for-
units.tr: Indeed, the Romans waged the Macedonian war with less upheaval in events than the Punic war, but it was more famous, in that the Macedonians surpassed the Carthaginians in nobility. Since they had subdued the glory of the East, they were also aided by the auxiliaries of all kings. Therefore the Romans enrolled more legions, and received auxiliaries from Masinissa, king of the Numidians, and from all their other allies. King Eumenes of Bithynia was ordered to help the war with his utmost strength. Besides the army of unconquered reputation, Perseus had in his treasuries and granaries the expenses of a ten-year war, which his father had prepared. Inflated by these things, and forgetting his father's fortune, he ordered his men to consider the old glory of Alexander.

units.la: tuna paterna, veterem Alexandri gloriam considerare suos iubebat. Prima equitum congressio fuit, qua victor Perseus suspensam omnium expectationem in fa-
units.tr: The first cavalry engagement took place, in which Perseus, the victor, drew to his own side the suspended expectation of all.

units.la: uorem sui traxit:misit tamen legatos ad consulem,qui pacem peterent, quam patri suo Romani etiam victo
units.tr: Nevertheless, he sent envoys to the consul to seek peace, which the Romans had even granted to his father when he was defeated,

units.la: dedissent,impensas belli lege victi suscepturus.Sed consul Sulpitius non minus graues quam victo leges dixit. Dum haec aguntur, metu tam periculosi belli, Romani AEmilium Paulum consulem creant, eiq; extra ordinem Macedonicum bellum decernunt : qui cum ad ex-
units.tr: had given, undertaking to bear the expenses of the war as the conquered party under the terms of the agreement. But the consul Sulpicius laid down terms no less severe than those for a defeated enemy. While these things were going on, out of fear of so dangerous a war, the Romans created Aemilius Paulus consul and decreed him the Macedonian war outside the ordinary course of business.

units.la: ercitum venisset, non magnam moram pugnae fecit. Pridie quam proelium conferretur,luna nocte defecit : triste id ostentum Perseo omnibus praesagientibus, sinemq; Macedonici regni portendi vaticinantibus.
units.tr: When he had come to the army, he did not delay long before fighting. On the day before the battle was to be joined, the moon was eclipsed at night. This was a dreadful omen for Perseus, and everyone foretold it, prophesying that it portended the end of the Macedonian kingdom.

units.la: 2 In ea pugna M. Cato,Catonis oratoris filius,dum inter confertissimos hostes insigniter dimicat, equo delapsus,pedestre proelium aggreditur. Nam cadentem manipulus hostium cum horrido clamore,veluti iacentem obtruncaturus circumsteterat;at ille citius corpore collecto, magnas strages edidit. Quum ad vnum opprimendum vndique hostes connolarent, dum procerum quendam petit, gladius ei e manu elapsus, in mediam cohortem hostium decidit:ad quem reciperandum vmbone se protegens inspectante vtroq;exercitu,inter mucrones se hostium immersit ; recollectoq;gladio , multis vulneribus exceptis,ad socios cum clamore hostium reuertitur.Huius audaciam ceteri imitati, victoriam peperere. Perseus rex fuga cum decem millibus talentum Samothraciam defertur : quem Cneus Octauius , ad per-
units.tr: 2 In that battle Marcus Cato, son of the orator Cato, fought conspicuously among the thickest of the enemy; but his horse slipped and fell, and he went on fighting on foot. For when he fell, a company of the enemy gathered around him with a fearsome shout, as though about to cut down a man lying prostrate; but he, gathering his body up more quickly, dealt out great slaughter. When the enemy were massing from every side to overwhelm him alone, while he was making for a certain leading man, his sword slipped from his hand and fell into the midst of an enemy cohort. To recover it he covered himself with his shield-boss and plunged in among the points of the enemy's spears, while both armies looked on; then, having recovered his sword and taken many wounds, he returned with a shout to his comrades through the enemy's ranks. The others, imitating his boldness, won the victory. King Perseus, in flight, was carried with ten thousand talents to Samothrace, where Gnaeus Octavius, sent by the consul to pursue him, took him together with his two sons, Alexander and Philip, and led him captive to the consul.

units.la: Q s persequendum missus à consule, cum duobus filiis, Alexandro & Philippo, cepit; captumq; ad consulem duxit. Macedonia à Carano, qui primus inea regnauit, usq; ad Perseum triginta reges habuit. Quorum sub regno fuit quidem annis noningentis & viginti tribus; sed rerum non nisi centum nonaginta duobus annis potita. Ita cum in ditionem Romanorum cessisset, magistratibus per singulas ciuitates constitutis, libera facta est, legesq; quibus adhuc vtitur, à Paulo accepit. AEtolorum vniuersarum vrbium senatus, cum coniugibus & liberis, qui dubia fide fuerant, Romam missus, ibiq; ne in patria aliquid nouaret, diu detentus; egreq; per multos annos legationibus ciuitatum senatu fatigato, in patriam quisq; suam remissus est.
units.tr: Sent in pursuit of him by the consul, Quintus [Cneus] Octavius took him, together with his two sons, Alexander and Philip, and led him, a captive, to the consul. Macedonia, from Caranus, who was the first to reign there, down to Perseus, had thirty kings. Under their rule it lasted for 923 years, but it had been in possession of its affairs for only 192 of them. So when it had passed into the power of the Romans, magistrates were set up in each state, and it was made free; and the laws which it still uses it received from Paulus. The senate of all the cities of Aetolia, together with their wives and children, who had been of doubtful loyalty, was sent to Rome, and there, lest they should stir up anything in their homeland, was kept under detention for a long time; and when, after many years, the senate had been worn out by the embassies of the cities, each man was sent back to his own country.
POMPEII TROGI EPITOMA HISTORIARUM
BOOK XXXIV. SUMMARY.

units.la: 1 In Achaeos Romani causas belli quaerunt & inuenint. Cruenta Achaeorum seditio. 2 Bellum, quo Achaei Roma profugus regno oppressi sunt, & Corinthus euersa. Prolemaeus AEgypto pulsus petit à Romanis auxilium. 3 Popilii ad Antiochum, in gratiam Prolemaei vere libera legatio. Antiocho mortuo, Demetrius frater ... 4 Prufias rex Bithyniae regno & vita à filio spoliatur.
units.tr: 1 The Romans seek and find grounds for war against the Achaeans. The bloody sedition of the Achaeans. 2 The war by which the Achaeans, having been overcome, were brought low, and Corinth destroyed. Ptolemy, driven from Egypt, seeks help from the Romans. 3 The Popilii's embassy to Antiochus, truly free, on behalf of Ptolemy. After Antiochus's death, his brother Demetrius ... 4 King Prusias of Bithynia is stripped of his kingdom and his life by his son.

units.la: OENIS ac Macedonibus subactis, AEtolorumque viribus principum captiuitate debi= debilitatis, foli adhuc ex Graecia vniuersa Achaei nimis potentes tunc temporis Romanis videbantur, non propter singularium ciuitatium nimias opes, sed propter conspirationem vniuersarum: Namq; Achaei, licet per ciuitates veluti per membra diuisi sint, vnum tamen corpus & vnum imperium habent: singularumque vrbium pericula mutuis viribus propulsant. Quærentibus igitur Romanis causas belli, tempestiue fortuna quærelas Spartanorum obtulit, quorum agros Achaei propter mutuum odium populabantur, Spartanis à senatu responsum est, legatos se ad inspiciendas res sociorum, & ad iniuriam demendam in Graeciam missuros: sed legatis occulta mandata data sunt, vt corpus Achaeorum dissoluerent, singulasq; vrbes proprij iuris facerent, quo facilius ad obsequia cogerentur; & si quæ vrbes contumaces essent, strangerentur. Igitur legati, omnium ciuitatium principibus Corinthum euocatis, decretum senatus recitant; quid consilij habeant, aperiunt. Expedire omnibus dicunt, vt singuke ciuitates sua iura & suas leges habeant. Quod vbi omnibus innotuit, velut in furorem versi, vniuersum peregrinum populum trucidant; legatos quoq; ipsos Romanorum violassent, nisi audito tumultu, trepidi fugissent.
units.tr: After the Aetolians and Macedonians had been subdued, and the Aetolians' strength had been weakened by the capture of their leaders, the Achaeans alone remained in all Greece, and at that time they seemed to the Romans far too powerful. This was not because of the excessive wealth of any single city, but because of the union of all of them. For the Achaeans, although divided into cities as if into limbs, nevertheless have one body and one government, and they ward off the dangers of each city with their combined strength. The Romans, then, were looking for grounds for war, and fortune opportunely offered them a complaint from the Spartans, whose fields the Achaeans were ravaging out of mutual hatred. The senate replied to the Spartans that it would send envoys to Greece to examine the affairs of its allies and to redress the wrong. But secret instructions were given to the envoys: they were to break up the body of the Achaeans and make each city independent, so that they could more easily be compelled to obedience; and any cities that proved obstinate were to be brought under control by force. Accordingly the envoys summoned the leading men of all the cities to Corinth, read out the decree of the senate, and revealed what they intended. They said it was advantageous to all that each city should have its own rights and its own laws. When this became known to everyone, they were as if driven mad, and they slaughtered the whole foreign populace. They would also have harmed the Roman envoys themselves, had they not, on hearing the uproar, fled in alarm.

units.la: 2 Hæc vbi Romæ nuntiata sunt, statim senatus Mummio consuli bellum Achaicum decernit: qui extemplo exercitu deportato, & omnibus strenue prouisis, pugnandi copiam hastibus fecit. Sed Achaei, velut nihil negotij Romano bello suscepissent, ita apud eos negleta omnia & soluta fuere. Itaq; prædam, non prælium cogitantes, & vehicula ad spolia hastium reportanda duxerunt, & coniuges liberosq; suos, ad spectaculum certaminis, in montibus posuerunt. Sed prælio cōmisso, ante oculos suorum casi, lugubre his spectaculū, & grauem luctus memoriam reliquerunt. Coniuges quoq; liberiq; eorum, de spectatoribus captiui facti, praeda ho-
units.tr: 2 When these events were reported at Rome, the senate at once voted the Achaean war to the consul Mummius. He immediately transported his army, made thorough provision for everything, and gave the enemy the chance to fight. But the Achaeans acted as if they had undertaken no business with Rome at all, so everything among them was neglected and disorganized. Thinking of plunder rather than battle, they brought wagons to carry off the enemy's spoils, and they posted their wives and children on the hills to watch the contest. When battle was joined, their own people fell before their eyes, leaving a grievous memory of mourning and a sorrowful spectacle for them. Their wives and children too, taken captive from among the onlookers, became the spoil of the enemy.

units.la: stium fuere. Vrbs ipsa Corinthus diruitur: populus ominis sub corona venditur: vt hoc exemplo ceteris ciuitatibus metus nouarum rerum imponeretur. Dum haec aguntur, rex Syriae Antiochus Ptolemaeo, maioris soro-ris suae filio, regi AEgypti, bellum infert, segni admodum, & quotidiana luxuria ita marcenti, vt nō solum regia maiestatis officia intermitteret, verumetiam sensu hominis nimia sagina careret. Pulsus igitur regno, ad fratrem minorem Ptolemaeum Alexandriam confugit: participatoque cum eo regno, legatos Romam ad fenatum mittunt; auxilia petunt; fidem societatis implorant. Mouere senatum preces fratrum.
units.tr: Corinth itself was razed. The people of military age were sold under the spear-crown, so that this example would strike fear of revolution into the other cities. While these things were happening, Antiochus, king of Syria, made war on Ptolemy, king of Egypt, the son of his elder sister. Ptolemy was a sluggish man, so enervated by daily luxury that he neglected not only the duties of royal majesty but even the use of his senses, through excessive fatness. Driven from his kingdom, he fled to his younger brother Ptolemy at Alexandria. Sharing the kingdom with him, they sent envoys to the senate at Rome, seeking aid and invoking the faith of the alliance. The brothers' entreaties moved the senate.

units.la: 3 Mittitur itaq; legatus Popilius ad Antiochum: qui abstinere illum AEgypto, aut si iam incepisset, excedere iuberet. Cum in AEgypto eum inuenisset, ofculumq; ei rex obtulisset (nam colurat inter ceteros Popilium Antiochus, cum Romae obses esset) tunc Popilius facessere interim priuatam amicitiā iubet, cum mandata patriae intercedant; prolatoq; senatus decreto, & tradito, cum cunctari eum videret, confultationemq; ad amicos referre; ibi Popilius virga quam in manu gerebat amplo circulo inclusum, vt & amicos caperet, consulere iubet; nec prius inde exire, quam responsum senatui daret, aut pacem, aut bellum cum Romanis habiturum. Adeoq; haec auctoritas animum regis fregit, vt parituru se senatui responderet. Reuersus in regnum Antiochus, decedit relicto parvulo admodum filio: cui cum tutores dati à populo essent, patruus eius Demetrius, qui obses Romae erat, cognita morte Antiochi fratris, senatum adiit, obfidemq; se viuo fratre venisse, quo mortuo, cuius obses fit, se ignorare: Dimitti igitur se ad regnum tegnum petendum æquum esse, quod sicuti iure gentium maiori fratri cesserit, ita nunc sibi, qui pupillum ætate antecedat, deberi. Cum se non dimitti animadverteret à senatu, tacito iudicio tutius, apud pupillum quam apud eum regnum futurum arbitrante, specie venandi ab urbe profectus, Hostia tacitus, cum fuga comitibus navem conscendit. Delatus in Syriam secundo fauore omnium excipitur; regnumq; ei, occiso pupillo, a tutoribus traditur.
units.tr: 3 Accordingly, the envoy Popilius was sent to Antiochus, with orders to bid him keep away from Egypt, or, if he had already begun, to withdraw. When he found him in Egypt, the king offered him an embrace (for Antiochus had been on familiar terms with Popilius while he was a hostage at Rome). Popilius told him to put aside private friendship for the time being, since he was carrying his country's orders. He produced the senate's decree and handed it over, and when he saw the king hesitating and wanting to refer the matter to his friends for consultation, Popilius drew a circle around him with the staff he carried in his hand, and ordered him to give an answer to take back to the senate before he stepped out of it, namely whether he would have peace or war with the Romans. Such was the authority of this command that it broke the king's spirit, and he replied that he would obey the senate. Antiochus returned to his kingdom, but died, leaving a very young son. Guardians were appointed for the boy by the people, but his uncle Demetrius, who was a hostage at Rome, learned of the death of his brother Antiochus and went before the senate. He said that he had come as a hostage while his brother was alive, and that since that brother had died, whose hostage he was, he did not know what to do. It was therefore fair that he be sent home to seek the kingdom, which, since by the law of nations it had passed to the elder brother, now ought to belong to him as the one who was older than the boy. When he saw that the senate was not releasing him, and judging that the kingdom would be safer with the boy than with himself, he left the city on the pretext of hunting, and secretly sailed from Ostia with his companions in flight. Carried to Syria, he was received with the goodwill of all, and after the boy was killed, the kingdom was handed over to him by the guardians.

units.la: 4 Eodem fere tempore Prusias rex Bithyniæ, consilium cepit interficiendi Nicomedis filii, dum consulere studet minoribus filiis, quos ex nouerca eius susceperat, [ & Romæ habebat. Sed res adolescenti ab his, qui facinus susceperant, ] proditur: hortatiq; sunt, ut crudelitate patris prouocatus, occupet insidias, & in auctorem retorqueat scelus: nec difficilis persuasio fuit. Igitur cum accitus in patris regnum venisset, statim rex appellatur. Prusias regno spoliatus à filio, priuatusque redditus, etiam à seruis deseritur: Cum in latebris ageret, non minori scelere, quam filium occidi iusserat, à filio interficitur.
units.tr: 4 At about the same time King Prusias of Bithynia formed a plan to kill his son Nicomedes, while he was anxious to provide for his younger sons, whom he had had by his stepmother, and who were living at Rome. But the plot was betrayed to the young man by those who had undertaken the crime. They urged him to anticipate the snares, provoked by his father's cruelty, and to turn the crime back upon its author; and the persuasion was not difficult. So when he came, summoned, into his father's kingdom, he was at once hailed as king. Prusias, stripped of his kingdom by his son and reduced to a private man, was also deserted by his slaves. While he was hiding in out-of-the-way places, he was killed by his son, with no less wickedness than that by which he had ordered his son to be killed.
POMPEII TROGI EPITOMA HISTORIARUM
BOOK XXXV. SUMMARY.

units.la: 1 Demetrius bella quæ- terat, eiusdem filio dat porens, ab hostibus opprimi- nas, proelio victus & interfectus, tur, & in acie cadit.
units.tr: 1 Demetrius, while he was seeking wars, is handed over by his father to the son of the same name; he is overwhelmed by enemies and falls in the line of battle.
2 [The man] who overthrew Demetrius...

units.la: {*}EMETRIVS occupato Syriae regno, novitati suae ocium periculosum ratus, ampliare fines regni, & opes augere finitimorum bellis statuit. Itaq; Ariarathi regi Cappadociae propter fastiditas sororis nuptias infestus, fratrem eius Orofernem per iniuriam regno pulsum, supplicem recepit; datumq; sibi honestum belli titulum gratulatus, restituere eum in regnum statuit. Sed Orofernes ingrato animo iniita cum Antiochensibus pactione, offensis iunc Demetrio, pellere ipsum regno, à quo restituebatur, consilium cepit. Quo cognito, Demetrius vita quidem eius, ne Ariarathes metu fraterni belli liberaretur, pepercit; ipsum autem comprehensum, vinctum Seleuciae custodiri iubet. Nec Anreges lacessit Tantum odium Demetrij apud omnes erat, vt æmulo eius non vires regiæ tantum, verumetiam generis nobilitas consensu omnium tribueretur. Igitur Alexander admirabili rerum varietate, pristinarum sordium oblitus, totius ferme Orientis viribus succinctus, bellum Demetrio infert, victumq; vita pariter ac regno spoliat: quamquam nec Demetrio animus in propulsando bello defuit: Nam & primo prælio hostem fugauit, & regibus bellū restituentibus, multa millia in acie cæcidit. Ad postremum tamen inuictlo animo inter confertissimos fortissime dimicans, cecidit.
units.tr: ALEXANDER, having seized the kingdom of Syria, thought that a quiet life would be dangerous for his new position, and resolved to enlarge his borders and increase his power by wars with his neighbours. So, angry with King Ariarathes of Cappadocia over the rejected marriage of his sister, he received as a suppliant Ariarathes' brother Orophernes, who had been driven unjustly from his kingdom. Pleased that this gave him an honourable pretext for war, he decided to restore Orophernes to the throne. But Orophernes, ungrateful, made a pact with the Antiochenes and, now offended with Demetrius, planned to drive from his kingdom the very man who was restoring him. When this was discovered, Demetrius spared his life, so that Ariarathes would not be freed from fear of a civil war with his brother, but he had Orophernes seized, bound, and kept in custody at Seleucia. Nor did he provoke the Anreges. So great was the hatred for Demetrius among all men that his rival was granted, by universal consent, not only royal power but also nobility of birth. Therefore Alexander, with a remarkable change of fortune, forgetting his former base origins, and girding himself with the forces of almost the whole East, made war on Demetrius and stripped him of both life and kingdom. Yet Demetrius' spirit was not lacking in defending himself in the war: in the first battle he put the enemy to flight, and when the kings renewed the war he cut down many thousands in the line of battle. At last, however, fighting most bravely with an unconquered spirit among the thickest ranks, he fell.

units.la: Initio belli Demetrius duos filios apud Gnidium hospi-
units.tr: At the start of the war Demetrius had entrusted his two sons at Gnidus to his host,

units.la: hostitem suum, cum magno auri pondere, commenda-
units.tr: together with a large weight of gold, for safekeeping,

units.la: uerat, ut belli periculis eximerentur, & si ita fors tulisset, paternae ultioni seruarentur: Ex his maior Demetrius annos pubertatis egressus, audita Alexandri luxuria, quem inseperatae opes, & alienae felicitatis ornamenta, velut captum, inter scortorum greges desidem in regia tenebant, auxiliantibus Cretensibus securum, ac nihil hostile metuentem, aggreditur. Antiochenses quoque veterem patris offensam novis meritis correcturi se ei tradunt: sed & milites paterni, fauore iuuenis accensi, prioris sacramenti religionem nouiregis superbia praeferentes, signa ad Demetrium transferunt: atque ita Alexander non minori impetu fortunae, destructus, quam elatus, primo proelio victus interficitur: deditque poenas & Demetrio, quam occiderat, & Antiocho, cuius mentitus originem fuerat.
units.tr: so that they would be spared the perils of war and, if fortune so willed, kept for their father's revenge. Of these, the elder Demetrius, now past the years of boyhood, learned of Alexander's luxury, which kept him idle among flocks of prostitutes in the palace, as though he were captivated by the unexpected wealth and the trappings of another's good fortune. Relying on the Cretans, who were secure and feared no enemy, he attacked him. The Antiochenes also, intending to make amends for their old offence to his father by new services, handed themselves over to him. And the soldiers of his father, inflamed with goodwill toward the young man, preferring the sanctity of their earlier oath to the arrogance of the new king, transferred their standards to Demetrius. And so Alexander, overthrown by fortune's assault no less than he had been raised up by it, was defeated in the first battle and killed. He paid the penalty both to Demetrius, whom he had killed, and to Antiochus, whose origin he had falsely claimed.

units.la: POMPEII TROGI EPI- TOMA HISTORIARVM LIBER XXXVI.
units.tr: THE EPITOME OF THE HISTORIES OF POMPEIUS TROGUS, BOOK XXXVI.
SUMMARY.

units.la: 1 Demetrius iunior bella importune mouet & infeliciter persequitur. Turbae in Syria, vbi Tryphon ab Antiocho Demetrii fratre oppriminitur. Iudaeos subigit Antiochus.
units.tr: 1 The younger Demetrius wages wars unseasonably and pursues them without success. Disturbances in Syria, where Tryphon is oppressed by Antiochus, brother of Demetrius. Antiochus subdues the Jews.

units.la: 2 De Iudaeorum origine & gestis Iustini sententia.
units.tr: 2 On the origin and deeds of the Jews, according to the opinion of Justin.

units.la: 3 Iudaeorum opes. Mare mortuum, à quibus Iudaei domiti sint.
units.tr: 3 The wealth of the Jews. The Dead Sea, and by whom the Jews were subdued.

units.la: 4 Attali Asiae regis delicta, mors, testamentum. Romanorum Asia fit propria: diuitias autem & vitia sua Romam transfinitt.
units.tr: 4 The faults and death of Attalus, king of Asia, and his will. Asia becomes a Roman province; but the Romans transfer its riches and its vices to Rome.

units.la: ​RECIPERAT O paterno regno, Demetrius & ipse rerum successu corruptus, vitiis adolescentia in segnitiam labitur; tantumq; contemptum apud omnes inertia, quantum odium ex superbia pater habuerat, contraxit. Itaq; cum ab imperio eius passim civitates deficerent, ad abolendam segnitiæ maculam, bellum Parthis inferre statuit: cuius adventum non inviti Oriētis populi videre; & propter Arsacidæ regis Parthorum crudelitatem, & quod veteri Macedonum imperio assueti, novi populi superbiam indigne ferebant. Itaq; cum & Persarum, & Elimæorum, Bactrianorumq; auxiliis invaretur, multis prœliis Parthos fudit. Ad postremum tamen pacis simulatione deceptus, capitur ʒ traductusq; per ora ciuitatium, popu- lis qui desciuerant, in ludibrium fauoris ostenditur. Missus deinde in Hyrcaniam, benigne & iuxta cultum pristinæ fortunæ habetur. Dum hæc aguntur, interim in SyriaTrypho, qui se tutorem Antiocho Demetrij priuigno substitui à populo laborauerat, occiso pupillo, regnum Syriæ inuadit. Quo diu potitus, tandem exolescente fauore recentis imperij, ab Antiocho puero admodum, Demetrij fratre, qui in Asia educabatur, bello vincitur: rursusq; regnum Syriæ ad subolem Demetrij reuertitur. Igitur Antiochus, memor quod & pater propter superbiam inuisus, & frater propter segnitiam contemptus fuisset, ne in eadem vitia incideret, recepta in matrimonium Cleopatra, vxore fratris, ciuitates quæ initio s̈aterni imperij defecerant, summa industria persequitur, domitasque rursus regni terminus adiicit, Iudæosq; qui in Macedonico imperio sub Demetrio patre armis se in libertatem vindicauerant, subigit. Quorum vires tanta fuere, vt post hunc nullum Macedonum regem tulerint, domesticisq; imperiu vsi, Syriæ magnis bellis infestaurint.
units.tr: Demetrius, having recovered his father's kingdom, was himself corrupted by his success; through the vices of youth he sank into sloth, and he drew upon himself as much contempt from everyone for his inactivity as his father had incurred hatred for his arrogance. Therefore, when cities were revolting everywhere from his rule, he resolved to wipe away the stain of his sloth by making war on the Parthians. The peoples of the East saw his coming not unwillingly, both because of the cruelty of the Parthian king Arsaces and because they, accustomed to the old Macedonian rule, resented indignantly the arrogance of a new people. And so, although he was aided by Persian, Elymaean and Bactrian forces, he routed the Parthians in many battles. At last, however, deceived by a pretence of peace, he was captured and led through the towns of those who had revolted, and was displayed to the people as an object of mockery. Then he was sent into Hyrcania, where he was treated kindly and given a state suited to his former fortune. While these things were happening, meanwhile in Syria Tryphon, who had tried to set himself up by the people as guardian of Antiochus, the stepson of Demetrius, killed the boy and seized the kingdom of Syria.
