Having held it for a while, at last, as the favour for his new rule faded, he was defeated in war by Antiochus, a mere boy, brother of Demetrius, who was being brought up in Asia; and so the kingdom of Syria returned to the offspring of Demetrius. Then Antiochus, mindful that his father had been hated for arrogance and his brother despised for sloth, so as not to fall into the same vices, married Cleopatra, his brother's wife; with the greatest diligence he pursued the cities which had revolted at the beginning of his father's rule, and, having subdued them, he added them again to the bounds of the kingdom; and he subdued the Jews, who in the Macedonian empire under his father Demetrius had asserted their liberty by arms. Their strength was so great that after this they endured no Macedonian king, and, ruling by their own government, they harassed Syria with great wars.

units.la: 2 Namq; Iudæis origo Damascena, Syriæ nobilissima ciuitas: unde & Assyriis regibus genus, ex regina Semiramidi fuit. Nomen vrbi à Damasco rege inditum: in cuius honorem, Syrii sepulchrum Arathis vxoris eius pro templo coluere; deamq; exinde sanctissimam religionis habent. Post Damascum Azelus, mox Adores & Abraham, & Israel reges fuere. Sed Israelem felix decem filiorum proventus maioribus suis clariorem fecit.
units.tr: 2 For the Jews had their origin in Damascus, the most noble city of Syria, whence also the Assyrian kings derived their line through Queen Semiramis. The city took its name from King Damascus; in his honour the Syrians worshipped the tomb of his wife Arathis as a temple, and from that time they regard her as a most holy goddess. After Damascus came Azelus, then Adores, and Abraham, and Israel were kings. But Israel's fortunate abundance of ten sons made him more famous than his ancestors.

units.la: Itaq; populum in decem regna diuisum filiis tradidit, omnesq; ex nomine Iudæ, qui post diuisionem decesserat, Iudæos appellauit; coliq; eius memoriam ab omnibus iussit: Eius portio omnibus accesserat. Minimus etate inter fratres Ioseph fuit: culus excellens ingenium veriti fratres, clam interceptum peregrinis mercatoribus vendiderunt. A quibus deportatus in AEgyptum, cum magicas ibi artes sollerti ingenio percepisset, breui ipsi regi carus fuit. Nam & prodigiorum sagacissimus erat, & somniorum primus intelligentiam condidit; nihilq; diuini iuris humanique, et incognitum videbatur: adeo, vt etiam sterilitatem agrorum ante multos annos prouiderit: periissetq; omnis AEgyptus fame, nisi monitu eius rex edicto seruari per multos annos
units.tr: Therefore he divided the people into ten kingdoms and handed them to his sons, and he called them all Jews after the name of Judah, who had died after the division; and he ordered that his memory be honoured by all. His portion had come to all of them. The youngest in age among the brothers was Joseph, whose outstanding talent made his brothers afraid; they seized him and sold him secretly to foreign merchants. Carried by them into Egypt, when he had learned the magic arts there with a clever mind, he soon became dear to the king himself. For he was most skilled in portents, and he was the first to establish the understanding of dreams; nothing of divine or human law seemed unknown to him; so much so that he foresaw the barrenness of the fields many years in advance; and all Egypt would have perished by famine, had not the king, at his advice, ordered grain to be preserved by edict for many years,

units.la: 25 fruges iussisset: tantaque experimenta eius fuerunt, vt non ab homine, sed à deo responsa dari viderentur. Filius eius Moses fuit, quem praeter paterna scientiæ hereditatem, etiam formæ pulchritudo commendabat. Sed AEgyptij quum scabiem, & vitiliginem paterentur,
units.tr: 25 and his trials of him were so great that his answers seemed to be given not by a man but by a god. His son was Moses, whom, besides his father's inheritance of knowledge, the beauty of his appearance also recommended. But when the Egyptians suffered from scabies and leprosy,

units.la: 30 responso moniti, eum cum aegris, ne pestis ad plures serperet, terminis AEgypti pellunt. Dux igitur exulum factus, sacra AEgyptiorum furto abstulit: quæ repetentes armis AEgyptij, domum redire tempestatibus compulsi sunt. Itaq; Moses Damascena antiqua patria repetita, montem Synam occupat: quo septem dierum ieiunio per deserta Arabia, cum populo suo fatigatus, cū tandem venisset, septimū diem more gentis Sabbatum appellatum, in omne aeuum ieiunio sacrauit: quoniam illa dies famem illis erroremq; finierat. Et quoniā metu contagionis pulsos se ab Aegypto meminerant, ne eadem causa inuisi apud incolas forent, caverunt, ne cum peregrinis communicarent: quod ex causa factum paulatim in disciplinam religionemq; couertit. Post Mosen etiam filius eius Aruas, sacerdos sacris AEgyptiis, mox rex creatur; semperq; exinde hic mos apud Iudaeos fuit, vt eosdem reges, & sacerdotes haberent: quorum intestitia religione permixta, incredibile quantū coaluere.
units.tr: 30 warned by an oracle, they drove him out with the sick beyond the borders of Egypt, lest the plague creep among more people. So, made leader of the exiles, he carried off the sacred objects of the Egyptians by theft; when the Egyptians took up arms to get them back, the exiles were driven by storms to return home. And so Moses, having returned to his ancient homeland of Damascus, occupied Mount Sinai; after a fast of seven days in the deserts of Arabia, wearied with his people, when at last he arrived, he consecrated the seventh day, called the Sabbath in the custom of their nation, to fasting for all time, because that day had ended their hunger and wandering. And because they remembered that they had been expelled from Egypt out of fear of contagion, lest for the same reason they should be hated by the inhabitants, they took care not to mix with foreigners; which practice, begun for this reason, gradually turned into a discipline and a religion. After Moses, his son Aaron, a priest of the Egyptian rites, was created king; and from then on it was always the custom among the Jews to have the same men as kings and priests; their religion, intermingled with their kingship, grew to an incredible extent.

units.la: 3 Opes genti ex pecudibus opobalsami creuere, quod in his tantum regionibus gignitur. Est namq; vallis, quae continuis montibus, velut muro quodam, adinstar castrorum clauditur. Spatium loci ducenta iugera, nomine arcus dicitur. In ea silua est & vbertate, & amoenitate insignis: siquidem palmeto & opobalsamo distinguitur. Arbores opobalsami formam similem piceis arboribus habent, nisi quod sunt humiles magis, & in vinearum morem excoluntur. Ea certo anni tempore balsamum sudant. Sed non minor loci eius opacitatis quam vbertatis admiratio est: quippe cum toto orbe regionis eius ardentissimus sol fit, ibi tepidi aeris naturalis quaedam ac perpetua opacitas inest. In ea regione Lacus est, qui propter magnitudinem & aquae immobilitatem, mortuum mare dicitur. Nam neq; ventis moue-tur, resistente turbinibus bitumine, quo aqua omnis stagnatur; neq; nauigationis patiens est, quoniā omnia vita carentia in profundum merguntur; nec materiam vllā sustinet, nisi quae alumine illinatur. Primū Xerxes rex Persarum, Iudæos domuit: postea cum ipsis Persis in ditionem Alexandri Magni venerat, diuque in potestate Macedonici imperij subiecti Syria regno fuerat. A Demetrio cum desciuissent, amicitiaRomanorum petita, pri-
units.tr: 3 The people's wealth grew from the flocks of balsam, which is produced only in these regions. For there is a valley, enclosed by continuous mountains as if by a kind of wall, on the model of a camp. The area of the place is two hundred acres, and it is called the Arch. In it is a forest distinguished both for fertility and for charm, since it is interspersed with palm groves and balsam. The balsam trees have a form similar to pitch trees, except that they are lower, and they are cultivated like vines. At a certain time of year they sweat out balsam. But the wonder at the shade of that place is no less than at its fertility; for although the sun there is the hottest in the whole world, a certain natural and perpetual shade of temperate air dwells in that region. In this region there is a lake which, on account of its size and the stillness of its water, is called the Dead Sea. For it is not moved by winds, bitumen resisting the whirlwinds, by which all its water is kept still; nor does it admit of navigation, since everything lacking life sinks to the depths; nor does it bear any material except what is smeared with alum. First, Xerxes, king of the Persians, subdued the Jews; afterwards, when they had come under the rule of Alexander the Great together with the Persians, they remained for a long time under the power of the Macedonian empire as a subject part of the kingdom of Syria. When they had revolted from Demetrius, they sought the friendship of the Romans, and they were the first of all the Orientals to recover their liberty, the Romans then readily giving away what belonged to others.

units.la: mi omnium ex Oricutalibus libertatem receperunt, facile tunc Romanis de alieno largientibus.
units.tr: First of all the Orientals regained their liberty, the Romans then being generous with what was not theirs.

units.tr: 4 At the same time, while the kingdom of Syria was passing back and forth between new kings, Attalus, king of Asia, who had received the most flourishing kingdom from his uncle Eumenes,

units.la: 10 gnum, cædibus amicorum & cognatorum supplicis fœdabat, nunc matrem anum, nunc Beronicen sobsam maleficiis eorum necatas confingens. Post hanc scelesta violentia rabiem, squalidam vestem sumit; barbam capillumq; in medium reorum summittit; nõ in publicum
units.tr: 10 defiled it with the murders of friends and kinsmen, feigning now that his old mother and now that his sister Berenice had been killed by their poisonings. After this wicked violence he took on a rabiid frenzy: he put on squalid clothing, let his beard and hair grow long in the manner of the accused, did not come out in public or show himself to the people, did not hold more lavish banquets at home, and showed no sign of a sound mind, so that he seemed to be paying the penalty to the hands of those he had killed.

units.tr: 15 Then, abandoning the administration of the kingdom, he dug gardens and sowed poisonous seeds, mixing harmful things with harmless ones,

units.la: 20 miscebat,eaq; omnia venenum succo infecta, velut peculiare munus amicis mittebat. Ab hoc studio ærariæ artis fabricæ se tradit, cærisque fingendis, & arte fundando, procudendoque oblectabatur. Matri deinde sepulchrum facere instituit; cui operi intentus, morbum ex 25 solis feruore contraxit, & septima die decessit: huius testamento heres populus Rom. tunc instituitur. Sed eratex Eumene Aristonicus, non iusto matrimonio, sed ex pellice Ephesia citharista cuiusdam filia genitus, qui post mortem Attali velut paternum regnum Asiam in-
units.tr: 20 and sent all these things, infected with venom, as a special gift to his friends. From this pursuit he turned to the craft of working bronze, and took pleasure in modelling figures, casting and beating metal. Next he resolved to build a tomb for his mother; while intent on this task he caught a sickness from the heat of the sun and died on the seventh day. By his will the Roman people was then named his heir. But Aristonicus, the son of Eumenes, was born not of a lawful marriage but of a concubine, a daughter of a certain Ephesian lyre-player; after Attalus's death he seized Asia as if it were his father's kingdom.

units.la: 30 uasit. Cum multa secunda prælia aduersus ciuitates, quæ metu Romanorum tradere se ei noluerant, fecisset; iussu, rex iam videretur, Asia Licinio Crasso cõsuli de-cernitur: qui intentior Attalicæ prædæ, quā bello, quum extremo anni tempore inordinata acie prælium conferuisset, victus pœnas inconsulta auaritia, sanguine dedit. In huius locum missus Perpenna consul, prima congressione Aristonicum superatum in potestatem suam redegit; Attalicasq; gazas hereditarias populi Romani nauibus impositas, Romam deportauit. Quod agre ferens successor eius Marcus Aquilius Consul, ad expediendum Aristonicum Perpennæ, veluti sui potius triumphi munus esse deberet, festinata velocitate contendit. Sed contentionem Consulum mors Perpennæ diremit. Sic Asia Romanorum facta cum opibus suis, vitia quoq; Romam transmisit.
units.tr: 30 After he had won many successes in battle against the cities that, from fear of the Romans, had refused to surrender to him, he was regarded as king already; Asia was assigned by decree to the consul Licinius Crassus. Being more eager for the Attalid plunder than for the war, he fought a battle at the very end of the year with a disordered line, was defeated, and paid the penalty in blood for his ill-considered greed. Consul Perperna was sent in his place; in the first encounter he defeated Aristonicus and brought him into his power, and he shipped the Attalid treasures, the inheritance of the Roman people, to Rome. Being vexed by this, his successor, the consul Marcus Aquilius, hurried with headlong speed to finish off Aristonicus, as though this should rather have been the reward of his own triumph than of Perperna's. But the death of Perperna ended the rivalry between the consuls. Thus Asia was made Roman together with its wealth, and its vices too were carried over to Rome.
POMPEII TROGI EPITOMA HISTORIARVM
Book 37. Summary.

units.la: 1 Massilienses in Phocaeenses beneficentia. In Cappadocia & Ponto tragœdiæ. 2 Mithridatis, Ponti regis, futura magnitudo prædicta, liberatio, occupationes. 3 Eiusdem res gestæ, & domi abuxore periculum. 4 Otii detectatio. Exercitia militaria. Cappadociæ sum.
units.tr: 1 The Massilians' kindness to the Phocaeans. Tragedies in Cappadocia and Pontus. 2 The future greatness of Mithridates, king of Pontus, foretold; his escape; his conquests. 3 His deeds, and the danger from his wife at home. 4 The exposure of his idleness. His military exercises. Summary of Cappadocia.

units.la: APTO Aristonico, Massilienses pro Phocensibus conditoribus suis, quorum urbem senatus, & omne nomen, quod & tunc, & antea Antiochi bello, infesta contra populum Romanum arma tulerant, deleri iusserat, legatos Romam deprecatum miserunt, veniamq; his a senatu obtinuere. Post hæc regibus, qui aduersus Aristonicum auxilia tulerant, premia persoluta: Mithridati Pontico Syria maior: filiis Ariarathis regis Cappadocia, qui eodem bello occiderat, Licaonia & Cilicia data fideliorq; populus Romanus
units.tr: After Aristonicus was defeated, the Massilians sent envoys to Rome to plead on behalf of the Phocaeans, their founders. The senate had ordered their city and every name associated with it destroyed, since they had taken up arms against the Roman people both then and earlier, in the war with Antiochus. The envoys obtained pardon from the senate. After this, rewards were paid to the kings who had brought aid against Aristonicus: Greater Syria went to Mithridates of Pontus, and Lycaonia and Cilicia to the sons of King Ariarathes of Cappadocia, who had fallen in the same war. The Roman people proved more faithful to the sons of their allies than the mother had been to her own children.

units.la: in socij filios, quam mater in liberos fuit: Quippe hinc paruulis auctum regnum, inde vita adempta. Namque Laudice ex numero sex filiorum, quos virilis sexus ex Ariarathe rege susceperat, timens ne non diutinam regni administrationem adultis quibusdam potiretur,
units.tr: For here the kingdom was enlarged for the little ones, while there life was taken away. Laodice, of the six sons whom King Ariarathes had had by her, was afraid that some of the grown sons might gain control of the long administration of the kingdom.

units.la: quinque parricidiali veneno necauit; unum paruulum sceleri matris cognatorum custodia eripuit, qui post necem Laudices (nam propter crudelitatem eam populus extinxerat) solus regno potitus est. Mithridates quoq; repentina morte interceptus, filium, qui & ipse Mithridates dictus est, reliquit. Cuius ea postea magnitudo fuit, vt non sui tantum temporis, verumetiam superioris aetatis omnes reges maiestate superauerit, bellaque cum Romanis per 46. annos varia victoria gesserit: Cū eum summis imperatoribus Sylla, Lucullus, ceterisque, in summa Cneus Pompeius ita vicerint, vt maior clariorq; in restaurando bello resurgeret, damnoq; suis terribilior redderetur. Denique, ad postremum non vt hostili victus, sed voluntaria morte, in auito regno senex, herede filio decessit.
units.tr: She had five of them killed with a parricidal poison. She rescued one little boy from his mother's crime by putting him under the guardianship of relatives. After Laodice's death (the people had destroyed her for her cruelty), he alone obtained the kingdom. Mithridates too was cut off by a sudden death and left a son, who was also called Mithridates. His greatness was such that he surpassed in majesty all the kings of his own and earlier times. He waged war with the Romans for forty-six years with varying success. The chief commanders, Sulla, Lucullus and the rest, and at last Gnaeus Pompey, defeated him, yet he rose again in renewing the war, greater and more famous, and by his losses became more formidable to his enemies. At last he died, not as one conquered by an enemy but by a voluntary death, an old man in his ancestral kingdom, leaving his son as heir.

units.la: 2 Huius futuram magnitudinem etiam caelestia ostenta praedixerant. Nam & quo genitus est anno, & eo quo regnare primum coepit, stellae cometes per vtrūq; tempus septuaginta diebus ita luxit, vt cœlum omne conflagrare videretur. Nam & magnitudine sui quartam partem cœli occupauerat; & fulgore sui solis nitorem vicerat; & cum oriretur occumberetque, quatuor spatium horarum consumebat. Puer tutorum insidias passus est, qui eum fero equo impositum, equitare iacu-lari, lariq latrig, cogebant: qui conatus cum eos fefellissent, supra etatem regente equum Mithridate, veneno cum appetiuere. Quod metuens, antidota fapius bibit, & ita fe aduersus insidias exquisitis tutioribus remediis stagnauit, vt ne volens quidem senex venenο inori potuerit. Timens deinde ne inimici quod veneno non potuerant, ferro peragerent, venandi studium finxit: quo per feplures annos neq; verbis, neq; ruris tecto vsus est; sed per siluas vagatus, diuersis montium regionibus pernoctabat, ignaris omnibus, quibus effet loci: affectus feras cursu aut fugare, aut persequi, cum quibusdam etiam viribus congredi. Quibus rebus, & insidias vitauit; & corpus ad omnem virtutis patientiam duraut.
units.tr: 2 Heavenly portents had also foretold his future greatness. In the year he was born, and again in the year he first began to reign, a comet shone for seventy days in each period, so that the whole sky seemed to be on fire. It occupied a quarter of the heavens by its size, and by its brilliance it outshone the splendour of the sun; from rising to setting it took four hours. As a boy he suffered the plots of his guardians, who made him mount a wild horse and forced him to ride, hurl the javelin and fight like a bandit. When these attempts failed them, they turned to poison: though Mithridates controlled the horse beyond his years, they attacked him with poison. Fearing this, he often drank antidotes, and so he fortified himself against the plots with carefully chosen and more reliable remedies, so that even if he had wished it, the old man could scarcely be killed by poison. Then, fearing that his enemies would finish with the sword what they had not been able to do with poison, he feigned a passion for hunting. For several years he used neither words nor the roof of a house, but wandered through the woods and spent his nights in different mountain regions, unknown to everyone as to where he was. He chased wild beasts, either outrunning them or pursuing them, and even contended with some of them in strength. By these means he both avoided the plots and hardened his body to every endurance of toil.

units.la: 3 Ad regni deinde administrationem cum accessif-set, statim non de regendo, sed de augendo regno cogitauit, Itaq; Scythas iniuictos antea, qui Sopyriona, Alexandri Magni ducem, cum triginta millibus armatorum deleuerant; qui Cyrum, Persarum regem, cum ducentis millibus trucidauerant; qui Philippum Macedonum regem fugauerant, ingenti felicitate perdomuit. Auctus igitur viribus, Pontum quoq;, ac deinceps Cappadociam occupauit. Cum de Asia tractaret, tacitus cum quibusdam amicis regno profectus, vniuersam ne-mine sciente peruagatus est, omniumq; vrbium situm ac regiones cognouit. Inde Bithyniam transcendit, & quasi dominus Asiae, opportuna quaq; victoria sua metatus est. Post hac in regnum, cum iam periisse crederetur, reuersus est, inuento paruulo filio, quem per absentiam eius Laudice soror vxorque eius, quae fuerat: sed inter gratulationem aduentus sui, & filij geniti, veneno periclitatus est. Siquidem Laudice soror cum periisse eum crederet, in concubitus amicorum proiecta, quasi admissum facinus maiore scelere tegere posset, venenum num aduenienti parauit. Quod cum ex ancilla Mithridates cognouisset, facinus in auctores vindicauit.
units.tr: 3 When he came to the administration of the kingdom, he at once thought not of governing but of enlarging it. Therefore he subdued, with remarkable success, the Scythians, who had until then been unconquered: they had destroyed Sopyrion, a general of Alexander the Great, with thirty thousand armed men; they had slaughtered Cyrus, king of the Persians, with two hundred thousand; and they had put to flight Philip, king of the Macedonians. Strengthened by this, he seized Pontus and then Cappadocia. While he was considering Asia, he set out secretly from his kingdom with some friends and wandered over the whole region, unknown to anyone, learning the situation and character of every city. From there he crossed into Bithynia, and as if lord of Asia he marked out every place that was favourable for his victories. Afterwards he returned to his kingdom, which was thought to be lost, and found his little son, whom his sister and wife Laodice had been holding in his absence. But amid the rejoicing at his return and at the birth of his son, he was endangered by poison. Laodice, believing he had perished, threw herself upon the couches of her friends. So that she might cover her crime with a greater one, she prepared poison for his arrival. When Mithridates learned of this from a maidservant, he avenged the deed upon its authors.

units.la: 4 Hieme deinde imminente, non in conuiuio, sed in campo; non in aduocationibus, [sed in exercitationibus: ] nec inter sodales sed inter coaequales, aut equo, aut cursu, aut viribus contendebat. Exercitum quoq; suum ad parem laboris patientiam quotidiana exercitatione durabat, atq; ita inuictum ipse inexpugnabilem exercitum fecerat. Inita deinde cum Nicomede societate Paphlagoniam inuadit, victamq; cum socio diuidit. Quam cum teneri à regibus senatui nuntiatum esset, legatos ad vtrumq; misit, qui gentem restitui in pristinum statum iuberent. Mithridates cum se iam parem magnitudini Romanorum crederet, superbo responso, hereditarium patri suo regnum obuenisse, respondit: mirarique se, quod ei relata controuersia non fuerit, sibi referatur. Nec territus minus, Galatiam quoq; occupat. Nicomedes quoniam se tueri iure non potuerat, iusto regi redditurum respondit. Atq; ita filium suum mutato nomine, Philiamenem Paphlagonum regum nomine appellat, & quasi stirpi regiæ reddidisset regnum, falso nomine tenet. Sic ludibrio habiti legati, Romam reuertuntur.
units.tr: 4 Then, with winter approaching, he competed not at banquets but on the field; not in lawsuits, nor among his companions, but against his equals, in horsemanship, running and strength. He also hardened his army by daily exercise to an equal endurance of toil, and so he made an army that was itself unconquerable and invincible. Then, having formed an alliance with Nicomedes, he invaded Paphlagonia and, after conquering it, divided it with his ally. When the senate was told that the country was held by kings, it sent envoys to each of them, ordering that the nation be restored to its former state. Mithridates, believing himself now a match for the greatness of the Romans, replied haughtily that the kingdom had come to his father by inheritance. He said he was surprised that the dispute, which had not been referred to him, was now being referred to him. Not in the least frightened, he also seized Galatia. Nicomedes replied that, since he could not defend his claim by right, he would return the kingdom to its rightful king. And so he gave his son a changed name, Philamenes, after the name of the Paphlagonian kings, and, as if he had restored the kingdom to the royal line, he held it under a false name. Thus the envoys were mocked, and they returned to Rome.

units.la: POMPEII TROGI EPI- TOMA HISTORIARVM LIBER XXXVIII.
units.tr: THE EPITOME OF POMPEIUS TROGUS' HISTORIES, BOOK 38.
SUMMARY,

units.la: 1 Mithridates regni sui cenfer, iustum bellum illud auspicia parricidiis pollut, ostendens. & callidis artibus Ariarathē Cappadocem trucidat. 6 Malas eorundem attes & originem de regit.
units.tr: 1 Mithridates reveals that his kingdom is sustained by unjust war, which he defiles with parricides by his auspices. And by crafty arts he slays Ariarathes the Cappadocian. 6 He sets forth the wicked arts of the same men and their origin.

units.la: 2 Nouæ tragœdiæ Mithridaris & Nicomedis, quas senatus Romanus vr- cunque sedat. 7 Sturpis suæ nobilitatē, suorumque libertatem ac fortitudinem opponit, nec non belli facilitatem, libertate ac munificētia mitiores alliciens.
units.tr: 2 The new tragedies of Mithridates and Nicomedes, which the Roman senate somehow quells. 7 He sets against them the nobility of his race, the freedom and courage of his people, and also the ease of war, attracting them by his liberality and generosity.

units.la: 3 Tigranem Mithridates in societatem belli adversus Romanos trahit, & proconsulibus Rom. praelio fusis, ingenti ciuitatū Asiarum fauore excipitur. 8 In Ægypto Ptolemæus Physcon multiplici scelere omnia turbat & a suis pellitur.
units.tr: 3 Mithridates draws Tigranes into alliance in war against the Romans, and after the Roman proconsuls are routed in battle, he is received with great favour by the cities of Asia. 8 In Egypt Ptolemy Physcon throws everything into confusion by many crimes and is driven out by his own people.

units.la: 4 Oratio Mithridatis, in qua rationes suis exponit cur bellum sit Romanis inferendum. 9 Demetrii Syriæ regis, fortunæ ludibrio, variiʃ casus.
units.tr: 4 Speech of Mithridates, in which he sets out his reasons why war should be waged against the Romans. 9 Demetrius, king of Syria, is the plaything of fortune and suffers various misfortunes.

units.la: 5 Romanos, dum occupati essent adoriendos esse 10 Antiochus Demetrii fraterParthos bello aggressus, in acie à suis desertus, occiditur.
units.tr: 5 The Romans, while they are occupied, should be attacked. 10 Antiochus, brother of Demetrius, attacks the Parthians in war, is deserted by his men in battle, and is killed.

units.la: ITHRIDATES parricidia nece vxoris auspicatus, sororis alterius Lau dicesfilios, cuius virum Ariarathem regem Cappadocie per Gordium infidiis occiderat, tollendos statuit: nihil actum morte patris exi-stimans, si adolescentes paternum regnū, cuius ille cupidit ate flagrabat, occupassent. Igitur dum in his cogitationibus versatur, interim Nicomedes rex Bithyniæ, vacuam morte regis Cappadociam invadit. Quod cum nuntiatum Mithridati suisset, per simulationem pietatis auxilia sorori ad expellendum Cappadocia Nicomedem mittit. Sed iam Laudice per pactionem se Nicomedi in matrimonium tradiderat. Quod agre ferens Mithridates, præsidia Nicomedis Cappadocia expellit, regnumq; sororis filio restituit: egregium prorsus factum, ni subsequuta fraus esset. Siquidem interiectis mensibus, simulat se Gordium, 5 quo ministro vsus in Ariarathe interficiendo fuerat, reflituere in patriam velle, sperans, si obsisteret adolescens, causas belli futuras; aut si permitteret, per eundem, filium tolli posse, per quem interfecerat patrem. Quod vbi Ariarathes iunior moliri cognouit, grauiter feres interfectorem patris per aununculum potissimum ab exilio reuocari, ingentem exercitum contrahit. Igitur cum in atiem eduxisset Mithridates peditum octoginta millia, equitum decem millia, currus falcatos 600. nec Ariarathi auxiliantibus finitimis regibus, minores copiæ essent, incertum belli timens, consilia ad insidias transfert: solicitatoq; iuuene ad colloquium, cum ferrum occultatum inter fascias gereret, scrutatori ab Ariarathe regio more missō, curiosus unum ventrem pertractanti, ait caueret ne aliud telum inueniret, quam quæreret. Atq; ita rursus protectis insidiis, euncatum ab amicis velut ad secretum sermonem, infpectante vtroq; exercitu interficit: regnum Cappadociæ octo annorum filio, in potesto Ariarathis nomine, additoq; ei rectore Gordio tradidit.
units.tr: Mithridates, having begun his parricides with the murder of his wife, decided that the sons of his other sister Laodice must be removed; he had treacherously killed their father Ariarathes, king of Cappadocia, through Gordius. He thought nothing would be achieved by his father's death if the young men were to seize the paternal kingdom, which he himself burned to possess. So while he was occupied with these thoughts, meanwhile Nicomedes, king of Bithynia, invaded Cappadocia, which lay empty after the king's death. When this was reported to Mithridates, under the pretence of loyalty he sent aid to his sister to drive Nicomedes out of Cappadocia. But Laodice had already given herself in marriage to Nicomedes by an agreement. Mithridates, taking this badly, expelled Nicomedes' garrisons from Cappadocia and restored the kingdom to his sister's son. It would have been an admirable deed indeed, had not treachery followed. For after some months, he pretended that he wished to restore Gordius, whom he had used as his agent in killing Ariarathes, to his homeland. He hoped that if the young man resisted, this would give him grounds for future war; or if he allowed it, that the son could be killed by the same man through whom he had killed the father. When the younger Ariarathes learned that this was being planned, he took it very hard that the murderer of his father was being recalled from exile, chiefly through his uncle, and he gathered a huge army. So when Mithridates had led out into the field eighty thousand foot soldiers, ten thousand horse and six hundred scythed chariots, and since the neighbouring kings who would have aided Ariarathes had smaller forces, fearing the uncertain outcome of war, he turned to ambush. He enticed the young man to a conference, but he was carrying a concealed blade between his bands. Ariarathes, as a king's custom, had sent a searcher; Mithridates, pretending to be curious, fingered one belly and said he should take care not to find some other weapon than the one he was looking for. And so, having again covered up the ambush, he had Ariarathes led away by his friends as if for a private talk, and killed him while both armies watched. He handed the kingdom of Cappadocia to the eight-year-old son, under the name of Ariarathes but in his power, and gave him Gordius as guardian.

units.la: 2 Sed Cappadoces crudelitate ac libidine prefectorum vexati, à Mithridate deficiunt: fratremq; regis, & ipsum Ariarathem nomine, ab Asia vbi educabatur, reuocant: cum quo Mithridates prælium renouat, vi-ctumEiusdem Cappadociæ regno expellit. Nec multo post adolescens, exagitatudine collecta infirmitate, decedit.
units.tr: 2 But the Cappadocians, vexed by the cruelty and lust of the governors, revolted from Mithridates. They recalled the king's brother, also named Ariarathes, from Asia where he had been brought up. Mithridates renewed the battle with him, defeated him, and drove him from the kingdom of the same Cappadocia. Not long afterwards the young man, weakened by a gathered illness, died.

units.la: Post huius mortem Nicomedes timens ne Mithridates Cappadociæ, etiam Bithyniam finitimam invaderet, subornat puerum eximiæ pulchritudinis, quasi Ariarathes tres, non duos filios genuisset, qui à senatu Romano paternum regnum peteret. Vxorem quoque Laodicen Romam misit, ad testimonium trium ex Ariarathe susceptorum filiorum. Quod vbi Mithridates cognovit, & ipse pari impudentia Gordium Romam mittit, qui senatui assereret, puerum qui Cappadociæ regnum traditerat, ex eo Ariarathe genitum qui bello Aristonici auxilia Romanis feres cecidisset. Sed senatus studio regum intellecto, aliena regna falsis nominibus furantium, & Mithridati Cappadociam, & Nicomedi, ad solatium eius, Paphlagoniam adem it. Acne contumelia regum foret, ademptum illis, quod daretur aliis, vterque populus libertate donatus est. Sed Cappadoces munus libertatis abnuentes, negant viuere gentē sine rege posse. Atque, ita rex illis à senatu Ariobarzanes con-
units.tr: After his death, Nicomedes, fearing that Mithridates would invade neighbouring Bithynia after Cappadocia, procured a boy of extraordinary beauty, pretending that Ariarathes had begotten three sons, not two, and that he should seek the paternal kingdom from the Roman senate. He also sent his wife Laodice to Rome, as witness to the three sons she had borne to Ariarathes. When Mithridates learned this, with equal shamelessness he sent Gordius to Rome, to assert to the senate that the boy who had received the kingdom of Cappadocia had been born of that Ariarathes who had fallen while bringing aid to the Romans in the war with Aristonicus. But the senate, perceiving the zeal of the kings who were seizing foreign kingdoms under false names, took Cappadocia from Mithridates and Paphlagonia for Nicomedes as a consolation. And so that it would not be an insult to the kings that what was taken from them was given to others, both peoples were granted liberty. But the Cappadocians refused the gift of liberty, saying that their nation could not live without a king. And so the senate established Ariobarzanes as king over them.
The Roman senate cuts through their knots. Ariobarzanes is restored.

units.la: 3 Erat eo tempore Tigranes rex Armenia, obses Parthis ante multum temporis datus, sed olim ab iisdem in regnum paternum remissus: Hunc Mithridates mire ad societatem Romani belli, quod olim meditabatur, pellicere cupiebat. Nihil igitur de offensa Romanorum sententiam, per Gordium impellit, vt Ariobarzani, regni admodum, bellum inferat: & nequis dolus subesse videretur, filiam suam ei Cleopatram in matrimonium tradit. Primo igitur aduentu Tigranis, Ariobarzanes sublatis rebus suis, Romam contendit. Atq; ita per Tigranem rursus Cappadocia iuris esse Mithridatis coepit. Eodem tempore morttuo Nicomede, etiam filius eius, & ipse Nicomedes{?}
units.tr: 3 At that time Tigranes was king of Armenia. He had been given as a hostage to the Parthians long before, but they had later sent him back to his father's kingdom. Mithridates was eager to win him over as an ally for the Roman war he had long been planning. So, without any mention of an offence against the Romans, he pushes him through Gordius to attack Ariobarzanes, a king of great standing, and so that no trickery should seem to lie behind it, he gives him his daughter Cleopatra in marriage. At Tigranes' first approach, Ariobarzanes gathered up his belongings and hurried to Rome. And so, through Tigranes, Cappadocia once again came under the control of Mithridates. At the same time, Nicomedes died, and his son, also named Nicomedes, was driven from his kingdom by Mithridates.

units.la: 25 30 line numbers as printed. comedes regno à Mithridate pellitur: qui cum supplex Romam venisset, decernitur in senatu, vt vterq; in regnum restituantur: in quod tū misi Aquilius & Manlius Maltinus legati. Hu cognitû Mithridates societatê 5. cū Tigrane, bellum aduersus Romanos gessurus, iungit: pactiq; inter se sunt, vt vrbes agriq; Mithridati, homines vero & quæcunq; auferri possent, Tigrani cederent. Post hæc Mithridates intelliges quantum bellum suscitaret, legatos ad Cimbros, alios ad Gallogræcos, & Sarmatas, Bastranasq; auxilium petitum mittit. Nam omnes hæ gentes, Romanum meditabundas bellum, variis beneficiorû muneribus iam ante illexerat. Ab Scythia quoq; exercitû venire iubet, omnemq; Orientê aduersus Romanos armat. Nõ magno igitur labore Aquilio & Maltino exercitum instructos vincit: quibus simul cũ Nicomede pulsis, ingeti sauore ciuitatium excipitur: multũ ibi auri argētiq;, studio veterû regum, magnûq; belli apparatû inuenit: quibus instructus, debita ciuitatib, publica priuataq; remittit, & vacationê quinquennij concedit. Tunc ad concionê milites vocat, eosq; variis exhortationibus ad Romana bella sine Asiana incitat. Quam orationem digna duxi, cuius exẽplum breuitati huius operis insererem, quam obliquam Pompeius Trogus exposuit: quoniã in Liuio & in Sallustio reprehẽdit, quod conciones directas, pro sua oratione operi suo inserendo, bistoria modum excesserint.
units.tr: 25 30 ...comedes is driven from his kingdom by Mithridates. Coming to Rome as a suppliant, he was decreed by the senate that both kings should be restored to their kingdoms, and Aquilius and Manlius Maltinus were sent as envoys for this purpose. When Mithridates learned of this, he joins forces with Tigranes to wage war against the Romans, and they agreed between themselves that the cities and lands should go to Mithridates, but the men and whatever could be carried off should go to Tigranes. After this, Mithridates, understanding how great a war he was stirring up, sent envoys to the Cimbri, others to the Gallo-Greeks, the Sarmatians and the Bastarnae, to seek help. For all these peoples, who were already contemplating war against Rome, he had won over beforehand with various gifts. He also orders an army to come from Scythia, and arms the whole East against the Romans. Without great effort he defeats Aquilius and Maltinus, who had drawn up their troops; with Nicomedes also driven out, he is received with immense favour by the cities. There he finds much gold and silver, left by the zeal of the old kings, and a great store of war equipment. Equipped with these, he remits to the cities their debts, public and private, and grants them a five-year exemption from tribute. Then he calls the soldiers to an assembly and, with various exhortations, urges them on to the Roman war as if it were a war in Asia. I have thought this speech worth inserting in this work, though briefly, in the form in which Pompeius Trogus set it out indirectly. For he criticises Livy and Sallust for having gone beyond the bounds of history by inserting direct speeches of their own composition into their works.

units.la: 4 Optandum sibi fuisse ait, vt de eo liceret consulere, bellumne fit cum Romanis, an pax habenda: quin vero sit resistendum impugnantibus, nec eos quidê dubitare, qui spe victoriæ careant: Quippe aduersus latrones, si nequeant pro salute, pro vltione tamen sua omnes ferrum stringere. Ceterum quia non id agitur, an liceat quiescere, non tantû animo hostiliter, sed etiam præpraelio congressis consulendum,qua ratione ac spe capta bella sustineant: Esse autem sibi victoria fiduciam, fi fit illis animus: Romanos, vinci posse, cognitum non sibi magis,quam ipsis militibus, qui & in Bithynia Aquilium,& Maltinum in Cappadocia fuderint. At si quem aliena magis exempla, quam sua experimenta moueant, audire se a Pyrrho rege Epiri, non amplius quam quinq;millibus Macedonum instructo,fusos tribus praeliis Romanos. Audire Annibalem (sexdecim annis Italiae victorem immoratum: & quin ipsam caperet vrbem,non Romanorum illi vires obstitisse,sed domestica emulationis atque invidiae studium. Audire populos Transalpinae Galliae Italiam ingressos, maximis eam plurimisq; vrbibus posidere; & latius aliquanto solum finium quā in Asia,qua dicatur imbellis,eo(dem Gallos occupasse; nec victam solum dici sibi Romam a Gallis, sed etiam captam, ita vt vnius illis montis tantum cacumen relinqueretur,nec bello hostem,sed pretio remotum; Gallorum autem nomen, quod semper Romanos terruit in partem virium suarum ipse numeret, Nam hos qui Asiam incolunt Gallos,ab illis, qui Italiam occupauerant,sedibus tantum distare: originem quidem ac virtutem,genusq; pugnae idem habere, tantoque his fagaciora esse quam illis ingenia, quanto longiori ac difficiliori spatio,per Illyricum Thraciamq; prodierint, pene operosius transitis eorum finibus,quam vbi consedere possessis. Tam ipsam Italiam audire se numquam, vt Roma condita sit, satis illi pacatam, sed assidue per omnes annos pro libertate alios,contra quosdam etiam pro iure imperij bellis continuis perfeucrasse, & a multis ciuitatibus Italiae deletos Romanorum exercitus ferro, a quibusdam nouo contumelia more subiugum missos. Ac ne veteribus immoremur exemplis, boc ipso temtempore vniuersam Italiam bello Marsico confurrexis- se, non iam libertatem, sed consortium imperij, ciuitatisq; poscentem: Nec grauius vicino Italiæ bello, quam domesticis principum factionibus vrbem premi multoque periculosius esse Italico ciuile bellum, simul & à Germania Cimbros, immensa millia ferorum atq; immitium populorum, more procellæ, inundasse Italiam: quorum tametsi singula bella sustinere Romani possent, vniuersis tamen obruantur, vt ne vacaturos quidem bello suo putet.
units.tr: 4 He says that he would have wished to be able to consult on whether there should be war with the Romans or peace should be kept. But since resistance must be offered to those who attack, and even those who lack hope of victory do not hesitate, for against robbers, even if they cannot save themselves, all men draw the sword to avenge themselves: since the question is not whether they may keep quiet, but how, and with what reason and hope, they may sustain the war, they must take counsel not only in their minds as enemies but also in the battle they are entering. Moreover, if they have the courage, he says, he has confidence in victory; that the Romans can be conquered is known to him no less than to the soldiers themselves, who routed Aquilius in Bithynia and Maltinus in Cappadocia. But if some men are moved more by other men's examples than by their own experience, he has heard that Pyrrhus, king of Epirus, with no more than five thousand Macedonians, routed the Romans in three battles. He has heard that Hannibal, victor in Italy for sixteen years, lingered there, and that it was not the strength of the Romans that stopped him from taking the city itself, but the rivalry and envy at home. He has heard that the peoples of Transalpine Gaul entered Italy and occupy it with its greatest and most numerous cities, and that they have seized a territory considerably wider than in Asia, which is said to be unwarlike; and that Rome was not only conquered by the Gauls but also captured, so that only the summit of one hill was left to them, and they were removed not by war but by ransom. The name of the Gauls, which has always terrified the Romans, he counts among his own forces. For those Gauls who inhabit Asia are separated from those who occupied Italy only by their dwelling places; they have the same origin and courage and the same manner of fighting, and their minds are the sharper for the longer and more difficult journey they made through Illyricum and Thrace, a journey almost more laborious than the settling of their lands once they had settled there. He has heard too that Italy itself was never at peace since Rome was founded, but that year after year it has continually fought wars, for freedom against some and for the right of empire against others; and that Roman armies have been destroyed by the sword in many Italian cities, and others have been sent under the yoke in a new kind of humiliation. And, not to dwell on old examples, at this very time all Italy has risen in the Marsian war, demanding not now freedom but a share in the empire and citizenship. Nor, he says, is the city more heavily pressed by the neighbouring Italian war than by the factions of its leaders at home, and the civil war in Italy is far more dangerous; and at the same time the Cimbri have flooded into Italy from Germany, like a storm, immense multitudes of savage and fierce peoples. Although the Romans could withstand each of these wars singly, they will be overwhelmed by them all together, so that he thinks they will not even have leisure for their own war.

units.la: 5 Vtendum igitur occasione, & rapienda incrementa virium, ne si illis occupatis quieuerint, mox aduersus vacuos, & quietos maius negotium habeant. Non enim quæri an capiendafint arma, sed vtrum sua potius occasione, an illorum. Nam bellum equidem iam tunc secum ab illis geri cœptum, cum sibi pupillo maiorem Phrygiam ademerint, quam patri suo pramium dati aduersus Aristonicum auxilij conCesserant, gentè quam & proauo suo Mithridati, Seleucus Callinicus in dotem dedisset. Quid cum Paphlagonia se decedere iusserunt, non alterum illud genus belli fuisse? quæ non vi, non armis, sed adoptione testamenti & regum domesticorum interitu, hereditaria patri suo obuenisset: cum inter hanc decretorum amaritudinem parendo, non tamen eos mitigaret, quin acerbius se in dies gerant, nō obtinuisse. Quod enim à se non præbitum illis obsequium? non Phrygiam, Paphlagoniamque dimissas? non Cappadocia filium eductum, quam iure gentium victor occupauerat? Raptam tamen sibi esse victoriam eius ab illis, quorum nihil est nisi bello quæsitum. Non regem Bithyniæ Chreston, in quem senatus arma decreuerat, à se in gratiam illorum oppugnatum? tamen nihilominus imputari sibi, siqua Gordius aut Tigranes faciat: libertatem etiam in contumeliam fui à senatu vltro delatam Cappadocia, quam reliquis gentibus abstulerunt: deinde populo Cappadocum, pro libertate oblata, Gordium regem orante, ideo tantum quoniam amicus suus esset, non obtinuisse. Nicomedem praecepto illorum belli sibi intulisse: quia vltum icrit se, ab ipsis ventu obtiam in eo, & nunc eam secum bellandi illis causam fore, quod non impune se Nicomedi lacerandum, saltaricis filio, praebuerit.
units.tr: 5 We must therefore use the opportunity and seize the growth of our strength, lest, if they are occupied and then keep quiet, they later have a harder struggle against us when we are idle and at peace. For the question is not whether arms should be taken up, but whether they should be taken up on our own opportunity or on theirs. Indeed the war was already begun against me by them when they took from me, while I was a ward, the greater Phrygia, which they had granted to my father as a reward for his help against Aristonicus, a land which Seleucus Callinicus had given as dowry to my great-grandfather Mithridates. When they ordered me to withdraw from Paphlagonia, was that not another kind of war? That land had come to my father by inheritance, not by force of arms but by adoption in a will and by the death of its domestic kings. Although I obeyed these bitter decrees, they did not soften their attitude, and they behave more harshly every day. What obedience did I not show them? Did I not give up Phrygia and Paphlagonia? Did I not bring up the son of Cappadocia, which I had seized as victor by the law of nations? Yet their victory over him was snatched from me, though it was won by nothing but war. Did I not attack King Chrestus of Bithynia, against whom the senate had decreed war, in order to please them? Yet whatever Gordius or Tigranes does is still charged against me. They offered freedom to Cappadocia, which they had taken from the other nations, but they offered it of their own accord, and only as an insult to me; and when the people of Cappadocia accepted the freedom offered, at the request of King Gordius, they did not allow it to stand, simply because he was my friend. They made war on Nicomedes at my instigation: because I had avenged myself, they came to meet me in that cause, and now they will have a further reason to make war on me, because I did not allow Nicomedes to be torn apart with impunity, though he was only a child.

units.la: 6 Quippe non deliberat regum illos, sed vires ac maiestatem infequineq, in se vno, sed in aliis quoq, omnibus hac semper arte grassatos. Sic & aliam suum Pharnacem, per cognationum arbitria, succedanum regi Perganeno Eumeni datum: sic rursus Eumenem, cuius classibus primum in Asiam fuere transfuecti; cuius excitu magis quam suo, & Magnum Antiochum, & Gallos in Asia, & mox in Macedonia regem Perseum dominatur, & ipsum pro hoste habitum, eiq, interdictum Italia; & quod cum ipso deforme sibi putauerant, cum filio eius Aristonico bellu gesisse. Nullius apud eos mai ora, quam Masinissae regis Numidarum habere merita.
units.tr: 6 Indeed those men are not deliberating about kings; they envy the power and majesty of kings. They have always attacked by this same method not only me alone but all the others too. Thus they gave my brother Pharnaces, through the decisions of their kinsmen, as a successor to Eumenes, king of Pergamum; and again Eumenes himself, by whose fleets they were first carried into Asia, and by whose army rather than their own they overcame Antiochus the Great, the Gauls in Asia, and soon afterward king Perseus in Macedonia. They treated Eumenes himself as an enemy, and forbade him Italy; and they made war on his son Aristonicus, because they thought he was a disgrace to themselves. Among them, the services of Masinissa, king of the Numidians, count for nothing.

units.la: Huic imputari victu Annibalem, huic captum Syphacem, huic Carthaginem deletam, hunc inter duos illos Africanos tertium seruatorem vrbis referri: tamen cum huius nepote bellum modo in Africa gestum adeo inexpiabile, vt ne victum quidem memoriae patris donaret, quin carcerem ac triumphi spectaculum experiretur.
units.tr: To him they attribute the defeat of Hannibal, to him the capture of Syphax, to him the destruction of Carthage. Between the two Africani he is named the third saviour of the city. Yet they waged war with his grandson in Africa so implacably that they did not even spare the defeated man out of respect for his father's memory, but tried him in prison and in the spectacle of a triumph.

units.la: Hanc illos regibus omnibus legem odiorum dixisse, scilicet quia ipsi tales reges habuerint, quorum etiam nominibus erubescant, aut pastores Aboriginum, aut aruspices Sabinorum, aut exules Corinthiorum, aut seruos vernasq, Thuscorum, aut, quod honoratissimum nomen fuit inter hac, Superbos: atq, vt ipsi ferunt, conditores suos, lupa uberibus altos: sic omnem illum populum luporum animos, inexplebiles sanguinis atq; imperij, diuitiarumq; auidos ac iciunos habere.
units.tr: They laid down this law of hatred for all kings, evidently because they themselves had such kings that they blush at their very names: shepherds of the Aborigines, soothsayers of the Sabines, exiles of the Corinthians, or slaves and servants of the Etruscans, or, the most honoured name among these, the Superbi. And, as they themselves say, their founders were nursed at the teats of a she-wolf. Thus that whole people has the spirit of wolves, insatiable for blood, empire and riches, hungry and greedy.

units.la: 7 Se autem, seu nobilitate illis comparetur, clariorem illa colluuie conuenarum esse, qui paternos maiores suos à Cyro Dario q, conditoribus Perfici regni, maternos à Magno Alexandro, ac Nicatore Seleuco, conditoribus imperij Macedonici, referat: seu populus illorum conferatur suo, earum se gentium esse, quae nō mo-do Romano imperio sint pares, sed Macedonico quoque obstiterint. Nullam subiectarum sibi gentium expertā peregrina imperia; nullis vmquam nisi domesticis regibus paruisse: Cappadociam velint, an Paphlagoniam recenseré; rursus Pontum an Bithyniam; itemq; Armieniam maiorem minoremque: quarum gentium nullam neq; Alexander ille, qui totam pacauit Asiam, nec quisquam successorum eius, aut posterorum attigisset. Scythiam ditos vmquam ante se reges non pacare, sed tantum intrare ausos Darium & Philippum; aegre inde fugam sibi expediisse, vnde ipse magnam partem aduersus Romanos virium haberet. Multoque se timidius ac diffidentius bella poutica ingressum, cum ipse rudis ac tyro esset: Scythiae praeter arma, virtutemq;, animi, locorum quoque solitudinibus, vel frigoribus instructa, per
units.tr: 7 As for myself, whether my nobility is compared with theirs, I claim to be more illustrious than that sewage of foreigners, who trace their paternal ancestors to Cyrus and Darius, founders of the Persian kingdom, and their maternal ones to Alexander the Great and Seleucus Nicator, founders of the Macedonian empire. Or if their people is compared with mine, I belong to those nations which are not only equal to the Roman empire but have also resisted the Macedonian one. No nation subject to me has ever experienced foreign rule; they have obeyed only native kings. Whether they wish to count Cappadocia or Paphlagonia; again Pontus or Bithynia; likewise Greater and Lesser Armenia: Alexander, who subdued all Asia, never touched any of these nations, nor did any of his successors or descendants. The Scythians, they say, never subdued by their kings before me; only Darius and Philip dared to enter their land, and they scarcely escaped from it, though from there I have a great part of my strength against the Romans. And he entered the Roman wars much more timidly and diffidently, since he himself was raw and inexperienced. Scythia is protected not only by arms and courage but also by the solitude of its places and its cold, through

units.la: 25 quae denuntiaretur ingens militiae labor ac periculum. Inter quas difficultates ne spes quidem praemij foret, ex hoste vago; nec tantum pecuniae, sed etiam sedis inopes. Nunc se diuersam belli conditionem ingredi. Nam neq; calo Asiae esse temperatius aliud, nec solo fertilius, nec
units.tr: 25 which was announced as a great labour and danger of campaigning. Amid these difficulties there was not even the hope of reward, since the enemy was wandering, and they lacked not only money but even a settled home. Now he is entering a different condition of war. For nowhere is the climate more temperate than in Asia, nor the soil more fertile, nor is anything more pleasant

units.la: 30 vrbium multitudine amoenius, magnamque temporis partem non vt militiam, sed vt festum diem altuos, bello dubiū facili magis an vberi, si modo aut proximas regni Attalici opes, aut veteres Lydiae Ioniaque audierint, quas non expugnatum eant, sed possessum: tantumq; se auida exspectat Asia, ut etiam vocibus vocet: adeo illis odium Romanorum incussit rapacitas Procoafulum, sectio publicanorum, calumniae litium. Sequantur se modo fortiter; & colligant, quid se duce pos- sit efficere tantus exercitus, quem sine cuiusquam militum auxilio, suamet vnius opera viderent Cappadociam caso rege cepisse; qui solus mortalium Pontum ominem Scythiamq; pacauerit, quam nemo ante transire tuto, atq; adire potuerit. Nam iustitiae atq; liberalitatis suae, ne ipsos milites, qui experiantur, tesides refugere: & illa indicia habere, quod solus regum omnium non paterna solum, verumetiam externa regna hereditatibus propter munificentiam acquisita possideat, Colcos, Paphlagoniam, Bosphorum.
units.tr: 30 in the multitude of its cities; and for a great part of the time they live not as soldiers but as if on a festival day. It is doubtful whether the war would be easier or more fruitful, if they had heard of the wealth of the neighbouring Attalid kingdom or of the old riches of Lydia and Ionia, which they would not conquer but possess. Asia is so eagerly waiting that it calls out with voices; so much has the rapacity of proconsuls, the plundering of the publicans, and the calumnies of lawsuits roused hatred of the Romans in them. Let them only follow him bravely, and let them consider what so great an army can accomplish under his leadership, which they saw had taken Cappadocia after killing the king, without anyone's soldiers' help, by his own work alone. He alone of mortals had subdued Pontus and Scythia, which no one before could cross safely or approach. For his justice and liberality are such that even the soldiers who test them do not flee in fear, and they have this evidence: he alone of all kings possesses by inheritance not only his paternal kingdoms but also foreign ones, acquired through his generosity: Colchis, Paphlagonia, and the Bosporus.

units.la: 8 Sic excitatis militibus, post annos tres & viginti sumpti regni in Romana bella descendit. At in Aegypto mortuo rege Ptolemaeo, ei qui Cyrenis regnabat Ptolemaeo per legatos regnum, & vxor Cleopatra regina foror ipsius defertur. Laetus igitur hoc solo Ptolemaeus, quod sine certamine fraternum regnum recepisset, in quod subornari & a matre Cleopatra, & fauore principum, fratris filium cognouerat. Ceterum infestus ominibus, statim vbi Alexandriam ingressus est, fautores pueri trucidari iussit. Ipsum quoq; die nuptiarum, quibus matrem eius in matrimonium recipiebat, inter apparatus epularum, & solemnia religionum, in complexu matris interficit: atq; ita thorum sororis, cede filii eius cruentus, ascendit. Post quod non mitior in populares, qui eum in regnum vocauerant, fuit. Siquidem peregrinis militibus licentia cadis data, omnia sanguine quotidie manabant: ipsam quoque sororem, filia eius virgine per vim fluprata, & in matrimonium adsci-
units.tr: 8 Thus with his soldiers roused, after reigning twenty-three years he descended into the Roman wars. But in Egypt, when King Ptolemy died, the kingdom was offered through envoys to Ptolemy, who ruled at Cyrene, together with his wife Cleopatra, the late king's sister. Ptolemy was glad of this alone, that he received his brother's kingdom without a struggle, although he had learned that his nephew was being incited to claim it by his mother Cleopatra and the favour of the leading men. But hostile to omens, as soon as he entered Alexandria he ordered the boy's supporters to be slaughtered. On the very day of his wedding, when he took his mother as his wife, amid the preparations for the feast and the solemn rites, he killed the boy in his mother's arms; and so, bloodied by the slaughter of her son, he climbed into his sister's bed. After this he was no milder toward the people who had called him to the kingdom. Foreign soldiers were given license to kill, and everything dripped with blood every day. His sister herself, whose virgin daughter had been raped by force and taken in marriage,

units.la: Concludit, ratione duo- bus in bello successibus. Munificetiae fuz praemiis militesalli- ciens. Ptolemaeo Philometore mortuo, Pto- lemaeus Phy- fcon regnum accipit. Parricidiis polluitur. Seuit in po- pulares.
units.tr: Summary: he concludes that in the war he had two successes, attracting soldiers with rewards of generosity. On the death of Ptolemy Philometor, Ptolemy Physcon receives the kingdom. He is polluted with parricides. He rages against the people.

units.la: adscita, repudiat. Quibus rebus territus populus, in diuersa labitur, patriamque metu mortis, exul relinquit. Solus igitur in tanta vrbe cum suis reliquis Ptolemaeus, cum regem se non hominum, sed vacuarum aedium videret, edicto peregrinos solicitat. Quibus confluentibus, obuius legatis Romanorum Scipioni Africano, & Spurio Mummio, & L. Metello, qui ad inspicienda sociorum regna venicbant, procedit. Sed quam cruentus ciuibus, tam ridiculus Romanis fuit. Erat enim & vultu deformis, & statura breuis, & sagina ventris non homini, sed bellua similis. Quam foeditatem nimia subtilitas perlucida vestis augebat, prorsus quasi aestu inspicienda praeberentur, quae omni studio occultanda pudibundo viro erant. Post discessum deinde legatorum (quorum Africanus, dum inspicit vrbem, spectaculo Alexandrinis fuit,) iam etiam populo peregrino inuisus, cum filio, quem ex sorore suscepterat, & cum vxore matris pellice, metu insidiarum, tacitus in exilium proficiscitur: contractoque mercenario exercitu bellum fratri parat ac patriae infert. Arcessitum maximum deinde a Cyrenis filium, ne eum Alexandrini contra se regem crearent, interficit. Tunc populus statuas & imagines eius detrahit. Quod factum studio fratris exaestimans, filium quem ex ea suscepterat, interfecit, corpusque in membra diuisum, & in cista compositum, matri die natalis eius, inter epulas offerri curat. Quae res non regina tantum, verumetiam vniuersae ciuitati acerba, & luctuosa fuit: tantumque moerorem festiuissimo conuiuio intulit, vt regia omnis repentino luctu incideretur. Verso igitur studio principum ab epulis in exsequias, membra lacera populo ostendunt, & quid sperare de rege suo debeant, filij caede demonstrant. 9 Finito luctu orbitatis, Cleopatra cum vrgeri se frafraterno bello videret, auxilium à Demetrio rege Syriæ, per legatos petit: cuius ipsius varij & memorabiles casus fuere. Namq; Demetrius, vt supra dictum est, cum bellum Parthis intulisset, & multis congressionibus victor fuisset, repente insidiis circumuentus, amisso exercitu capitur. Cui Arsacides [Parthorum rex, magno & regio animo misso ] in Hyrcaniam non cultum tantum regium praestitit, sed & filiam in matrimonium dedit, regnumq; Syriæ, quod per absentiam eius Thrypho occupaverat, restituturum promisit. Post huius mortem desperato reditu, non ferens captivitatem Demetrius, priuatam etsi opulentam vitam pertæsus, tacitus in regnum fugam meditatur. Hortator illi & comes Gallinander amicus erat: qui post captivitatem eius à Syria per Arabiam deserta, ducibus pecunia coparatis, Parthico habitu Babylonem peruenerat. Sed fugientē Phrahates, qui Arsacidæ successerat, equitum celeritate, per compendiosos tramites occupatum retrahit. Vt est deductus ad regē, Gallimandro quidē non tantum venia, verumetiam priorum fidei datum. Demetrium autē & graviter caesatum ad coniugem in Hyrcaniā remittit, artioribusq; custodiis observari iubet. Interiecto deinde tempore, cum fidem illi etiam suscepti liberi facerent, eodem amico comite repetita fuga est: sed pari infelicitate prope finis regni sui deprehenditur, ac demum perductus ad regē, vt innisus à confectu summouetur. Tunc quoq; vxori & liberis donatus, in Hyrcaniam, poenalem sibi ciuitatem, remittitur, talisq; aureis ad exprobrationem puerilis leuitatis donatur. Sed hanc Parthorum tam mitem in Demetrium clementiam non misericordia gentis facie bat; nec respectus cognationis, sed quod Syriæ regnū affectabant, vsuri Demetrio aduersus Antiochum fratrē, prout res, vel tempus, vel fortuna belli exegisset.
units.tr: adscita, repudiat. Terrified by these things, the people scattered in different directions, and in fear of death they left their country as exiles. Alone then in so great a city with his remaining followers, Ptolemy, seeing that he was king not of men but of empty houses, invited foreigners by an edict. When they flocked to him, he went out to meet the Roman envoys Scipio Africanus, Spurius Mummius and Lucius Metellus, who had come to inspect the kingdoms of the allies. But as bloody as he was to his citizens, so ridiculous was he to the Romans. For he was ugly of face and short of stature, and the bulk of his belly made him resemble a beast rather than a man. This foulness was increased by his excessively fine, transparent clothing, so that what a modest man should hide with every care was exposed as if in the heat. Then, after the envoys had left (Africanus, while he was looking over the city, became a spectacle for the Alexandrians), he was hated even by the foreign population. Fearing ambushes, he silently went into exile with the son he had had by his sister, and with his mother's concubine as his wife. Having raised a mercenary army, he prepared war against his brother and brought it upon his country. Then he summoned his eldest son from Cyrene, lest the Alexandrians make him king against himself, and killed him. The people then pulled down his statues and images. Thinking this had been done at his brother's instigation, he killed the son he had had by her, and had the body cut into pieces, placed in a chest, and offered to his mother among the feasts on her birthday. This deed was bitter not only to the queen but to the whole city, and it brought such grief to the most festive banquet that the whole palace was suddenly turned to mourning. So the attention of the leaders turned from feasts to funerals; they showed the people the torn limbs, and by the killing of his son they demonstrated what they should hope for from their king. 9 When the mourning for her child was over, Cleopatra, seeing herself pressed by a war with her brother, sought help through envoys from Demetrius, king of Syria. His own fortunes had been varied and memorable. For Demetrius, as was said above, after waging war on the Parthians and winning many battles, was suddenly surrounded by ambushes, and captured with the loss of his army. The Arsacid king, of great and royal spirit, not only gave him royal treatment in Hyrcania but also gave him his daughter in marriage, and promised to restore the kingdom of Syria, which Tryphon had seized in his absence. After the Arsacid's death, despairing of a return and unable to bear captivity, Demetrius, weary of a private life, though a wealthy one, secretly planned to flee to his kingdom. His encourager and companion was his friend Gallinander, who, after Demetrius's captivity, had crossed the desert of Arabia from Syria, with guides bought for money, and reached Babylon in Parthian dress. But Phraates, who had succeeded the Arsacid, overtook the fugitive by the speed of his horsemen along shorter paths, and brought him back. When he was brought before the king, Gallinander was granted not only pardon but also restored trust from his former service. Demetrius, however, was severely punished, and the king sent him back to his wife in Hyrcania, and ordered him kept under closer guard. After an interval, when his children, too, gave him a pledge of loyalty, the flight was attempted again with the same friend as companion; but he was caught with equal misfortune almost at the border of his kingdom, and finally brought to the king, and removed from his council. Then too, he was given back to his wife and children, and sent back to Hyrcania, the city of his punishment, and given golden fetters as a reproach to his childish levity. But this mild clemency of the Parthians toward Demetrius was not due to any kindness of their people, nor to regard for kinship, but to the fact that they coveted the kingdom of Syria, intending to use Demetrius against his brother Antiochus, as circumstances, time, or the fortune of war might require.

units.la: {y} Ec irridetur à Parthis, qui eius nomine vti conflitutur.
units.tr: {y} And he is mocked by the Parthians, who make it their practice to use his name.

units.la: 10 Iis auditis, Antiochus occupandum bellum ratus, exercitum, quem multis finitimorum bellis indurauerat, aduersus Parthos ducit. Sed luxuria non minor apparatus, quam militiae fuit: quippe 80. millia armatorum sequuta sunt 300. millia lixarum; ex quibus coquorum, pistorum, scenicorumq; maior numerus fuit. Argenti certe aurique tantum, ut etiam gregarij milites caligas auro figerent, procul carentq; materiam, cuius amore populi ferro dimicant. Culminarum quoq; argentea instrumenta fuere, prorsus quasi ad epulas, non ad bella pergerent. Adnenienti Antiocho multi Orientales reges occurrere, tradentes se, regnaq; sua cum execratione superbia Parthica. Nec mora congressioni fuit. Antiochus tribus proeliis victor cum Babyloniam occupaf15 set, magnas haberi coepit. Iraq; omnibus ad eum populis deficientibus, nihil Parthis reliqui praeter patrios fines fuit. Tunc Phrahates Demetrium in Syriam ad occupandum regnum cum Parthico praesidio mittit, ut eo pacto Antiochus ad sua tuenda a Parthia revocaretur.
units.tr: 10 Hearing this, Antiochus thought the war could be seized upon, and he led his army, which he had hardened in many wars with his neighbours, against the Parthians. But his luxury was no less than his military preparation. Indeed, 80,000 armed men were followed by 300,000 camp-followers, among whom the number of cooks, bakers and entertainers was greatest. There was so much silver and gold that even the common soldiers fastened their boots with gold; no doubt this was the very material for whose sake peoples fight with iron. There were also kitchen utensils of silver, as if they were marching to feasts rather than to war. As Antiochus advanced, many eastern kings came to meet him, surrendering themselves and their kingdoms, and hating Parthian arrogance. There was no delay in engaging. Antiochus won three battles and, when he had taken Babylon, he began to be held in great esteem. With all the peoples deserting to him, nothing remained to the Parthians except their ancestral borders. Then Phraates sent Demetrius into Syria with a Parthian garrison to seize the kingdom, so that by this means Antiochus would be recalled from Parthia to defend his own territory.

units.la: 20 Interim quoniam viribus non poterat, insidiis Antiochum ubique tentabat. Propter multitudinem homi- num, exercitum suum Antiochus per civitates in hyberna diuiserat: quae res exitij causa fuit. Nam cum graruari se copiarum praebitione, & iniuriis militum, civitates viderent, ad Parthos deficiunt; & die statuta omnes apud se diuisum exercitum per insidias, ne inilicem ferre auxilia possent, aggrediuntur. Quae cum huntiata Antiocho essent, auxilium proximis laturus, cum ea manu, quae secum hyemabat, progrediter. In iti30 nere obuiam regem Parthorum habuit, aduersus quem fortius, quam exercitus eius dimicauit. Ad postremum tamen cum virtute hostes vicerunt, metu suorum desertus, occiditur: cui Phrahates exsequias regio more fecit filium, Demetrij, quam secū Antiochus adduxerat, captus amore virginis, uxorem duxit. Pœnitere deinde dimissi Demetrij cœpit: ad quem retrahēdum cum turmas equitum festinato misisset, Demetrium hoc ipsum metuentem, iam in regno misi inuenerunt: fru-straq; omnia conati, ad regem suum reuersi sunt.
units.tr: 20 Meanwhile, since he could not prevail by force, Phraates attacked Antiochus everywhere by treachery. Because of the number of men, Antiochus had divided his army among the cities for winter quarters, and this was the cause of his ruin. For when the cities saw themselves burdened by the supplying of troops and by the injuries of the soldiers, they went over to the Parthians; and on an appointed day they attacked the army, which had been divided among them, by ambush, so that they could not bring aid to one another. When this was reported to Antiochus, he set out with the force that was wintering with him, to bring help to the nearest places. On the march he met the king of the Parthians, against whom he fought more bravely than his army did. In the end, however, although he defeated the enemy by valour, he was deserted through fear by his own men and was killed. Phraates gave him a funeral in the royal manner. Captivated by love of a maiden, Phraates married the daughter of Demetrius, whom Antiochus had brought with him. Then he began to regret having released Demetrius. To bring him back he hastily sent squadrons of cavalry, but they found Demetrius, fearing exactly this, already in the kingdom. After trying everything in vain, they returned to their king.
THE EPITOME OF THE PHILIPPIC HISTORIES OF POMPEIUS TROGUS
BOOK XXXIX. SUMMARY.

units.la: 1 Demetrius interfecto fratre Antiocho dum Ægyptum tentat Syriam amittit & tandem cruento fato tol-litur. 2 Alexander, exignobili rex factus, dum fortunam suam nō reuerenter habet, fœde perit, interfectus à Grypho, qui matrem & fratrem extinguit.
units.tr: 1 Demetrius, after his brother Antiochus was killed, attempts Egypt, loses Syria, and at last is carried off by a bloody fate. 2 Alexander, made king from a lowly origin, while he does not hold his fortune with moderation, perishes disgracefully, killed by Grypus, who also destroys his mother and his brother.

units.la: 3 In Ægypto Cleopatra entalia regna excurrētibus, regina mater grauissimas Syria & Ægyptus vexanturbas concitat, unde hor-tur.
units.tr: 3 In Egypt, Cleopatra, while the kingdoms are running into one another, her mother's rage stirs up the most grievous disturbances in Syria and Egypt, from which...

units.la: 4 Peculiares tragœdiæ quas Cleopatra inter suos excitat. Tandem illa à filio Alexandro occupata inter-ira, quarum interitus deseri-bitur. Alexander in exilium agitur, reuocato Ptolemæo Notho. Romanis ad Ori-
units.tr: 4 Peculiar tragedies which Cleopatra stirs up among her own people. At last she is seized by her son Alexander and perishes, and her death will be described. Alexander is driven into exile, and Ptolemy Nothus is recalled. The Romans, at Ori-

units.la: NTIOCHO in Parthia cum exercitu deleto, frater eius Demetrius obsidione Parthorum liberatus, ac restitutus in regnum, cum omnir Syria in luctu propter amissum exercitum esset, quasi Parthica ipsius ac fratris bella, quibus alter captus, alter occisus erat, prospere gesisset, ita AEgypto bellum inferre statuit; regnum AEgypti Cleopatra sorori pretium auxilij aduersus fratrem suum, pollicente.
units.tr: Antiochus, having lost his army in Parthia, was freed from the Parthian siege by his brother Demetrius and restored to the kingdom. Although all Syria was in mourning over the lost army, Demetrius, as if he had successfully conducted the Parthian wars of himself and his brother (one of whom had been captured and the other killed), resolved to make war on Egypt, Cleopatra her sister promising him the kingdom of Egypt as the price of his help against her brother.

units.la: Sed dum aliena affectat, vt assolet fieri, propria per desectionem Syriae amisit. Siquidem Antiochenses primi, duce Tryphone, exercitantes superbiam regis, quae couersatione Parthica crudelitatis intolerabilis facta erat, mox Apameni, ceteraque ciuitates exemplum sequuta, per absentiam regis à Demetrio defecere. Ptolemaeus quoq; rex AEgypti, bello ab eodem petitus, cum cognouisset Cleopatram sororem suam opibus AEgypti nautibus impositis, ad filiam & Demetrium generum in Syriam profugisse, immisit iuuenem quendam AEgyptium, Protarchi negotiatoris filium, qui regnum Syriae armis peteret. Et compositā fabula, quasi per adoptionem Antiochi regis receptus in familiam regiam esset, nec Syrijs quemlibet regem aspernantibus, ne Demetrij paterentur superbiam; nomen iuueni Alexandri imponitur, auxiliaq; ab AEgypto ingentia mittuntur.
units.tr: But while he aims at what belongs to others, as usually happens, he lost his own possessions through the revolt of Syria. For first the Antiochenes, under the leadership of Tryphon, roused by the king's pride, which had become unbearable cruelty through his Parthian way of life, soon revolted from Demetrius in his absence, and the Apameni and the other cities followed their example. Ptolemy, king of Egypt, who was also being attacked by Demetrius, when he learned that his sister Cleopatra had fled with the wealth of Egypt, on ships, to her daughter and her son-in-law Demetrius in Syria, sent into Syria a certain young Egyptian, son of the merchant Protarchus, to seize the kingdom of Syria by arms. And a story was invented that he had been received into the royal family by adoption by King Antiochus; and since the Syrians would not reject any king, lest they suffer the pride of Demetrius, the young man was given the name Alexander, and huge forces were sent from Egypt to help him.

units.la: Interea corpus Antiochi interfecti à rege Parthorum, in loculo argenteo ad sepulturam in Syriam remissum peruenit: quod cum ingenti studio ciuitatum & regis Alexandri, ad firmandam fabulam fidem excipitur: quae res illi magnum fauorem popularium conciliauit, omnibus non fictas in eo, sed veras lacrymas exhibentibus. Demetrius autem victus ab Alexandro, cum vndiq, circumstantibus malis premeretur, ad postremum etiam ab vxore filiisque deseritur. Relictus igitur cum paucis seruulis, cum Tyrum religione templi se defensurus petisset, naui egrediens, praefecti iussu interficitur. Alter ex filiis Seleucus, quoniam fine matris auctoritate diadema sumpsisset, ab eodem interficitur; alter cui propter nasi magnitudinem, cognomen Grypo fuit: rex amaà matre hactenus constituitur, vt nomen regis penes filium, ius autem omnis imperij penes matrem esset.
units.tr: Meanwhile the body of Antiochus, killed by the king of the Parthians, was sent back to Syria in a silver coffin for burial and arrived there. This was received with great zeal by the cities and by King Alexander, to lend credibility to the fiction; and this won him great favour with the people, since all shed not feigned but real tears over it. Demetrius, however, defeated by Alexander and pressed on every side by misfortunes, was at last deserted even by his wife and sons. Left with a few slaves, he sought Tyre to defend himself under the protection of the temple, but as he disembarked from his ship he was killed on the orders of the governor. Another of his sons, Seleucus, having taken the diadem without his mother's authority, was killed by the same man; another, who had the surname Grypus because of the size of his nose, was set up as king by his mother until then, so that the title of king rested with the son, but the power of the whole realm rested with the mother.

units.la: 2 Sed Alexander occupato Syriæ regno, tumes fuc- cessu rerum, spernere iam etiam ipsum Ptolemæum, à quo fuerat subornatus in regnum, superba insolentia {5}capit. Itaque Ptolemæus reconciliata sororis gratia, destruere Alexandri regnum, quod odio Demetrij, virtus suis acquisierat, summis opibus instituit. Mittit igitur ingentia Grypo auxilia, & filiam Tryphenam Grypo nuptuam, vt populos in auxilium nepotis, non socie{10}tate tantum belli, verum & affinitate sua solicitaret. Nec res frustra fuit: nam cum omnes Grypum instructum Ægypti viribus viderent, paulatim ab Alexandro deficere coepere. Fit deinde inter reges prælium, quo {15}victus Alexander, Antiochiam profugit: sibi inops pecunia, cum stipendia militibus deessent, templo Iouis solidum ex auro victoriæ signum tolli iubet, facetis iccis sacrilegium circumscribens: nam victoriam commodatam sibi ab Iouc esse dicebat. Interiectis deinde die{20}bus, cum ipsius Iouis aureum simulacrum infiniti ponderis tacite euelli iussisset, deprehensusque in sacrilegio, concursu multitudinis effect in fugam versus, magna vi {25}tempestatis oppressus ac desertus à suis, à latronibus capitur; perductusque ad Grypum, interficitur. Grypus porro reciperato patrio regno, externisque periculis liberatus, insidiis matris appetitur. Quà cum cupiditate dominationis prodito marito Demetrio, & altero filio interfecto, huius quoque victoria inferiorem dignitatem suam factam doleret, venieti ab exercitatione po{30}culum veneni obtulit. Sed Grypus prædictis iam ante insidiis, veluti pietate cum matre certaret, bibere ipsum iubet; abnuenti instat. Postremum prolato indice eam arguit, solam defensionem sceleris superesse affirmans, si bibat, quod filio obtulit. Sic victa regina facile rein se verso, veneno, quod aliy paraverat, extinguitur. Parta igitur regni securitate, Grypus octo annis quiete {•} & ipse habuit, & regno praefuit. Natus deinde illi est {5} aemulus regni frater ipsius Cyzicenus, eadem matre genitus, sed ex Antiocho patruo suscepta: quem cum veneno tollere voluisset, ut maturius armis cum eo de regno contenderet, excitauit.
units.tr: 2 But Alexander, having seized the kingdom of Syria, swelling with success, began to despise even Ptolemy himself, by whom he had been installed in the kingdom, and assumed a proud insolence.
