Therefore Ptolemy, having restored the favour of his sister, resolved with all his resources to destroy Alexander's kingdom, which he had acquired by virtue for the hatred of Demetrius. He therefore sent great forces to Grypus, and gave his daughter Tryphena in marriage to Grypus, so as to win over the peoples to help his nephew, by an alliance not only of war but also of kinship. Nor was this without effect: for when all saw Grypus equipped with the strength of Egypt, they gradually began to desert Alexander. Then a battle took place between the kings, in which Alexander, defeated, fled to Antioch. Lacking money, and with no pay for his soldiers, he ordered the golden statue of Victory to be taken from the temple of Jupiter, claiming to cover the sacrilege with a clever pretext: for he said that the victory had been lent to him by Jupiter. Some days later, when he secretly ordered the golden statue of Jupiter himself, of infinite weight, to be torn down, he was caught in the sacrilege; a crowd gathered, and he was put to flight. Overwhelmed by a great storm and abandoned by his own men, he was captured by robbers, brought to Grypus, and killed. Grypus, moreover, having recovered his father's kingdom and freed from foreign dangers, was attacked by the plots of his mother. Since she, in her lust for power, had betrayed her husband Demetrius and killed her other son, and grieved that her own dignity had been lowered by his victory, she offered him a cup of poison at a festive banquet. But Grypus, the plots having been anticipated, ordered her to drink it herself, as if he were contending with his mother in devotion; she refused, and he pressed her. At last he produced an informer who accused her, asserting that the only defence left for her crime was to drink what she had prepared for her son. Thus the queen, conquered, was easily turned by her own poison, which she had prepared for another, and died. Having therefore secured the kingdom, Grypus both enjoyed quiet for eight years and ruled the kingdom. Then a rival for the kingdom was born to him, his brother Cyzicenus, born of the same mother but fathered by Antiochus, his uncle. When she wished to remove him by poison, so that he would contend with him for the kingdom more quickly by arms, she stirred up this conflict.

units.la: 3 Inter has regni Syriae parricidiales discordias, {10} moritur rex AEgypti Ptolemaeus, regno AEgypti vxori & alteri ex filiis, quem illa legisset, relicto: videlicet quasi quietior AEgypti status, quam Syriae regnum esset, quum mater altero ex filiis electo, alterum hostem esse habitura. Igitur cum prior in minorem filium esset, a populo compellitur maiorem eligere: cui prius quam regnum daret, vxorem ademit; compulsumque repudiare carissimam sibi sororem Cleopatram, minorem sororem Selenen ducere iubet, non materno inter filias iudicio, cum alteri maritum eriperet, alteri daret.
units.tr: 3 Amid these parricidal discords of the Syrian kingdom, Ptolemy, king of Egypt, died, leaving the kingdom of Egypt to his wife and to whichever of his sons she should choose. Evidently the state of Egypt was thought quieter than that of the Syrian kingdom, since the mother, having chosen one of the sons, would have the other as an enemy. Therefore, since the mother was inclined toward the younger son, the people forced her to choose the elder. Before giving him the kingdom, she took away his wife, and ordered him, compelled to repudiate his dearest sister Cleopatra, to marry the younger sister Selene, not by a maternal judgement among her daughters, since she took a husband from one and gave him to the other.

units.la: {20} Sed Cleopatra non tam a viro repudiata, quam a matre dinortio viri dimissa, Cyzicceno in Syria nubit: eiq; ne nudum vxoris nomen afferret, exercitum Cypri folicitatum, velut dotalem, ad maritum deducit. Par igitur viribus fratris Cyzicenus, praelium committit: ac {25} victus in fugam vertitur, Antiochiamq; venit. Tunc Antiochiam Grypus, in qua erat Cyziceni vxor Cleopatra, obsidere coepit: qua capta, Tryphena vxor Grypi nihil antiquius quam sororem Cleopatrā requiri iuffit: non vt captiua opem ferret, sed ne effugere captiuitatis mala posset, quae sui aemulatione in hoc potissimū regnum inuaserit, hostiq; foroꝛis nubendo hostem se eius esse cerit. Tum peregrinos exercitus in certamina fratrum adductos, tum repudiatam a fratre, contra matris
units.tr: Cleopatra, however, was not so much repudiated by her husband as dismissed by her mother's divorce of her husband, and she married Cyzicenus in Syria. Lest she bring him only the bare name of wife, she led to her husband an army stirred up in Cyprus, as if it were her dowry. Cyzicenus, equal in strength to his brother, joined battle; but he was defeated, turned to flight, and came to Antioch. Then Grypus began to besiege Antioch, where Cyzicenus' wife Cleopatra was. When it was taken, Tryphena, the wife of Grypus, gave no thought more urgent than to have her sister Cleopatra sought out, not so that she might bring aid as a captive, but so that she could not escape the evils of captivity, which she had incurred through rivalry with her, invading this kingdom in particular and, by marrying an enemy of her country, making herself his enemy. Then she accused her of bringing foreign armies into the strife of brothers, and of marrying outside Egypt after being repudiated by her brother, against their mother's will.

units.la: voluntatem, extra AEgyptum nuptam accusat. Contra Grypus orare, ne tam foedâ facinus facere cogatur: a nullo vmquam maiorum suorum inter tot domestica, tot externa bella post victoriâ in feminas seuitum, quas sexus ipse & periculis bellorum, & seuitia victorum eximat: in hac vero praeter commune bellantium fas, accedere necessitudinem sanguinis: quippe ipsius quae tam cruente seuiat, sororem equidem germanam esse suam vero consobrinam: liberorum deinde commu-
units.tr: Grypus, on the other hand, pleaded that she should not be compelled to commit so foul a deed: that none of his ancestors, through so many domestic and foreign wars, had ever raged against women after victory, women whom their sex itself, and the dangers of war, and the cruelty of victors, spare; and that in this case, beyond the common law of combatants, there was added the bond of blood: for she who raged so cruelly was indeed his own sister by blood, and his cousin; and then the aunt of their common children.

units.la: nium materteram. His tot necessitudinibus sanguinis adiicit superstitionem templi, quo abdita profugerit, tantoque religiosius colendos sibi decs, quo magis his propitiis ac fauentibus vicisset: tum nec occisa illa, se viriu quicquam Cyziceno dempturum, nec seruaturum redita. Sed quanto Grypus abnuit, tanto soror muliebri pertinacia accenditur, rata non misericordiae hec verba, sed amoris esse. Itaq; vocatis ipsa militibus, mittit qui sororem confoderent. Qui vt in templum intrduerunt, cum euellere eam non possent, manus amplexantis deae simulachrum praecederunt. Tunc Cleopatra execratione parricidarum, mandata violatis numinibus vltione sui, decedit. Nec multo post repetita praelij congressione, victor Cyziceus vxorem Grypi Tryphenam, quae paulo ante sororem interfecerat, capit; eiusq; supplicio vxoris manibus parentauit.
units.tr: To these many ties of blood he added the sanctity of the temple, into which she had fled for refuge, and the gods whom she must worship all the more devoutly, the more she had conquered with their favour and goodwill; then that if she were killed he would not take anything from Cyzicenus' strength, and if she were spared and returned he would not preserve it. But the more Grypus refused, the more his sister was inflamed with womanly obstinacy, thinking these words were not of pity but of love. So she summoned soldiers herself and sent men to stab her sister. When they entered the temple and could not tear her away, they cut off the hands of the goddess's statue which she was embracing. Then Cleopatra, cursed by the parricides, having entrusted the violated divinities with avenging her, died. Not long afterwards, when the battle was renewed, the victorious Cyzicenus captured Tryphena, the wife of Grypus, who had shortly before killed her sister, and by her wife's punishment he avenged the dead.

units.la: 4 At in AEgypto Cleopatra cum grauaretur socio regni, filio Ptolemaeo, populum in eum incitat; abductaq; ei Selene vxore, eo indignius, quod ex Selene iam duos filios habebat, exulare cogit, arcesito minore filio Alexandro, & rege in locum fratris constituto: nec filiû regno expulisse contenta, bello Cypri exulantem persequitur. Vnde pulso, interficit ducem exercitus sui, quod viuum eum é manibus dimisisset: quamquam Ptolemaeus maeus verecundia materni belli, non viribus minor ab infula recessisset. Igitur Alexander territus hac matris crudelitate, & ipse eam reliquit, periculosò regno fecuram ac tutam vitam anteponens. Cleopatra vero timens, ne maior filius Ptolemaeus ab Cyziceno ad reciperandum Aegyptum auxiliis iuuaretur, ingetia Grypo auxilia, & Selenen vxorem nupturam hosti prioris mariti, mittit; Alexandrumq, filium per legatos in regnum reuocat: cui cum occultis insidiis exitiū machi- naretur, occupata ab eodem interficitur, spiritumq, nō fato, sed parricidio dedit: digna prorsus hac mortis insamia, quae etiam matrem thoro expulit; & duas filias viduas, alterno fratrum matrimonio, fecit; & filio alteri in exilium acto, bellum intulit, alteri erepto regno exitium per insidias machinata est.
units.tr: 4 But in Egypt, Cleopatra, being burdened by her co-ruler, her son Ptolemy, stirred up the people against him. She took his wife Selene from him, and, all the more outrageously since she already had two sons by Selene, she forced him into exile. She summoned her younger son Alexander and set him on the throne in his brother's place. Not content with having driven her elder son from the kingdom, she pursued him in exile to Cyprus. There, once he had been expelled, she had killed the commander of her own army, because he had let him go alive out of his hands, although Ptolemy, less strong in arms but more restrained out of reverence for his mother's war, had withdrawn from the island. Alexander, terrified by his mother's cruelty, therefore abandoned her too, preferring a safe and secure life to a perilous kingdom. Cleopatra, fearing that her elder son Ptolemy would be aided by the Cyzicene with troops to recover Egypt, sent auxiliaries to Grypus and sent Selene, who was to marry the enemy of her former husband. She also recalled her son Alexander from exile by envoys. While she was plotting his destruction by secret ambushes, he was seized by the same man and killed, and he gave up his life not by fate but by parricide. Such an infamy of death was entirely worthy of her, who had also expelled her own husband from his marriage bed; she made two daughters widows by a double marriage to their brothers; she waged war on one son after he had been driven into exile, and plotted the destruction of the other by treachery after his kingdom had been taken from him.

units.la: Sed nec Alexandro cedes tam nefanda inulta fuit. Nam vbi primum compertum est, scelere filij matrem interfectam, concursu populi in exilium agitur, reuocatoq, Ptolemaeo regnum redditur: qui neque cum matre bellum gerere voluisset, nec à fratre armis repetere; quod prior possedisset. Dum haec aguntur, frater eius ex pellice susceptus, cui pater Cyrenarum regnum testamento reliquerat, herede populo Romano instituto, decedit. Iam enim fortuna Romana porrigere se ad Orientalia regna, non contenta Italiae terminis, coeperat. Itaq, & ea pars Lybiae prouincia facta est: postea Creta, Ciliciaq, piratico bello perdomita, in formam prouinciae rediguntur. Quo facto, & Syria, & Aegypti regna Romana vicinitate artata, quae incrementa de finitimis bellis quaerere solebant, adempto vagandi arbitrio, vires suas in perniciem mutuam conuerterunt; adeo, vt assiduis proeliis consumpti, in contemptum finitimorum venerint, praedaq, Arabum genti, imbelli antea
units.tr: But Alexander's own crime was not left unavenged, for as soon as it became known that his mother had been killed through her son's wickedness, she was driven into exile by a popular uprising, and the kingdom was restored to Ptolemy. He had not wished to wage war against his mother, nor to demand by arms from his brother what the latter had held first. While these things were happening, their brother, born of a concubine, to whom their father had left the kingdom of Cyrene by will, with the Roman people named as heir, died. For already Roman fortune had begun to extend itself toward the eastern kingdoms, no longer content with the bounds of Italy. And so that part of Libya was made a province; afterwards Crete and Cilicia, subdued in a war against pirates, were reduced to the form of provinces. With this done, Syria and the kingdoms of Egypt, hemmed in by their proximity to Rome, which had been accustomed to seek their increase from neighbouring wars, with the freedom to wander taken away, turned their strength to mutual destruction; so much so that, worn out by constant battles, they came into contempt among their neighbours and became prey to the Arab people, who previously had been unwarlike.
Libya, Crete and Cilicia become provinces.

units.la: Syria & Aegyptus bellis mutuis attrita fiunt praeda latronib, antea fuerint. Quorum rex Eurotimus, fiducia septingentorum filiorum, quos ex pellicibus susceperat, diuisis exercitibus nunc AEgyptum, nunc Syriam infestabat: magnumq; nomen Arabum, viribus finitimorum exsanguibus fecerat.
units.tr: Syria and Egypt, worn down by mutual wars, became prey to robbers, who had previously been [unwarlike]. Their king Eurotimus, trusting in seven hundred sons whom he had had by concubines, attacked now Egypt, now Syria, with his armies divided; and he had made the great name of the Arabs by the strength of neighbours who had been drained of their blood.
POMPEIUS TROGUS'S EPITOME OF THE HISTORIES
BOOK XL. SUMMARY.

units.tr: 1 Tigranes the Armenian, the son of Antiochus Cyzicenus, is set up, and the Syrians choose him as their king. The kingdom of Syria, which was afterwards reduced to the form of a province

units.la: 2 Victo Tigrane, Antio- uinciæ formam redigitur. [illegible, ~1 letters]VTVIS fratrum odiis, & mox filiis inimicitiis parentum succedentibus, cum inexpiabili bello & reges, & regnum Syria consumptum esset, ad externa populus auxilia concurrit, peregrinosque sibi reges circumspicere coepit. Itaq; cum pars Mithridatem Ponticum, pars Ptolemaum ab AEgypto arcessendum censeret; occurreretque quod Mithridates implicitus bello Romano esset, Ptolemaus quoque semper hostis fuisset Syriae, omnes in Tigranem regem Armeniae consensere, instructum praeter domesticas vires, & Parthica societate & Mithridatis assinitate. Igitur accitus in regnum Syriae, per 18. annos tranquillissimo regno potitus est: neque bello alium lacessere, neque lacessitus inferre alii bellum necesse habuit. 2 Sed sicut ab hostibus tuta Syria fuit,ita terræmotu vastata est,quo centū septuaginta millia hominum, & multa vrbes perierunt. Quod prodigium mutationem rerum portendere aruspices responderunt. Igitur 5 Tigrane à Lucullo victo,rex Syriæ Antiochus,Cyziceni filius, ab eodem Lucullo appellatur. Sed quod Lucullus dederat,postea ademit Pompeius : qui poscenti regnum respondit, ne volenti quidem Syriæ, nedum recusanti daturum se regem, qui 18. annos, quibus Tigranes Sy-
units.tr: 2 Tigranes having been defeated, Syria was reduced to the form of a province. The kings and the kingdom of Syria were worn down by hatreds between brothers, and soon afterwards by enmities passed from parents to sons, and by a war without end. The people therefore turned to foreign help and began to look about for foreign kings for themselves. Some wanted Mithridates of Pontus to be summoned, others Ptolemy from Egypt. But Mithridates was caught up in a war with Rome, and Ptolemy had always been an enemy of Syria, so all agreed on Tigranes, king of Armenia, who was strong in his own resources, in his alliance with the Parthians, and in his kinship by marriage with Mithridates. So he was called to the kingdom of Syria, and for eighteen years he held it in complete peace. He had no need to provoke another power to war, nor, when no one provoked him, to make war on anyone. 2 But as Syria was safe from enemies, it was laid waste by an earthquake, in which one hundred and seventy thousand men and many cities perished. The soothsayers answered that this portent foretold a change of affairs. Then, when Tigranes was defeated by Lucullus, Antiochus, the son of Cyzicenus, was named king of Syria by the same Lucullus. But Pompey took away what Lucullus had given. To Antiochus, who demanded the kingdom, he replied that he would not give a king to Syria, even if Syria wanted one, much less to one who refused it; the man who had lain hidden in a corner of Cilicia during the eighteen years in which Tigranes held Syria, and who now, after Tigranes had been beaten by the Romans, demanded the rewards of another man's work. Therefore, just as he had not taken the kingdom from the man who held it, so he would not hand it to Tigranes' successor, since he did not know how to defend it, lest he expose Syria again to the raids of the Jews and Arabs. And so he reduced Syria to the form of a province, little by little, and it became the Roman East, the discord of its kinsmen's kings having made it so.

units.la: 10 riam renuit,in angulo Cilicia latuerit,victo autem eodem Tigrane à Romanis, alieni operis præmia postulet. Igitur vt habenti regnum non ademerit, ita quo cesserit Tigrani non daturum,quod tueri nesciat, ne rursus Syriam Iudæorum & Arabum latrociniis infestâ red-15 dat.Atq; ita Syriam in prouinciæ formam redigit:paulatim, Oriens Romanorum , discordia consanguineorum regum,factus est.
units.tr: 10 ...in whose time he had kept out of Syria and hidden in a corner of Cilicia, and who, after Tigranes had been defeated by the Romans, asked for rewards for work that was not his own. Therefore, just as he had not taken the kingdom from the one who held it, so he would not give it to the one who came after Tigranes, since that man could not defend it, lest he make Syria again a prey to the robberies of the Jews and Arabs. And so he reduced Syria to the form of a province, gradually, and the East became a possession of the Romans.
The Epitome of the Histories of Pompeius Trogus
BOOK XLI. SUMMARY.

units.tr: 1 The origin of the Parthians, the obscurity of their name, their successes, and their deeds, briefly described. 4 The affairs and rule of the Parthian kings. 5 Arsaces, the most wise king of the Parthians, and his peaceful death.

units.tr: 2. The administration of the Parthian kingdom. The Parthian speech, dress, arms, army, and manner of plundering. Arsaces' successors.

units.tr: 3. Domestic customs, burial, religion, character, and the virtues and vices of the Parthians. Under Eucratides, who is oppressed by his son. The Parthian wars and their successes.

units.la: ARTHI,penes quos, velut diuisione orbis cum Romanis facta, nunc Orientis imperium est, Scythatum exulles fuere. Hoc etiam ipsorum vocabulo manifestatur: namScythico ser-
units.tr: The Parthians, by whose power the empire of the East now lies, as if the world had been divided with the Romans, were exiles of the Scythians. This is also shown by their very name, for in the Scythian language the Parthians are called exiles.

units.la: mone Parthi exules dicuntur. Hi & Assyriorum & Medorum temporibus,inter Orientis populos obscurifsimi fuere. Postea quoq; cum imperium Orientis à Medis, ad Persas translatum est, veluti vulgus sine nomine, praeda victorum fuere. Postremo Macedonibus triumphato Oriente feruierūt: vt cuius mirum videatur, ad tantam eos felicitatem per virtutem prouectos, vt imperent gentibus, sub quarum imperio veluti servile
units.tr: In the times of the Assyrians and Medes, they were among the most obscure of the peoples of the East. Later, too, when the empire of the East passed from the Medes to the Persians, they were like a nameless common people, the booty of the victors. Finally, when the East was conquered by the Macedonians, they served them. It may seem remarkable that they, who had once been subject to such peoples as a servile crowd, were raised by their courage to such good fortune that they now rule over nations.

units.la: vulgus fuere. A Romanis quoq; trinis bellis per maximos duces florentissimis temporibus lacessiti, foli ex omnibus gentibus non pares solum, verumetiam victores fuere: quamquam plus gloriae fit, inter Assyria & Medica, Persicaq; memorata olim regna, & opulentif-
units.tr: Harassed by the Romans in three wars, waged by very great generals at the height of their power, they alone of all nations were not only equal but also victorious. Yet more glory belongs to the Parthians for having risen to rule the Bactrian empire, rich in a thousand cities, among the kingdoms once renowned in Assyria, Media and Persia, than for having won distant wars.

units.la: simum mille vrbium Bactrianum imperium emergere potuisse, quam longinqua bella vicisse, praeterea cū grauibus Scythicis & vicinalibus bellis assidue vexati, va-
units.tr: Moreover, they were constantly vexed by heavy wars with the Scythians and their neighbours, and pressed by many conflicts and dangers.

units.la: riis periculorum certaminibus vrgerentur. Ii domestiis seditionibus Scythia pulsi, solitudines inter Hyrcaniam, & Dahas, & Areos, & Spartanos, & Maggianos furtim occupauere. Fines deinde non intercedentibus primo finitimis, postea etiam prohibentibus, in tantum protulere, vt non iminenfa tantum, ac profunda
units.tr: Driven out of Scythia by domestic sedition, they secretly occupied the deserts between Hyrcania, the Dahae, the Areioi, the Spartani and the Magiani. Then, with no neighbours at first opposing them, and later even forbidding them, they extended their borders so far that they occupied not only vast and deep plains but also the steep slopes and heights of hills and mountains.

units.la: camporum,verumetiam praerupta collium,montiumq; ardua occupauerint. Ex quo fit, vt Parthiae pleraq; frigus aut aestus, aut frigoris magnitudo posideat, quippe cum montes [nix] & campos aestus infestet.
units.tr: As a result, most of Parthia is held either by cold or by heat, or by extreme cold: snow harasses the mountains, and heat the plains.

units.la: 2 Administratio gentis post defectionem Macedonici imperij, sub regibus fuit. Proximus maiestatis regi,
units.tr: 2. After the defection from the Macedonian empire, the nation was governed by kings. Next in rank to the king is the order of the people; from this order they draw their commanders in war and their magistrates in peace.

units.la: populorum ordo est: ex hoc duces in bello, ex hoc rectores in pace habent. Sermo his inter Scythicum Medicumq; medius, & utrisq; mixtus. Vestis olim sui moris, postea quam accesserant opes, ut Medi perlucida, ac flui-
units.tr: Their speech is midway between Scythian and Median, and mixed with both. Their dress was once in their own fashion, but after their wealth increased they adopted the Median, which is light and flowing. Their weapons follow the ancestral and Scythian custom.

units.la: da. Armorum patrius ac Scythicus mos. Exercitum nō ut alia gentes liberorum, sed maiorem partem seruorū habent: Quorum vulgus, nulli manumittendi potestāte permissa, ac per hoc omnibus seruis nascentibus, in dies crescit: Hos pari ac liberos suos cura habent; & e- quitare & sagittare magna industria docent. Locupletissimus ut quisq; est, ita plures in bello equites regi suo praebet. Deniq; Antonio bellum Parthis inferenti, cum quinquaginta millia equitum occurrerent, soli 400. liberi fuere. Cominus in acie praeliari, aut obsessas expugnare urbes nesciunt. Pugnant autem procurrentibus equis, aut terga dantibus: saepe etiam fugam simulant, ut incautiores aduersum vulnera insequentes habeant. Signum bis in praelio non tuba, sed tympano datur. Nec pugnare diu possunt: ceterum intolerandi forent, si quantus his impetus est, vis tanta & perseverantia esset. Plerumq; in ipso ardore certaminis praelia deserunt, ac paulo post pugnam ex fuga repetunt: ut cum maxime viciisse te putes, tunc tibi difcrimè subeundum fit. Munimentū ipsis equisq;, lorica plumata sunt, quae utrumq; toto corpore tegunt. Auri argentiq; nullus nisi in armis usus.
units.tr: They do not have an army of free men, as other nations do, but mostly of slaves. This common mass of slaves, since no one is permitted to manumit them, and since every slave born adds to their number, grows daily. They treat these slaves as they do their own children, and teach them with great diligence to ride and to shoot arrows. The wealthier each man is, the more horsemen he supplies to his king in war. Indeed, when Antony made war on the Parthians, and fifty thousand horsemen met him, only four hundred were free men. They do not know how to fight at close quarters in battle, or how to storm besieged cities. They fight with their horses charging forward or turning their backs, and often they feign flight so that they may have pursuers too careless to guard against their wounds. In battle the signal is given not by trumpet but by drum, twice. Nor can they fight for long; yet they would be unbearable if such violence and such endurance went with their attack. Most often, in the very heat of the fight, they abandon the battle, and a little later they renew it from their flight, so that just when you think you have most surely won, you must then face the greatest danger. For themselves and their horses, their protection is a plumed breastplate, which covers both the rider and the horse over the whole body. They use gold and silver only for their arms.

units.la: 3 Vxores dulcedine varia libidinis singuli plures habent: nec ulla delicta adulterio grauius vindicant. Quamobrem feminis non consuetudine tantum virorum, verumetiam conspectum interdicunt. Carne non nisi venatibus quasita vescuntur. Equis omni tempore vestantur; illis bella, illis conuiuia, illis publica ac priuata officia obeunt; super illos ire, cōsistere, mercari, colloqui.
units.tr: 3. Each man has several wives, because of the varied sweetness of lust, and they punish no offence more severely than adultery. For this reason they forbid women not only the company of men but even the sight of them. They feed on meat only when it has been got by hunting. They are always mounted on horses: on horseback they carry out wars, feasts, and public and private duties; on horseback they go, stop, trade, and converse.

units.la: Hoc denique discrimen inter seruos liberosque est, quod serui pedibus, liberi non nisi equis incedunt. Sepultura vulgo aut auium, aut canum laniatus est. Nuda demum offa terra obruit. In superstitionibus atque cura deorum, praecipua omnibus veneratio est. Ingenia genti tumida, sed ditiosa, fraudulenta, procacia: quippe violentiam viris, mansuetudinem mulieribus afignant. Semper aut in externos, aut in domesticos motus inquieti: nam tura taciti: ad faciendum, quam ad dicendum promptiores: proinde secunda, aduersaq; silentio tegunt. Principibus metu, non pudore parent. In libidinem proiecti, in cibum parci: fides dictis promissiq; nulla, nisi quatenus expedit.
units.tr: This, finally, is the difference between slaves and free men: slaves go on foot, free men only on horseback. The burial of the common people is the mangling of birds or dogs; only then does the bare earth cover the bones. In superstitions and in the care of the gods they show the greatest reverence of all. Their character is proud yet wealthy, deceitful and insolent: they ascribe violence to men and gentleness to women. They are always restless, moving against foreigners or against their own people. They are readier to act than to speak, and so they hide their successes and their setbacks in silence. They obey their princes from fear, not from respect. They are given to lust and sparing in food. Their word and their promises are worth nothing, except so far as it suits them.

units.la: 4 Post mortem Alexandri Magni, cum inter fuccessores eius, Orientis regna diuiderentur, nullo Macedonum dignante Parthorum imperium, Stagnori externo socio traditur. Hi postea deductis Macedonibus, in bellum ciuile, cum ceteris superioris Asiae populis Eumenem sequuti sunt, quo victo, ad Antigonum transfere. Post hunc a Nicatore Seleuco, ac mox ab Antiocho & successoribus eius possessi: a cuius pronepote Seleuco primum defecere, primo Punico bello L. Manlio Bulsone, M. Attilio Regulo consulibus. Huius defectionis impunitatem illis duorum fratrum regum, Seleuci & Antiochi discordia dedit: qui dum sibi inuicem eripere regnum volunt, persequi defectores omiserunt. Eodem tempore etiam Theodotus mille urbium Bactrianarum praefectus, defecit, regemq; se appellari iussit: quod exemplum sequuti totius Orientis populi, a Macedonibus defecere. Erat eo tempore Arsaces vir, sicut incerta originis, ita virtutis experta. Hic solitus latrociniis & rapto viuere, accepta opinione Seleucum a Gallis in Asia victum, soluius regis metu, cum praedonum manu Parthos ingref-sus, sus, prafectum eorum Andragoram oppressit, sublatoq, eo, imperium gentis inuasit. Non magno deinde post tempore, Hyrcanorum quoq, regnū occupauit: atq, ita duarum ciuitatium imperio praeditus grandem exerci-
units.tr: 4. After the death of Alexander the Great, when his successors divided the kingdoms of the East, and since none of the Macedonians deigned to hold the rule of the Parthians, it was handed to Stagnor, a foreign ally. Later, when the Macedonians were withdrawn, he followed Eumenes in the civil war, together with the other peoples of Upper Asia; when Eumenes was defeated, they passed over to Antigonus. After him they were held by Seleucus Nicator, and soon afterwards by Antiochus and his successors. They first revolted from Seleucus, the great-grandson of Nicator, in the time of the First Punic War, when Lucius Manlius Vulso and Marcus Atilius Regulus were consuls. The discord between the two brother kings, Seleucus and Antiochus, gave them impunity for this revolt: while they wanted to snatch the kingdom from each other, they neglected to pursue the rebels. At the same time Theodotus, governor of the thousand Bactrian cities, also revolted and ordered himself to be called king. Following this example, the peoples of the whole East revolted from the Macedonians. At that time there was a man named Arsaces, uncertain in origin but proven in courage. He had usually lived by brigandage and plunder. Hearing that Seleucus had been defeated by the Gauls in Asia, and being freed from fear of the king, he entered Parthia with a band of robbers, overpowered their governor Andragoras, and, having killed him, seized the rule of the nation. Not long afterwards he also occupied the kingdom of the Hyrcanians. Thus, possessing the rule of two peoples, he prepared a large army,

units.la: 5 tum parat, metu Seleuci & Theodoti Bactrianorum regis. Sed cito morte Theodoti, metu liberatus: cum filio eius, & ipso Theodoto foedus ac pacem fecit: nec multo post cum Seleuco rege ad defectores persequendos veniente, congressus, victor fuit: quem diem Parthi exinde solemnem, velut initium libertatis, obseruant.
units.tr: 5. for fear of Seleucus and of Theodotus, king of the Bactrians. But soon, with Theodotus dead, he was freed from fear, and he made a treaty and peace with Theodotus's son and with Theodotus himself. Not long afterwards, when King Seleucus came to punish the rebels, he engaged him and was victorious. The Parthians have since observed that day as a solemn feast, as the beginning of their freedom.

units.la: 10 § Reuocato deinde Seleuco, nouis motibus in Asiam, dato laxamento, regnum Parthicum format, militem legit, castella munit, ciuitates firmat, vrbe quoq, nomine Daram, in monte Zapacrtenon condit: cuius
units.tr: 10 § Seleucus was then recalled, and with new disturbances in Asia, and given a respite, Arsaces established the Parthian kingdom, levied soldiers, fortified castles, and strengthened cities. He also founded a city called Dara, on Mount Zapaortenus.

units.la: 15 loci ea conditio est, vt neque munitius quicquam esse, neq, amoenius possit: ita enim & praeruptis rupibus vndique cingitur, vt tutela loci nullis defensoribus egeant; & soli circumiacentis tanta vbertas est, vt proprijs opibus expleatur: iam fontium ac fluuiorum ea copia est,
units.tr: 15 The site is such that nothing could be stronger or more pleasant: it is surrounded on all sides by steep cliffs, so that the protection of the place needs no defenders, and the soil around it is so fertile that it supplies its own riches. Moreover, there is such an abundance of springs and rivers

units.la: 20 vt & aquarum abundantia irrigetur, & venationum voluptatibus exornetur. Sic Arsaces quaesito simul, constituto, regno, non minus memorabilis Parthis, quam Persis Cyrus, Macedonibus Alexander, Romanis Romulus, matura senectute decedit. Cuius memoria hunc honorem Parthi tribuerunt, vt omnes exinde reges suos
units.tr: 20 that it is watered by an abundance of waters and adorned with the delights of hunting. So Arsaces, having at the same time sought out and established his kingdom, died in ripe old age, no less memorable to the Parthians than Cyrus was to the Persians, Alexander to the Macedonians, or Romulus to the Romans. In memory of him the Parthians granted this honour: that from then on all their kings should be called by the name of Arsaces.

units.la: 25 Arsacis nomine nuncupent. Huius filius & successor regni, Arsaces & ipse nomine, aduersus Antiochum Seleuci filium, centum millia peditum, & 20. millibus equitum instructum, mira virtute pugnauit: ad po-
units.tr: 25 His son and successor in the kingdom, also named Arsaces, fought with remarkable courage against Antiochus, son of Seleucus, with a hundred thousand foot soldiers and twenty thousand horsemen. In the end he was received into alliance with him.

units.la: 30 stremum in societatem eius assumptus est. Tertius Parthorum rex Priapatius fuit, sed & ipse Arsaces dictus: nam, sicut supra dictum est, omnes reges suos hoc nomine, sicuti Romani Caesares, Augustosque cognominauere. Hic
units.tr: 30 The third king of the Parthians was Priapatius, but he too was called Arsaces; for, as was said above, they all bore this name as kings, just as the Roman Caesars were called Augusti. This one

units.la: His actis in regno quindecim annis decessit, relictis duobus filiis, Mithridate & Phrahate: quorum maior Phrahates more gentis, heres regni, Mardos validam gentem bello domuit; nec multo post decessit, multis filiis relictis: quibus praeteritis, fratri potissimum Mithridati, insignis virtutis viro, reliquit imperium: plus regio quam patrio deberi nomini ratus, potiusque patria, quam liberis consulendum.
units.tr: After these events he died, having reigned fifteen years, and left two sons, Mithridates and Phraates. The elder, Phraates, as was the custom of the nation, succeeded to the kingdom and subdued the Mardi, a powerful people, in war. Not long after, he died, leaving many sons. Passing over these, he left the kingdom to his brother Mithridates, a man of outstanding courage, judging that more should be owed to the royal title than to the paternal name, and that the welfare of the country should be considered before that of his children.

units.la: 6 Eodem fere tempore, sicuti in Parthis Mithridates, ita in Bactris Eucratides, magni vtergi viri, regna inceunt. Sed Parthorum fortuna felicior, ad summum, hoc duce, imperii fastigium eos perduxit. Bactriani autem per varia bella iactati, non regnum tantum verumetiam libertatem amiserunt: siquidem Sogdianorum & Drangaritanorum, Indorumque bellis fatigati, ad postremum ab inualidioribus Parthis, velut
units.tr: At about the same time, just as Mithridates began to reign among the Parthians, so Eucratides, a great man in both respects, began to reign in Bactria. But the fortune of the Parthians was the happier, and under this leader it raised them to the summit of power. The Bactrians, however, tossed about by various wars, lost not only their kingdom but also their liberty. For, worn down by wars with the Sogdians, the Drangians and the Indians, they were at last overwhelmed by the more vigorous Parthians, and were reduced to a bloodless state.

units.la: exsangues, oppressi sunt. Multa tamen Eucratides bella magna virtute gesserit: quibus attritus, cum obsidionem Demetrii regis Indorum pateretur, cum 300. militibus, 60. millia hostium assiduis eruptionibus vicit. Quinto itaque mense liberatus, Indiam in potestatem redegit.
units.tr: Yet Eucratides fought many great wars with great courage. Worn down by them, when he endured a siege by Demetrius, king of the Indians, he defeated sixty thousand enemies with three hundred soldiers, by constant sallies. Thus, after five months, he was freed, and he reduced India under his power.

units.la: Vnde cum se reciperet, a filio quem socium regni secerat, in itinere interficitur: qui non dissimulato parricidio, velut hostem, non patrem interfecisset, & per sanguinem eius currum egit; & corpus abiici insepultum iussit. Dum haec apud Bactros geruntur, interim inter Parthos & Medos bellum oritur: cum varius vtriusque populi casus fuisset, ad postremum victoria penes Parthos fuit. His viribus auctus Mithridates, Media Bacaque & Elimaeos, sin praeponit; ipse in Hyrcaniam profici scitur. Vnde recu
units.tr: On his way back from there he was killed in the course of his journey by his son, whom he had made his partner in the kingdom. The son did not conceal the parricide: he had killed his father as if he were an enemy, not a father; he drove his chariot through his blood and ordered his body to be thrown out unburied. While these things were happening among the Bactrians, meanwhile war arose between the Parthians and the Medes. After the fortunes of each people had varied, victory at last rested with the Parthians. Strengthened by these forces, Mithridates placed Media, Bactria and the Elymaeans under his governors, and himself set out, it is said, for Hyrcania.

units.la: ucrsus, bellum cum Elimaeorum rege gessit: quo victo, hanc quoque gentem regno adiecit, imperiumque Parthorum a monte Caucaso, multis populis in ditionem redactis, dadiis, dafis, vfq; ad flumen Euphratem protulit. Atq; ita aduersa valetudine arreptus, non minor Arfacefproauo gloriosa senectute decedit.
units.tr: From there he returned and waged war with the king of the Elymaeans. When he had defeated him, he added this nation too to his kingdom, and extended the empire of the Parthians from Mount Caucasus, with many peoples brought under his sway, as far as the river Euphrates, including the Dahae. Then, seized by ill health, he died in a old age no less glorious than that of his ancestor Arsaces.

units.la: OST necem Mithridatis, Parthorũ regis, Phrahates filius eius, rex confituitur: qui cum inferre bellum, in vltionem tentati ab Antiocho Parthici regni Syriæ slatuisset, Scytharum motibus ad sua defendendā reuocatur. Namq; Scytha in auxilium Parthorum acuersus Antiochum, Syriæ regem, mercede solicitati, cum confecto iam bello superuenirent, & calumnia tardius lati auxilij mercede fraudaretur, dolentes tantum iis itinerib frustra emensum, quum vel stipediũ pro vexatione, vel alium hostem dari sibi poscerent, superbo responso offensi, fines T ParParthorum vastare coeperunt. Igitur Phrahates cū adueꝛsus eos proficisceretur,ad tutelam regni reliquit Hymerum quendam, pueritiæ sibi slore conciliatum : qui tyrannica crudelitate,oblitus & vitæ praeteritæ, & vicarij officij,Babylonios,multàsq́ alias ciuitates importune vexauit. Ipse autem Phrahates exercitum Græcorum, quem bello Antiochi captum superbe crudeliter, tractauerat,in bellum secum ducit : immemor prorsus, quod hostiles eorum animos nec captiuitas minuerat, & insuper iniuriarum indignitas exacerbauerat. Itaq́ cum inclinatam Parthorum aciem vidissent, arma ad hostes transtulere; & diu cupitam captiuitatis vltionem exercitus Parthici, & ipsius Phrahatis regis crudeha caude exsequuti sunt.
units.tr: After the death of Mithridates, king of the Parthians, his son Phraates was made king. He had resolved to wage war in revenge against Antiochus, king of Syria, who had attacked the Parthian kingdom, but he was called back to defend his own lands against the movements of the Scythians. For the Scythians, hired to help the Parthians against Antiochus, king of Syria, arrived when the war was already finished, and since they were cheated of their pay on the pretext that they had come too late, they complained only that they had marched in those parts in vain. When they asked either for wages to compensate for the trouble, or for another enemy to be given them, they were offended by the proud reply and began to lay waste the territory of the Parthians. So when Phraates set out against them, he left in charge of the kingdom a certain Hymerus, who had won his favour in boyhood. Forgetting both his past life and the duty of a deputy, Hymerus harassed the Babylonians and many other cities with tyrannical cruelty. Phraates himself took with him to war the Greek army which he had captured in Antiochus' war and treated proudly and cruelly, quite forgetting that captivity had not blunted their hostile spirit, and that the indignity of their injuries had made it worse. So when they saw the Parthian battle line wavering, they turned their arms against the enemy, and the Parthian army and King Phraates himself paid the long-desired penalty for their captivity, at the hands of the cruel fellows.

units.la: 2 In huius locum Artabanus,patruus eius,rex subsituitur : Scythae autem contenti victoria, depopulata Parthia, in patriam reuertuntur. Sed Artabanus bello Thogarus illato,in brachio vulneratus, statim decedit.
units.tr: 2 In his place Artabanus, his uncle, was made king. The Scythians, content with their victory, laid waste Parthia and returned to their homeland. But Artabanus, having waged war against the Thogarus, was wounded in the arm and soon died.

units.tr: Mithridates, his son, succeeded him. Because of his exploits he was given the surname "the Great": inflamed by rivalry in virtue, he surpassed the fame of his parents in greatness of spirit. He therefore waged many wars with his neighbours with great courage, and added many peoples to the Parthian kingdom. He also fought the Scythians successfully on several occasions, and was the avenger of his fathers' wrongs. At last he made war on Ortoadistes, king of the Armenians. But since we are passing over into Armenia, its origin must be traced back a little further. It is not right to pass over in silence a kingdom whose territory, after Parthia, surpasses all other kingdoms in size. Armenia extends from Cappadocia as far as the Caspian for 1,100,000 paces, and in breadth it stretches 700,000 paces. It was founded by Armenius, a companion of Jason the Thessalian.

units.la: perditum propter insignem periculosamque regno suo virtute Pelias vex cuperet, denuntiata militia, in Colchos enim abire iubet; pellemque arietis memorabilem gentibus reportare: sperans interitum viri, aut ex periculis
units.tr: When Pelias feared him, because of his outstanding and dangerous valour, he ordered him to be sent on a military mission: he was to go to Colchis and bring back the famous ram's fleece to the peoples, hoping that the man would perish either from the dangers of so long a voyage or from so distant a war among barbarians.

units.la: Culis tam longe navigationis, aut ex bello tam profundo de barbaria. Igitur Iason diuulgata opinione tam gloriosa expeditionis, cum ad eum certatim principes iuuentutis totius ferme orbis concurrerent, exercitii fortissimorum virorum, qui Argonautae cognominati sunt, comparauit quem cum magnis rebus gestis incolumem reduxisset, rursus a Pelia filio Thessalia pulsus, magnae Iasonis fata.
units.tr: Jason, therefore, spread abroad the report of so glorious an expedition, and when the leading young men of almost the whole world came running to him eagerly, he assembled a band of the bravest men, who were called the Argonauts. After great deeds he brought them back safe, but he was again driven out of Thessaly by Pelias's son. Such was the fate of the great Jason.

units.la: Virtum ingenti multitudine, quae ad famam virtutis eius ex omnibus gentibus quotidie confluebat; comite Medea uxore, quam repudiatam miseratione exitii rursus sum receperat, et Medio primigeno ab Aegeo rege Atheniensium genito, Colcho repetiuit, socerumque, etiam regno pulsum restituit.
units.tr: With a huge crowd, which flocked to him every day from all nations, drawn by the fame of his valour, and with his wife Medea as companion, whom he had repudiated but had afterwards taken back out of pity for her ruin, and with Medus, the firstborn son of King Aegeus of Athens, he returned to Colchis and restored his father-in-law to the kingdom from which he had been driven.

units.la: Magna deinde bella cum finitimis gessit, expugnatisque ciuitates partim regno soceri, ad abolendam superstitionem militiae iniuriam, qua et filiam eius Medeam abduxerat, et filium Aegialeo interfecerat, adiunxit; partim populus quos secum adduxerat, assignauit. Primumque hunc manorum post Herculem et Liberum, qui reges Orientis fuisse traduntur, eam caeli plaga domuisse dicitur. Post
units.tr: He then waged great wars with his neighbours. Some of the cities he took he added to his father-in-law's kingdom, in order to abolish the superstition and to avenge the wrong of the expedition, by which the Colchians had carried off his daughter Medea and killed the son of Aegialeus. Others he assigned to the peoples he had brought with him. He is said to have been the first of his people, after Hercules and Bacchus, who were believed to have been kings of the East, to subdue that quarter of the sky.

units.la: pulcherrimos Fratrum et Amphitritae aurigas Castoris et Pollucis, duces assignauit; cum Albanis foedus pepigerat: qui Herculi ex Italia ab Albano monte, cum Geryone extincto, armenta eius per Italiam duxerat, secerunt diuitias; quique memores Italiae originis, exercitu Cn. Pompeii bello Mithridatico fratres salutauerunt. Itaque Iasoni totus ferme Orientis, ut conditori, diuinos honores tribuit, et sub Alexandro constituit; quae Parmenion, dux Alexandri Magni, post multos annos dirui iussit, ne quisquam nomen in Oriente venerabilius, quam Alexandri effet. Post mortem Iafonis, Medius emulus virtutis eius, in honorem matris, Medeam vrbem condidit: regnumq; ex nomine suo Medorum constituit, sub cuius maiestate Orientis postea imperium fuit. Albanus vicina Amazones fuit: quarum reginam Thalestrem concubitum Alexandri petisse, multi auctores prodidere. Armenius quoque ipse Theffalus, vnus de numero ducum Iasonis, recolleta multitudine, qua amisso Iasone rege passim vagabatur, Armenium condit: a cuius montibus Tigris fluimodicis primo incrementis nascitur, interiecto deinde aliquanto spacio, sub terra mergitur, atq; ita postquinque & viginti millia passuum grande iam flumen in regione Sophene emergit, ac sic in paludes Euphratis recipitur.
units.tr: After the most handsome charioteers, Castor and Pollux, sons of Amphitrite, he assigned leaders; he had made a treaty with the Albanians, who, when Hercules had killed Geryon and driven his cattle through Italy from the Alban mountain, had settled there and grown rich, and who, mindful of their Italian origin, greeted the army of Gnaeus Pompey as brothers in the Mithridatic War. Thus almost the whole of the East paid divine honours to Jason as its founder, and set them up under Alexander. Parmenion, the commander of Alexander the Great, ordered these honours destroyed many years later, so that no name more venerable than Alexander's should exist in the East. After Jason's death, Medus, a rival of his valour, founded the city of Media in honour of his mother Medea, and established the kingdom of the Medes named after himself, under whose majesty the empire of the East later existed. The neighbouring Amazons were Albanian; many authors have recorded that their queen Thalestris sought intercourse with Alexander. Armenius himself, the Thessalian, one of Jason's leaders, gathered together the multitude which had wandered about aimlessly after the loss of their king Jason, and founded Armenia. From its mountains the Tigris rises as a small stream at first, then after a short stretch sinks underground, and so, after twenty-five thousand paces, emerges as a large river in the region of Sophene, and is then received into the marshes of the Euphrates.

units.la: 4 Igitur Mithridates rex Parthorum, post bellum Armeniae, propter crudelitatem a senatu Parthico repulsus, gno pellitur. Frater eius Orodes cum regnum vacans occupasset, Babyloniam, quo Mithridates confugerat, diu obsidet; & fame coactos, in deditionem oppidanos compellit. Mithridates autem fiducia cognationis, vl-tra se in potestatem Orodis tradit. Sed Orodes plus hostem quam fratrem cogitans, in conspectu suo trucidari eum iussit: & post hac, bellum cu Romanis gessit, Crassum & Crassum imperatorem cum filio, & omni exercitu Romano deleuit. Huius filius Pacorus missus ad persequendas Romani belli reliquias, magnis rebus in Syria gestis, in Parthiam patri suspectus revocatur: quo absente, exercitus Parthorum relictus in Syria, a Cassio Quaestore Crassi cum omnibus ducibus trucidatur. His itaque gestis, non magno post tempore Romanis inter Caesarem Pompeium peiumq; ciuile bellum oritur: in quo Parthi Pompeiarum partium fuere, & propter amicitiam cum Pompeio
units.tr: 4 Now Mithridates, king of the Parthians, after the war with Armenia, was rejected by the Parthian senate because of his cruelty and driven from his kingdom. His brother Orodes, having seized the vacant throne, besieged Babylon, where Mithridates had taken refuge, for a long time; and, forcing the townspeople by famine, compelled them to surrender. Mithridates, trusting in their kinship, voluntarily gave himself into Orodes' power. But Orodes, thinking of him more as an enemy than a brother, ordered him to be slaughtered in his sight. After this he waged war with the Romans and destroyed Crassus, and Crassus's son, the commander, and the whole Roman army. Orodes' son Pacorus was sent to pursue the remnants of the Roman war; after great achievements in Syria he was recalled to Parthia, as his father grew suspicious of him. In his absence, the Parthian army left in Syria was slaughtered with all its leaders by Cassius, quaestor of Crassus. After these events, not long afterwards, a civil war broke out among the Romans between Caesar and Pompey, and a worse one followed. In this war the Parthians took the side of Pompey's party, both because of their friendship with Pompey

units.la: pcio bello Mithridatico iunctam, & propter Crasi necem, cuius filium in partibus Cæsaris esse audierant: quem vltorem patris victore Cæsare futurum non dubitabant. Itaq; victis partibus Pompeiani, & Cassio & Bruto auxilia aduersus Augustum & Antonium miserè; & post belli finem rursum Pacoro duce, inita cum Labieno societate, Syriam & Asiam vastauere, castraq; Ventidij, qui post Cassium absente Pacoro exercitum Parthicum fuderat, magna mole aggrediuntur: sed ille simulato timore, diu continuit se & insultare feliciter oppugnat. Partbos aliquantisper passus est. Ad postremum infecuros latosq; partem legionum emisit: quarum impetu fusi Parthi, in diuersa abiere. Pacorus cum fugientes suos abduxisse secum legiones Romanas putaret, castra Ventidij, veluti sine defensoribus, aggreditur. Tū Ventidius reliqua parte legionum emissa, vniuersam Parthorum manum cum rege ipso Pacoro interfecit: nec vllo bello Parthi vmquam maius vulnus acceperunt. Hæc cum in Parthia nuntiata essent, Orodes pater Pacori, qui paulo ante vastatam Syriam, occupatam Asiam à Parthis audierat, victoremque Pacorum Romanorum gloriabatur, repente filij morte, & exercitus clade audita, ex dolore in furorem vertitur. Multis diebus non alloqui quemquam, non cibum sumere, non voce mittere, ita vt etiam mutus factus videretur. Post multos deinde dies, vbi dolor vocem laxauerat, nihil aliud quā Pacorum vocabat; Pacorus illi videri, Pacorus audiri videbatur; cum illo loqui, cum illo consistere; interdum quasi amissum flebiliter dolebat. Post longum deinde luctum, alia solicitudo miserandum senem inuadit, quem ex numero 30. filiorum in locum Pacori regem destinet. Multa pellices, ex quibus generata tanta inuentus erat, pro suis quaq; solicita, animum senis obsidebant. Sed fatum Parthia fecit, in qua iam quasi sol& shy;lemne est reges parricidas haberi, vt sceleratissimus omnium, & ipse Phrahates nomine, rex statueretur.
units.tr: formed in the Mithridatic War, and because of Crassus's death, whose son they had heard was on Caesar's side; they did not doubt that he would avenge his father once Caesar was victorious. So when Pompey's party was defeated, they sent help to Cassius and Brutus against Augustus and Antony; and after the end of the war, under the command of Pacorus again, having formed an alliance with Labienus, they ravaged Syria and Asia, and attacked with a great force the camp of Ventidius, who had routed the Parthian army after Cassius, in Pacorus' absence. But Ventidius, feigning fear, kept himself under cover for a long time, and then successfully attacked the insulting enemy. He allowed the Parthians to go on for a while; at last he sent out part of his legions against the careless and scattered enemy. The Parthians, routed by their charge, fled in different directions. Pacorus, thinking he had drawn the Roman legions away with his fleeing men, attacked Ventidius's camp, as though it were without defenders. Then Ventidius sent out the rest of his legions and destroyed the whole Parthian force, together with King Pacorus himself; and the Parthians never received a greater wound in any war. When this news reached Parthia, Orodes, the father of Pacorus, who had only just heard that Syria had been devastated and Asia occupied by the Parthians, and who had been boasting that Pacorus had conquered the Romans, was suddenly struck by the news of his son's death and the army's defeat, and his grief turned to madness. For many days he spoke to no one, took no food, and uttered no sound, so that he seemed even to have become mute. Afterwards, many days later, when his grief had loosened his voice, he called for nothing but Pacorus; it seemed to him that he saw Pacorus and heard Pacorus; he spoke with him and stood beside him; at times he mourned him tearfully as though he had been lost. After this long mourning, another anxiety seized the pitiable old man, who was to appoint a king in Pacorus' place from among his thirty sons. Many concubines, from whom so many young men had been born, each anxious for her own, besieged the old man's mind. But fate made Parthia a place where it is now almost customary for kings to be parricides, so that Phraates, the most wicked of all, was made king.

units.la: 5 Itaq; statim quasi nollet mori, patrem interfecit; fratres quoq; 30. trucidat: sed nec in filiis cessant parricidia. Nam cum infestos sibi optimates propter assiduam sceleram videret, ne esset qui nominari rex posset, adultum filium interfici iubet. Huic Antonius propter auxilium aduersus se, & Caesarem latum, bellum cum sedecim validissimis legionibus intulit; sed graviter multis praeliis vexatus, a Parthia refugit: qua victoria insolentior Phrahates redditus, cum multa crudeliter consuleret, in exilium a populo suo pellitur. Itaq; cum magno tempore finitimas civitates, ad postremum Scythas precibus fatigasset, Scytharum maximo auxilio in regnum restituitur. Hoc absente, regem Parthi Tyridatem quendam constituerant: qui audito aduentu Scytharum, cum magna amicorum manu ad Cæsarem, in Hispaniam bellum tunc temporis gerentem, profugit, obsidem Cæsari minimum filium Phrahatis ferexs: quem negligentius custoditum rapuerat. Quo cognito, Phrahates legatos statim ad Cæsarem mittit, seruum suum Tyridatem, & filium remitti sibi postulat. Cæsar & legatione Phrahatis audita, & Tyridatis postulatis cognitis (nam & ipse restitui in regnum desiderabat, iuris Romanorum futuram Parthiam affirmans, si eius regnum muneris eorum fuisset) neq; Tyridatem deditum se Parthus dixit, neq; adductus Parthos Tyridati auxilia datur um. Ne tamen per omnia nihil a Cæsare obtentum videretur, Phrahati filium sine pretio remisit; & Tyridati quoad manere apud Romanos vellet, opulentum sumptum præberi iussit. Post hæc hac finito Hispaniensi bello, cum in Syriam ad componendum Orientis statum venisset, metuens Phrahati insufficiens, ne bellum Parthiæ vellet inferre. Itaq; tota Parthia captiuos ex Crasso, siue Antonij exercitu recollectos,
units.tr: 5 Immediately, as though unwilling to die, he killed his father and then slaughtered thirty of his brothers. Yet the murders did not stop with his brothers, for he also turned on his own sons. Seeing that the nobles were hostile to him because of his constant crimes, and fearing that there would be no one left who could be named king, he ordered his grown son to be put to death. Antony, because this son had sought his help against Augustus and Caesar, made war on him with sixteen very strong legions. But after being badly harassed in many battles, Antony retreated from Parthia. Phraates, growing more arrogant after this victory, behaved with great cruelty, and was driven into exile by his own people. Accordingly, after he had long wearied the neighbouring peoples and at last the Scythians with his entreaties, he was restored to the kingdom with the great help of the Scythians. During his absence the Parthians had set up a certain Tiridates as king. When he heard of the Scythians' arrival, he fled with a large band of friends to Caesar, who was then waging war in Spain, and he brought with him as a hostage the youngest son of Phraates, whom he had seized after it had been carelessly guarded. When this became known, Phraates immediately sent envoys to Caesar, demanding that his slave Tiridates and his son be sent back to him. Caesar heard both the embassy of Phraates and the demands of Tiridates. (For Tiridates himself wanted to be restored to the kingdom, and Caesar declared that Parthia would become subject to Roman law if the kingdom was given to him as a favour from Rome.) The Parthian refused to surrender Tiridates, and Tiridates was not given the troops he had asked for. Yet, so that Caesar should not seem to have gained nothing at all, he returned the son to Phraates without ransom, and ordered that lavish provision be made for Tiridates for as long as he wished to stay with the Romans. After this, once the Spanish war was over, Caesar came to Syria to settle the state of the East, fearing that Phraates, who was not to be trusted, might wish to make war on Parthia. Therefore, the whole of Parthia returned the captives taken from Crassus, or gathered from the army of Antony, together with the standards and military emblems, which were sent back to Augustus.

units.la: signa, cum his militaria Augusto remissa. Sed & filij nepotesq; Phrahatis obsides Augusto dati: plusq; Cæsar magnitudine nominis sui fecit, quam armis alius imperator facere potuisset,
units.tr: But the sons and grandsons of Phraates were also given to Augustus as hostages. Caesar achieved more through the greatness of his name than another commander could have achieved with arms.
The Epitome of the Histories of Pompeius Trogus
Book XLIII. Summary.

units.la: 1 Romani imperii initia. subacti. Phocenses Tarquinii Vrbis origo. Primi Italiæ rei temporibus Massiliam condunt, Liguribus inuicti cultores & reges. condunt, Liguribus inui-
units.tr: 1 The beginnings of the Roman empire. Subjugated. The Phocaeans. The origin of the city under Tarquin. In the time of the first founders, Massilia was founded; the Ligurians, unconquered cultivators and kings.
2 Rhea, daughter of Numitor, bears twins.

units.la: Remum & Romulum parit, qui mira quadam ratio ne educati emerguntur. Varia Massiliensium fortuna & felices successus.
units.tr: She bears Remus and Romulus, who, raised by a strange method, come forth. The varied fortune and happy successes of the Massilians.

units.la: 3 Roma à Remo Romu foedera. Eorundem beneloque condita: Senatus consilia & munificentia institutus: rapre Sabinę: vicini Romanos.
units.tr: 3 Rome founded by Romulus after Remus. Treaties of the same, and the city founded by their benefits. The counsels and generosity of the Senate established. The rape of the Sabine women. The neighbours oppose the Romans.

units.la: ARTHICIS, Orientalibusque ac totius propemodum orbis rebus explicitis, ad initia Romana vrbis Trogus, velut post longam peregrinationem domum reuertitur; ingrati ciuis ossicium exsistimans, si cum omnium gentium res gestas illustrauerit, de sola tantum patria taceat. Breuiter igitur Vrbis origo. initia Romani imperij perstringit: vt nec modo ppositi operis excedat, nec vtiq; originem vrbis, quae est caput totius orbis, silentio pratermittat. Italiae cultores primi Aborigines fuere: quorum rex Saturnus tanta iustitia fuisse traditur, vt neq; seruierit sub illo quisquam, neq; quicquam priuatae rei habuerit; sed omnia communia, & induisa omnibus fuerint, veluti vnum cunctis patrimonium esset. Ob cuius exempli memoriam cautum est, vt Saturnalibus exaequato omnium iure pasim in conuiuiis ferui cum dominis recumbant. Itaque Italiae regis nomine, Saturnia appellata est: & mons in quo habitabat, Saturnius; in quo nunc, veluti a Ioue pulso sedibus suis Saturno, Capitolium est. Post hunc tertio loco regnasse Faunum ferunt, sub quo Euander ab Arcadiae urbe Pallanteo, in Italiam cum mediocri turba popularium venit: cui Faunus & agros & montes, quae ille postea palatii appellauit, benigne assignauit. In huius radicibus templum Lycaeo, quae Graeci Pana, Romani Lupercum appellant, constituit: ipsum dei simulacrum nudum caprina pelle amictum est, quo habitu nunc Romae Lupercalibus decurritur. Fauno fuit vxor nomine Fatua, quae assidue diuino spiritu impleta, velut per surorem, futura praemonebat. Unde adhuc qui inspirari solent, fatuari dicuntur. Ex filia Fauni & Herculis, qui eodem tempore extincto Geryone, armenta victoriae praemia per Italiam ducebat, siupro conceptus Latinus, procreatur. Quo tenente regnum Aeneas ab Ilio, Troia a Graecis expugnata, in Italiam venit: statimq; bello exceptus, cum in aciem exercitum eduxisset, ad colloquium vocatus, tantam admirationem sui Latino praebuit, vt & in societatem regni reciperetur; & Lauinia in matrimonium ei data, gener ascisceretur. Post haec commune vtriusq; bellum aduersus Turnum Rutulorum regem, propter fraudatas Lauiniae nuptias, fuit: in quo & Turnus & Latinus interierunt. Igitur cum AEneas iure victoria vtroq; populo potiretur, vrbem,ex nomine vxoris, Lauiniam condidit. Bellum deinde aduersus Mezentium,regem Ethruscorum,gessit: in quo cum i-
units.tr: Having set out the affairs of the Arsacids, the Orientals, and almost the whole world, Trogus returns home, as after a long journey, to the beginnings of the Roman city. He thinks it the duty of an ungrateful citizen, if he had illustrated the deeds of all nations, to remain silent about his homeland alone. Briefly, then, he sketches the origin of the city and the beginnings of the Roman empire, so that he neither departs from the purpose of his work nor passes over in silence the origin of the city, which is the head of the whole world. The first inhabitants of Italy were the Aborigines, whose king Saturn is said to have been of such justice that no one served under him and no one had any private property; all things were common and shared by all, as if all had one inheritance. In memory of this example it was decreed that at the Saturnalia, when everyone's right is made equal, slaves recline with their masters at banquets everywhere. Thus from the name of the king of Italy the land was called Saturnia, and the mountain on which he lived, Saturnius; on it now stands the Capitol, as if Saturn had been driven from his seat by Jupiter. After him, in the third place, they say Faunus reigned. Under him Evander came into Italy from the Arcadian city of Pallanteum, with a modest band of countrymen, and Faunus kindly assigned to him the fields and mountains which Evander afterwards called the Palatine. At the foot of this hill he set up a temple to Lycaean Pan, which the Greeks call Pan and the Romans Lupercus. The statue of the god is naked, wrapped in a goatskin, and in this dress the Lupercalia are now run at Rome. Faunus had a wife named Fatua, who, constantly filled with divine spirit, foretold the future as if in frenzy; whence even now those who are wont to be inspired are said to be fatuari. From the daughter of Faunus and Hercules, who at the same time, having killed Geryon, was driving the cattle, the prize of victory, through Italy, Latinus was born, conceived in an unlawful union. While he held the kingdom, Aeneas came into Italy from Ilium, after Troy had been captured by the Greeks. Received at once in war, and having led his army into battle line, he was called to a parley, and so impressed Latinus with admiration that he was admitted to partnership in the kingdom, and was given Lavinia in marriage and taken as son-in-law. After this there was a joint war of both peoples against Turnus, king of the Rutulians, on account of the broken marriage of Lavinia, in which both Turnus and Latinus perished. Therefore, when Aeneas held both peoples by right of victory, he founded a city, named after his wife, Lavinium. Then he waged war against Mezentius, king of the Etruscans, in which battle

units.tr: 15 sacred to Mars, she gave birth to two boys, uncertain whether they were conceived in unlawful intercourse or from Mars. When this became known, Amulius, his fear multiplied by the birth of two sons, ordered the boys exposed and burdened the girl with chains, and she died from the mistreatment. But Fortune, looking ahead to the origin of Rome, offered the boys to a she-wolf to be nourished.

units.tr: 20 The she-wolf, having lost her cubs and wishing to empty her swollen teats, offered herself as nurse to the infants. When she often returned to the little ones as if to her cubs, the shepherd Faustulus noticed the matter, and, having taken the boys from the beast, raised them in rustic life among the flocks.
