units.tr: 25 It was believed, as on manifest evidence, that they were sons of Mars, either because they were born in the grove of Mars or because they were nursed by the she-wolf, who is under Mars's protection. The boys were named Remus and Romulus. Grown up among the shepherds, their daily contests of courage increased both their strength and their swiftness.

units.la: 30 re. Igitur cum latrones à rapina pecorum industrie frequentera,fuminonerent , Remus ab iisdem latronibus captus , veluti ipse effet , quod in aliis prohibebat, regi offertur; crimini datur , quasi greges Numitoris infestare solitus esset. Tunc à rege Numitori in vltio‑ nem traditur. Sed Numitor adolescentia iuuenis per‑ motus, & in suspicionem expositi nepotis adductus, cū cum nunc lineamentorum filia similitudo, nunc atas expositionis temporibus congruens, anxium tenerent, repente Faustulus cum Romulo superuenit: à quo co‑ gnita origine puerorum, facta conspiratione, & adole‑ scentes in vltionem materna necis, & Numitor in vin‑ dictam erepti regni armantur.
units.tr: 30 Once robbers were industriously raiding the flocks, Remus was captured by those same robbers, and was handed over to the king as if he himself were doing what he forbade in others. He was charged with the crime, as if he were in the habit of harassing Numitor's flocks, and was then handed over by the king to Numitor for punishment. But Numitor, moved by the young man's youth and led to suspect the grandson who had been exposed, was held in anxiety, now by the resemblance of his features to his daughter's, now by an age fitting the time of the exposure. Suddenly Faustulus arrived with Romulus. From him, having learned the origin of the boys, they made a conspiracy, and the youths armed themselves to avenge their mother's death, and Numitor to avenge his seized kingdom.

units.la: Occiso Amulio, regnum Numitori restituitur, & vrbs Romana ab adolescentibus conditur. Tunc & fe‑ natus centum seniorum, qui patres dicti sunt, consti‑ tuitur; tunc & vicinis, connubia pastorum dedignan‑ tibus, virgines Sabinae rapiuntur; finitimisque populis armis subiectis, primum Italiae, & mox orbis imperium quaesitum. Per ea adhuc tempora reges hastas pro dia‑ demate habebant, quas Graeci sceptra dixere. Nam & ab origine rerum, pro diis immortalibus veteres hastas coluere: ob cuius religionis memoriam, adhuc decrum simulacris hastae adduntur. Teporibus Tarquinij regis, ex Asia Phocensium iuuentus, ostio Tyberis inuecta, amici‑tiam cum Romanis iunxit: inde in vltimos Galliae fi‑nus navibus profecta, Massiliam inter Ligures, & feras gentes Gallorum condidit; magnaque res, sive dum ar‑mis se aduersus Gallicam feritatem tuentur, sive dum vltro lacessunt, à quibus fuerant ante lacesiti, gesserunt. Namque Phocenses exiguitate ac macie terra coacti, flu‑ diosius mare quam terras exercuere; piscando, mercando, plerumque etiam latrocinio maris (quod illis temporibus gloriae habebatur) vitam tolerabant. Itaque, in vltimam Oceani oram procedere ausi, in finum Gallicum ostio Rhodani amnis deuenere. Cuius loci amoenitate capti, reuersi domum, referentes qua viderant, plures solici‑tanetauere. Duces classis Simos & Protis fuere. Itaq; regem Segobrigiorum, Nannum nomine, in cuius finibus vrbem condere gestiebant, amicitiam petentes conueniunt. Forte eo die rex occupatus in apparatu nuptiarum 5 Gyptis filia erat: quam more gentis electo inter epulas genero, nuptum tradere illic parabat. Itaq; cum ad nuptias inuitati omnes processissent, rogatur etiam Graci hospites ad conuiuium. Introducta deinde virgo, cum iuberetur à patre aquam porrigere ei quem virum eli10 geret, tunc omissis omnibus adGraecos conuersa, aquam Proti porrigit; qui factus ex hospite gener, locum condende vrbis a socero accepit. Condita igitur Massilia est prope ostia Rhodani amnis, in remoto sinu, veluti in angulo maris. Sed Ligures incrementis vrbis inuiden15 tes, Graecos assiduis bellis fatigabant. Qui pericula propulsando intantum eniterentur, vt victis hostibus in captius agri multas colonias constituerent. 4 Ab hiis igitur Galli & vsu vita cultioris, deposita & mansuefacta barbaria, & agrorum cultus, & vrbes 20 mœnibus cingere didicerunt. Tunc & legibus, non armis viuere, tunc & vitem putare, tunc oliuam ferere consueuerunt: adeo, magnus & hominibus, & rebus impositus est, nitor, vt non Graecia in Galliam emigrasse, sed Gallia in Graeciam translata videretur. Mortuo 25 rege Nanno Sogobrigiorum, a quo locus acceptus conden- dæ vrbis fuerat, cum regno filius eius Comanus successisset, affirmante regulo quodam, quandoq; Massiliam exitio finitimis populis futurâ, opprimendam, in ipso ortu, ne mox validior ipsum obruerat, subiectit & illam sa- 30 bulam: Caneu aliquando partu grauidam locu a pastore precaria petisse, in quo pareret: quo obtento, iterata petisse vt sibi educare eodem in loco catulos liceret: ad postremum adultis catulis, sultam domestico prasidio, proproprietatem loci sibi vindicasse. Non aliter Masilienfes, qui nunc inquilini videantur, quandoque dominos regionum futuros. His incitatus rex, insidias Masilioensibus extruit. Itaq; solemni Floraliorum die, multos fortes ac strenuos viros hospitio iure in urbe misit: plures scirpiis latentes, frondibusq; superductos induci vehiculis iubet, & ipse cum exercitu in proximis montibus delirescit: vt quum nocte à praedictis aperta porta forent, tempestiue ad insidias adesset; vrbemq; somno ac vino sepultam armatis inuaderet. Sed has insidias mulier quaedam, regis cognata, prodidit, quae adulterare cum Graeco adolescente solita, in amplexu iuuenis miserata forma eius, insidias aperuit, periculumq; declinare iubet. Ille rem statim ad magistratus defert: atq; ita patefactis insidiis, cuncti Ligures comprehenduntur, latentesq; de scirpiis protrahuntur. Quibus o-nibus interfectis, insidianti regi insidiae tenduntur. Caesa sunt cum ipso rege hostium septem millia. Exinde Masilienses festis diebus portas claudere, vigilias agere, stationem in muris obseruare, peregrinos recognoscere, curas habere, ac veluti bellum habeant, sic vrbem pacu temporibus custodire: adeo illic bene institura non temporum necessitate, sed recte faciendi consuetudine seruantur.
units.tr: Amulius was slain, the kingdom was restored to Numitor, and the youths founded the Roman city. Then also a senate of one hundred elders, who were called fathers, was established. Then the Sabine virgins were seized from their neighbours, who scorned marriage with shepherds; and, with the neighbouring peoples subdued by arms, first the rule of Italy and soon of the world was sought. In those times kings still held spears in place of the diadem, which the Greeks called sceptres. For from the beginning of things the ancients also worshipped spears as immortal gods, and in memory of this religion spears are still attached to the statues of the gods. In the time of King Tarquin, a youth of the Phocaeans came from Asia, sailed into the mouth of the Tiber, and joined friendship with the Romans. Thence, setting out in ships to the furthest bay of Gaul, they founded Massilia among the Ligurians and the savage tribes of the Gauls; and they performed a notable deed, whether while defending themselves with arms against Gallic ferocity, or while attacking of their own accord those by whom they had previously been attacked. For the Phocaeans, compelled by the poverty and barrenness of their land, pursued the sea more eagerly than the land; they lived by fishing, by trade, and often even by piracy, which in those times was considered a glory. Therefore, having dared to advance to the furthest shore of the Ocean, they arrived in the Gallic gulf at the mouth of the river Rhone. Captivated by the charm of that place, they returned home and, relating what they had seen, stirred up many others. The leaders of the fleet were Simos and Protis. Therefore they came to King Nannus of the Segobrigians, in whose territory they were eager to found a city, seeking his friendship. By chance the king was that day occupied with the preparations for a wedding: his daughter Gyptis was to be given in marriage there, the bridegroom having been chosen, according to the custom of the tribe, among the banquet guests. Therefore, when all the invited guests had come to the wedding, the Greek strangers too were asked to the feast. Then the maiden was brought in, and when her father bade her offer water to the man she chose as husband, she turned from all the others to the Greeks and offered the water to Protis. He, having become son-in-law from a stranger, received from his father-in-law the site for founding a city. Massilia was therefore founded near the mouth of the river Rhone, in a remote bay, as it were in a corner of the sea. But the Ligurians, envious of the city's growth, harassed the Greeks with constant wars. The Greeks, repelling these dangers, struggled so hard that, with the enemy defeated, they established many colonies on the captured land. 4 From these Greeks, the Gauls learned the way of life of a more cultivated people: they put aside and tamed their barbarism, and learned to till the fields and to surround their towns with walls. Then they began to live by laws rather than by arms; then they also learned to prune the vine and to plant the olive. So great was the splendour bestowed on both men and things that Greece seemed not to have emigrated into Gaul, but Gaul to have been transplanted into Greece. When King Nannus of the Segobrigians, from whom the site for founding the city had been received, died, his son Comanus succeeded to the kingdom. A certain petty king maintained that Massilia would one day prove destructive to the neighbouring peoples, and that it should be crushed at its very birth, before it could soon grow too strong to be overthrown. He therefore also told that tale: that Caneus, once pregnant, had asked a shepherd for a place in which to give birth; having obtained it, he again asked that he be allowed to raise his puppies in the same place; and at last, when the puppies were grown and strong from their domestic protection, he claimed the ownership of the place for himself. The Massilians, who now seem to be lodgers, would in the same way one day become masters of the regions. Stirred by this, the king laid an ambush for the Massilians. So, on the solemn day of the Floralia, he sent many brave and vigorous men into the city under the right of hospitality. He ordered more men, hidden in rushes and covered with leafy branches, to be brought in carts, while he himself lay hidden with the army on the nearby mountains, so that when the gate had been opened by those already inside at night, he would be at hand at the right moment for the ambush, and would attack the city buried in sleep and wine with armed men. But a certain woman, a relative of the king, betrayed this ambush. She was in the habit of committing adultery with a young Greek, and, moved with pity by the young man's beauty in his embrace, she revealed the ambush and urged him to avert the danger. He at once reported the matter to the magistrates. The ambush having thus been exposed, all the Ligurians were seized, and those hiding in the rushes were dragged out. When all of them had been killed, the traps were set for the king who had laid the ambush. Seven thousand of the enemy were slain along with the king himself. Thereafter the Massilians, on festival days, closed the gates, kept watches, maintained guard on the walls, examined strangers, and took care; and even in times of peace they guarded the city as if they were at war. So well instituted are their customs there, maintained not by the necessity of the times but by the habit of doing right.

units.la: 5 Post haec magna illis cum Liguribus, magna cum Gallis fuere bella: quae res, & vrbis gloriam auxit; & virtutem Gracorum multiplicata victoria; celebrem inter finitimos reddidit. Carthaginiensium quoq; exercitus, cum bellum captis piscatorum nanibus ortum esset, saepe fuerunt, pacemq; victis dederunt: cum Hispanis amicitiam iunxerunt; cum Romanis prope ab initio condita vrbis foedus summa fide custodierunt, auxiliisq; in omnibus bellis induistrie socii fuerunt: quaeres illis & virium fiduciam auxit, & pacem ab hostibus praestitit. Cum igitur Massilia fama rerum gestarum, & abundantia opum, & virium gloria virente floreret, finitimi populi ad nomen Massiliensium delendum, veluti ad commune extinguendum incendium concurrunt. Dux consensu omnium Catumandus regulus eligitur: qui cum magno exercitu lectissimorum virorum urbem hostium obsideret, per quietem speciem torua mulieris, quae se deam dicebat, exterritus, vltro pacem cum Massiliensibus fecit: petitoque, ut intrare illi urbem, & deos eorum adorare liceret, cum in arcem Minervae venisset, conspecto in porticibus simulacro deae, quam per quietem viderat, repente exclamat, illam esse, quae se nocte exterruisset; illam quae recedere ab obsidione iußißet. Gratulatusq; Maßilienßibus,quod animaduerteret eos ad curam deorum immortalium pertinere, torqueaureo donata dea, in perpetuum amicitiam cum Maßilienßibus iunxit. Parta pace,& securitate fundata,reuertentes à Delphis Maßilienßiam legati, {a}quo mißi munera Apollini tulerant, audierunt vrbem Romanam à Gallis captam, incensamq;. Quam rem domi nuntiatam publico funere Maßilienses profequuti sunt: aurumq; & argentum publicum priuatumque contulerunt, ad explendum pondus Gallis,à quibus redemptam pacem cognouerant. Ob quod meritum & immunitas illis decreta, & locus spectaculorum in senatu datus,& fœdus aequo iure percussum. In postremo libro, Trogus maiores suos à Vocontiis originem ducere, auum suum Trogum Pompeium, Sertoriano bello, civitatem à Cn.Pompeio percepisse dicit; patruum Mithridatico bello turmas equitum sub eodem Pompeio duxisse; patrem quoq; sub Caio Caesare militasse,epistolarum,& legationum, simul & anuli curã habuisse.
units.tr: After this, Massilia had long wars with the Ligurians and then with the Gauls. These wars increased the city's glory, and the victories multiplied the courage of the Greeks and made them famous among their neighbours. The armies of the Carthaginians also often fought against them, after a war began over the seizure of fishing boats, but they gave peace to the defeated. They made friendship with the Spaniards, and they kept the covenant made with the Romans, almost from the founding of that city, with the utmost good faith, and they were eager allies in all the Roman wars. These dealings both increased their confidence in their own strength and secured peace from their enemies. So when Massilia was flourishing, with the fame of its achievements, the abundance of its wealth and the glory of its growing power, the neighbouring peoples gathered together to destroy the name of the Massilians, as if to put out a fire common to all. By the agreement of all, Catumandus, a petty king, was chosen as leader. He besieged the enemy's city with a large army of the most select men. But in his sleep he was terrified by the appearance of a fierce woman who said she was a goddess, and he voluntarily made peace with the Massilians. He asked that it be permitted to him to enter the city and worship their gods. When he came into the citadel of Minerva and saw in the porticoes the statue of the goddess whom he had seen in his sleep, he at once cried out that she was the one who had terrified him at night, the one who had ordered him to withdraw from the siege. He congratulated the Massilians because he saw that they were concerned for the immortal gods, and the goddess, presented with a golden torque, bound her friendship with the Massilians forever. When peace had been made and their security established, the Massilian envoys returning from Delphi, where they had carried gifts to Apollo, heard that the city of Rome had been captured and burned by the Gauls. When this news was announced at home, the Massilians conducted a public funeral for it, and they contributed gold and silver, both public and private, to make up the weight of ransom for the Gauls, from whom they had learned that peace had been bought back. For this service, an exemption from taxes was granted to them, a place for public shows was given to them in the senate, and a treaty was struck on equal terms. In the last book, Trogus says that his ancestors derived their origin from the Vocontii; that his grandfather, Trogus Pompeius, received citizenship from Gnaeus Pompeius in the Sertorian war; that his uncle led troops of cavalry under the same Pompey in the Mithridatic war; and that his father also served under Gaius Caesar, and had charge of the letters, the embassies, and at the same time the seal.
POMPEII TROGI EPITOMA HISTORIARVM
LIBER XLIV. BREVIARIVM.

Hæc inter Africam & Galliam posita Oceani freto,& Pyrenæis montibus clauditur. Sicut minor vtraq; terra, ita vtraq;fertilior. Nam neq; vt Africa violento sole torretur,neq; vt Gallia assiduis ventis fatigatur;sed media inter vtramq;,hinc temperato calore, inde felicibus & tempestiuis imbribus , in omnia fugum genera fecunda est,adeo vt non ipsis tantum incolis,verumetiā Italiæ, vrbiq; Romanæ cunctarum rerum abundantia sufficiat. Hinc enim non frumenti tantū magna copia est, verū & vini,mellis,oleiq;nec ferri solum materia precipua est , sed & equorum pernices greges ; nec summa tantum terra laudāda bona, verum & abstrusorū metallo-
units.tr: Spain, just as Europe closes off its limits, so too shall it be the end of this work. The ancients called it first Iberia, from the river Iberus, and afterwards Spain, from Hispanus. It lies between Africa and Gaul, and is bounded by the strait of the Ocean and the Pyrenean mountains. As it is smaller than either land, so it is more fertile than both. For it is neither scorched by the violent sun, as Africa is, nor worn down by constant winds, as Gaul is; but lying between the two, it is fruitful in every kind of produce, with moderate heat on one side and favourable, seasonable rains on the other. So great is its abundance that it suffices not only for its own inhabitants but also for Italy and the city of Rome in all things. For it has not only a great quantity of grain but also of wine, honey and oil; it is the chief source of iron and of swift herds of horses; and its goods are worthy of praise not only on the surface of the land but also in its rich veins of hidden metals. Moreover, there is a great supply of flax and esparto grass; no land is more productive of vermilion. Its rivers do not rush in torrents that harm, but flow gently, and they irrigate its vineyards and fields; its estuaries of the Ocean abound in fish. Many people are also rich in gold, which they carry away from the marshes. Gaul clings to the Pyrenees along a single ridge; on all other sides it is encircled by the sea. The shape of the land is nearly square, except that the shores of the strait narrow it where it joins the Pyrenees. The length of the Pyrenean range is six hundred miles. The healthiness of the climate is equal throughout all of Spain; the air is not tainted by any heavy mist from the marshes. To this is added the sea breeze, blowing constantly from every quarter, which penetrates the whole province, refreshes the land air, and gives its people excellent health.

units.la: Situs. tallorum felices diuitiæ: Iam lini, spartiq, vis ingēs; minij certe nulla feracior terra. In hac cursus amnium nō torrentes, rapidiq, vt noceant, sed lenes, & vineis campiq, irrigui, æstuariiq, Oceani affatim pisci: Pleriq, etiam diuites auro, quod in paludibus vehunt. Vno tantum Pyrenei montis dorso adhæret Gallia; reliquis partibus vndiq, in orbem mari cingitur. Forma terræ prope quadrata, nisi quod artantibus freti littoribus in Pyrenæum coit. Porro Pyrenei montis spatium sexcentæ millia passuum efficit. Salubritas cœli per omnem Hispaniam æqualis, quid aëris spiritus, nulla paludium graui nebula inficitur: Huc accedunt & marinæ auræ, vndiq, versus afiduiflatus, quibus omnem prouinciam penetrantibus, euentilato terrestri spiritu, præcipua hominibus sanitas redditur.
units.tr: Situation. The rivers' courses are not torrents, rapid enough to harm, but gentle; and the fields and vineyards are watered, and the estuaries of the Ocean supply fish in plenty. Many are also rich in gold, which they carry in the marshes. Gaul is attached to the Pyrenees by one ridge only; on all other sides the sea surrounds it in a circle. The shape of the land is nearly square, except that the shores of the strait narrow it where it runs into the Pyrenees. The Pyrenean range measures six hundred miles. The healthiness of the air is the same throughout all of Spain; no air is infected by heavy fog from marshes. Add to this the sea breezes, blowing constantly from every side, which penetrate the whole province and, by freshening the air of the land, give its people remarkable health.

units.la: 2 Corpora hominum ad inediam, laboremq;, animi ad mortem parati. Dura omnibus & adstricta parcimonia. Bellum quam otium malunt: si extraneus deest, domi hostem quærunt. Sæpe tormentis profilentio rerum creditarum immortui: adeo illis fortior taciturnitatis cura, quā vitæ. Celebratur etiā bello Punico serui illius patientia, qui vlus dominũ inter tormēta risu exultauit, ferenaq, lætitia crudelitate torquentiū vicit. Velocitas genti pernix; inquies animus: plurimis militares equi, & arma, sanguine ipsorū cariora. Nullus in sestos dies epularū apparatus. Aqua calida lauari post secundū bellum Punicum à Romanis didicere. In tanta sæculorum serie nullus illis dux magnus, præterViriatū, fuit: qui annis decem, Romanos varia victoria fatigauit, (adeo seris propiora, quā hominibus ingenia gerūt) quem ipsum non iudicio populi electum, sed vt cauendi scientem, declinandorumque periculorum peritum: sequuti sunt. Cuius ea virtus continentiaq, fuit, vt cum Consulares exercitus frequenter vicerit, tantis rebus gestis non armorum, non vestis cultum, non deniq; vitium mutauerit; sed in eo habitu, quo primum bellare coepit, perseuerauerit, vt quiuis gregarius miles ipso imperatore opulentior videretur.
units.tr: 2 The bodies of the men are ready for hunger and toil, their minds ready for death. Their thrift is harsh and strict for all. They prefer war to leisure; if no foreign enemy is at hand, they seek one at home. Often they die under torture without betraying what has been entrusted to them; so much stronger is their care for silence than for life. Also celebrated in the Punic war is the endurance of a certain slave who, while his master was being tortured, laughed and rejoiced, and by his cheerful bearing overcame the cruelty of his torturers. The people are swift and vigorous, their spirit restless; most of their horses and weapons are dearer to them than their blood. There is no elaborate preparation of feasts on holy days. They learned to bathe in warm water from the Romans after the second Punic war. In so long a succession of ages, the people had no great leader except Viriathus, who for ten years wore down the Romans with varied success. (So much more do they bear the natures of wild beasts than of men.) His followers did not choose him by the people's judgment, but followed him because he knew how to take precautions and was skilled at avoiding dangers. His virtue and self-restraint were such that, although he often defeated consular armies, and though he accomplished such great deeds, he never changed his dress, his fare, or even his vices; he persisted in the same habit in which he had first begun to make war, so that any common soldier appeared wealthier than the commander himself.

units.la: 3 In Lusitanis iuxta fluuium Tagum, vento equas fetus concipere multi auctores prodidere: quae fabula ex equarum fecunditate, & gregum multitudine nata fuit: qui tanti in Gallecia, & Lusitania, ac tam pernices visuntur, vt non immerito vento ipso concepti videantur. Galleci autem Gracam sibi originem afferunt. Siquidem post finem Troiani belli, Teucrum morte Aiacis fratris inuisum patri Telamoni, quum non reciperetur in regnum Cyprum concessisse, atq; ibi urbem nomine antiquae patriae Salaminam condidisse. Inde accepta opinione paternae mortis, patriam repetisse. Sed quum abEuryface Aiacis filio, acceßu prohiberetur, Iispania littoribus appulsum, loca, vbi nunc est Carthago noua, occupasse, inde Galleciam transisse, & positis sedibus genti nomen dedisse. Gallecie autem portio, Amphilochi dicuntur. Regio cum aeris ac plumbi vbertima, tum & minio, quod etiam vicino flumini nomen dedit. Auro quoq; ditissima, adeo vt etiam aratro frequenter glebas aureas exscindant. In huius gentis finibus sacer mons est, quem ferro violari nefas habetur: sed si fulgure terra proscissa est, quae in his locis assidua res est, detectum aurum velut dei munus colligere permittitur. Feminae res domesticas, agrorumq; culturas administrant, ipsi armis, & rapinis seruiunt. Praecipua his quidem ferri materia, sed aqua ipso ferro violentior: quippe temperamento eius, ferrum acrius redditur: nec ullum apud eos telum probatur, quod non aut Bilbili fluuio, aut Chalybe tinguatur. Vnde etiam Chalybes fiunt. fluuij huius finitimi appellati; ferroq; ceteris praestare dicuntur.
units.tr: 3 Many authors have reported that among the Lusitanians, near the river Tagus, mares conceive by the wind. This fable arose from the fecundity of the mares and the multitude of the herds, which are seen in Gallaecia and Lusitania in such numbers and so swift that they are rightly thought to have been conceived by the wind itself. The Gallaecians, however, claim a Greek origin. For after the end of the Trojan war, Teucer, hated by his father Telamon because of the death of his brother Ajax, was not received back into the kingdom, and so went to Cyprus, where he founded a city named Salamis after his old homeland. Then, having received word of his father's death, he sought to return to his country; but, being prevented from landing by Eurysaces, son of Ajax, he put in on the coast of Spain, occupied the places where New Carthage now stands, and from there passed over into Gallaecia, settled there, and gave his name to the people. A part of Gallaecia is called the Amphilochian. The region is very rich in copper and lead, and also in vermilion, which gave its name to the neighbouring river. It is also very rich in gold, so that they often turn up golden clods even with the plough. Within the borders of this people is a sacred mountain, which it is considered wrong to violate with iron; but if the earth has been split by lightning, which is a frequent occurrence in these places, the uncovered gold may be gathered, as a gift of the god. The women manage the household affairs and the cultivation of the fields, while the men serve in arms and in raiding. Their chief material is iron, but water is more powerful than iron itself: by its tempering the iron is made sharper, and no weapon is approved among them that is not dipped in the river Bilbilis or in the Chalybs. From this the Chalybes are said to take their name, a river neighbouring these lands; and they are said to excel all others in iron.

units.la: 4 Saltus vero Tartesiorum, in quibus Titanas bellum aduersus deos gestisse proditur, incoluere Cure-
units.tr: 4 The wooded region of the Tartessians, where it is related that the Titans waged war against the gods, was inhabited by the Cure-

units.la: 5 tes: quorum rex vetustissimus Gargoris, mellis colligendi vsum primus inuenit. Huic cum ex filia stupro nepos prouenisset, pudore flagitij variis generibus extingui paruulum voluit: sed per omnes casus fortuna quadam seruatus, ad postrentum ad regnum tot periculorū mi-
units.tr: 5 tes; their oldest king, Gargoris, first discovered the use of gathering honey. When a grandson was born to him from his daughter through an illicit union, he wished to destroy the infant in various ways, to hide the shame of the crime. But the child was preserved by a certain good fortune through all the dangers, and at last came to the kingdom, after so much...

units.la: 10 feratione peruenit. Primum omnium cum eum exponi iußisset, & post dies ad corpus expositi requirendum 'mififfet,inuentus est vario feraruin lacte nutritus. Deinde relatum domum,tramite angusto, per quem armentà commeare consueuerant, proiici iubet: crudelis
units.tr: 10 ...suffering. First of all, when he had ordered the child to be exposed, and afterwards sent men to fetch the body of the exposed child, he was found nourished on the milk of various wild beasts. Then, when he had been brought home, he ordered him to be thrown onto a narrow path by which the herds were accustomed to pass; he was cruel enough to prefer that his grandson be trampled rather than killed by a simple death.

units.la: 15 prorsus qui proculcari nepotem, quam simplici morte interfici maluit. Ibi quoq; cum inuiolatus effet, nec alimentis egeret, canibus primo ieiunis, & multorum dierum abstinentia cruciatis, mox etiam suibus obiecit. Itaq; cum non solum non noceretur, verumetiam quasundam vberibus aleretur, ad vltimum in Oceanum
units.tr: 15 ...Even there, when he was unharmed, and needed no food, he first threw him to hungry dogs, tormented by abstinence for many days, and afterwards even to swine. And so, since he was not only not harmed but was even suckled at the udders of some animals, at last he ordered him to be cast into the Ocean.

units.la: 20 abiici iußit. Tum plane manifesto quodam numine inter furentes æstus, ac reciprocantes vndas, velut naue non fluctu veheretur, leni salo in littore exponitur: nec multo post ceruca affuit, qua vbera paruulo offerret. In-
units.tr: 20 ...Then, clearly by some manifest divine power, amid the raging tides and the returning waves, as if he were carried not by the surge but by a ship, he was set down on the shore in calm water; and not long after, a hind came up to offer her udders to the little child. ...

units.la: 25 s[?]ledeniq; conuersatione nutritis eximia puero pernicitas fuit; interq; ceruorum greges diu montes saltusque, haud inferior velocitate peragrauit. Ad postremum laqueo captus, regi dono datus est. Tunc & lineamentorum similitudine, & notis corporis, qua inusta paruu-
units.tr: 25 Moreover, through the constant care of his foster-mother, the boy developed remarkable swiftness. He roamed the mountains and wooded valleys for a long time among herds of deer, and was no less fast than they. At last he was caught in a snare and given as a gift to the king. Then, from the likeness of his features and the marks on his body that had been branded on him as a child, he was recognized as the king's grandson.

units.la: 30 lo fuerant, nepos agnitus. Admiratione deinde tot casuum periculorum a, ab eodem successor regni destinatur. Nomen illi impositum Habidis: qui vt regnum accepit, tanta magnitudinis fuit, vt non sustra deorum
units.tr: Amazed at so many dangers he had escaped, the king named him successor to the throne. He was called Habidis. When he received the kingdom, he was of such stature that he seemed to have been rescued from so many perils not without the majesty of the gods:

units.la: V maiemaiestate tot periculis ereptus videretur: quippe barbarum populum legibus iunxit; & boues primus aratro domari, frumentaque, sulco quaerere docuit; & ex agresti cibo mitiore vesci, odio eorum quae ipse passus fuerat, homines coegit. Huius casus fabulosi viderentur, nisi & Romanorum conditores lupa nutriti, & Cyrus rex Persarum cane alitus proderetur. Ab hoc & ministeria servilia populo interdicta, & plebs in septem urbes divisa. Mortuo Habyde regnum per multa saecula a successoribus eius retentum est. In alia parte Hispaniae, & quae ex insulis constat, regnum penes Geryonem fuit. In hac tanta pabuli laetitia est, ut nisi abstinentia interpellata sagina fuerit, pecora rumpatur. Inde deniq; armenta Geryonis, quae illis temporibus sola opes habebantur, tanta fama fuere, ut Herculem ex Asia praeda magnitudine illexerint. Porro Geryonem ipsum non triplicis naturae, ut fabulis proditur, fuisse ferunt; sed tres fratres tanta concordia extitisse, ut uno animo omnes regi viderentur: nec bellum Herculi sua fonte intulisse; sed cum armenta sua rapi vidissent, amissa bello repetisse.
units.tr: For he united the barbarous people under laws; he was the first to tame oxen for the plough and taught them to seek grain by furrowing the soil; and he compelled men to eat a milder food than wild fare, out of hatred for the things he himself had suffered. His careers would seem fabulous, were it not that the founders of Rome, nursed by a she-wolf, and Cyrus, king of the Persians, reared by a dog, are also recorded. From him, menial services were also forbidden to the people, and the common folk were divided into seven cities. After Habyis died, the kingdom was kept for many centuries by his successors. In another part of Spain, and in the islands that belong to it, the kingdom was held by Geryon. In that land there is such abundance of pasture that, unless the cattle are checked by restraint, they burst from overfeeding. Hence the herds of Geryon, which were then the only wealth, became so famous that they drew Hercules from Asia by the greatness of the booty. Moreover, they say Geryon himself was not of a triple nature, as the fables relate, but that three brothers were so united in harmony that they all seemed to rule with one mind; nor did Hercules make war upon them from any personal quarrel, but when they saw their herds carried off, they sought them back by war.

units.la: § 5. Post regna deinde Hispaniae, primi Carthaginienses imperium prouinciae occupauere. Nam cum Gaditani a Tyro, unde & Carthaginiensibus origo est, sacra Herculis, per quietem iussi, in Hispaniam transtulisse liffent, vrbemque, ibi condidissent, inuidentibus increvit mentis nova urbs finitimis Hispaniae populis, ac pro-
units.tr: § 5. After the kingdoms of Spain, the Carthaginians were the first to seize control of the province. When the people of Gades, having been ordered in a dream to carry the sacred rites of Hercules from Tyre, whence the Carthaginians also derive their origin, into Spain, had founded a city there, the new city grew in strength, to the envy of the neighbouring Spanish peoples, and

units.la: terea Gaditanos bello lacessentibus, auxilium confanguineis Carthaginienses misere. Ibi felici expeditione & Gaditanos ab iniuria vindicaverunt, & maiorem partem provinciae imperio suo adiecerunt. Postea quoque, hortantibus prima expeditionis auspiciis, Hamilcarem imperatorem cum magna manu ad occupandam pro-vin-
units.tr: since they harassed the Gaditani with war, the Carthaginians sent aid to their kinsmen. There, by a successful campaign, they both protected the Gaditani from injury and added the greater part of the province to their empire. Afterwards, too, encouraged by the omens of their first expedition, they sent the general Hamilcar with a large force to occupy the province
Hamilcar is lured into an ambush and killed.

units.la: Iustini ad taticum obiectum resp. / Geryon alia Hispaniae partem regit. / Cur triplex fabulis dicitur. / Carthaginiensium imperium. ninciam misere: qui magnis rebus gestis, dum fortunam inconsultius sequitur, in insidias deductus, occiditur. In huius locum gener ipsius Hasdrubal mittitur: qui & ipse à seruo Hispani cuiusdam, vlciscente domi-ni iniustam necem, interfectus est. Maior vtroq; Annibal imperator, Hamilcaris filius succeddit. Siquidem vtriusq; res gestas supergressus, vniuersam Hispaniam domuit: inde Romanis illato bello, Italiam per annos sexdecim variis cladibus fatigauit: cum interea Romani missis in Hispaniam Scipionibus, primo Pœnos prouincia expulerunt. Postea cum ipsis Hispanis grauia bella gesserunt: neceprius perdomita prouincia iugum Hispaniæ accipere potuerunt, quam Cæsar Augustus perdomito orbe, victricia ad eos arma transstulit, populumq; barbarum & ferum, legibus ad cultiorem vitæ vsum traductum, in formam prouinciæ redegit.
units.tr: Justin's answer to the objection of Taticus. / Geryon rules another part of Spain. / Why he is called threefold in the fables. / The Carthaginian empire. ...to Spain. Hamilcar, who, after great achievements, followed fortune too recklessly, was lured into an ambush and killed. His son-in-law Hasdrubal was sent in his place, and he too was killed by a servant of a certain Spaniard who was avenging his master's unjust death. Hannibal, the elder of the two, a general and son of Hamilcar, succeeded. Surpassing the exploits of both, he subdued all of Spain; then, after bringing war on the Romans, he wore out Italy for sixteen years with various disasters. Meanwhile the Romans sent the Scipios into Spain, and at first drove the Carthaginians out of the province. Afterwards they waged serious wars with the Spaniards themselves, and the province, not yet thoroughly subdued, could not accept the yoke of Spain until Caesar Augustus, having subdued the world, turned his victorious arms against them and reduced the barbarous and savage people, who had been brought to a more civilised way of life by laws, into the form of a province.
THE END.
[woodcut ornament, no text]
