units.la: RECTE iudicas, Francisce, eum ad iudicandum sapientiorem, & ad agendum parationem fore. Vidisse autem non is solum putandus est, qui oculatus testis, regiones longinquas, & vltimas peragrauit; sed & is qui & mores hominum, & regionum situs, & rerumpublicarum conuersiones animo tenet. Sedentibus nobis, id praestant historicorum libri. Unde enim, vt est apud M. Tullium, facilius quam ex annalium monumentis, aut bellica res, aut omnis Resp. disciplina cognoscitur? Itaque, dum tu Italiæ, discendi & cognoscendi causa, inhæres; & doctorum qui illic sunt hominum, doctis colloquiis frueris: ego historicos Græcos & Latinos magnam partem percucurri. Hi mihi Iustinum emendanti, & quamplurimis locis cæcutienti, facem prætulerunt. Reliqui erant in Pompei historias prologi, Latine, arbitror, numquam editi: è quibus stercoris plus exhausi, quam olim ex Augiæ cloacis, Hercules ipse: Sed ita contaminata erant omnia, & fœde conspurcata, vt ceteris historiis, tamquam auxiliaribus copiis, inter medios hostes destitutus, coactus tandem sim, victus, manum dare. Tu nobis isthic alterum Herculem quærito. Eos intetim tibi, amicissime Francisce, amicitiæ nostræ restificandæ, lub. mer. do dico. Gozio & Puchotio multam à me salutem. Vale.
units.tr: You are right, Francisco, to judge that he will be the wiser for judging and the readier for acting. But a man should not be thought to have seen the world only if he has been an eyewitness who has travelled through distant and remote regions. He who keeps in mind the customs of men, the lie of lands, and the changes of states has seen it too. Even when we sit still, the books of the historians provide this. For, as Marcus Tullius says, where else can one learn more easily about warfare or the whole science of government than from the records of the annals? So while you stay in Italy for the sake of learning and study, and enjoy the learned conversation of the scholars who are there, I have run through a great part of the Greek and Latin historians. They have held a torch for me as I corrected Justin and stumbled in very many places in the dark. There remained the prologues to Pompeius's histories, which I think have never been published in Latin. From these I have drawn out more dung than Hercules himself once drew from the sewers of Augeas. But everything was so contaminated and foully fouled that, abandoned among the enemy in the midst of them, with the other histories as my auxiliary forces, I was at last forced to give up, beaten. You there must look for another Hercules for us. I gladly give these to you, most friendly Francisco, as is my due, to renew our friendship. Many greetings from me to Gozius and Puchotius. Farewell.
BOOK

units.la: LIBER HISTORIARVM PHILIPPICARVM, ET TOTIVS MVNDI origines, & terræ situs.
units.tr: BOOK OF THE PHILIPPIC HISTORIES, AND THE ORIGINS OF THE WHOLE WORLD, AND THE SITUATION OF THE EARTH.

units.la: PRIMO volumine continentur hæc, Imperium Assyriorum à Nino rege, vsque ad Sardanapalum. Post quem translatum est per Arbactum ad Medos, vsq; ad vltimum regem Astiagen. Is à nepote suo Cyro pulsus regno: & Persæ regno potiti. Vt Croeso Lydiæ regi bellum intulit Cyrus; victumque cepit. Hic in excessu dicti Æolicarum & Ionicarum vrbium situs; originesque Lydorum, & in Italia Tuscorum. Post Cyrum, filius Cambyses Ægyptum in domuit. Repetitæ Ægypti origines vrbium. Extincto Cambyse, Darius occisis Magis regnum Persicum accepit; captaque Babylone, bella Scythica molitus est.
units.tr: The first volume contains the following: the empire of the Assyrians from King Ninus down to Sardanapalus. After him it passed through Arbactus to the Medes, down to their last king, Astyages. He was driven from his kingdom by his grandson Cyrus, and the Persians seized the kingdom. How Cyrus made war on Croesus, king of Lydia, and after defeating him took him prisoner. Here, by way of digression, the situation of the Aeolian and Ionian cities, and the origins of the Lydians and, in Italy, of the Tuscans. After Cyrus, his son Cambyses subdued Egypt. The origins of the Egyptian cities are traced back. With Cambyses dead, Darius, after the Magi were slain, received the Persian kingdom; and after capturing Babylon, he undertook the Scythian wars.
PROLOGUE OF BOOK II.

units.la: SEcundo volumine continentur hæc; Scythiæ & Ponti situs; originesque Scythiæ, vsque ad bellum quo est inde pulsus Darius: qui post hanc fugam Græciæ bellum intulit, per Datin & Tisafernem, quod soli Athenienses tenuere. Hic origines Athenarum repetitæ, & reges vsque ad Pisistrati tyrannidem, qua extincta vicere Persas. Vt, mortuo Dario filius Xerxes bellum Græciæ intulit: ac repetitæ origines Thessaliæ: expulsoque Græcia Xerxe bellum ab Atheniensibus translatum in Asiam, vsque ad Xerxis interitum.
units.tr: The second volume contains the following: the situation of Scythia and Pontus, and the origins of Scythia, down to the war in which Darius was driven out of it. After this flight he made war on Greece, through Datis and Tissaphernes, a war which only the Athenians withstood. Here the origins of Athens are traced back, and its kings down to the tyranny of Pisistratus; with that tyranny ended, they overcame the Persians. Then, on the death of Darius, his son Xerxes made war on Greece. The origins of Thessaly are traced back. With Xerxes expelled from Greece, the war was carried by the Athenians into Asia, down to the death of Xerxes.
Prologue of Book III.

units.la: TErtio volumine continentur hæc. Vt mortuo Xerxe filiusArtaxerxes, occiso interfectore patrisArtabano, bellum cum defectore Ægypti habuit: primoque dux eius Achæmenes victus eltiterum per Megabyzum Ægypto recepta. Vt Græcis cum rege pacificatis, bella inter ipsos orta sint. Inde repetitæ Peloponnensium origines: ut ab Herculis posteris Dorico populo sit occupata. Dein inde bella Argolica & Messaniæ coalitique Sicyonix & Corinthi tyranni. Bellum Thyreum & quod Athenienses primo cum Bœotis, dein cum Peloponnesiis gesserunt.
units.tr: Third, the volume contains the following. After the death of Xerxes, his son Artaxerxes, having put to death Artabanus, the murderer of his father, waged war with the rebel of Egypt; first his general Achaemenes was defeated, and then Egypt was recovered through Megabyzus. When the king had made peace with the Greeks, wars arose among the Greeks themselves. Then the origins of the Peloponnesians are traced back: how the Dorian people took possession of it, descended from the posterity of Hercules. Then the wars of Argos and Messenia, and the coalition of the tyrants of Sicyon and Corinth. The Thyrean war, and the wars which the Athenians first waged with the Boeotians and then with the Peloponnesians.
Prologue of Book IV.

units.la: QVarto volumine continentur res Siculæ, ab vltima origine, vsque ad deletam Syracusis Atheniensium classem.
units.tr: Fourth, the volume contains the affairs of Sicily, from their earliest origin down to the destruction of the Athenian fleet at Syracuse.
Prologue of Book V.

units.la: QVinto volumine continentur hæc. Bellum inter Athenienses & Lacedæmonios, quod Decceleicum vocatur, vique ad captas Athenas. Vt expulsi sunt Athenis triginta tyranni. Bellum quod Lacedæmonii in Asia cum Artaxerxe gesserunt, propter Cyrum initum. Hinc repe- titum in excessu Cyri cum fratre bellum; & Græcorum qui sub eo militaverunt.
units.tr: Fifth, the volume contains the following. The war between the Athenians and Lacedaemonians, called the Decelean War, down to the capture of Athens. How the thirty tyrants were expelled from Athens. The war which the Lacedaemonians waged in Asia with Artaxerxes, undertaken on account of Cyrus. Hence, by way of digression, the war of Cyrus with his brother, and of the Greeks who served under him.
Prologue of Book VI.

units.la: SExto volumine continentur hæc. Bellum Lacedæmoniorum gestum in Asia cum Perficis præfectis, ducibus belli Herculide & Agesilao, vsque ad proelium nauale factum Cnidi: quo victis illis, Athenienses repetiere imperium. Dein bellum Corinthiacum, & bellum Bœotium quo, Leuctris & Mantinea victi Spartani, amisere imperium. In Thessalia deinde Iasonis & post illum Alexandri Phæreï coalitum atque extinctum imperium. Tum sociale bellum gestum adversus Athenienses Achæis & Rhodiis, & Byzantiis. Transitus hinc ad res Macedonicas.
units.tr: Sixth, the volume contains the following. The war waged by the Lacedaemonians in Asia against the Persian governors, with Herculidas and Agesilaus as commanders of the war, down to the naval battle fought off Cnidus; in that battle they were defeated and the Athenians regained their empire. Then the Corinthian War, and the Boeotian War, in which the Spartans, defeated at Leuctra and Mantinea, lost their empire. Then in Thessaly, the coalition and extinction of the empire of Jason, and after him of Alexander of Pherae. Then the Social War waged against the Athenians by the Achaeans, Rhodians and Byzantines. Transition from here to Macedonian affairs.
Prologue of Book VII.

units.la: SEptimo volumine continentur origines Macedonicæ, regesque à conditore gentis Carano, vsq; ad magnum Phi-
units.tr: Seventh, the volume contains the origins of the Macedonians, and their kings from the founder of the nation, Caranus, down to the great Phi-

units.la: LIBER HISTORIARUM PHILIPPICARUM, ET TOTIUS MUNDI origines, & terrae situs.
units.tr: Book of the Philippic Histories, and the origins of the whole world and the situation of the earth.

units.la: PRIMO volumine continentur haec, Imperium Assyriorum à Nino rege, vsque ad Sardanapalum. Post quem translatum est per Arbactum ad Medos, vsq; ad vltimum regem Astiagen. Is à nepote suo Cyro pulsus regno: & Persae regno potiti. Vt Croesso Lydiae regi bellum intulit Cyrus; victumque cepit. Hic in excessu dicti Aeolicarum & Ionicarum vrbium situs; originesque Lydorum, & in Italia Tuscorum. Post Cyrum, filius Cambyses Aegyptum domuit. Repetitae Aegypti origines vrbium. Extin. Cto Cambysē, Darius occisis Magis regnum Persicum accepit; captaque Babylone, bella Scythica molitus est.
units.tr: The first volume contains the following: the empire of the Assyrians from King Ninus down to Sardanapalus. After him the empire was transferred by Arbactus to the Medes, down to their last king, Astyages. He was driven from his kingdom by his grandson Cyrus, and the Persians took possession of the kingdom. Cyrus made war on Croesus, king of Lydia, and after defeating him took him prisoner. Here, in a digression, is the location of the Aeolian and Ionian cities, and the origins of the Lydians, and of the Tuscans in Italy. After Cyrus, his son Cambyses subdued Egypt. The origins of the cities of Egypt are traced again. After Cambyses' death, Darius, having put the Magi to death, received the Persian kingdom; and after Babylon was taken, he undertook the Scythian wars.
PROLOGUE TO BOOK II.

units.la: SEcundo volumine continentur haec; Scythiae & Ponti situs; originesque Scythiae, vsque ad bellum quo est indepulsus Darius: qui post hanc fugam Graeciae bellum intulit, per Datin & Tisafernem, quod soli Athenienses tenuere. Hic origines Athenarum repetitae, & reges vsque ad Pisistrati tyrannidem, qua extincta vicere Persas. Vt, mortuo Dario filius Xerxes bellum Graeciae intulit: acrepetitae origines Thessaliae: expulsoque Graecia Xerxe bellum ab Athenienses translatum in Asiam, vsque ad Xerxis interitum.
units.tr: The second volume contains the following: the location of Scythia and Pontus, and the origins of the Scythians, down to the war in which Darius was driven off, who, after this flight, made war on Greece through Datis and Tisaphernes, which only the Athenians held out against. Here the origins of Athens are traced, and its kings down to the tyranny of Pisistratus, after whose overthrow they defeated the Persians. Then, when Darius died, his son Xerxes made war on Greece; the origins of Thessaly are traced again; and after Xerxes was expelled from Greece, the war was carried by the Athenians into Asia, down to the death of Xerxes.
PROLOGUE TO BOOK III.

units.la: TErtio volumine continentur hæc. Vt mortuo Xerxe filiusArtaxerxes, occiso interfectore patrisArtabano, bellum cum defectore Ægypti habuit: primoque dux eius Achæmenes victus eiectus per Megabyzum Ægypto recepta. Vt Græcis cum rege pacificatus, bella inter ipsos orta sint. Inde repetitæ Peloponnenfium origines: vt ab Herculis posteris Dorico populo fit occupata. Deinde bella Argolica & Messania: coalitique Sicyonix & Corinthi tyranni. Bellum Thyreum: & quod Athenienses primo cum Boeotis, dein cum Peloponnesiis gesserunt.
units.tr: The third volume contains these matters. After the death of Xerxes, his son Artaxerxes, having put to death Artabanus, the murderer of his father, waged war against the rebel of Egypt; first his general Achaemenes was defeated and driven out, and then Egypt was recovered through Megabyzus. Then, the Greeks having been brought to peace with the king, wars arose among themselves. Next the origins of the Peloponnesians are traced back, how the Dorian people took possession of it, descended from the posterity of Hercules. Then follow the Argive and Messenian wars, and the coalition of the tyrants of Sicyon and Corinth. The Thyrean war, and the wars which the Athenians waged first against the Boeotians and afterwards against the Peloponnesians.
Prologue to Book IV.

units.la: Varto volumine continentur res Siculæ, ab vltima origine, vsque ad deletam Syracusis Atheniensium classem.
units.tr: The fifth volume contains the affairs of Sicily, from their earliest origin down to the destruction of the Athenian fleet at Syracuse.
Prologue to Book 5.

units.la: Vinto volumine continentur hæc. Bellum inter Athenienses & Lacedæmonios, quod Decceleicum yocatur, viique ad captas Athenas. Vt expulsi sunt Athenis triginta tyranni. Bellum quod Lacedæmonii in Asia cum Artaxerxe gesserunt, propter Cyrum initum. Hinc repetitum in excessu Cyri cum fratre bellum; & Græcorum quisque militaverunt.
units.tr: The fifth book contains the following: the war between the Athenians and the Lacedaemonians, called the Decelean War, and indeed up to the capture of Athens; the expulsion of the thirty tyrants from Athens; the war which the Lacedaemonians waged in Asia against Artaxerxes, begun on account of Cyrus; and then, on the death of Cyrus, the war renewed with his brother, in which individual Greeks served as soldiers.
PROLOGUE TO BOOK VI.

units.la: Exto volumine continentur hæc. Bellum Lacedæmoniorum gestum in Asia cum Perficis prefectis, ducibus belli Herculide & Agesilao, vsque ad prælium navale facturn Cnidi: quo victis illis, Athenienses repetierem imperium. Dein bellum Corinthiacum, & bellum Bœotium quo, Leuctris & Mantineæ victi Spartani, amiserunt imperium. In Theffalia deinde Iasonis & postea illum Alexandri Phærei coalitum atque extinctum imperium. Tum sociale bellum gestum aduersus Athenienses Achæis & Rhodiis, & Byzantiis. Transitus hinc ad res Macedonicas.
units.tr: The following are contained in this sixth volume. The war waged by the Lacedaemonians in Asia against the Persian commanders, with Herculidas and Agesilaus as leaders of the war, up to the naval battle fought at Cnidus; after they were defeated in it, the Athenians regained their empire. Then the Corinthian war, and the Boeotian war, in which the Spartans, defeated at Leuctra and Mantinea, lost their empire. Next in Thessaly the empire of Jason, and afterwards that of Alexander of Pherae, was joined together and then extinguished. Then the Social War waged against the Athenians by the Achaeans, Rhodians and Byzantines. A transition from here to Macedonian affairs.
Prologue to Book 7.

units.la: Eptimo volumine continentur origines Macedonicæ, regesque à conditore gentis Carano, vsque ad magnum Phi-
units.tr: The seventh book contains the origins of the Macedonians and their kings, from the founder of the nation, Caranus, down to the great Philip.

units.la: Philippum : ipsius Philippi res gestæ vsque ad captam vrbem Methonem. Addit æ in excessu Illyriorum & Pæonum origines.
units.tr: It contains the deeds of Philip himself up to the capture of the city of Methone. It also adds the origins of the Illyrians and Paeonians at the end.
PROLOGUE TO BOOK VIII.

units.la: OCtauo volumine continentur res gestæ Philippi magni, post captam vrbem Methonem, à principio belli Phocensis quod sacrum vocant, vsque ad finem eius : intenectamque huic bellum quod Philippus cum Calchidoniis vrbibus gessit, quarum clarissimam deleuit Olynthon. Vtillyrici reges ab eo victi sunt; & Thracia atque Thessalia ab eo subacta : & rex Epiro datus Alexander, eiecto Atyba : & strustra Perinthos oppugnata.
units.tr: The eighth volume contains the deeds of Philip the Great from the capture of the city of Methone, from the beginning of the so-called Sacred War of the Phocians until its end. Connected with this is the war which Philip waged against the Chalcidian cities, the most famous of which, Olynthus, he destroyed. The Illyrian kings were defeated by him; Thrace and Thessaly were subdued by him; Alexander was given the kingship of Epirus after Arybbas was expelled; and an unsuccessful attack was made on Perinthus.
PROLOGUE TO BOOK IX.

units.la: NOno volumine continentur hæc. Vt Philippus à Perintho summotus. Byzanti origines, à cuius obsidione summotus Philippus, Scythiæ bellum intulit. Repetitæ inde Scythicæ res, ab his temporibus, in quibus illa prius finierant, vsqueadPhilippi bellum quod cum Athea, Scythiæ rege, gessit. Vnde teuersus, Græciæ bellum intulit : victorque Cheronex, cum bella Persica moliretur, præmissa classe cum ducibus, à Paufania occupatis angultiis, nuptiarum die occcisus est, priusquam bella Persica inchoaret. Repetitæ res inde Persicæ à Dario notho cui successit filius Artaxerxes cognomine Mnemon: qui post fratrem Cyrum victum, pulsaq; Cnido per Conona classe Lacedæmoniorum, bellum cum Euagora rege Cyprio gessit : originesque Cypri repetitæ.
units.tr: The ninth volume contains the following: how Philip was driven away from Perinthus; the origins of Byzantium, from whose siege Philip was driven off, and then his war against the Scythians. The Scythian affairs are then taken up again, from those times at which they had previously ended, down to Philip's war with Atheas, king of the Scythians. From there he turned back and waged war on Greece; and after he had conquered Chaeronea, while he was preparing the Persian war, he sent his fleet ahead with its commanders, and was killed on his wedding day by Pausanias, who had seized the narrow passes, before he could begin the Persian war. The Persian affairs are then taken up again, from Darius Nothus, whom his son Artaxerxes, surnamed Mnemon, succeeded. After Artaxerxes defeated his brother Cyrus, and with the Lacedaemonian fleet under Conon drove the Cnidians out, he waged war with Evagoras, king of Cyprus; and the origins of Cyprus are also taken up.
PROLOGUE TO BOOK X.

units.la: DEcimo volumine continentur Persiæ res, vt Artaxerxes Mnemon pacificatus cum Euagora rege Cyprio, bellum Ægyptium in vrbe Ace comparariti splein Cadusiis victor : defectores in Asia purpuratos suos persequutus, primum Dopanem præfectum Paphlagonum origo repetita : Dein præfectum Hellespont Ariobarzanen: deindein Syria præfectum Armeniæ Orontem, omnibusq; victis decesserit, filio successore Ocho. Is deinde occisis optimatibus Sidona cepit : Ægypto bellum ter intulit. Vt post mortem Ochi regnarit Arsen: Deinde Darius, qui cum Alexandro Macedonum rege bello conflixit.
units.tr: The tenth volume contains the affairs of Persia: how Artaxerxes Mnemon, having made peace with Evagoras, king of Cyprus, prepared a war against Egypt in the city of Ace, and was victorious over the Cadusians. Pursuing the rebel nobles in Asia, he first dealt with Dopanes, prefect of the Paphlagonians, whose origin is traced back; then with Ariobarzanes, prefect of the Hellespont; then in Syria with Orontes, prefect of Armenia. Having defeated them all, he died, and his son Ochus succeeded him. Ochus then, after killing the leading nobles, took Sidon, and he waged war on Egypt three times. After Ochus's death, Arses reigned, and then Darius, who fought with Alexander, king of the Macedonians.
Prologue to Book 11.

units.la: VNdecimo volumine continentur res gestæ Alexandri Magni, vsque ad interitum regis Persarum Darii. Dictæque in excessu origines & reges Cariæ.
units.tr: The eleventh volume contains the deeds of Alexander the Great, down to the death of Darius, king of the Persians. In the digression are also set out the origins and kings of Caria.
PROLOGUE TO BOOK XII.

units.la: DVodecimo volumine continentur Alexandri Magni bella Bactriana, & Indica, vsque ad interitum eius. Dictæque in excessu res à præfecto eius Antipatro in Græcia gestæ, & ab Archidamo rege Lacedæmoniorum Molossoque Alexandro in Italia, vbi est cum exercitu delectus. Additæ his origines Italicæ Apulorum, Samnitum, Sabinorum; & vt Zopyrion in Ponto cum exercitu periit.
units.tr: The twelfth volume contains the wars of Alexander the Great in Bactria and India, down to his death. And at the end are recounted the events in Greece carried out by his deputy Antipater, and by Archidamus, king of the Lacedaemonians, and by Alexander of Molossia in Italy, where he raised an army. Added to these are the Italian origins of the Apulians, the Samnites and the Sabines; and how Zopyrion perished with his army in Pontus.
Prologue to Book XIII.

units.la: TErtiodecimo volumine continentur hæc: vt mortuo Alexandro, optimates castrorum eius, prouinciarum imperia sint partiti: vt veterani qui ab eodem lecti erant in colonias, moliti, relictisillis, in Græciam redire, à Phithone sint deleti. Bellum Lamiacum, quod Antipater in Græcia gessit. Bellum quo Perdiccas regem Ariarathem occidit, & occisus est. Bellum quo Eumenes Neoptolemum & Craterum occidit. Additæ in excessu origines regesque Cyrenarum.
units.tr: The thirteenth volume contains the following: after Alexander's death, the leading men of his camp divided the provincial commands among themselves; the veterans whom he had enlisted into colonies, planning to leave them and return to Greece, were destroyed by Phithon; the Lamian War, which Antipater waged in Greece; the war in which Perdiccas killed King Ariarathes and was himself killed; and the war in which Eumenes killed Neoptolemus and Craterus. At the end are added the origins and kings of the Cyrenians.
PROLOGUE TO BOOK XIV.

units.la: QVartodecimo volumine continentur hæc: Bellum inter Antigonum & Eumenem gestum: Quem vt Cappadocia expulit Antigonus, sic Phrygia maiore Atidæum & Cliton: victus in Hellespontonaiuali bello. Repetitum rursus bellum ab Eumene per Argyrasspidas, quo victus ab Antigono, interiit. Vt in Macedonia Cassander victo Polyperchonte, receptaque à defectore Munychia matrem Alexandri Olympiada Pydnæ obsessam interfecit.
units.tr: The fourteenth volume contains these matters: the war waged between Antigonus and Eumenes. Just as Antigonus drove Eumenes out of Cappadocia, so in Greater Phrygia Eumenes overcame Atidaeus and Cliton, who were defeated in the Hellespontine naval war. The war was renewed by Eumenes against Antigonus through the Argyraspides, and in it Eumenes, defeated by Antigonus, perished. In Macedonia, Cassander, after defeating Polyperchon, and after Munychia had been received from the defector, put to death Olympias, the mother of Alexander, who had been besieged at Pydna.
PROLOGUE TO BOOK XV.

units.la: QVintodecimo volumine continentur hæc, Vt Demetrius Antiochi filius Galamæ victus est ab Ptolemæo. V s Vs Vt Cassander in Macedonia filium Alexandri regis interfecit: ac alterum Polyperchontes. Vt Ptolemæum vicit classe Demetrius: idemque ab obsidione Rhodi summotus est. Repetita in excessu origo Rhodiorum: vnde digressus Demetrius liberauit à Cassandro Græciam. Dein pater eius Antigonus bellum cum Lysimacho & Seleuco habuit. Repetitæ Seleuci res, & regis Indiæ sandrocotti. Vt victus bello Antigonus interiit; reliquiaeque imperii sunt à filio collectæ.
units.tr: The fifteenth volume contains these matters: how Demetrius, son of Antiochus, was defeated at Galatia by Ptolemy; how Cassander in Macedonia killed the son of King Alexander, and Polyperchon the other son. How Demetrius defeated Ptolemy at sea, and was himself driven off from the siege of Rhodes. The origin of the Rhodians is taken up again in a digression, after which Demetrius left and freed Greece from Cassander. Then his father Antigonus waged war against Lysimachus and Seleucus. The affairs of Seleucus are taken up again, and those of Sandrocottus, king of India. How Antigonus, defeated in war, perished; and how the remains of the empire were gathered together by his son.
PROLOGUE TO BOOK XVI.

units.la: Extodecimo volumine continentur hæc. Vt mortuo Cassandro, ortisque inter filios eius certaminibus, Demetrius adiutor alteri adhibitus, occiso eo, Macedoniæ regnū tenuit: quo mox, victus à Pyrrho Epiri rege, translatis in Asia bellis, captus à Seleuco decessit. Ptolemæus nuncupato successore filio Philadelpho decessit. Vt Lysimachus in Ponto captus ac missus à Dromichete, rursus in Asia ciuitates quæ sub Demetrio fuerant, & in Ponto Heracleam occuparit. Repetitæ inde Bithyniæ & Heracleotice origines; tyrannique Heraclea Clearchus & Satyrus & Dionysius, quorum filiis interfectis Lysimachus occupauit vrbem.
units.tr: The sixteenth volume contains these matters. How, after the death of Cassander and the strife that arose among his sons, Demetrius was called in as helper by one of them; and when that son had been killed, he held the kingdom of Macedonia. Soon afterwards, defeated by Pyrrhus, king of Epirus, and with the wars transferred to Asia, he was captured by Seleucus and died. Ptolemy died after naming his son Philadelphus as successor. How Lysimachus, captured in Pontus and released by Dromichetes, again seized the cities in Asia that had been under Demetrius, and Heraclea in Pontus. Then the origins of Bithynia and of Heraclea are taken up again, and the tyrants of Heraclea: Clearchus, Satyrus and Dionysius; after their sons were killed, Lysimachus occupied the city.
PROLOGUE TO BOOK XVII.

units.la: Eptimodecimo volumine continentur hæc. Vt Lysimachus occiso filio Agathocle, per nouercam Arsinoen, bellum cum rege Seleuco habuit, quo victus interiit: vltimumque certamen commilitonum Alexandri fuit. Vt Seleucus amissis in Cappadocia cum Diodoro copiis, interfectus est ab Ptolemæo fratre Arsinoes vxoris Lysimachi, in cuius vicem Ptolemæus cognomine Ceraūnus, creatus ab exercitu rex, Macedoniā occupauit: bella cum Antiocho & Pyrrho composuit, datis Pyrrho auxiliis quibus iret contra Romanos, defensum Tarentum. Inde repetitæ origines regum Epiroticorum, visque ad Pyrrhum: ipsiusque Pyrrhi res gestæ, priusquam in Italiam traiecit.
units.tr: The seventeenth volume contains these matters. How Lysimachus, after killing his son Agathocles through his stepmother Arsinoe, waged war against King Seleucus, and was defeated and perished in it; and this was the last struggle among the comrades of Alexander. How Seleucus, having lost his forces in Cappadocia together with Diodorus, was killed by Ptolemy, brother of Arsinoe, the wife of Lysimachus. In his place Ptolemy, surnamed Ceraunus, was made king by the army and occupied Macedonia; he ended the wars with Antiochus and Pyrrhus, and gave Pyrrhus auxiliaries with which to go against the Romans, and defended Tarentum. Then the origins of the kings of Epirus are taken up again, down to Pyrrhus, and the exploits of Pyrrhus himself, before he crossed into Italy.
PROLOGUE TO BOOK XVIII.

units.la: Trauodecimo volumine, continentur resà Pyrrho Epirota in Italia gestæ contra Romanos; postquam id bellum.
units.tr: The eighteenth volume contains the deeds of Pyrrhus of Epirus in Italy against the Romans, after that war was finished.

units.la: Note: marginal numerals 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35, 40 mark line references. bellum, transfitus eius in Siciliam aduersus Carthaginienses. Inde origines Phoenicum, & Sidonis, & Tyri Carthaginiensiumque res gestæ in excellu dictæ.
units.tr: The war, his crossing into Sicily against the Carthaginians. Then the origins of the Phoenicians, of Sidon and of Tyre, and the exploits of the Carthaginians are recounted in a digression.
PROLOGUE TO BOOK XIX.

units.la: Ndeuicefimo volumine continentur res Carthaginiensium in Africa per numerum multorum annorum gestæ: vt in Sicilia cum Selinuntem, Agrigentum, Camerinam & Gelam ceperunt: quo bello Dionysius Syracusanus, Siciliæ regnum occupauit. Bellum quod cum co Pœni per Imilconem gellere, quo obsidione Syracusanorum exercitum & classem amiserunt.
units.tr: The nineteenth volume contains the affairs of the Carthaginians in Africa, carried on over many years: how they took Selinus, Agrigentum, Camarina and Gela in Sicily; in which war Dionysius of Syracuse seized the kingdom of Sicily. The war that the Carthaginians waged through Himilco, in which they lost their army and fleet through the siege of the Syracusans.
PROLOGUE TO BOOK XX.

units.la: Vicesimo volumine continentur res gestæ Dionysii Siculi patris, Vt pulsis Pœnis Italica bella fit molitus, Indè repetitæ origines Venetorum & Græcorum, & Gallorum qui Italiam incolunt. Deductæque Dionysii rebus ad interitum eius, dictæ quas Hanno magnus in Africa gessit.
units.tr: The twentieth volume contains the exploits of Dionysius the Elder of Sicily: how, after the Carthaginians were driven off, he undertook wars in Italy. Then the origins of the Veneti and the Greeks, and of the Gauls who inhabit Italy, are taken up again. And after Dionysius' affairs are carried down to his death, the deeds of Hanno the Great in Africa are recounted.
PROLOGUE TO BOOK XXI.

units.la: No & vicesimo volumine continentur hæc. Vt in Siciliam Dionysius filius à patre amissio tractarit imperium. Vt per Dionem eiectus bellum cum Siculis gessit donec amissis liberis & fratribus Corinthum fecerit. Vt à Timoleonte Carthaginiensium bello fit liberata Siciliæ liarum mortuoque Pisistrato iterum facta seditione arcessiti ad bellum Carthaginienses obsederunt Syracusas: quo bello Agathocles nactus imperium est.
units.tr: The twenty-first volume contains these matters. How Dionysius the Younger, having lost his father, took up the rule in Sicily. How, driven out by Dion, he waged war with the Sicilians until, having lost his children and brothers, he went to Corinth. How, through Timoleon, Sicily was freed from the Carthaginian war; and after the death of Pisistratus, a new sedition arose and the Carthaginians were summoned to the war and besieged Syracuse. In this war Agathocles obtained power.
PROLOGUE TO BOOK XXII.

units.la: Ecundo & vicesimo volumine continentur hæc. Res gestæ Agathoclis: vt à Pœnis nactus imperium, bellum cum ipsis gessit primum in Sicilia, dehinc victus, traiecit in Africam; vbi possessa prouincia Aphellam regem Cyrenarum interfecit. Vt rursus in Siciliam reuertisse, occupata totius infulæ dominatione, cum reuertisset in Africam cum, amissis copiis, solus inde profugit in Siciliam: bellum ibi repetitoque cum Pœnis pacem composuit, & dissidentes à se Siculos subiecit.
units.tr: The twenty-second volume contains these matters. The deeds of Agathocles: how, having obtained power from the Carthaginians, he first waged war against them in Sicily; then, defeated, he crossed into Africa, where, having taken the province, he killed Aphetas, king of the Cyrenaeans. How he returned again to Sicily, and having occupied the rule of the whole island, went back to Africa, where, having lost his forces, he fled alone to Sicily. There he renewed the war with the Carthaginians, made peace, and subdued the Sicilians who had revolted from him.
PROLOGUE TO BOOK XXIII.

units.la: Etrio & vicesimo volumine continentur hæc. Vt Agathoclis dominata Siciliæ, bello in Italia Bruttiis intulerit.
units.tr: The twenty-third volume contains these matters. How the rule of Agathocles in Sicily carried the war into Italy, against the Bruttians.

units.la: ReperRepetitæ inde Brutiorum origines. omnibus subactis, rex, sed ditione filii exhæredati ac nepotis oppressus, interiit. Inter peregrinos deinde milites eius & Siculos bellum motum: quæ causa Pyrrhum regem Epiri in Siciliam adduxit: bellaque Pyrrhus cum Pœnis & Mamertinis ibi, & gessit. Et à Sicilia reuertsus in Italiam, victus proelio à Romanis reuertit in Epirum.
units.tr: Then the origins of the Bruttians are taken up again. When all had been subdued, the king perished, oppressed by the rule of his disinherited son and grandson. Afterwards a war arose between his foreign soldiers and the Sicilians; this cause brought Pyrrhus, king of Epirus, into Sicily. There Pyrrhus waged wars with the Carthaginians and the Mamertines, and returning from Sicily to Italy, he was defeated in battle by the Romans and went back to Epirus.
PROLOGUE TO BOOK XXIV.

units.la: Varro & vicesimo volumine continetur bellum quod inter Antigonum, & Antiochum Seleuci filium in Asia gestum est. Bellum quod Ptolemæus Ceraunus in Macedonia cum Monio Illyrio & Ptolemæo Lysimachi filio habuit: vtque Atfinoen sororem suam imperio Macedonicarum vrbium exuit. Ipse, cum Belgio Gallorum duce congressus, interiit. Repetitæ inde Gallorum origines, qui Illyricum occupauerant; atque vt ingressi Græciam, Brenno duce, Delphis victi deletique sunt.
units.tr: The twenty-fourth volume contains the war waged in Asia between Antigonus and Antiochus, son of Seleucus. The war that Ptolemy Ceraunus waged in Macedonia against Monunius the Illyrian and Ptolemy, son of Lysimachus; and how he stripped his sister Arsinoe of the rule of the Macedonian cities. He himself, having met Belgius, leader of the Gauls, perished. Then the origins of the Gauls who had occupied Illyricum are taken up again; and how, having invaded Greece under Brennus, they were defeated and destroyed at Delphi.
PROLOGUE TO BOOK XXV.

units.la: Vinto & vicesimo volumine continentur hæc. Vt Antigonus Gallos deleuit: deinde cum Apollodoro Cassandreæ tyranno bellum habuit. Vt Galli transierint in Asiam, bellumque cum rege Antigono & Bithynio gesserunt: quas regiones occuparunt. Vt Pyrrhus ex Italia reuertsus, regno Macedonię Antigonum exuerit; Lacedæmoniam obsedit; Argis interiit; filiusque eius Alexander cum Illyricis & aliis bellum habuerit.
units.tr: The twenty-fifth volume contains these things: how Antigonus destroyed the Gauls; then he waged war with Apollodorus, tyrant of Cassandreia. How the Gauls crossed into Asia and waged war with King Antigonus and the Bithynian, and which regions they occupied. How Pyrrhus, returning from Italy, stripped Antigonus of the kingdom of Macedonia, besieged Lacedaemon, and died at Argos; and his son Alexander waged war with the Illyrians and others.
PROLOGUE TO BOOK XXVI.

units.la: Eito & vicesimo volumine continentur hæc. Quibus in vrbibus Græciæ dominationem Antigonus Gonatas conflituerit: Vt defectores Gallos Megaris delevit: regemque Lacedæmoniorum Aream Corinthii interfecit. Dehinc cum fratris sui Crateri filio Alexandro, bellum habuerit. Vt princeps Achaiæ Aratus Sicyonem & Corinthum & Megaram occuparit. Vt in Syria rex Antiochus, cognomine Soter, altero filio occiso, altero rege nuncupato Antiocho, decesserit. Vt in Asia filius Ptolemæi regis socio Timarcho desciuerit à patre. Vt frater Antigoni Demetrius, occupato Cyrenis regno, interiit. Vt mortuo rege Antigono, filius eius Seleucus Gallinicus regnum accepetit.
units.tr: The twenty-sixth volume contains these things: in which cities of Greece Antigonus Gonatas established his dominion; how he destroyed the Gauls who had revolted at Megara; and how the Corinthians killed Areus, king of the Lacedaemonians. Then he waged war with Alexander, the son of his brother Craterus. How Aratus, leader of the Achaeans, seized Sicyon, Corinth and Megara. How King Antiochus in Syria, surnamed Soter, died, one of his sons having been killed and the other proclaimed king as Antiochus. How in Asia the son of King Ptolemy revolted from his father with his associate Timarchus. How Demetrius, brother of Antigonus, died after seizing the kingdom of Cyrene. How, on the death of King Antigonus, his son Seleucus Callinicus received the kingdom.
PROLOGUE TO BOOK XXVII.

units.la: SEptimo & vicesimo volumine continentur hęc. Seleuci bellum in Syria aduersus Ptolemæum. Item in Asia aduersus fratrem suum Hieracem: quo bello Anguræ victus est à Gallis. Vtque Galli Pergamio victi ab Attalo Lambitunum occiderint. Vt Ptolemæus eum denuo cæptum interfecerit: & Antigonum prælio nauali vicerit. Deinde à Gallinico fusus, in Mesopotamia Antiochus insidiantem sibi effugit Artamenem. Vt postea amisso regno, equo præcipitatus Seleucus, decesserit, maioréq; filiorum eius Epacorios occiderit.
units.tr: The twenty-seventh volume contains these things: the war of Seleucus in Syria against Ptolemy; likewise in Asia against his brother Hierax, in which war he was defeated by the Gauls at Angora. And how the Gauls, defeated at Pergamum by Attalus, destroyed Lambitunum. How Ptolemy, having begun it again, killed him and defeated Antigonus in a naval battle. Then, routed by Callinicus, Antiochus escaped in Mesopotamia from Artamenes, who was lying in wait for him. Afterwards, Seleucus, having lost the kingdom, was thrown from his horse and died, and the elder of his sons killed Epacorius.
PROLOGUE TO BOOK XXVIII.

units.la: OCtauo & vicesimo volumine continentur hæc. Vt mortuo rege Epiri Alexandro, Laudamiam Epirotæ occiderint. Dictique in excessu Bastarnici motus. Vtex Macedonia Demetrius sit à Dardanis fusus,quo mortuo tutelam filii eius Philippi suscepit Antigonus, qui Thessaliam, Mæsiam, Cariam subiecit: & adiutis Achæis contra regem Spartanum Cleomenem, coepit Lacedæmona: amissoque regno Cleomenes Spartanus confugit Alexandriam, atque ibi interiit. Dictum in excessu bellum Illyricum,quod Romani gessere cum Teuta.
units.tr: The twenty-eighth volume contains these things: how, on the death of Alexander, king of Epirus, the Epirots killed Laodamia. And the Bastarnian movements are mentioned in digression. How Demetrius was defeated by the Dardanians and driven out of Macedonia, and on his death Antigonus took up the guardianship of his son Philip; he subjected Thessaly, Moesia and Caria, and with the aid of the Achaeans against the Spartan king Cleomenes he took Lacedaemon. Having lost his kingdom, Cleomenes fled to Alexandria and died there. The Illyrian war which the Romans waged with Teuta is mentioned in digression.
PROLOGUE TO BOOK XXIX.

units.la: NDetricefimo volumine continentur hæc: res gestæ Philippi regis aduersus Dardanos & Ætolos. Repetitæque inde Creticæ origines: Post cuius insulæ societatem , Philippus cum Illyriis & Dardanis & rursus Ætolis bello congressus est: adiuuantibus Ætolos Romanis: Quo finito intulit Ætolis bellum.
units.tr: The twenty-ninth volume contains these things: the deeds of King Philip against the Dardanians and Aetolians. Then the origins of Crete are recounted. After the alliance with that island, Philip engaged in war with the Illyrians and Dardanians, and again with the Aetolians, who were aided by the Romans; when that was finished he declared war on the Aetolians.
PROLOGUE TO BOOK XXX.

units.la: RIcesimo volumine continentur hæc. Vt mortuo Ptolemæo Vtruphonæ, filius eius Philopator Antiochum regem vicit. Vtque amore Agathoclæ correptus decessit,relicto filio pupillo: in quem cum Philippo rege Macedonum consensit Antiochus. Philippi deinde gesta
units.tr: The thirtieth volume contains these things: how, on the death of Ptolemy Vtruphon, his son Philopator defeated King Antiochus; and how, seized by love of Agathoclea, he died, leaving a son as a ward, against whom Antiochus made an agreement with Philip, king of the Macedonians. Then the deeds of Philip in Asia, after he had stirred up the Aetolian wars.

units.la: in Afia,cum mouiffecÆtola bella.A quibus reuerfus bellum habuit cum ducibus Romanis Sulpicio & Flaminino,à quibus victus, pax. Tranfitus deinde ad res Antiochi, qui poft regnum acceptum perfequutus defectores in Media Molonem, in Afia Maccheum, quem obfedit Sardibus;pacata fuperioreAfia Bactris tenus, in Romana bella defcendit.
units.tr: Having returned from these, he waged war with the Roman commanders Sulpicius and Flamininus, by whom he was defeated, and peace followed. Then the narrative passes to the affairs of Antiochus, who, after receiving the kingdom, pursued the rebels: in Media Molon, in Asia Maccheus, whom he besieged at Sardis; having pacified Upper Asia as far as Bactria, he descended to the Roman wars.
PROLOGUE TO BOOK XXXI.

units.la: No & tricefimo volumine, continetur bellum,quod cum Lacedæmonio NabideTitus Flamininus & Philopœmen dux Achæorum geffit. Item bellum quod cum Antiocho in Achaia per Acilium confulem & in Afia per Scipionem geftum eft. Denique Annibalis ad regem ab Carthagine fuga. Bellum cum Ætolis geftum pereundem Acilium,qui Antiochum Græciaexpulerat.
units.tr: The thirty-first volume contains the war waged against the Lacedaemonian Nabis by Titus Flamininus and Philopoemen, leader of the Achaeans. Likewise the war waged against Antiochus in Achaia by the consul Acilius, and in Asia by Scipio. Finally, Hannibal's flight from Carthage to the king. The war with the Aetolians waged by the same Acilius, who had expelled Antiochus from Greece.
PROLOGUE TO BOOK XXXII.

units.la: Ecundo & tricefimo volumine continentur hæc. Defectio ab Achæis Lacedæmoniorum & Meffeniorum, qua Philopœmen interiit. Romanorum in Afia, duce Manlio, adverfum Gallos bellum. Regis Philippi, prae ablatas fibi civitatesalienatusinRomanos animus; & ob hocaliter filiorum Demetrius occifus: Concitatio abeo Bafternæ,tranfire conati in Italiam.Indein excelfa dictæ res Illyricæ: vt Galli qui occupaerant Illyricum rur. fusredieruntin Galliam, originesque Pannoniorum, & incrementa Daciorum, per Rubobofien regem. In Afia bellum arege Eumene geftum aduerfus Gallum Ortiagontem, Pharnacem Ponticum & Prufiam, adiuuante Prufiam Annibale Pœno. Res geftæ Annibalis poft victu Antiochum,& morsmortuo Scleuco filio magniAntiochi fucceffit regno frater Antiochus.
units.tr: The thirty-second volume contains these things: the revolt of the Lacedaemonians and Messenians from the Achaeans, in which Philopoemen died; the Roman war in Asia under Manlius against the Gauls; King Philip's estrangement of mind from the Romans, because cities had been taken from him, and for this reason his son Demetrius was put to death by the other son; the stirring up of the Bastarnians by him, who attempted to cross into Italy. Thence, in digression, the Illyrian affairs: how the Gauls who had occupied Illyricum returned again into Gaul, and the origins of the Pannonians, and the growth of the Dacians, through King Rubobostes. In Asia a war was waged by King Eumenes against the Gaul Ortiagon, Pharnaces of Pontus and Prusias, with the Carthaginian Hannibal aiding Prusias. The deeds of Hannibal after he was defeated by Antiochus; and, on the death of Seleucus, son of the great Antiochus, his brother Antiochus succeeded to the kingdom.
PROLOGUE TO BOOK XXXIII.

units.la: Ertio & tricefimo volumine continentur hæc. Vtcu Perfeo Philippi filio rege Macedonum Romani bellum geflerint:quo capto deleta eft Epiros: Ætolicæ ciuitates ab vnitate corporis deducta,inter Achæos & Lacedæmonios certamine orto. Bellum rurfum in Macedonia geftum à Roman's cum Pfeudophilippo.
units.tr: The thirty-third volume contains these things: how the Romans waged war with Perseus, son of Philip, king of the Macedonians; on his capture Epirus was destroyed; the Aetolian cities were separated from the unity of the body, a dispute having arisen between the Achaeans and Lacedaemonians; and the war waged again by the Romans in Macedonia with Pseudophilippus.
PROLOGVS LIB. XXXIV.

units.la: Varro & tricesimo volumine continentur hæc. Bellum Achaicum quòd Romani per Marcellum & Mummium gesserunt: quo diruta est Corinthus. Bellum regis Eumenis cum Gallogræcis, & in Pisidia cum Selgenfibus. Res quas gessit Syriæ rex Antiochus, & rex Ægypti Ptolemæus Epiphanes. Repetitæ inde origines regum Cappadocum. Vt mortuo Ptolemæo, relicti abeo filii duo Philometor & Euergetes, primum cum Antiocho habuere bellum, quod per Romanos finitum est, deinde inter se, quo maiore est expulsus: restitutoque, Romani inter fratres regna diuiserunt. Vt mortuo rege Syriæ Antiocho Demetrius, cognomine Soter, qui Romæ fuerat obses, clam fugit, occupataque Syria bellum cum Tigranes marcho Medorum rege habuit, & Ariarathe rege Cappadocum. Vt habita inter Ariatathen & Orophernem regni certamina. Vt mortuo rege Alexandro Eumene, suffectus Attalus bellum cum Selgęfibus habuit, & cum rege Prusia.
units.tr: Varro, in his thirtieth volume, also covers the following. The Achaean War, which the Romans waged through Marcellus and Mummius, in which Corinth was destroyed. The war of King Eumenes with the Gallo-Greeks, and in Pisidia with the Selgians. The deeds of Antiochus, king of Syria, and of Ptolemy Epiphanes, king of Egypt. The origins of the kings of Cappadocia are traced back. How, after Ptolemy died, his two sons Philometor and Euergetes were left behind; they first waged war with Antiochus, which was ended by the Romans, and then fought each other, in which the greater one was driven out; but when he was restored, the Romans divided the kingdoms between the brothers. How, after Antiochus, king of Syria, died, Demetrius, surnamed Soter, who had been a hostage at Rome, secretly fled; and when he had seized Syria, he waged war with Tigranes, king of the Medes, and with Ariarathes, king of the Cappadocians. How contests for the kingdom arose between Ariarathes and Orophernes. How, after King Alexander Eumenes died, Attalus was appointed in his place and waged war with the Selgians and with King Prusias.
PROLOGUE TO BOOK XXXV.

units.la: Vinto & tricesimo volumine continentur hæc. Bellum Viraticum inter Cretas & Rhodios: sedicio Gnidiorum adueruus Cerinenses. Aduersus Demetrium Soter a Syria, tamquam genitus Epiphane Antiocho: quo bello victus Demetrius, inuisum Ptolemæo Philometore, qui eo bello interiit. Vt deinde orta Demetrio bella sint cum Diotoro Tryphone: expulsusque a Tryphone regno Syriæ Demetrius. Repetit inde superionis Asiæ motus, factos per Aretheum & Arsaceum Parthum.
units.tr: The thirty-fifth volume contains these matters: the Viratic war between the Cretans and the Rhodians; the sedition of the Gnidians against the Cerinthians. Against Demetrius Soter, who was from Syria, as if born of Epiphanes Antiochus; in which war Demetrius was defeated, hated by Ptolemy Philometor, who died in that war. Then how wars arose for Demetrius with Diodotus Tryphon, and Demetrius was expelled from the kingdom of Syria by Tryphon. He then returns to the disturbances of upper Asia, caused by Arethaeus and Arsaces the Parthian.
Prologue to Book XXXVI.

units.la: Exto & tricesimo volumine continentur hæc. Vt Tryphone pulsus Syria Demetrio, captoq; a Parthis, bellum gessit cum fratre eius Antiocho cognomine Sedete. Vt Antiochus inter secto Hyrcano, fudæos subegit. Repetitainde in excessu origo Iudæorum. Vt rex Asiæ Attalus Cenoftracas subegit: successoremque imperii Attalum Philometora reliquit. Mortuo deniq; Philometore Ariaonicus regno Asiæ occupato, bellum cum Romanis gessit, quo captus est.
units.tr: The thirty-sixth book contains these matters: how Demetrius, driven from Syria by Tryphon and captured by the Parthians, waged war with his brother Antiochus, surnamed Sidetes. How Antiochus, with Hyrcanus cut off, subdued the Jews. Thence the account goes back, in a digression, to the origin of the Jews. How Attalus, king of Asia, subdued the Cenoftracae, and left as successor to his realm Attalus Philometor. Finally, after Philometor's death, Aristonicus seized the kingdom of Asia and waged war with the Romans, by whom he was captured.
PROLOGUE TO BOOK XXXVII.

units.la: SEptimo & tricesimo volumine continentur hæc. Repetitis regum Ponticorum originibus, vt vltimum in Mithridatem Eupatora series imperii deducta fit: Atque vt ingressus ille regnum, subegit Pontum & Paphlagoniam, priusquam in bella Romana descendit. Dictaque in excessu regum Bosphoranorum & Colchorum origines, & res gestæ.
units.tr: The thirty-seventh volume contains the following. The origins of the kings of Pontus are traced back, and the line of rule is brought down to the last of them, Mithridates Eupator. It is told how, on entering upon his kingdom, he subdued Pontus and Paphlagonia before he went down into the Roman wars. At the end, the origins and deeds of the kings of Bosporus and Colchis are also related.
PROLOGUE TO BOOK XXXVIII.

units.la: OCtavo & tricesimo volumine continentur hæc. Vt Mithridates Eupator occiso Ariarathe, Cappadociam occuparit; victoque Nicomede & Malthino Bithyniam. Vt mortuo Prolemæo Philometore, frater eius Phiscon, accepto regno Ægypti seditione populi, deinde bellum cum vxore sua Cleopatra & cum rege Syriæ Demetrio habuit. Inde repertum vt Demetrius captus fit à Parthis, [bellumque] intulerit, quo cum exercitu suo deletus est.
units.tr: The thirty-eighth volume contains the following: how Mithridates Eupator, after killing Ariarathes, seized Cappadocia; and how, having defeated Nicomedes and Malthinus, he took Bithynia. How, after the death of Ptolemy Philometor, his brother Physcon, having received the kingdom of Egypt by a popular uprising, then waged war against his own wife Cleopatra and against Demetrius, king of Syria. Next, it is related how Demetrius was taken captive by the Parthians, and then made war on them, and was destroyed with his army.
PROLOGUE TO BOOK XXXIX.

units.la: NOno & tricesimo volumine continentur hæc. Vt extinco à Parthis Antiocho Sedete, frater eius Demetrius dimissus regnum Syriæ recepit: subornatoque in bellum aduersus eum Alexàdro Zabineo interiit: filiusque Antiochus Gryppos, victo Zabineo regnum occupauit. Dehinc cum fratre suo Antiocho Cyziceno, bellum in Syria Cilicicaque gessit. Vt Alexandria, mortuo rege Ptolemæo Physcone, filius eius Ptolemæus Lathyros, accepto regno expulsus est a matre Cyprum; & in Syria bello petirus ab eadem, suffecto in locum eius Alexandro, donec occisa per Alexandrii matre recepit Ægypti regnum. Vt post Lathyrum filius Alexandri regnarit, expulsoque eo suffectus fit Ptolemæus Nothus. Vt Syriam Iudæi & Arabes terrestribus latrociniis infestarint. Mari Cilices piraticum bellum mouerunt, quod in Cilicia Romani per Auronium gesserunt. Vt in Syria Eracleo post mortem regis occuparit imperium.
units.tr: In the thirty-ninth volume these things are contained: how, after Antiochus Sidetes was killed by the Parthians, his brother Demetrius, released, recovered the kingdom of Syria; but having been incited to war against him by Alexander Zabinas, he perished; and his son Antiochus Grypus, after defeating Zabinas, seized the kingdom. Then he waged war in Syria and Cilicia against his brother Antiochus Cyzicenus. How, when King Ptolemy Physcon died at Alexandria, his son Ptolemy Lathyrus, having received the kingdom, was expelled by his mother and went to Cyprus; and, sought in war in Syria by the same mother, Alexander was put in his place, until, after the mother was killed by the Alexandrians, he recovered the kingdom of Egypt. How, after Lathyrus, a son of Alexander reigned, and when he was expelled, Ptolemy Nothus was set in his place. How the Jews and Arabs harassed Syria with land robberies. The Cilicians stirred up a piratical war at sea, which the Romans waged in Cilicia through Aurelius. How Heraclio seized the rule in Syria after the king's death.
Prologue to Book 40

units.la: QVadragesimo volumine continentur hæc. Vt mortiruo Cypro rege, Cizycenus cum filiis eius bello congressus, interiit. Hi deinde à filio Cizyceni Eusebe extinctaque regali Antiochorum domo, Tigranes Armenius Syriam occupauit. Cui mox victo, Romani abstulere eam. Vt Alexandriam post interitum Ptolemæi Lathiri substituti sint eius filii: alteri data Cypros, cui post Claudii rogationem Romani abstulerunt eam; alter seditione flagitatus Alexandria Romam profugit: belloque per Gabinium gesto recepit imperium; quo mortuo successit filius, qui cum sorore Cleopatra certamine insumpto, & Pompeium magnum interfecit, & bellum cum Cæsare Alexandri gessit. Vt successit eius soror regno Cleopatra; quæ inligato in amorem suum M. Antonio, belli Actiaci fine extinxit regnum Prolemæicorum.
units.tr: The fortieth volume contains the following. After the death of Cyprus, the king, Cyzicenus fought a war with his sons and perished. Afterwards, these sons were overthrown by Cyzicenus's son Eusebes, and with the royal house of the Antiochi extinguished, Tigranes the Armenian seized Syria. Soon after he was defeated, and the Romans took it from him. After the death of Ptolemy Lathyrus, his sons were set up as rulers in Alexandria: to one was given Cyprus, which the Romans later took from him after the proposal of Clodius; the other, demanded by a rebellion, fled from Alexandria to Rome, and after the war waged by Gabinius he recovered the throne. When he died, his son succeeded him, who, having taken up a contest with his sister Cleopatra, both killed Pompey the Great and waged war against Caesar in Alexandria. After this, his sister Cleopatra succeeded to the kingdom; becoming entangled in love with Mark Antony, she brought the kingdom of the Ptolemies to an end at the close of the war of Actium.
PROLOGUE OF BOOK XLI.

units.la: VNo & quadragesimo volumine continentur res Parthicæ & Bactrianæ. In Parthicis, vt est constitutum imperium, per Arsacen regem. Successores deinde eius Artabanus, & Tigranes cognomine Deus; à quo subacta est Media & Mesopotamia. Dictusque in excessu Arabiæ situs. In Bactrianis autem rebus, vt à Diodoro rege constitutum est: deinde quo repugnante Scythicæ gentes Sarancæ & Arani Bactra occupauere & Socdianos. Indicæ quoque res additæ, gestæ per Apollodorum & Menandrum reges eorum.
units.tr: The forty-first volume contains the affairs of the Parthians and the Bactrians. Concerning the Parthians: once the empire was established by King Arsaces, his successors were Artabanus and Tigranes, surnamed "the God," by whom Media and Mesopotamia were subdued; and the position of Arabia, at its far edge, is described. As for the affairs of the Bactrians, the empire was founded by King Diodotus; then, in the time of his successor (who opposed them), the Scythian tribes of the Saranci and the Arani occupied Bactra and the Sogdians. The affairs of India are also added, carried out by its kings Apollodotus and Menander.
PROLOGUE TO BOOK XLII.

units.la: SEcundo & quadragesimo volumine continentur Parthicæ res. Vt præfectus Parthis Phrahates bellum intulit in Babylonios & à Græcis cæsus est: vt Phrahati successit rex Mithridates cognomine Magnus, qui Armenis bellum intulit. Inde repetitæ origines Armeniorum, & situs. Vt varia complurium regum in Parthis successione, imperium accepit Orodes, qui Crassum deleuit: & Syriam per filium Pacorum occupauit. Illi successit Phrahates, qui & cum Antonio bellum habuit, & cum Tiridate. Addiæ res Scythicæ. Reges Thoclatorum Asiani, interitusque Sarducarum.
units.tr: The forty-second volume contains the affairs of the Parthians. How the prefect of the Parthians, Phraates, made war on the Babylonians and was slain by the Greeks; how King Mithridates, surnamed the Great, succeeded Phraates and made war on the Armenians. Thence the origins of the Armenians and their situation are traced back. The various succession of several kings among the Parthians; Orodes received the kingdom, who destroyed Crassus and seized Syria through his son Pacorus. Phraates succeeded him, who waged war both with Antony and with Tiridates. Scythian affairs are added. The Asian kings of the Thoclatae, and the destruction of the Sarducae.
X PRO-
PROLOGUE TO BOOK XLIII.

units.la: TErtio & quadragesimo volumine continentur origines [priscorum] Latinorum,situs vrbis Romæ, & res vsque ad Priscum Tarquinium. Origines [deinde] Liguriæ,& Massilicusium res gestæ.
units.tr: The forty-third volume contains the origins of the early Latins, the situation of the city of Rome, and events down to Priscus Tarquinius. Then the origins of Liguria, and the deeds of the Massiliots.
PROLOGUE TO BOOK XLIV.

units.la: QVarro & quadragesimo volumine continentur res Hispanicæ & Punicæ.
units.tr: The forty-fourth volume contains the Spanish and Punic affairs.
END.

units.la: INDEX EORVM QVÆ HOC LIBRO CONTINENTVR.

units.la: EIVM quendam Apellicontem,lectorbeneuole, hominem φιλάβιβλον magis, quam φιλόσοφον, Aristotelis libros, quos lacunis plenos magna pecunia parauerat, & emendandos susceperat, fœdismendis refertos edidisse refert Strabo, quum temere & imperite suppleret quæ passim deerant: Neque hic stetisse eorum depravationem. Nam & bibliopolas nobis, negligenter à librariis trascriptos libros, reliquisse. Hæc quasi tabes, ita processit, vt scriptu Aristotelicis tantum non exitium adferret. Qui à summi Philosophi libris manus impuras non abstinuerant, quid non auderent, in ceteris? Oës sane qui lucri causa exscribuntur libri, Sirempse lege iusdit esse Iuppiter. Sed hæc omnia correctorum audaci ignorantia, aut fœdalibrariorum negligentia tribuamus; Vetustas non pauca depravat, multa tollit. Huic morbo medicinam vt faciamus, in his saltem aduersiis quorum necdum desperata est salus, conquirendi sunt meliori, & pudentiori sæculo scripti libri; & in his conferendis & exprimendis nō religentes solum, sed & religiosi esse debemus, vt id sequamur quod exemplarium multitudo in fidem trahit, vt præcipit Eusebius: Si cubi haereas prudentiores consulendi. Iam in imprimendo adhibēda exacta & extrema diligentia, ne emendationem, quam titulus profitetur, opus ipsum redarguat. Hac in edēdo Iustino, secutus certe sum; an assecutus, tuū, Lector, iudicium est. Vsus sum primum codice Oliuarii Aligretii Charantonai, nobilis adolescentis, & eruditi, & quod hoc sæculo perrarum est, pij; quem
units.tr: Strabo reports that a certain Apellicon, a man who loved books more than wisdom, published the books of Aristotle, which he had bought at great expense in a damaged state and undertook to emend, filled with monstrous errors, since he rashly and unskilfully supplied whatever was missing here and there. Nor did their corruption stop there, for booksellers left us books carelessly copied by scribes. This plague spread so far that it nearly destroyed the Aristotelian writings. If men who did not keep their unclean hands off the books of the greatest philosopher, what would they not dare with the rest? Indeed, all books that are copied for profit, as Jupiter has ordained, are thrown into confusion. But let us attribute all this to the bold ignorance of correctors or the foul carelessness of copyists. Age corrupts many things and destroys many more. To apply a remedy to this disease, at least in those works whose health is not yet despaired of, we must seek out books written in a better and more discerning age. In comparing and printing them we must be not only careful but scrupulous, so that we follow what the multitude of copies confirms, as Eusebius advises: if you are in doubt anywhere, consult the wiser ones. In printing, too, exact and extreme diligence must be applied, so that the work itself does not refute the emendation the title promises. In editing Justin I have certainly followed this method; whether I have achieved it, Reader, is for your judgement. I used first the manuscript of Oliverius Aligretus Charantonus, a noble and learned young man, and, what is very rare in this age, pious; whom, recently slain by the crime of a wicked robber, I mourn as I ought.

units.la: quēnuper impio scelerati latronis facinore interempti, prout ac debeo,doleo:Moueor adolescentis ipsius,mouer necesitate quæ mihi cū ipso intercedebat maxima: Obuersantur oculis casti labores, & infructuosi, iuuenis optimi, & ad summa nati; quæ profecto conjecuturus esset si virtutes eius maturuisset. Accedit lacrymis meis, genus ipsum mortis: Quamuis,si bene calculum ponas, parum interest morbo,an ferro, an vero mala ætate pereas: attamen amico graue est, hominem amicum primo ætatis flore,nōin acie virtute hostis,sed insidiis fraudelatronis & sicarij perire. His moribus,his temporibus nati sumus, vt vitam viri boni latronibus debeamus. Itē nunc mortales, & magnis cogitationibus pectora implete. Quidquid tot annis, tot laboribus cumulauerīs, id horula vnius momentum destruet: Id quoque quod tenetur, per manus exit. Igne-scē lector, sapiens,& bonum ferre potest modice; & malum fortiter acleniter. Hominis tamen est, etiam non insipientis,hominis amicissimi, indigna morte peremti,desiderio cōmoneri. Τὰ ςε ἀλλο Ὁ τῶν λόγων, vt est apud antiquū poetam, ἀνἔχω ἐμὶ Homo sum;humana humanitas fero. Non potui in illius mentione, nō affici dolore; quem leui hoc scripto tegstatum relinquo,vt qui me amasse illum viuū sciunt,mortui apud me gratam esse,& sanctam memoriam intelligant. Spero lacrymis meis,abudus te paratam veniam. Igitur cum veteris illius exemplaris beneficio, multa emendassem, neq; tamen videretur huic auctori perpurgando sufficere, duos etiam manu descriptos libros accepi à P. Daniele populari meo; duos deinde à Fr. Pithoeo:tum duos alios à CL. V. Iacobo Cuiacio domꝭ tore meo : Octauus optimæ nota est Cl. Puteani viri clarissimi, & regij in senatu Parisiensi Senatoris. His nonus accessit, & tandem etiam decimus P. Pithoei beneficio: Tres item impressi ad vetera exemplaria collati, vnus Petri, alter Francisci Pithoeorum fratrum, tertius Io. Pelerini, doctoris regij. Horum summmorum & doctissimorum virorum, non libri tantum, verum & iudicium & doctrina, multis locis errantem docuerunt, hafitantem confirmarunt. Non est huius loci, Lector, eorum tibi minime obscuram dignitatem, erudítionem, humanitatem praedicare: sed hac te scire volui, vt intelligeres quibus viris huius auctoris emendatio debeatur. Est enim benignum, & plenum ingenuí pudoris, fateri per quos profeceris. Ergo decem illos veteres codices, & tribus impressis adscriptas lectiones, cum vulgatis editionibus itaftudiose & diligenter contuli, vt ceteris qui in hoc auctore conantur aliquid, nihil fere praeter coniecturas reliqui fit. Iam in ipso auctoris contextu ita religiose versatus sum, vt vbique veterum librorum scripturam bona fide exhibuerim; nullas omnino coniecturas admiserim; lectiones vulgo editas, contra libros non receperim, nisi, siquando in veteribus sententia non constabat; tum enim antiquam scripturam inter varias lectiones retuli, vt liberum esset suum cuique iudicium. Quadam in vno tantum manuscripto reperta, eoque non ita probo, inclusi hac nota[ ]. Ex meis & aliorum paucissimis coniecturis, confeci notas, additis ex Graecis Latinisque auctoribus, observationibus, quibus quae diuersa auctores prodiderunt, breuiter sub nominibus ipsorum trado. Quapassim a me Vett. exemplariorum fide restituta sunt & emendata, ea si omnia in notas conicere voluissem, quod plerique nunc faciunt, exigui laboris inani ostentatione, immane opus conficiendum suisset, & iustus commentarius scribendus, imo iusto maior: Quo, cum eo hic auctor non indigeret, neq; te, neq; typographum onerare volui; neque in eo conficiendo abuti otio meo. Vale.
units.tr: I am moved by the young man himself, and by the very close intimacy that bound me to him. There rise before my eyes his chaste and fruitless labours, of a most excellent youth born for great things, which he would surely have attained had he lived to mature his virtues. To my tears is added the manner of his death. Although, if you reckon properly, it makes little difference whether one perishes by disease, by the sword, or by the misfortune of a bad age, yet it is grievous for a friend that a friend in the first flower of youth should perish not in battle against an enemy, but by the ambush and fraud of a robber and an assassin. We were born in such times and with such customs that we must owe the life of a good man to brigands. So, mortals, fill your hearts with great thoughts: whatever you have piled up over so many years and labours, one hour will destroy; even what you hold slips from your hands. Forgive me, Reader; a wise and good man can bear good things moderately and bad things bravely and gently. Yet it belongs to a human being, even one who is not foolish, and to a man most dear, to be moved by the loss of one taken from us by an unworthy death. Bear with me: as the ancient poet says, "I am a man; I think nothing human foreign to me" [ἀνέχου ἐμοῦ]. I could not mention him without being moved to grief. I leave him this memorial in a slight writing, so that those who knew that I loved him while he lived may understand that his memory is dear and holy to me even now that he is dead. I hope that with my tears I bring you a readily granted pardon. Therefore, with the help of that old exemplar, I had emended many passages, yet this seemed insufficient for thoroughly purging this author. I then received two manuscripts copied by hand from Pierre Daniel, my fellow citizen; then two more from F. Pithou; then two others from the most distinguished man Jacques Cujas, my teacher. The eighth is of excellent quality, belonging to the most illustrious Puteanus, a royal councillor in the Parisian Senate. To these a ninth was added, and finally a tenth through the kindness of P. Pithou. Likewise three printed editions collated with the old manuscripts: one of Pierre, another of François Pithou, brothers, and a third of Jean Pélerin, royal doctor. These most eminent and learned men, through their books, judgement and learning, taught me where I was wrong in many places and confirmed me where I hesitated. It is not the place, Reader, to proclaim to you their dignity, erudition and humanity, which are by no means obscure; but I wished you to know this, so that you understand to what men the emendation of this author is owed. For it is a kindly thing, and full of genuine modesty, to acknowledge through whom one has made progress. Therefore I have so carefully collated those ten old manuscripts and the readings noted in the three printed copies with the common editions that, for those who try anything further on this author, almost nothing remains but conjectures. Moreover, in the text of the author itself I have dealt so scrupulously that everywhere I have faithfully presented the reading of the old books; I have admitted no conjectures at all, and I have not accepted readings commonly printed against the books, except where in the old texts the sense was not settled; in such cases I have placed the ancient reading among the variant readings, so that each reader's judgement remains free. Some things found in only one manuscript, and that not very trustworthy, I have enclosed with this mark[ ]. From my own and a few others' conjectures I have composed notes, adding observations drawn from Greek and Latin authors, in which I briefly set down, under their names, what different authors have reported. As for the many passages that I have restored and emended on the authority of the old copies, if I had wished to put all of them into notes, as many do now, it would have been a huge task of empty display for little labour, and a full commentary would have had to be written, indeed larger than the work itself. Since this author does not need that, I did not wish to burden you or the printer, nor to misuse my leisure in producing it. Farewell.
DE

units.la: DE TROGO POM- PEIO ET IVSTINO.
units.tr: On Trogus Pompeius and Justin.

units.la: {D}E Trogi Pompeii genere, hæc Iustinus ipse, ad finem libri 43. In postremo libro Trogus maiores suos à Vocontiis (ita Mss. omnes, non vt vulgo Volsis) originem duxere; auum suum Trogum Pompeium Sertoriano bello à Cn. Pompeio ciuitatem percepisse dicit: patruum Mithridatico bello turmas equitum sub eodem Pompeio duxisse: patrem quoq; sub Caio Cæsare militasse, epistolarumque, & legationum simul & annuli curam habuisse. Caium Cæsarem intelligit, illū qui superato Pompeio Rempub. tenuit, vt loquitur in epistolis Seneca; nō eum qui post Tiberium imperio potitus. Dubitanter hoc scribo, & mihi ipsi pæne diffidens, quum sciam aliter videri doctissimo, & historiarum, omnisque antiquitatis prudentissimo viro: quem quominus possim hoc tempore consulere, eiusque colloquio atque familiaritate doctior fieri, facit hæc clades nova pestilitasq;: propter quam hic & Musæ alumnis suis spoliatæ conticuerunt; & mœsti, tot tantasque intuemur vastitates funerum; vt merito dixerit M. Varro, nasci nos spissius quam emori. Vix duo homines, inquit, decem menses edolatum Cnum reddunt puerum: contra, Qna pestilentia, hostica acies, pundo tempora; immanes accruos facit. Iraq; siquid in his notis est, aut non notatum, aut male notatum, id adscribes, Lector, doctorum virorum, quos vt oracula consulebam, absentiæ; & meæ tot imminentibus periculis, solicitudini. Sed, vt eo vnde excessit, redeat oratio, à Mithridatico bello, quo Trogi nostri patrem iam fuisse, nemo negauerit, ad Cæsarem Caligulam, sunt vt minimum anni centum. Vixisse ergo Trogum iudico, Augusti & Tiberii temporibus: quibus floruisse & Q. Curtium Rufum, vt ab humanissimo & scriptorum veterum peritissimo P. Pithoeo didici, ita docebo ad eius historias. Trogus autem noster, quum forte Sallustio
units.tr: Concerning the family of Trogus Pompeius, Justin himself says this at the end of Book 43: "In the last book, Trogus states that his ancestors derived their origin from the Vocontii (so all the manuscripts read, not, as is commonly printed, the Volsci). He says that his grandfather, Trogus Pompeius, received citizenship from Gnaeus Pompey in the Sertorian war; that his uncle led squadrons of cavalry under the same Pompey in the Mithridatic war; and that his father also served under Gaius Caesar and had charge of the correspondence, the embassies and the signet ring." By Gaius Caesar he means the one who, after defeating Pompey, held the Republic, as Seneca puts it in his letters, and not the one who later obtained the empire after Tiberius. I write this tentatively, and I distrust my own view, since I know that a most learned man, and one most skilled in history and in all antiquity, sees it otherwise. What prevents me from consulting him at present, and from becoming wiser through his conversation and friendship, is this new calamity and plague. Because of it, the Muses have been stripped of their nurslings and have fallen silent, and we, sorrowful, look upon such great and numerous devastations of the dead that Marcus Varro was right to say that we are born more thickly than we die. He says: "Scarcely two men, in ten months, produce a child of the Cnus kind; on the other hand, a pestilence, a hostile army, and a pounding of times make huge heaps of dead." Therefore, if anything in these notes is unmarked or badly marked, reader, please attribute it to the absence of the learned men whom I consulted as oracles, and to my own anxiety amid so many threatening dangers. But let me return the discussion to where it left off. From the Mithridatic war, in which our Trogus's father was already serving, no one would deny, to Caligula Caesar, there are at least one hundred years. I therefore judge that Trogus lived in the times of Augustus and Tiberius, and that Quintus Curtius Rufus also flourished in those times, as I learned from the most courteous and most expert in ancient writers, Pierre Pithou; I shall demonstrate this from his histories. Our Trogus, then, when he chanced to see the Roman state recounted by Sallust and Livy, set about writing a Greek and foreign history.

units.la: Liuio resPop. Rom. memoratas videret, ad Grzcam & peregrinam hiftoriam fcribendam aggreffus eft. Trogi nomen,arbitror, barbarum;Pompeii ab auo eft. Solebat enim peregrini in eorum nomina tranfire, quorum beneficio ciues Rom. erant. M. Cicero ad Acilium, de Demetrio Megar: Dolabella, inquit, rogatu meo ciuitatem à Cæfare impetrauit:qua in re, ego interfui: Itaq; nunc P. Cornelius Vocatur. M. Varro lib. 5. de L. L. meminit cuiufdam T. Quintii Trogi: & Tacitus 11. Annal. SaufelJam (vel vtis cui magnam partem faluiem debet Tacitus;Saufeius) Trogum commemorant, qui fortaffe Senecæ eft M. Heluius Trogus.
units.tr: The name Trogus, I think, is foreign; Pompeius came from his grandfather. For foreigners were accustomed to take the names of those through whose favour they had become Roman citizens. Marcus Cicero, writing to Atticus about Demetrius of Megara, says: "Dolabella, he says, obtained citizenship from Caesar at my request; in this matter I took part. And so now he is called Publius Cornelius." Marcus Varro, in Book 5 of On the Latin Language, mentions a certain Titus Quintius Trogus. And Tacitus, in Book 11 of the Annals, mentions Saufeius (or, as others read, Saufeius Trogus), to whom Tacitus owes a large part of his safety; perhaps this is the Marcus Helvius Trogus of Seneca.

units.la: Iuftinus Trogi abbreuiator,quo tempore vixerit,non habeo dicere: fortaffe quis eum imperio Conftantinopolim translato floruiffe colliget ex eius libro 8. quum inquit, Graciam etiam nunc, & Syribus & dignitate orbis terrarum principem: quæ tamen coniectura leuis eft nimis. Nam quod quidam Methodici claruiffe eum anno Christi centefimo quinquagefimo fcripferunt, nullo auctore fcripferunt:In errorem induxi,quod hæc epitoma, in vulgo editus libris, Antonino Imp. inferiatur, contra vetetum codicum fidem.Vixit quidem sub Antonino Iuftinus martyr & philofophus, cuius exrant opera Græca; & qui anno 143. librum pro noftra religione có pofitum, Antonino tradidit, vt eft in Chronico Eufebii. Hunc illi eundem cum noftro facere videntur, & ante eos neefcio quis Martinus Polonus,nulla probabilitatione. Iuftinum, cuius hæc eft epitoma, nemo D. Hieronymo antiquior commemorat:eius mihi locum, ex præfatione in Danielem, notauit doctiffimus P. Pithoeus. Præne præterieram in bibliotheca Medicæa vidiffe me beneficio Fr. Victorii, Petrinepotis Iuftini codicem litteris Longobardicis in quo hic auctor M. Iunianus Iuftus. nunc dicitur:qui & in Ant. Arnaldi ampliffi viri ms. Iuftinus Frontinus.
units.tr: Justin, the abridger of Trogus, I cannot say in what period he lived. Perhaps someone might gather from his eighth book, where he says that Greece is still now the leader of the Syrians and of the world in dignity, that he flourished after the empire was transferred to Constantinople; but this conjecture is far too slight. As for certain Methodists who wrote that he flourished in the hundred and fiftieth year of Christ, they wrote this on no authority. What misled me is that this epitome, as printed in common books, is dedicated to the emperor Antoninus, contrary to the faith of the older manuscripts. Indeed, Justin the martyr and philosopher, whose Greek works survive, lived under Antoninus, and in the year 143 he presented to Antoninus a book composed in defence of our religion, as is recorded in the Chronicle of Eusebius. Those writers seem to identify him with our Justin, and before them I know not who, Martinus Polonus, with no probability at all. No one mentions Justin, whose epitome this is, earlier than Saint Jerome; the most learned Pierre Pithou pointed out to me that passage from Jerome's preface to Daniel. I had almost passed over the fact that, in the Medici library, through the kindness of Fr. Victorius, I saw a codex of Justin, the grandson of Petrus, written in Lombardic script, in which this author is named Marcus Iunianus Iustus. He is also called, in the manuscript of the most distinguished Antonius Arnaldus, Justinus Frontinus.
ON THE PREFACE OF JUSTIN.

units.la: Pag. 1. lin. 17. Se segregati] Mire hic variant scripti libri: ego lectionem quam sine litura habebant duo Mss, secutus sum, explosa vulgata, quæ nulli rei est: imo contra mentem auctoris est.
units.tr: Page 1, line 17. Se segregati] The manuscripts vary here in a remarkable way. I followed the reading that two manuscripts have without any erasure, rejecting the vulgate reading, which makes no sense and is indeed contrary to the author's meaning.

units.la: Pag. 2. lin. 6. Cato.]in principio Originum. M. Cicero pro Plancio: meminit & Columella fine lib. 2. Symmach. 1. ep. 1. contra apud Suetonium Galba.
units.tr: Page 2, line 6. Cato.] At the beginning of the Origines. Cicero, Pro Plancio. Columella also mentions him at the end of book 2. Symmachus, Epistles 1.1. On the contrary, see Suetonius, Galba.
ON BOOK I.

units.la: Historiarum Philippicarum ιστορία à Trogo esse, vetetum librorum consensus arguit. Philippicas autem quare inscripserit, difficile est iudicium. Nam velle ex hac epitoma, de integro Trogi opere iudicare, desipere est: ita Trogum male accepit hic, quisquis fuit, Iustinus: Qui dum resecare cupit, quæ nec iucunda erant & minime necessaria, optimum auctore prorsus euitauit, vt vetus poeta loquitur. Ego putauerim Philippicam historiam, Trogo Macedonicam esse, princeps nempe huius operis argumentum. Nam à 7. lib. ad 41. regnum Macedonicum describit: cuius à Philippo Alexandri patre, dignitas coepit, ita vt id Græcia & Asia cerucibus, Gelut iugum seruitutis, imponeret, vt extr. lib. 6. Iustinus: & eum auctor Prologorum Magnum vocat. Quae autem Philippico imperio præmisit, arbitror esse Mundi origines, quas vett. librorum titulus iactat. Terræ autem situs, quos eadem pollicetur inscriptio, esse descriptiones regionum, quæ in Iustino fere nullæ sunt, in Trogo frequentes fuerunt, vt indicant Prologi quos ex Mss. codicibus produxi in lumine eras-
units.tr: That the Philippic Histories (ιστορία) are by Trogus, the agreement of the old books proves. Why he entitled them Philippic is hard to judge. For to wish to judge Trogus' whole work from this epitome is foolish. This man, whoever he was, Justin, treated Trogus badly: in trying to cut out what was neither pleasant nor very necessary, he entirely avoided the best author, as the old poet says. I would think that the Philippic history is Trogus' Macedonian history, its principal subject. For from book 7 to book 41 he describes the Macedonian kingdom, whose greatness began with Philip, the father of Alexander, so that he placed Greece and Asia under the yoke of servitude, like a burden on the neck, as Justin says at the end of book 6. The author of the Prologues calls him "the Great." What he placed before the rule of Philip, I believe, are the origins of the world, which the title of the old books proclaims. The situation of the lands, which the same inscription promises, are descriptions of regions. These are almost absent in Justin but were frequent in Trogus, as the Prologues indicate, which I have brought forward from manuscripts in the light of the erased-

units.la: Φιλιππικὰ Theopompi citantur ab Athenæo passim; quibus hist[?]oriam Philippi libris 48. complexus est, vt Diodorus refert lib. 11. Quinque autem libros eum inseruisse ab Philippi historia alienos, idem Diodorus auctor est, è quibus tres, res Siculas continebant. Non est autem alperanda P. Pithoei coniectura, Trogum Theopompi ꝥ mulatione atque exemplo historias suas, vt Demosthenis M. Tullium orationes suas in Antonium, Philippicas inscripsisse.
units.tr: The Philippica of Theopompus is cited by Athenaeus passim. In it he embraced the history of Philip in 48 books, as Diodorus reports in book 11. Diodorus also states that he inserted five books foreign to the history of Philip, three of which dealt with Sicilian affairs. But P. Pithoeus' conjecture should not be dismissed: that Trogus, by the imitation and example of Theopompus, entitled his histories Philippic, just as Demosthenes named his orations against Philip, and Cicero his orations against Antony.
