units.la: Pag. 3. lin. 1. PRINCIPIO. totum hunc locum transcripsit Augustinus lib. 4 cap. 6. de ciuitate Dei. Compara hæc cum iis quæ initio Catilinarii Sallustius, cuius flumen diofum fuisse Iustinum aut Trogum ipsum, & hic locus & alii satis indicant: & quæ in principio lib. 2. ait de rebus Scythicis, quæ satis ample, magnificeque fuerunt eadem totidem verbis, de Atheniensibus Sallustius. Vide ad hunc locum M. Ciceronem 3. de Legib. & 2. de offic. Aristot. 1. Polit. Tacit. 3. Annal.
units.tr: Page 3, line 1. PRINCIPIO.] Augustine transcribed this whole passage in book 4, chapter 6 of De civitate Dei. Compare these words with what Sallust says at the beginning of the Catiline. Whether this passage and others sufficiently show that the flowing style was Justin's or Trogus' own, I leave open. And what Trogus says at the beginning of book 2 about Scythian affairs, which were treated fully and magnificently, Sallust says in the same words about the Athenians. See on this passage Cicero, De legibus 3 and De officiis 2, Aristotle, Politics 1, and Tacitus, Annals 3.

units.la: P. 4. v. 4. Primus omnium Ninum.] Orosius lib. 2. ca. 2. Omnis historia antiqua à Nino incipiunt: omnis historia Romana à Procla exorsa est: ita habet Ms. popularis mei P. Danielis, viri studiis bonarum artium præclarissimi, cum ininprestis desit prius membrum. Est autem Ninus primus τῶν εἰς ἱστορίαν ... Diodorus lib. 2. quem vide: Et a Nino Chronici initium sumpsit Eusebius.
units.tr: Page 4, line 4. Primus omnium Ninum.] Orosius, book 2, chapter 2: "All ancient history begins with Ninus; all Roman history began with Proca." So my fellow countryman P. Daniel's manuscript has it, a man most distinguished in the liberal arts, since in the printed editions the first clause is missing. Ninus is the first of those who entered history [τῶν εἰς ἱστορίαν ...]. See Diodorus, book 2. Eusebius also began his Chronicle with Ninus.

units.la: V. 5. Auitum.] Ms. habitum. Habitum pro Auitum, & Habe, pro Aue, scripsisse veteres, notum est: Varro apud Nonium. Quibus inflabilis animam ardens mutabiliter habet habere, & non habere ibi enim habet, est auet.
units.tr: Line 5. Auitum.] The manuscript has habitum. That the ancients wrote habitum for avitum and habe for ave is well known: see Varro, quoted by Nonius, where habet is the same as avet.

units.la: V. 10. Tanaum.] Is fortasse, quem Iornandes, Taunafin vocat.
units.tr: Line 10. Tanaum.] He is perhaps the one whom Jordanes calls Taunafin.
Line 19. Zoroastre.] In Diodorus he is called Oxyartes (Ὀξύαρτης).

units.la: V, 22. 23. Ninya.] Ita vno excepto vett. omnes: & Eusebius & Cassiodorus: Græcis est Νίνυας & ita apud Agathiam reflituit Leunclaius lib. 2. Variaflee in hoc nomine auctores refert Augustus lib. 18. de ciuitate Dei, cap. 2.
units.tr: Lines 22–23. Ninya.] So all the old books except one read; so do Eusebius and Cassiodorus. In Greek it is Ninyas (Νίνυας), and Leunclavius restored it so in Agathias, book 2. The author reports the variants of this name in Augustine, De civitate Dei, book 18, chapter 2.

units.la: V. 23 Semiramide.] Præter Diodorum, vide Plutarchum in ἐγκωμίῳ & Ælianum τῶν ἰδίων lib. 7.
units.tr: Line 23. Semiramide.] Besides Diodorus, see Plutarch in the Encomium and Aelian, book 7 of his Varia.

units.la: V. 30. Velamentis.] Vett. alii Virtus Gefferalii, calciamentis, placet vulgata lectio. lib. 2. priusquam aduersus calorem Gelsi signa Gelamenta corporis inuenire tentur. Virgil. Purpureasq; super Gestes, Gelamina nota, Intexunt.
units.tr: Line 30. Velamentis.] Other old books have a different word, and "shoes" (calciamentis) is the vulgate reading that pleases me. In book 2: before they found, against the heat of the sun, coverings for the body. Virgil: They weave in purple coverings, marked garments.

units.la: P. 5. v. 7. Harenae Vice.] sequutus sum Cuiacii doctoris mei codicem quod in constructione murorum Babylonis nemo harenae, aut picis meminerit. Diod. τὰς τῶν λίθων ... vide Curtium Rufum lib. 5. Anim. Marcellinum lib. 13. Orosium lib. 2. cap. 7. Optimus optimi & clarissimi viri Cl. Puteani liber, habet harenapicc. Aşulani edicio arena & calcis Vice.
units.tr: Page 5, line 7. Harenae Vice.] I followed the codex of my teacher Cuiacius, in which no one mentions sand or pitch in the construction of the walls of Babylon. Diodorus [τὰς τῶν λίθων ...]. See Curtius Rufus, book 5; Ammianus Marcellinus, book 13; Orosius, book 2, chapter 7. The excellent book of the most distinguished Claude Puteanus has sand and pitch. The Aldine edition [Asulani] has in place of sand and lime.

units.la: V. 8. E terra exaftuat] plerique veteres, & erecta flamma. Semiramidem in regia ... potuisse referre Diod. Et in templo Iouis, inquit ... μαται χευσέα σφυρήλατα Διὸς, Ηρᾶς, Πίας. sed vulgata lectio confirmatur Cuiacii libro.
units.tr: Line 8. E terra exaftuat] Many old books, and erected flame. Diodorus reports that Semiramis could have ... in the palace. And in the temple of Jupiter, he says, golden statues, hammered, of Zeus, Hera and Rhea [χρυσέα σφυρήλατα Διὸς, Ἥρας, Ῥέας]. But the vulgate reading is confirmed by the book of Cuiacius.

units.la: V. 14. Duos & 40.] praeter vnum, Mss. omnes: duo & triginta, duo, antique pro duos, & statim quidam vett. regnum potita. quomodo lib. 12. qui postea regnum Indorum potitus est. & lib. 6. potitus Siciliorum, & lib. 10. Siltonem potita. & lib. 37. ne non diutinam administrationem regni potiretur. Vide Prisc. 18: qui ex Iugurth. Sallustii adfert, Adherbalis potiretur. quo loco Vetus codex Sallust. habet Adherbalem.
units.tr: Line 14. Duos & 40.] Except for one, all the manuscripts have duo et triginta, "two and thirty." Duo is the old form for duos. Soon after, some old books have regnum potita, as in book 12, who afterwards gained the kingdom of the Indians; book 6, gained possession of the Sicilians; book 10, having gained Siltonem; and book 37, that he might not hold the administration of the kingdom for long. See Priscian, book 18, who quotes from Sallust's Jugurtha, Adherbal should gain possession, where an old codex of Sallust has Adherbalem.

units.la: V. 22. Sardanapalus.] tricesimus à Nino, inquit Diod: Vt Velleius lib. 1. tertius & tricesimus. Praefectus qui hic Arbactus, in prologo est Arbaces: Diodoro & Straboni lib. 16. & Athenaeo & Agath. 2. Α'ρβάκης. Velleio mendose Pharnaces, pro Arnaces. Orosio lib. 1. cap. 19. & lib. 2.
units.tr: Line 22. Sardanapalus.] The thirtieth from Ninus, says Diodorus. Velleius, book 1, says the thirty-third. The prefect who here is Arbactus is in the Prologue Arbaces. Diodorus, Strabo book 16, Athenaeus and Agathias book 2 have Ἀρβάκης. Velleius wrongly has Pharnaces for Arnaces. See Orosius, book 1, chapter 19 and book 2.

units.la: cap 2. Arbatus: quem, inquit, alij Arbacem vocant.
units.tr: Chapter 2. Arbatus: whom, he says, others call Arbaces.
Line 27. Purpuram.] Plutarch, On the Fortune of Alexander, book 2.

units.la: V. 30. Tractantique lanam.] Recte. Tracta, enim in veteri glossario sunt ... Sed ea dicta videntur à trahendo. Varro. sed simul manibus trahere lanam.
units.tr: Line 30. Tractantique lanam.] Correct. For tracta in an old glossary means ... but these words seem derived from trahere. Varro: but at the same time to draw wool with the hands.

units.la: Veteres omnes excepto Cuiacii codice tractantes, ferrum & arma habentes. & ita Saresb. Policratici 6. cap. 14.
units.tr: All the old books, except the codex of Cuiacius, have tractantes, ferrum & arma habentes (handling iron and holding arms), and so Saresbury, Policraticus, book 6, chapter 14.

units.la: P. 6. v. 11. Astyagen.] Vide Herodotum lib. 1 & Orosium lib. 1. cap. 19 Astyagis filiam Mandanen vocat Herodotus & Valer. Max. lib. 1. ca. 7. quae Aelianο lib. 12. est Mandana. ... Sed videtur emendandus Valerius cum inquit, Astya-
units.tr: Page 6, line 11. Astyagen.] See Herodotus, book 1, and Orosius, book 1, chapter 19. Herodotus and Valerius Maximus, book 1, chapter 7, call Astyages' daughter Mandane, which in Aelian, book 12, is Mandana. But Valerius seems to need emending where he says Astya-

units.la: Assyages duos prænuntios somnii finstra discutere tentasse, legendum enim duo prænuntia somnia, vt in quodam Ms. legere memini. De Cyro præter Herodotum & Oxyslo lege Ctefiæ ἱκ λοyάς, & Xenophontis ςυμουταυδιας, quam quidem non ad historiæ fidem scripsit, sed ad effigiem iusti imperii, inquit, 1. ad fratrem M. Cicero.
units.tr: Astyages tried to dispel by a trick the two forewarnings of his dream. For one should read two omens of the dream, as I remember reading in a certain manuscript. About Cyrus, besides Herodotus and Oxyles, read Ctesias' Persica and Xenophon's Cyropaedia, which he wrote not as a faithful history but, as M. Cicero says in his first letter to his brother, as the image of a just empire.

units.la: V. 21. Arcessit. Ea st omnium fere veterum libtorū in hoc auctore scriptura. dicitur autem arcesso ab arcio, vt à capio, capesso, facio, facesso. Itrifcianus lib. 8. & arcio est accidit: ar pro ad ἀεχαικώς. vide Scaurum de orthogr.
units.tr: Line 21. Arcessit.] This is the reading of almost all the old books for this author. But arcesso is derived from arcio, as capesso from capio and facesso from facio. Priscian, book 8: arcio is accio, with ar for ad, in the archaic manner. See Scaurus on orthography.

units.la: P. 7. v. 16. Seruilibus Verberibus. lib. 2. Verbera in ea- siem, non armaferenda, omissoque ferro, sirgas acflagella, ceteraque seruilia metus parandla infrumenta. Et redte Accursius ad. 1 12. D. dꝛiure fisci seruilia verbeta interpretatur flagella, vt l. 10. §. pen. D. de inius vocando, iun&a. l. 7. §. præterea. D. de iniuriis: probat. Petronius seruiles pœnas dixit: Sallust. 1. hist. abunde libertatem rati, quia tergus abstinetur, Vide Senecam extr. ἀπολο- κων.
units.tr: Page 7, line 16. Seruilibus Verberibus.] Book 2: Blows are to be borne in the manner of slaves, not arms carried; iron omitted, straps and whips and other servile instruments of fear prepared. And Accursius rightly, on Digest 1.12, de iure fisci, interprets servile blows as whips (flagella), as in D. 47.10, de iniuriis vocando, §pen., joined with D. 47.10, §praeterea, de iniuriis, confirms. Petronius called them servile punishments. Sallust, Histories book 1: thinking liberty enough, because the back is spared. See the end of Seneca's Apocolocyntosis.

units.la: V. 25. Filium ]Commemorat & Seneca de Ira lib. 3. P. 8 v. 2. Exinterato.] Ita Mss. Glossa Interata. ιξιντριδίντος voce ab interioribus ducta.
units.tr: V. 25. Filium] Seneca also mentions this in On Anger, book 3, chapter 8, verse 2. Exinterato] So the manuscripts read. The gloss has Interata, from the Greek [ιξιντριδίντος], a word derived from the inner parts.

units.la: V. 13. Iòs conuocato populo.] Frontinus lib. 1. cap. 11.
units.tr: V. 13. Ios, the people being called together] Frontinus, book 1, chapter 11.

units.la: P. 9. v. 1. Matres & Ϙxores.] Plutarchus hbello de virtutibus mulierum.
units.tr: P. 9, v. 1. Matres & Ϙxores] Plutarch, in his book on the virtues of women.

units.la: V. 9. Maxima genti.]Lectionem vulgatam, quam Cuiaci codex & Orofius lib. 1. cap. 19. comprobant, sequutus sum. Veteres enim plerique pro maxima, habent, desumum. Ex voce maxima, solum X. forte remanserat, in eo libro ex quo multi deinde transcripti sunt, ceteris litteris aliquo casu deletis.ea nota librariis imposuit: in Cl. Puteani Ms. legitur ducem.
units.tr: V. 9. Maxima genti] I have followed the common reading, which the codex of Cujacius and Orosius, book 1, chapter 19, confirm. Most of the old copies have desumum instead of maxima. Only the letter X of maxima had perhaps survived in the exemplar from which many copies were later made, the other letters having been lost by some accident. Scribes then put that mark in place. In the manuscript of Puteanus it reads ducem.

units.la: V. 19. Vrbs Barce.] Mss. quidam Vrbs Vero concessa: alii Vero & concessa: alii Baragon cessa. vulgata lectio probari non potest: est enim Barce in Cyrenaica prouincia, vrbs Pentapoleos, quo Persarum arma victricia nondum peruenerant. Herodotus initio lib. 3. Absurdius est Beroea, quomodo Asilanus edidit: est enim oppidum Macedonia, Ptolemæo Βέρροια Ctefias vrbem Croso dono datam Batenè vocat, πόλις μυγάλωτις ExGardar, de qua & Stephanus. P.10.
units.tr: V. 19. Vrbs Barce] Some manuscripts read Vrbs Vero concessa, others Vero & concessa, others Baragon cessa. The common reading cannot be approved. Barce lies in the province of Cyrenaica, a city of the Pentapolis, to which the victorious Persian arms had not yet come; see Herodotus at the beginning of book 3. Beroea, as Asilanus edited it, is more absurd: that is a town of Macedonia, which Ptolemy calls [Βέρροια]. Ctesias calls the city given as a gift to Croesus Batenè, [πόλις μυγάλωτις ExGardar], and Stephanus also speaks of it. P. 10.

units.la: Fuere Lidû.]Herodotus lib. 1. De Gyge, vide & Plutarchi, 1. συμπροσιακῶν.
units.tr: Fuere Lidû] Herodotus, book 1, on Gyges. See also Plutarch, Symposiacs, book 1 [συμπροσιακῶν].

units.la: V.27 Tamyris.]Frontinus lib. 2. & Iornandes & noftrâ vett. omnes conftanter Tamiris, vno excepto, qui habet Tomeris. Orofii Ms. Thameris. Valerii editio poftrema Thamyris Herodoto eft Τόμυρις: aliis τάμυρις, præter Herodotum lib. 1. vide Valer. Max. lib. 9. cap. 10. De Cyri morte diffentit à ceteris Diod. libro 2. in Scytharum hiftoria.
units.tr: V. 27. Tamyris] Frontinus, book 2, Jordanes, and all our old authorities consistently read Tamiris, with one exception, who has Tomeris. The Orosius manuscript has Thameris, and the last edition of Valerius has Thamyris. In Herodotus it is [Τόμυρις]; in others [τάμυρις], apart from Herodotus, book 1. See Valerius Maximus, book 9, chapter 10. On the death of Cyrus, Diodorus, book 2, in his history of the Scythians, disagrees with the others.

units.la: P.11. v.9 Saucios.]Ea eft vetus lectio. Strabo (qui lib. 11, hæc in Sacis gefta fcribit) ἱξοἱνους καὶ ταραχλήγεως. infra lib. 24. mero faucios dicit. quomodo Ennius & Lucretius amore faucios. Inde apud Tibullum percuffus tem.pora Baccho, qui Græcis dicitur οἰνοπλήξ.
units.tr: P. 11, v. 9. Saucios] This is the old reading. Strabo, who in book 11 writes these things as done among the Sacae, has [ἱξοἱνους καὶ ταραχλήγεως]. Later, in book 24, he says mero saucios (wounded with wine), as Ennius and Lucretius say amore saucios (wounded with love). Hence in Tibullus, percussus tempora Baccho (struck in the temples by Bacchus), which in Greek is called [οἰνοπλήξ].

units.la: Plautus Cafina quid eft, nifi hac meraclo Se Vfbiam percuffit flore Liberi?
units.tr: Plautus, Casina: "What is it, unless she has struck herself with this unmixed wine, with the flower of Liber?"

units.la: Ea videtur effe eius loci vera lectio. flos Liberi & Plauto fape & Turpilio apud Nonium, eft vinum.
units.tr: This seems to be the true reading of that passage. In Plautus, who often uses it, and in Turpilius as quoted by Nonius, flos Liberi (the flower of Liber) means wine.

units.la: V.26. Cambyfes.]quæ paucis auctor noftep, ea Herodotus lib. 2 & 3. tractat fulius. Cambyfis frater qui hicin vett. eft Mergis, apud Herodotum eft Σμέρδις, quo nomine etiam magum Oropaften vocat: & Cometes magus qui in editionibus vulgatis dicitur Comaris contra libros, apud eundem Herodotum eft Παναδώρας: & Oftanes, qui vulgo Orthanes, Herodoto dicitur Ὀτάνης: & Darius Hyftaspis filius, in vetë noftris eft Hyptafi: Hæc vt in Herodoto habentur; edidit Aulanus. Sed αἱ τῶν ὀνομάτων μετα- πλάσεις, καὶ μέλιγα τὸν βαρβαρικὸν, ὡσπερ, vt eft apud Strabonem. Et quanta eft inter Trogum & Herodotum varietas; tanta eurlonge etiam maior inter Herodotum & Ctefiam in ipfa hiftoria diffenfio.
units.tr: V. 26. Cambyses] What our author touches on briefly, Herodotus treats at length in books 2 and 3. Cambyses' brother, who in the old copies here is Mergis, is in Herodotus [Σμέρδις], whom he also calls by the name Oropastes the magus. Cometes, the magus who in the common editions is called Comaris (contrary to the manuscripts), is in the same Herodotus [Παναδώρας]. Ostanes, commonly Orthanes, is called [Ὀτάνης] by Herodotus. Darius, son of Hystaspes, is in our old copies Hyptafi. These things stand thus in Herodotus, as Aulanus edited them. But changes of names, and barbarian forms softened [μέλιγα τὸν βαρβαρικὸν], as in Strabo... And as great as the variety is between Trogus and Herodotus, so much greater still is the disagreement between Herodotus and Ctesias in the history itself.

units.la: V.29 ad Ammenis.]Meminit & Plutarch. Alexand & Seneca natur. quæft. 2. cap. 30.
units.tr: V. 29. ad Ammenis] Plutarch, in his Life of Alexander, also mentions this, and Seneca in Natural Questions, book 2, chapter 30.

units.la: P.12.v 4. Gladio fua ffcen:e.]Strabo extr. lib.15. à magis fublatum tradit: ab auctore noftro eft Herod. 3. & Marcellinus libro 17. cuius mihi locus demendo fufpectus eft.
units.tr: P. 12, v. 4. Gladio sua sceneae] Strabo, at the end of book 15, reports that it was taken away by the magi. Our author has it from Herodotus, book 3, and Marcellinus, book 17, whose passage I suspect of having been tampered with.

units.la: V.7 Magus ante famam.]Magi duo fuerunt, vt ex Herodoto conftat, & Orofiolib. 2. cap. 8. apud quem vox duæ quæ quæ est in Ms. deest in impressis. Septem commemorat Valer. lib. 9. cap. 2. & Marcell. 23.
units.tr: V. 7. Magus ante famam] There were two magi, as is clear from Herodotus and from Orosius, book 2, chapter 8, where the word duae (two) found in the manuscript is missing in the printed editions. Valerius Maximus, book 9, chapter 2, and Marcellinus, book 23, mention seven.

units.la: Gobryas medium. Valer. lib. 3. cap. 2. Paullo post fortuna tamen ita regente, malim ita illum regente. Magophoniæ meminit & Agat. 2.
units.tr: Gobryas medium] Valerius Maximus, book 3, chapter 2. A little later, in fortuna tamen ita regente, I would prefer ita illum regente (with fortune thus guiding him). Agathias, book 2, also mentions the Magophonia (the slaughter of the magi).

units.la: V. 7. Principum. dixit pro principum, ut vbique cinitatium, penatium, apium paludium, sapientium, antiquo genitiuo, quem & Pandectæ Fl. & plerique libri vett. agnoscunt. Hominium dixit Salluft. luguth. neq; illi res, neque consilium, aut quisquam hominum fati: placebat: monuit flos delibatus litteratorum Scaliger. Principum pro principum scripsisse Licinium tit. de stupratoribus, docuit me doctor meus lac. Cuiacius, & agreste illud ad prisci conditoris libus robur, fractum moliter plebe tenuatum, convicium seculi, vel conditorum inrogare. Vel principum Leg. fort. & agreste illud ab conditoribus robur. Quod cū indicasset ingenioso & erudito amico meo Ant Arnaldo, subiecit eadem sententia dixisse Horatiū lib. 3. Od. 6; Sed rusticorum mascula multum Proles.
units.tr: V. 7. Principum] He wrote principum for principum, as everywhere cinitatium, penatium, apium, paludium, sapientium, using the old genitive ending in -ium, which the Florentine Pandects and most old books also recognize. Sallust, in the Jugurtha, wrote hominium: "it did not please him, neither the business nor the plan, nor did any of men..." The flower of scholars, Scaliger, pointed this out. That the form principum for principum was written by Licinius in the title on stuprators, my teacher Jacques Cujas taught me. And that rustic robur (strength), broken and softened by the plebs, is a reproach of the age, or to impute it to the founders. Or principum, in the Leges fortunae, and that rustic strength from the founders. When I had pointed this out to my clever and learned friend Antoine Arnauld, he added that Horace expressed the same sentiment in book 3, Ode 6: "But the manly offspring of the rustics, of great strength..."

units.la: P. 14. v. 8. Zophyrus. Græcis Herodoto lib. 3. Plutarch. Apopht. Zopyrus π. ιπ φ. vt lib. 2. Palanthus, qui aliter est Phalanthus. & in prologis Pæni, Phæni dicuntur, sunt enim à Phœnicibus.
units.tr: P. 14, v. 8. Zophyrus] In Herodotus, book 3, and Plutarch's Apophthegms, [Ζώπυρος]. As in book 2, Palanthus, which otherwise is Phalanthus. And in the prologues the Punic and Phoenician peoples are called Paeni and Phaeni, for they are descended from the Phoenicians.
On Book II.

units.la: QVafatis ample. Eadem verba vsurpat & Sallustius, in Catilinario, de Atheniensibus. Scythicum autem Daritibellum, & Herodoto occasionem dedit res Scythicas altius repetendi initio lib. 4.
units.tr: QGreatly shaken. Sallust uses the same words in the Catiline, about the Athenians. Herodotus took his occasion for the Scythian matters, and for tracing them back further at the beginning of book 4, from the Scythian tale of Darius.

units.la: P. 19. v. 2. Scytharum gens antiquissima. Herodotus, ipsos Scythas ait, dicere ... Et de gentis antiquitate, Ægyptios non cū Scythis, sed cum Phrygiis, certasse refert lib. 2. quod confirmat in Eutropium Claudianus. Sed Marcellinus lib. 22. Æ-y ptiam gentem, inquit, omnium Getuftissimam, nisi quod juper antiquitate certat cum Scythis.
units.tr: P. 19, v. 2. The Scythian nation is most ancient. Herodotus says that the Scythians themselves claim this. On the antiquity of the nation, he reports in book 2 that the Egyptians did not contend with the Scythians but with the Phrygians. Claudian confirms this against Eutropius. But Marcellinus, book 22, says: The Egyptian nation, he says, is the most ancient of all, except that it vies with the Scythians in antiquity.

units.la: P. 20. v. 5. Scythiam adeo editorem. Virg. 1 Georg. Mundus ut ad Scythiam, Riphæasque arduus arces Consurgit, premitur Libya denexus in Austros. Sed constat inter Mathematicos, in globo nullum esse alio editiorem locum.
units.tr: P. 20, v. 5. They make Scythia so high. Virgil, Georgics 1: As the world rises high toward Scythia and the Riphaean heights, Libya is pressed down, tied to the south winds. But mathematicians agree that on a globe no place is higher than another.

units.la: V. 8. Ægyptum.] Strato quidam apud Strab. lib. 1. Ægyptum ait, τὸ παλαιὸν ἰωλεσίτης κλύζειος, &c.
units.tr: V. 8. Egypt. Strato, cited by Strabo book 1, says of Egypt: In former times it was [τὸ παλαιὸν ἰωλεσίτης κλύζειος, &c.]

units.la: V. 13. Aggerationibus regum] Inde Titulus Codicis, de Nihil aggeribus non rumpendis. Cicero moles vocat oppositas fluctibus.
units.tr: V. 13. By the mounds of kings. Hence the title of the Code, Concerning not breaking the dykes. Cicero calls such works mounds set against the waves.

units.la: V. 19. Phasi flumine.] Ita legendum etiam contra libros, qui habent Ithasi. De Phasi vide Plinium lib. 6. ca. 4. & Solinum cap. 20. & libellum de fluminibus nomine Plutarchi editum. De Scythis praeter Herodotum lib. 4. vide Diodorum Siculum lib. 2. & Strabonem lib. 7. vbi eorum integritatem multis praedicat: de qua Horatius lib. 3. Ode 24. Vide & pauca apud Marcell: lib. 22. & cōfer quæ lib. 31. de Hunnis scribit & Alanis, quos discurrere, ait latrocinando & venando. ita enim videtur locus ille supplendus.
units.tr: V. 19. By the river Phasis. This must be read so, against the books that have Ithasis. On the Phasis see Pliny book 6, chapter 4, Solinus chapter 20, and the little book on rivers published under Plutarch's name. On the Scythians, besides Herodotus book 4, see Diodorus Siculus book 2 and Strabo book 7, where he extols their integrity at length; Horace speaks of it in Odes 3.24. See also a few points in Marcellinus book 22, and compare what he writes in book 31 about the Huns and Alans, whom he says roam by robbery and hunting. That is how the passage there seems to need to be supplied.

units.la: V. 23. In plaustris ἁμαξοῖσιν. Plaustra autem ait coriis tecta, pro quo Marcellinus lib 22. habet corticibus, nescio an recte.
units.tr: V. 23. In wagons [ἁμαξοῖσιν]. He says the wagons were covered with hides. Marcellinus, book 22, has bark in place of this; I do not know whether rightly.

units.la: V. 25. Iustitia gentis ingenii.] δικαιοσύνη ἀνθρώπων. Homero, Strabo, & Arrianus lib. 4. Ideo infra lib. 12. gentem innoxiam dicit. Ingenium vocat quod paulo post natura ram. Naevius - Vbi Ingenio arbustla nata sunt, non obsita.
units.tr: V. 25. The justice of the people's nature. [δικαιοσύνη ἀνθρώπων.] Strabo and Arrian book 4 say this of Homer. Hence below, book 12, he calls the nation harmless. He calls it nature (ingenium), which a little later he calls natural disposition. Naevius: Where the shrubs have grown up in their own nature, unplanted.

units.la: Notavit ad Ausonium Scaliger. Petronius. Crines ingenio suo flexi. Tacitus. cū honestα suopte ingenio peterētur. alii.
units.tr: Scaliger noted this on Ausonius. Petronius: Hair curled by its own nature. Tacitus: when an honourable thing was sought by its own nature. And others.

units.la: V. 29. Non perinde.] Ita vett. omnes. Tacitus de Germanis: Possessione, inquit, & ipsa haut perinde afficiuntur. V. 30. Lacte.] Inde Homero Γαλακτοφάγοι. Strabo lib. 7. & 11. addit carne, & caseo, equino maxime.
units.tr: V. 29. Not in the same way. All the old copies read so. Tacitus on the Germans: They are not affected by possession in the same way, he says. V. 30. Milk. Hence Homer's milk-drinkers [Γαλακτοφάγοι]. Strabo, books 7 and 11, adds meat and cheese, especially of horses.

units.la: V. 32. Pellibus tamen.] malim tantum. Pelles Nomadicas merces commemorat Strabo lib. 11. de Hunnis Marcellinus indumentis, inquit operiuntur lintels, vel ex pellibus filiostrium murium consarcinatis.
units.tr: V. 32. Yet only with skins. I would prefer only. Strabo book 11 mentions skins as the nomads' goods. Of the Huns, Marcellinus says: They are covered with clothing, he says, linen, or with skins of field mice sewn together.

units.la: P. 21. v. 22. Vexoris.] Ita boni libri, alii Vixoris, quidam Befoxis: Orosius Ms. lib. 1. cap. 14. Vefoges. Florentina editio hoc loco & initio libri primi, (supposuit Sefoftres, contra libros: opinor, quia Herodotus lib. 2. refert eum, Scythas subegisse. Iornandi est Vefofis.
units.tr: P. 21, v. 22. Vexoris. So the good books; others have Vixoris, and some Befoxis. Orosius, manuscript, book 1, chapter 14, has Vefoges. The Florentine edition here and at the beginning of book 1 has put Sesostris, against the books, I suppose because Herodotus book 2 relates that he subdued the Scythians. Jornandes has Vesofis.

units.la: V. 23 Primo lenonibus.] Hanc vocem omnes, præter Vetetes agnoscunt: & probat P. Daniclis Ms. Glossarius. Leno, id est, mediator, inquit, qui apud Italos dicitur Ambassator, Unde Trogus Pompeium in secundo historiarum, Pramissis lenonibus, qui hostibus parcendi legem indicerent.
units.tr: V. 23. First, the pimps. All read this word except Vetetes, and the manuscript glossary of P. Daniel confirms it. Leno, that is, mediator, it says, what is called an ambassador among the Italians. Hence Trogus, in the second book of his histories, about Pompey: With the go-betweens sent ahead, who would announce a law of sparing the enemy.

units.la: V. 26. Stolide aduersum.] Ms. colendi. Vnus italide, quod ad vulgatam lectionem proxime accedit, quam sequutus est Orosius. Hic locus explicat quod Scythicus legatus apud Curtium Rufum lib. 7. air, suis patuisse iter ad Ægyptum.
units.tr: V. 26. Foolishly against. A manuscript reads colendi. One reads italide, which comes closest to the common reading, the one Orosius followed. This passage explains what the Scythian envoy in Curtius Rufus, book 7, says, that his route to Egypt lay open.

units.la: P. 22. v. 11. Duo regii iuuenes.] Totum hunc locum confer cum Orosii capite 15. libri primi. Et de Amazonibus quædam Herodotus 4. Multa Diodorus lib. 2. & Strabo lib. 11. qui hæc fabulosa iudicat. Vide & Ammianum lib. 15, 22 & Eustathium in Dionysium, & Stephanum in Ἔφεσος.
units.tr: P. 22, v. 11. Two royal youths. Compare this whole passage with Orosius book 1, chapter 15. On the Amazons, Herodotus book 4 says some things, Diodorus book 2 and Strabo book 11 say many, and Strabo judges them fabulous. See also Ammianus book 15, Eustathius on Dionysius, and Stephanus under Ephesus.

units.la: V. 14. Cappadocia orn.] Orosius Cappadocia Pontica ora. Legendum ex Ms. Ponticæ.
units.tr: V. 14. Cappadocian shore. Orosius has the Pontic shore of Cappadocia. It should be read Pontic, from the manuscript.

units.la: V. 25. Viros q. d r. interficiunt.] Inde Ἀιόρνατα dicta; id est, ἀνδροκτόνοι. Herod.
units.tr: V. 25. They kill men. Hence they were called Aiornata, that is, [ἀνδροκτόνοι], man-slayers. Herodotus.

units.la: P. 23. v. 3. Genitas fe Marte.] De vna tantum id narrat Diodorus, cuius nomen non exprimit: & Apollonius 2. Amazonas, Martis & Harmoniæ Naiadis, genus esse tradit. Quæ hic Marthesia dicitur, eam lornandes Marpe siam vocat.
units.tr: P. 23, v. 3. Born of Mars. Diodorus says this of one woman only, whose name he does not give. Apollonius says the Amazons were the offspring of Mars and a Naiad of Harmonia. The woman here called Marthesia is called Marpesia by Jornandes.

units.la: V. 13, xii. Stipendia.] De duodecim certaminibus, quæ tamquam stipendia, Eurystheo debebat Hercules, vt immortalitatem consequeretur, legendæ fabulæ, & Diodorus lib. 4. Amazonum regina, Orithya est, in omnibus scriptis libris, & in preflis quibusdam: Vulgo Orrera: & apud Apollonium lib. 2.
units.tr: V. 13, xii. Service. On the twelve labours, which Hercules owed to Eurystheus as service in order to win immortality, the fables should be read; also Diodorus book 4. The Amazon queen is Orithyia in all written books and in some printed ones; commonly Orrera; and in Apollonius book 2:
[Queens of the Amazons, Orithyia and Antiope.]

units.la: Sed in hac historia mire variant auctores. Vide Plutarchum in Theseo, & Diodorum libro 2. & 4. Paufaniam Atticis.
units.tr: But the authors vary wildly in this story. See Plutarch in Theseus, Diodorus books 2 and 4, and Pausanias in Attica.

units.la: P. 24. v. 21. Scythæ autem.] Vide Herodotum initio 4. qui non octo annos, sed viginti octo, domo absuisse Scythas
units.tr: P. 24, v. 21. But the Scythians. See Herodotus at the beginning of book 4, who says the Scythians were away from home not eight years but twenty-eight. This is certainly more probable; yet here, against the agreement of the books, I change nothing.

units.la: Nota: the marginal numerals 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35 and 40 run down the text column as line references. thas narrat, quod sane probabilius est: hic tamen contra consensum librorum nihil muto.
units.tr: ...thas narrates, which is certainly more probable: here, however, against the consensus of the books, I change nothing.

units.la: Ita Mss. Herod. οἱ δὲ ἱκ πλαγίῳ-πες.
units.tr: So the manuscripts of Herodotus: [οἱ δὲ ἐκ πλαγίῳ-πες].

units.la: Ea est sex Mss. constans lectio. Hunc regem Orosius lib. 2. cap. 8. vocat Attyrum. Ms. Accirum. Herodotus 4. Γ'νδαθύρσων: qui & Σκώ-παι, & Ταξάκιι duarum aliarum Scythiae partium reges, commemorat. Ctesiae Σκυδάρης dicitur. Antriregyrus dicitur Iornandi.
units.tr: This is the reading that is constant in six manuscripts. Orosius book 2, chapter 8, calls this king Attyrus; one manuscript has Accirus. Herodotus book 4 has [Γνδαθύρσων], and also mentions the kings of the two other parts of Scythia, [Σκώπαι] and [Ταξάκιι]. In Ctesias he is called [Σκυδάρης]. Jornandes calls him Antriregyrus.
V. 16. The Ionians also. Herodotus book 6, at the beginning.

units.la: V.28. Innati solo. Indigena, αὐτόχθονες, γηγενεῖς, terrigenis patribus. Ausonius in ordine nobilium Vrbium; M. Cicero pro Flacco.
units.tr: V. 28. Born of the soil. Native, [αὐτόχθονες], [γηγενεῖς], earth-born fathers. Ausonius in his list of noble cities; Cicero, Pro Flacco.

units.la: V. 29. Primi. de Atheniensium inventis Lucretius lib. 6. Aelianus lib. 3. M. Cicero pro Flacco.
units.tr: V. 29. The first. On the inventions of the Athenians, Lucretius book 6, Aelian book 3, and Cicero, Pro Flacco.

units.la: V.33. Regem habuere. De statu & mutationibus Reip. Athenien-sium, multa paucis Strabo lib. 9. Vide & quae Paterculus lib 1. Primum regem fuerunt Cecropem: Alii Actaeum sive Actaeonem αὐτόχθονα. Paus anias Atticis, Eusthatius in Dionysium, alii. De variis appellationibus Atheniensium praeteriam citatos, vide Herodotum Vrania.
units.tr: V. 33. They had a king. On the condition and changes of the Athenian state, Strabo book 9 says much in little. See also what Paterculus book 1 says. Some say the first king was Cecrops; others Actaeus or Actaeon, [αὐτόχθων]. Pausanias in Attica, Eustathius on Dionysius, and others. On the various names of the Athenians, I pass over the authors cited; see Herodotus in Urania.

units.la: Biformem] Δι. Φυγ. Eusebius & Hieronymus in Chronicis. Plutarchus de sera numinis vind. Eusthatius in Dionys. Vide & Diodorum libro 1. de Pete Mnesthei patre.
units.tr: Biform. [Δι. Φυγ.] Eusebius and Jerome in the Chronicles. Plutarch, On the Delay of Divine Vengeance. Eustathius on Dionysius. See also Diodorus book 1, on Pete, the father of Menestheus.

units.la: V.4. Amphictyon. Vett. Amphictyonides, vulgo Amphiryon: & ita Orosius Ms. lib.1.cap.9. Verum nomen ex Paulania restituit. Et Fabricius in Orosio & Iustino. Et ex Mss. emendanda est editio Chronicorum Eusebii, quae Amphitryonem quintum Athenien-sium regem facit,quod fit Amphictyon 3. Athen. Errori causam praebuit Amphitruo Thebanorum rex, vulgo notior Amphictyone. De tempore diluuii Deucalionis discrepat ab auctore nostro Varro & Eusebius, quod notauit Augustinus lib. 18. de ciuit. Dei, cap. 10.
units.tr: V. 4. Amphictyon. The old copies have Amphictyonides; the common reading is Amphiryon, and so Orosius, manuscript, book 1, chapter 9. The true name is restored from Pausanias, and Fabricius in Orosius and Justin agrees. The edition of Eusebius's Chronicle, which makes Amphitryon the fifth king of the Athenians, must be corrected from the manuscripts, so that it reads Amphictyon, third king of Athens. The cause of the error was Amphitryon, king of the Thebans, better known than Amphictyon. On the time of Deucalion's flood, Varro and Eusebius disagree with our author, as Augustine noted in The City of God, book 18, chapter 10.
V. 7. Greece of the peoples. Orosius has Thessaly.

units.la: V 11. Erechtheum. Vett. in hoc nomine variè corrupti sunt. Ab hoc rege Homerus Iliad. 2. Athenienses vocat
units.tr: V. 11. Erechtheus. The old copies are variously corrupted in this name. Homer, Iliad 2, calls the Athenians after this king:

units.la: Δήμος Ἐρεχθεύς. Hic à Paufania, Eusebio, quem Augustinus ca 11.lib.18. de ciu.Dei sequitur, dicitur Erisichthonius. Quod hic ait per ordinem successionis, repugnat Paufanias Atticis, quem vide, & Diod. lib.1. qui eum ait Ægyptium fuisse.
units.tr: [The people of Erechtheus.] Pausanias and Eusebius, whom Augustine follows in The City of God, book 18, chapter 11, call him Erisichthonius. What he says here, by order of succession, is contradicted by Pausanias in Attica, which see, and by Diodorus book 1, who says he was an Egyptian.
V. 16. Medo. See book 4, 2. The good books have Medio.

units.la: V. 18. Demophoon qui auxilium. Hic variat historia. Mnesthei Atheniensium regis anno 18. captam Troiam auctore Eusebius: & Homerus in catalogo navium, & Diod. lib 1. eundem faciunt Atheniensium ducem. Collocatur autem inter Thefeum & Demophoentem.
units.tr: V. 18. Demophoon qui auxilium. Here the history varies. Eusebius, in the eighteenth year of the Athenian king Mnestheus, places the capture of Troy. Homer in the catalogue of ships, and Diodorus book 1, make the same man leader of the Athenians. He is placed between Theseus and Demophon.

units.la: V. 20. Dorienses. Herodotus lib. 5. Vide & Valerium lib.7.cap.6. & Augustinum lib.18. cap.18. de ciuitate Dei. Paufanias Atticis & Achaicis, Orofius lib.1. cap. 18. Peloponnenses vocant, & Eusebius in Chronicis: Velleius Paterculus lib.1. Lacedæmonios, quæ eadem sunt. Fuit autem Codrus Melanthi exsulis filius. Plutarchus de exilio. Strabo lib. 9. Hunc locum transcripsit Saresb. Polica.lib.4 cap.3.
units.tr: V. 20. Dorienses. Herodotus book 5. See also Valerius book 7, chapter 6, and Augustine, On the City of God, book 18, chapter 18. Pausanias in the Attica and Achaica, and Orosius book 1, chapter 18, call them Peloponnesians; Eusebius in the Chronicles, and Velleius Paterculus book 1, call them Lacedaemonians, which is the same thing. Codrus was the son of Melanthus, an exile. Plutarch, On Exile. Strabo book 9. Saresberiensis, Policraticus book 4, chapter 3, copied this passage.

units.la: P.27.v.2. Annuis magistratibus. Paterc. & Eusceb. post mortem Codri principes aiunt constitutos, quos mors finiebat: Multis autem post annis constitutos annuos magistratus.
units.tr: P.27.v.2. Annuis magistratibus. Paterculus and Eusebius say that after the death of Codrus rulers were appointed who held office only until they died. But many years later annual magistrates were appointed.

units.la: V.3. Nulla leges. ex Plutarchi Solone, & aliis notum Draconis legibus Atheniensis vsos ante Solonem. Vide Gell. lib 11 cap.18.
units.tr: V.3. Nulla leges. From Plutarch's Solon and others it is known that the Athenians used the laws of Draco before Solon. See Gellius book 11, chapter 18.

units.la: V.5 Tanto temperamento. Dicere enim solebat, τὸ ἴσον πολλῶν ἢ πολέων. Vide Plutarchum, & Laertium. De Solonis legibus præter ceteros, vide & Herodotū lib.1. Emendandus Ammianus lib.16. ex rhetoris Lycurgi, id est, Axonibus. Leg. & Axonibus, vt Rhetræ Lycurgi, ita Axones Solonis, Plutarch.
units.tr: V.5. Tanto temperamento. For he used to say, τὸ ἴσον πολλῶν ἢ πολέων [equality among many rather than among a few]. See Plutarch and Diogenes Laertius. On the laws of Solon, above all others, see also Herodotus book 1. Ammianus book 16 must be corrected from the orator Lycurgus, that is, from the Axones. Read "and Axones", just as "Rhetrae" belongs to Lycurgus, so "Axones" belongs to Solon, Plutarch.

units.la: V.12 Capital. Θεανάτῳ ζημίᾳ Plutarch. Festi mutilator Paulus. Capital facinus, quod capitis pœna luitur. Ea est plerisque locis apud bonos auctores vetetum librorum scriptura.
units.tr: V.12 Capital. Θανάτῳ ζημίᾳ [penalty of death], Plutarch. Festus's abridger Paulus: capital facinus, quod capitis poena luitur [a capital crime, which is expiated by the penalty of the head]. This is the spelling of older books in most places among good authors.

units.la: V.15. Dementiam. in primis versutum & callidum factum Solonis vocat M. Cicero t de Officio. Versus eius, vide apud Laertium. Totam historiam quaere apud Plutarchum memoriter & Paufanias in Atticis, & Ælianus fine libri 7. Vbi interpres δύο τινὰ μισθοφόρων ἀγαθὰς. male vertit,captis duobus templis,cum fit,Duabus Megarensium nauibus poticus. Vide etiam Frontinum lib. 4. cap, vlt. Controuerfiam de Salamina infula exponit Strabo lib.9.vbi de Megara.
units.tr: V.15. Dementiam. M. Cicero, On Duties, calls this the most crafty and cunning act of Solon. For his verses, see Diogenes Laertius. Look up the whole story in Plutarch, from memory, and Pausanias in the Attica, and Aelian at the end of book 7. Where the translator renders δύο τινὰ μισθοφόρων ἀγαθὰς [two mercenary ships of good quality] badly as "captis duobus templis" [two temples having been taken], since it is "Duabus Megarensium navibus" [with two ships of the Megarians]. See also Frontinus book 4, last chapter. Strabo book 9, where he treats Megara, sets out the dispute about the island of Salamis.

units.la: P.23.v.2. Ita Megarenses.] Vett.omnes Dorenses.inepte &ἀνισοφητως,irrepfit forte ex fiperioribus.
units.tr: P.23.v.2. Ita Megarenses.] All the older copies have "Dorenses", foolishly and ἀνισοφήτως [without consistency]; it perhaps crept in from the lines above.

units.la: V.3. Pififtratus. ] Praeter Plurarchum & Herodotum lib.1. lege Valerium lib.1. cap.3. & lib.8. cap.9 Ælianum lib. 8. Qui autem ratione Pififtratidatum tyrannide liberati fiunt Athenienses docet Herodotus 5. & Paufanias Laconicis.
units.tr: V.3. Pisistratus.] Besides Plutarch and Herodotus book 1, read Valerius book 1, chapter 3, and book 8, chapter 9, and Aelian book 8. Herodotus book 5 and Pausanias in the Laconica show how the Athenians were freed from the tyranny of the Pisistratids by a plan.

units.la: V.28. Auxilium a Lacedaemoniis.] Per Φιλαξιδλω,ἠμετ-ρόφορος. Herodot.lib.6. Probus in Milriade. Meminit & Plato 3. de Leg. De quattridui religione, Lycurgi legem commemorat, Lucianus de Astrologia. Vide & Strabonem libro 9. Confet cum auctore noftro Orofium cap. 8. libro 2.
units.tr: V.28. Auxilium a Lacedaemoniis.] Through Φιλαξίδλω, ἠμετρόφορος [unclear Greek as printed]. Herodotus book 6. Probus, in the Life of Miltiades. Plato also mentions it, in book 3 of the Laws. Concerning the religion of the fourth day, he recalls a law of Lycurgus; Lucian, On Astrology. See also Strabo book 9. Compare our author with Orosius, book 2, chapter 8.

units.la: P.29.v.1.Dux belli.] Στρατηγὸς, vnus è decè. Πολέμαρχος Ο-antem erat Καλλικράτης Ο· Αφιδράτης Ο· Herodotus & Paufanias.
units.tr: P.29.v.1. Dux belli.] Στρατηγὸς [general], one of ten. Polemarch was Callicrates, and Aphidrates [as printed]. Herodotus and Pausanias.

units.la: V.14. Cynagiri.] De quo praeter Herodotum Valerius lib 3.cap.2. & Ammianus lib. 26. qui eum & Callimachus vocat Medicorum bellorum fulmina.
units.tr: V.14. Cynagiri.] On him, besides Herodotus, see Valerius book 3, chapter 2, and Ammianus book 26, who, like Callimachus, calls him "the thunderbolt of the Median wars".

units.la: V.24 Duscenta millia.]Herodotus è barbaris ἐξακοσίους ... ex Athenienfibus vero centum nonaginta duo cecidiffe auctor eft.
units.tr: V.24 Ducenta millia.] Herodotus says that of the barbarians 600,000 fell, but of the Athenians only 192.
V.25. Hippias.] M. Cicero, book 9, To Atticus, letter 12.

units.la: V.26. Concitor.] quidam conditor, vulgo concitator, & initio lib.3. fed illud Mss. approbantibus malo. Tacit. 4. Annal. miffosq, in Galliam concitores belli.
units.tr: V.26. Concitor.] Some read conditor, commonly concitator, and at the beginning of book 3; but I prefer that reading, with the approval of the manuscripts. Tacitus, Annals 4: "sent instigators of war into Gaul" [missosque in Galliam concitores belli].

units.la: V.30. Artemenes.) Herod.lib 7.A'προζαζίλω vocat.& hanc controuerfiam viuo patre motam,& ab ipfo Dario iudicatam effe refert. Idem paulo poft Achaemenem nominat Darii filium Xerxis frarrem. Plutarchus in Artaxerxe,ab Atfica,qui poftea Artaxerxes dictus eft,& Cyto eandem quaestionem tenouatam fcribit,& Darii contrariam huic fententiam commemorat.
units.tr: V.30. Artemenes.] Herodotus book 7 calls him Ἀρτοζάζιλω [as printed], and reports that this dispute was raised while his father was alive and was judged by Darius himself. The same author shortly afterwards names Achaemenes, son of Darius, brother of Xerxes. Plutarch, in the life of Artaxerxes, writes that the same question was renewed by Atossa and Cyrus, and records Darius's opinion contrary to this one.

units.la: P.30.v.14. Artafernem.) Ita ex Herod. emendani. Vett. habent Ariafernem, facili lapfu. Vni fupra fcriptum legendum effe Tisapherneм.
units.tr: P.30.v.14. Artafernem.] Corrected thus from Herodotus. The older copies have "Ariafernem" by an easy slip. Above one of them is written that we should read "Tisapherne".

units.la: V.14. Quinquennium instruxit. ]Vulgo, per quinquennium, & Orosius lib. 2. cap. 9. sed antiqua scriptura recta est. Infra lib. 12. Triduum luctum indixit. Lege 12. Tabul. Vsus, auctoritas fundi, biennium esto. Quintilianus declamatione 196 Ex lege, in exsilium quinquennium missus est. Notauit Iac. Cuiacius cum interpretaretur titulum Cod. de vsucap. pro emptore, vel pro transfacto.
units.tr: V.14. Quinquennium instruxit.] Commonly per quinquennium, and Orosius book 2, chapter 9; but the old reading is correct. Later, in book 12: Triduum luctum indixit. Read the Twelve Tables: Usus, auctoritas fundi, biennium esto. Quintilian, declamation 196: Ex lege, in exsilium quinquennium missus est. Jacques Cujas noted this while interpreting the title of the Code, On Usucaption, for a buyer or a transferee.

units.la: V.15. Demaratus ] Herodotus fine lib. 7. fugam eius ad Persas lib. 6. explicat.
units.tr: V.15. Demaratus.] Herodotus, at the end of book 7, explains his flight to the Persians in book 6.

units.la: P.31.v.3 Soror reg. Leonidæ.]Herodoto est vxor Leonidæ Γοργὼ, cuius meminit Plutarchus in Apophth. Laconi.
units.tr: P.31.v.3. Soror reg. Leonidae.] In Herodotus, the wife of Leonidas is Gorgo [Γοργὼ], whom Plutarch mentions in the Sayings of the Spartans.

units.la: V.5. Iam Xerxes septingenta ] Variant in numero auctores. Herod. lib. 7. Diod. 11. Isocrates Panathenaico. & Plin. lib. 33. cap. 10. Quomodo autem exercitum Xerxes dinumerauerit, vide Herod. & Plin. l. 4. cap. 11.
units.tr: V.5. Iam Xerxes septingenta.] The authors differ on the number. Herodotus book 7, Diodorus 11, Isocrates in the Panathenaicus, and Pliny book 33, chapter 10. For how Xerxes counted his army, see Herodotus and Pliny book 4, chapter 11.

units.la: V.6. Vt non immerito praeditum.]Herodotus enumeratis copiis. ... inquit, ... tà ἐπιθέσεσ, &c.
units.tr: V.6. Ut non immerito praeditum.] Herodotus, having listed the forces, says: "...", tà ἐπιθέσεσ [as printed], etc.

units.la: V. 8. Naues decies. ] Nauium numeros in veteribus omnibus depravatus. Arbitror legendum mille ducentas: litteris quibusdam immutatis, & vocibus inuersis: Convenit numerus cum Herodoto, Diodoro, Probo, Isocrate, Orosio, qui tamen onerariarum, sive τεσσαρᾶ, addunt tria millia, & ἐπτακόσιαι, octingentas & quinquaginta. Vt ille superior numerus fit trite mium, seu rostratorum, vt Orosius vocat.
units.tr: V. 8. Naves decies.] The number of ships is corrupt in all the old copies. I think we should read mille ducentas [1,200], with some letters changed and words transposed. The number agrees with Herodotus, Diodorus, Probus, Isocrates and Orosius, who add to the transport ships, or τεσσαρᾶ [as printed], three thousand, and ἑπτακόσιαι [seven hundred], eight hundred and fifty. So that the higher number is of triremes, or beaked ships, as Orosius calls them.

units.la: V.22. Leonida. ]Lege praeter Herodotum & Diodorum, & Orosium, Strabonem lib. 9. Ælianum lib. 3. Valerium lib. 3. cap. 2 & Paulanian Laconicis. meminit & Seneca epist. lib. 13. Vide & Ctesiae excerpta; variat hic multum a ceteris.
units.tr: V.22. Leonida.] Read, besides Herodotus, Diodorus and Orosius, Strabo book 9, Aelian book 3, Valerius book 3, chapter 2, and Pausanias in the Laconica. Seneca also mentions it, Letters book 13. See also the excerpts of Ctesias; he differs here a great deal from the others.

units.la: P 32.v.17 Sexcenti Giri]Quingentos habet Diodorus, quem in hac narratione fere expressisse auctor noster videtur. M Cicero 2 de finibus trecentos, & Seneca in Suasoriis, & Ælianus: cuius interpres τριακοσίους imperite vertit triginta.
units.tr: P 32.v.17 Sexcenti Greci.] Diodorus has five hundred, which our author seems to have mostly followed in this account. M. Cicero, On Ends book 2, has three hundred, and Seneca in the Suasoriae, and Aelian, whose translator wrongly renders τριακοσίους [three hundred] as "triginta" [thirty].
V.18. Praetorium.] Diodorus: τὴν τοῦ βασιλέως σκηνήν [the king's tent].

units.la: V.25. Tarter d ei]Ms. die antique pro diei. Sallust. Iugurt. Vix decima partedie reliqua. vide quæ notat Aulus GelGellius lib. 9. cap. 14. quæ Prifcianus lib. 7. exprima historia Sa!luftii, & quæ Probus in Catholicis.
units.tr: V.25. Tarter die.] A manuscript has the old form die for diei. Sallust, Jugurtha: Vix decima parte diei reliqua [with scarcely a tenth part of the day left]. See what Aulus Gellius notes in book 9, chapter 14; and what Priscian in book 7 says from the history of Sallust, and what Probus says in the Catholica.

units.la: V.30. Ionas] Herod.lib.8. Plutarch.in Themist. Ortos autem Ionas ab Atheniensibus notum ex Herod. lib.1. & aliis.
units.tr: V.30. Ionas.] Herodotus book 8; Plutarch in the Life of Themistocles. That the Ionians were descended from the Athenians is known from Herodotus book 1 and others.

units.la: V.33.Symbolos.] Symbolum & Symbola, & Symbolae dicunt Latini, Plautus Pseud. Sc.1. & Bacchid. Sc.sbo sn Piraeum. Ms. vnus hoc loco habet Symbolas, quomodo & Plautus sæpe.
units.tr: V.33. Symbolos.] The Latins say symbolum, symbola and symbolae; Plautus, Pseudolus scene 1, and Bacchides scene 3: ...ibo in Piraeum [as printed]. One manuscript here has Symbolas, as Plautus often does.
P.33.v.3. An ideo,] An old poet.
Men' servasse, si essent qui me perderent?

units.la: V.9. Cessim.] Ita recte libri vetetes. Varro apud Non.
units.tr: V.9. Cessim.] So rightly the older books. Varro, in Nonius.

units.la: Vereor ne me quoque,cum domum ab Iilo
units.tr: Vereor ne me quoque, cum domum ab illo
I'll slip back home quietly; let no one recognise me except the dog.

units.la: L. fi ex plagis s2. D.ad leg. Aquil. eadem ratione Plautus Cafina.
units.tr: L. si ex plagis 52 D. ad leg. Aquil.; in the same way Plautus, Casina.
Recessim cedam ad parietem.

units.la: V.9. Ante nauali] Hæc vide apud Herodot. Plutarc. Diodorum, Æmilium Probum, Orofium lib. 2. cap.10.
units.tr: V.9. Ante navali.] See these matters in Herodotus, Plutarch, Diodorus, Aemilius Probus, and Orosius book 2, chapter 10.

units.la: apud quem initio capitis, vox, ʃʃ, abest à Ms. & sane inducenda est.
units.tr: to which, at the beginning of the chapter, the word ʃʃ is absent from a manuscript; and it certainly should be added.

units.la: V. 23. Themistocles nauium præfi lium, M. Cicero ad Att. epist. 7. consilium Themistoclcum. Fronlib.1.c.3. Aristotel. 1. Rhet.
units.tr: V. 23. Themistocles navium praefectus.] M. Cicero, To Atticus, letter 7: "the plan of Themistocles". Frontinus book 1, chapter 3. Aristotle, Rhetoric book 1.
P.34.v.4. Per servum.] Frontinus book 1, chapter 2.

units.la: V.11. Artemisia.] Ἀρτεμισίᾳ. Herod. lib. 7. & 8. Pausa. Lacoinicis. Vnus è manuscriptis Artemidora scriptum habet,quomodo & Orofius.
units.tr: V.11. Artemisia.] Ἀρτεμισίᾳ [as printed]. Herodotus books 7 and 8. Pausanias in the Laconica. One of the manuscripts has "Artemidora", as does Orosius.
V.20 Multa millia.] Two hundred, says Diodorus.
P.35.v.2. Themistocles timens.] Frontinus book 2, chapter 6.

units.la: V.6. Eundem seruum.] Sicinnum nomine, Herod. At Diod.ait fuisse pædagogum filiorum ipsius:ad instituendos liberos,vtebantur seruorum operâ veteres.Plutarch. Aristide Arnacem vocat Eunuchum.
units.tr: V.6. Eundem servum.] Named Sicinnus, in Herodotus. But Diodorus says he was the tutor of his sons: the ancients used slaves' labour for teaching children. Plutarch, in the Life of Aristides, calls Artabanus a eunuch.

units.la: V.24.Olynthum.] Artabazo, non Mardonio id tribuit Herodotus.
units.tr: V.24. Olynthum.] Herodotus attributes this to Artabazus, not to Mardonius.

units.la: V.25. Athenienses quoque.] Herodot. sine libri 8. & Diod.
units.tr: V.25. Athenienses quoque.] Herodotus, at the end of book 8, and Diodorus.

units.la: V.32. Vitus Mardonius.] Hæc est memorabilis illa Græcorum apud Platæas victoria, de qua Herodotus 9. Z Diod. 11. Plutarch. Ariftide, Æmilius Probus Ariftide & Paufania,quos vide,& Ælian.lib.11. & Strab.lib.9.& Paufan. Laconicis & Bœoticis. Interfeƈtum eo prœlio Mardonium præter Ctefiam fcribunt omnes: hunc fequitur auctor nofter.
units.tr: V.32. Vitus Mardonius.] This is the famous Greek victory at Plataea, of which Herodotus book 9, Diodorus book 11, Plutarch in the Life of Aristides, Aemilius Probus in the Lives of Aristides and Pausanias, whom see, and Aelian book 11, and Strabo book 9, and Pausanias in the Laconica and Boeotica, all write. Apart from Ctesias, all write that Mardonius was killed in that battle; our author follows them.

units.la: P.36. v.3 Mycale.)Libri fcripti hoc loco omnes deprauate legûnt M-sia,alii Mofia, alii aliter. Vulgatam lectionem contra libros retinui ex Herodoto & Diodoro. Est autem Mycale mons Ioniæ & vrbs, Stephano. Famæ velocitatem, de qua auctor nofter, tedarguit Diodorus: ait enim rumorem istum sparsum à Leotychida ϲφέϲόω. Vide Plutarch. in Æmilio. Et hic, vt & Diodorus notauit,deficit H:rodoti historia.
units.tr: P.36. v.3 Mycale.) All the manuscripts read this place name corruptly, some as "M-sia", others as "Mofia", and others differently. Against the manuscripts I have kept the common reading, following Herodotus and Diodorus. Mycale is a mountain and a town of Ionia, according to Stephanus. Diodorus refutes our author on the speed of the rumour, for he says that the rumour was spread by Leotychidas at [ϲφέϲόω]. See Plutarch in the Life of Aemilius. And here, as Diodorus also noted, the history of Herodotus breaks off.

units.la: V.16. Cum mania.) Præter Diodorum, vide Thucydidem lib.1. & Frontinum lib.1.cap.1. Meminit & Paufanias initio lib. 1.
units.tr: V.16. Cum moenia.) Besides Diodorus, see Thucydides book 1 and Frontinus book 1, chapter 1. Pausanias also mentions it at the beginning of book 1.

units.la: P.37.v.11. Dixcem.) Naυαρχων constituerunt.Diod.Thucyd.lib 1.Probus quos lege.
units.tr: P.37. v.11. Ducem.) They appointed [ναυάρχων] (admirals). See Diodorus and Thucydides book 1, and Probus, whom you should read.

units.la: V.16. Nuntios.) Libri veteres optimi alii pontios,alii pe-tios,barbaram vocem Iustini ꝛcatè vsitatam,quis fortasse sufpicetur: nihil mutare aufus fum, quum vulgata lectio duobus Mss. confirmetur,non tamen antiquissimis.
units.tr: V.16. Nuntios.) The best old books variously read "pontios" and "petios", a barbarous word which Justin commonly uses, as someone might perhaps suspect. I have not dared to change anything, since the common reading is confirmed by two manuscripts, though not by the most ancient ones.

units.la: V. 23. Cimonem. ) Cuius vitam,vide apud Plutarchum & Probum,de eo & Herodotus extremo lib. 6. Valer. lib. 5.cap.3.
units.tr: V.23. Cimonem.) For his life, see Plutarch and Probus. Herodotus also speaks of him at the end of book 6. See Valerius Maximus book 5, chapter 3.

units.la: V.30. Xerxem ) Ad Eurymedontem, ἀστρ ἀλλὰ τὰς ἀ-νοσ μίκρα μὴ δύο καθηρρικὰς ἀφιρόμενα. Plutarch. vide & Thucyd. lib.1. & Diod.11.
units.tr: V.30. Xerxem.) Concerning Eurymedon: [ἀστρ ἀλλὰ τὰς ἀνοσ μίκρα μὴ δύο καθηρρικὰς ἀφιρόμενα]. See Plutarch, and also Thucydides book 1 and Diodorus book 11.
On Book III.

units.la: Vippe Artabanus.)Legendus Diodor.lib.11. & Ctefias, & Probus, qui hic Bacabafus, illis Megabyzus dicitur. Artabanus autem Aristeleli 5. de republica , est Αγεταμάνης.
units.tr: Vippe Artabanus.) Diodorus, book 11, and Ctesias should be read here, and Probus, who calls this man Bacabasus, whereas those others call him Megabyzus. Aristotle, in book 5 of the Politics, calls Artabanus Agetamanes [Αγεταμάνης].

units.la: P.42.v.15 Et eadem patris.) τὸν φονίᾳ τὴν παρεὸς. Diod. nam illa,& necem fratru;absunt à vett.
units.tr: P.42.v.15 And of the same father.) [τὸν φόνον τὴν παρα...] Diodorus. For the words about the murder of the brothers are absent from the older texts.

units.la: V. 28. Lycurgus. ) De quo in eius vita Plutarchus & Herodotus libro primo, & Strabo libro 10. & Paufanias Lacon.
units.tr: V.28. Lycurgus.) On him see Plutarch in his Life, Herodotus book 1, Strabo book 10, and Pausanias, Laconica.

units.la: V.18. Polybita.) Ita Vett. Graeci Πολυδίζτης. At Charillus quomodo & Heraclides, illis est Charilaus. Herodoto Ἀισωδῶτης.
units.tr: V.18. Polybita.) The older Greek writers have Polydectes [Πολυδέκτης]. But Charillus, as both Heraclides and others have it, is Charilaus. In Herodotus he is Aisodotes [Ἀισωδῶτης].

units.la: P.43. v.3. Leges.) De quibus praeter citatos, vide Xenophonte in πολιτεία Lacedaemoniorum. Strabo lib. 8. & 10.
units.tr: P.43. v.3. Leges.) On these, besides the authors cited, see Xenophon in his work on the Spartan constitution, and Strabo, books 8 and 10.

units.la: V. 7. Parcimoniam omnibus sua sit.) Vett.omnes. Parcimoniam omnibus. Item existimans, &c. quae lectio quid velit non video. Paterc. lib.1. Lycurgum vocat, disciplina consentientissima Spirum: malim, contentissima.
units.tr: V.7. Parcimoniam omnibus sua sit.) The older texts have omnes. The reading Parcimoniam omnibus. Item existimans, etc., I do not see what it means. Paterculus, book 1, calls Lycurgus one whose discipline was most unanimous [Spartan]; I would rather read contentissima, most strenuous.

units.la: V.32. Dotis fienis.) Titinnius. Viri enim(ita legendum arbitror) dotibus deliniti, Sltro etiam Quoribus ancillantur. Plautus passim.
units.tr: V.32. Dotis fienis.) Titinnius: For men (I think it should be read thus), soothed by dowries, even serve their wives. Plautus passim.

units.la: P.44.v.17. Cum Messenius propter stupratas.) Strabo libro 6. & 8. & Paufan. lib.3. & 4. Orof. lib.1. cap. 21. habet propter sprctas Virgines, vitiose; Strabo enim ὑπὸ φθορᾶς τῶν παρθένων. De hoc bello vatie Seruius P. Danielis in 3. Aeneid.
units.tr: P.44.v.17. Cum Messenius propter stupratas.) Strabo, books 6 and 8, and Pausanias, books 3 and 4. Orosius, book 1, chapter 21, has propter sprctas Virgines [on account of the scorned virgins], wrongly; for Strabo says [it was] by the violation [ὑπὸ φθορᾶς] of the maidens. On this war, see variously Servius and P. Daniel on the third book of the Aeneid.

units.la: P.45.v.2. Parthenia.)Ita vett. & Graeci, non Parthenii, vt vulgo. Vide praeter caeteros Enstath.in Dionyl.
units.tr: P.45.v.2. Parthenia.) So the older writers and the Greeks have it, not Parthenii, as is commonly printed. See above all Eustathius on Dionysius.

units.la: V.4 Nulli enim pater exstiterat.) Ἀπάτορες & spurii filii. Infra lib.20.
units.tr: V.4 Nulli enim pater exstiterat.) [Ἀπάτορες], that is, spurious sons. See below, book 20.

units.la: V.5. Palantum.) Graeci Φαλάντιοι. & Horat. Ode 6.l.2. Euftathio Φιλαρθ. De Tarentinorum origine, vide etiam Paufaniam in Phocicis.
units.tr: V.5. Palantum.) The Greeks have Phalantians [Φαλάντιοι]. Also Horace, Odes 2.6. Eustathius [Φιλαρθ.]. On the origin of the Tarentines, see also Pausanias in his Phocica.

units.la: P.46. v.3. Oraculo Delphis.) Praeter Strab. lib. 8. Lege Paufaniam lib. 4.
units.tr: P.46. v.3. Oraculo Delphis.) Besides Strabo, book 8, read Pausanias, book 4.

units.la: V.29. Tertium quoque bellum.) De quo praeter ceteros iam citatos, Diod lib.11.&15.
units.tr: V.29. Tertium quoque bellum.) On this, besides the others already cited, see Diodorus, books 11 and 15.

units.la: 33. Athenienses.) Inter quos erat Cimon Miltiadis filius Paufanias. Thucyd.lib.1.
units.tr: 33. Athenienses.) Among them was Cimon, son of Miltiades, Pausanias. Thucydides, book 1.

units.la: P.47.v.2. A Delo.)Id enim commune aerarium esse voluerunt. Probus in Aristide. Thucyd. lib.1.
units.tr: P.47.v.2. A Delo.) For they wished this to be the common treasury. Probus on Aristides. Thucydides, book 1.

units.la: V.6. Peloponnenses.)Bellum Peloponnesiacum, 8 libris à Thucydide comprehensum: De quo & Plutarch. in Pericle & Diod. lib.12.
units.tr: V.6. Peloponnenses.) The Peloponnesian War, comprised in eight books by Thucydides. On this see also Plutarch in his Life of Pericles and Diodorus, book 12.

units.la: V. 7. Parua tunc.) Hunc locum male accepit Orosius lib.1. cap.vlt. Athenienses autem, inquit, missa in Aegyptu parua classe, auctor noster non paruam classem, sed paruas vires, dicit Atheniensibus fuisse, missa classe ducentarum navium in Aegyptum. Thucyd.lib.1.
units.tr: V.7. Parua tunc.) Orosius, book 1, final chapter, has misunderstood this passage. He says, "The Athenians, however, having sent a small fleet into Egypt," whereas our author says the Athenians had small strength, not a small fleet, when they sent a fleet of two hundred ships into Egypt. Thucydides, book 1.

units.la: V. 13. Periclem sp. s. v. & Sophoclem.] Meminit M. Cicero 1. de Offic. qui Prætores vocat, στρατηγούς.
units.tr: V. 13. Periclem sp. s. v. & Sophoclem.] Marcus Cicero, in book 1 of On Duties, mentions this, calling the praetors [στρατηγούς] generals.

units.la: V.28.In annos xxx.] Paus. Eliacis. vide & supra notat.
units.tr: V.28. In annos xxx.] Pausanias, Elian affairs. See also what is noted above.

units.la: P.48.v.10.Agros in populat.] Idem Fabio Maximo cum Annibal ad vrbem esset, accidit, Plutarch. & Ciuili. Taeitus s. histor. qui notam artem ducum vocat.
units.tr: P.48.v.10. Agros in populat.] The same happened to Fabius Maximus when Hannibal was at the city. Plutarch, and Civilis. Tacitus in his Histories, who calls it a well-known art of generals.

units.la: V.17.Nauali prælio.] Ad Naupactum, duce Phormione. Thuc. lib. 2.
units.tr: V.17. Nauali prælio.] At Naupactus, under the command of Phormio. Thucydides, book 2.

units.la: V. 21.In annos quinquaginta.] Thuc. lib. s.
units.tr: V. 21. In annos quinquaginta.] Thucydides, book 5.
IN BOOK IV.

units.la: Siciliam.] Vide Thuc. lib. 6. Melam 1. 2. cap. vlt. Plin. lib. 3. cap. 8. Diod. lib. s. quem πρότοπος βίβλον vocat. Strab. lib. 6. Solin cap. 11. Virgilium 3. Æneid. Eustath. in Dionys. Lucret. lib. 1. Claud. lib. 1. de raptu. De incolis Siciliæ, vide etiam Pausan. Eliacis.
units.tr: Sicily.] See Thucydides book 6; Mela 1.2 last chapter; Pliny book 3 chapter 8; Diodorus book 5, whom he calls "the first book" [πρότοπος βίβλον]; Strabo book 6; Solinus chapter 11; Virgil, Aeneid 3; Eustathius on Dionysius; Lucretius book 1; Claudian, On the Rape of Proserpina book 1. On the inhabitants of Sicily see also Pausanias, Eliaca.

units.la: V. 18. Eructet.] Mss. eructuet. Scruius ad illud 3. Æneid,
units.tr: V. 18. Eructet.] The manuscripts have eructuet. Servius on that line of Aeneid 3,

units.la: Interdum scopulos, aunlsaq; siscera montis Eruit eructans --
units.tr: Sometimes it belches up rocks and the torn-out entrails of the mountain --
He notes that only eructo, eructas is said.

units.la: V. 22. Rhegium.] Διὰ τὸ συμβαίνειν τὴν χώραν... Strabo. Dicitur ergo διὰ τῆς ῥήξεως. Eustath. Sallustius apud Seruium in 3. Æneid. ibi. Hæc loca si quondam, &c.
units.tr: V. 22. Rhegium.] Because the land is joined [to Italy]... Strabo. It is therefore said "through the breaking" [διὰ τῆς ῥήξεως]. Eustathius. Sallust in Servius on Aeneid 3, there: If these places once, etc.

units.la: V.29. Terga dantes in imum.] Ita boni libri, alii, Virgilius in imum desidere, alii Vorticibus. Errorinde manauit, quod quis forte ad oram libri Virgilii nomen notauerat, quod in contextum assumptum, trāsiit in Vorticibus: alii vt sententia constaret, ad τὸ Virgilius, addiderunt scribat. Certe videtur in hac Siciliæ descriptione auctor noster, ex 3. Æneid. imitatus pleraque, obseruatu facillima.
units.tr: V. 29. Terga dantes in imum.] So the good books read; others have Virgilius in imum desidere, others Vorticibus. The error arose because someone had perhaps noted the name Virgil in the margin of a copy of Virgil; this was taken into the text and passed into Vorticibus. Others, to make the sense stand, added scribat to the word Virgilius. Certainly in this description of Sicily our author seems to have imitated most things from Aeneid 3, which is very easy to observe.

units.la: P.52.v.7.Ætna.] Vide præter locos supra notatos, Plin. lib. 2. cap. 106. Lucret. lib. s. De Scylla & Charybdi vide præterea Sallustii fragmenta apud Seruium 3. Æneid.
units.tr: P. 52, v. 7. Aetna.] See, besides the places noted above, Pliny book 2 chapter 106; Lucretius book 5. On Scylla and Charybdis see also the fragments of Sallust in Servius on Aeneid 3.
P. 23. Cyclopes.] Thucydides: "said to be the most ancient" [παλαιότατοι μὲν λεγόμενοι] ...

units.la: V.24. Cocalus.] Ita vet. omnes & historia. de Cocalo lege Diod. extremo lib. 4. & 17. Strab. lib. 6. Eufebius in Chron. apud quem Cotalus dicitur, librariorū, arbitror errore.
units.tr: V. 24. Cocalus.] So all the old books and the history. On Cocalus read Diodorus at the end of book 4 and in book 17; Strabo book 6; Eusebius in the Chronicle, where he is called Cotalus, I think by an error of the copyists.

units.la: V.17. Anaxilaus. ]Oʼ τύραννος τῶν Ρηγίων. Strab. Thucyd. lib. 7. Micalum Herod. 7. Mixvδες vocat, Anaxilai αἰxίτλω, & Strab. 7. Micythus quidam est Messanæ princeps. Vide Macrob. 1. Saturn.
units.tr: V. 17. Anaxilaus.] ὁ τύραννος τῶν Ῥηγίων [the tyrant of the Rhegians]. Strabo; Thucydides book 7. Herodotus book 7 calls Micalus "Micythus" [Μίκυθος], the one who was the [adoptive] son of Anaxilas; and Strabo book 7 says Micythus is a certain prince of Messana. See Macrobius, Saturnalia book 1.

units.la: P.53.v.2. Carthaginienses ] Ad id à Xerxe ineitati. Diod. l.11. apud quem initio narrationis legendum γερμανοί εἰλοντο Ἀμιλκαρ, non Ἀμίλκαρα. Vide & Herodotum libro 7.
units.tr: P. 53, v. 2. Carthaginians.] Incited to this by Xerxes. Diodorus book 11, where at the beginning of the narrative one should read the Carthaginians chose Hamilcar [γερμανοί εἰλοντο Ἀμιλκαρ], not Ἀμίλκαρα. See also Herodotus book 7.

units.la: V.17. Cat'inienses. Ita vett. ferme omnes, & Orosius Ms.lib.2.cap.14. quidam, Cathenienses.Graecis Καταναῖοι & Καταναῖ Latinis plerumque Catina. Cicero ni 5.in Ver. Catina Sενυς.
units.tr: V. 17. Catinienses.] Nearly all the old books have this, and some manuscript copies of Orosius book 2 chapter 14 have Cathenienses. The Greeks have Καταναῖοι and the Latins mostly Catina. Cicero, in the fifth Verrine: Catina in Sicily [Κατάνη Σικελίας].

units.la: V.20 Quod Afiam. ]legendum arbitror, quo Afiam Graeciamque penitus occupavarent:aut,quo Afiam,&c occupauerant. Vt dicat, Athenienses studio illo maioris imperii, Asiam & Graeciam animo iam, & praesumptione quodammodo, penitus occupasse.
units.tr: V. 20. Quod Asiam.] I think one should read by which they had thoroughly occupied Asia and Greece, or by which they had occupied Asia, etc. The sense is that the Athenians, through that zeal for a greater empire, had in intention, and in a sense by presumption, already thoroughly occupied Asia and Greece.

units.la: V.17. Cariade.]Ita vett. Thueyd. 3.χαριᾶδες vocat,& hos non Catinienfibus,fedLeontinis in auxilium missos scribit.
units.tr: V. 17. Cariade.] So the old books. Thucydides book 3 calls them χαριάδες [chariades], and writes that these were sent to help the Leontines, not the Catinians.

units.la: P 54.v.6. Nicias]Thuc. lib.6. Diod. extremo lib.12. & initio lib.13. Plutarch. & Probus Alcibiade, ille etiam in Nicia.
units.tr: P. 54, v. 6. Nicias.] Thucydides book 6; Diodorus at the end of book 12 and the beginning of book 13; Plutarch and Probus in the Life of Alcibiades, and the former also in the Life of Nicias.

units.la: V 14. Sed in quo.]Ita & Orosius lib.2.cap.14.vet.noftri, fed quo,forte,qui.
units.tr: V. 14. Sed in quo.] So also Orosius book 2 chapter 14 in our old books: but in which; perhaps qui.
V. 23. Demosthenem.] Thucydides book 7; the others likewise.

units.la: V.33. Furent.]Ita boni auctores loquuntur:&inprimis Salluft. Iugurth. S P.Q.R. Verbis nuntient,Selle & censere eos ab arm is discedere: ita seque, illisque dignum sore. Vulgatae editiones, esse.
units.tr: V. 33. Furent.] Good authors speak this way, especially Sallust in the Jugurthine War: the Senate and people of Rome, let them announce in words that they think those men should withdraw from arms; thus it will be fitting for themselves and for those others. The common editions have esse.

units.la: P.55.v.9. Eurymedon ] Miror Mss. oēs hoc loco mendose prorsus legere Eurylocus. quomodo & Orof. Ms.Ego in vulgata lectione contra historiam nihil mutare aulus sum.
units.tr: P. 55, v. 9. Eurymedon.] I am surprised that all the manuscripts here wrongly read Eurylocus, as does the Orosius manuscript. I have not dared to change anything in the common reading against history.
V. 10. Triginta.] Orosius has fifteen.

units.la: V.11. Demosthenes ] Vtrumque à Syracusanis interfectum refert Thucyd. extr. libro 7. & Plutarch.
units.tr: V. 11. Demosthenes.] Thucydides at the end of book 7, and Plutarch, report that both were killed by the Syracusans.
ON BOOK V.

units.la: A Lcibiades absent.) Thucyd.7.Diod.13.Plutarch.&Probus in Alcib. Ælian. lib. 13. Accusatur & de truncatis, vt Thuc. autdeiectis Hermis,vt Probus.
units.tr: Alcibiades absent.) Thucydides 7; Diodorus 13; Plutarch and Probus in the life of Alcibiades; Aelian book 13. He is also accused of mutilating the Hermae, as Thucydides [reports], or of casting down the Hermae, as Probus [reports].

units.la: V.37. Bellum inferre.) Quod,munita à Lacedæmoniis, s concilio Alciabidis, Decelia, Decelicum appellatum est.
units.tr: V.37. Bellum inferre.) Because it was fortified by the Lacedaemonians at the suggestion of Alcibiades, it was called Decelea, Decelicum.

units.la: P. 58.v.14. Quam Vidi.) Vulgo Vidi. Lucil. Populus Romanus Vidius s, superatum præliis.
units.tr: P.58 v.14. Quam Vidi.) Commonly read as "Vidi." Lucilius: "The Roman people, Vidius, overcome in battles."
V.30. Ad Tissaphernem.) Thucydides 8; others noted above.

units.la: P.59.v.31. Imperium ad Senatum.) Ad quadringentos : quorum meminit & Strab.9.
units.tr: P.59 v.31. Imperium ad Senatum.) To the Four Hundred, whom Strabo 9 also mentions.

units.la: P. 60. v.1. Revocatur.]Id valde contendente Pifandro, & aliis optimatum fautoribus. Thucyd. lib. 8. Probus à Pifandro destitutum scribit. 15
units.tr: P.60 v.1. Revocatur.) This happened while Pisander and other supporters of the aristocrats strongly contended for it. Thucydides book 8. Probus writes that he was removed by Pisander.

units.la: Ibid. Dux.)Probus. Prætor. Plutarch. Hucusque Thucydides quem excipit Xenophon.
units.tr: Ibid. Dux.) Probus: praetor. Plutarch. Up to here Thucydides, whom Xenophon takes up.

units.la: V.10. Mindarus.] Ita Græci, & hic vulgati libri Mss. Xefromindarus. Is nauali ad Cyzicum pugna periit. Xenoph. 1. Diod. 13. Plut. Alcibiade, à quibus histo- 20 riæ huius fuliior explicatio petenda.
units.tr: V.10. Mindarus.) So the Greeks write, and so the manuscripts here read; the printed text has "Xefromindarus." He fell in the naval battle at Cyzicus: Xenophon book 1; Diodorus 13; Plutarch in Alcibiades. A fuller account of this history should be sought from these.

units.la: V 17. Quibus ea res quastum præb.) Diod. Οἱ πολλοὶ ... 25
units.tr: V.17. Quibus ea res quaestum praeb.) Diodorus: [Οἱ πολλοὶ ...]

units.la: V.18. Illatum à Carthag.)De quo vide Diod.lib.13. 25
units.tr: V.18. Illatum à Carthag.) On this see Diodorus book 13.

units.la: V.25. His omnibus præliis.) Quinque terrestribus & tribus naualibus. Probus.
units.tr: V.25. His omnibus praeliis.) Five on land and three at sea. Probus.

units.la: V.31. De cælo missum.) Minutius Oct. In hc diernum inopinato Visos cælo missos, ignobiles & ignotos, terræ filios nominamus. 30
units.tr: V.31. De caelo missum.) Minucius Octavius: "In this day, we call those who have suddenly appeared, as if sent from heaven, ignoble and unknown, sons of the earth."
P.61 v.1. Tantum in uno viro.) Isocrates, Philippus.

units.la: V.18.Lysander.)Post Xenophontem, vide Plutarchum & Probum in eius vita, Diod. lib.13. quieum Sardis ad Cyrum profectum scribit; M. Cicero in Cat. maiore, ex Xenoph. OEconom. 35
units.tr: V.18. Lysander.) After Xenophon; see Plutarch and Probus in his life. Diodorus book 13 writes that he went to Cyrus at Sardis. M. Cicero in Cato Maior, from Xenophon's Oeconomicus.

units.la: V.26 Oppressere.) Non Alcibiadem, sed Antiochum, qui quidem erat ... Plut. alii & Paufan. Bœoticis.
units.tr: V.26. Oppressere.) Not Alcibiades but Antiochus, who indeed was ... Plutarch, others, and Pausanias, Boeotica.

units.la: P.62.V.6 Conon.)Eius vitam descripsit Probus,qui eum prœlio ad Ægos flumen, quo Atheniensium imperium concidit,non interfuisse scribit,cóera quam Xenophon, lib.2. Exlw.Plut Lysandro.Diod. 13
units.tr: P.62 v.6. Conon.) Probus wrote his life, and he writes that Conon was not present at the battle of Aegospotami, by which the empire of the Athenians collapsed, contrary to what Xenophon says in book 2 of the Hellenica. Plutarch in Lysander. Diodorus 13.

units.la: V. 29. Cum octo nauibus.) Plutarch. At Diodorus: Τὰν μὲν ἐν τεσσαρῶν δύο μόνον διεξέπεσον, ἂν μίαν ἴχων Κάραν ὁ σφε- ς τὴν ἱὸς, τὴν μὲν εἰς Αθήνας ἐπανοδον ἀπίχνω, &c.
units.tr: V.29. Cum octo navibus.) Plutarch. But Diodorus: [Τὰν μὲν ἐν τεσσαρῶν δύο μόνον διεξέπεσον, ἂν μίαν ἴχων Κάραν ὁ σφε- ς τὴν ἱὸς, τὴν μὲν εἰς Αθήνας ἐπανοδον ἀπίχνω, &c.]
P.63 v.32. Malts delendum.) Lysander and Agis. Pausanias, Laconica.

units.la: P.64.v.1. Si demissa Piraum.) Ἐ̓στι τὰ μικρὰ σκίλη καὶ τὰ τείχη τὰ πυρὸς ὡς ἀπλάξαν. Diod.extr. l.13. Plut. Lysandro,quos vide & Xenoph. Exlw.β. Et ita bello Peloponnesiaco finis impositus,quod Thucyd. ἀξιολογώτερον vocat τῶν ἀγεχρονῶν, & μικρότατον: in annum enim 26, protractum est.
units.tr: P.64 v.1. Si demissa Piraum.) [Ἐ̓στι τὰ μικρὰ σκίλη καὶ τὰ τείχη τὰ πυρὸς ὡς ἀπλάξαν.] Diodorus at the end of book 13; Plutarch in Lysander, which see; and Xenophon Hellenica 2. And so the Peloponnesian War was brought to an end, which Thucydides calls [ἀξιολογώτερον τῶν ἀγεχρονῶν] more notable than the earlier wars, and [μικρότατον] the smallest; for it was drawn out over 26 years.

units.la: V,9. Triginta rectores.) Vide præter citatos Diod.initio lib. 41.
units.tr: V.9. Triginta rectores.) See, besides those cited, Diodorus at the beginning of book 14.

units.la: V.14. Cadesd c.ab Alcib] De morte Alcibiadis, ad cuius cædem 30. tyranni Lysandrum impulerunt, vide Plutarch. Diodorum, Probum, Ciceronem 2. de Diuinat. Val.lib.1. cap.8. De Theramene,vno de 30. vide Xenoph, Exlw.6.lib.2 & M.Cic.Tusc.
units.tr: V.14. Caedes ab Alcib.) On the death of Alcibiades, for whose murder the Thirty Tyrants urged Lysander, see Plutarch, Diodorus, Probus, Cicero De Divinatione 2, and Valerius book 1 chapter 8. On Theramenes, one of the Thirty, see Xenophon Hellenica book 2, and M. Cicero, Tusculan Disputations.

units.la: V.31. Thra∫ybulus.]Τυρισὺς ὀνομάζονται Diod.14.vide Xenoph. Exlw β. Paufan.Atticis.
units.tr: V.31. Thrasybulus.) [Τυρισὺς ὀνομάζονται] Diodorus 14; see Xenophon Hellenica 2; Pausanias, Attica.

units.la: V.32. Nobilis.] Probus,multi eū nobilitate pracurrerunt. P.65.vet. Phylen.]Steph. de Vrbibus. χώρια vocant Xenoph & Diod.
units.tr: V.32. Nobilis.) Probus: "many surpassed him in nobility." P.65 vet. Phylen.) Stephanus, On Cities. Xenophon and Diodorus call them [χώρια].

units.la: V.5. Lysias ]Paulo aliter Plutarch. in vitis Rhetorum, quem vide.
units.tr: V.5. Lysias.) Somewhat differently Plutarch, in the Lives of the Orators, which see.

units.la: V.18. Crit:as.]Τὴν ἡγεμονίαν τυραννόρων Diod. dux tyrannorum, Probus, crudelissimum omnium tyrannorum vocat Laἐtant. lib.3. de falsa sap. Hippolochi,(ita habent. Vett.omnes)uon meminerunt. Xenoph.2. Exlw. Hippomachi vocat,quomodo habet editio vulgata.
units.tr: V.18. Critias.) Diodorus: [Τὴν ἡγεμονίαν τυραννόρων], "leadership of the tyrants." Probus: "leader of the tyrants." Lactantius book 3 of De falsa sapientia calls him the most cruel of all tyrants. All the older copies have "Hippolochus," which the others do not mention. Xenophon Hellenica 2 calls him Hippomachus, as the printed edition has.

units.la: V. 21. Magna Voce Thra∫ybulus.] Non Thrasybulus, scd Cleocritus κάρδας μάλιστα ἐπὶ Θεόν ἀν. Xenoph.
units.tr: V.21. Magna voce Thrasybulus.) Not Thrasybulus but Cleocritus, [κάρδας μάλιστα ἐπὶ Θεόν ἀν], as Xenophon says.
V.32. Substitutus decem.) Probus: praetors.

units.la: P.66. v.3. Paulanias.] Ἐ̓τ ἄντε cum Lysander,cum 40. nauibus. Diod. Hic autem pacem fecit non misericor- dia : scd φόνων Ἀνδρὶ , & ἴσως τὴν ἀρχὴν ἀδικῶσι, &c. vide Diod. & Xenoph.
units.tr: P.66 v.3. Paulanias.) [Ἐ̓τ ἄντε] with Lysander, with 40 ships. Diodorus. But he made peace not out of mercy but [φόνων Ἀνδρὶ], and perhaps they were acting unjustly from the start, etc. See Diodorus and Xenophon.
V.16. Discordiarum oblivionem.) [Αμνηστία.] M. T. Cicero, Philippics 2.

units.la: Val. Max. lib. 4. cap. 1. Plutar. Cicerone. Mi μυησικακεῖν. Xenoph. Et ita Siculos pacem fecisse refert Thuc. lib. 4. ἐχοντες ἀ ἐνσπονδοι.
units.tr: Valerius Maximus book 4 chapter 1; Plutarch; Cicero. [μυησικακεῖν.] Xenophon. And so Thucydides reports that the Sicilians made peace, book 4, [ἐχοντες ἀ ἐνσπονδοι].

units.la: V. 22. Darius. Diod. lib. 13. De Cyri ἀναβάτ, id est, ut Hieronymus loquitur, a scenis, Xenoph. Diod. lib. 14. & 15. Plutarch. in Artaxerxe, qui ante regnum Arsices, vel ut Ctesias, Arsaces dicebatur, post Mnemon est cognominatus.
units.tr: V.22. Darius.) Diodorus book 13. On Cyrus's [ἀναβάτ], that is, as Jerome puts it, "from the stage," Xenophon; Diodorus books 14 and 15; Plutarch in Artaxerxes, who before his reign was called Arsices, or, as Ctesias has it, Arsaces, and after whom Mnemon was added as a surname.

units.la: P. 67. v. 6. Fors praelii] H τυχη. Diod.
units.tr: P.67 v.6. Fors praelii.) [ἡ τύχη.] Diodorus.
IN BOOK VI.

units.la: Hercyllides. ] Ἀεχυλλίδας. Xenoph. libro 3. & Diod. 14. Plutarch. in Artaxerxe, quos vide. Huc spectat Trogi Pompeii fragmentum apud Prisc. lib. 6. cuiusetiam Mss. habent, ab Herculide. Orosius lib. 3. cap. 1. vocat Hitcilidem. Dercyllidae meminit & Plutarchus in Apophth. Lacon.
units.tr: Hercyllides. Hercyllidas [Ἀεχυλλίδας]. Xenophon, book 3, and Diodorus, book 14; Plutarch in the Life of Artaxerxes, which see. To this refers the fragment of Pompeius Trogus in Priscian, book 6, whose manuscripts also read "ab Herculide." Orosius, book 3, chapter 1, calls him Hitcilides. Plutarch also mentions Dercyllidas in the Sayings of the Spartans.

units.la: V. 23. Criminatur.] Orosius lib. 3. cap 1. defert et praeditorem. Ms. P. Danielis, differt. vide Noniu. Tacit. 1. Anoali. Pars multo maxima imminentes dominos Cariu rumoribus differebant Petronius. Alioqui mille causas nos quotidie collident, & per totam urbem rumoribus differunt, itamalo. quam deferent.
units.tr: V. 23. Criminatur. Orosius, book 3, chapter 1, has "defert" and "praeditorem." The manuscript of P. Daniel differs; see Nonius. Tacitus, Annals 1: "The greater part of them spread rumours about the masters who threatened them." Petronius: "Otherwise a thousand causes crush us daily, and they spread them through the whole city with rumours, so that I would rather they informed against me."

units.la: V. 21. Quam gerant.] Plauto familiaris locutio subinteligendum potius, quod in uno codice reperitur, aut magis. Plautus Rud.
units.tr: V. 21. Quam gerant. A phrase familiar from Plautus; it should rather be understood as what is found in one manuscript, or in more. Plautus, Rudens.

units.la: Tacita bona'st mulier semper, quam loquens. Terent. in Eunuch. Qui placere se studeat bonis, Quam plurimis.
units.tr: A silent woman is always better than a talkative one. Terence, in the Eunuch. He who strives to please the good rather than the very many.

units.la: V. 29 Hortatur, et in locum.] Ita & Diodor. lib. 14. Pausanias Atticis id Euagorae Cypri o regi tribuit. Vide Probum Conone.
units.tr: V. 29. Hortatur, et in locum. So also Diodorus, book 14. Pausanias attributes this to the Athenians and to Evagoras, king of Cyprus. See Probus, Conon.

units.la: P. 71. v. 3. Hercinione.] Vett. hic variant, quidam Mercinionis, alii Mercimoni, alii Inercinioni. Hercynione habet etiam Orosius. Eum Diodorus vocat NiΦρια.
units.tr: P. 71. v. 3. Hercinione. The early editions vary here: some have Mercinionis, others Mercimoni, others Inercinioni. Orosius also has Hercynione. Diodorus calls him Νιφρια [NiΦρια].

units.la: V. 9. Respon sum oraculi.] Quod extat apud Paufan. Lacon. & Plutar. Agesilao. Vide etiam Xenoph. 3. Exn. & in Agesil. Vide & Probum ibid.
