units.tr: V. 9. Response of the oracle. This is found in Pausanias, Laconica, and in Plutarch's Agesilaus. See also Xenophon, Hellenica 3, and the Agesilaus. See Probus there too.

units.la: V. 29. Adorare] Probus, Venerari, quod προσκυνεῖν illi vocant.
units.tr: V. 29. Adorare. Probus has "venerari," which they call προσκυνεῖν [proskynein].
P. 71. v. 1. Ministrum. Ταξιαν [Taxian]. Diodorus.

units.la: V.8. Pyfandrus ]Ita Mss.omnes,vulgo Lyfander,contra hiftoriam. Græcis eft Πεισανδρος. Xenophon lib. 4. Plut. Agefilao, & Probus. Diodoro eft Περιεχων, vt alii notarunt,mendofe.
units.tr: V. 8. Pyfandrus. All the manuscripts have this; the common printed text has Lysander, against the history. In Greek it is Πεισανδρος [Peisandros]. Xenophon, book 4, Plutarch's Agesilaus, and Probus have it. In Diodorus it is Περιεχων [Periechon], as others have noted, through error.
V. 14. Contuntione Agefilai. He was the brother of Agesilaus's wife.
V. 32. Victi Lacedam. At Cnidus.

units.la: P.73.v.4. Lacedamonii habende.] Ifocrates ad Philip. Λακεδαιμονιους εξιβαλον εκ των αερων, &c. Orofius. Magnitudine atque atrocitate belli iflius, inclinatus ex hoc semper in posterum Lacedamoniorum flatus: Prona namque, ex illo fluere, & retro fublapfa referri spes Spartanorum sisa est. Ita locus ille ex Ms.P.Danielis legendus est.
units.tr: P. 73. v. 4. Lacedamonii habende. Isocrates to Philip: they drove the Lacedaemonians out of the seas [Λακεδαιμονιους εξιβαλον εκ των αερων], etc. Orosius: "Because of the magnitude and atrocity of that war, the fortunes of the Lacedaemonians inclined downward from then on; for the hope of the Spartans, sliding down from that point and falling back, was checked." That passage must therefore be read as it stands in the manuscript of P. Daniel.

units.la: V.6. Thebani.] Et alii ad id pecunia Persarum inducti. Paufan.lib.4.
units.tr: V. 6. Thebani. Others too were induced to this by Persian money. Pausanias, book 4.

units.la: V.7.Infimus] Ita quidam impreffi, recte: alii infinitus. Mss.finitimus.
units.tr: V. 7. Infimus. Some printed editions have this, rightly; others have infinitus. The manuscripts have finitimus.

units.la: V 8 Epaminonda.) De quo praeter ceteros Plutarch.in Pelopida & Probus in eius vita. Non vult Iuftinus eum praelio interfuisse,quod Orofius putauit, fed eius virtute auctam rem Thebanam.
units.tr: V. 8. Epaminonda. On him, above all others, see Plutarch in the Life of Pelopidas and Probus in his Life. Justin does not mean that he took part in the battle, as Orosius thought; rather, the Theban cause was enlarged by his valour.

units.la: V.11. Lyfander.) Apud Haliartum. Xenoph. 3. Plut. & Probus Lysandro. Diod. 14. Paufan. Laconicis.
units.tr: V. 11. Lysander. At Haliartus. Xenophon, book 3; Plutarch and Probus in the Life of Lysander; Diodorus, book 14; Pausanias, Laconica.

units.la: 18. Ex Asia,qui ibi.) Paufanias libro 3. & 4. De pugna ad Coronæam, vide supra citatos auctores; qui non superuenisse pugnæ,sed ab initio interfuisse referunt.
units.tr: 18. Ex Asia, qui ibi. Pausanias, books 3 and 4. On the battle at Coronea, see the authors cited above, who report that he was present from the beginning of the battle, not that he arrived after it had begun.

units.la: V.32. Iphicratem.) De quo praeter superiores, Probus in eius vita. Hoc autem bellum quia circa Corinthū gerebatur,Corinthium est appellatu, Κορινθιακος πολεμος. P.74.v.16 Manibus eorum.) recte. vulgo contra libros & mentem auctoris,manubiis,Orofius,Perfis aedificantibus. Legendus Xenoph. 4. Diod. 14. Paufa. Atticis.
units.tr: V. 32. Iphicratem. On him, besides the authors above, see Probus in his Life. This war, since it was waged around Corinth, is called the Corinthian War, Κορινθιακος πολεμος [Korinthiakos polemos]. P. 74. v. 16. Manibus eorum. The correct reading; the common text, against the manuscripts and the author's meaning, has manubiis (spoils). Orosius: "Persian builders." Read Xenophon, book 4; Diodorus, book 14; Pausanias, Attica.

units.la: V.22. Artaxerxes.) Pax Antalcidæ, dicta quod esset eius operæ impetrata. Xenoph. 5. Diod.14. Plutarch. in Ages. & Artaxer.
units.tr: V. 22. Artaxerxes. The Peace of Antalcidas, so called because it was secured through his effort. Xenophon, book 5; Diodorus, book 14; Plutarch in the Lives of Agesilaus and Artaxerxes.

units.la: V. 27. Ægyptio bello.) Κυπριακον πολεμον, comme-morat Diodorus in quod pace constituta incubuerit Artaxerxes. Nisi hæc de ea pace accipias, de qua Diodotus 15. Αρταξερξης μαλλον πολεμειν προς Αιγυπτιους, η παντων δαν ειρη-νην δυναμιν αξιολογον συσησασθαι, διδοντα συμμαχους τους εν τηΝ τὴν ἰλλάδα πολέμους, &c. quæ compara cum Iustini vetustis. Sed de Ægyptio bello, vide Gemiftum, & Plutarch; Artax.
units.tr: V. 27. Aegyptio bello. Diodorus mentions the Cyprian War, after which Artaxerxes turned to the peace. Unless you take these words of that peace, of which Diodorus, book 15, says: "Artaxerxes preferred to wage war against the Egyptians rather than to establish any peace of considerable strength for all, giving allies the wars in Greece" [Αρταξερξης μαλλον πολεμειν προς Αιγυπτιους, η παντων δαν ειρηνην δυναμιν αξιολογον συστησασθαι, διδοντα συμμαχους τους εν τη Ελλαδι πολεμους], etc.; compare this with the old text of Justin. On the Egyptian war, see Gemistus and Plutarch, Artaxerxes.
Roman city. Strabo, at the end of book 6.

units.la: Lacedæmonii fecurii.] Lubet ex Ms. voces aliquot Orofio lib 3. cap. 2. restituere. Lacedæmonij, inquit, inquieti magis[quam strenui; & furore potius]quam virtute intolerabiles,post bellapofita,tentant furta bellorum.
units.tr: Lacedaemonians secure. It is worth restoring a few words from the manuscript of Orosius, book 3, chapter 2. "The Lacedaemonians," he says, "restless rather than vigorous, and intolerable through frenzy rather than valour, after the wars were ended, attempt the thefts of war."

units.la: Caftellum.] Κρᾶνον. Xenoph. Ελλὰν. 6. ciuitas est Peloponnesi. Steph. De hoc bello vide Xenoph.
units.tr: Castellum. Κρᾶνον [Kranon]. Xenophon, Hellenica 6. A city of the Peloponnese, according to Stephanus. On this war, see Xenophon.

units.la: Hoc est enim fignum:] Diod. 17. αἰτιον τῶν ῥσκρῶν, ait ἀεὶ εἰχίων ἀπὸ ὀρχηστρων.
units.tr: Hoc est enim signum. Diodorus, book 17: the cause of wars [αἴτιον τῶν πολέμων] is always, he says, from dancers [ἀπὸ ὀρχηστῶν].

units.la: Tacito confenfu inducia.] quæ indutia tacita dicuntur Liuio lib. 2. & 23.
units.tr: Tacito consensu inducia. Truces of this kind are called tacit truces (indutiae tacitae) in Livy, books 2 and 23.

units.la: Principio nctis.] Vide Plut. Agefilao. Front. lib.1. cap. 11.
units.tr: Principio noctis. See Plutarch, Agesilaus; Frontinus, book 1, chapter 11.

units.la: Nec bellum diu dilatum.] Proeliū ad Mantineam, de quo Xenoph. lib. 7. Diod. 15. Plutarch. Agefilao & Apophr. Lacon. Probus Epaminonda, Paufan. Bœoticis, Strab. lib. 8 præter quos de Epaminondæ morte, legendus Cicero epist. ad Lucceium. Val. lib.3. cap 2. Ælian.12. Paufanias Atticis, & Arcadicis, quem sequitur Orofius lib. 3. cap. 2. Hucusque Xenophon,cuius historiam prosequitur Diod.15. & Gemiffus Plecho.
units.tr: Nec bellum diu dilatum. The battle at Mantinea, on which see Xenophon, book 7; Diodorus, book 15; Plutarch in Agesilaus and the Sayings of the Spartans; Probus in the Life of Epaminondas; Pausanias, Boeotica; Strabo, book 8. Besides these, on the death of Epaminondas, read Cicero's letter to Lucceius; Valerius, book 3, chapter 2; Aelian, book 12; Pausanias, Attica and Arcadica, whom Orosius, book 3, chapter 2, follows. Thus far Xenophon, whose history Diodorus, book 15, and Gemistus Plethon continue.
IN BOOK VII.

units.la: Macedonia.] Dicta à Macedone Ofiridis filio: Diod. lib. 1. alias Ioius filio & Deucalionis nepote. Steph. de verb. Solinus cap.14. Euftath.in Dionyf. apud quem & Hefychium Macetia dicuntur,& Macchab.1 cap.1. terra Cethim.Eft autem Cethim Gen.10.filius Iauan, &Danielis 11. per Iauan Graeci intelliguntur. Inde Macetæ, sunt Macedones. Aufon. Macetumq, attollite nomen.
units.tr: Macedonia.] Named from Macedon, son of Osiris: Diodorus, book 1; elsewhere, son of Ioius and grandson of Deucalion. Stephanus, On Words; Solinus, ch. 14; Eustathius on Dionysius, where Hesychius also has the forms Macetia; and Maccabees 1, ch. 1, "the land of Cethim." Cethim is a son of Javan, Gen. 10, and in Daniel 11 Javan means the Greeks. Hence the Macetae are the Macedonians. Ausonius: "Raise up the name of the Macetae."

units.la: Emathionis.] Ita Probus in 1. Geor. Virg. Emathia vocat Solinus, quem facit genuinum terræ, id est αὐτὸ-χθονα.
units.tr: Emathionis.] So Probus on Virgil, Georgics 1. Solinus calls it Emathia, and makes it native to the land, that is, autochthonous [αὐτόχθονα].

units.la: Paonia.]A qua olim Macedonia Pæonia dicebatur. Liuius ab vrb.cond. lib 40.
units.tr: Paonia.] Macedonia was once called Paeonia after this people. Livy, from the founding of the city, book 40.

units.la: Telegonus.] Πηλίων Homero Iliad. φ. vt notauit Glareanus. Vett. omnes Telegenus, quod est Vlyssis filii nomen, ab hoc loco alienum.
units.tr: Telegonus.] In Homer, Iliad phi, it is Pelion [Πηλίων], as Glareanus noted. All the old copies have Telegenus, which is the name of Ulysses' son and out of place here.
Eustathius.
Eusebius.
Edessa.
Aegeae.

units.la: Perdicca] Herodotus, ὁ ἀρχὴν, inquit, quia primus rex in Macedonia nominatus est. Solinus: Eusebius hunc, 4. facit. Quomodo hic ad regnum peruenerit, vide Herodotum. meminit & Thuc. extr. lib. 2.
units.tr: Perdiccas.] Herodotus says he was the first (ho archēn [ὁ ἀρχήν]) because he was the first king named in Macedonia. Solinus: Eusebius makes this the fourth king. How he came to the throne, see Herodotus. Thucydides also mentions him, at the end of book 2.
Argaeus.
Europus.
Their king, brought forth in the cradle.
To this Amyntas.
Mygabazus.
Sons.
Bubares.
In order.
Three sons.
At home, Epaminondas.

units.la: Insidiis Eurydices. interemit Perdicca;cui ,cum aduersus Illyrios cecidisset, successit Philippus,cum adhuc Thebis esset,vt Diod. Iustinus enim , quem libro 3. cap.12. sequitur Orof. triennium tantum obsidem fuisse scribit: accurate haec Gemistus.
units.tr: By the plots of Eurydice, Perdiccas killed him. When Perdiccas had fallen in the war against the Illyrians, Philip succeeded him while he was still at Thebes, as Diodorus reports. For Justin, whom Orosius follows in book 3, ch. 12, writes that he was a hostage for only three years. Gemistus treats this accurately.

units.la: P. 83. v. 5. Inopia , continui belli &c.) Forte legendum, continuis belli exhausti regni, imm. at. fyr. Orgerent, & bella qua, &c.
units.tr: P.83, v. 5. Inopia, continui belli &c.) Perhaps one should read something like "a kingdom exhausted by continuous war, and the wars which..., &c."

units.la: V. 13. Contemptum sibi hostium demeret.) malim, contemptum sui hostibus demeret.
units.tr: V.13. Contemptum sibi hostium demeret.) I would rather read that it removed the enemies' contempt for themselves.

units.la: V.14. Cum Athenien sibus certamen.) Diod. lib. 16. Regem Macedoniae Argeum facere volebant Athenienses, misso Mantia duce cum exercitu. de victis Illyriis, vide eundem sub anno secundo Philippi.
units.tr: V.14. Cum Athenien sibus certamen.) Diodorus, book 16: the Athenians wanted to make Argaeus king of Macedonia, sending Mantias as commander with an army. For the defeat of the Illyrians, see the same author under the second year of Philip.

units.la: V.18. Lariffam capit, &c.) Vett. Lariseam, Lariffas plures recensent lib. 9. &13. Strab. & Steph. de vrbibus: nullam quae huic loco conueniat, nisi legas, Lariffam in Thessalia, & ea lectio uno Ms. confirmatur, habet is Lariffam hine in Thessaliam. Ceteri, Lariffam capit, hic in Thessaliam. Glareanus Liffam, legit, quae est urbs Illyriiae, Ptolem. Steph. Thessaliam aggressus est Philippus, contra tyrannos vocatus Diodorus anno IV.
units.tr: V.18. Lariffam capit, &c.) The old copies have Lariseam. Several authors list Larissas in books 9 and 13, and Strabo and Stephanus in their works on cities. None suits this passage unless you read Larissam in Thessalia, and that reading is confirmed by one manuscript, which has Larissam hinc in Thessaliam. The others have Larissam capit, hinc in Thessaliam. Glareanus reads Lissam, a city of Illyria, according to Ptolemy and Stephanus. Philip set out for Thessaly, called there against the tyrants, as Diodorus reports under the fourth year.

units.la: 25. Fratre patruele, altore.) Vett. auctore, forte tutore. De hoc loco dicam lib. 17.
units.tr: 25. Fratre patruele, altore.) The old copies have auctore; perhaps it should be tutore. I will discuss this passage in book 17.

units.la: V.32. Methona] Vett. Mothana. Methana Strab.l.8.aliter est Μεθώνη. Praeter Dio. sub an.8. vide & Solinum ca.14. & Plin. lib.7. cap.37. Sagittam autem iecerat Aster oppidanum inscriptam suo nomine, locoque Culneris, & nomine (id est nomine Philippi) quem petebat: vt est apud Solin.
units.tr: V.32. Methona.) The old copies have Mothana. Strabo, book 8, has Methana; in Greek it is Μεθώνη [Methōnē]. Besides Diodorus under the eighth year, see Solinus, ch. 14, and Pliny, book 7, ch. 37. He had shot an arrow inscribed with the name of Aster, a townsman, and in place of Culnerus, and in the name of the man he was aiming at, that is, Philip, as it is in Solinus.
IN BOOK VIII.

units.la: OMnibus perire.) Ita Vett. omnes & Orosius: nullo sensu, vt mihi quidem videtur. P.Pithoeus,sagaci eorde & ingenio vnico coniecit legendum, Omnibus peruia, proxime ad antiquam scripturam. Ego leuissima vnius litterulae mutatione lego, omnibus perire quod singula amitterent non nisi oppressae senserunt. Vult amittere omnes quod amitterent singulae: quae singulis perirent, perire omnibus: sed id non sensisse, nisi oppressas. nam quod vulgo legitur, ab omnibus vitæ periere: Nugæ. De hac ciuili Græcorum discordia apud Plutarch. Callilthenes.
units.tr: Omnibus perire.) So all the old copies and Orosius read, which makes no sense as far as I can see. P. Pithoeus, with a keen mind and unique talent, conjectured omnibus peruia (open to all), very close to the old script. I read it with the smallest change of one letter: "to perish for all, because they lost singly, which only the oppressed felt." It means that they lost, one by one, what they had each lost; what was lost by individuals perished for all; but they did not feel this until they were oppressed. As for the common reading, "by all their lives perished," it is nonsense. On this civil discord of the Greeks, see Plutarch, Callisthenes.

units.la: Ἐν δὲ ... (Greek line as printed: Ἐν δὲ τῷ χρόνῳ ... ἁλλὰ πηγῆς.)
units.tr: Ἐν δὲ τῷ χρόνῳ ... ἀλλὰ πηγῆς. [Ἐν δὲ τῷ χρόνῳ ... ἁλλὰ πηγῆς.] In the meantime ... but of the spring.

units.la: Cum diceret illam Philippo magnitudinis, & potentiæ occasionem & causam excitisse.
units.tr: Since he said that she had given Philip the occasion and cause of his greatness and power.

units.la: V. 17. Thebani.) Hoc est initium belli Sacri, seu Phocici, quod in annum nonum durauit, Diodorus lib. 16. sub anno 6. Philippi: decennium durasse scribit Pausan. in Bœoticis, & Phocicis. Vide & Gemist.
units.tr: V.17. Thebani.) This is the beginning of the Sacred, or Phocian, War, which lasted into the ninth year. Diodorus, book 16, under the sixth year of Philip. Pausanias, in Boeotica and Phocica, writes that it lasted ten years. See also Gemistus.

units.la: V.21. Græcia concilium.) Amphictyonum. Diod. Pauf. Ælianus 12.
units.tr: V.21. Graecia concilium.) Of the Amphictyons. Diodorus, Pausanias, Aelian 12.

units.la: P.86 v f. Dimicans ceciderit.) Diod. & Paufanias præcipitem se è rupe dedisse referunt, anno Philippi 7.
units.tr: P.86, v. f. Dimicans ceciderit.) Diodorus and Pausanias report that he threw himself headlong from a rock, in the seventh year of Philip.

units.la: V.6. Onomarchus.) Ita Græci in Vett. est ΟΕnomenaum, aut ΟΕnomaus, vt in Orosio Ms.
units.tr: V.6. Onomarchus.) The Greek name in the old copies is Oenomenaum or Oenomaus, as in the Orosius manuscript.

units.la: V. 13. Angustias Thermopyl.) Ad quas occupandas Philippus contendebat. Diod.
units.tr: V.13. Angustias Thermopyl.) Philip was hurrying to occupy them. Diodorus.

units.la: P.87.v.17. In Cappadociam.) Hellespónti vrbes Micybernam & Toronem Philippum anno 13. occupasse refert Diod. Putauì aliquando, legendum, Chalcidem, ex eodem Diodoro.
units.tr: P.87, v. 17. In Cappadociam.) Diodorus reports that in the thirteenth year Philip occupied the Hellespontine cities Micybernē and Toron. I once thought one should read Chalcidem, from the same Diodorus.

units.la: V. 27. Olynthios.) Vide præter Diodorum, Demosth. Olynth. & Libanii argumenta.
units.tr: V.27. Olynthios.) See, besides Diodorus, Demosthenes' Olynthiacs and the Arguments of Libanius.

units.la: P.88.v.1. Auraria in Thessalia.) Circa Pydnā fuisse χρυσέας, auctor est Diodorus, è quib. Philippus annua talenta mille colligebat. De iis & Gemistus.
units.tr: P.88, v. 1. Auraria in Thessalia.) Diodorus is the authority that there were gold mines (chrysai) near Pydna, from which Philip collected a thousand talents a year. Gemistus also writes about them.

units.la: V.5. Duo reges Thraciæ.) Cotys Thraciæ rex, filios tres Berisaden, Amadocum & Cersoblepten reliquit: Berisades mature obiit: Videtut igitur Iustinus de duobus illis loqui. Vide Demosthenem κατ' Ἀριστοκράτους. Diodorus, sub anno quinto refert Philippum reges Thraciæ, Illyriæ, & Pœoniæ imperatos oppressisse: & de Cersoblepte sub anno 8. & 18.
units.tr: V.5. Duo reges Thraciae.) Cotys, king of Thrace, left three sons: Berisades, Amadocus and Cersobleptes. Berisades died early, so it seems Justin is speaking of those two. See Demosthenes, Against Aristocrates. Diodorus, under the fifth year, reports that Philip subdued the kings of Thrace, Illyria and Paeonia; and on Cersobleptes under the eighth and eighteenth years.

units.la: V.15. Pax facta.) De qua passim in orationibus Demosthenes.
units.tr: V.15. Pax facta.) Demosthenes speaks of this throughout his orations.

units.la: V.17. Thessali Bœotique.) Anno Philippi 14. Vide Diodorum, qui hæc latius persequitur.
units.tr: V.17. Thessali Boeotique.) In the fourteenth year of Philip. See Diodorus, who treats this more fully.

units.la: P.90.v.12. Alexandrum priuignum.) Quomodo Arrybæ priuignus sit Alexander, non video. Legę quæ notaui ad lib.17. & Diodorum sub anno 19.
units.tr: P.90, v. 12. Alexandrum priuignum.) I do not see how Alexander is stepson of Arrhybas. Read what I noted on book 17, and Diodorus under the nineteenth year.
Aa IN

units.la: P.92. v.15. Ἰζ antium]ld tétauitPhilippus quod Perinthiis quos oblessos tenebat, Byzantini auxilia misserunt: Cum ergo arbitraretur, optimos quosque Perinthum misso, cum parte copiarum, ἀφ' ὧν τῷ Βυζαντίῳ. Diod. 9 anno xx & xxi. De Byzantii appellatione, vide Eustath. in Dionys. & Steph. de urb. ante Lygos dictum. Plin. 4. cap.11. Cassiodorus Tulli Hoftilii temporibus conditum scribit. Vide & Tacitum Ann.12.
units.tr: P.92, v. 15. Ἰζ antium] Philip was troubled because the Byzantines sent help to the Perinthians, whom he held besieged. Since he thought the best men should be sent to Perinthus with part of the forces, from which [ἀφ' ὧν τῷ Βυζαντίῳ] ... Diodorus, under the twentieth and twenty-first years. On the name Byzantium, see Eustathius on Dionysius and Stephanus, On Cities: it is said to be named after Lygos. Pliny, book 4, ch. 11. Cassiodorus writes that it was founded in the time of Tullus Hostilius. See also Tacitus, Annals 12.

units.la: V.30. Alexandrum decem & octo]Decem & sex annos natum fuisse Alexandrum, cum Byzantium oppugnaret Philippus, scribit Plutarch.
units.tr: V.30. Alexandrum decem & octo.) Plutarch writes that Alexander was sixteen years old when Philip besieged Byzantium.

units.la: P.93.v.1. Athenæ]Ita è Mss. vnus, & Orosius Ms. lib. 3. cap.13 & Front. lib.2. cap.4. Ceteri partim Methe, partim Mirtheas vitio librariorum, qui litteram m ex vocis Scytharum extrema, addiderunt. Straboni lib.7. est Ariæ. & Plut. in Apophr. & 2. de fort. Alexand.
units.tr: P.93, v. 1. Athenae.) So one manuscript, and the Orosius manuscript, book 3, ch. 13, and Frontinus, book 2, ch. 4. The others have partly Methe, partly Mirtheas, through the error of copyists who added the letter m from the end of the word for the Scythians. In Strabo, book 7, it is Ariae. Plutarch, in the Apophthegms, and in On the Fortune of Alexander.

units.la: V.4. Rex decedens]Vert. rex recedens: vulgaram lectionem & sequentia comprobant, & Orosius sequitur. Ifri- anorum rege mortuo, inquit, &c.
units.tr: V.4. Rex decedens.) Some read rex recedens; the common reading and what follows confirm it, and Orosius follows it: "When the king of the Ifrianorum had died," he says, etc.

units.la: V.17. Alimentis exhibeat]Exhibere est alere, & alimenta præstare. Infra lib 11. & 22. L.1.§ 1. D. de ossi. præf. vrb. L. Nesennius 36. de negot. gest. L.fi quis à liberis, in prin. de liber. agnosc.
units.tr: V.17. Alimentis exhibeat.) To exhibit is to nourish and to provide maintenance. Below, book 11 and 22; Law 1, §1, D. de officio praefecti urbi; L. Nesennius 36, de negotiis gestis; L. si quis a liberis, in principio, de liberali agnoscendo.

units.la: P.94.v.12 Bellum Athenienses]Anno xxii. Diodorus. Iunxerunt se Atheniensibus 1 hebani, Demosthenis eloquentia persuasi. Diod. Plutarchus in Demosthene. Gemistus lib.2.
units.tr: P.94, v. 12. Bellum Athenienses.) In the twenty-second year, Diodorus. The Thebans joined the Athenians, persuaded by the eloquence of Demosthenes. Diodorus; Plutarch in Demosthenes; Gemistus, book 2.

units.la: V. 22. Pralio commisso] Ad Chæronæam, quo victor Philippus, πατρὶς τῆς Ἐλλάδος κύρα, præter Diod. & Plutarch. Gemist. vide Strab.9. Paufaniam Achaic. & Bæoticis, Ælian. 12.
units.tr: V.22. Proelio commisso.) At Chaeronea, where Philip was victor, "the fatherland of Greece" [πατρὶς τῆς Ἑλλάδος]. Besides Diodorus, Plutarch and Gemistus, see Strabo, book 9; Pausanias in Achaica and Boeotica; Aelian 12.
V.30. Dissimulata laetitia.) Read Aelian, book 8.

units.la: P.95.V.11.Sepulturam Vendidit]Emendandus est Orosius lib. 3. cap. 14. ex Ms. Mortuorum mortes, Venditiones captiuitatis, Viatorum Cnius regis frans, ferocia, d'minatus agricauit, a Ms. abest vox mortes. mortuorum venditionem hunc intellige.
units.tr: P.95, v. 11. Sepulturam vendidit.) Orosius, book 3, ch. 14, must be emended from the manuscript: "deaths of the dead, sales of captivity, of travellers ..."; the word mortes is absent from the manuscript. Understand here "the sale of the dead."

units.la: V.33. Ducetillo]Erat enim declaratus ςυγμὸς αὐτοκράτωρ ἐκ Ἐλλάδος. Diod. sub anno xxiv. Geoig. Gemist. 2. P.96.. P.96.v.7. Amyntam] Eius Gemiftus nullam mentione facit neq; Diod. De Philippi morte, vide Diod. Ciceronē de Fato. Ælian.extr. lib 3. Valerium lib.1. cap. vlt. & Plutarch.Alexand.& Pauf.Arcad.
units.tr: V.33. Ducetillo.) For he had been declared supreme commander (autokrator) from Greece. Diodorus under the twenty-fourth year; Georgius; Gemistus, book 2. P.96. P.96, v. 7. Amyntam.) Gemistus makes no mention of him, nor does Diodorus. On the death of Philip, see Diodorus; Cicero, On Fate; Aelian, end of book 3; Valerius, book 1, last ch.; Plutarch, Alexander; and Pausanias, Arcadica.

units.la: Ibid. Cuius soror erem] Attalum Cleopatræ θείου, id est auunculum,aut patruum vocat Plutarch Alexãd. Diod. & Gemiftus ἀδελφιδοῦν, id eft, ἀδελφῆς υἱόν, pro quo forte Iuftinus aut Trogus, apud Græcum auctorem legerat ἀδελφόν.
units.tr: Ibid. Cuius soror erem.) Plutarch, in Alexander, calls Attalus the theios of Cleopatra, that is, her uncle or paternal uncle. Diodorus and Gemistus call him adelphidous, that is, son of a sister; perhaps Justin or Trogus, in the Greek author, had read adelphon [ἀδελφόν].

units.la: V.28. Ducatu]Vtitur hac voce ex tr.lib.2.& inf. lib.30. & Sueton.Tiber.cap.19. & Neronc cap.35. Vtitur & Suetonio antiquior,Curtius:& in Gloffario veteri, Ducatus eft ηγεμονία.
units.tr: V.28. Ducatu: He uses this word here, as in Trogus book 2 and below in book 30, and Suetonius in Tiberius ch. 19 and Nero ch. 35. Curtius, who is earlier than Suetonius, also uses it, and in an old glossary ducatus is rendered as leadership [ἡγεμονία].

units.la: P.97. v. 3. Exnouerca] Quæ inclufa videt abfúntab optimis libris,habetur tamen in vno Cuiacii codice, neq; videntur reiicienda. Ad ea vide Plut. in Alexandro.
units.tr: P.97. v. 3. Exnouerca: The words enclosed in brackets are absent from the best manuscripts, but they are found in one of Cuiacius's manuscripts, and they do not seem to be rejected. On these see Plutarch in Alexander.

units.la: V.24. Cleopatram] Paufaniæ in Arcadicis non conuenit cum hac narratione.
units.tr: V.24. Cleopatram: Pausanias in the Arcadica does not agree with this account.

units.la: P.98. v. r. Fair rex]Locum hunc adducit Saresb. Policratici lib.5.cap.12.& Mss. lectionem comprobat.
units.tr: P.98. v. r. Fair rex: John of Salisbury cites this passage in Policraticus book 5, chapter 12, and confirms the reading of the manuscripts.

units.la: V. 10. Perfidia ] Notat Paufanias supradicto loco,& Plutarch. Pelopida,
units.tr: V. 10. Perfidia: Pausanias notes this in the passage mentioned above, and Plutarch in Pelopidas.
IN LIB. X.

units.la: A Rhaxerxi]Qui Mnemon dictus est:eius vitam fcripfit Plutarchus, quem vide, & Ælianum fine lib. 9. Iuftitiæ eum fama floruiffe Probus & idem Plutarchus auctores funt.
units.tr: Rhaxerxi] Who was called Mnemon. Plutarch wrote his life, which see, and Aelian (without book 9 of his Varia Historia). Probus and Plutarch himself are the authorities that he flourished with a reputation for justice.
V.34. Ariaratcs] The older copies read Aralratus; Plutarch has Ariaspes.

units.la: P.101.v.19. Darius pofthalaucrat] Lex erat apud Perfas, ὅπερ ἀπὸ τὸν ἀναδιξάμενον τὸ αἴτημα, ἡ ἀδικος τὸν ἀναδιξαμένον παῖς τὸ αἴτημα, ἀνυπέρ ἡ ἄδωρος. Plutarch.
units.tr: P.101 v.19. Darius posthac laudavit] There was a law among the Persians, [ὅπερ ἀπὸ τὸν ἀναδιξάμενον τὸ αἴτημα, ἡ ἀδικος τὸν ἀναδιξαμένον παῖς τὸ αἴτημα, ἀνυπέρ ἡ ἄδωρος.] Plutarch.

units.la: V. 22. Solis eam ] Plutarch. Dianæ quæ eft Ecbatanis, ἢ ἀναιτήν καλλισ̓ιν
units.tr: V.22. Solis eam] Plutarch, of Diana who is at Ecbatana, [ἢ ἀναιτήν καλλισ̓ιν].

units.la: V. 24. In iurgia ] quidam Ms. in Iniuriam. Iniuria etiã verbis fit, vt IC. docent, Tertull. Omnis iniuria fen in-gua,fen manu incuffa.
units.tr: V.24. In iurgia] Some manuscript reads in iniuriam. An injury is also done by words, as the jurists teach. Tertullian: "Every injury is inflicted either by the tongue or by the hand."

units.la: V.29.Ex dolore] Τῷ λυπῆς ἡ δυσφυίας. Plut.Artax.In libello περὶ φιλαδελφίας mendosè legitur Ξέρξης pro Ae- πιξίξης
units.tr: V.29. Ex dolore] [Τῷ λυπῆς ἡ δυσφυίας.] Plutarch, Artaxerxes. In the little book On brotherly love it is wrongly read "Xerxes" for "Artaxerxes" [Ξέρξης ... Ἀρταξέρξης].

units.la: Aa 2 V. 31. V.31. Ocho) Qui & ipse Artaxerxes dictus est. Diod. extremo lib.17.
units.tr: V.31. Ochus] Who is himself also called Artaxerxes. Diodorus, end of book 17.

units.la: P.102 v.3. Cadusii) Ita Ms. vnus, ceteri Adusij, alii aduerfij. Vulgo male Armenij, quia in fequentibus legerant Codomannum Armeniis praefectum. Sed Cadusij legendum conftat, ex Diodoro libro 17. a quo haec penitenda.
units.tr: P.102 v.3. Cadusii] So one manuscript reads; the others read Adusii, and others Aduersii. Commonly, and wrongly, Armenii, because in what follows they had read that Codomannus was prefect of the Armenians. But Cadusii is established as the correct reading, from Diodorus book 17, from whom these things are to be taken.

units.la: V.9 Rex à pop.) Cum prius fuiffet Asdyès, feu Asdyès, id est, ἀμφιθέρηος, vt Hefychius interpretatur. Plut. Alex. & oratione prima & fecunda de fort. Alex.
units.tr: V.9. Rex a pop.] Whereas previously he had been called Asdyes, or Asdyes, that is, [ἀμφιθέρηος], as Hesychius interprets. Plutarch, Alexander, and in the first and second orations on the fortune of Alexander.
ON BOOK XI.

units.la: DVobus libris 11. & 12. Alexandri Magni Philippi F. res geftæ continentur: quas libris 8. Arrianus Nico. medentis complexus est: Exstat de iis etiam Q. Curtii Rufi hiftoria manca & lacera: Eam emendatam & quantum potest ex Vett. codicibus restituere in animo est: Eroideo in horum duorum librorum explicatione breuior. Legedus praeterillos 17. Diodori liber, & Plutar. chi Alexader, & orationes duae περὶ τῆς Αλεξάνδρου τύχης ἀρετῆς. & Ælianus lib.3.
units.tr: The deeds of Alexander the Great, son of Philip, are contained in books 11 and 12. Arrian of Nicomedia summarised them in eight books. There also survives Q. Curtius Rufus's history of these events, though it is incomplete and mutilated. I intend to emend it and restore it as far as possible from old manuscripts. My explanation of these two books will be brief. Besides these, one may read the seventeenth book of Diodorus, Plutarch's Life of Alexander, the two orations on the fortune or the virtue of Alexander, and Aelian, book 3.

units.la: P.106 v.1. Prima illi cura) Diod. περὶ μὲν τοὺς Φορέας τὰ πολεμικὰ τῆς ἀρμονίας πυρικὰ ἡξιωσε, &c.
units.tr: p.106 v.1. First care: Diodorus: "περὶ μὲν τοὺς Φορέας τὰ πολεμικὰ τῆς ἀρμονίας πυρικὰ ἡξιωσε, &c."

units.la: V.3. Lyncestarum) Populus est Macedoniae, qui Aufidicitur Thucyd. extr. lib. 2. & Plinio, & Ptolemaeo. Strabo libro 7. Aufiacei. quomodo habent hic vett. libri.
units.tr: v.3. Lyncestae: a people of Macedonia, who are called Aufi(...) by Thucydides at the end of book 2, by Pliny and by Ptolemy. Strabo, book 7, has "Aufiacei", as the old books here read.

units.la: V.7. Gentes rebellantes compescuit) Τὰ μὲν ἃ βαρβάρα κινήσεται, ἡ τῆς ἐκ ποιήσεως ἀγκύρας αὐτοῦ. Plut. Multa in hoc auctore quę iuftum commentarium scribenti, cum Graecis comparare operae pretium esset: Ea hic annotare nou eft inftituti noftri.
units.tr: v.7. He subdued the rebellious nations: "Τὰ μὲν ἃ βαρβάρα κινήσεται, ἡ τῆς ἐκ ποιήσεως ἀγκύρας αὐτοῦ." Plutarch. There are many things in this author which it would be worth comparing with the Greeks for someone writing a full commentary. To annotate them here is not part of my plan.

units.la: V.13. Athenienses & Lacedaemonios) Haec est vett. librorum lectio: ex hiftoria & fequentibus pro Lacedaemoniis legendum Thebanos: non enim defecerunt Lacedaemonii, qui Philippi & Alexandri pacem semper fpreuerant: Supra lib 9. & infra lib.12.
units.tr: v.13. Athenians and Lacedaemonians: this is the reading of the old books. From the history and what follows, one should read "Thebans" instead of "Lacedaemonians", for the Lacedaemonians did not revolt; they had always scorned the peace of Philip and Alexander. See above, book 9, and below, book 12.

units.la: V.16. A 7ιβαλλις ab Illyriis habet Arrianus lib. 1.
units.tr: v.16. Arrian, book 1, has "Pelion" from the Illyrians.

units.la: V.25. Sub Eucidarum gente) Diod. ἀφ' Ἡρακλέους.
units.tr: v.25. Under the tribe of the Eucidae: Diodorus, "ἀφ' Ἡρακλέους" (from Heracles).

units.la: Erat autem Alexander paterno genere Hεγαλείδης, matemo Aιαxίδης Plutarch. alii: erat Hercules Thebanus, non Theffalus. In eundem lapidem impingit Iuftinus cū paulo poft, aitabHerculeÆacidarum gentem originem trahere.
units.tr: Alexander was, on his father's side, a descendant of Heracles, and on his mother's side a descendant of Aeacus, as Plutarch and others say. Hercules was a Theban, not a Thessalian. Justin stumbles over the same stone a little later, saying that Hercules traced his origin to the tribe of the Aeacidae.
p.107 v.8. Allies: "Σύνεδροι" (fellow-councillors).

units.la: V.18. Cleadas] Liber ἀνάγνωσμα de vita Alexandri, quem mihi ex bibliotheca reginæ matris vtendum dedit doctiffimus Fr. Pithœus, refert Ifmeniam quendam Thebanū τῆς αὐλομεσλοδίας ἱματίσον ἀνθρώπων, τῷ σοφὸν τῇ γραμμῇ τυγχάνοντα, in Thebanorum gratiam apud Alexandrum dixiffe.
units.tr: v.18. Cleadas: a book of readings on the life of Alexander, which the most learned Fr. Pithoeus lent me from the library of the queen mother, reports that a certain Ismenias the Theban, "τῆς αὐλομελοδίας ἱματίσον ἀνθρώπων, τῷ σοφὸν τῇ γραμμῇ τυγχάνοντα", spoke before Alexander in the Thebans' favour.

units.la: P.108.v.1. Vrbs diruitur] Præter Arrianum. Diod. Plutarch. vide Ælianum lib.13. Paufan.Arcad. & Strabo lib. 9. quiThebas fuo tempore vix tueri fcnbit ὁὶ καμέτις ἐξι-ολόγου τύπου.
units.tr: p.108 v.1. The city is destroyed: besides Arrian, see Diodorus and Plutarch, Aelian book 13, Pausanias in Arcadia, and Strabo, book 9, who writes that in his own time Thebes could hardly be made out: "ὁὶ καμέτις ἐξι-ολόγου τύπου."

units.la: V.2. Captiui] quorum erat 30000. Ceciderant autem 90000. Plut. Ælian.
units.tr: v.2. Captives: there were 30,000 of them. Ninety thousand had fallen. Plutarch, Aelian.

units.la: V.12. Ad Darium profecti] Arrianus folum Charidemum nominat.
units.tr: v.12. Having set out to Darius: Arrian names only Charidemus.
p.109 v.3. Javelin: Diodorus, year 2, "Δοχὴ".

units.la: V.10. In exercitu eius] Plutarchus fcribit quofdam Alexandro tribuere τεσσαρύρες πεζὸς, & totedit Diodor. & Arrianus:Alios πεζαχισμὸς ἱππεῖς.Equitum autem illi quinque millia, hi quatuor fuiffe tradiderunt. Diodorus in numero equitum confentit cum Iuftino: Nauibus autem longis fexaginta traiecifle Hellefpontū refert. Front. 4.cap. 2. folis hominum 40.millibus, orbe terrarum aggreffum fcribit.
units.tr: v.10. In his army: Plutarch writes that some ascribe to Alexander "τεσσαρύρες πεζὸς", and so Diodorus and Arrian; others "πεζαχισμὸς ἱππεῖς". Of the cavalry, some have handed down that he had five thousand, others four thousand. Diodorus agrees with Justin about the number of cavalry. He reports that he crossed the Hellespont with sixty long ships. Frontinus, book 4, ch. 2, writes that he attacked the world with only 40,000 men.

units.la: V.24. Affirmans fuis occulta] Sapor apud Marcellinū lib.17. Illud apud nos numquam acceptum fuit, quod adferitis ‹os exfultates, nullo diferimine virtutis ac doli, prosperes omnes laudari debere bellorum euentus. Diodorus. ἀναξίου id ait, τῆς Πηροῖς μεγαλοψυχίας.
units.tr: v.24. Asserting that his plans were hidden: Sapor, in Ammianus Marcellinus, book 17: "What you say, that exulting over successes, with no distinction between courage and trickery, all the outcomes of wars ought to be praised, was never accepted by us." Diodorus says it is unworthy of the magnanimity of the Persians: "ἀναξίου id ait, τῆς Πηροῖς μεγαλοψυχίας."

units.la: V.28. Adrastius] Steph. Ἀδράστιας πόλεως, per quod fluit Granicus fluuius, a quo hoc proelium dicitur ad Granicum, Strabo lib.13.
units.tr: v.28. Adrasteia: Stephanus, "Ἀδράστιας πόλεως", through which flows the river Granicus, from which this battle is called the battle of the Granicus. Strabo, book 13.

units.la: Ib. In acie Persarum] Diod.peditum C. mil.equitū X. qui hoc proelio Persarum peditum 10000. equitu 2000. cecidisse auctor est:Plutarch. peditum 20000.
units.tr: In the Persian battle line: Diodorus says that in this battle 10,000 Persian infantry and 2,000 cavalry fell. Plutarch says 20,000 infantry.

units.la: V.32. Novem pedites] Idem ex Aristobulo refert Plutarchus, & confirmat Orosius lib.3.cap.16. & lib.4.cap.1. ne quis cum Glareano, mendum hic esse suspicetur. Arrianus ex Macedonum auxiliis xxv. cecidisse: ex reliquis, equites xx. pedites xxx. Plutarch.ex Aristobulo, τεγάσμενα ꝑ νεκρὸς γίνεσθαι τῶς πάντας.
units.tr: v.32. Nine foot soldiers: Plutarch reports the same from Aristobulus, and Orosius, book 3, ch. 16, and book 4, ch. 1, confirms it, so that no one, with Glareanus, should suspect an error here. Arrian says that of the Macedonian auxiliaries 25 fell; of the rest, 20 cavalry and 30 infantry. Plutarch, from Aristobulus: "τεγάσμενα ꝑ νεκρὸς γίνεσθαι τῶς πάντας."
v.33. Lavishly: Diodorus, "Μεγαλεπρεπῶς."

units.la: P.110.v.1 Statuæ equestribus] Τῶν χαλκαῖ εἰκόνες ἐν Διὰ ἱερᾶσιν. Arrian.
units.tr: p.110 v.1. Equestrian statues: "Τῶν χαλκαῖ εἰκόνες ἐν Διὰ ἱερᾶσιν." Arrian.

units.la: V 2. Maior pars Asiæ] Ἡ οὗτος τῶ ταύρου ἡ τῆς Εὐφράτην. Strabo.
units.tr: v.2. The greater part of Asia: "Ἡ οὗτος τῶ ταύρου ἡ τῆς Εὐφράτην." Strabo.

units.la: V.11. Gordien] Ira vett. omnes: Græci, Γορδίων. Et ita fortasse libtari scripserat, ut infra multis locis Craterοn, τῶ facilis est in e mutatio. Stephanus vocat Fορδίδων. Hic initium habent quæ ad nos peruenerunt Q. Curtii fragmenta.
units.tr: v.11. Gordian: all the old books have this, and in Greek it is Γορδίων. Perhaps the author had written it so, as at many places below he has Craterus, since the change of i to e is easy. Stephanus calls it Gordidon. Here begin the fragments of Q. Curtius that have come down to us.

units.la: 28. Regem opus esse] Cic. ad Attic. Video mihi opus esse Gladium, vide Nonium. hic vulgo regi.
units.tr: 28. I see that I need a sword: Cicero to Atticus, "Video mihi opus esse gladium"; see Nonius. Here it is commonly read as "regi" (for the king).

units.la: P.111.v.14. Cydni] Τυχῶν δὲ Φασις ταχὺ τὸ ρεῦμα τῆς Κυδ-νου. Euftath. Vide præter Plut. Valerium lib.3.ca.vlt. Diodorus caufam morbi nullam affert.
units.tr: p.111 v.14. Cydnus: "Τυχῶν δὲ Φασις ταχὺ τὸ ρεῦμα τῆς Κυδ-νου." Eustathius. See besides Plutarch and Valerius, book 3, last chapter. Diodorus gives no cause of the illness.

units.la: V.16. In præfrigidam Cndam] Malim in præfrigidam mudam.
units.tr: v.16. Into the very cold wave: I would prefer "in præfrigidam undam".

units.la: V.30. Cum qua tringentis] Dc. millia habet Arrianus, quem numerum Persas prima congressione habuisse scriplit Iustinus, vereor ut recte: qui enim iam moueretur Alexander, Dc. millibus primo prælio superatis? Vulgo hic legitur ccc. tts millibus quod probat Orof.
units.tr: v.30. With which three hundred: Arrian gives 600,000, a number which Justin says the Persians had in the first encounter. I doubt whether this is correct, for how could Alexander already be moving, if 600,000 had been overcome in the first battle? The usual reading here is "ccc. tts millibus", which Orosius confirms.

units.la: P.112.v.16 Prælium inq.an.committitur] Ἐν Ἰσσῷ τῆς Κιλικίας. Diod. anno iii. M.Cic.ep.ad Cœlium. Hoc prælio ex millia cæsa. Plut. vt Diodorus peditum duodecim myriades, equitum x.millia.
units.tr: p.112 v.16. Battle is joined: "Ἐν Ἰσσῷ τῆς Κιλικίας." Diodorus, year 3. M. Cicero to Caelius. In this battle six thousand were slain. Plutarch, like Diodorus, gives twelve myriads of infantry and 10,000 cavalry.

units.la: V.21 GXXX.] Mitor Fr. Fabricium diligentissimum hominem notare ad Orosium, cum Iustino facere Diodorum: qui ἱππάρχους habet, id est ttecentos.
units.tr: v.21. GXXX.: I wonder that the most diligent man, Fr. Fabricius, notes in Orosius that Diodorus agrees with Justin, for Diodorus has "ἱππάρχους", that is, three hundred.

units.la: V.28. Non mortem] Malim vitam, vt quidam ediderunt contra librorum Mss. fidem. Deprecari enim hoc loco est valde precari. Vide Gellium lib.6. cap.16. Infra lib.12. auxilia aduerfus Bruttios deprecantibus. Quamuis & apud hunc auctorem diuersam significationem habeat.
units.tr: v.28. Not death: I would prefer life, as some editors have published against the faith of the manuscripts. For to deprecate here is strongly to pray. See Gellius, book 6, ch. 16. Below, in book 12: auxilia adversus Bruttios deprecantibus. Although with this author it also has a different meaning.

units.la: {y} Marginal reference numbers 35, 40, 30, 25, 20, 15, 10 run down the margins beside the lines.
units.tr: {y} Marginal reference numbers 35, 40, 30, 25, 20, 15, 10 run down the margins beside the lines.

units.la: P.113.v.4. Barsenen] Barsinen Darii filiam commemorat Arria.lib.7. quam deuicto Dario Alexander in vxorem duxit:de ea lib. 13.infra.
units.tr: p.113 v.4. Barsene: Arrian, book 7, mentions Barsine, daughter of Darius, whom Alexander took as his wife after defeating Darius. About her see below, book 13.

units.la: V.15. Abdalonimus] Diod. βασιλισμος vocat, non Sidonis,sed Tyri regem constitutum:vide Curt. Vet.noftri mire variant.
units.tr: v.15. Abdalonymus: Diodorus calls him "βασιλισμος". He says that he was set up as king not of Sidon but of Tyre. See Curtius. Our old texts vary remarkably.

units.la: V.24. Ideum in Tyro] Vet. deum Tyro: legendum arbitror id eum in Tyro vetere,antiquiore templo:sine copula. Dicebatur enim locus ille παλαίυτε. Curtium vide & Arrian.lib.2. Diod.anno iv. & Plut.
units.tr: v.24. Ideum in Tyro: the old reading is deum Tyro. I think one should read id eum in Tyro vetere, antiquiore templo, without a conjunction, for that place was called ancient. See Curtius, Arrian, book 2, Diodorus, year 4, and Plutarch.

units.la: P.114.v.3. Inde Rhodum] Orosius hanc lectionem sequitur lib.3. cap.16. & 17. quae mihi propter Mss. varietatem,suspecta est: Eorum plerique habent. Inter haec dum Alexander Aeg.Cil scer.recepit,ad Iouem Hammone,&c.
units.tr: p.114 v.3. Thence to Rhodes: Orosius follows this reading in book 3, chs. 16 and 17. Because of the variety of the manuscripts it seems suspect to me. Most of them have: Meanwhile, while Alexander received Egypt and Cilicia, he went to Jupiter Ammon, etc.

units.la: P.115.v.4. Quadringenti millibus] Ita Vet. omnes, antea mendose legebatur xl. millibus. Etiam hoc numero differunt scriptores. Videndus Curtius.
units.tr: p.115 v.4. Four hundred thousand: so all the old books have it; formerly it was wrongly read as forty thousand. Writers differ even on this number. Curtius should be consulted.

units.la: P.116.v.2. Cum etiam in otio] Legendum forte cuius.
units.tr: p.116 v.2. Although also in leisure: perhaps one should read cuius (whose).

units.la: V.23. Praelium committitur)E'v Ταυχαμηλοις προς ποτα-μῷ Βυμαδών,ἀπίχων Α'φοίλων τῆς πολιος ὄντα ἐξαργοις πα-δίας Att. 3. Inde dicta pugna ad Arbela. Orosius nescio quo auctore apud Tarsum pugnatum scripsit,lib.3.ca.17. Tacit.12. Annal. vocat castellum infigne fama, suppressio nomine.
units.tr: v.23. Battle is joined: "Ἐν Ταυχαμηλοις προς ποταμῷ Βυμαδών, ἀπίχων Α'φοίλων τῆς πολιος ὄντα ἐξαργοις πα-δίας", Arrian, book 3. Hence the battle is called the battle at Arbela. Orosius, on I know not what authority, wrote in book 3, ch. 17, that the fight took place at Tarsus. Tacitus, Annals 12, calls it a castle of famous name, with the name suppressed.

units.la: P.117.v.7. In Urbe clausa)Lego Susa ex Diod.princ.posterioris partis lib. 17. vbi agnoscit eundem pecuniae numerum.
units.tr: p.117 v.7. In the closed city: I read Susa, from Diodorus at the beginning of the latter part of book 17, where he records the same sum of money.

units.la: V.9. Persepolin) Ita & Steph. Straboni Περσεπολις lib. 15. ἢ δὲ ἡ Περσέπολις ἔχουσα βασιλέως σκηνάς καὶ κλίσεα τῇ φολυτελείᾳ τῶν κειμένων.
units.tr: v.9. Persepolis: so Stephanus also has it. Strabo, book 15: "Persepolis, however, possessing the king's tents and couches, is remarkable for the sumptuousness of its furnishings": "ἢ δὲ ἡ Περσέπολις ἔχουσα βασιλέως σκηνάς καὶ κλίσεα τῇ φολυτελείᾳ τῶν κειμένων."

units.la: V.31. Applicito capsino) Locus absque dubio mendosus: legendum arbitrabar, applicato capite. Veteres cum vulgatis consentiunt.
units.tr: v.31. Applicito capsino: the passage is doubtless corrupt. I would read "applicato capite"; the old books agree with the printed text.
p.118 v.11. Royal gods: "Θεὸς βασιλείας." Plutarch.

units.la: V.18. Pignus fidei regiae dexteram) Probus in Datame fidemque de eare more Persarum dextra dedisset. Diod. lib.16. Καὶ τὴν δεξιὰν ἔδωκε τοῦ Φερνάβαζου, ἐπὶ δὲ ἡ πίστις αὐτὴ βασιλεωτάτη παρὰ τοῖς Πέρσαις. Gemitus lib.2.
units.tr: v.18. Pledge of royal faith, the right hand: Probus, in the life of Datames: "and he gave his faith on it by right hand, in the manner of the Persians." Diodorus, book 16: "And he gave his right hand to Pharnabazus, and this faith is the most royal among the Persians": "Καὶ τὴν δεξιὰν ἔδωκε τοῦ Φερνάβαζου, ἐπὶ δὲ ἡ πίστις αὐτὴ βασιλεωτάτη παρὰ τοῖς Πέρσαις." Gemitus, book 2.

units.la: V.19. Porreda) Plut. λαμβανόμενος τῆς τῆς Πολυχρατης χειρὸς καὶ ξλίαν. Pene fugerat me,notare in Mss. Δαρείου esse Dareum Dareum sine, vt apud Horatium & auctorem nostrum Alexandrea, & infra Cassandrea, lib. 24. Græcis Ἀλέξανδρια, & Κασσανδρ[ε]ια. Et Balneum hiisdem est βαλανεῖον.
units.tr: v.19. Porreda: Plutarch: "λαμβανόμενος τῆς τῆς Πολυχρατης χειρὸς καὶ ξλίαν." I had almost failed to note that in the manuscripts "Δαρείου" is Dareum, written "Dareum" without the other letter, as in Horace and in our author Alexandrea, and below Cassandrea, book 24. In Greek, Ἀλέξανδρια and Κασσανδρ[ε]ια. And the bath is likewise βαλανεῖον.
On Book XII.

units.la: Ecbatana] Ex vestigiis scripturæ veteris odoratus sum leg. Ecbatana congesta. Vet. enim habent & batanis congesta: quidam ex ebatanu: alii aliter. Diod. posteriore parte lib. 17. Parmenioni commissos refert τὰς βασιλέως θησαυρούς ἐν Ἐκβατάνοις ἴχοντας πολλῶν ὀκτωκαιδεκα μυ-ριάδας. Vide & Strab. ‹s.
units.tr: Ecbatana] From traces of the old text I have guessed the reading should be "Ecbatana congesta." The old manuscripts have "et batanis congesta," and some have "ex ebatanu," and others differ again. Diodorus, toward the end of the latter part of book 17, reports that the king's treasures were entrusted to Parmenio at Ecbatana, amounting to more than eighteen myriads [ὅντας τοὺς βασιλέως θησαυροὺς ἐν Ἐκβατάνοις ὄντας πολλῶν ὀκτωκαίδεκα μυριάδας]. See also Strabo.

units.la: V.16. Gracia]Diod. extremo partis prioris lib.17.Curtius lib. 6.
units.tr: V.16. Gracia] Diodorus, at the end of the first part of book 17; Curtius, book 6.

units.la: V.27. Alexander rex Epiri]Vide Liuium lib.8. Strabo lib. 6. contra Mellapios & Lucanos euocatum scribit.
units.tr: V.27. Alexander, king of Epirus] See Livy, book 8. Strabo, book 6, writes that he was summoned against the Messapians and Lucanians.

units.la: P.121.v.3. Amnemque Acherufium]Strabo τὸν Ἀχερούσιον: & ita in sequentibus Mss. Plin. 3. cap. 11. Oraculum exstat apud Strab. & Stephanum.
units.tr: P.121.v.3. Amnemque Acherusium] Strabo has "the Acherusian" [τὸν Ἀχερούσιον], and the manuscripts have it so in what follows. Pliny, book 3, chapter 11. The oracle survives in Strabo and Stephanus.

units.la: V.10. Brundufium]Vet. Brundisium. Græci, Βρεντέσιον, vnde a poetis Brenda dictum, Festus: aut potius Brenta, a. in a. voce duabus syllabis truncata, quod est Ennio familiare. de eo Strabo lib. 6. & Steph. In Mss. pro Æoli, legitur Æsculi, aut Esculi, aut etiam Etcoli. Habitatum à Gretensibus Brundusium auctor est Strabo, & Lucanus lib. 2. & 5.
units.tr: V.10. Brundusium] The old form is Brundisium. The Greeks have "Brentesion" [Βρεντέσιον], from which the poets called it Brenda, as Festus says; or rather Brenta, with the word shortened to two syllables by dropping the final vowel, which is a habit of Ennius. Strabo, book 6, and Stephanus speak of it. In the manuscripts, for "Aeoli" one reads "Aesculi," or "Esculi," or even "Etcoli." Strabo is the authority that Brundusium was settled by the Cretans, and so is Lucan, books 2 and 5.

units.la: V. 23. Et Pediculis.]Italiæ populi.Plin.l.3.c.7.Strab.lib. 6. Ποιδίκλαος vocati, in Mss. Legitur Peditulí. Inde qui libros imprefios emendarunt, fecerunt Rutuli, longe petita coniectura.
units.tr: V.23. And the Pediculi.] Peoples of Italy; Pliny, book 3, chapter 7; Strabo, book 6, who call them Pedicli [Ποιδίκλαοι]. In the manuscripts one reads "Peditulí." From this, those who edited the printed books made it "Rutuli," a conjecture far fetched.

units.la: P.122.v.13. Mardosque] Quidam hoc loco legerunt Medos, quomodo & in Eusebio editum est, contra libros.
units.tr: P.122.v.13. And the Mardi] Some have read "Medi" here, as is also printed in Eusebius, against the books.

units.la: V.14. Thalestris] Strabonis. est Θαλέστρια. Trecentis mulieribus edidi, vnius codicis fidem sequutus, & Diodorum sub anno 7.
units.tr: V.14. Thalestris] Strabo's form is Thalestria [Θαλέστρια]. I printed "three hundred women," following the authority of a single manuscript, and Diodorus under the year 7.

units.la: P.123.v.3. Patria nomen eiuraret] Quomodo patriæ nomen eiurarit Alexander non capio: à moribus quidem patriis discessisse manifestum est: non ideo tamen Persa haberi voluit. Quid si legamus,patris nomen: Ilouis enim filium fe, non Philippi dicebat. Plerique Mss. patrie nominem uraret. Simili mendo infectus Gellius cap. 2. lib.1. sanctissime disciplinae nomine mentirentur. Leg. nomen ementirentur.
units.tr: P.123.v.3. Should renounce the name of his country] I do not understand how Alexander could renounce the name of his country. He had certainly departed from his native customs, but he did not therefore wish to be thought a Persian. What if we read the name of his father? For he called himself the son of Jupiter, not of Philip. Most manuscripts have should disown the name of his country. Gellius, book 1, chapter 2, is infected by a similar error: would lie under the name of a most holy discipline. Read should falsely claim the name.

units.la: Laborem militiae] Tacitus lib.3.Annal. bella plane accindis obeunda; sed reuertentibus post labrem, quod bone sless quam vxorum lenamentum? Difputatur eo loco, An magistratum in prouinciam euntem comitari vxor debeat.
units.tr: The toil of soldiering] Tacitus, Annals book 3: they must undertake wars in full armour; but when they return after their toil, what is more pleasant than a wife's flattery? The passage discusses whether a wife ought to accompany a magistrate going out to a province.

units.la: V.26. Epigoni] Quo nomine, & eorum qui ad Thebas cum Polynice occubuerant, posteri cenfebantur.
units.tr: V.26. Epigoni] By this name were called the descendants of those who had fallen with Polynices at Thebes.

units.la: P.124.v.14. Parimas Parapammenos] Ex Diodoro fub anno 8, & aliis legendum arbitror Paropamisadas. Adafpii qui fiut non inuenio: quod vulgo legitur Hydaspii, nomen eft ab Hydafpe Indiae fluuio confictum: Nec placet quod Cafpios quidam ediderunt: Quid fi Arios legamus? Omnino arbitror duas syllabas priores ta Adafpios, ex voce Paropamisadae, adhaefiffe fequenti vocabulo, vnde factum fit Adafarios. Inde Adafpios. Sed his vocib. reftituendis diuino eft opus.
units.tr: P.124.v.14. Parimae, Parapamenae] From Diodorus under the year 8, and in my opinion other authors, we should read Paropamisadae. I cannot find the Adaspii who are mentioned; what is commonly read as Hydaspii is a name invented from the river Hydaspes in India. Nor do I approve of the reading Caspii that some have printed. What if we read Arii? I think the first two syllables, ta of Adaspios, have clung to the following word, from the word Paropamisadae, whence came Adasarii, and then Adaspii. But restoring these words needs a divine.

units.la: P.126.v.5. Chorafmos] Arriano lib. 4. xwgoμívos. Strab. xwgoμουνοσ. Plinio Chorafmii. Daha, Graecis func Δάα. Pro quo hic quidam Saca repofuerunt, Curtius 7. Chorafmios, Dahas, & Sacas coniungit, & Solinus capi- te fr.
units.tr: P.126.v.5. Chorasmi] Arrian, book 4, has "Chorasmians" [χωρασμίους]; Strabo "Chorasmuni" [χωρασμουνοί]; Pliny "Chorasmii." The Dahae are called by the Greeks "Daai" [Δάαι]. In place of this, some here have put "Sacae"; Curtius, book 7, joins the Chorasmians, Dahae and Sacae, and Solinus in the chapter on...
V.18. Nysan] So Stephanus and Strabo, book 14. Arrian has "Nysaean" [νύσαιαν].

units.la: P.127.v.3. Saxum] Πέτρα Α᾽ογρ fcu Α᾽ογυς, vt habet Diod. fub anno 8.& Q. Curtii Mss, lib.8.
units.tr: P.127.v.3. Rock] Petra [Πέτρα], or Aornos or Aornus [Ἄορνος / Ἄορνος], as Diodorus has it under the year 8, and in the manuscripts of Q. Curtius, book 8.

units.la: V.25. Adreftae] Mss.plerique Arefas, Arrian. 5. Adpai-sus vocat. Diod. Arefiros, vt hie quidam ediderunt. Gedeami, (ita habent Mss. aut Gefani) in Ms. Orofio func Cathens, Fabricius ex Arriano edidit Cathaei, eos Kaefaeos vocat Diodorus. Prafidae, feu Prafidia Curtio libro 9. funt Pharrasii. Idem habet Gargaridas, vt hic edidi ex Mss. Graecis Παργαριτῶν, & Παρσαγειδῶν, de quibus ad Curtium plenius.
units.tr: V.25. Adrestae] Most manuscripts have Arestas; Arrian, book 5, calls them Adraistai. Diodorus has Arestiri, as some here have printed. The Gedeami (so the manuscripts, or Gefani): in one manuscript of Orosius it reads Cathens; Fabricius, following Arrian, printed Cathaei; Diodorus calls them Kaesaeans. The Prasidae, or Prasidia in Curtius, book 9, are the Pharrasii. The same author has Gargaridae, as I have printed here from the Greek manuscripts, Pargaritai [Παργαριτῶν] and Parsageidai [Παρσαγειδῶν]; more fully on these in my notes on Curtius.

units.la: V.27. Cufites] Hic, vt caeteris locis omnibus Mss. librorum feqhutus fum lectionem. Orofius Ms. Cefides, quo loco Fr. Fabricius arbitratur accipienda haec effe de So-phite, phite, de quo Curtius 9. sed Sophiten Strab. Ζωπίτλω ildelevocat, Cathea præfuisse lib.17. scribit, quam iam ante deuictam esse ab Alexandro patet ex superioribus, si pro Gefteanos legamus Cathenos, aut Carbaos, vt in Orosio Fabricius. Ista ad Curtium pluribus.
units.tr: V.27. Cusites] Here, as in all other places, I have followed the reading of the manuscripts. The Orosius manuscript has Cesides, which Fr. Fabricius thinks should be understood of the Sophites, of whom Curtius speaks, book 9. But Strabo calls the Sophites Zopyrion [Ζωπύριον] and writes that he governed Cathaea, book 17, which had already been subdued by Alexander, as is clear from what precedes, if for Gesteanos we read Cathenos, or Carbaos, as Fabricius does in Orosius. More on these matters in my notes on Curtius.

units.la: V.32. Ostendere aliud canicicm) Tacit.lib.1. Ann. hi Verberum notas, illi canicicm, plurimi detrita tegmina, & nudum corpus exprobrantes.
units.tr: V.32. To show another dog] Tacitus, Annals book 1: some reproach them with the marks of the lash, others with the dog, most with their worn cloaks and naked bodies.

units.la: P.128.v.14. Huacensianas Sileosque) Quidam Ms. Agefimas Syrosq., forte Acefinas Sibosque, vt illi sint fluuii Acefinis accoleshi sint quos Sobos vocat Curtius Strabo 16 & Steph. & Arrianus Sibas Diod. mendose 1655.
units.tr: P.128.v.14. Huacensians and Sileans] One manuscript has Agesimas and Syros, perhaps Acesinas and Sibos, so that they are the people living by the river Acesines, whom Curtius calls the Sobi. Strabo, book 16, Stephanus, and Arrian call them Sibae; Diodorus, carelessly, 1655.

units.la: V.16. In Ambros & Sugambros) Mandros & Subagras habet Orosius Ms. Fabricius emendauit Mallos & Oxydracas, vt hoc loco quidam ediderunt. Plin. lib.12. cap.6. Sydracas, vocat expeditionum Alexandri terminum. Curtius 9. Sudracas, quomodo & Iustinus, & Orosius, & Diodorus emendandi.
units.tr: V.16. Among the Ambri and Sugambri] Orosius in the manuscript has Mandros and Subagras. Fabricius emended to Mallos and Oxydracas, as some here have printed. Pliny, book 12, chapter 6, calls the Sydracae the limit of Alexander's expeditions. Curtius, book 9, has Sudracae, as also Justin, Orosius and Diodorus, to be corrected.

units.la: P.129.v.9. Ambigeri) Forte is est quem Sambam vocat Diodorus: Samam Curtius, Ambyram Orosius.
units.tr: P.129.v.9. Ambigeri] Perhaps this is the one Diodorus calls Sambas; Curtius Samas, Orosius Ambyras.

units.la: V.19. Curru circa metam acto) Quod solebant qui ad metam peruenerant, inde Horat. Metaque feruidis euitata rotis. Vett. plerique curru certamine iam acto, aut peracto. Sed & Orosius & vnus Ms. vulgatam lectionem tuentur.
units.tr: V.19. Driven round the turning-post in a chariot] Because those who had reached the turning-post used to do so; hence Horace: and the goal avoided by the glowing wheels. Most old editions have in a chariot-race now driven, or finished. But Orosius and one manuscript support the common reading.

units.la: V.27. Babyloniam redit) Μυπρογινὸν Iustini ἀμέγπρο: Inquit enim paulo post. Hac ex causa Babyloniam sestissamus: Et quæ sequuntur Sufis magnam partem acta esse ex Diodoro, & Arriano, & ceteris constat.
units.tr: V.27. He returns to Babylon] Justin's phrase is in the meantime; for he says a little later: for this reason he hastened to Babylon. And what follows, that the events of Susa were largely taken from Diodorus, Arrian and the others, is clear.

units.la: V.31. Optimatibus Macedonum) Διανέμων τὰς ἀρίσας τοῖς ἀρίσοις. Plut.
units.tr: V.31. To the Macedonian nobles] Distributing the best things to the best men [Διανέμων τὰ ἄριστα τοῖς ἀρίστοις]. Plutarch.

units.la: P.130.v.f. Magis, quam à creditoribus gratiam) Magis comparatiuo iunctum. Prisc.lib.3. Plautus magis maiores mugas dixit.
units.tr: P.130.v.f. Rather than favour from creditors] Magis joined to a comparative. Priscian, book 3: Plautus said magis maiores, more greater.

units.la: V.14. Cum patre inire bella) Dixit vt Arrianus 7. μετὰ τῶ πολεὶς προσπτόις. Vulgo finire minus recte.
units.tr: V.14. To wage war with his father] He said it as Arrian, book 7, has with the citizens [μετὰ τῶν πολιτῶν]. The common reading finire ("to end") is less correct.

units.la: Ibid. Quatinus) Ita Vett. est autem quatinus, quoniam Festo & Frontino.
units.tr: Ibid. Inasmuch as] So the old texts have it; but quatenus is also quoniam, as in Festus and Frontinus.

units.la: P.131.v.13. Ephastion decedit) Ecbatanis: præter sepe citatos auctores, vide Ælia lib. 7. Eum vt heroë coluit Alexander. Arria.
units.tr: P.131.v.13. Hephaestion dies] At Ecbatana. Besides the authors often cited, see Aelian, book 7: Alexander honoured him as a hero. Arrian.

units.la: Quidam ex magis) Vide Senecæ suasoriam 4. in ea censeo legendum Babylone excluditur, cui patuit Oceanus, vulgo Babylone cluditur: nili mauis Babylone es cluditur.
units.tr: Some of the Magi] See Seneca's suasoria 4. In that place I think we should read Babylon is shut out, to which the Ocean lay open; the common reading is Babylon is shut in, unless you prefer Babylon is shut in.

units.la: V.29 Byrfi.an) Huius loci nemo præter hunc meminit. P.132.v.4. Medicus Theffalus) In omnibus libris etiam scriptis mendum est: legendum enim Medus, Μηδ•ὁ Θέσσαλος, Attia, lib.7. Diod extr.lib.17. Plut.
units.tr: V.29 Byrsa-] No one but this author mentions this place. P.132.v.4. Thessalian physician] In all the books, even the manuscripts, there is an error: we should read Medus, the Thessalian [Μῆδος ὁ Θεσσαλός]. Aelian, book 7; Diodorus at the end of book 17; Plutarch.

units.la: V.6. Velutsi tele) Ο ὑσπερ λόγχη πταλαγὼς. Plutarchus, qui hæc confiĉta scribit, neque Alexandrum veneno interiisse, quod & Arrianus.
units.tr: V.6. As if from a spear] As if a spear had dripped [ὥσπερ λόγχη πταλαγῶς]. Plutarch, who writes these things as fiction, says that Alexander did not die from poison, as Arrian also says.

units.la: V.29. Præguffare) Plutarch. vocat ἀχίσους. Hieronymo ειρογὸς, dicitur minister vinarius.
units.tr: V.29. Pre-tasting] Plutarch calls them ἀχίσους; Jerome ειρογὸς; the term denotes a wine-steward.

units.la: P.133. v.17. Stbi parentatura) Αγαῦρα ἱππάφιον, vocat, Diod.17.&18.
units.tr: P.133. v.17. Would prepare the funeral rites for himself] Diodorus, books 17 and 18, calls him Agaura, the horseman [Ἀγαῦρα ἱππάφιον].
V.20 Most worthy] To the excellent one [Τῷ ἐξθρίσῳ]. Diodorus.

units.la: V.32. Voce nuncupatus heres) Nuncupatiuum teftamentum quid sit explicant I C. eo vtebantur cum vrgente vi valitudinis non sufficerent ad obsignandas testamenti tabulas. Suet. in vita Horatii: in qua nomen consulis emendandum est, vt pro C. Mario Censorino, legamus C. Marcio Censorino, ex Cassiodoro, & Dione.
units.tr: V.32. Named heir by voice] The jurists explain what a nuncupative will is: people used it when the urgency of illness did not allow them to seal the tablets of a will. In Suetonius's life of Horace the name of the consul must be corrected: instead of C. Marius Censorinus we should read C. Marcius Censorinus, from Cassiodorus and Dio.

units.la: P.134.v.1. Annos iii. & xxx) M.Cicero Philipp. 5. ceteri, annos xxxii. menses viii.
units.tr: P.134.v.1. Years iii and xxx] Cicero, Philippics 5. Others have years xxxii, months viii.

units.la: V.10. Prodigia) De quibus Plutarch. in eius vita.
units.tr: V.10. Portents] Of which Plutarch speaks in his life.
In Book XIII.

units.la: Sed Iamici) Vulgo legitur, sed nec amici. Nec, quod in vno tantum Ms. reperi, inducendum curaui. Frustra ex- (pectabat regnum cum omnes pares essent, & æqualitas discordiam augeret, vt paulo post lib. 16. dicet. Æquales enim æqualibus imperare contra naturam est, & qui in alios regnū exercere vult, ὡς ὅσος οἱ ἀνθρώποις esse debet, vt Aristot. loquitur.
units.tr: But Iamici: the common reading is sed nec amici. I have not thought it right to introduce that reading, since I found it in only one manuscript. It vainly awaited a kingdom, since all were equals, and equality increases discord, as he says a little later in book 16. For equals to rule over equals is contrary to nature, and one who wishes to exercise kingship over others ought to be [ὡς ὅσος οἱ ἀνθρώποις], as Aristotle puts it.

units.la: V.13 Spectabant) Vulgo exspectabant Supra lib. 2. rex Gelut spectator pugna. Vet. plerique spectabant pugna. M. Cicero epist. ad Cassium ea, quæ est 16. lib 15. Longiores enim exspectabo, vel potius exigam. Nonius exiecre, citat hoc modo. Longiores enim spectabo, vel potius exigam, quando hercle eo tempore exigam. locum eo adscripsi, quia poltre-
units.tr: V.13 Spectabant: the common reading is exspectabant. Above, in book 2, we have rex Gelon spectator pugnae, and most of the old copies have spectabant pugnae. M. Cicero, in the letter to Cassius which is the 16th of book 15: For I shall wait longer, or rather I shall drive out. Nonius, under exigere, quotes it in this way: For I shall wait longer, or rather I shall drive out, since by Hercules I shall drive out at that time. I have quoted the passage there because the last words

units.la: postrema verba in Cicetonis editionibus nulla sunt: quæ Nonius tamen, vt Ciceronis, adsert.
units.tr: the last words are absent from the editions of Cicero, yet Nonius quotes them as Cicero's.

units.la: P. 137. v. 3. Roxanis] Ea etat Oxyattis Bactriani filia. Art. lib. 7. vide Curtium lib. 9.
units.tr: P. 137, v. 3. Roxanis: she was the daughter of Oxyartes the Bactrian. See Arrian book 7 and Curtius book 9.

units.la: V. 18. Maternas sordes] Vide Plutarchum exttemo vitæ. Alexandri.
units.tr: V. 18. Maternas sordes: see Plutarch at the end of the Life of Alexander.

units.la: V. 30. Arideum Al. fr. regem] Legendus Diod. initio lib. 18. & Curt. lib. 10. Seneca de benef. Quid sibi voluit prouid. nisa, quæ Arrhideum regno imposuit? illi putas hoc datum patri eius datum est, & fratri.
units.tr: V. 30. Arideum, Alexander's half-brother, as king: read Diodorus at the start of book 18 and Curtius book 10. Seneca, On Benefits: What did that far-sighted woman intend, who set Arrhideus over the kingdom? Do you think this was given to his father? It was given to his father and to his brother.

units.la: P. 138. v. 9. Attalus, ad interf.] Mcleagro id tribuit Curt. lib. 10.
units.tr: P. 138, v. 9. Attalus, to the killing: Curtius book 10 attributes this to Meleager.

units.la: 32. Corpus Alexandri] Quod ad id tempus infepultū fuerat. Ælian. extr. lib. 12. Alexandria autem deportatum à Ptolemæo, idem auctor est, & Strabo 17. & Diod. 18.
units.tr: 32. The body of Alexander: it had lain unburied up to that time. Aelian, extract from book 12. That it was carried to Alexandria by Ptolemy the same author says, and Strabo 17 and Diodorus 18.

units.la: P. 139. v. 8. Arabiaque pars] Mss. vnum & Orofium lib. 3. cap. 23. expressi. Mss. enim ceteri Asia Libyaque pars.
units.tr: P. 139, v. 8. And the part of Arabia: I have followed one manuscript and Orosius book 3 chapter 23. The other manuscripts read Asia and the part of Libya.

units.la: V. 11. Cleomenes] Dinocrates dicitur Val. Max lib. 1. ca. 5. & Solino. Cleomenes autem Africæ & Ægypti vectigalibus fuerat præpositus. Curt. lib. 4.
units.tr: V. 11. Cleomenes: Valerius Maximus book 1 chapter 5 and Solinus call him Dinocrates. Cleomenes, however, had been placed over the revenues of Africa and Egypt; Curtius book 4.

units.la: V. 12. Laumedon] Infra lib. 15. Laudice pro Laodice Veteres Latinos Laumento pro Laomedonte dixisse, docuit nos Josephus Scaliger in Festum, quem vide. In 14. Annalium Taciti quæ Boodicea, eadem statim Boudicea dicitur, in vita Agricolæ Voadica, vitiose fortassis: & apud Petronium Laucoon pro Laocoon.
units.tr: V. 12. Laumedon: below, in book 15, Laudice for Laodice. Joseph Scaliger, in his commentary on Festus, which see, has taught us that the old Latins said Laumento for Laomedon. In Tacitus, Annals 14, what is Boodicea is immediately called Boudicea; in the Agricola it is Voadica, perhaps wrongly; and in Petronius Laucoon for Laocoon.

units.la: V. 14. Acropatos] Legendum ex Arriani 7. Atropates li. 6. Ἀτροπάτης. Is Diodoro Ἀτροπάτης mendose, pro Ἀτροπάτης. Diligenter comparandus est hic locus cum principio lib. 18. Diod. Siculi. Videndus & Curtius & Appianus Συεμαχῆ.
units.tr: V. 14. Acropatos: it should be read from Arrian book 7 as Atropates, book 6 [Ἀτροπάτης]. Diodorus wrongly has [Ἀτροπάτης] for [Ἀτροπάτης]. This passage should be carefully compared with the beginning of book 18 of Diodorus Siculus. Curtius and Appian should also be consulted, in the passage on the alliance [Συμμαχῆ].

units.la: V. 15. Phrygia maior] Omnino emendandum, Phrygia maior Ant. Phil filio assignatur, cum Lycia & Pamphilia: Cariam, &c. ex Diod. App. Curtio. τόπω mutarunt in Nearcho, cum vni tot regiones assignari ægre ferrent: Inue: so inde ordine legerunt, Liciam & Pamphiliam Nearco. Et mihi quidem ita videtur.
units.tr: V. 15. Phrygia maior: this must be emended entirely. Greater Phrygia is assigned to Antipater, son of Philip, together with Lycia and Pamphylia; then Caria, and so on, from Diodorus, Appian and Curtius. Others changed the name into Nearchus, since it was hard to bear that so many regions should be assigned to one man; then they read in that order, Lycia and Pamphylia to Nearchus. And to me indeed it seems so.

units.la: 24. Terras inter] Seras edidit in Orofio Fabricius quomodo habet è Mss. nostris vnus: ceteri, Terras quod malo. Nam & vrbs Taxila, cui imperabat Taxiles, siue Ta{*}xilus, ut eum Strabo vocat, inter Hydaspen & Indum sita est. Arrian. 5. Strab. 15. Et Taxili regnum suum relictum Diodorus refert.
units.tr: 24. Terras inter: Fabricius printed Seras in Orosius, as one of our manuscripts also has; the others have Terras, which I prefer. For the city of Taxila, which Taxiles ruled (or Taxilus, as Strabo calls him), lies between the Hydaspes and the Indus. Arrian book 5; Strabo book 15. And Diodorus reports that Taxiles' kingdom was left to him.

units.la: 27. Pithon] Mediam ei datam Diodorus & Curtius auctores funt.
units.tr: 27. Pithon: Diodorus and Curtius are the authorities that Media was given to him.

units.la: 27. Extarches] Οξυάρτης Roxanis pater, habet Diodorus.
units.tr: 27. Extarches: Diodorus gives [Ὀξυάρτης] as Roxana's father.

units.la: Ibid. Aracoffi] Deerant haec in impressis, quae Mss. agnoscunt & Diodorus. Plutarchus in Eumene extremo habet Ἰούρτιν mendose pro Σιούρτιν. sed qui hic Statanor, Diodoro & Arriano lib. 6. est σαταναρ. Quae sequuntur variant ab iis quae Diodorus scribit. Sed de istis plura ad Curtium.
units.tr: Ibid. Aracoffi: these words were missing from the printed editions, but the manuscripts and Diodorus recognise them. Plutarch, at the end of the Life of Eumenes, has [Ἰούρτιν] wrongly for [Σιούρτιν]. As for Statanor here, in Diodorus and in Arrian book 6 he is [Σαταναρ]. What follows differs from what Diodorus writes. More on these matters may be found at Curtius.

units.la: V. 31. Archos] Diod. Α'ρχων. Et pro Arcesilaus, quod & Diodorus & vett. uno excepto omnes agnoscunt, Fabricius in Orosio, legit Arcelaus.
units.tr: V. 31. Archos: Diodorus has [Ἄρχων]. And for Arcesilaus, which Diodorus and all the old copies except one acknowledge, Fabricius in Orosius reads Arcelaus.

units.la: P.140.v 1. Incrementorum materia] Mitor Vett. omnes pro materia habere memoria. Praefecturas vocat, Satrapias. Σατράπης Persis, Latinis praefectus dicitur.
units.tr: P. 140, v. 1. Incrementorum materia: I am surprised that all the old copies have materia. He calls them prefectures, that is satrapies. The Persian [satrapes] is called praefectus in Latin.

units.la: V.5. Athenienses & AEtoli] Lamiacum bellum de quo Diod. 17. & 18. & Strab. 9. meminit & Plutarch. in Pyrrho. & Demoft. & Paufanias Atticis. Ita appellatum quod ad Lamiam in quam se receperat Antipater gestum sit. Iustinus aut memoria lapsus, aut alios sequutus auctores Helacleam pro Lamia vocat.
units.tr: V. 5. Athenienses & AEtoli: the Lamian War, which Diodorus mentions in books 17 and 18, Strabo book 9, Plutarch in Pyrrhus, and Demosthenes and Pausanias in Attica. It is so called because it was fought near Lamia, into which Antipater had withdrawn. Justin, whether through a lapse of memory or following other authors, calls Heraclea Lamia.

units.la: V.11. Cadis damnati] Et Ιερόσυλοι Diod.
units.tr: V. 11. Cadis damnati: Diodorus also has [Ἱερόσυλοι] (temple-robbers).

units.la: 27. Harpalo] Mss. Harpago. librarios in errorem induxit, Aftyagis Harpagus, de quo lib. 1. De hoc lege supra notatos. & emenda Eusebii Chronicum, in quo legitur Harpalus fugit in Asiam, scribe ex Asia. De Demosthenis exfilio videndus Plutarc. & Paufan. in Corinth.
units.tr: 27. Harpalo: the manuscripts have Harpago, which misled the copyists; this is Harpagus of Astyages, of whom book 1. See the notes above on him, and emend Eusebius' Chronicle, where it is read Harpalus fled into Asia; write from Asia. On Demosthenes' exile see Plutarch and Pausanias in Corinthiaca.

units.la: P.141. v.8. Equestri prelio] Ducibus Antiphilo & Menone Thessalo. Plut. Diod.
units.tr: P. 141, v. 8. Equestri proelio: led by Antiphilus and Menon the Thessalian. Plutarch, Diodorus.

units.la: V.17. Ariarathi] Regnabat is in Cappadocia. Diodor. Plut. in Eumene. Erat enim Cappadocia Eumeni dicta non data. Probus. Quae hic de Cappadocibus narrantur, ea Diod. de Ifauriis refert: a quo & eorum quae sequuntur plenior narratio petenda est.
units.tr: V. 17. Ariarathi: he reigned in Cappadocia. Diodorus, Plutarch in Eumenes. For Cappadocia was called Eumenes' by name, not given to him, according to Probus. What is related here about the Cappadocians, Diodorus reports of the Isaurians; a fuller account of what follows must be sought from him.

units.la: P.142. v.14. Et Aegyptios insignis] Τοῖς μὲν ἱππεῦσι Φι- λιπποῦ ἡσσαρἔκουσι... ἐν ἰσχύῳ ... φίλοι δ' ὅλως... ὁ ἐπὶ πλοῖα {Greek} Diod. apud quem lege quà ratione Cyrenem acquisierit Ptolemæus.
units.tr: P. 142, v. 14. Et Aegyptios insignis: [Τοῖς μὲν ἱππεῦσι Φιλίππου ... ἐν ἰσχύῳ ... φίλοι δ' ὅλως ... ὁ ἐπὶ πλοῖα] Diodorus, where you should read by what method Ptolemy acquired Cyrene.

units.la: V. 30. Cyrene autem condita] Vide Herod. lib. 4. Pausan. Laconicis, & Phocicis. Strabo lib. 1. & 17. & excerpta ex Heraclide {Greek}, & Ammian. lib. 22. & Callimachi hymnos. & Euseb. & Solinum cap. 30. Sallust. Iugurth. & Pindarum Ode 4. Pith.
units.tr: V. 30. Cyrene autem condita: see Herodotus book 4; Pausanias in Laconica and Phocica; Strabo books 1 and 17; the excerpts from Heraclides; Ammianus book 22; the hymns of Callimachus; Eusebius; Solinus chapter 30; Sallust, Jugurtha; and Pindar, Pythian Ode 4.

units.la: Ibid. Arissæo] Hic à Callimacho, hymnoinApollinem Aristoteles dicitur, & ab Heraclide, & in Mss. Eusebii libris.
units.tr: Ibid. Arissaeo: here Callimachus, in the hymn to Apollo, calls him Aristaeus; so do Heraclides and the manuscripts of Eusebius.

units.la: V. 31. Battos] Mss. Battos, vt suprà Ariaraftes, & lib. 15. Sandrococtus, duplex, in d. frequens in vernacula Italorum lingua mutatio.
units.tr: V. 31. Battos: the manuscripts have Battos, as above Ariaraftes, and in book 15 Sandrococtus. The doubling, and the change of the letter d, is frequent in the Italian vernacular.

units.la: V. 32. Cirnus] Herodoto transpositis litteris {Greek}, facit autem non regis, sed Polymnesti filium Battum.
units.tr: V. 32. Cirnus: by transposing the letters in Herodotus, [Κύρνος] makes him not a king but the son of Polymnestus, Battus.

units.la: Nomen initiale, ceteris omnibus est Thera, Spartanorum colonia, quo omnium auctorum consensu moueor, vt pro Theramenis, legam Therae. Vnde negligentes libraril primum fecerunt Theras, inde Therame, tandem Theramenis.
units.tr: The initial name, in all the other authorities, is Thera, a colony of the Spartans. I am moved by the agreement of all the authors to read Therae for Theramenis. From this, careless copyists first made Theras, then Therame, and finally Theramenis.

units.la: P. 143. v. 18 Ab Apolline raptam] Vide Callimachum, & eius scholiasten.
units.tr: P. 143, v. 18. Ab Apolline raptam: see Callimachus and his scholiast.

units.la: V. 21. Arissæum] Cuius Sallustium mentionem fecisse, indicat Seruius in 1 Georg. Quare apud Probum Catholicis Sallustii fragmentum ita leg. arbitror. Apollonis F. (id est filius, vulgo filia) & Cyrenes, vt Aristæum intelligat.
units.tr: V. 21. Arissaeum: Servius on Georgics 1 indicates that Sallust mentioned him. Therefore, in the fragment of Sallust in Probus, I think it should be read thus: Apollonis F. (that is, filius, commonly given as filia) and Cyrenes, so that he is understood as Aristaeus.

units.la: P. 144. v. 12. Polyperchon] Crateron legendum esse praeterquam ex Diodoro, Plutarcho, & Probo in Eumene, etiam ex sequente libro constat; vt Polyperchontae Graeciae in Macedoniam cognovit: non igitur hoc praesilio cecidesat, quamuis eandem illam lectionem Orosius sequutus sit lib. 3. cap. 23.
units.tr: P. 144, v. 12. Polyperchon: that Craterus should be read is clear not only from Diodorus, Plutarch and Probus in Eumenes, but also from the following book, where it is recorded that the Polyperchontes came from Greece into Macedonia. So this slip did not arise from that source, although Orosius followed that same reading in book 3 chapter 23.

units.la: V. 17. Perdicca occiso] De eius morte, dissentientes opiniones Diodori & Probi, vide apud ipsos auctores. Vide & Paulsan. Atticis, & Orosium.
units.tr: V. 17. Perdicca occiso: the opinions of Diodorus and Probus differ about his death; see the authors themselves. See also Pausanias in Attica, and Orosius.

units.la: V. 18. Pheltone & Illyrio] Horum non meminit Diod. Plutarchus vero & Appianus in Syriaca historia, Eumenē solum commemorat: Phiton ist qui supra Pithon, Diodoro {Greek}.
units.tr: V. 18. Pheltone & Illyrio: Diodorus does not mention these men. Plutarch and Appian in the Syrian history mention only Eumenes. Phiton is the one who above is Pithon, in Diodorus [Πίθων].
ON BOOK XIV.

units.la: Vmenes] Legenda eius vita apud Plutarchum & Probum: historiae autem series petenda est è Diodoro.
units.tr: Eumenes: his life is to be read in Plutarch and Probus, but the sequence of events is to be taken from Diodorus.

units.la: P.146. v.11. Victus, in munitum quoddam castellum] Vi-ctus proditione Apollonidæ Eumenes, Noram confugit, quod est castellum Phrygiæ, vt Probus; situm in Cappadociæ & Lycaoniæ finibus, vt Plutarchus.
units.tr: P. 146, v. 11. Overcome, into a certain fortified castle: Eumenes, betrayed by Apollonides, fled to Nora, which, according to Probus, is a castle of Phrygia, and, according to Plutarch, lies on the borders of Cappadocia and Lycaonia.

units.la: P. 147. v. 9. Dum ducis imperia contemnunt] Nam non parere sed ducibus, sed imperare potestatem habent, Probus, de hac pugna, vide Diod. 19. Plutarc. & Probum. Victus est autem Eumenes solo equitatu, cum ceteris copijs superior esset.
units.tr: P. 147, v. 9. While the commanders scorn his orders: for they have the power not to obey the generals but to give commands, Probus. On this battle see Diodorus book 19, and Plutarch and Probus. Eumenes was defeated with his cavalry alone, although he was superior in his other forces.

units.la: P.148. v. 6. Cernitis, milites] Confer hanc orationem cum ea quæ apud Plutarchum extat.
units.tr: P. 148, v. 6. You see, soldiers: compare this speech with the one found in Plutarch.

units.la: v. 9. Quater intra hunc annum] Ter habet Probus.
units.tr: v. 9. Four times within this year: Probus has three times.

units.la: P.149. v. 11. Affignari caffedibus] A quibus iugulatus est. Plutarc. Probus.
units.tr: P. 149, v. 11. To be assigned to the assassins: by whom he was strangled, Plutarch, Probus.
v. 15. Summoned to Olympias: Diodorus book 18.

units.la: 26. Murorum praesidio] Liuius lib.34. Fuerat quondam fi-ne muro Sparta: tyranni nuper locis patentibus planisq; obiecerant murum. Paufan. Achaic.
units.tr: 26. The garrison of the walls: Livy book 34. Sparta had once been without a wall; the tyrants had recently placed a wall around its open and level places. Pausanias, Achaica.

units.la: v. 30. Caffandrum à Gracia] Diod. 19. hæc late persequitur.
units.tr: v. 30. Cassander from Greece: Diodorus book 19 pursues this at length.

units.la: P.150. v.2. Magnitudine filij] Τῶν ὑπηρετῶν ἀναμιμνη-σκόμενοι τῶν Ἀλεξάνδρου. Diod.
units.tr: P. 150, v. 2. The greatness of the son: "remembering the attendants of Alexander" [Τῶν ὑπηρετῶν ἀναμιμνησκόμενοι τῶν Ἀλεξάνδρου]. Diodorus.

units.la: V.7. Muliebris magis] Τὴν ἐντυχίαν ἐκ ὑπερηφανίας ἀνδρωπίνως. Ideo Antipater καθάπερ χρησμωδῶν, ἐπὶ τῆς πλάνης παρεκλέσαντο μηδέποτε συγχωρῆσαι γυναικὶ τῆς βασιλείας ἀντεξαλλάξαι. Diod. Vide Paufan. in Att.
units.tr: v. 7. More womanish: "the encounter, from arrogance, in a human manner" [Τὴν ἐντυχίαν ἐκ ὑπερηφανίας ἀνθρωπίνως]. Therefore Antipater, as if prophesying, in the wandering, urged that the kingship never be allowed to pass to a woman [μηδέποτε συγχωρῆσαι γυναικὶ τῆς βασιλείας ἀντεξαλλάξαι]. Diodorus. See Pausanias on Attica.

units.la: V.10. Nepote Herc.] Barfines hic filius erat; Roxanis Alexander vocabatur, Paufan. Atticis & Bœoticis: quo de hic agitur, vt patet ex Diodoro. Videtur ergo hic, Iustinus lapsus memoria,
units.tr: v. 10. Grandson of Hercules: this one was the son of Barsine; the son of Roxane was called Alexander, Pausanias on Attica and Boeotia. It is of this one that the present passage treats, as is clear from Diodorus. It seems, therefore, that Justin slipped in his memory here.

units.la: V.31. Non refugiétem gladium] Οὐδ᾽ ἡμίας ἀ̈σφονῆ ἡ γυναικὶ ἀξίωσιν ἀξιώσιν. Diod. cum quo hæc comparanda, & qui si ex aduerso ponenda sunt.
units.tr: v. 31. Not refusing the sword: "Nor does he think it worthy for a woman to claim a worthy..." [Οὐδ᾽ ἡμίας ἀσφονῆ ἡ γυναικὶ ἀξίωσιν ἀξιῶσιν]. Diodorus, with whom these things are to be compared, and which, if so, are to be set over against them.

units.la: P.151. v.4. Theffalonicen regis Aridei] Theffalonice erat Philippi τῆς Αμύντα filia, & Alexădri ἀδελφὴ ἁρμοτάς. Diod. Paufan. in Bœoticis. & eam supra Olympiadis priuignam vocauit. Iustino impofuit, quod Trogus forte regis Philippi filiam scripserat, & Aridæus, Philippus post mortem Alexandri cognominatus est.
units.tr: P. 151, v. 4. Thessalonice, the daughter of King Aridaeus: Thessalonice was the daughter of Philip, son of Amyntas, and half-sister [ἀδελφή] of Alexander. Diodorus; Pausanias in Boeotica. He also calls her the stepdaughter of Olympias. Justin is mistaken here, perhaps because Trogus had written that she was the daughter of King Philip, and Arrhidaeus was surnamed Philip after the death of Alexander.
IN BOOK XV.
