units.la: APud Galaman] Legendum Gazam ex Diod. Plutarc. in Demetrio, Appiano in Syriaca, & huius libri Periocha. Meminit huius prælii Paufan. in Atticis: quo loco Ptolemæi res gestas breuiter & accurate recenset.
units.tr: Apud Galaman: Read "Gaza", from Diodorus, Plutarch in Demetrius, Appian in Syriaca, and the Periocha of this book. Pausanias in Attica also mentions this battle, and there he briefly and accurately recounts the deeds of Ptolemy.

units.la: V.15. Priuatum omne instrumentum] Τὴν βασιλικὴν ἀπο-κτεινὴν. Diod.
units.tr: V.15. Priuatum omne instrumentum: [Τὴν βασιλικὴν ἀπο-κτεινὴν] i.e. the royal baggage. Diodorus.

units.la: V. 25. Ranarum murium-que multitudinem] Plinius libro 8. cap. 29. ab tanis ciuitatem in Gallia pultam memorat, si modo locus mendo caret. De muribus libro 10. cap. 65.
units.tr: V.25. Ranarum murium-que multitudinem: Pliny, book 8, chapter 29, records a town in Gaul called Tanis, plagued by these, if only the place is not corrupt. On mice, book 10, chapter 65.

units.la: V. 25. Herculesi] Quem reducere in regnum tentabat Polyperchon, eum tamen à Cassandro corruptus, intermisit, annos natum ἐπτακαιδέκα. Diod. 20. quomodo hic reponendum arbitror. Iā enim annos quindecim defecerat esse Alexander M. Et ex XVII. quinarii nota maleiunctâ, aut negligenter expressa, leui errore fit XIIII. Paufan. in Bœoticis Herculem & Alexandrum, Alexandri M. filios à Cassandro veneno sublatos refert.
units.tr: V.25. Herculesi: Polyperchon tried to restore him to the kingdom, but, having been bribed by Cassander, he dropped the attempt, when he was seventeen years old [ἐπτακαιδέκα]. Diodorus, book 20, which is how I think this should be read here. For Alexander the Great had already ceased to be fifteen years old. And from XVII, through a carelessly joined or carelessly written quinarius mark, a slight error produces XIIII. Pausanias in Boeotica relates that Hercules and Alexander, the sons of Alexander the Great, were removed by poison by Cassander.

units.la: P.153.v.2. Admissa classe] Plutarchus in Demetrio. Diodorus lib. 20.
units.tr: P.153.v.2. Admissa classe: Plutarch in Demetrius. Diodorus, book 20.

units.la: V.11. Regem se] Probus, nemo Eumene Simo rex appellatus est, sed prefectus: idem post huius occasum statim regiâ ornatum nomenque sumpserunt. Lege Plutarch. & Diod. & Appiam.
units.tr: V.11. Regem se: Probus: no one called Eumenes or Simo was named king, but prefect; the same men, after the fall of this one, at once assumed the royal dress and name. Read Plutarch, Diodorus and Appian.

units.la: V.14. Lysimachus] Agathoclis filius, unus è Custodibus Alexandri. Vide Paus. in Atticis Plin. 8. cap. 16. Curt. lib. 8. quæ hic de Lysimacho leoni obiecto referuntur, fabulam vocat.
units.tr: V.14. Lysimachus: son of Agathocles, one of the Bodyguards of Alexander. See Pausanias in Attica, Pliny book 8, chapter 16. Curtius, book 8. What is related here about Lysimachus being thrown to a lion, he calls a fable.

units.la: P.155. v.13. Figura anchore] Lege Appianum in Syriaca historia. Ausonius de Antiochia — Illa Seleucum Nuncupat, ingenuum cui sues fuit anchora signum; Qualis inusta solet generis nota certa per omnem Nam subolis seriem natiua cucurrit imago.
units.tr: P.155. v.13. Figura anchore: Read Appian in the Syriaca historia. Ausonius on Antioch: "That city names Seleucus, to whom the anchor was the sign of his noble birth; just as a branded mark of a family is usually a certain sign, for the natural image ran through the whole succession of his offspring."
Hic
is called. Appian.
V.25. Babylonem cepit: Diodorus, book 19; Appian.
V.29. Sandrocottus: Old editions read Sandrocottus. Arrian, book 5.

units.la: § Σανδρόκοττος. Plutarcho in Alexandro Ἀνδροκόττος. Appiano Ἀνδροκόττος. Oros. Ms. Andracote Fabricius Sandrocottus edidit ex Strabonis 15.
units.tr: Σανδρόκοττος [Sandrocottus]. In Plutarch's Alexander it is Ἀνδροκόττος [Androcottus], and in Appian also Ἀνδροκόττος. Orosius manuscript: Andracotus. Fabricius edited Sandrocottus from Strabo, book 15.

units.la: P.156.v.16. Bellum Antigoni]Lege Plut.in Demet.Pauf. in Att.Dimicatum autem est ad Ipsum. Appianus.
units.tr: P.156.v.16. Bellum Antigoni: Read Plutarch in Demetrius, and Pausanias in Attica. But the battle was fought at Ipsus, according to Appian.
IN BOOK XVI.

units.la: Dost Gaffandri] Legendus Paufanias in Boeoticis. Plut. in Demetrio & Pyrrho.
units.tr: Dost Gaffandri] Read Pausanias in the Boeotica. Plutarch in the Demetrius and Pyrrhus.

units.la: V. 28 In parricidio, nulla satis iusta causa] Spartianus refert, Bassianum occiso fratre, Papiniano mandasse, ut in Senatu pro se, & apud populum facinus diluceret: Illum telspondisse, Non tam facile parricidium excusari, quam fieri. Fuit illa principis I Cæs, Cygnæa vox: quam miror hominem si dis placet politicum, & I Cæsum, & Christianum, in libris suis de Republica, reprehendere, pessimo exemplo: Recte enim & ordine fecit Papinianus, & viri boni officium functus est, qui mori praeoptauit, quam tyranno impia & iniqua imperanti parere. Idem illeim eo peccat, quod Papinianum imperatoris confanguineum facit, contra quam Spartianus, quem ille auctorem laudat. I Cæsum cognationem & affinitatem nescit distinguere. Facit quod rhetores solent, quibus concessum est ementiri in historiis aliquid, ut dicere videatur argutius.
units.tr: V. 28 In parricidio, nulla satis iusta causa] Spartianus reports that Bassianus, after killing his brother, ordered Papinian to clear the deed in the Senate and before the people on his behalf. Papinian replied that parricide is not so easily excused as committed. That was the emperor's famous swan-song saying. I am surprised that a man, by God a political writer, criticises this in his books on the Commonwealth, and that he does so to the worst example, since Papinian acted rightly and in good order, and performed the duty of a good man, in choosing to die rather than obey a tyrant who commanded impious and unjust things. The same writer also errs in making Papinian a kinsman of the emperor, contrary to Spartianus, whom he himself cites as authority. He does not know how to distinguish kinship from affinity. He does what rhetoricians usually do, who are allowed to invent something in their histories so as to seem to speak more subtly.

units.la: P.158.v.24. Dorscetis regis] Dromuchaeta, legit Fabricius in Orosium ex Plutarcho, Paufania in Atticis, Strabone lib. 7.qui eum Getarum regem faciunt. Ego contra libros nihil muto: neque nouum est historiarum scriptores in barbaris nominibus variare.
units.tr: P.158.v.24. Dorscetis regis] Dromuchaeta, reads Fabricius on Orosius, following Plutarch, Pausanias in Attica, and Strabo book 7, who make him king of the Getae. I, on the other hand, change nothing in the books. Nor is it new for historians to vary in barbarian names.

units.la: v. 30.Ptolomaeus, Seleucus, & Lysimachus] Plutar. in Demetrio,& Pyrrho, Paufan. in Atticis, quos in hac historia, consule.
units.tr: v. 30. Ptolomaeus, Seleucus, & Lysimachus] Plutarch in Demetrius and Pyrrhus, Pausanias in Attica; consult these in this history.

units.la: P.159.v. 13. Ptolemaeum cum magna] Regū Ægypti seriē, vide apud Strabon.lib.7.quaedam apud Paus.in Attic.
units.tr: P.159.v. 13. Ptolemaeum cum magna] For the succession of the kings of Egypt, see Strabo book 7; some things are in Pausanias in Attica.

units.la: P.160.v.3.In Pontum]Ita omnino legendum est ex uno Cuiacij codice.Est.n.Heraclea hoc loco πόλις Θεάκης ἐν τῷ Πον-
units.tr: P.160.v.3. In Pontum] It must be read exactly so, from a single Cuiacius manuscript. For Heraclea in this place is the city of Theakes in Pontus [πόλις Θεάκης ἐν τῷ Πον-
Bb

units.la: τὰ Πόντα, Stephanus: de qua Strabo 11. Et Eustathius in Dionysium. Ceteri omnes & impressi, & scripti, Metapontum: turpi errore. Metapontum & Heraclea, Italiae urbes, librarios in errorem induxerunt. Ex eodem libro scripti Lamachus non Malachus quomodo alii Vet. habent.
units.tr: τὰ Πόντα] [τὰ Πόντα], Stephanus, about which see Strabo book 11, and Eustathius on Dionysius. All the others, both printed and manuscript, have Metapontum, a shameful error. The cities of Metapontum and Heraclea in Italy led the copyists into this mistake. From the same book, the manuscript has Lamachus, not Malachus, as some other old copies have.

units.la: 25.Paffi funt inter pl. ma. etiā tyrannidem] Ενγαγνίδη ἐχόντες τινὰς. Strabo. De Clearcho tyranno Diod. lib. 15. & 16. & Plutarch. 2. de fortuna Alexandri.
units.tr: 25.Passi sunt inter pl. ma. etiam tyrannidem] [ἐνγαγνίδη ἐχόντες τινὰς]. Strabo. On the tyrant Clearchus, Diodorus books 15 and 16, and Plutarch, On the Fortune of Alexander, 2.

units.la: P.163.v. 6. Frater Clearchi Satyrus] Diod. li. 16 filium Timotheum ei succeßiße refert: qui & eum interfectum ait Διονυσίων ὑπὸ τῶν, ἐπὶ ἑαυτὸν βασιλεύοντα. Consule Memnonis excerpta.
units.tr: P.163.v. 6. Frater Clearchi Satyrus] Diodorus book 16 reports that his son Timotheus succeeded him. He also says that he was killed [Διονυσίων ὑπὸ τῶν, ἐπὶ ἑαυτὸν βασιλεύοντα] by the Dionysians, who were ruling over themselves. Consult the excerpts of Memnon.
IN BOOK XVII.

units.la: Ilsimachia] Prius Cardia dicta. Steph. Paufan. in Attuc. Eam suo tempore deletam fuisse scribit Strabo lib 10.
units.tr: Ilsimachia] Formerly called Cardia. Stephanus. Pausanias in Attica. Strabo, book 10, writes that it was destroyed in his time.

units.la: v.29. Agathoclem] Lege Paufaniā in Atticis, & Strab. lib. 13. qui Lysimachum ait ἐν τοῖς οἰκείοις ἀφανισθέντα, filium necasse. per ἐχώρα οἰκία, domesticas calamitates intelligit, quae hic & apud Paufaniam recensentur, nõ improbos familiares, quod putauit doctissimus Fabricius.
units.tr: v.29. Agathoclem] Read Pausanias in Attica, and Strabo book 13, who says that Lysimachus was destroyed [ἐν τοῖς οἰκείοις ἀφανισθέντα] among his own household, and that he killed his son. By [ἐχώρα οἰκία] domestic calamities are meant, which are listed here and in Pausanias, not wicked intimates, as the very learned Fabricius thought.

units.la: P.164.v. 16. In eo bello Lysimachus] Praeter Paufan. & Strab. vide Appianum συγγραφῆ.
units.tr: P.164.v. 16. In eo bello Lysimachus] Besides Pausanias and Strabo, see Appian's history [συγγραφῆ].

units.la: 24 A Ptolomeo] Cerauno. erat hic filius Ptolemaei Soteris, & Eurydices Antipatri filiae. Appianus, qui Seleucum tres & lxx. annos vixisse scribit, quod cū iis quae Iustinus supra retulit, non congruit.
units.tr: 24 A Ptolomeo] Ceraunus. This man was the son of Ptolemy Soter and Eurydice, daughter of Antipater. Appian, who writes that Seleucus lived seventy-three years, does not agree with what Justin reported above.

units.la: P.165.v. 23 Molossorum] Chaones primum, Molossos deinde regnasse refert Strab. 7. quem lege.
units.tr: P.165.v. 23 Molossorum] Strabo, book 7, reports that the Chaones reigned first and the Molossians afterwards. Read him.

units.la: v.29.Lanassam] Sic Vett. & Plutar. in Pyrrho, qui eam facit filiam τῶ Κλεοδίου, qui filius erat Herculis.
units.tr: v.29. Lanassam] So the old copies have it, and Plutarch in Pyrrhus, who makes her the daughter of Cleodius [τοῦ Κλεοδίου], who was the son of Hercules.

units.la: P.166.v. 3.Infidiis Orestae.] Μαχαιρίας Ἀτάφῶν ἀνδρῶν ἀντιλήτος αὐτὸν. Strab.9. Regū Epiri genus, vide apud Paufaniam in Atticis & Plutarc. in Pyrrho.
units.tr: P.166.v. 3. Infidiis Orestae.] [Μαχαιρίας Ἀτάφῶν ἀνδρῶν ἀντιλήτος αὐτὸν]. Strabo, book 9. For the royal line of Epirus, see Pausanias in Attica and Plutarch in Pyrrhus.

units.la: v 4. Pylades] Pielum vocat Paufan. Pylades hic imperiti librarij substituerant, Oreftis nomine, inducti. Erat hic Andromaches filius, Paufan.
units.tr: v 4. Pylades] Pausanias calls him Pielus. An unskilled copyist substituted Pylades here, led by the name Orestes. This man was the son of Andromache, according to Pausanias.

units.la: v. f. Arrylam] Ita ex veteri scriptura legendum iudicaui, eaui,habetenim Vett. tribam,alii hiribam.nisi quis malit ex Plutarch. Tharrytam, quod accedit ad Tarriba, quod in vno veteri legitur. Et quae de eo Plutarc. refert cum auctore nostro conueniunt Θαρρύτας τρῶτον ἱσρέξ-
units.tr: v. f. Arrylam] I judged that it should be read thus from the old manuscript, which has tribam (others hiribam), unless someone prefers Tharrytam from Plutarch, which comes close to Tarriba, as read in one old copy. What Plutarch reports about him agrees with our author: [Θαρρύτας πρῶτον ἱσρέξ-

units.la: § σιν, ἀπλωικοῖς ἤχει τῷ χρὴ μησι, τὴ ροµοις φιλαρχοῦντες δ' ἀκροσμένην τὰς πολίς, ὁ ἀκρίως γίνεσις. Tharypū hunc vocat Paufanias: eius filius Alcetas pater Arrybba, siue Aryba, vt Plutarch. feu Aryrube, vt Diodorus lib. 16. & Neoptolemi. Arrybae filius Aeacides, à quo Pyrrhus. Neoptolemi filiae Troas,Olympias Alexandri Mag. mater; & Alexander filius, de quo fup. lib. 12. Haec ex Plutarcho & Paufan. Hinc fupra lib. 7. legendum arbitror, concilia-ante nuptias patruo,tutore Virginis, Arrybba,rege Molossorum; & lib. 8. Siquidem Arrybam regem Epiri, &c. atque Alexandrum pupillum eius, Sxoris Olympiadis fratrem, &c. Lector fagax & eruditus iudicet.
units.tr: [σιν, ... ] Pausanias calls this man Tharypus. His son Alcetas was the father of Arrybba, or Aryba, as in Plutarch, or Aryrube, as in Diodorus book 16 and Neoptolemus. The son of Arrybas was Aeacides, from whom came Pyrrhus. The daughter of Neoptolemus was Troas, and Olympias, mother of Alexander the Great, and her son Alexander, of whom above in book 12. These things are from Plutarch and Pausanias. Hence I think that above, in book 7, it should be read: concilia-ante nuptias patruo, tutore Virginis, Arrybba, rege Molossorum; and in book 8: Siquidem Arrybam regem Epiri, &c. atque Alexandrum pupillum eius, Sxoris Olympiadis fratrem, &c. Let the shrewd and learned reader judge.

units.la: v.16. Frater Acacides)Frater patruelis, vt ex ijs constat quae fupra notaui.
units.tr: v.16. Frater Acacides)] A paternal cousin, as is clear from what I noted above.

units.la: P. 20. Vtuum admodum parvulum] Plutarch. ῥήτωρ ὄντα. Lego bimum admodum, vt parvulum ex gloffa fit.
units.tr: P. 20. Vtuum admodum parvulum] Plutarch [ῥήτωρ ὄντα]. I read bimum admodum, since parvulum comes from a gloss.
v.23. Glauci)] [Γλαυκίαν]. Plutarch calls him this.
v.29. Annorum XI.)] [Ἀνωγιδίκαιτ' ἀν]. Plutarch.
ON BOOK XVIII.

units.la: Gitur Pyrrhus] De Pyrrhi in Italiam expeditione, Plut. P.167. v.14. in Pyrrho, Paufan. lib. 1. L. Florus lib. 1. Orofii. 4. cap. 1. & epitome Liuiana.
units.tr: Igitur Pyrrhus] On Pyrrhus' expedition into Italy, see Plutarch, p. 167, line 14, in his Life of Pyrrhus; Pausanias, book 1; L. Florus, book 1; Orosius, book 4, chapter 1; and the Epitome of Livy.
P. 168, line 4. Adductis) Read abductis.

units.la: v 5.Valerius Laurinus]Plutarcho Ἀλβινο, literis transpositis & intetie6to, legendum Ἀὰ6ιν. Pugna cómisfaest ε. Plut. Heraclea autem,auctore Plinio,inter Sirin est & Acirin fluuios. Vndein Orofio legere audeo; apud Herad-leam Campaniae Orbem Clusidem: qua muis Ms. habeat Heracleam Campaniae Orbem flumisque Lirin, cum pulla sit Campaniae Heraclea, & Liris fluuius ab hoc loco alienus sit. Sequutus est autè Orosii Flori corrupti exemplar. Ideo vt Orosius, ira & Florus emendandus.
units.tr: Line 5. Valerius Laurinus] In Plutarch the name is Albinus, with its letters transposed and corrupted; it should be read as Laurinus. The battle was fought. Plutarch. Pliny says that Heraclea lies between the rivers Siris and Aciris. Hence I venture to read in Orosius: "at Heraclea in Campania, the Orbis Clusidis", although one manuscript has "Heraclea of Campania, the Orbis, and the river Liris". But there is no Heraclea in Campania, and the Liris is a river far from this place. Orosius, however, followed a corrupted copy of Florus. So, just as Orosius must be emended, so must Florus.

units.la: v. 9 Insufitata ante elephantorum) Plinius lib. 8. cap. 6.
units.tr: Line 9. Insuefacta ante elephantorum) Pliny, book 8, chapter 6.
Bb 2, line 18.

units.la: De quibus versus Ennii elegantes sunt apud M Cic.1.de offic.
units.tr: On these, the elegant verses of Ennius are quoted by M. Cicero, De Officiis, book 1.

units.la: CXXX. habet Valer. Max. lib. 3. cap. 7.
units.tr: CXXX. Valerius Maximus has this, book 3, chapter 7.

units.la: Alii hunc misum ferunt, ut de capitis redimendis ageret. De Romanorum continentia lege Val.lib.4. cap.3. Hoc voluit Varro lib.2. de vita pop. Rom. Qua abstinentia viri mulieresque Romæ fuerint, quod a tege munera eorum noluerit nemo accipere.
units.tr: Others report that this man was sent to negotiate the ransom of prisoners. On Roman self-restraint, see Valerius Maximus, book 4, chapter 3. Varro meant this in his second book On the Life of the Roman People: with what abstinence the men and women of Rome lived, since no one would accept gifts from a king.

units.la: Plutarchus de senatu tantum:βα- σιλέων πολεων συνεδρίον.
units.tr: Plutarch speaks only of the senate: [βασιλέων πόλεων συνέδριον], a council of kings and cities.
Strabo, books 1 and 16.

units.la: Ibid. Assyrium flagnum Lacum intelligit Τιννοπεῖνα de quo Strabo lib.16. De Sidone & Tyro, vide eundem Strabonem & Q. Curtium.
units.tr: Ibid. By the Assyrian marsh he means the lake [Τιννοπεῖνα], of which Strabo speaks in book 16. On Sidon and Tyre, see the same Strabo and Quintus Curtius.
In Greek it is [Τρύκη].

units.la: Malim Tyri, & supra pro conualuere, legendum forte coaluere. Didonis autem pater Agenor, filius Beli.
units.tr: I would prefer "of Tyre", and above, for "conualuere", perhaps read "coaluere". Dido's father was Agenor, son of Belus.

units.la: Id est, sororis maritum, ut ex Sophoclis OEdipo tyranno, & Probi Paufania, notauit vir incomparabilis Iac. Cuiacius Obseruat 6. Quomodo & Ditmarus & Vvitichindus Saxo lib.1. loquuti sunt. Sed & Cedrenus, Iothor socerum Moysis vocat. Vt quicunque vxorem alteri dat, aut filiam, aut sorørem, eius gener dicatur: Fortasse & qui ducit, generi dicitur; quo sensu ἐπιγαμβρεύειν legimus Matth.22. Acerbum autem hic vocat qui vulgo, & à Marone Sicharæum dicitur. In ora Mss. aliquot adscriptum est, Hiarba legendum: falso Mauritanorum principem cum Didonis marito confundentes. Alii Acceruas habent, u pro b. Seruius in Virgilium notat Sicharbam eundem appellatum & fragmentum de Didone, quod mihi ex veteri libro transcriptum communicauit popularis meus P. Daniel: in quo totus hic locus adducitur ex Trogo Pompeio in Epitomis.
units.tr: That is, the husband of his sister. The incomparable Jacques Cujas noted this from Sophocles' Oedipus Tyrannus and from Pausanias' treatment of Probus, in his Observations, book 6. Thus Dithmar and Widukind the Saxon also speak, in book 1. Cedrenus calls Jethro the father-in-law of Moses. Whoever gives a wife, a daughter or a sister to another man is called that man's son-in-law; perhaps whoever takes a wife is also called a son-in-law, and in this sense we read [ἐπιγαμβρεύειν] in Matthew 22. Here he calls Acerbas the man who is commonly called Sichaeus, and by Maro (Virgil). Some manuscript margins note that "Hiarba" should be read, the writers wrongly confusing him with the Mauretanian prince and Dido's husband. Others have "Acceruas", with u for b. Servius on Virgil notes that the same man is called Sicharbas. Also, my fellow countryman P. Daniel copied for me from an old book a fragment about Dido, in which this whole passage is quoted from Trogus Pompeius' Epitome.

units.la: Virg. 1. Æneid. Strab.17. Appianus Ἀνδρίους. Dionysius in Euftathium: Et ceteri pafsim auctores de Carthagine multa: de qua silere rectius putat Salluftius, quam parum dicere.
units.tr: Virgil, Aeneid 1. Strabo, book 17. Appian [Ἀνδρίους]. Dionysius, in Eustathius. And other authors everywhere write much about Carthage, about which Sallust thinks it better to keep silent than to say too little.

units.la: P.173.v.14. Equi caput]Ideo Καzxαὸς dicta, quod ipsorum lingua est caput equinum. Steph.
units.tr: P. 173, line 14. "Horse's head"] It is called [Καρχηδὸς] because in their language it means a horse's head. Stephanus.

units.la: V.19. Maxitanorum]Vet.quidam Muxitanorum, vulgo Maurstanorum:eum Euftathius regem facit Maζιxων, apud Steph. Maζυς sunt, οἱ Αἰϑίης ropudφεὶ, εἰσὶ δὲ χρῆ ἱτπο-ροι Μαξυςς, χρῆ ἱτρίροι Μαχυςς. docto lectori iudicium reli-nquo.
units.tr: Line 19. Maxitanorum] Some old copies have Muxitanorum, and commonly Maurusianorum. Eustathius makes him a king of the [Μαζίκων], in Stephanus. The [Μαζύες] are those who [...], and there are others called [Μαξύες] and [Μαχύες]. I leave the judgement to the learned reader.

units.la: P.174.v.6. L XXII. annis] Hic plurimum variant auctores: quidam ante Troiam captam conditam volunt, inter quos Philistus apud Eusebium & Appianus: quidam post captam Troiam, ante quam Romam conderetur: neque hi in numero annorum consentiunt. Paterculus annos quinque & lx. ante Romam. Liuii epitoma libro 1. annos DCC. stetiffe Carthaginem refert; euerfa autem est, anno vrbis DCVII. fuerat ergo ante vrbem conditam annos XCIII. Solinus cap.30. annos DCCXXXVII vel vtin veteri codice Vineti legitur DCLXXVII. Eusebius veniffe in poteftatem Romanorum anno a conditione sui DCLXXIII. (ita eft in Ms.) vel vt alii affirmant DCCLVIII. prior numero annorum plus habet, quam Paterculi ratio. M.Cic.1. de Repub. Nectantum Carthago habuiffet opum fexcentos fere annos, fine confiliis & difciplina. Sed haec accuratius explicabunt Bochelli mei ad Eusebium obferuationes Chronicae.
units.tr: P. 174, line 6. "Twenty-two years"] Here the authors differ greatly. Some want it founded before Troy was taken, among them Philistus, cited in Eusebius, and Appian; others want it founded after Troy was taken but before Rome was founded. Nor do these agree on the number of years. Paterculus says sixty-five years before Rome. The Epitome of Livy, book 1, says that Carthage stood for 700 years; but it was overthrown in the year 607 of Rome, so it had stood 93 years before the city was founded. Solinus, chapter 30, says 737 years, or, as is read in an old Venetian codex, 677. Eusebius says it came under Roman power in the 673rd year of its founding (so it is in the manuscript), or, as others affirm, the 758th. The former figure gives more years than Paterculus' reckoning. M. Cicero, De Re Publica, book 1: "Nor would Carthage have had so great a store of wealth for about six hundred years without counsel and discipline." But these matters will be explained more accurately in my Bochart's Chronological Observations on Eusebius.
Line 10. "Men as the Sidonians"] See Curtius Rufus, book 4.

units.la: V.16. Diufeliciter pugnaffent] Duo Mss. & vulgati, & Orofius lib.4 cap.9. infeliciter, quod non probo: fequitur enim Siciliae partem domuerant.
units.tr: Line 16. "Fought unsuccessfully for a long time"] Two manuscripts, the printed editions, and Orosius, book 4, chapter 9, have "infeliciter" (unsuccessfully), which I do not accept, since it is followed by "they had subdued part of Sicily".

units.la: V.18. Maleum] Mazeum edidit in Orofio Fabricius, quomodo habet vnus Ms.
units.tr: Line 18. "Maleum"] Fabricius, in his edition of Orosius, printed "Mazeum", as one manuscript has.
ON BOOK XIX.

units.la: Ortuorum corp.cr.p q.terra obruere] Ipsum cremare non fuit apud Romanos veteris instituti: terra condebantur, Plin.lib.7. cap.54. & ludaeorum morem notat Tacit hist 5.
units.tr: "To bury the bodies of the dead in earth rather than burn them"] Cremating the body was not an ancient custom among the Romans: they were buried in earth. Pliny, book 7, chapter 54. Tacitus, Histories, book 5, notes the Jewish custom.
P. 177, line 6.
Line 12. "Hamilcar in the Sicilian war"] Above, book 4. Diodorus, book 11.

units.la: V.25.Imilco)Diod.lib.14. Ιμιλκων, Is totam fetme Sicilia m exceptis Syracufis occupauerat.
units.tr: Line 25. "Imilco"] Diodorus, book 14: [Ἰμίλκων], who had occupied almost all of Sicily except Syracuse.

units.la: P.178.v.33. Mortem sibi consciuit) Εαυτὸ ἀγηγγύς Ἀρα-τὸν, ἀπὸ ἀπογέτιγνοι. Diod.
units.tr: P. 178, line 33. "He took his own life"] He hanged himself [ἑαυτὸν ἀπήγξατο]. Diodorus.

units.la: Dionysius] Quo pacto hic Sicilia deuicta Italiam aggressus sit lege Diod 14.
units.tr: "Dionysius"] On how this man, after subduing Sicily, attacked Italy, see Diodorus, book 14.

units.la: v. 28. Thusconum populi] Tyrrheni, à Tyrrheno Atys filio, Herculis nepote. Strab. li. 5. ceteri: Seneca de conf. lol. ad Albinam Tuscos Asia sibi Vendidat. Confer hunc locum cum Solini cap. 8. Vid. & Virgilium 1. 7. & 11. Æneï. & Tacit. 4. Annal.
units.tr: Line 28. "The people of Tuscany"] The Tyrrhenians, named from Tyrrhenus, son of Atys, grandson of Hercules. Strabo, book 5. Others: Seneca, in his consolation To Albina, says: "Asia claims the Tuscans for itself." Compare this passage with Solinus, chapter 8. See also Virgil, Aeneid 7 and 11, and Tacitus, Annals, book 4.

units.la: v. 31. Arpos] Prius Argiripa dicta. Virg. 11. Æneid. quo loco lege Seruium.
units.tr: Line 31. "Arpi"] Formerly called Argyrippa. Virgil, Aeneid 11, where see Servius.

units.la: Et Spinambrii] probatur mihi Glareani conjectura, vt legamus Tarquinij à Thessalis, & Spina & Ravenna. Ravennā enim à Thessalis conditam docet Strabo. Malim tamē & Spina Vrbs quod à veteri lectione prōpius abest. Spina autem, πόλις Ἰκκα ἐκ τῆς πόλεως ἰδρύθη. Strabo lib. 5.
units.tr: "And Spina"] I accept Glareanus' conjecture that we should read "Tarquinii, from the Thessalians, and Spina and Ravenna", for Strabo teaches that Ravenna was founded by the Thessalians. I would prefer, however, "and the city of Spina", which is closer to the old reading. Spina is [πόλις Ἰκκα ἐκ τῆς πόλεως ἰδρύθη], a city founded from the city of ... Strabo, book 5.

units.la: v. 3. Ceren] Ceren alij scribunt: quam à Pelasgis conditam refert Strabo. De urbium conditoribus, auctorum dissensiones hic notare, non est mei propositi: & tanta est inter eos varietas, vt ne vrbis quidem Romæ origo constet.
units.tr: Line 3. "Cere"] Others write Caere. Strabo reports that it was founded by the Pelasgians. It is not my purpose to note here the disagreements of authors about the founders of cities, and the variety among them is so great that not even the origin of the city of Rome is certain.
Line 10. "Hercules' arrow"] Aristotle, On Marvellous Reports [περὶ θαυμαστῶν ἀκουσμάτων].

units.la: 16. Maior Gracia] Vide Festum, & quæ ad eum Iof. Scaliger, & Strabonem lib. 6. Seneca ad Albinam. Totum Italia latus quod infero mari alluitur Maior Graciæ fuit.
units.tr: Line 16. "Magna Graecia"] See Festus, and what Joseph Scaliger wrote on him, and Strabo, book 6. Seneca to Albina: "The whole side of Italy washed by the lower sea was Magna Graecia."

units.la: v. 19. Sirim] Italiæ ciuitas πόλις Μεσσηνίων Steph. deinde Heraclea dicta: Plin. lib. 3. Σίρις vocat Strabo lib. 6.
units.tr: Line 19. "Siris"] A city of Italy, [πόλις Μεσσηνίων], "a city of the Messenians", according to Stephanus; afterwards called Heraclea. Pliny, book 3. Strabo, book 6, calls it [Σῖρις].

units.la: cum in aciem processissent] Ad Sagram fluuium, Strabo lib 6. M. Cicero 2. & 3. de Nat. deorū. Plurare. in Æmylio. Locrensium cum Rheginis fuisse x. millia; Crotoniensium cxxx. millia Strabo refert: & ortum inde proverbium Ἀλλὰ ἐπὶ Σάγρα: cuius meminit & Cicero.
units.tr: "When they had advanced into battle"] At the river Sagra. Strabo, book 6. M. Cicero, On the Nature of the Gods, books 2 and 3. Plutarch, in his Life of Aemilius. Strabo reports that the Locrians with the Rhegians numbered 10,000, and the Crotoniates 130,000. From this arose the proverb [Ἀλλὰ ἐπὶ Σάγρα], which Cicero also mentions.

units.la: Nuntiata est Victoria] Ludis Olympiæ auditam, scribit M. Cicero, & ceteri: Strabo pro fabula id habet.
units.tr: "Victory was announced"] Cicero and others write that it was heard of at the Olympic Games. Strabo regards this as a fable.

units.la: v. 3. Crotoniensibus nulla virtutis] De corū pristina virtute præter Strabonē lege M. Ciceronem 2. Rhet. de luxuria autem & vitæ genere post attritas bellis frequentibus vires, vide Petronium in Satyrico, apud quem pro scenas, ne idem bis dicat, legendum arbitror cænas quis-quis suos heredes habet, inquit, nec ad cænas, nec ad spectacula culas admittitur.
units.tr: Line 3. "The Crotoniates had no virtue"] On their former virtue, besides Strabo, read M. Cicero, Rhetoric, book 2. On their luxury and way of life after their strength was worn down by frequent wars, see Petronius in the Satyricon, where, instead of "scenas", to avoid saying the same thing twice, I think we should read "cenas". He says: "Whoever has heirs of his own is admitted neither to dinners nor to shows."

units.la: Pythagoras] Vide Laertium in eius vita M. Cicero n. 5. Tusculul.
units.tr: "Pythagoras"] See Laertius in his life, and M. Cicero, Tusculan Disputations, book 5.

units.la: v. 8. Adperdifcendos] Φιλομυθίας χαέιν tyrannidem sugiens. Strabo lib. 14.
units.tr: Line 8. "To learn"] [φιλομαθίας χάριν], for the sake of learning, fleeing tyranny. Strabo, book 14.

units.la: 26. Velut instrumenta luxuria] Tertullian. lib. 6. de habitu muliebri, instrumenta muliebria gloria vocat. eo loco, vbi legitur, medicamenta exsuco, quibus lana colorantur, emendandum videtur mala.
units.tr: Line 26. "Like the instruments of luxury"] Tertullian, book 6, On Women's Apparel, calls them women's instruments of vanity. In the place where it reads "medicines of juice, with which wool is dyed", it seems that we should emend to "mala".

units.la: P.183.v.17. Romam incenderant.] De Roma à Gallis capta & incensa pleni sunt auctorum libri.
units.tr: P. 183, line 17. "They had burned Rome"] The books of the authors are full of accounts of Rome being captured and burned by the Gauls.
v.29. The Rhetorae peoples] Steph., on the word Pœrtoi: a peculiarity of the blind [τυφλωικὸν ἴδιον].

units.la: P.184.v.9. Insidiis ad postremum] M Cic.3.de Nat.deorum. Atque (mallem namque) in suo lectulo mortuus in Tympanidiis in regum illatus est. Diod.lib.15. refert eum epulantem & largius bibentem in morbum incidisse: fieri autem potest vt cum insidiis suorum peritet, id ebrietati tribueretur, quod Alexandro Ma. euenit. Vide Plutarchum & Probum in Dione.
units.tr: P.184.v.9. Killed by ambush in the end] M. Cic., De Nat. Deor. 3: "But (I would rather say) he died in his own bed, and was carried into the tombs of the kings among the Tympanidia." Diodorus, bk. 15, reports that he fell ill from feasting and drinking too heavily. It is possible that, since he perished by the ambushes of his own people, this was attributed to drunkenness, as happened to Alexander the Great. See Plutarch and Probus in the Life of Dion.
IN BOOK XXI.

units.la: Aturam eius] Plerique veteres natura eius, ex quo natura ius, fecit doctor meus Iac. Cuiacius, ad L.§. D.de pactis, quem vide. Error hinc natus est. In vet. libris diphthongus scribitur litteris separatis. Cum ergo in veteri esset natura ius, negligens exscriptor, natura eius, exscripsit, quod deinde audax corrector supraducta linea emendauit, vt legeretur naturam eius: Id & alij postea, maiori etiam audacia, mutarunt in maturam ætatem eius. Similibus mendis infectum Senecam, oltendit mihi CL. & doctissimus vir Nic. Faber libro de Ira 2. cap. 30. vbi legitur, pater est: tantum profuit, vt illi donanda iniuria eius sit: cum in libris Mss. sit, vt illi etiam iniuria eius sit, nemo non doctissimo viro assentiatur, leg. iniuria sua sit. Et lib.1.de Clement.cap.19. Cum liceat innoxium alius & ob hoc fecerunt salutarem potentiam esse tractare. Vett.codices,salutare potentia esse: Quis nō videat leg. potentia esse? Sed Cuiacii emendationem probat auctor ipse, lib 2. aetatis primilegium dicit, quod ius ordo nascendi, natura ipsa gentibus dedit. Su.lib.3. vocat, ius gentium. Vnde libenter emendarem locum libri XLI. infra, quorum maior Phraates, more gentis, heres regni. Vt legeremus more gentium, vel iure gentium, imperitus librarius, pro tore, ut scribebant veteres, coniecit legendum, more, inde more gentium, tandem more gentis. supra lib. 16. de Ptolemæo. Is contra ius gentium, minimo natu ex filio, ante infirmitatem, regnum tradiderat, eius rei populo rationem reddidërat, quæ postrema verba notanda sunt, ut intelligamus; regem contra ius & receptos mores, nihil absq; consensu populi innouare posse. Nam & infra lib.39. cum Ægypti regina minorem filium regē facere vellet, à populo compellitur, maiorem eligere. Herodotus lib. 7. ait Greek. Neque lex Diuina quicquam patitur primogenito derogari. Deuteron. 21. Ius autem naturæ esse eius gētium notum est ex I Ctorum libris M. Cicero 3. de Offic. Neque vero hoc solum natura, idest, iure gentium, &c. De Dionysio iuniore, lege Plutarchum & Probum in Dione. & Diodorum lib.16.& Gemistum.
units.tr: Aturam eius] Most older writers have natura eius [his nature], from which my teacher Jacques Cujas made natura ius [the right of nature], at L. §. D. de pactis, which see. The error arose from this. In old books a diphthong is written with separate letters. Since the old copy had natura ius, a careless copyist wrote natura eius, which a bold corrector then emended by drawing a line through the stroke, so that it was read naturam eius. Others later changed it, with even greater boldness, into maturam ætatem eius [his mature age]. That Seneca was infected with similar faults was shown to me by the distinguished and learned man Nic. Faber, in Book 2 of On Anger, chapter 30, where it reads pater est: tantum profuit, vt illi donanda iniuria eius sit: [he is a father: it has been so beneficial that his wrong must be forgiven him], whereas the manuscripts have vt illi etiam iniuria eius sit [so that even his wrong is to him]. Everyone must agree with that learned man that we should read iniuria sua sit [it is his own wrong]. And in Book 1 On Clemency, chapter 19: Cum liceat innoxium alius & ob hoc fecerunt salutarem potentiam esse tractare. The old codices have salutare potentia esse [that power is healthful]; who does not see that we should read potentia esse [that it is power]? But the author himself supports Cujas's emendation in Book 2, where he calls it aetatis primilegium [a privilege of age], quod ius ordo nascendi, natura ipsa gentibus dedit [which the order of birth, nature itself, gave to peoples as a right]. In Book 3 he calls it ius gentium [the law of nations]. Hence I would gladly emend the passage in Book 41 below, quorum maior Phraates, more gentis, heres regni [of whom the elder, Phraates, was heir to the kingdom by the custom of the people]. A clumsy copyist, reading the abbreviation tore for iure [or more] as the old writers wrote it, proposed more [by custom], so that we would read more gentium [by the custom of the nations] or iure gentium [by the law of nations]; then more gentium, and finally more gentis [by the custom of the people]. Above, in Book 16, on Ptolemy: Is contra ius gentium, minimo natu ex filio, ante infirmitatem, regnum tradiderat, eius rei populo rationem reddidërat [he had handed over the kingdom, against the law of nations, to the youngest of his sons, before his illness, and had given the people an account of that matter]. These final words must be noted, so that we understand that a king cannot introduce anything against law and accepted custom without the consent of the people. For also below, in Book 39, when the queen of Egypt wished to make the younger son king, she was compelled by the people to choose the elder. Herodotus, Book 7, says [Greek]. Nor does divine law allow anything to be taken away from the firstborn: Deut. 21. That natural law is the same as the law of nations is known from the books of the jurists; M. Cicero, On Duties, Book 3: Neque vero hoc solum natura, idest, iure gentium [Nor indeed is this by nature alone, that is, by the law of nations], etc. On the younger Dionysius, read Plutarch and Probus in the life of Dion, and Diodorus Book 16, and Gemistus.

units.la: Pag.186. v. 1. Dionysius pellitur) Opera Dionis inprimis.
units.tr: Page 186, line 1. Dionysius is driven out: chiefly the work of Dion.

units.la: V.3. A Locrensibus) Vide Strabonem lib. 6. & Ælianum lib. 9.
units.tr: Line 3. By the Locrians: see Strabo book 6 and Aelian book 9.
Page 187, line 2. Hanno, prince of the Carthaginians: Orosius book 4, chapter 6.

units.la: V.30. Depsito imperio arcem Syracusanis) Timoleonti & Corinthius legendus Plutarchus & Probus in Timoleonte. Diodotus libro 16.
units.tr: Line 30. Having laid down his rule, he handed the citadel to the Syracusans: for Timoleon read Corinthian; see Plutarch and Probus in Timoleon, and Diodorus book 16.

units.la: V.32. Corinthum in exsilium) Diod. inde natum Proverbium, Dionysium Corinthi.
units.tr: Line 32. Into exile at Corinth: from Diodorus comes the proverb Dionysius at Corinth.

units.la: P.188. v.24. Rhodanum) Quidam Mss. Rodonum, alii Rodanum. Front.lib.1.cap.2. Rodinum.
units.tr: Page 188, line 24. Rhodanus: some manuscripts read Rodonus, others Rodanus. Frontinus, book 1, chapter 2, has Rodinus.

units.la: P.189. Pag.189.v.3. Venditasset) Ita Vet. quomodo etiam legendum in Orosio libro 4. cap. 6. cuius Ms. habet, indicasset.
units.tr: Page 189, line 3. Venditasset: so the old copies read, and it should likewise be read thus in Orosius, book 4, chapter 6, whose manuscript has indicasset.
ON BOOK XXII.
From Agathocles) Read Diodorus, book 19.

units.la: V.33. Patre figulo) Plutarch. in Apophth.
units.tr: V.33. Father a potter) Plutarch, in the Apophthegms.

units.la: P.190.v.2. Forma) Τὴν πτ ὄψιν ἰναγεισιν, καὶ τὸ ὀνομα ἰνεμ-ζονεσ. Diod.
units.tr: P.190.v.2. Form) The appearance is described as [Τὴν πτ ὄψιν ἰναγεισιν, καὶ τὸ ὀνομα ἰνεμ-ζονεσ] in Diodorus.

units.la: V.15. Sui Syracusani) Inclusa absunt à bonis libris, quia tamen sine iis manca esset oratio, & in uno Ms. repperiuntur, nihil mutare ausus sum: quamuis ea mihi valde suspecta sint. Belli in Agrigentinos & Crotoniatas meminit Diodorus: de Ætneis & Campanis nullum verbum.
units.tr: V.15. The Syracusans themselves) The bracketed words are absent from the good books. Because the sentence would be incomplete without them, and they are found in one manuscript, I have dared to change nothing, although I hold them in strong suspicion. Diodorus mentions the war against the Agrigentines and the Crotonians, but says nothing about the Aetnaeans and the Campanians.

units.la: & Damasco, illi est Δάμας. Plurimum autem in tota hac narratione ab auctore uostro discrepat Diodorus, vt quibus ex lib.19. & 20. videre potest.
units.tr: And Damasco; in Greek it is Δάμας. Diodorus differs greatly from our author throughout this whole narrative, as one can see from books 19 and 20.

units.la: P.192.v.3. Inaudita mors) Locus hic cum depravatus legeretur Clareano negotium fecit: ego Mss. lectionem expressi, in qua nihil est quod lectorem morari possit.
units.tr: P.192.v.3. An unheard-of death) Since this passage was read in a corrupt form, it caused trouble for Clareanus. I have expressed the reading of the manuscripts, in which there is nothing that could delay the reader.

units.la: V.8. A quo Gictus) Diod. extremo lib.19. apud quem de Syracusarum obsidione nihil.
units.tr: V.8. By whom Gictus) Diodorus, at the end of book 19, says nothing about the siege of Syracuse.

units.la: V.14. Statuit bellum in Africam) Confer haec cum Diodor.lib.20.
units.tr: V.14. He resolved on war in Africa) Compare these things with Diodorus, book 20.

units.la: V.31. Ceteros omnes ad tutelam) Cum fratre Antandro. Nequid autem se absente Syracusani moverent διεξιόντες τὰς συμβουλίας ἀπ' ἀπάλων, καὶ μάλιστα ἀδελφοὺς ἀπ' ἀδελ-φῶν, καὶ πατέρας ἀπὸ παίδων, ut qui domi manebant, de amicis & propinquis qui cum Agathocle erant solicitij quiescerent. Diod.
units.tr: V.31. All the others to the guardianship) Along with his brother Antander. That the Syracusans might not stir while he was absent, [διεξιόντες τὰς συμβουλίας ἀπ' ἀπάλων, καὶ μάλιστα ἀδελφοὺς ἀπ' ἀδελ-φῶν, καὶ πατέρας ἀπὸ παίδων], that is, going through their counsels with everyone, especially brothers with brothers and fathers with sons, so that those who stayed at home, anxious about friends and relatives who were with Agathocles, might be quiet. Diodorus.

units.la: V.33. Septimo igitur) Restituendus est numerus in Diodoro, initio lib.19. Cum enim lib.20. dicat à Troia capta ad Agathoclis in Africam expeditionem esse annos σχεδὸν ΒΡΙ τῶν ἐκατονταετιῶν ἡμερῶν, id est, DCCCLXXXIII.
units.tr: V.33. Therefore in the seventh) The number needs to be restored in Diodorus, at the beginning of book 19. For since book 20 says that from the capture of Troy to Agathocles' expedition into Africa there were nearly [σχεδὸν ΒΡΙ τῶν ἐκατονταετιῶν ἡμερῶν], that is, 883 years,

units.la: & in Africa profectus sit vii.anno imperij sui: vt & ex ipso Diodoro constat: à capta Troia ad eius tyrannidem erunt anni DCCCLXXVI. Male igitur in Diodoro legitur ἐκατονταετίας ἑξ, id est DCCCLXVI. cum sit legendum ἐπτακοσιοστῷ ἑξ. Nisi superior numerus emendandus videatur, vt legamus ἑπτακοσιοστῷ pro ἐκατοστῷ. Et hoc veilus.
units.tr: and he set out for Africa in the seventh year of his reign, as is also clear from Diodorus himself, then from the capture of Troy to his tyranny there would be 876 years. Therefore it is wrongly read in Diodorus as [ἐκατονταετίας ἑξ], that is, 866, when it ought to be read [ἐπτακοσιοστῷ ἑξ]. Unless the earlier number seems to need correcting, so that we read [ἑπτακοσιοστῷ] for [ἐκατοστῷ]. And this is what I would prefer.

units.la: P.193. v.11. Odio diuturni imperii] Βαρωοµένους τοῖς ἀεσ- φάγμασιν, ἐκ πολλῶν χρόνων, λύψεσς καιρὸν τῆς δυσαρέστως, Diod.
units.tr: P.193. v.11. Hatred of a long-standing rule] [Βαρυνομένους τοῖς ἐπαχθήμασιν, ἐκ πολλῶν χρόνων, ζητοῦντας καιρὸν τῆς ἀπαλλαγῆς], Diodorus. Being weighed down by the burdens of a long time, they were seeking an opportunity for release.

units.la: P.194.v.21. Hanno] Ἐt Βοµίλκας. Diod. qui auctori nofiro dicitur Bomilcar, aut Vomilcar. Habuerunt autem in exercitu xl. millia peditum, equites mille. Diod. Orofius Ms. pro xxx.millia habet viginti, & ita vnus è noftris. Nec magis in cæforum numero conueniunt. Orofius qui cetera hinc tranfcripfifle videtur, duo millia Pœnorum, Siculos duos: Diodorus illorum mille, horum duecentos cecidiffe fcribit.
units.tr: P.194.v.21. Hanno] And [Βομίλκας], Diodorus, who in our author is called Bomilcar or Vomilcar. They had in the army forty thousand foot and a thousand horse, according to Diodorus. The manuscript of Orosius has twenty thousand instead of thirty thousand, and so does one of ours. Nor do they agree better on the number of the slain. Orosius, who seems to have copied the rest from here, writes that two thousand Carthaginians and two Sicilians fell; Diodorus writes that a thousand of the former and two hundred of the latter fell.

units.la: P.197.v.14. Afdlas] Diodoro Οφίλας dicitur, is ἀξιοῦ ξάλσρο, inquit, τοῖς ἰλλίοι μείζονα δυναστίαν.
units.tr: P.197.v.14. Ophilas] In Diodorus he is called Ophilas, who, he says, [ἀξιοῦ ... τοῖς ... μείζονα δυναστείαν], claimed a greater power than the others.

units.la: V.27. Bomilcar rex Pœnorum] Carthaginienfium ducces, etiam reges dicuntur. Hannonis Periplus infcribitur Αννῶνος Καρχηδονίων βασιλέως. & Imilco de quo fupra lib. 19. rex Carthaginiensium ab Orofio dicitur. Ideo, opinor quia plerunq; perpetuam auctoritatem obtinebant. Procopius 1. de bello Goth. barbaros ait duces fuos, reges vocare. Vide quæ notaui ad lib. 31. inf.
units.tr: V.27. Bomilcar, king of the Carthaginians] The leaders of the Carthaginians are also called kings. The Periplus of Hanno is entitled [Ἁννῶνος Καρχηδονίων βασιλέως], "of Hanno, king of the Carthaginians." Imilco, of whom above in book 19, is called king of the Carthaginians by Orosius. I suppose this is because they generally held their authority for life. Procopius, in book 1 of the Gothic War, says that barbarians call their leaders kings. See what I have noted on book 31 below.

units.la: P.196. v.17. Cum Archagatho] Diodorus defcruiffe filios fcribit, qui à militibus fuga cognita, interfectifint. Quam crudeliter autem in Sicilia verfatus fit poft reditum Agathocles, lege apud Diodorum.
units.tr: P.196. v.17. With Archagathus] Diodorus writes that the sons deserted him, and that when the flight became known to the soldiers, they were killed. For how cruelly Agathocles behaved in Sicily after his return, read Diodorus.
ON BOOK XXIII.

units.la: P.198, v.27. Ruttiosq; fe ex nomine] Strabo lib. 6. Bruttios dictos ait à Lucanis, βριττίους ἀπὸ παλαιοῦ τοὺς δούλους: cum enim eorum effent pastores, rebus temporeDionyfii turbatis, ab iis defecerant: Stephanus à Brettio Herculis filio dictos vult. vide Euftath. in Dionyf. qui eos Βρεττίους vocat, & Diod. 16.
units.tr: P.198, v.27. The Bruttians, named after themselves] Strabo, book 6, says the Bruttians were named by the Lucanians, [Βρεττίους ἀπὸ παλαιοῦ τοὺς δούλους], "the slaves of old." For since they had been their shepherds, when affairs were disturbed in the time of Dionysius they revolted from them. Stephanus wants them named after Brettius, son of Hercules. See Eustathius on Dionysius, who calls them [Βρεττίους], and Diodorus, book 16.

units.la: P.199.v.6. Opinionis eius] Opinio huic auctori eft fama & rumor. Nonius fignificationem notat, fed exempla, vtipfius eft mos, adfcripfit parum accómodata. Tacitus in vita Agricolæ. Comitante opinione Britanniam ei promisciam dari. Cic.11. ad Attic.epift.16. & 18.
units.tr: P.199.v.6. Of his opinion] For this author, opinio means report and rumour. Nonius notes this meaning, but as is his habit he added examples that are not very fitting. Tacitus, in the Life of Agricola: with rumour accompanying, that Britain would be given to him as a province. Cicero, letters to Atticus, book 11, letters 16 and 18.
V. 20. Texena] One of the manuscripts has Teonexa, perhaps Theoxena.

units.la: P.200.v.14. Pyrrhus aduerfus] Vide Plutarchum in eius vita, & Paufaniam in Atticis: qui cum primum Carthaginienses infula fugasse referunt, tandem cum ob crudele imperium à sociis desereretur, ν δωαέρμ⊙ κεχρηῖν Σιχιλίας, ᾧσπερ ναῦς ποσὶ ἀνέχ ιόμενοι, vocatus a suis, Italiam repetiit, nauali proelio in itinere à Carthaginiensibus supes ratus.
units.tr: P.200.v.14. Pyrrhus against] See Plutarch in his Life, and Pausanias in the Attica. They report that at first he put the Carthaginians to flight in the island, but finally, deserted by his allies because of his cruel rule, [as if carrying a ship on their feet, ὥσπερ ναῦς ποσὶ ἀνεχόμενοι], he was called back by his own people and returned to Italy, having been defeated in a naval battle on the way by the Carthaginians.

units.la: Heleno filio ] Plutarchus non hunc, sed Alexandrum ait ex Lanassa Agathoclis filia susceptum.
units.tr: To his son Heleno] Plutarch says that this son was not the one born to him, but Alexander, born of Lanassa, daughter of Agathocles.

units.la: P.201 v.4. Necin Italia ] Praeter Plutarchum legeFlorum & Orofium lib. 4. cap. 2. & Front. lib. 4. cap. 1. apud quem pro Statuentum, quod & Mss. agnoscunt ex Plutarch legendum Beneuentum: victus autem magno praelio à Manio Curio confule.
units.tr: P.201 v.4. Nor in Italy] Besides Plutarch, read Florus, and Orosius, book 4, chapter 2, and Frontinus, book 4, chapter 1, where instead of Statuentum, which the manuscripts also recognise, one should read, from Plutarch, Beneventum; he was defeated there in a great battle by the consul Manius Curius.

units.la: V.8. Adstruxerat ] vulgo, attraxerat. & ita Mss. quidam; illud malo, statim enim destruens, inquit, qua cumulauerat. Tacit. de vita Agric. & confularibus ac triumphalibus ornamentis praedito, quid aliud adstruere fortuna poterat?
units.tr: V.8. Had added] Commonly attraxerat, and so some manuscripts; I prefer the former, for he says that immediately destroying what he had heaped up. Tacitus, in the Life of Agricola: endowed with consular and triumphal honours, what else could fortune add?

units.la: v.18. Quippe genitus] Quae hic de Hierone referuntur citat Saresbi Policraticilio. 1. cap. 13. Deeo Plautus Me- nach. sc. fine fores.
units.tr: v.18. For he was born] What is related here about Hiero is cited from Saresberiensis, Policraticus, book 1, chapter 13. Plautus, in the Menaechmi, scene: fine fores.
ON BOOK 24.

units.la: Irraum campum] De quo Paufaniasin Phocicis. Diod. lib. 16. & Plin. 4. cap. 3.
units.tr: On the Irraean plain: see Pausanias in the Phocica, Diodorus book 16, and Pliny book 4, chapter 3.

units.la: Arean] Ita veteres: Plutarc. in Pyrrho, & Paul. Ati- cis Rex Lacedaemoniorum est A᾽ρεύς.
units.tr: Arean: so the ancients wrote it. See Plutarch in the Life of Pyrrhus, and Pausanias in the Attica. The king of the Lacedaemonians is Areus [Ἀρεύς].

units.la: P.204.v.17. Ptolemaofilio] Lysimachum & Philippum paulo post commemorat, Ptolemaei nō meminit: id mouit quosdam vt hoc loco pro Ptolemaeo, Lysimachum reponerent: ego nihil muto, cum praesertim in Prologo huius libri, Ptolemaeum quendam Lysimachi filium nominet.
units.tr: P.204, v.17. Ptolemy's son: He mentions Lysimachus and Philip shortly after, but makes no mention of Ptolemy. This led some to replace Ptolemy with Lysimachus at this point. I change nothing, especially since in the Prologue of this book he names a certain Ptolemy, son of Lysimachus.

units.la: P.205.v.15. Cum eos nō caperent terra] Strabo lib.4. Verisimile esse ait, Gallos δωσεῖσθαι κατὰ ἐνεχθῆναι τε- σοῦτον, ὥς ςάσπως ἰμπρισίοντος, ἐξελάσας κολὺ ἀλλὰ ἐξ ἰεω- τῶν ὀκτῶν οἰκείας, &c.
units.tr: P.205, v.15. Since the land could not hold them: Strabo, book 4, says it is likely that the Gauls [...] so that [...] , &c. [the Greek is corrupt in the scan].

units.la: V.17. Versacrum ] Primus hunc locum ex vet. librisemendauit P. Pithoeus aduersar. lib. 1. cap. 6. quid sit ver sacrum docent Festus in Ver sacrum, & in Mamertugi: Liuius lib. ab v. c. xxxi. & xxxiv. Sifenna iv. historiarum, apud Nonium in Ver sacrum, & in damnare, nam duo illa fragmenta coniungenda esse notarunt alij. Eusebius in Chronico, Lacedæmonij Ver sacrum deflinantes Heracleam Vrbem condunt.
units.tr: V.17. Ver sacrum: P. Pithoeus first emended this passage from old manuscripts, Adversaria book 1, chapter 6. Festus explains what a ver sacrum is, under "Ver sacrum" and under Mamertugi. Livy, book 31 and book 34 (ab urbe condita). Sisenna, Histories book 4, cited by Nonius under "Ver sacrum" and under "damnare"; others have noted that these two fragments must be joined. Eusebius in the Chronicle: the Lacedaemonians, intending a ver sacrum, founded the city of Heraclea.
"Beyond the rest they are skilled": I would rather read "they were renowned".

units.la: Audax, bellicosa) Strabo lib. 4. genus Gallorum aitesse θυμικὸν καὶ ταχὺ πρὸς μάχλησιν ἀπλῶς ἐαυτοὺς καὶ οὐ κρ- ισίως. Et Gallos bellicosissimos gentem vocat Saluftius, & gloria belli ante Romanos fuisse (sic enim est in vet. codice) quasi habuerant, alia omnia virtuti sue prona esse, cum Gallis pro salute, nō pro gloria certare. Cic. de arusp. resp. Nec numero Hispanos, nec robore Gallos superauimus. D. Hieron. contra Vigil. Sola Gallia monstra non habuit, sed viru semper fortibus & eloquentissimis abundauit. De eloquentia Gallorum vide eundem Hieron. ep. 39. part. 3.
units.tr: Bold and warlike: Strabo, book 4, says the Gauls' nation is spirited and quick to fight, throwing themselves into battle without judgement [θυμικὸν καὶ ταχὺ πρὸς μάχλησιν]. Sallust also calls the Gauls "the most warlike nation", and says that they had "the glory of war" before the Romans (for so the old manuscript has it), while all other things were subordinate to their courage, since the Gauls fought for safety, not for glory. Cicero, On the Responses of the Haruspices: "We have not surpassed the Spaniards in numbers, nor the Gauls in strength." St Jerome against Vigilantius: "Gaul alone has produced no monsters, but has always abounded in brave and most eloquent men." On the eloquence of the Gauls see the same Jerome, letter 39, part 3.

units.la: Prolomæus) Paufaniasin Atticis, & l'hocicis, quæ lege de hac Gallorum in Græcia irruptione, & Delphorum obsidione.
units.tr: Ptolemy: see Pausanias in the Attica and the Phocica, where you will read of this invasion of the Gauls into Greece and the siege of Delphi.

units.la: P.207. v.2. Non Gotis agendum) Salluft. Catil. & r. historia. non Gotis paranda auxilia. Restituenda hæc vox Afranio apud Nonium. Nullam profecto accessi ad aram, quin deos supplicis, sumptu Gatis, donis, precibus, ploransibus obsecrans, nequicquam fatigarem. leg. supplicis, sumptu Gotis &c.
units.tr: P.207, v.2. Not to be dealt with by the Goths: Sallust, Catiline, and Histories: "help is not to be procured from the Goths". This word is to be restored to Afranius in Nonius: "I never approached an altar without beseeching the gods as a suppliant, with expense to the Goths, with gifts, prayers, and weeping and entreaties, in vain would I weary them." Read "supplicis, sumptu Gotis", etc.

units.la: v.27. Templum autem Appollinis) Præter Paufaniam, vide & Straboneм lib. 9.
units.tr: v.27. But the temple of Apollo: Besides Pausanias, see also Strabo, book 9.
P.208, v.2. In the form of a theatre: Strabo calls it an amphitheatre [ἀμφιθέατρον].

units.la: P. 209.v.32. Et terræmotu portio) Compara cum hoc loco Gallicæ cladis descriptionem, quæ est in Phocicis Paufaniæ. Is xxvi. millia Gallorum, partim ferro, partim tempestate & metu Panico, partim fame scribit in Phocide cecidisse. De Brenni morte, vide præterea Val. 1. cap. 2.
units.tr: P.209, v.32. And a portion by earthquake: Compare with this passage the description of the Gallic disaster in Pausanias' Phocica. He writes that 26,000 Gauls fell in Phocis, partly by the sword, partly by storm and Panic terror, partly by famine. On the death of Brennus see also Valerius, book 1, chapter 2.

units.la: P.210.v.14. Nemo ex tanto exercitu) Polybius lib.4. eos qui superauerint, circa Byzantium constitisse, ibiq; imperium condidisse scribit.
units.tr: P.210, v.14. No one from so great an army: Polybius, book 4, writes that those who survived settled around Byzantium and founded a kingdom there.
ON BOOK 25.

units.la: T Asiam omnem) Vide Strabonē lib.12. Oraculum de eorum in Asiam transitu exstat in Paufaniæ Phocicis.
units.tr: All Asia: See Strabo, book 12. The oracle concerning their crossing into Asia is found in Pausanias' Phocica.

units.la: v.46. Maiestatem suam tutam] Quid fi tutari? & ita quidem olim impressi.
units.tr: v.46. To keep their majesty safe: What if it should read "tutari"? And so indeed the old printed editions have it.

units.la: In auxilium à Bithynia]Strabo Gallos scribit, Attalicorum regum terras diu populasse; tandem ab iis Bithyniam obtinuisse, quæ & Gallogræcia.
units.tr: Called to aid from Bithynia: Strabo writes that the Gauls for a long time laid waste the lands of the Attalid kings; at last they took Bithynia from them, which is also called Gallograecia.

units.la: V. 23. Pyrrhus] Quomodo Pyrrhus Italia & Sicilia excesserit, & in Græciam reuersus Antigonum, & Gallos strenuè pugnantes viceriť, legendus in eius vita Plutarchus & Pau'anias in Atticis.
units.tr: V.23. Pyrrhus: How Pyrrhus left Italy and Sicily, returned to Greece, and defeated Antigonus and the Gauls who fought stoutly, should be read in Plutarch's Life of him, and in Pausanias' Attica.

units.la: P.213. v.16. Vt ad deuincenda regna]Ideo cum Antigonus comparabat xυϛ ... ιχ ἰσ ἀ.
units.tr: P.213, v.16. In order to subdue kingdoms: On this account Antigonus was compared [the Greek is corrupt in the scan].

units.la: v.19. Cherroneso]Glareanus ex historia legit Peloponeso, & sequentia comptobant. Vet. alii cerroneso, alii cerronefto. Vide Plutarc.& Paus in Attic. & Lacon.
units.tr: v.19. Chersonese: Glareanus reads Peloponnese from the history, and the following words agree. Other old copies have "cerroneso", others "cerronefto". See Plutarch and Pausanias in the Attica and the Laconica.

units.la: P.214. v.8. Saxo de muri] Probus, lapide ætiua, Plut. & Paufan. & Strabo lib. 8. id est, tegulam vocant.
units.tr: P.214, v.8. A stone from the wall: Probus [...]; Plutarch, Pausanias and Strabo, book 8, call it a tile (tegula).

units.la: v.9. Caput eius] Val. Max. lib. 5. cap. 1.
units.tr: v.9. His head: Valerius Maximus, book 5, chapter 1.

units.la: v. 14. Comparandum Pyrrho] ἡ πολεμικὴ ... μὲν ἐν τῷ τοῦ ... ταῦτα αὐτὸν βασιλέων.
units.tr: v.14. To be compared with Pyrrhus: his military skill [...] these kings [the Greek is corrupt in the scan; cf. Plutarch].
ON BOOK XXVI.

units.la: Pirorum quoque urbs]Locus manifesto mendosus, nec Vett. auxilio sunt. Glareanus nescio quo auctore Epidauriorum legit. Ex Paufaniæ Eliacis, & Plutarchi libello de virtutibus mulierum, omnino legendum Eliorum.
units.tr: The city of the Piri as well: The passage is manifestly corrupt, and the old witnesses do not help. Glareanus, on some authority I cannot identify, reads Epidaurians. From Pausanias' Elian books and Plutarch's treatise on the virtues of women, it must certainly be read Eleans.

units.la: P.216. v. 6. Hellanicus] Ita Vett.& Paufan.& Plut. quos lege, vulgo Helematus. Statim autem edidi pigneris, ex Vett.omnibus. Vide Prisc. lib.6. frequens est o in e mutatio. Inde Apellinem dicebant veteres, pro Apollinem, Festus. & Amplocis pro amplectiapud Sallustium, & à tegendo, toga dicta, Prisc. lib. 1. & à pendeo, pondus. Inde quod in Vett. Mss. semper legitur Ptolomæus rectum arbitror; est enim Græcis Πτολεμαῖος. Vt quæ iis est Κίρχυρα. Latinis est Corcyra: & Beguivix, est Beronice. Pignus autem hic vocat natos.
units.tr: P. 216, v. 6. Hellanicus: So the old copies read, and Pausanias and Plutarch, whom you should consult; commonly it is printed Helematus. Immediately afterwards I have printed pigneris from all the old copies. See Priscian, book 6: the change of o into e is frequent. Hence the ancients said Apellinem for Apollinem (Festus), and Amplocis for amplectia in Sallust, and toga is derived from tegere (to cover), Priscian book 1, and pondus from pendere (to hang). Hence I think Ptolemaeus is correct, as it is always read in the old manuscripts; for in Greek it is Ptolemaios [Πτολεμαῖος]. So too the Greek Kirchyra [Κίρχυρα] is Corcyra in Latin, and Beguivix is Beronice. Here he calls the sons pledges.

units.la: v. 16. Quinto post quam] Sex menses tyrannidem tenuisse refert Paufan. Internecinum] Duobus praeterea locis, vocem hanc huic auctori restitui, quæ & hic & lib. 6. & 11. varie corrupta erat. Alii internecinum scribunt: sed Festus internecinum dicit, & ita plerisq; Amm. Marcell: locis editū est: P.217. v. 11. Bellum Athenien sibus] Eius meminit Pauf. in Atticis.
units.tr: v. 16. Fifth after: Pausanias reports that he held the tyranny for six months. Internecinum: In two other places I have restored this word to this author, where it was variously corrupted, both here and in books 6 and 11. Others write internecinum, but Festus gives internecinum, and it is printed so in most places in Ammianus Marcellinus. P. 217, v. 11. The war against the Athenians: Pausanias mentions it in his Attica.
v. 25. Agat: Here Pausanias has Magat.
ON BOOK XXVII.

units.la: Ege Antiocho] Is Θεὸς dicebatur, Appianus Σωσ. qui eum ab vxore Laudice interfectum scribit, quod doleret sibi adiunctam Berenicem, vel, vt est in nostris Mss. Beronicem.
units.tr: Ege, to Antiochus] He was called God [Θεὸς]. Appian [Σωσ.] writes that he was killed by his wife Laodice, because she resented having Berenice joined to her; or, as it is in our manuscripts, Beronice.

units.la: P.219. v.4. Daphne] Daphne Stephano est Δάφνη τῆς ἐν Ἀρνοχίας μεγάλου πόλεως. Strabo 16. oppidum mediocre dicit esse.
units.tr: P.219, v.4. Daphne] Stephanus gives Daphne as "Daphne of the great city in Arnochia" [Δάφνη τῆς ἐν Ἀρνοχίας μεγάλου πόλεως]. Strabo, book 16, calls it a middling town.

units.la: P.220. v.15. Interpellatur a fratre] Belli inter Seleucum Callinicum & Antiochum Hieracem meminit Strabo lib. 16.
units.tr: P.220, v.15. Is pressed by his brother] Strabo, book 16, mentions the war between Seleucus Callinicus and Antiochus Hierax.

units.la: V.24. Rex Bithynia Eumenes] Regum Bithyniæ originem & successionem lege lib. 13. Strabonis.
units.tr: V.24. King Eumenes of Bithynia] Read the origin and succession of the kings of Bithynia in Strabo, book 13.

units.la: P.221. v.16. Non amici debito quam hostiis] Ea est bonorum librorum scriptura, ex qua legendum arbitror, non amicus dedito quam hostis factus id est, non tam amicus, &c. Similes loquutiones notaui supra initio lib 6.
units.tr: P.221, v.16. Not as a friend owed rather than as enemies] This is the reading of the good books, but I think one should read "non amicus dedito quam hostis factus", that is, not so much a friend, and so on. I noted similar expressions above at the beginning of book 6.

units.la: V.22. Germanis] Mallem, germani, vt germanos & fratres fuisse intelligat non natura tantum; sed cabius etiam, & fortuna,
units.tr: V.22. Germanis] I would prefer "germani", so that he understands them to have been brothers, not only by nature, but also by chance and by fortune.
IN BOOK XXVIII.

units.la: Tiam] Scribendum Phthiam, quomodo apud Plutarch. vocatur Pythri mater.
units.tr: Tiam: read Phthiam, as Plutarch calls Pyrrhus' mother.

units.la: P.223. v.5. Qui soli quondam aduersus Troianos] Strabo id ex Ephoro docet lib. 10.
units.tr: P.223, v.5. "Qui soli quondam adversus Troianos": Strabo teaches this from Ephorus, book 10.

units.la: V.24 Pastores, qui latrocinio] Hieronymus in Chronico, pastorum & latronum manum dicit: inde forte Gallica dictio, pastres, pro latronibus.
units.tr: V.24. "Pastores, qui latrocinio": Jerome in the Chronicle calls them "a band of shepherds and robbers" [pastorum et latronum manum]. Perhaps from this comes the French word "pastres" for robbers.

units.la: V.29. Æyolos autem] Strabo ex Ephoro lib. 10. Τοῦτε Αἰτωλυσίν ... ἐν Ἰλιάδι ... πρὸς Τυρία ... ἀ-χ-ὄ ... propter locorum asperitatem & difficilem aditum, & belli vsum: à quo Homero πολυχάλκου dicuntur.
units.tr: V.29. "Aetolos autem": Strabo, from Ephorus, book 10 [Τοῦτε Αἰτωλυσίν ... ἐν Ἰλιάδι ... πρὸς Τυρία ... ἀ-χ-ὄ ...]: on account of the roughness of the country, the difficult access, and their practice of war, from which Homer calls them "rich in bronze" [πολυχάλκου].

units.la: P.225. v.6. Ipsi regem quarant] Vett. omnes quia forte quare regem quarant.
units.tr: P.225, v.6. "Ipsi regem quaerant": all the old copies have "quia", perhaps read "quare regem quaerant" (why they seek a king).

units.la: V. 10. Bellum Spartanis infert] Vide Plutar. in Cleomene & Arato, & Paufaniam Corinth.
units.tr: V.10. "Bellum Spartanis infert": see Plutarch in the lives of Cleomenes and Aratus, and Pausanias of Corinth.

units.la: V.21. Patentibus omnes] Ita ex vno Ms. legendum: ceteri patentibus. Tacit 4 Annal. Ceterum sub recentem clades patuere procerum domus, fomenta & medici passim prabiti, &c.
units.tr: V.21. "Patentibus omnes": this should be read so from one manuscript; the others have "patentibus". Tacitus, Annals 4: "But after the recent disaster the houses of the nobles lay open, and remedies and physicians were everywhere offered," etc.

units.la: P.226. v.1. Dignatione] Idest, dignitate, vtirur Tacitus passim, M. Cicero ad Attic. epist. 10 lib. 10. Curtius, Seneca, alii: Cleomenem autem sibi ipsi manus attulisse Paufan. & Plutarc. auctores sunt.
units.tr: P.226, v.1. "Dignatione": that is, "dignitate" (dignity). Tacitus uses it throughout, and M. Cicero in his letter to Atticus, book 10; also Curtius, Seneca and others. Pausanias and Plutarch are the authorities that Cleomenes laid violent hands on himself.
IN BOOK XXIX.

units.la: Interfecto Seleuco] Callinici filio, qui pharmaco ab amicis sublatus est, relicto fratre Antiocho successore, qui Magnus dictus est, Appian. Syriaca.
units.tr: "Interfecto Seleuco": the son of Callinicus, who was removed by poison given by his friends, leaving his brother Antiochus as successor, who was called the Great. Appian, Syriaca.

units.la: V. 9. Ætate immatura] Minor quinque & viginti annis, cum nouem annos natus odium Romanorum patri iucassset. Probus.
units.tr: V.9. "Aetate immatura": younger than twenty-five years, since at the age of nine he had inherited his father's hatred of the Romans. Probus.

units.la: V. 12. Demetrius] De quo Appianus in Illyrica historia, Polybius, Liuius. Fuit autem L. Æmilius Paulus, consul cum M. Liuio Salinatore.
units.tr: V.12. "Demetrius": on whom Appian in the Illyrian history, Polybius and Livy. There was L. Aemilius Paulus, consul with M. Livius Salinator.

units.la: P.229.v.12. Legatum deinde ad Annibalem] Vide Liuium lib. ab.v. c.33. qui in vincula conditos Philippi legatos scribit.
units.tr: P.229, v.12. "Legatum deinde ad Annibalem": see Livy, book [...], chapter 33, who writes that the envoys of Philip were thrown into chains.

units.la: v.17. Lauinum praetorem) M. Valerius Lœuinus praetor M. Marcello & Q. Fabio Maximo Coss. à Romanis, precibus Apolloniatum, contra Philippum missus. Liuius 24. &c.
units.tr: v.17. "Lavinum praetorem": M. Valerius Laevinus, praetor, sent by the Romans against Philip at the request of the Apolloniates, in the consulship of M. Marcellus and Q. Fabius Maximus. Livy, book 24, etc.
IN BOOK XXX.

units.la: A Antiochus rex Syriae) Appianus Syriaca; D. Hieronymus in 11. cap. Danielis.
units.tr: "A Antiochus rex Syriae": Appian, Syriaca; St Jerome on Daniel, chapter 11.

units.la: V.14. Agathoclia) Meminit Plutarch. in ἐρμῆς. vulgo Agathoclea: quomodo habet & Hieron. in Dan.
units.tr: V.14. "Agathoclia": Plutarch mentions it in Hermes; commonly "Agathoclea", as Jerome also has it in Daniel.

units.la: V.18. Crepundia) Vulgo tripudia. lectionem veterē in tanto librorū consensu, si non amplectar, impudens sim.
units.tr: V.18. "Crepundia": commonly "tripudia". If I did not embrace the old reading, in such agreement of so many books, I would be shameless.

units.la: Nimis Basilicum est, & Alexandreum, quod soluere non possis, rescindere. Crepundia videntur hic esse κρότο μει-ψια, crepitacula, sistra Ægyptiaca, crotala, quibus in saltationibus vtebantur veteres, maxime orientales populi, vt apud Maronem Syra,
units.tr: It is too much of a Basilican and Alexandrian thing to be loosened and cut away. Here "crepundia" seem to be the things called krotala [κρότο...], rattles, Egyptian sistra, castanets, which the ancients used in their dances, especially the eastern peoples, as Virgil says of the Syrian woman:

units.la: Crispum sub crotalo docta mouere latum.
units.tr: "to move the supple flank skilfully beneath the castanets."

units.la: Crepundia Plauto Milite glor. sunt instrumenta puerilia.
units.tr: In Plautus' Miles Gloriosus, "crepundia" are childish toys.

units.la: Vt faciem quasi puero in collo pendeant crepundia. Martialis Apophor, crepitacula vocat. Vulgata lectio confirmari potest loco Salluftij, qui in Catil. Pallere, saltare elegantius quam necesse est probae: multa alia, quae sunt instrumenta luxuriae. Sed fi ei cartora quam decus atque pudicitia semper omnia fuere, ita in Mss. libris Salluftij legi.
units.tr: "As if they hung rattles from a child's neck." Martial in the Apophoreta calls them "crepitacula". The Vulgate reading can be confirmed by the passage of Sallust in the Catiline, who says: "to be pale, to dance more elegantly than is needed for an honest woman, and many other things which are instruments of luxury. But since these things were always valued more than honour and modesty..." So it is read in the manuscripts of Sallust.

units.la: P.232.v.24. Legiones q; cum cons.] Ita manuscripti duo: ceteri omnes, legationesque cum conditionibus pacis: error ex notarum compendio: cum CONS. interpretati sunt cum conditionibus, & ad id sequentia inuitabant, deinde cum exposita conditiones pacis à Rom.effent. Missus autem est consul post P.Sulpitium Galbam, & P.Villium Tappulum, T. Quintius Flamininus, ita Vett.libri, & rec, ne Flamininos patritios cum plebeiis Flaminiis confundamus: Hoc non animaduertfum; auctorem libelli de viris illustribus, fiue is Aur. Victor, fiue quis alius, in fedum errorem induxit, vt hunc, Flaminii eius qui ad Thrafimenum lacum occubuit filium arbitrarentur, vt alii docuerunt, inepte. Hic tamen Plutarcho vbique Φλαμίνιος dicitur.
units.tr: P.232, v.24. "Legiones q; cum cons.": two manuscripts read thus; all the others read "legationesque cum conditionibus pacis" (embassies with conditions of peace). The error came from the abbreviation in the notes: "cum CONS." was taken as "cum conditionibus", and the following words invited this: "then the conditions of peace were set out by the Romans." The consul sent after P. Sulpicius Galba and P. Villius Tappulus was T. Quinctius Flamininus, so read the old books and the recent ones, lest we confuse the patrician Flamininus with the plebeian Flaminius. This was not noticed: the author of the little book on illustrious men, whether it was Aurelius Victor or someone else, led into a serious error by thinking this man was the son of that Flaminius who fell at Lake Trasimene, as others have shown, foolishly. Here, however, Plutarch everywhere calls him Φλαμίνιος [Flaminios].

units.la: P.233.v.7. Theramenem & Therafiam] Theramenis infula hic, vt & supra lib.13. pro Thera accipitur. Strabo lib.1. ἀγὰ μέσον Θήρας καὶ Θηραϊας. Vide & Plinium lib.2. cap.87. & Eusebium in Chronico, & Senecam lib.6. natur. quæst. cap.21. cuius locus mendosus est, nec fatis explicatus ab annotatore:
units.tr: P.233, v.7. "Theramenem & Therafiam": the island of Thera (Theramenis) here, as also above in book 13, is taken for Thera [ἀγὰ μέσον Θήρας καὶ Θηραϊας]. See also Pliny, book 2, chapter 87, Eusebius in the Chronicle, and Seneca, Natural Questions, book 6, chapter 21, whose passage is corrupt and not sufficiently explained by the annotator.

units.la: v.12. Labe] A labendo labem dixit, vt & supra initio lib.17. & Cic. 2.de legib. Quamobrem ille quidem fapientiffimus Gracia Cir, longeque doctissimus, Salde hanc labem Ceretur. Labem etiam χαλκὸς clic, & hiatu notarum est ex I Ctorum libris, & M.Cic.1. de diuinat. Hæc vox cū librarij esset infolens, versit in mole. Hoc terræmotu Rhodium colossum ruisse Eusebius refert.
units.tr: v.12. "Labe": he called it "labes" from "labi" (to slip), as also at the beginning of book 17; and Cicero, On the Laws, book 2: "Wherefore that man, the wisest of Greece and by far the most learned, should be cleansed of this stain." "Labes" is also in the jurists' books, with a hiatus in the notes, and in Cicero's On Divination, book 1. Since this word was unfamiliar to the scribes, they changed it to "mole". Eusebius reports that the Colossus of Rhodes fell in this earthquake.

units.la: P. 234. v. 1. Romana fortuna suscit] Ad Cynoscephalas, s
units.tr: P.234, v.1. "Romana fortuna suscitat": at Cynoscephalae, s...

units.la: V. 11. Gracia Orbibus] Debetur hæc lectio codici Cuiacianu: nam ceteri optimæ notæ Thracia contra histo-riam. Plutarch. τὴν μὲν Μακεδονικὴν ἀπίδωκεν αὐτοῦ βασι-λείαν, τὴς δὲ Ἑλλάδος ἀσφαλισάμενος λαφηναι.
units.tr: V.11. "Gracia Orbibus": this reading is owed to the Cuiacian codex; all the other manuscripts of the best mark read "Thracia", contrary to history. Plutarch: [τὴν μὲν Μακεδονικὴν ... ἀσφαλισάμενος λαφηναι] he gave him the Macedonian kingdom, and having secured Greece...

units.la: V. 17. Legatos ad Antiochum] Asiaticum bellum Romanis suscitauit Thoas Æoliæ princeps, & Annibal. An. Florus.
units.tr: V.17. "Legatos ad Antiochum": the Asiatic war was stirred up against the Romans by Thoas, prince of Aeolia, and by Hannibal. Florus.
IN BOOK XXXI.

units.la: Mortuo Ptolemæo] Hæc latius & accuratius persequicurAppianus in Syriaca.
units.tr: Mortuo Ptolemæo] Appian pursues these matters more fully and accurately in the Syriaca.

units.la: V. 26. Nabis tyrannus] Liu. lib. 34. Plut.in Flaminio, & Philopœmene. Paus. in Messenicis, Achaicis, & Arcadic.
units.tr: V. 26. Nabis the tyrant] Livy book 34. Plutarch in the lives of Flamininus and Philopoemen. Pausanias in the Messenian, Achaean and Arcadian books.
V. 32. Hannibal's] Appian and Livy book 34.

units.la: P. 236. v. 26. Ac tum temp. con/.] Suffetes Carthaginiensibus erant, qui Romæ confules, Liuius lib. 30. quos Æmilius Probus in Annibale, binos reges, vocat. Erat & apud illos Dictatoris imperium, Liu. lib. 23. & Quæstorū dignitas; habebantur hi proximi iudicibus, idem Liuius lib. 34. Iudices erant centum, sup. lib. 19. & Senatus erat triginta seniorum consessus, Liuius lib. 30. erant apud eos & Prætores, Probus Annib. Liuius 33.
units.tr: P. 236 v. 26. At that time...] The Suffetes were the magistrates of the Carthaginians, who were called consuls at Rome (Livy book 30). Aemilius Probus in his Hannibal calls them two kings. They also had the power of a dictator (Livy book 23) and the dignity of quaestors. These were held next to the judges (Livy book 34 again). There were a hundred judges (above, book 19). The Senate was an assembly of thirty elders (Livy book 30). They also had praetors (Probus in Hannibal; Livy book 33).

units.la: P.237. v. 11. Flaminino R. imp. comparetur] Quod Flamininum male habebat: & Plutarchus inter causas finiti cum Nabide belli recenset Flaminini φιλοτιμίαν ἡ ζῆλο-τυπίαν τῶν Φιλοποίμενος πυθῶν.
units.tr: P. 237 v. 11. Compared with the Roman commander Flamininus] Because it vexed Flamininus. Plutarch, among the causes of ending the war with Nabis, also lists Flamininus' ambition or jealousy on learning of the honour of Philopoemen [φιλοτιμίαν ἢ ζηλοτυπίαν τῶν Φιλοποίμενος πυνθανόμενος].

units.la: V. 19. Mille equites] Vett.plerique equitum, vnde mendosum locum esse suspicor: & sane in Io. Peleriui vet.cod. legitur tria millia equitum.
units.tr: V. 19. A thousand horsemen] Most old copies read equitum (of horsemen), so I suspect a faulty passage here. Indeed the old manuscript of Io. Pelerinus reads tria millia equitum (three thousand horsemen).

units.la: V.21. Regi sedenti] Id est otioso. M.Cicero 10.ad Att. e-pist. Et res ipsa, & epist. Quid nam mihi.
units.tr: V. 21. To the king sitting] That is, at leisure. M. Cicero, Letters to Atticus book 10: the passages beginning "Et res ipsa" and "Quid nam mihi".

units.la: V.28. Vnus ex comitibus] Aristonem mercatorem TyGc rium, προφάσεις τῆς ἐμπορίας missum scribit Appianus, quæ lege, & Liuium.
units.tr: V. 28. One of the companions] Appian writes that Aristo, a Tyrian merchant, was sent on the pretext of trade [προφάσει τῆς ἐμπορίας]. Read this, and Livy.

units.la: Ad Antiochum legatos] Inter quos erat Scipio, qui Annibalem denicerat. P. ꝛter Liuium & Appianum, vide Lucianum in dialogis Νεκρικοῖς, & Plutar. & Flaminio. Consilium autem legatorum, explicat & Fronti. lib. 1 cap. 8.
units.tr: Envoys to Antiochus] Among them was Scipio, who had put Hannibal to death. Besides Livy and Appian, see Lucian in the Dialogues of the Dead and Plutarch in Flamininus. The purpose of the envoys' counsel is also explained by Frontinus, book 1, chapter 8.

units.la: P. 239 v. 3 Omnibus quæ perrogatis] Appianus Annibalem primum sententiam rogatum scribit.
units.tr: P. 239 v. 3. When all the questions had been put] Appian writes that Hannibal was asked for his opinion first.

units.la: V. 21. Suis eos opibus] Quod in Africa contra Carthaginenses iam antea fecerat Agathocles, eleganter Appianus: Τὰς πολίμους ἀπὸ ... ὑπὸ ... ἐπιχειρούμενον, ἐξω δὲ κυφωτίας.
units.tr: V. 21. With their own resources] This is what Agathocles had already done earlier against the Carthaginians in Africa, as Appian elegantly says [Τὰς πόλεις ... ὑπὸ ... ἐπιχειρούμενον, ἐξω δὲ κυφωτίας].

units.la: V. 26. Ministerium] Ita Mss, vt supra lib. 24. arbitrium pro arbitrum. & lib. 6. postulat sibi dari ministerium impensæ. vt est in vulgatis libris, nam ibi Mss. ministrum.
units.tr: V. 26. Ministerium] So the manuscripts read, as above in book 24 arbitrium for arbitrum, and in book 6 postulat sibi dari ministerium impensae, as is in the printed books; for there the manuscripts have ministrum.

units.la: I' 240. v. 6. Affectationum adulationibus] Assentantium, quod est in vet. cod. Pelecini, rectum puto.
units.tr: P. 240 v. 6. With the flatteries of affectations] I think assentantium (of flatterers), which is in the old codex of Pelecinus, is the correct reading.

units.la: V 9. Acilius Romanus cos.] Manius Acilius Glabrio: apud Appianum mendose legitur Αχίλιος inuerso A. pro Αχίλιος. erat hic cos. cum P. Corn. Scipione Nasica. vulgo Attilium, inepte, vt apud auctorem de viris illustribus. Vide Liuium 36. Florum, Front. l. 2 cap. 4.
units.tr: V. 9. Acilius the Roman consul] Manius Acilius Glabrio. In Appian the name is wrongly read with an inverted A, as [Αχίλιος] for [Ἀκίλιος]. He was consul with P. Cornelius Scipio Nasica. Commonly printed as Attilium, foolishly, as in the author On Illustrious Men. See Livy book 36, Florus, and Frontinus book 2, chapter 4.

units.la: V. 20. Æmilium] Ita vet. cod. Pelerini. Cuiacianus. Æmilium E pro A. Veteres enim Atrylius scribebant ceteri variæ corrupti, quidam es Gnium, alii ei Lentum. Scripsiffe auctorem arbitror, nuntiatur et Lucium Aemilii, pro quo impresserunt quidam Lucium Neuium: quidam Liuium M nenium. Est autem hic L. Æmilius Regillus Liuio lib. 37. & Floro: Appiano Ἀεύκιος Αἰμίλιος, Πνγῦ λ pro Πυγίας.
units.tr: V. 20. Aemilium] So the old codex of Pelerinus reads, and the Cuiacian has Aemilium E for A. For the old writers wrote Atrylius, and the others are corrupted in various ways, some reading es Gnium, others ei Lentum. I think the author wrote nuntiatur et Lucium Aemilii, for which some printers put Lucium Neuium, and some Liuium Mnenium. This is L. Aemilius Regillus in Livy book 37 and Florus. In Appian he is [Λεύκιος Αἰμίλιος], and [Πυγῦλ] stands for [Πυγίας].

units.la: V. 33. Cos. L Scipio] Et cum eo C. Læliu: præter citatos G. Illius l. 6. c. 4. Scipio hoc bello cōfecto A.fi.aticus dictus.
units.tr: V. 33. Consul L. Scipio] And with him C. Laelius; besides those cited, see G. Illius book 6, chapter 4. Scipio, after this war was finished, was called Asiaticus.

units.la: P. 241. v. 9. I. filius filium] P. Æmyl'i, qui P. cum vicit n tura filium. P. Scipionis, adoptione inquit Appianus, contra quam ceteri: non enim ipse Africanus, sed eius filius, Paoli Æ nihil filium eum qui Carthaginem euertit, adoptauit. P 1. in Æmilio, Cicero, alii.
units.tr: P. 241 v. 9. Son of the son] The son of P. Aemilius, who conquered Perseus, by adoption, says Appian, contrary to the others: for it was not Africanus himself but his son who was adopted by the son of Paulus, the one who destroyed Carthage. See Plutarch in Aemilius, Cicero, and others.

units.la: I' 242. v. 6 Præliam cum Antiocho] Ad montem Sipylum: abscente Africano, qui Elax ægrotabat. Appian. 40
units.tr: P. 242 v. 6. The battle with Antiochus] At Mount Sipylus, Africanus being absent, as he was sick. Appian, book 40.

units.la: Οὐχ ὑφίζομεν τῆς σὺν ἀγλαΐας, ἀλλ᾽ ἐπιτάξομεν τῆς ἐτέρου ἀτυχίας, inquit apud Appianum Africanus.
units.tr: "We do not ... of glory, but we will impose ... of another's misfortune," says Africanus in Appian [Οὐχ ὑφίζομεν τῆς σὺν ἀγλαΐας, ἀλλ᾽ ἐπιτάξομεν τῆς ἐτέρου ἀτυχίας].

units.la: V. 21. Aptiorem gloriam] Ea est duorum tantum Mss. lectio: ceteri vulgatam confirmant, nisi quod vulgo Gelonta/tas legitur.
units.tr: V. 21. More fitting glory] This is the reading of only two manuscripts; the others confirm the printed text, except that commonly Gelonta/tas is read.
ON BOOK XXXII.

units.la: Ἄξ Toli] De Aetolico bello quod gesit M. Fulvius Nobilior cos. cum Gn. Manlio Vulsone, lege Liuiam lib. 38. Florum 2.
