units.tr: Aetoli [Ἄξ Toli]: On the Aetolian war which M. Fulvius Nobilior, consul, waged with Gn. Manlius Vulso, read Livy book 38 and Florus book 2.

units.la: P 244 v.2. Ἠολοφαμενε.) Praeter Liuium 39 & Plutarchum lege Paulanian Arcadicis.
units.tr: P. 244, v. 2. [Ἠολοφαμενε]: Besides Livy book 39 and Plutarch, read Pausanias, Arcadica.

units.la: V.17. Lygortas) Mss. Lygortas, facili lapsu, pro Grae-ci Αυκόργας.
units.tr: V. 17. Lygortas: The manuscripts read Lygortas, through an easy slip, for the Greek [Αυκόργας].

units.la: V.28 D.dymai) Strabo lib. 16. interfectum à barbaris cum templum Beii spoliare conatertur: Auctor de viris illustribus, a sodalibus quos temulentus in convivio pulsauerat, o citum esse refert. D.H eron.in 11.Daniel cum aduerfus Elimaeos pugnatet, eu omni exercitu delerum.
units.tr: V. 28. Dardymai: Strabo, book 16, says he was killed by barbarians while trying to plunder the temple of Bel. The author of De viris illustribus reports that he was killed by his companions, whom he had struck in a drunken quarrel at a banquet. Jerome, on Daniel 11, says that when he was fighting against the Elymaeans, he was destroyed with his whole army.

units.la: P 245. w23 Occifo Demetrio] De Perseo in fratrem Demetrium fraude, & Philippi morte, vide Liuium lib. 40. & Paulan in Cornuthiacis.
units.tr: P. 245, v. 23. Occiso Demetrio: On Perseus' treachery against his brother Demetrius, and on the death of Philip, see Livy book 40 and Pausanias in the Corinthiaca.

units.la: P.246. v.1 Scordifcos] Hos ad Istrum habitasse etiam Strabo auctor est lib. 7. Paulo potius Sabos ex Vett. edidit: Strabonis Σαβοι est, & Plinio lib.3 Saues.
units.tr: P. 246, v. 1. Scordiscos: Strabo also states that these people lived near the Ister, book 7. Paulus rather edited "Sabos" from the older copies: Strabo's [Σαβοι], and in Pliny book 3, "Saves."

units.la: V.18. Aurum argentumque] Lege Strab.lib.4 Fuit autem Q. Seruilius Caepio cos. cum Atilio Seranno, & insequenti anno a Cimbris victus, epitome Liuiana lib. 67.
units.tr: V. 18. Aurum argentumque: Read Strabo, book 4. Now Q. Servilius Caepio was consul with Atilius Serranus, and in the following year was defeated by the Cimbri; see the Livian epitome, book 67.

units.la: Ogosius lib.5 cap.16. Sallustius extremo lugurthino, vbi pro C.Manlio, vetus codex legit M. Aiallio. De eius morte Strabo, & Valerius l.b. 6. cap.11. qui inter se variant: & ipse Valerius secum pugnat lib.4.cap.7.
units.tr: Orosius, book 5, chapter 16. Sallust, at the end of the Jugurthine War, where an old manuscript reads "M. Aiallio" in place of "C. Manlio." On his death, see Strabo and Valerius, book 6, chapter 11, who disagree with each other; and Valerius himself contradicts himself in book 4, chapter 7.

units.la: V.23. Aetta] Graecis est Aiame, quod autem statim dicit Argonautas nauem humeris tulisse, vide Apollo.lib.4. Τρίτος ὤ γε ὠς ἐδ ἀρίχα Ϛειμεροί ὕπερ ἀνάκτων Ἡ ἴδιῃ ἢ ἀρέτῃ Αἰόλης ἀπὸ ἔμας ἐχήμενος Νᾶν μεταχερδοίτων, ἔοτι τε ἀνδοι νησαρχαῖς, Ἀδισμοῦς ἀχθίαι ζων ἐνεκλιδεν ἀπὸ νῶτα Ἡ ρ᾽ ὁ ὀρηοῦ νύκτας τι, &c. 28. Magnitudinem nauis] Vulgo longitudinem nauis. Nauis pro nauigationis dixit.
units.tr: V. 23. Aetta: In Greek it is Aiame, but as for what he says next, that the Argonauts carried the ship on their shoulders, see Apollonius, book 4. Third, indeed, when they had ... they bore the ship on their shoulders, [Τρίτος ὤ γε ὠς ἐδ ἀρίχα Ϛειμεροί ὕπερ ἀνάκτων Ἡ ἴδιῃ ἢ ἀρέτῃ Αἰόλης ἀπὸ ἔμας ἐχήμενος Νᾶν μεταχερδοίτων, ἔοτι τε ἀνδοι νησαρχαῖς, Ἀδισμοῦς ἀχθίαι ζων ἐνεκλιδεν ἀπὸ νῶτα Ἡ ρ᾽ ὁ ὀρηοῦ νύκτας τι, &c.] 28. Magnitudinem nauis: The usual reading is "the length of the ship." He used "ship" for "voyage."

units.la: V.31. Dacei]De Dacis & Getis lege Strabonem lib. 7.
units.tr: V. 31. Dacei: On the Dacians and Getae, read Strabo, book 7.

units.la: P. 247. v. 14. Cretam defertur] Vide Probum in Annibalis vita. Quo commento Euinenem viceric refert & Front. lib.4. cap.12. Et de eius morte Plutarch.in Flaminino, Appianus in Syriaca, Liuius lib. 39. vbi & Africani mortem commemorat. Val.lib.9.cap.2.Varro περὶ ἰξαγω-γῆς apud Nonium. Quaeris ibidem ab Annibale, cur biberet medicamentum: Quia Romanis, inquit, me Prusiades tradere volebat.
units.tr: P. 247, v. 14. Cretam defertur: See Probus in the Life of Hannibal. By this stratagem he is said to have defeated Eumenes; see also Frontinus, book 4, chapter 12. On his death, see Plutarch in Flamininus, Appian in the Syriaca, and Livy book 39, where he also records the death of Scipio Africanus. Valerius, book 9, chapter 2. Varro, in [περὶ ἐξαγωγῆς], as cited in Nonius: "You ask in the same place why Hannibal drank the medicine. Because, he said, Prusias wanted to hand me over to the Romans."
ON BOOK XXXIII.

units.la: Acedonicum)De hoc bello Plutarch.in Paulo Æmilio, Liuius lib.41, & sequentibus,Flor.lib.2.& Paterculus lib.1. Paufanias Achaicis, Diodorus lib.31. cuius habemus tantum excerpta.
units.tr: Macedonicum) On this war, see Plutarch in the life of Paulus Aemilius, Livy book 41 and the following books, Florus book 2, and Paterculus book 1. Pausanias in the Achaica, and Diodorus book 31, of whom we have only excerpts.

units.la: P.249.v.3 Decennis)Ita legendum ex vestigiis antiquae lectionis, ea est, decentu Supra pro denunciatum, malim denuntiarunt.
units.tr: P. 249, v. 3. Decennis) It should be read thus, following the traces of the older reading, which gives "decentu". Above, for denunciatum, I would prefer denuntiarunt.

units.la: V.10. Cos. Sulpicius)Huius consulis nemo praeter hunc auctorem meminit: aut igitur fœdum mendum est in libris; aut Iustinus turpiter lapsus est. Est enim hic P. Licinius qui cos. fuit cum C. Cassio Longino, Liuius lib. 42. & Plutarch. in Apopht. quod notauit Glareanus, nescio tamen quo auctore eum L. Licinium vocet.
units.tr: V. 10. Cos. Sulpicius) No one but this author mentions this consul. Either there is a foul error in the manuscripts, or Justin has slipped badly. For this is P. Licinius, who was consul with C. Cassius Longinus (Livy book 42, and Plutarch in the Apophthegms), as Glareanus noted. I do not know, however, on what authority he calls him L. Licinius.

units.la: V.16. Luna nocte defecit) M. Cicero dialogo de Senectute, ex eius 1. de officiis, constat Catonem filium in Macedonia Persico bello militasse: totus is locus Ciceronis adducitur a Saresberiensi lib. 6. Policr. cap. 7. a quo abest glossa illa Adeo summa erat obseruatio in bello moruendo, quae in textum Ciceronis impudenter irrepsit.
units.tr: V. 16. Luna nocte defecit) From Cicero's dialogue on old age, and from his first book of De Officiis, it is established that Cato's son served in the Macedonian war against Perseus. Saresberiensis, book 6 of the Policraticus, chapter 7, cites the whole of this passage of Cicero, but he lacks that gloss, "So great was the regard for dying in war", which has shamelessly crept into the text of Cicero.
ON BOOK XXXIV.

units.la: Chaei) Bellum Achaicum,& eius originem multis describit Paufanias in Achaicis, vide Liuium lib. 52. & Florum lib.2. Paterculus lib.1. & Orofium lib.5. cap. 3.
units.tr: Chaei) The Achaean War and its origin are described at length by Pausanias in the Achaica. See Livy book 52, Florus book 2, Paterculus book 1, and Orosius book 5, chapter 3.

units.la: V.22. Legatos quoq; ipsos) Florus de Critolao concitore huius belli legatos Romanos, dubium an eis manus, certe oratione violauit. Et M.Cicero pro lege Manilia, propter legatos superbius appellatos Corinthum euersam dicit: vide & 1. de offic.
units.tr: V.22. Legatos quoque ipsos) Florus, speaking of Critolaus, the instigator of this war, says he violated the Roman envoys, if not with their hands (it is doubtful), then certainly with his words. M. Cicero, in the speech for the Manilian Law, says that Corinth was destroyed because of the envoys who had been addressed insolently. See also On Duties, book 1.

units.la: L. Mummius cum Cn. Cornelio Lentulo cos.fuit: & ab Achaia deuicta Achaicus dictus. Orosius, Paterculus, ceteri. Corinthum capram esse anno 111, Olympiadis CLVI. scribit Plinius lib.34 cap.2.
units.tr: L. Mummius was consul with Cn. Cornelius Lentulus, and from his conquest of Achaia he was called Achaicus. Orosius, Paterculus and others. Pliny, book 34, chapter 2, writes that Corinth was taken in the 111th year, in the 156th Olympiad.

units.la: P.252. v.6. Antiochus] Epiphanes dictus, Magni filius: eius soroits Cleopatræ, hic Ptolemæus filius erat. De Popillio legato, vide Liuium 45. Plutarch. in Apopht. Valerium lib 6.cap.4. à quibus C. Popillius dicitur: Paterculo est Marcus, & Hieronymo in 11 Daniel. Hic vulgo est P. Popilius.
units.tr: P.252. v.6. Antiochus) Called Epiphanes, son of Magnus. His sister was Cleopatra, and this Ptolemy was her son. On the legate Popillius, see Livy book 45, Plutarch in the Apophthegms, and Valerius book 6, chapter 4, by whom he is called C. Popillius. In Paterculus he is Marcus, and in Jerome on Daniel 11. Here in the common editions he is P. Popilius.

units.la: V.29. Antiochus decedit] Appian. τὰ τῆς Ελυμαίας Ἀφο- ... Hierod. in Daniel. ex Polybio
units.tr: V.29. Antiochus decedit) Appian, on the affairs of Elymais [τὰ τῆς Ελυμαίας Ἀφο...]. Jerome on Daniel, from Polybius

units.la: & Diodoro bibliothecarum scriptoribus referreum, cum templum Dianæ in Elimaide spoliare conaretur, oppressum a custodibus templi, & vicinis gentibus, quibusdam phantasiis in amentiam versum, morbo interisse, in Tabes oppido Perfidis.
units.tr: and Diodorus, the writers of libraries, report that when he tried to plunder the temple of Diana in Elymais, he was overwhelmed by the guardians of the temple and the neighbouring peoples; driven out of his wits by certain apparitions, he died of illness in Tabae, a town of Persia.

units.la: V.30. Patruus eius Demetrius] Appianus Syriaca. Demetrium hunc dicit Σελευκου μὲν υἱὸν, Αντιόχου δὲ τοῦ ἐπιφανοῦς ἀδελφὸν... Non ergo patruus, sed patruelis; erant enim ambo duorum fratrum filii. Lege Appianum, & epitomam Liuii 46.
units.tr: V.30. Patruus eius Demetrius) Appian, Syriaca. He calls this Demetrius "son of Seleucus, but brother of Antiochus Epiphanes" [Σελευκου μὲν υἱὸν, Αντιόχου δὲ τοῦ ἐπιφανοῦς ἀδελφὸν...]. So he was not his paternal uncle but his cousin, since both were sons of two brothers. Read Appian, and the epitome of Livy, book 46.

units.la: P 253. v. 10. Præfius] Strabo lib. 13. scribit interfectum ab Attalo, alii à filio adiuuante Attalo. Epitoma Liuiana 50. Appian.
units.tr: P 253. v. 10. Praefectus) Strabo, book 13, writes that he was killed by Attalus; others say by his son, with Attalus helping. Livy's epitome, book 50. Appian.
ON BOOK XXXV.

units.la: NOuitati suæ otium] Supra libro 20. grave otium regnè P.254.v.2 suo. Catullus. Otium reges prius & beatas Perdidit urbes.
units.tr: Novitati suae otium) Above, in book 20: "Leisure is grave for kings who rule by their own will." Catullus: "Leisure has before now destroyed kings and happy cities."

units.la: Vulgo odium hic legitur, pro otium, quod & quæ sequuntur, & quæ superiore libro dixit, impugnant.
units.tr: It is commonly read here as odium instead of otium, but both what follows and what he said in the previous book contradict this.

units.la: V.6 Orofernem] Ita Vet. Appianus Ολοφέρνης, & Diodorus 31.
units.tr: V.6 Orofernem) So the old copies have it. Appian has Holophernes [Ολοφέρνης], and Diodorus, book 31.

units.la: V.18. Subornant] De hoc Alexandro, incertæ stirpis & ignoto homine, Liuii epitoma 52. & Appian.
units.tr: V.18. Subornant) On this Alexander, of uncertain stock and an unknown man, see Livy's epitome, book 52, and Appian.

units.la: Commendauerat] Ita est in veteribus. Commendare est deponere L. & si quis tiv. D. de religiosis E. 196. D. de verb. signif. Cic. 2. de legibus. Lar familiaris in Quirolo, mihi the saurum commendauit, id est, confidedit thesaurum auri, ut id seruarem sibi, vt est in Plauti Aulularia.
units.tr: Commendauerat) So it stands in the old copies. To commend means to deposit: Digest, de religiosis, law 196; Digest, de verborum significatione; Cicero, On the Laws, book 2. The household god in the Querolus: "He entrusted a treasure to me" (mihi thesaurum commendauit), that is, he entrusted a hoard of gold to me so that I would keep it for him, as in Plautus' Aulularia.
IN BOOK XXXVI.

units.la: Demetrius] Nicator dictus. vide App. Liuii 52. epitoma hæc paulo aliter. Demetrius, inquit, ob crudelitatem, quam per tormenta in suos exercebat, a Diodoro quodam, uno ex subditis, qui Alexandri filio bimulo admod-um, regnum afferebat, bello superatus Seleuciam fugit.
units.tr: Demetrius] Called Nicator. See Appian and Livy, book 52. This epitome tells the story a little differently: "Demetrius," it says, "on account of the cruelty which he practised on his own people through torture, was defeated in war by a certain Diodorus, one of his subjects, who brought the kingdom to the infant son of Alexander, then about two years old, and fled to Seleucia."

units.la: *V.10. Arfacidæ] Arsacidæ pro Arsace. Arsaces dicebantur omnes Parthorum reges, infra lib.41. Sed & lib.2. Amphictyon, in Mss. est Amphictyonides: Prusiades, est Prusias apud Vatronem, cuius locum supra notauimus: & Callias sub quo Athenas Xerxes incendit Diodoro dicitur Callindes: & quod mitius est, auctor vocatur sup. lib. 2. pro Thespias, poluit Thespiadæ, ita enim veteres libri manuscripti omnes.
units.tr: V.10. Arfacidæ] Arsacidæ for Arsace. All the kings of the Parthians were called Arsacae, as below in book 41. But also in book 2, Amphictyon, in the manuscripts, is Amphictyonides; Prusiades is Prusias in Varro, whose passage we noted above; and Callias, under whom Xerxes burned Athens, is called Callindes by Diodorus. What is milder: the author, in book 2 above, has Thespiadæ for Thespias, for all the old manuscripts read it so.

units.la: V.19. Tryphe] Dictus Diodorus, Strabo lib.14. & 16. Apianus & Livius.
units.tr: V.19. Tryphe] Called Diodorus by Strabo, books 14 and 16, by Appian and by Livy.

units.la: Ibid. Antiochoprimogeno] Alexandrum Alexandri nothi F. vocant Appian. Liu. 52 & 55. quos legę.
units.tr: Ibid. Antiochoprimogeno] Appian and Livy, books 52 and 55, call him Alexander, son of Alexander the bastard. Read them.

units.la: V.31. Iudæosque] Tacit. 5. hist. Vide historiam Macchabæorum. Statim malum legete, Mac edonico.
units.tr: V.31. Iudæosque] Tacitus, Histories, book 5. See the history of the Maccabees. Read Macedonico at once in place of the faulty reading.

units.la: P.257. v.6. Arathu] Hermolaus in 5. Plinii dubitat an hoc loco, permutatis litteris legendum sit Atharan, quæ est Syriorum deastriam Acargacis dicta, Strabo 16. cuius meminit & Macrob. 1. Saturnal.
units.tr: P.257. v.6. Arathu] Hermolaus, on book 5 of Pliny, doubts whether here, with the letters transposed, one should read Atharan, which is the Syrian goddess called Atargatis, as Strabo book 16 says, and whom Macrobius also mentions in Saturnalia book 1.

units.la: V.29. Vitiliginem] Ita ex Mss. legendum, & Orosio lib. 1. cap. 8. & 10. Vitiligo, Arnobio est lepra, vt me docuit doctorum princeps Iac. Cuiacius. Ille notas albicantium Vitiliginis, manu admota detersit. Ec Seneca 3. natur. quæst. capite 25. vitiliginem, vocat sedam ex albo Varietatem. Græcis λεύκη. Exodi 4. & Numer. 12. lepra dicitur canens ἀπὸ χιῶν. Hæc debeo, lepius a me commemorato, numquam tamen satis laudato, doctori meo; cuius de humanitate & doctrina, numquam quisquam ita magnifice dicet, quin id virtus eius exsuperet. Sed clarissimi viri gloriæ, neq; inea prædicatione accedere quidquam poterit; neque tenebrionum quorundam obtrectatione decedere. Illud reuertor. Vitiligineam hanc Tacitus lib. 5. hiit.tabem, vocat, quæ corpora fædaret. De Mosco alicer Strabo lib.16.
units.tr: V.29. Vitiliginem] So it should be read according to the manuscripts, and in Orosius book 1, chapters 8 and 10. Vitiligo is leprosy in Arnobius, as the prince of scholars, Jacques Cujas, taught me. "He wiped away with a hand applied the marks of the whitening vitiligo." And Seneca, Natural Questions book 3, chapter 25, calls vitiligo a patch of white discoloration. In Greek it is leukē. In Exodus 4 and Numbers 12, leprosy is said to be white [ἀπὸ χιῶν] as snow. I owe this to my teacher, whom I have often mentioned but never praised enough. No one will ever speak of his humanity and learning so magnificently that his virtue does not surpass it. But the glory of that distinguished man can gain nothing from any praise, nor lose anything through the disparagement of certain shadowy nobodies. I return to my point. Tacitus, Histories book 5, calls this vitiligo a blight, which would disfigure bodies. Of Moschus elsewhere, see Strabo book 16.

units.la: P.258. v. 14. Iustitia religione] Strabo διχωλογ ... ἱερωτατος ἀντες.
units.tr: P.258. v. 14. Iustitia religione] Strabo: "...most holy" [ἱερώτατοι].

units.la: V.18. Ducenta iugera] Vulgo ducenta millia iugera: iumanis, & supra fidem numeratus. Veteres plerique ducenti iugera nomine arcus dicitur, quod si legamus Sigin's iugerum Hieronymus dicitur? & id Plinius lib. 12. cap. 25. & Solinus cap. 38. confirmant, & Strabo lib. 16. Ιεγαρως ἱεί πέδιον χώλας ἀξιοχόμου ὁρίσῃ ... ἐξεῖ χρη ἱεχρώξοις ... τρίτος αὐτὸ κύκλω ... &c. is tamen spatium loci facit centum stadiorum.
units.tr: V.18. Ducenta iugera] Commonly read as ducenta millia iugera, two hundred thousand acres, which is monstrous and beyond belief. Most old texts read ducenti iugera, and it is called the measure of an arch. If we read Sigin's iugerum, does Jerome say so? Pliny, book 12, chapter 25, and Solinus, chapter 38, confirm it, and Strabo book 16 [Ιεγαρως ... ] makes the extent of the plain a hundred stadia.

units.la: V.22. Piceis arboribus) Veteres plerique specie, transpositis litteris, Strabo, cytiso, & tetrabitho similes facit. Vide Plinium & Solinum.
units.tr: V.22. Piceis arboribus] Most older authorities, with the letters transposed, read specie; Strabo makes them like cytisus and tetrabitha. See Pliny and Solinus.

units.la: V.24. Opacitatis] In Mss. manifesto errore legitur apricitatis.
units.tr: V.24. Opacitatis] In the manuscripts, by an obvious error, it is read as apricitatis (sunniness).

units.la: V.27. In ea regione lacus) Mss. quidam latus lacus, alii Non longe est lacus Alphaltides. postremam hanc lectionem neu non reicio: loquitur enim hoc loco de Asphaltite lacu, quem cum Sirbone eund. in facere videtur Strabo lib 16. cum eos distinguat Plin.r.cap.13. & 15 & 16.
units.tr: V.27. In ea regione lacus] Some manuscripts read latus lacus (a wide lake), others Non longe est lacus Alphaltides (not far off is the Asphaltite lake). I do not reject this last reading, for here he is speaking of the Asphaltite lake, which Strabo, book 16, seems to make the same as Sirbonis, though Pliny, book 5, chapters 13, 15 and 16, distinguishes them.

units.la: P.259.v.9. Ab Eumene; arque Ex Strabone lib 13 constat Eumenem huius A. tali patrem fuisse, & ita quidam hi cediderunt contra libros: Dictos est hic Attalus, Philometor: & morbo interiit, pop. Romano herede instituto. Strab.epitoma Liuii 58. Florus extrem. li.2. Orosius lib.5.cap.8. alii.
units.tr: P.259.v.9. Ab Eumene; atque] From Strabo, book 13, it is established that Eumenes was the father of this Attalus; and so some have written, contrary to the books. This Attalus was called Philometor, and died of disease, having named the Roman people his heir. See Strabo; Livy's epitome, book 58; Florus, end of book 2; Orosius, book 5, chapter 8; and others.

units.la: V.27. Aristonicus) De bello Aristonici, præter Liuiam epitomam, Florum, Velleium, lege Sciabonem lib. 14. Licinius Crassus qui à nostro consul dicitur, Floro est prætor, Paterculo Proconsul, qui eum iuris scientissimus vocat: a nostro auctore sunt Liuius, Orosius, M. Cicero 41 Philipp.
units.tr: V.27. Aristonicus] On the war of Aristonicus, besides Livy's epitome, Florus and Velleius, read Strabo, book 14. Licinius Crassus, whom our author calls consul, is praetor for Florus and proconsul for Paterculus, who calls him most learned in law. Our author's sources are Livy, Orosius and Cicero, Philippics 41.

units.la: P.260.v.7. Marcus Aquilius) In fastis Marius, & Perpenna, Perperna. Vide supra notatos auctores.
units.tr: P.260.v.7. Marcus Aquilius] In the Fasti it is Marius, and Perpenna for Perperna. See the authors noted above.
IN BOOK XXXVII.

units.la: {a}Tria maior] Quidam impressi codices Phrygia maior: quod probo. Infra lib.38. fibi pupillo maiorem Phrygiā ademerint, quam patri suo premium dati aduersus Arionicum auxilii, concesserant. Vide Appianum Mithridatico.
units.tr: {a}Tria maior] Some printed copies have Phrygia maior (Greater Phrygia), which I approve. Below, in book 38: "they had taken from his ward the Greater Phrygia, which they had granted to his father as a reward for help given against Aristonicus." See Appian, Mithridatic War.

units.la: V.13. Mithridates quoque] Hic Euergetes dictus, filius autem eius quem xi. annos natum regni successorem reliquit, Eupator. Strabo lib.10. Vide Appiani Mithridaticum. Mithridates, est in nostris Mss. in uno Mithridatis. Quod quidam Mithradates scribendum censent, ex numismatibus antiquis, non probo. Miθραδάτης enim Græcum est, Mithridates Latinum: a in i. Vt Μασσυλία, Massilia: Κατάνη, Catina: Νόμαδες, Numida: Ἀγρίγεντum, Agrigentum, & forta sic etiam Μασσυνίσσης, qui in Eclogis Diodori vitiose dicitur Μαυασσῆς, Masinissa. Sed & in Latinis vocibus τὸ a in i vertitur, Sapiens, ut sapiens: cano tibicines, &c.
units.tr: V.13. Mithridates also] This one is called Euergetes; his son, whom he left as successor at eleven years of age, was Eupator. Strabo, book 10. See Appian's Mithridatic War. In our manuscripts the form is Mithridates, and in one Mithridatis. Some think it should be written Mithradates, on the evidence of ancient coins, but I do not approve. For the Greek form is Μιθριδάτης [Mithridátēs] and the Latin Mithridates, with a changed to i, as Μασσαλία [Massalía] becomes Massilia, Κατάνη [Katánē] becomes Catina, Νόμαδες [Nómades] becomes Numida, Ἀκράγαντας [Akrágantas] becomes Agrigentum, and perhaps so also Μασσυνίσσης [Massynissēs], which in the Eclogues of Diodorus is wrongly written Μαυασσῆς [Mauassēs], Masinissa. But in Latin words too the a is turned into i, as in sapiens for sapiens, cano for tibicines, and so on.

units.la: V.18. Per XLVI] Orosius, alii XXX. inquit, alii XL. annos gestum seruerunt. Florus lib. 3. habet xi. Appianus xlii. si rationem inicris xxix. annos inuenies ab ortu ipso Mithridatici belli ad Pompeii triumphum.
units.tr: V.18. For 46 years] Orosius says: "others have recorded thirty years, others forty." Florus, book 3, gives eleven. Appian gives forty-two. If you reckon the sum from the very beginning of the Mithridatic war to Pompey's triumph, you will find twenty-nine years.

units.la: P.262. v. 3. Antidota sapius bibit] Plin. lib. 25. cap. 2. & lib.23. cap.8. & lib.29 cap.1.
units.tr: P.262 v.3. He often drank antidotes] Pliny, book 25, chapter 2; book 23, chapter 8; and book 29, chapter 1.

units.la: V.16. Iraq, Scythae] Strabo lib.7. Idem lib.1.&2. refert Mithridatem hunc, barbaros ad Mæotidem paludem, & inde Colchos vsque deuicisse. Vide Memnonis excerpta.
units.tr: V.16. And the Scythians] Strabo, book 7. The same Strabo, in books 1 and 2, reports that this Mithridates subdued the barbarians as far as the Maeotian marsh and from there all the way to Colchis. See the excerpts of Memnon.

units.la: P. 263. v. 21. Filiamenem] Pylamenem ex Homero legendum docuit Glareanus. Πυλαιμένεω Πυλαιμένως. Homerus ext. lib.2. Iliad. eiusdem meminit, Eustath. in Dionysium & Strabo libro 12. & Probus in Datame, qui eum, memoria lapsus, a Patroclo interfectum ait, cum ex Homeri lib. 5. constet Menelaum eum hasta confodisse. Ab hoc Paphla, onia aliquando Pylamenia dicta: Plinius libro 6. capite 2. Nicomedem autem & Pylamenem reges commemorat Orosius lib. 6. cap. 2.
units.tr: P.263 v.21. Filiamenes] Glareanus taught that it should be read Pylaemenes, from Homer: Πυλαιμένεω, Πυλαιμένως [Pylaimeneōs, Pylaiménōs]. Homer mentions him in Iliad, book 2; so do Eustathius on Dionysius and Strabo, book 12. Probus, in his life of Datames, says through a lapse of memory that he was killed by Patroclus, although it is clear from Homer, book 5, that Menelaus ran him through with a spear. From him Paphlagonia was sometimes called Pylaemenia; Pliny, book 6, chapter 2. Orosius, book 6, chapter 2, mentions the kings Nicomedes and Pylaemenes.
ON BOOK XXXVIII.

units.la: {M}Ithridates] Φοινικώντης ἐκ παίδος ὁ Μιλεσάδης ἦν.
units.tr: Mithridates] Miletades was a Phoenicontes from boyhood [Φοινικώντης ἐκ παίδος ὁ Μιλεσάδης ἦν].

units.la: Vide ἐπιλογὰς Memnonis: In iis filius sororis Mithridatis Arathes dicitur, vt & in Prologo huius libri.
units.tr: See the Epilogues of Memnon: in them the son of Mithridates' sister is called Arathes, as also in the Prologue of this book.

units.la: P.265.v.30. Sed Cappadoces] Strab. l.12. Romani, inquit, Ἰωνιάσαντες εἰ̈ησαν οὔτως εἰεν ἀπρόφηκόπες πρὸς τὴν ἀλλόφυλ ἐθνη, ἐπιτίχισθαι αὐτοῖς ἐξ ἑαυτῶν ἐλισθ κατὰ χρόνον ὁ ἀν Βιλοιπο, &c.
units.tr: P. 265, v. 30. Sed Cappadoces] Strabo, book 12: "The Romans," he says, "having become ... were so ... toward the foreign nations, that from among themselves there were set over them, in turn, ..., as ..." [Ἰωνιάσαντες εἰ̈ησαν οὔτως εἰεν ἀπρόφηκόπες πρὸς τὴν ἀλλόφυλ ἐθνη, ἐπιτίχισθαι αὐτοῖς ἐξ ἑαυτῶν ἐλισθ κατὰ χρόνον ὁ ἀν Βιλοιπο], etc.

units.la: P. 266. v.22. Tigranes] Lege Strabonem extr. lib.11. ex quo & ex vno Ms. scripsi obses Parthis, cum in ceteris sit obses a Parthis, inepte. Appianus Ariobarzanē à Mithra 10 & Bagoa Cappadocia pulsum scribit, & in eius locum Ariarathen constitutum: Nicomedem vero Bythinia à Socrate fratre, eiectum.
units.tr: P. 266, v. 22. Tigranes] Read Strabo at the end of book 11, from which, and from one manuscript, I have written obses Parthis; the rest read obses a Parthis, which is absurd. Appian writes that Ariobarzanes was driven out of Cappadocia by Mithras and Bagoas, and Ariarathes was set up in his place; and that Nicomedes was driven out of Bithynia by his brother Socrates.

units.la: V.29. Filiam suam Cleopatram] Inde Appianus Τυγάτηρ (legendum Τιγράνης) ὁ Ἀρμένιος αὐτοῦ κ̃δεσθῆς ἐν. socer 35 vertit interpres, cum hoc loco κηδεστὴς fit gener. De Nicomede filio pulso. vide Strab. 12.
units.tr: V. 29. Filiam suam Cleopatram] Hence Appian: Tigranes the Armenian, his son-in-law [Τιγράνης ὁ Ἀρμένιος αὐτοῦ κηδεστής] (the Greek should read Tigranes, not Tygater); the translator renders the word as "father-in-law", though here kēdestēs means "son-in-law". On Nicomedes' expelled son, see Strabo, book 12.

units.la: P.267.v.3. Aquilium & Manlium Maltinum] Legendum arbitror Manium Aquilium & M. Attilium. Vett. quidam Aquilium & Marcum Altinium. Appianus missos legatos 20 αἰτῶν Μάνιον Αὐλίον ἡχείσθαι: quem superatum à Mithridate, docet Epit Liuii.77.
units.tr: P. 267, v. 3. Aquilium & Manlium Maltinum] I think we should read Manium Aquilium & M. Attilium. Some old copies have Aquilium & Marcum Altinium. Appian says that, after sending legates, Manius Aquilius was put in command [Μάνιον Αὐλίον ἡγεῖσθαι]. The Epitome of Livy 77 shows that he was defeated by Mithridates.

units.la: V.14. Non magno igitur labore] Quā ratione Mithridates Aquilium & C. Cassium Romanos duces vicerit, lege Appianum.
units.tr: V. 14. Non magno igitur labore] For how Mithridates defeated the Roman commanders Aquilius and C. Cassius, read Appian.

units.la: 35 V.25. Quod concriones direct.] De iis qui ὑπερμήκεις διηγήσεις historiae inserunt, & ita historiam concionum ἀποδηκλω faciunt, vide initium lib.2. Diodori.
units.tr: 35 V. 25. Quod concriones direct.] On those who insert overly long speeches into history, and so make the history of speeches a display piece [ἀποδηκλω], see the beginning of book 2 of Diodorus.

units.la: P.269.v.1. Bello Marsico] Dictum à Marsis belli auctoribus, Strabo lib. 5. dictum etiam Italicum, & sociale: de 30 eo lege Appianum, & Florum, alios: apud quos, & apud Plutarchum, vide & historiam belli civilis Mariani, & Cimbrici, quorum mox meminit. Orosius lib. 5. cap.19. eodem anno bellum civile commotum, & Mithridaticum coeptum scribit.
units.tr: P. 269, v. 1. Bello Marsico] So called from the Marsi, the originators of the war. Strabo, book 5, also calls it the Italian and the Social War. On this, read Appian and Florus, and others, among whom also Plutarch; see also the history of the Marian and Cimbrian civil wars, which he mentions shortly. Orosius, book 5, chapter 19, writes that in the same year the civil war broke out and the Mithridatic war began.

units.la: 35 P.270.v.6. Vltum ierit] Ita ex Vett. emendauit: quomodo & apud Tacitum legendum docuit me P. Pithoeus, Annal.6. Mox Artabanus tota mole regni Vltimi id perstiä locorum Lege, Vltimum sit. Vt doctissimus & diligentissimus Lipsius annotauit.
units.tr: 35 P. 270, v. 6. Vltum ierit] Thus corrected from the old copies. Likewise in Tacitus, P. Pithoeus taught me it should be read so, Annals 6. Soon afterwards, Artabanus, with the whole weight of the kingdom ... the place ... read Vltimum sit, as the most learned and diligent Lipsius noted.

units.la: 40 V.10. Non delicta regum] Sallustius in epistola Mithridatis ad Arfacem. Namque Romanis cum nationibus, populis, regibus cunctis, sna & ea Gerimus, causa bellandi est, cupido profunda imperii & diuitiarum, &c. Idem & Iugurtha apud eundem Sallustium.
units.tr: 40 V. 10. Non delicta regum] Sallust, in the letter of Mithridates to Arsaces: "For we are at war with the Romans, with all nations, peoples and kings; the cause of the war is the deep desire for empire and riches," etc. The same also in Sallust's Jugurtha.

units.la: Appianus de Mithridate originis huius auctore, ἀπὸ γένους Βασιλείου Περσικοῦ. Flotus lib. 5.
units.tr: Appian, on the origin of this Mithridates: he was "of a royal Persian stock" [ἀπὸ γένους Βασιλείου Περσικοῦ]. Florus, book 5.
Strabo, book 12.

units.la: Post Ptolemaeum Philometorem ordo successionis regum Ægypti mutatus est: huicusque enim patri filius succederat. At Philometori frater successit Euergetes 2. dictus, & Physcon. Strabo lib.17. Vide epitomam Liuianam 59. & Orosium lib. 5. cap.10.
units.tr: After Ptolemy Philometor the order of succession of the kings of Egypt was changed: up to this point a son had succeeded his father. But after Philometor his brother succeeded, called Euergetes II, and Physcon. Strabo, book 17. See Livy's epitome, book 59, and Orosius, book 5, chapter 10.
Strabo, book 14, mentions this embassy.

units.la: Qui Sedetes dictus est, eius in Patthos expeditionis meminit Liuii epitoma lib.59. & Otosius 5.cap.10. & Appianus Syriaca, qui Antiochum victum, sibi ipsi manus attulisse refert.
units.tr: Of the one called Sedetes, mention is made of his expedition into Patthos in Livy's epitome, book 59, and in Orosius, book 5, chapter 10; and Appian in the Syriaca relates that Antiochus, after his defeat, laid violent hands on himself.

units.la: Orosius: centum millia armatorum, ducenta millia amplius calonum atque lixarum, immixta scortis & histrionibus.
units.tr: Orosius: "a hundred thousand armed men, and more than two hundred thousand camp-followers and sutlers, mixed with prostitutes and actors."
ON BOOK XXXIX.

units.la: Emetrius autem Gitus) Appianus interfectum ait ab vxore Cleopatra ... & post eius mortem Seleucum filium ab ea veneno sublatum. Vide & epitomam Liuii 60.
units.tr: Emetrius, however, of Gitus: Appian says he was killed by his wife Cleopatra, and after her death Seleucus, her son, was poisoned by her. See also the epitome of Livy, book 60.

units.la: Ita Vct. & Appianus Γρυπὸς. Est autem Grypus κᾰμψυλόππιν, ὁ ἐπικαμπὴ τὴν ῥίνα ἔχων. Hesychius. De his cognominibus lege elegantem locum Plutarchi, in Coriolano. Huius frater vterinus Antiochus Kυζικηνὸς dictus, quod Cyzici esset educatus: lege Appianum extrema historia Syriaca.
units.tr: So the Vetus and Appian read Γρυπὸς [Grypus, "hook-nosed"]. Grypus is kampsylopprin [καμψυλόππιν], that is, one who has a bent nose [ὁ ἐπικαμπὴ τὴν ῥίνα ἔχων]. Hesychius. On these nicknames read the elegant passage of Plutarch in the Coriolanus. His half-brother Antiochus was called Kyzikenos [Κυζικηνός], because he had been brought up at Cyzicus. Read Appian at the end of the Syrian history.

units.la: Ptolemaeus Apio dictus, populum Romanum testamento heredem reliquit, Eusebius in Chronicis: eius regni ciuitates liberas esse senatus voluit, Liuianæ epitomæ lib. 70. contra auctorem nostrum.
units.tr: Ptolemy, called Apion, left the Roman people his heir by will, as Eusebius reports in the Chronicle. The senate wished his cities to be free. Livy's epitome, book 70, is against our author.

units.la: Bellum piraticum & maritimū, àP Seruilio, quiexpugnato Ifauro arce Cilicię, Ifaurici cognomen teportauit,coeptum. Pompeius confecit,mira felicitate & celeritate, intra xl. diem nimirum, aut vt alii intra xlix. vide Plutarchum, Appianum, M. Ciceronem pro lege Manilia.Cretam Q. Cæcilius Metellus debellauit, qui inde Creticus. Florus lib.3.
units.tr: The war against the pirates on sea and land, begun by P. Servilius, who took the stronghold of Isauria in Cilicia and brought back the surname Isauricus, was finished by Pompey with remarkable good fortune and speed, namely within forty days, or as others say within forty-nine; see Plutarch, Appian, and M. Cicero in his speech for the Manilian law. Crete was subdued by Q. Caecilius Metellus, who for this reason was called Creticus. Florus, book 3.
ON BOOK XL.

units.la: {1}N Tigranem) Tigranes Syria vltra Euphratem & Cilicia potitus, rex regum dictus est, Appianus, Strabo in fine lib 11. Eo à Lucullo superato, Antiochus ἐπιφανὴς dictus, Cyziceni filius, ἐχὼν τῶν Σύρων ἐκόλων: duxerat in patris vxorem Selenem, quam deinde Tigranes interfecit Strabo 16.
units.tr: {1} Tigranes, the king: Tigranes, who held Syria beyond the Euphrates and Cilicia, was called king of kings, as Appian and Strabo (end of book 11) say. After he was defeated by Lucullus, Antiochus was called Epiphanes [ἐπιφανὴς], son of the Cyzicene, holding the Syrian cities [ἐχὼν τῶν Σύρων ἐκόλων]. He had taken as wife of his father Selene, whom Tigranes afterwards killed. Strabo, book 16.

units.la: P. 283. v. 7. Ademit Pompeius) Oʼπ τὰς Σελευκίδας ὑπὸ Τιγράνης οκκοτόντας, ὑκ εἶχος ἡ ἑτι Συρίας ἀρχὴν μᾶλλον, ἢ Ρωμαίοις Τιγράνῃ ὑπηκόους. Appianus. De Lucullo autem & Pompeii rebus in Syria contra Mithridatem & Tigranem gestis, lege præter Appianum, Plutarchum in vi-ta quæ-que vita, & Dionem.
units.tr: P. 283, v. 7. Pompey took away: since the Seleucid cities were held by Tigranes, Syria no longer had its own rule but was rather subject to the Romans, as Tigranes was. Appian. On the deeds of Lucullus and Pompey in Syria against Mithridates and Tigranes, read besides Appian, Plutarch in each of their lives, and Dio.
ON BOOK XLI.

units.la: Parthi) Vide Strabonem lib. 11. & Dionysium, & quæ in eum notauit Eustathius. & Agathiam lib. 2. & fornandem, qui hunc locum citat ex Trogo Pompeio. Stra-bo cos dicit ἀντιπάλλης τῶν Ῥωμαίων, καὶ μίγαδος τῆς ἀρ-χῆς.
units.tr: Parthians: see Strabo, book 11, and Dionysius, and what Eustathius noted on him, and Agathias, book 2, and Fornandes, who cites this passage from Trogus Pompeius. Strabo calls them rivals of the Romans and co-sharers in power [ἀντιπάλους τῶν Ῥωμαίων καὶ μίγαδος τῆς ἀρχῆς].

units.la: V. 24. Et Dahæ) Veterum librorum Mss lectionem exhibui. Legendum autem & Dahæ, & Arios, & Ariana-nos & Magianos, ex Strabone: Ptolemæo: Plinio libro 6.
units.tr: V. 24. And Dahae: I have given the reading of the old manuscripts. But one should read Dahae, and Arii, and Arianians and Magians, from Strabo, Ptolemy, and Pliny, book 6.

units.la: Parthi, inquit, habent ab ortu Arios, à meridie Carmaniā & Arianos.
units.tr: The Parthians, he says, have Arii on the east, Carmania on the south, and the Arians.

units.la: P. 286. v.16 Stagnori] Legendum Statanzri vt supra lib.13. cui tamen Drancas & Areos tribuit, vt & Diodorus lib. 18. Patrhos autem Nicanori assignauit. Diodorus Parthiam & Hyrcaniam Phratafernicuenisse refert, & Strabo à Macedonibus Hyrcaniam Parthiæ iunctam scribit.
units.tr: P. 286, v. 16. Stagnori: read Statanzri, as above in book 13, to whom however he assigns the Drangae and Areians, as Diodorus also does, book 18. He assigned the Patrhi to Nicanor. Diodorus reports that Phrataphernes conquered Parthia and Hyrcania, and Strabo writes that Hyrcania was joined to Parthia by the Macedonians.

units.la: V. 22. B. Alfone, M. Atilio) Vett. plerique Balfone. Legendum Valfone. in fallacit C. Atilium, non M. At-tilius.
units.tr: V. 22. B. Alfonus, M. Atilius: most old copies have Balfonus. Read Valfonus. In the fasti it is C. Atilius, not M. Atilius.

units.la: Constitutum est Parthorum imperium, & conditum, Seleuco Callinico Asiam obtinente. Strabo 11. Eusebius Chronico-Lubet adscribere ortum regni Parthici ex Georgii Monarchi chronico, cuius mihi copiam fecit praestantissimus vir Fr. Pithoeus, Σευέας καὶ Αρίας δ' ἰδαυιλάδ- σι Αρσάκης ὁ ἐπικληθεὶς καὶ Μίνιος ὁ αὐτὸς ἐκ Σελεύκου. paulo post. Ἐπιτυτ τῆ Αρσάκου Πέρσαι τῆς Μακεδόνων καὶ Αρ- σάκην ἀρχῆς ἀπέσχοντο ὑπ' αὐτοὺς πλήρης ἀπὸ Αλεξάνδρου τὸ κτίσαι· διὰ τοιαῦτα αἰτίαν. Ασσάκης καὶ Τηρίδατης ἀδελφοὶ, τὸ γένος ἐλαγρτες ἀπὸ τῆ Περσῶν Αρτακίξες, ὁμο- πέλαντες Βασιλέων ἐπὶ Αρσακίδου Μακεδόν ἐπίγραφον ἐπὶ πάντες Περσέως. ὃς Αρσάκης ἐχοὶ ἐκαίωσεν Τηρίδατης Αρσάκης ἔφησι. ἑνὸς τῶν ἀδελφῶν, ἡ τὸν πάντων ἀπολειπομένη ἐπὶ Ασσυρίας· διαμεμηνυμένους ἐναντίαν ἐπιπλέον αὐτὸν, ἡ βασιλεύοντος Περσῶν Αρσάκης· ἀφ' ὧν οἱ Πέρσαι βασιλεῖς Αρσα- κίδαι ἐχρημάτισαν ἐπὶ β. ἡ ἀναιρεῖται. καὶ μετ' αὐτὸν Τηρι- δάτης ἀδελφὸς ἐπὶ λ. Integrum locum adscripsi quia editus non est; & narrationem continet memoria dignam.
units.tr: The Parthian empire was established and founded when Seleucus Callinicus held Asia. Strabo, book 11. I choose to add to Eusebius's Chronicle the origin of the Parthian kingdom from the chronicle of George the Monk, a copy of which was given to me by the most distinguished man Fr. Pithoeus. Arsaces, who was also called Minios, the same from Seleucus [Σευέας καὶ Ἀρίας ... Ἀρσάκης ὁ ἐπικληθεὶς καὶ Μίνιος ὁ αὐτὸς ἐκ Σελεύκου]. A little later: Under Arsaces the Persians kept away from the Macedonian and Arsacid rule, which had been full since Alexander's founding; for this reason Arsaces and Tiridates, brothers of Persian Artakian stock, having been kings under the Macedonians, were called Persian kings. Arsaces, when he was struck, ... Tiridates says Arsaces, one of the brothers, leaving all behind in Assyria, and with the Persians' king Arsaces; from them the Persian kings were called Arsacids for two hundred (?) years, and after him his brother Tiridates for thirty. I have added the whole passage because it is unpublished and contains a narrative worth remembering. [Ἐπιτυτ τῆ Ἀρσάκου Πέρσαι τῆς Μακεδόνων καὶ Ἀρσάκην ἀρχῆς ἀπέσχοντο ὑπ' αὐτοὺς πλήρης ἀπὸ Ἀλεξάνδρου τὸ κτίσαι· διὰ τοιαῦτα αἰτίαν. Ἀσσάκης καὶ Τηρίδατης ἀδελφοὶ, τὸ γένος ἐλαγρτες ἀπὸ τῆ Περσῶν Ἀρτακίξες, ὁμοπέλαντες Βασιλέων ἐπὶ Ἀρσακίδου Μακεδόν ἐπίγραφον ἐπὶ πάντες Περσέως.]
V.27. Theodotus: in Strabo, Diodotus.

units.la: P. 287. v. 1. Andragoram] Unum ex Audragorae posteris, de quo lib.12. quem Atrianus Ammynapeum vocat lib. 3. Georgius hunc vocat Agathoclem.
units.tr: P. 287, v. 1. Andragoras: one of the descendants of Audragoras, of whom in book 12, whom Arrian calls Ammynapeus in book 3. George calls him Agathocles.

units.la: V.14. Daram in monte Zapaortenon] Scripturam veterem expressi, ut ex ea veram lectionem quilibet assequi conetur, pro Daram, putaui aliquando legendum Choaram ex Plinii lib. 6. cap. 15. sed videat lectorem ex cap. 6. facilius possit erui vera lectio, A Caspiis, inquit, orientem versus regio est Zapaortene dicta, & in ea fertilitatis insignis locus Darieum dictus. ibi Hermolaus Dafan hoc loco legit, non Daram.
units.tr: V.14. Daram in the mountain Zapaorteni: I have expressed the old reading, so that anyone may try to reach the true reading from it. I once thought that instead of Daram one should read Choaram, from Pliny, book 6, chapter 15. But let the reader see from chapter 6 that the true reading can more easily be drawn out: "Toward the east from the Caspians," he says, "there is a region called Zapaortene, and in it a place notable for its fertility called Darieum." There Hermolaus reads Dafan in this place, not Daram.

units.la: V. 26. Arsacis nomine] Apud Parthos, inquit, Strabo 15. Αρσάκης καὶ Ὠρτάνης ἐτέραις ἰδίας δὲ ὁ μὲν Ὀρόδης, ὁ δὲ Φρα- άτης, ὁ δὲ ἀλλοιν.
units.tr: V. 26. In the name of Arsaces: among the Parthians, says Strabo, book 15, Arsaces and Ortanes are different names of their own: one is Orodes, another Phraates, another [ἄλλος] ...

units.la: P.288. v.5. Mithridati) Sextum ab Arsace facit Orosius lib 5. cap. 4.
units.tr: P. 288, v. 5. Mithridates: Orosius, book 5, chapter 4, makes him the sixth from Arsaces.

units.la: V.10 Eucratides) Eius meminit Strabo initio libro 15. & lib.11.
units.tr: V.10. Eucratides: Strabo mentions him at the beginning of book 15 and in book 11.

units.la: V. 31. Elymeorum regę) De horum potentia & viribus, quibus fretu Parthorum imperia contemnebant. Strabo libro 16.
units.tr: V. 31. The king of the Elymeans: on their power and forces, on which the Parthians relied when they despised empires. Strabo, book 16.
IN LIB. XLII.

units.la: Hogariu) Ita libri veteres, quidam tamen Theogarii: vnus Thocarii, Tocharios Scytichum genus commemorat Plinius lib 6. cap.17. & Toxaporus Dionysius Periegetes, & Ptolemaeus.
units.tr: Hogariu) The old books read thus; some, however, have Theogarii, and one has Thocarii. Pliny in book 6, chapter 17, mentions the Tocharii, a Scythian people, and Toxaporus is found in Dionysius Periegetes and Ptolemy.

units.la: V.25. Orroadifli) Agraxadorus Armeniae regis nomen est in Strabone lib.11. & Plutarcho in Antonio.
units.tr: V.25. Orroadifli) Agraxadorus is the name of an Armenian king in Strabo, book 11, and in Plutarch's Antony.

units.la: De Armenia lege Strabonem 11. Plin.6. cap.9. Dionysium & Eustathium: qui in magnitudine ab auctore nostro dissentiunt.
units.tr: On Armenia, read Strabo book 11, Pliny book 6 chapter 9, and Dionysius and Eustathius, who differ from our author on its size.

units.la: V.33. Ab Argenio) Armenum vocant Strabo & Eustathius, ἐξ Ἀρμενίας πόλεως, Θεσσαλικῆς. Stephanus ex Antipatro Rhodium fuisse dicit.
units.tr: V.33. Ab Argenio) Strabo and Eustathius call him Armenus, from the Thessalian city of Armenia [ἐξ Ἀρμενίας πόλεως, Θεσσαλικῆς]. Stephanus says, on the authority of Antipater, that he was from Rhodes.

units.la: P.291. v.15. Medio priuigno) Ita boni libri, vnus Medo, quomodo cum Strabo, Stephanus, & Eustathius vocant.
units.tr: P.291. v.15. Medio priuigno) So the good books read; one has Medo, as Strabo, Stephanus and Eustathius call him.

units.la: Qui paulo post Ægialus dicitur, Apollonio, & Strab. 7. est Abfyrtus.
units.tr: The man who is called Aegialus shortly afterwards is, in Apollonius and in Strabo book 7, Absyrtus.

units.la: V.25. Frudium (?) Straboni & Eustathio Περὶ Ἀμφίτρυονος ... a quibus populi isti Heniochi dicti. Solinus cap.20. Ammianus Marcel.22. Amphitus & Telchius Spartani, auriga Castoris & Pollucis.
units.tr: V.25. Frudium (?) In Strabo and Eustathius [under the heading] Περὶ Ἀμφίτρυονος ..., from whom those peoples were called Heniochi. Solinus chapter 20; Ammianus Marcellinus book 22: Amphitus and Telchius of Sparta, charioteers of Castor and Pollux.

units.la: V.27. Qui Herculem) Tacitus lib.6. Annal. Hiberos & Albanos Thessalis ortos scribit.
units.tr: V.27. Qui Herculem) Tacitus, Annals book 6, writes that the Iberians and Albanians were descended from Thessalians.

units.la: V 31. Templaq, constituit) Iaroína vocat Strabo, & Ιαρότα ... qualia multa reguli eueterunt; Parmenion autem id quod erat Abderis, diruit.
units.tr: V 31. Templaq, constituit) Strabo calls it Iaroína, and Ιαρότα ... many such petty rulers arose; but Parmenion destroyed what was at Abdera.

units.la: P. 292. v.10. Tigris) Praeter Strabonem, lege Plinium lib.6.cap.27. & Solinum eap.40. & libellum Plutarchi de fluuiis.
units.tr: P. 292. v.10. Tigris) Besides Strabo, read Pliny book 6 chapter 27, Solinus chapter 40, and Plutarch's little book on rivers.

units.la: V.18. Orodes) Ab hoc fratrem regno pulsum scribit Appianus in Parthica, & Syriaca historia: sed in hac Ηροδης editum est. Plutarcho in Crasso dicitur Ηροδης, in Antonio Ηροδης.
units.tr: V.18. Orodes) Appian, in his Parthian and Syrian histories, writes that a brother of his was driven from the kingdom by him; but in this passage the text is printed as Ηροδης. In Plutarch's Crassus he is called Ηροδης, and in his Antony Ηροδης.

units.la: V.29. A Cassio) Lege M.Cic. f. ad Attic. epist.10. Oros. lib.5. cap.13. Patercul. lib.2. De Paeoro à Ventidio caeso Plutarchus in Antonio, Appianus in Parth. alii.
units.tr: V.29. A Cassio) Read Cicero, letters to Atticus book 10; Orosius book 5 chapter 13; Paterculus book 2. On Pacorus being slain by Ventidius, see Plutarch in Antony, Appian in the Parthica, and others.

units.la: P.294.v.3 Phrahates) Φραάτης vocat Plutarch.in Antonio, quem lege & Appianum. Totus hic locus explicat, quod Horatius Ode 1. lib.2. ait.
units.tr: P.294.v.3 Phrahates) Plutarch in Antony calls him Φραάτης; read also Appian. This whole passage explains what Horace says in Ode 1 of book 2.

units.la: Redditum Cyri folio Phrahatem, & quod Od. 26. lib. 1. Quid Tyridatem teireat, Snice Securus.
units.tr: Restored Phrahates to Cyrus's standards, and what Horace says in Ode 26 of book 1: "What should frighten Tyridates, you who alone are free from care?"

units.la: Quod primus notauit Glareanus, non tam ineptus quā eum quidam haberi volunt.
units.tr: Glareanus was the first to note this, and he is not as foolish as some want him to be thought.

units.la: P.295.v.3. Tota Parthia captiui) Meminit Strabo lib. 6, & 16. Suetonius in Octauio cap.21. Horatius Oda vlt. li. 4. de Augusto. E fi͏gna nostro restitutt Ioui, &c. Suetonii locus confirmat antiquam scripturam Crassiano, vulgo enim legitur Cassiano.
units.tr: P.295.v.3. Tota Parthia captiui) Strabo mentions this in books 6 and 16. Suetonius in Augustus chapter 21, and Horace in the last ode of book 4, on Augustus: Restored the standards to our Jupiter, etc. Suetonius's passage confirms the old reading Crassiano; the commonly printed reading is Cassiano.
ON BOOK XLIII.

units.la: P.296. v. 14. Palanteo) Steph Παλάντιον πόλις Αρκαδίας. de Palatio, vide Virgilium 8. Æneid. Varronem 4. de ling. Lat. & Festum. Ouidii fastos. Propertii lib.4.
units.tr: P.296. v. 14. Palanteo) Stephanus: Palantion, a city of Arcadia [Παλάντιον πόλις Αρκαδίας]. On Palatium see Virgil, Aeneid 8; Varro, On the Latin Language, book 4; Festus; Ovid's Fasti; Propertius, book 4.

units.la: V. 20. Fatua) Soror eademque coniux Fauni: quam Fatuam nominatam tradit C. Bassus, quod mulieribus fata canere consueuisset, vt Fauuus viris, Lactant. libro 1. Vide Seruium in illud 6. Æneid.
units.tr: V. 20. Fatua) She was the sister and also the wife of Faunus. C. Bassus reports that she was called Fatua because she was accustomed to foretell fates to women, as Faunus did to men. Lactantius, book 1. See Servius on the passage in Aeneid 6.
Castrum, Inui, Bolamque, Coramq, & 7.

units.la: Hunc Fauno & nympha genitum Laurente Marica Accepimus.
units.tr: We have received that he was born to Faunus and the nymph Marica of Laurentum.

units.la: Quo loco Virgilius a Trogo diffidet: facit enim Latinum Fauni & Maricæ filium.
units.tr: Here Virgil differs from Trogus, for he makes Latinus the son of Faunus and Marica.

units.la: P.297.v.11. Filiam eius Rheam) Quæ & Siluia. Apud Ælian. libro 7. mendose legitur Σηβία pro Σιλβία. Quæ hic de verbis origine referuntur peruulgata sunt.
units.tr: P.297.v.11. Filiam eius Rheam) who is also called Silvia. In Aelian, book 7, Σηβία is wrongly read for Σιλβία. What is said here about the origin of the names is very well known.

units.la: P.298. v.16. Reges hasta) Iude Homero ἀκνταῖοι reges: supra lib. 2. cum Hieroni aquila in clypeo, noctua in hasta consedisset, consilio cautum, & mana promptū, regemque futurum significabatur. Paufanias in Boeoticis Chæronenses refert, ex Diis sceptrum colere, quod Vulcanus Iouifabricauit, & id hastam vocare.
units.tr: P.298. v.16. Reges hasta) Homer calls them kings [ἀκνταῖοι]. Above, in book 2, when an eagle sat on Hiero's shield and an owl on his spear, it was signified that he would be prudent and ready in action and would become king. Pausanias, in the Boeotica, reports that the Chaeronenses worship as a god a sceptre which Vulcan made for Jove, and they call it a spear.

units.la: V 21. Phocensium) Φωκαίων scribunt Græci, id est Phocensium, a Phocæa Ioniæ vrbe: Gellius libro 10. cap.16. terram Phocidem dixit. De Massilia, vide Strabonem lib. 4. Solinum cap. 8. Ammianum lib. 15. & Gellium: hi condi. eonditam Massiliam à Phocæensibus Persicam feruitutem fugientibus referunt, cum ipsorum vrbs ab Harpalo(Harpagum vocat Herodotus lib.1 iobsidetur. Plutarchus in Solone conditam scribit à Proto: eum Iustinus Protin vocat. Plutarchi sensum non sunt assequuti interpretes.
units.tr: V 21. Phocensium) The Greeks write Φωκαίων, that is, of the Phocaeans, from Phocaea, a city of Ionia. Gellius, book 10, chapter 16, calls it the land of Phocis. On Massilia see Strabo, book 4; Solinus, chapter 8; Ammianus, book 15; and Gellius. These authors report that Massilia was founded by Phocaeans fleeing Persian slavery when their own city was besieged by Harpalus (Herodotus, book 1, calls him Harpagus). Plutarch, in the Life of Solon, writes that it was founded by Protis; Justin calls him Protis. The interpreters have not grasped Plutarch's meaning.

units.la: P.299.v 1. Segobrigiorum) Quidam Vett. Segobriorum: Qui sint hi Galliæ populi, non memini legere. Plinius Segobrienses in Celtiberia collocat, & Strabo Segobrigam. In Gallia Narbonensi sunt Segalauns, qui Plinio lib.3.dicuntur Segouellauns: quo pacto hic fortasse repe̅nendum est.
units.tr: P.299.v 1. Segobrigiorum) Some old copies read Segobriorum. I do not recall reading which Gallic peoples these are. Pliny places the Segobrienses in Celtiberia, and Strabo places Segobriga there. In Narbonese Gaul there are the Segalauni, whom Pliny, book 3, calls Segovellauni; perhaps the matter should be sought there.

units.la: V. 2f. Comanus) Ptolemæus Massiliam vocat Κομμονὴ πόλιν, forte ab hoc rege, aut eiusdem nominis alio. Plinius tamen circa Massiliam Cenomannos habitasse in Volcis, refert: vnde dubito an in Ptolemæo mendum sit.
units.tr: V. 2f. Comanus) Ptolemy calls Massilia Κομμονὴ πόλιν [Κομμονὴ πόλιν], perhaps after this king, or after another of the same name. Yet Pliny reports that the Cenomani lived around Massilia among the Volcae, so I doubt whether the error lies in Ptolemy.

units.la: P.300.v 28. Carthaginiensiam quoque exercitu) Thucid. libro 1. Φωκαεῖς Μασσαλίαν οἰκιζοντες, Καρχηδονίους ςυίχων ναυμαχοῦντες.
units.tr: P.300.v 28. Carthaginiensiam quoque exercitu) Thucydides, book 1: the Phocaeans, founding Massilia, fought sea battles against the Carthaginians [Φωκαεῖς Μασσαλίαν οἰκίζοντες, Καρχηδονίους ναυμαχοῦντες].

units.la: P.301.v.12. Simu' acro Dea) Quod sedens fuisse in Massilia, Strabo refert lib.13.
units.tr: P.301.v.12. Simu' acro Dea) Strabo reports, book 13, that she was worshipped sitting in Massilia.

units.la: V. 28. A Vocontiū) Vulgo inepte, à Volscis. cui lectioni Volcæ, Galliæ ad Rhodanum populi, causam dederunt. Vocontii sunt in Gallia Narbonensi, qui in Ptolemæo mendose ςοχόνδοι, pro ςοκόντιοι. Est & Massilia eiusdem Narbonensis Galliæ ciuitas: Inde occasionem sumpsit Trogus originem suam edisserendi.
units.tr: V. 28. A Vocontiū) Commonly and foolishly read "a Volscis." The reading Volcae gave rise to the people of Gaul on the Rhone, the Volcae. The Vocontii are in Narbonese Gaul; in Ptolemy they are wrongly called Σοχόνδοι for Σοκόντιοι. Massilia is also a city of the same Narbonese Gaul, and from this Trogus took occasion to set out its origin.
ON BOOK XLIV.

units.la: Hispania) Confer Strabonem lib. 3. Melam 2. cap. 6. Plinium lib.3.cap.1. Solinum cap.26. vide & Currium Rufum libro decimo, Iberiam quidam ab Ibero dictam putant, Herculis filio, fratre Celti, Eustathius in Dionysium.
units.tr: Hispania) Compare Strabo, book 3; Mela, book 2, chapter 6; Pliny, book 3, chapter 1; Solinus, chapter 26. See also Currius Rufus, book 10. Some think Iberia was named after Iberus, son of Hercules and brother of Celtus, as Eustathius says on Dionysius.

units.la: P.303.v.13. Vndique Cersus assidui) Vulgati & duo Mss. Vndique aduersus assidui: malim Vndique aduersi & assi-dui fluctus.
units.tr: P.303.v.13. Vndique Cersus assidui) The printed editions and two manuscripts read Vndique aduersus assidui; I would prefer Vndique aduersi & assidui fluctus.

units.la: V.21. Celebratur etiam bello punico) Vide Liuium 21 ab 40 r c. & Valerium lib. 3. cap.3.
units.tr: V.21. Celebratur etiam bello punico) See Livy, book 21, from chapter 40, and Valerius, book 3, chapter 3.

units.la: V. 2f. V.25. Et arma sanguine ipsorum cariora.) Livius libro 34. Hispanos plerosque sibi manus attulisse refert, ob admissam arma. Ferox gens, inquit, nullam sibi statuam rati sine armis esse.
units.tr: V. 2f. V.25. Et arma sanguine ipsorum cariora.) Livy, book 34, reports that many Spaniards killed themselves because their arms had been taken away. A fierce people, he says, thinking that without arms they were nothing.

units.la: V.27. In tanta seculorum serie) Ἐπὶ ... Strabo. Cum Viriatho bellum gestum annos xiv. (Florus lib. 2. & Orosius lib. 5. scribunt.
units.tr: V.27. In tanta seculorum serie) [Ἐπὶ ...] Strabo. The war with Viriathus lasted fourteen years, as Florus, book 2, and Orosius, book 5, write.

units.la: P.304.v.6.In Lusitania) Rem incredibilem dicit Varro, sed verum lib. 2. de re rustica cap.5. & Columella lib.6. & Plin.lib.8. cap.42. vide & Maronem 3. Georg.
units.tr: P.304.v.6.In Lusitania) Varro calls it an incredible thing, but it is true: On Agriculture, book 2, chapter 5; also Columella, book 6, and Pliny, book 8, chapter 42. See also Virgil, Georgics 3.

units.la: V.11. Gallaci) A quibus deuictis Decimus Brutus Gallæcus dictus. Hi Strab. sunt Καλλαϊκοί, & Brutus Καλλαϊκός. Idem non ipsum Teucrum ibi consedisse, sed τῶν μετὰ Τεύκρου συμπνευσάντων τινὰς. De Amphilochis lege eundem.
units.tr: V.11. Gallaci) From those whom he conquered, Decimus Brutus was called Gallaecus. Strabo calls these people Καλλαϊκοί, and Brutus Καλλαϊκός. The same author says that it was not Teucer himself who settled there, but some of those who sailed with Teucer. On the Amphilochi read the same author.

units.la: V.22. Minio, quod etiam) Minius amnis, Plinius lib. 4. cap.20. qui & Βαῖνις, Straboni: cui Sacer mons est ἱερὸν ἀ-χρονικὸν. de quo idem initio lib.3.
units.tr: V.22. Minio, quod etiam) The river Minius: Pliny, book 4, chapter 20, who is also called Βαῖνις by Strabo, near which is the Sacred Mountain, ἱερὸν ἀχρονικόν [ἱερὸν ἀχρονικόν]; of which the same author speaks at the beginning of book 3.

units.la: P.305.v.3. Tartessiorum) Eorum regem Arganthonium. ad quem venerint Phoenices commemorat Herodotus lib.1. quem annos centum viginti refert vixisse: meminit & M. Cicero lib. de Senect. Tartessios omnium bonorum affluentes esse, & cœlo salubri, maximaq; aeris temperie frui, ideoq; longæuos dictos Strabo auctor est.
units.tr: P.305.v.3. Tartessiorum) Their king was Arganthonius. Herodotus, book 1, mentions the Phoenicians who came to him, and says he lived a hundred and twenty years. Marcus Cicero also mentions this in his book On Old Age. Strabo is the authority that the Tartessians enjoyed every blessing, had a healthy climate and a very mild air, and for this reason were called long-lived.

units.la: V. 5. Gargoris) Iohannes episcopus Gerundensis Paralipom. Hispaniæ lib. 1. Gorgonium vocat, eius nepotem Abium.
units.tr: V. 5. Gargoris) John, bishop of Gerona, in the Paralipomena of Spain, book 1, calls him Gorgonius, and his grandson Habis.

units.la: P.306.v.11.Et quæ ex insulis) Malim, ea quæ. De Geryone quæ referuntur notiora sunt, quam vt quidquam tari ad ea debeat: narratio extat in 4. Diodori. Cum autem dicit, Herculem ex Asia, &c. Herculem Tyrium intelligit, vide Arrianum lib. 2.
units.tr: P.306.v.11.Et quæ ex insulis) I would prefer ea quae. What is reported about Geryon is too well known to need any comment here; the account is in Diodorus, book 4. When he says Hercules from Asia, etc., he means the Tyrian Hercules; see Arrian, book 2.

units.la: V.23. Cum Gaditani à Tyro) Hæc prolixe narrat Strabo extremo lib. 3.
units.tr: V.23. Cum Gaditani à Tyro) Strabo tells this at length at the end of book 3.

units.la: V.32. Hamilcarem) Cuius cognomen Barcas: Lege Polybium lib. 2. Appianum in Iberica, Probum in eius vita. De Hasdrubale a feruo, cuius supra hoc ipso libro auctor meminit interfecto, vide eosdem.
units.tr: V.32. Hamilcar) Whose surname was Barcas. Read Polybius, book 2; Appian, in the Iberica; Probus, in his life. On Hasdrubal, killed by a slave, whom the author mentioned above in this same book, see the same authors.

units.la: P.307.v.10. Scipionibus) Cn. & P. intelligit, quos, duo
units.tr: P.307.v.10. Scipionibus) He means Gnaeus and Publius, whom

units.la: fulmina imperii Romani vocat M. Cicero pro Balbo, Liuius li. 25. De Hispania ab Augusto domita, lege Dionē, Suetonium, Florum, Orosium, Horatium Oda14. lib. 3. Sed hic, vt Augusto bellicorum certaminum, ita & mihi commentationis huius, laboriosę quam gloriosę magis, finis esto: &, vacuo tunc duellis orbe terrarū, Ianus Quirini ab illo clusus, leue hoc, non futurum tamen inutile, opus claudat.
units.tr: M. Cicero calls the two thunderbolts of the Roman empire, in the Pro Balbo. Livy, book 25. On Spain as subdued by Augustus, read Dio, Suetonius, Florus, Orosius, and Horace, Ode 14, book 3. But here, as Augustus brought an end to warlike contests, so let this be the end of my commentary, more laborious than glorious; and, with the orb of lands now free from wars and the gates of Janus, closed by him, shut, may this slight work close, which nevertheless will not be useless.
CONCERNING THE PROLOGUES: NOTES.

units.la: Librorum Trogi ἀπόξας edere, non erat animi mei sententia: tam crebra, tam foeda erant in iis vulnera, noux cicatrici, vt locus non esset, & mihi desperata eorū videretur salus. Tandem & amicorum auctoritate compulsus, & meo etiam iudicio persuasus, sententiam mutaui. Itaque vitam illis dedisse, hoc tempore satis sit: nam integram valitudinem aliis deberi, facile patiar. Attamē ne protsus eorum curam viderer omisisse, periculum faciundum duxi, an & coniecturis nostris sanari quaedam possent: sagaciores, in ceteris ἐυσχία suam exerceant. Namque a libris an sperandum aliquid sit, nescio: hoc scio septem Mss. codices, in difficillimis & contaminatissimis locis, quasi conspiratione quadam, consentire, aut lectionum monstris certare. Vidi Italicam interpretationem, olim editam, quae ne uno quidem loco, a librorum nostrorum scriptura discedit. Cuiusmodi sunt, Iustini abbreuiatoris negligentiam detegunt; & historiarum Trogi seriem oscendunt. Auctoris nomen in libris nullum est: Nam quod in duobus legitur. In Trogi sequitur Iustini epitoma libros, non arbitror huc spectare, sed ad maius opus, id est vulgatam Iustini epitomam. Quisquis est, non in Iustinum, sed in Trogum argumenta scripsit, vt in Liuium Florus. Nam in his quaedam sunt non pauca, quae in Iustino frustra quaeras; vt non immerito integrum Trogi ipsius opus, historia desideret. Sunt autem prologi ὑπο͂θεσις, singulorum librorum argumenta continentes.
units.tr: It was never my intention to publish Trogus' books in fragments [ἀπόξας]. They were so thickly and foully wounded, with scars piled on scars, that there seemed to be no room left for a cure, and I had given up hope of saving them. Finally, moved by the urging of friends and persuaded by my own judgement, I changed my mind. So for now it is enough to have given them life; I will gladly allow that their full health be owed to others. Still, lest I seem to have wholly neglected their care, I thought I should try whether some passages could be healed by my conjectures. Sharper minds may exercise their leisure [εὐσχολία] on the rest. For I do not know whether anything is to be hoped for from the manuscripts. I know this much: seven manuscripts, at the most difficult and most corrupted passages, agree as if by some conspiracy, or else vie with one another in monstrous readings. I have seen the Italian translation, published long ago, which does not depart from the wording of our books even at a single point. Such things expose the carelessness of the abridger Justin and show the sequence of Trogus' histories. No author's name appears in the manuscripts. As for the words that are read in two of them, "In Trogi sequitur Iustini epitoma libros," I do not think they refer here but to a larger work, namely the common epitome of Justin. Whoever he is, he did not write arguments on Justin but on Trogus, as Florus did on Livy. For in these there are not a few things that you would look for in vain in Justin, which is why the complete work of Trogus himself is rightly missed in history. The prologues, however, are summaries [ὑπόθεσις], containing the argument of each book.
Dd

units.la: V. 34. Tisafernem] ex Herodoto & Probo in vita Miltiadis, leg. Ariaphernem.
units.tr: Book 5, verse 34. Tisafernem: from Herodotus and from Probus in the life of Miltiades, read Ariaphernem.

units.la: V. 36. Tyrannidem, qua ext.] Coniectura legendum auguro, quæ extincta, ad Marathonem vic. Pers. aut propius veterem scripturam, tyrannidem extinctam: Qua ratione vic. Pers.
units.tr: Verse 36. Tyrannidem, qua ext.: I guess the correct reading is "quae extincta," that the tyranny, extinguished at the battle of Marathon against the Persians; or, closer to the old reading, "tyrannidem extinctam": in which way the victory over the Persians.

units.la: P. 311. v. 3. Pulso interfectore] Lego interfectio interfectore: prior vox, ob affinitatem sequentis ab exscriptore omissa, peperit falsam lectionem, & historiæ contrariam.
units.tr: Page 311, verse 3. Pulso interfectore: I read "interfectio" for "interfectore." The former word, having been omitted by the copyist on account of its similarity to the following one, produced a false reading contrary to the history.

units.la: V. 6. Achamenes] Diod. Ἀχαιμένης: & pro Agabazum, lege Megabazum. Μεγάβυζος, Diod. lib. 11.
units.tr: Verse 6. Achamenes: Diodorus has Achaimenes [Ἀχαιμένης]; and for Agabazum, read Megabazus, Μεγάβυζος, Diodorus book 11.

units.la: V. 10. Sicronia] Leg. Sicyonia & Corinthi tyranni, de quorum regno Eusebius Chronico, & Paufan. Corinth. Bellum autem Crisæum mihi neque lectum neque auditum est: suspicor leg. Thyreum, de quo Herod. libro 1. & Eusæb. Chron,
units.tr: Verse 10. Sicronia: read Sicyonia, and of the tyrant of Corinth, about whose rule Eusebius in his Chronicle and Pausanias in Corinthiaca. But I have neither read nor heard of the Crisaean war; I suspect we should read Thyreum, which Herodotus mentions in book 1 and Eusebius in the Chronicle.

units.la: V. 35. Eporei] Emenda Pharei. & statim Rhodiis. Alexandri Pherzei nomen, restituendum videtur & Diod. lib. 15. sub anno quarto, Olympiadis 102. ... (de Pelopida loquitur) ... Leg. ex Plutarcho in Pelopida τῷ φιλίῳ.
units.tr: Verse 35. Eporei: emend to Pharei. And immediately "Rhodiis." The name Alexander of Pherae seems to need restoring, and Diodorus book 15 under the fourth year of the 102nd Olympiad ... (he speaks of Pelopidas) ... Read from Plutarch in the Life of Pelopidas, "tōi philiōi."

units.la: P 312. v. 1. Magnum Phil] Ceteris regibus præstitisse Plutarchus, ... refert in Apophth. ex Theophrasto. Inde ergo Philippi historiæ Trogi, quod hic regum maximus Philippus Macedonici imperii fundamenta, eaque firmissima iccirco. Trogi autem historia nihil aliud quam Macedonica historia.
units.tr: Page 312, verse 1. Magnum Phil: Plutarch, in the Apophthegms, citing Theophrastus, reports that he surpassed the other kings. Hence, then, Trogus' history of Philip, because this greatest of kings, Philip, laid the foundations of the Macedonian empire, and those the firmest for that reason. Trogus' history, moreover, is nothing other than a Macedonian history.
Verse 20.

units.la: Mathea] Legendum Athea,docui ad Iustinum. Ponticarum gentium antiquissimum regem Atheam confimemorat Florus lib.3. qui in Mss. dicitur Eras. Sequenti linea scribendum Gidorg, Charonea.
units.tr: Mathea: read Athea; I showed this in my notes on Justin. Florus in book 3 mentions Athea, king of the Pontic peoples, who in the manuscripts is called Eras. In the following line read Gidorg, Charonea.

units.la: V.34. Ace]Strabo 16. Πτολεμαιος μεγάλη πόλις, ἡν Αἴχνη ἀνόμασαν πρὸς πρότ. ἡ ἐχεσῶντε ἐχυρώτεγεια πρὸς τὴν Αιχαικὴν οἱ Πῦσταί. emendandus Probus Datarne:& nuntium ad exercitum acrem misit. Leg. Acen.
units.tr: Verse 34. Ace: Strabo book 16: "Ptolemais, a great city, which they called Aichne [Πτολεμαιος μεγάλη πόλις, ἡν Αἴχνη ἀνόμασαν] ..." Probus should be emended in Datames. And "sent a messenger to the army" ["nuntium ad exercitum acrem misit"]. Read Acen.

units.la: Ib. In Cadusiis] Meminit Probus Datame. Statim autem tem leg. defectores, vt prologo lib.3.Diod. τὰς ἀΦεσκόμενος, eos qui defecerant, Probus. Cui praefectus seu dynastes Paphlagonum, est Thyas, in v.c. Thuys. Arsabarzanes Diod.15 & Gemisto,qui ex Diodoro exscripsit,praefectus Phrygiae:Probo,Lydiae,& Ionis,totiusque Phrygiae:cum Lydiam Antiphradati Diodorus tribuat, Orontes,illis effatrapes Mysiae.
units.tr: Ibid. In the Cadusians: Probus mentions Datames. Immediately, read "defectores" (deserters), as in the prologue to book 3; Diodorus has "tas aphestkomenos" [τὰς ἀΦεσκόμενος], "those who had revolted," in Probus. To him the prefect or dynast of the Paphlagonians is Thyas; in the Latin text, Thuys. Arsabarzanes in Diodorus book 15, and in Gemistus, who copied from Diodorus, prefect of Phrygia; in Probus, of Lydia and Ionia and all Phrygia. Since Diodorus assigns Lydia to Antiphradates, Orontes [is the satrap] of Mysia.

units.la: V.40. Sidon accep.] Lege Sidonis cepit, ex Diod.16. & Gemisto lib.2. qui cum loleat exscriptor esse Diodori, Mentorem facit Rhodium,ducem auxiliariorum: Tenen autem regem Sidoniorum,contra quam Diodorus, cui Mentor rex est, Tennes Rhodius dux. Quae subscquuntut ita emenda. Deinde Darcus, qui cum Alex. &c.
units.tr: Verse 40. Sidon accep.: read "Sidonem cepit," from Diodorus book 16 and Gemistus book 2, who, since he seems to be a copyist of Diodorus, makes Mentor a Rhodian, leader of the auxiliaries. Tennes, however, king of the Sidonians, contrary to Diodorus, for whom Mentor is king and Tennes the Rhodian leader. What follows should be emended thus: "Deinde Darius, qui cum Alexandro etc."

units.la: P.315.v.13. Molossaque] Scribe Molossaque.De Archidamo,pro Tarentinis contra Lucanos pugnante,interfecto.Diod.16. & Gemistus 2.
units.tr: Page 315, verse 13. Molossaque: write "Molossaque." Concerning Archidamus, who fought for the Tarentines against the Lucanians and was killed: Diodorus book 16 and Gemistus book 2.

units.la: V.25. Occidit, & occisus est] vereor vt absque libris testimonii posfitui:interim vt seutentia constet,legamus,occidit; & deinde occisus est. de nece Perdiccae lege Diod.18. & Probum Enmene.
units.tr: Verse 25. Occidit and occisus est: I fear it cannot be placed without witness from the manuscripts; meanwhile, so that the sense stands, let us read "occidit" and "deinde occisus est." For the killing of Perdiccas see Diodorus book 18 and Probus on Eumenes.

units.la: V.40. Antiochi] Scribe Antigoni. Paulo postemenda Polyperchontes. Is Hercules Barsines filium corruptus a Catlandro interfecit. Plutarchus περὶ Ἰουμαῖος,Diod.20. Paufan. Bœot.
units.tr: Verse 40. Antiochi: write "Antigoni." A little later emend "Polyperchontes." He, Hercules, the son of Barsine, was corrupted by Cassander and killed. Plutarch in "Peri Ioumaias" [περὶ Ἰουμαῖος]; Diodorus book 20; Pausanias, Boeotica.
Page 314, verse 17. Dromichaete: in Justin it is called "Doricetes."

units.la: V.20. Cleanchus] Lege Cleoxyas Memnonis, Diod. 15. 16. 20. hic Satyri non meminit: & Dionysii filii eidem sunt Zaleucus ἡ Καλαρχω: ex Memnone videtur,legendum Οξύδρης ἡ Καλαρχω.
units.tr: Verse 20. Cleanchus: read "Cleoxyas" of Memnon; Diodorus books 15, 16, 20. He makes no mention of Satyrus here, and the sons of Dionysius are the same, Zaleucus and Kalarchos. From Memnon it seems we should read Oxydres and Kalarchos.

units.la: V 25. Vt Lyfimachi] Vide excerpta ex Menonis historiis.
units.tr: V 25. Ut Lysimachi] See the excerpts from Memnon's histories.
P.315.v.2. Tyri] From Justin I read Velia, for Strabo, at the beginning of book 6, is the authority that it was founded by the Phocaeans.

units.la: initio lib. 6. auctor est à Phocaenfibus conditam. Pro Carthaginiumque, lege Carthaginiensiumque.
units.tr: For Carthaginiumque, read Carthaginiensiumque.

units.la: V.6 In Africam] Scribe in Africa, & paulo post in Si-cilia. Quae sequuntur ita deformata sunt, ut nulla fere historiae species appareat. Adid per rubellum annorum. f Ms.P. Pithoei adscriptum habet, per Afdrubalem, Amilcarem, & Annonem, quod ablque dubio rectum est.
units.tr: Verse 6. In Africam: write "in Africa," and a little later "in Sicilia." What follows is so corrupted that almost no trace of the history appears. In the manuscript of Pithou, "per rubellum annorum" is annotated as "per Hasdrubalem, Hamilcarem, and Hanno," which is without doubt correct.

units.la: Illa autem, cum felinum, temetegantum, & gamerinâ, & gelâ ceperunt, italegenda cóiicio cum Selinuntem, & Agrigentum, & Gam. & Gel. cep. Est autem Gamerina, aliter Camerina. G. & C. inuicem permutantur, xuoipnd, guberno, gladius, Varronia clade ... nobis est legife. Et in Mss. Cobriae, Gobryae, adici, pro adigi: Graecis Kapaγεῖα. Strabo, Steph. Paulo post, scribe Paniper Imulconem.
units.tr: But those things which they took, "Felinum, Temetegantum," and "Gamerina," and "Gela," I conjecture should be read as "Selinuntem, and Agrigentum, and Gamerinam and Gelam." Gamerina is also called Camerina. G and C are interchanged, as in "xuoipnd" [κυβερνῶ], guberno, gladius. In the manuscripts "Cobriae" and "Gobryae" appear for "adici" (for "adigi"); the Greeks write it [Καπαγεῖα]. See Strabo, Stephanus. A little later, write "Paniper" for "Imulconem."

units.la: V.21. Apatre] Tò videtur abundare. Statim leg. per Dionem ciecium bellum cum Sic. gessit: dom. amiff. lib. & fratre Corinthum secessit: Vt à Timoleonte Carthaginiensium bello, &c. Paulo post legas arcessiti ad bellum Carth. Ita quodammodo expressimus mentem auctoris.
units.tr: Verse 21. Apatre: "Tò" seems superfluous. Immediately read: "by Dion he waged a long war with Sicily; having lost his domestic affairs, and with his brother he withdrew to Corinth; so that by Timoleon ..." in the Carthaginian war, etc. A little later read "summoned to the Carthaginian war." Thus we have in some measure expressed the author's meaning.

units.la: P.317. v.7. Angura] Straboni lib. 4. &12. Ἀγκυρα, est castellum Tectosagum: Memnoni est vrbs Trogmorum.
units.tr: Page 317, verse 7. Angura: according to Strabo, books 4 and 12, Ankyra [Ἀγκυρα] is a fortress of the Tectosages; for Memnon it is a city of the Trogmorians.

units.la: V.26. Teuta] Florus lib.2. habet Teuca, sed in Mss. est Teutana: quomodo & in Iornande. Plinio lib. 34. cap. 6. Teuca.
units.tr: Verse 26. Teuta: Florus, book 2, has "Teuca," but in the manuscripts it is "Teutana," as also in Jordanes. In Pliny, book 34, chapter 6, "Teuca."

units.la: V.37. Ptolemaeo Virufphona] Hic est Ptolemaeus Euergetes: Virufphona quid ut, viderint doctores. Sed & quod sequitur rapi et paramare gathoclea corr. dec. quomodo restituendum sit, assequi coniectura non potest: hoc quilibet intelligit, amore Agathoclea corruptum decesse.
units.tr: Verse 37. Ptolemaeo Virufphona: this is Ptolemy Euergetes. What "Virufphona" means, let the scholars judge. But what follows, "rapi et paramare gathoclea corr. dec.," cannot be restored by conjecture; this much anyone understands: he died, corrupted by love of Agathoclea.

units.la: P.318.v.21. Duce Manlio, Liuius 38. Florus lib.2. Mitor in historia, miscella Pauli diaconi Fuluio hoc tribuicum Fuluius qui collega erat Manlii, paene iisdem dieb. cum Aetolis bellum gesserit, quibus Manlius cum Gallis. Plutarch. de virtutibus mulierum Ταϊσαν vocat, quod Manlii praenomen est: Interpres noster, de Cnaeo Scipione Plutarchum loqui arbitratus est.
units.tr: Page 318, verse 21. Duce Manlio: Livy 38; Florus book 2. I think in the history, in the miscellany of Paulus the Deacon, this is attributed to Fulvius, who was a colleague of Manlius and waged war against the Aetolians at almost the same time that Manlius did against the Gauls. Plutarch, in "On the Virtues of Women," calls him "Taisan" [Ταϊσαν], which is Manlius' praenomen. Our translator thought Plutarch was speaking of Cnaeus Scipio.

units.la: V.28. Gallium Ortiag.] Florus lib. 2. illum Orgiacontè vocat, ita est in Ms.
units.tr: Verse 28. Gallium Ortiag.: Florus book 2 calls him "Orgiacontes"; so it is in the manuscript.
Verse 37.

units.la: V.37. Epiros] De directa Epiro Plutarchus Æmilio, Eutropius lib. 4. statim pro Ærolica scribe Achaica, &c mox Pseudophilippo.
units.tr: Verse 37. Epiros: On the Epirote Pyrrhus, Plutarch in the Life of Aemilius; Eutropius book 4. Immediately, for "Aerolica" write "Achaica," and soon after, "pseudophilippo" (a false Philip).

units.la: P.319.v.5. Cum Selgensitæ] Selga vrbs Pisidiæ, Strabo lib. 12. Steph.
units.tr: Page 319, verse 5. Cum Selgensitae: Selga is a city of Pisidia; Strabo book 12; Stephanus.
Verse 27. Diodoro: read "Diodoto."

units.la: , V.32. Vt Trypho] Lego, Vt Trypho, pulso Syriæ Demetrio, captoq; a Parthis bel. gest. cum fr. eius Ant. cognomine Sedete. Vt Antiochus, &c.
units.tr: Verse 32. Ut Trypho: read: "As Trypho, Demetrius having been driven from Syria and captured by the Parthians, waged war with his brother Antiochus, surnamed Sidetes. As Antiochus, etc."

units.la: P.320.v.5. Eupatore] Leg. Eupator. paulo post. Vt mort. Ptol. Philometore frater eius Physcon accepit regnum Æg. Si mauis acceptoregno decerunt quaedam.
units.tr: Page 320, verse 5. Eupatore: read "Eupator." A little later: "When Ptolemy Philometor died, his brother Physcon took the kingdom of Egypt." If you prefer "acceptoregno" (having received the kingdom), some words are missing.

units.la: V.39 Bellumque] Locus hic ita supplevi potest, bellumq; ia intulerit Antiochus, quas, &c.
units.tr: V.39 Bellumque: This place can be supplied thus: and Antiochus made war, which, etc.

units.la: P. 321. v. 3. Cypra] Leg. Grypo. & mox, a filio Cyziceni Eusebe interfecti: extinctaque regalis (aut regum) Antiochorum, &c.
units.tr: P. 321, v. 3 Cypra: Read Grypo. And soon after: killed by the son of Cyzicenus Eusebes; and the royal line (or kings) of the Antiochi was extinguished, etc.

units.la: V. 7. Quo] Malim Quos, aut cai. paulo post legendum videtur, Vt Alexandria post int. Ptol. Latyri subst. sint eius filii, alteri, &c. & mox, Seditione exagitatus, Alexandrea Romam profugit.
units.tr: V. 7 Quo: I would prefer Quos, or cai. A little later it seems to be read: So that after Alexandria was taken, Ptolemy Lathyrus's sons are, the others, etc. And soon after: Harassed by sedition, he fled from Alexandria to Rome.

units.la: V.26. Sarance] Plin.lib.6 cap.16. Sarangæ, Herod. lib.3. Σαραγγαῖοι lib.7. Σαραγγαι. Mox. leg. fortasse, Arriani Bactra occupauere & Sogdianos.
units.tr: V. 26 Sarance: Pliny, book 6, chapter 16, has Sarangae; Herodotus, book 3, has Σαραγγαῖοι [Sarangaioi]; book 7 has Σαραγγαι [Sarangai]. Soon after, perhaps read: The Arians occupied Bactra and the Sogdians.

units.la: V.39. Thoclarorum] Nescio an legendum Tochariorum, de quibus dixi ad xlii. Iustini. Ita, lector, haec argumenta paulo meliora reddidi: Omnia sanare, non est ingenii mei. Sed nemo Smquam reprehensus, quis e segete, ad spicilegium reliquit stipulam.
units.tr: V. 39 Thoclarorum: I do not know whether it should be read Tochariorum, about which I spoke at chapter 42 of Justin. Thus, reader, I have rendered these arguments somewhat better; to heal everything is not within my talent. But no one has ever been reproved for leaving a straw from the crop for the gleaning.
THE END.
