units.la: VOD oculus olim Polyphemo, id nobis in historiarum lectione notatio temporum: quæ apud Iustinum nulla est. Quid itaq; aliud esse dicemus, quam Monstrum, horrendum, informe, ingens, cui lumen ademptum?
units.tr: As the eye was once to Polyphemus, so for us in reading history is the marking of times, and this is missing in Justin. What else shall we call it than a monster, horrible, shapeless, huge, with its light taken away?

units.la: Trogum ipsum negligentiæ accusandum, nemo mihi persuadeat: Iustini abbreviatoris facinus est. Ergo ne quid huic auctori àme deesset, ex Eusebii & Hieronymi chronico, ad optima & antiquissima exemplaria manuscripta CL. V. Claudii Puteani; & doctissimi mihique amicissimi P. Danielis, à me collato, excerpsi & exscripsi, quæ lucis aliquid afferre lustrino nostro poterant: non quidem omnia, sed summa fastigia rerum. Nam illud, iniuriam esset facere amico nostro Laur. Bochello, à quo veteres chronologos emendatiores & auctiores exspectamus. Comparaui autem cum Eusebio, Georgium monachum, cuius Græcum codicem mecum vir eruditionis singularis Franciscus Pithoeus communicauit; & è nostris Beroaldum, Funccium. Illi LXX. interpretes, hi Hebraeos sequuntur codices: tanta opinionum varietate ut Eusebio, Nini regis annus primus, incurrat in annum mundi III. CXLI. Georgio in III. CCLXXI. Beroaldo in an. MDCCCLXV. Funccio in MDCCCCVI. Hujus varietatis originem, pluribus persequerer, nisi laborè istum mihi, amici illius nostri, leuaret labor. Interim lumè hoc tibi, carissime Noëli, accendi, ne forte in historiæ huius tenebris aberres: Et vt illius
units.tr: Let no one persuade me that Trogus himself is to be blamed for carelessness; it is the fault of Justin the abridger. So that nothing might be lacking to this author on my part, I have excerpted and copied out from the chronicle of Eusebius and Jerome whatever could cast some light on our darkness, taken from the best and most ancient manuscript copies, which I collated with those of the most illustrious Claudius Puteanus and of the most learned P. Daniel, my dearest friend. I have not included everything, but only the principal summits of events. For it would be an injustice to our friend Laurentius Bochellus, from whom we look for more correct and fuller ancient chronologers. I have also compared Eusebius with George the monk, whose Greek codex the singularly learned Franciscus Pithoeus shared with me, and among our own writers with Beroaldus and Funccius. The former follow the Seventy interpreters, the latter the Hebrew manuscripts, and their opinions vary so widely that for Eusebius the first year of King Ninus falls in the year of the world III. CXLI, for George in III. CCLXXI, for Beroaldus in the year MDCCCLXV, and for Funccius in MDCCCCVI. I would pursue the origin of this variety at greater length, were it not that the labour of that friend of ours lightens this labour for me. Meanwhile I have kindled this light for you, dearest Noël, lest by chance you go astray in the darkness of this history; and, as the line says:
The maimed torch-pine guides the hand and steadies the steps.

units.la: ita hæc velim amplectatis excerpta, quo tutius possis, & firmius ingredi: Adferent tibi fortasse in huius auctoris lectione, non paruum adiumentum. Ad historiarum studium vt accedas, requirit etas tua; requirunt hęc tempora, quibus mature firmare animum expedit constantibus exemplis: Ea vnde petas, nisi ex historiis? Historiarum autem cognitionem, si inchoare à Sallustii, Liuii, Taciti lectione volueris, neque recte feceris, neque ordine: Abrupta est, aut interrupta in eorum libris, historiæ series. Ab hoc tibi auctore principium sit historici studii.
units.tr: So I would have you embrace these excerpts, so that you may enter more safely and more firmly; they will perhaps bring you no small help in reading this author. Your age requires that you come to the study of history, and these times require that the mind be early strengthened by steadfast examples. Where else should you seek them but in histories? But if you wish to begin the knowledge of history with the reading of Sallust, Livy and Tacitus, you will do neither rightly nor in order, for the sequence of history is broken off, or interrupted, in their books. Let this author be for you the starting point of the study of history.

units.la: 'Hic à Nino, qui primus est τῶν εἰς ἱστορίαν ἡγοῦμενων, ad Augustum Cæsarem, non vt Atticus apud M. Ciceronem, septingentorum, sed vt Corn. Nepos omne ævum, id est, duûm millium annorum memoriam, vno libro colligauit. Tu, Noeli dulcissimé, vtere fruere hac qualicunque opera mea, quæ si promouendis studiis tuis fuerit, satis magnum laboris mei fructum tulero. Vale.
units.tr: From Ninus, who is the first of those who lead in history [τῶν εἰς ἱστορίαν ἡγουμένων], down to Augustus Caesar, he has gathered the memory of the whole age, not of seven hundred years as Atticus does in Cicero, but of two thousand years, as Cornelius Nepos does, in a single book. You, most sweet Noël, make use of and enjoy this work of mine, whatever it is worth; if it serves to advance your studies, I shall have reaped a sufficiently great fruit from my labour. Farewell.

units.la: NOTASSE me tempora quæ cum eo non omnino conueniunt, ipse agnosco, vt de conditione Tyri & Carthaginis. Sed cum professus sim me Eusebium & Hieronymum sequi, non licuit ab eorum ratione discedere. Tribuendum hoc duxi antiquitati, & eruditioni, & diligentiæ illorum: Cum præsertim, in tanta nouarum opinionum copia & varietate, quid potissimum sequerer non haberem: & si noui alicuius hominis chronologiam potiorem duxissem, fuisset ea nouis rationibus, multisque confirmanda: quod erat ab instituto nostro alienum. Hoc enim volui, χρονολογίας regum, & clarorum virorum, aliquo modo ob oculos ponere: Quod si successit ex animi mei sententia, bene est; sin minus, laudanda est opera, qua & iuuentuti prodesse, & auctorem si non optimum, saltem non malum, & in historia necessarium, illustrare volui.
units.tr: I myself acknowledge that I have noted dates which do not wholly agree with him, for instance concerning the condition of Tyre and Carthage. But since I professed to follow Eusebius and Jerome, I was not permitted to depart from their reckoning. I have judged this to be owed to their antiquity, their learning and their diligence, especially since, amid such a great abundance and variety of new opinions, I had no clear choice of what to follow most closely; and if I had preferred the chronology of some recent writer, it would have needed to be supported by new arguments and many proofs, which was foreign to my purpose. For what I wished was to set before the eyes, in some measure, the chronology of kings and famous men. If this has succeeded according to my intention, it is well; if not, the effort is still to be commended, since I wished both to be of service to young people and to illustrate an author who, if not the best, is at least not bad, and necessary for history.

units.tr: Note on the readings of page 120, line 3: the manuscript has "expensis". The phrase "indolis; cladis, etc." is rightly cancelled in line 15. Line 23: "si non felicitate par. virt." (the sixth manuscript has "fuer." written above; another reading is "si felicitate, non virt."). Line 24: the seventh edition reads "clim."; a manuscript has "infelicior". Line 25: a manuscript has "ex Ecbatana nuper" and "tantas strages", while a conjecture reads "exhibita nuper". Line 25, "extremum": a conjecture reads "& batanu", and another manuscript has "mum, si a multe", with "hæc batanus" in a conjecture. Line 27: a manuscript has "in Italia aux." and "Tarenc nuper". I think the words "quod est in textu" in line 29 should be deleted altogether. Line 29, "velud": manuscripts read "ve[l]. stro". Line 31: "& tibi" with "Oc." and "præficitur" in the edition. Page 121, line 2: "ve. 91." Line 3: "Antipatris" is restored from Macedonia. Ioannes Peleus, Historia: beware. The following are cited above. Line 10: a manuscript has "Agedis". Line 11: the edition reads "Græcia"; Alexander, seven manuscripts have "Apulis".

Line 25: the MSS have "Polyperchonta" (Polyperchon, accusative). Line 21: the MSS have "catpere" (to seize), with the verb in the singular. Line 29: the edition has "discordia quippe" (for discord indeed). Line 22: the MSS have "priuatim" in the singular (privately). Line 31: the edition has "Prædam" (plunder) in the front position. Line 23: the MSS have "inferre" (to inflict). Line 33: the edition has "descenderat" (he had come down). Also, the MSS have "voluit" (he wished); see p. 172, line 2, where some MSS have "velle", as in Alexander. Line 33 (MSS): "philosophiam ipsam" (philosophy itself). Line 5: the MSS have "vnita" (united) and "viriumque gloria" (and the glory of their strength). Line 6: the MSS have "irruunt" (they rush in). The edition has "instruebat" (he was arraying). See p. 174, line 4: the MSS have "ratus finx" and the edition "ratus", with the reading "ratus esset" (supposing he was) in another MS. Line 9: one MS has "partes" and the Oxford reading is "ratus esset". Line 11: one MS has "Galmam", and the edition "Calamam" (Calama, a place name). Also in the MSS "finxisset" (had feigned), and "crudele" (cruel). Line 12: the edition has "victoria" (victory) in the final position. Line 5: the edition has "crudeliter" (cruelly) with "membris" (limbs). Line 14: the edition has "rebus dimisit" (he dismissed the affairs) and "verumet" (and truly). Line 9: the edition has "recipere virt" (to recover the strength). Folio: "iam" is to be added below, "honorauit" (he honoured). Line 11: the edition has "remedium" (remedy) and "ipsius Dem." (of Demetrius himself). Line 13: the MSS have "perferociff" (very fierce). Line 17: the MSS do not have "propter digni-tatem" (on account of dignity) and have "iniffe b." units.la: Et hæc quidem hactenus curiosè fortasse nimis: sed non sine magnorum & doctissimorum virorum consensu, atque etiam exemplo.
units.tr: These matters have perhaps been treated here too minutely so far, but not without the agreement and even the example of great and very learned men.

units.la: In Prologis, non est quod eandem quis à me diligentiam requirat: Nam & meræ[?] alio meæ vocant, & in iis nihil adeo dignum notatione visum est. Hoc solum monebo, proponi cos Iustinos, in omnibus libris nostris praterquam in Uno P. Pithœi, in quo sub titulo argumentorum, singulis libris Iustinis singuli Prologi præfiguntur.
units.tr: In the Prologues there is no reason for anyone to demand the same care from me, for they are called by other names, both "meræ" and "meæ", and nothing in them seemed so worthy of note. I will only point out that the Justins are printed with them in all our books, except in the edition of P. Pithoeus, in which, under the heading of arguments, a separate prologue is placed before each book of Justin.
THE END.
